**Unreliable examination (sedated, obtunded) → measure: delta-P = DIASTOLIC BP − compartment pressure; an absolute pressure over 30 alone ignores perfusion; measurement is an adjunct, not infallible.** Perfusion depends on the gradient, so a pressure of 30 is dangerous in a hypotensive patient and tolerable in a hypertensive one. In the ICU patient who cannot report pain, measurement (or repeated measurement) replaces the history.

**Not relieved, or delta-P under 30 mmHg → emergency fasciotomy (ideally within 6 hours).** Muscle tolerates about 4–6 hours of ischaemia before irreversible necrosis. Fasciotomy opens all compartments (four in the leg), and the wounds are left open. Afterwards, watch for rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemia.

**Never more opioids, and never delay for imaging.** Escalating analgesic need is itself a warning sign, and treating it hides the diagnosis; regional blocks can mask it too. Compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis: X-ray, Doppler or MRI only waste the time the muscle has.
mimic: Compartment syndrome vs arterial injury
Arterial injury: pulse lost early, cold pale limb. Compartment syndrome: pulse present until late, with pain on passive stretch.
Delta-P vs absolute compartment pressure
Delta-P (diastolic minus compartment) under 30 mmHg is the threshold; an absolute pressure of 30 ignores the patient’s blood pressure.
traps: “A palpable pulse excludes compartment syndrome”
Pulses are lost late; pain on passive stretch is early.
“Compartment pressure over 30 is the fasciotomy threshold”
Use delta-P: diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure under 30.
“Elevate the limb and give more analgesia”
Remove dressings, keep the limb at heart level, and decompress; rising opioid need is a warning.
decode: Tibial fracture, pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, pulses present — next step? [DocT GT]
Remove dressings and decompress (fasciotomy), not more opioids or imaging.
Sedated patient, tense calf — which measurement decides? [DocT GT, Marrow]
Delta-P = diastolic BP − compartment pressure; under 30 → fasciotomy.
x.punch: Compartment syndrome is diagnosed by pain on passive stretch while pulses are still present, measured by delta-P (diastolic minus compartment pressure) in the sedated, and treated by removing dressings and fasciotomy within about 6 hours.

topups.q: After emergency splenectomy, vaccinate at ____ days.
a: - ≥14 days after surgery (better response), or before discharge if follow-up is doubtful; elective: ≥2 weeks BEFORE.
- Pneumococcal (PCV20, or PCV15 then PPSV23 ≥8 weeks later), meningococcal ACWY + B, Hib, yearly influenza.
- Asplenia → overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (encapsulated organisms), mortality ~50%.

x.sub: Polytrauma → After surgery → Post-splenectomy vaccination
x.intro: Step 4 includes splenectomy for an uncontrollable splenic bleed. Without a spleen, the patient cannot clear encapsulated bacteria well, so vaccination is part of the operation’s aftercare. One DocT GT question asks the timing after an emergency splenectomy.
why: **Vaccinate 14 days or more after surgery (better response), or before discharge if follow-up is doubtful; for elective splenectomy, at least 2 weeks BEFORE.** Antibody responses are better when vaccination is delayed to about 2 weeks after the operation, probably because surgery and trauma blunt the immune response. If the patient may not return, an earlier dose is better than none.

**Pneumococcal (PCV20, or PCV15 then PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later), meningococcal ACWY and B, Hib, and yearly influenza.** PCV21 alone is now also accepted (ACIP 2024). These cover the encapsulated organisms the spleen normally clears (pneumococcus above all, then meningococcus and Haemophilus). Influenza is added because it predisposes to secondary pneumococcal infection. Antibiotic prophylaxis and a standby course are usually advised as well.

**Asplenia → overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (encapsulated organisms), mortality about 50%.** The spleen filters unopsonised bacteria and makes IgM against polysaccharide capsules. Without it, sepsis from pneumococcus can progress from fever to purpura fulminans and death within hours, and the risk lasts for life.
mimic: Emergency vs elective splenectomy
Emergency: vaccinate at about 14 days after surgery. Elective: at least 2 weeks before.
traps: “Vaccinate on day 1 after emergency splenectomy”
Responses are better at 14 days; vaccinate earlier only if the patient may not return.
“Pneumococcal vaccine alone is enough”
Meningococcal, Hib and yearly influenza vaccines are also given.
decode: After emergency splenectomy, vaccinate at how many days? [DocT GT]
14 days.
x.punch: After emergency splenectomy, vaccinate at about 14 days (or before discharge if follow-up is uncertain) against pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib and influenza, because overwhelming post-splenectomy infection kills about half of those it affects.

topups.q: First-line VTE prophylaxis in major trauma with normal renal function = ____.
a: - LMWH: enoxaparin 30 mg SC 12-hourly (or 40 mg 12-hourly/anti-Xa guided), within 24–48 h once bleeding is controlled.
- Beats UFH 5000 U 8-hourly (fewer DVT/PE, less HIT).
- IPC alone only while pharmacological prophylaxis is contraindicated; fondaparinux for HIT.

x.sub: Polytrauma → Drugs → VTE prophylaxis in major trauma
x.intro: Step 6 covers drugs given during bleeding; this is the drug given after it stops. Trauma patients swing from the early coagulopathy of step 2 to a prothrombotic state within a day or two, and DVT is common without prophylaxis. One DocT GT question asks the first-line agent.
why: **LMWH: enoxaparin 30 mg SC 12-hourly (or 40 mg 12-hourly or anti-Xa guided), started within 24–48 h once bleeding is controlled.** Trauma patients often have low anti-Xa levels on standard doses (oedema, high clearance), so twice-daily or weight- or anti-Xa-adjusted dosing is used. Starting is timed against bleeding risk: once haemorrhage is controlled and, in TBI or solid organ injury, once imaging is stable. The European trauma guideline (6th edition) recommends drug prophylaxis plus IPC within 24 hours of bleeding control (Grade 1B).

**It beats UFH 5000 U 8-hourly (fewer DVT and PE, less HIT).** In the trial by Geerts (1996), enoxaparin 30 mg 12-hourly reduced DVT compared with UFH 5000 U 12-hourly (31% vs 44%; proximal DVT 6% vs 15%), with no significant excess of major bleeding; the trial was not powered for PE. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is also less frequent with LMWH. UFH remains the choice in severe renal failure.

**IPC alone only while drug prophylaxis is contraindicated; fondaparinux for HIT.** Mechanical compression is a bridge for the patient still bleeding, not an equal alternative. In fracture patients, PREVENT CLOT (NEJM 2023) found aspirin 81 mg twice daily non-inferior to enoxaparin for death at 90 days, though with slightly more DVT.
mimic: LMWH vs UFH in trauma
LMWH: fewer DVT, less HIT, first line. UFH: for renal failure or when rapid reversal may be needed.
traps: “UFH 5000 U is first line in major trauma”
LMWH is, with normal renal function.
“Compression devices alone are equivalent”
Only while drug prophylaxis is contraindicated.
decode: First-line VTE prophylaxis in major trauma with normal renal function? [DocT GT]
LMWH (enoxaparin 30 mg twice daily).
x.punch: Once bleeding is controlled, usually within 24–48 hours, give LMWH (enoxaparin 30 mg twice daily) rather than UFH; compression devices are only a bridge while drugs are contraindicated.

spine: Shock feeds the lethal triad

Hypoperfusion makes the patient cold and acidotic, cold and acid stop clots forming, and the bleeding that follows deepens the shock, so lactate and base deficit measure how far down that spiral he already is.
Coagulopathy begins before any fluid
A quarter of the badly injured arrive coagulopathic because shock activates protein C and fibrinolysis and consumes fibrinogen; dilution, cold and acid add the late, iatrogenic layer.
Damage control resuscitation
When physiology is exhausted, keep the pressure low but adequate, give blood products instead of crystalloid in about a 1:1:1 ratio, and choose the patient for a short operation, not a complete one.
Stopping the bleeding mechanically
Bleeding stops only with pressure, a binder, a tourniquet, packing, embolisation or an abbreviated operation; REBOA is a temporary bridge with doubtful benefit.
Blood in ratio, to targets

Massive transfusion starts on a bedside score with group O cells and AB plasma, runs in a fixed ratio, then switches to laboratory and viscoelastic targets, with fibrinogen the first factor to replace.
Drugs, guideline and the sweep
Tranexamic acid within 3 hours, calcium kept normal and rFVIIa only as a last resort complete the bundle that the European guideline sets out.
SPECIAL05B.primer: Haemorrhage is the commonest preventable cause of death after injury, and most of those deaths happen in the first few hours. A clot needs enough fibrinogen, platelets, ionised calcium, working enzymes (which need a normal temperature and pH) and an endothelium that is not being broken down. Shock alone disturbs all of these, which is why the bleeding trauma patient is treated as a coagulopathy from the start, not just as a volume problem. SPECIAL05A covered definitions, scores, the primary survey and the ATLS shock classes; this deck covers what happens to blood and physiology and how they are rescued.

CVS-01.intro: Step 1 starts with the structure, because every later card depends on one fact: the outer layer is stiff. The sac holds a little lubricating fluid; a sudden addition to it has nowhere to go.
why: **A double-walled sac: a serous visceral layer and a fibrous parietal layer.** This is the ESC wording. Anatomically the outer fibrous pericardium is lined by the parietal layer of the serous pericardium, which folds back over the heart as the visceral layer (the epicardium); ‘parietal pericardium’ in clinical use means the fibrous layer with its serous lining. The fibrous layer is collagen-rich and stiff in the short term, which is why a small rapid bleed causes tamponade (CVS-20).

**20–50 mL of fluid in the pericardial cavity.** The ESC 2015 text gives 10–50 mL, a plasma ultrafiltrate; either way it is far below the 200 mL or so needed before a chest X-ray shows a big heart (CVS-11).

**It fixes the heart in the mediastinum, protects against infection and limits distension of the chambers.** Limiting acute dilatation is also what couples the two ventricles (interdependence), the basis of pulsus paradoxus and the discordant pressures of constriction.
mimic: Visceral pericardium vs myocardium
The visceral layer is the epicardium; its inflammation spills into the outer myocardium, which is why pericarditis has ECG changes and sometimes a troponin rise (CVS-11).
traps: “The pericardium stretches easily, so only large effusions matter”
Over minutes it barely stretches; it stretches only with slow accumulation (CVS-20).
decode: Normal pericardial fluid volume? [pattern]
Up to about 50 mL (ESC 10–50 mL).
CVS-01.punch: The sac is stiff and holds only about 50 mL. Everything about tamponade follows from a stiff bag with no spare room filling quickly.

CVS-02.sub: Pericarditis → Definitions → Acute, incessant, chronic, recurrent
CVS-02.intro: Step 3 names the form of pericarditis by its time course, because the name changes the treatment: how long colchicine runs and whether second-line drugs are justified.
why: **Acute: no more than 1–2 weeks.** ESC defines acute simply as a new episode; 1–2 weeks is the usual course with treatment and the usual length of full-dose NSAID (CVS-15).
**Incessant: more than 4–6 weeks but less than 3 months, without remission.** Symptoms never go away; this is ongoing disease, not relapse.
**Chronic: more than 3 months.** Usually a persistent effusion or a constrictive process.

**Recurrent: recurrence after a symptom-free interval of 4–6 weeks or longer.** The free interval is what separates it from incessant disease; recurrence affects 15–30% after a first episode and about half after a first recurrence without colchicine.
mimic: Incessant vs recurrent
Both can last months; incessant has never remitted, recurrent had at least 4–6 symptom-free weeks.
traps: “Symptoms back 2 weeks after stopping NSAIDs = recurrent pericarditis”
Without a 4–6-week symptom-free gap it is incessant (incompletely treated) disease.
decode: Symptoms persisting 8 weeks without remission — which form? [pattern]
Incessant.
Pericarditis lasting over 3 months? [pattern]
Chronic.
CVS-02.punch: The gap decides it: a symptom-free interval of at least 4–6 weeks makes it recurrent, no gap makes it incessant, and over 3 months it is chronic.

CVS-03.intro: Step 1 places acute pericarditis among the four pericardial syndromes. It is common, usually benign and rarely fatal, which is why most patients are treated as outpatients (CVS-12). The one real question asked something the card does not show: how pericarditis is classified by its pathology over time.
why: **The most common pericardial disease.** The four pericardial syndromes are pericarditis, effusion, tamponade and constriction; they overlap, and one can lead to another.
**27.7 per 100,000 per year in Europe.** This is an Italian urban population figure; many mild cases never reach hospital, so the true incidence is higher.
**0.2% of hospital cardiovascular admissions.** Most patients are low risk and do not need admission.
**5% of emergency-room admissions for chest pain.** That is why it must be separated from ACS on the ECG (CVS-08).
**In-hospital mortality about 1.1%.** Death comes mainly from tamponade, a specific cause (bacterial, neoplastic) or associated myocarditis, not from idiopathic pericarditis.
mimic: Acute pericarditis vs ACS in the chest-pain room
Pericarditis: young, pleuritic, positional pain with diffuse ST elevation; ACS: pressure-like pain with territorial ST changes (CVS-08).
traps: “Constrictive or effusive-constrictive pericarditis is an acute form”

Only 14% of the cohort got this right. By time course, acute pericarditis (under 6 weeks) is fibrinous or effusive; effusive-constrictive and constrictive are subacute (6 weeks to 6 months), and constrictive, adhesive or effusive are chronic (over 6 months in this pathological scheme).
decode: Which is classified under acute pericarditis: fibrinous, effusive-constrictive, adhesive, constrictive? [DocT GT]
Fibrinous: acute pericarditis is fibrinous or effusive; constriction and adhesion take weeks to months.
Most common pericardial disease? [pattern]
Acute pericarditis.
CVS-03.punch: Acute pericarditis is the commonest pericardial syndrome and rarely kills. Pathologically the acute forms are fibrinous or effusive; constrictive and adhesive forms come later.

parts.q: How is pericarditis classified by pathology and time course?
parts.a: Acute (under 6 weeks): fibrinous or effusive (serous, purulent, haemorrhagic). Subacute (6 weeks to 6 months): effusive-constrictive or constrictive. Chronic (over 6 months): constrictive, adhesive or effusive. This older pathological scheme uses 6 months; the ESC clinical time definitions (CVS-02) call disease chronic after 3 months.

CVS-04.intro: Step 1 asks what inflames the sac. In the developed world most cases are idiopathic, and idiopathic is presumed to be viral or immune; a specific cause matters because it changes treatment. The one question tested exactly this, in a patient whose background tempted people towards a specific cause.
why: **Idiopathic: presumed viral or autoimmune.** No cause is found in most patients in developed countries; an extensive search is not recommended in low-risk cases because it rarely changes management.

**Viral: Coxsackie, HHV-6, parvovirus B19, EBV, HIV, HCV, COVID-19. Bacterial: TB, Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, H. influenzae. Fungal: Histoplasma, Candida, Aspergillus. Parasitic: spirochaetes (as the card lists).** TB is the commonest specific cause worldwide and dominates in Africa (CVS-14); purulent bacterial pericarditis is rare but carries a high risk of tamponade and constriction (20–30% for bacterial causes).

**Malignancy (lung and nearby organs), blunt or penetrating trauma, radiation.** Lung and breast cancer and lymphoma are the usual malignant causes; a malignant effusion is often large and bloody (CVS-13).

**Cardiac: myocarditis, post-MI (Dressler’s syndrome) and ACS.** Early post-infarction pericarditis appears within days over a transmural infarct; Dressler’s syndrome (a post-cardiac injury syndrome) appears weeks later and is immune-mediated.
**Drugs: hydralazine, procainamide.** Both cause drug-induced lupus; isoniazid does too.
mimic: Uraemic or dialysis pericarditis vs viral pericarditis
Uraemic pericarditis usually lacks the diffuse ST elevation, because the epicardium is not inflamed; fever with diffuse ST elevation points to viral or idiopathic disease even in ESRD.
Early post-infarction pericarditis vs Dressler’s
Days after a transmural MI, local; versus weeks later, immune, diffuse.
traps: “An ESRD patient with pericarditis must have uraemic pericarditis”

Only 23% chose correctly. Fever and diffuse ST elevation are the viral/idiopathic picture; uraemic pericarditis typically has no ST elevation. The key (viral) is the exam-day answer, though renal failure is a real cause in the right picture.
“Diffuse ST elevation in an elderly patient means MI”
Elevation in I, II, III, aVF and aVL together fits no single artery (CVS-08).
decode: 79-year-old with ESRD, fever, pleuritic pain, diffuse ST elevation — commonest cause? [DocT GT]
Viral infection: the ECG and fever make this ordinary viral/idiopathic pericarditis, not uraemic.
Drugs causing pericarditis? [pattern]
Hydralazine, procainamide (and isoniazid): drug-induced lupus.
CVS-04.punch: Idiopathic or viral pericarditis is the commonest cause in every background in the developed world. A specific cause is suggested by the setting, but diffuse ST elevation with fever still points to viral disease, even on dialysis.

CVS-05.intro: Step 2 begins with the symptom present in almost every patient. Its character comes from where the pain fibres run: the parietal pericardium is supplied by the phrenic nerve, and only its lower part is pain-sensitive.
why: **Present in more than 90% of cases.** ESC gives over 85–90%; it is the main criterion (CVS-10).

**Sharp and pleuritic, different from ACS pain (which the card calls stabbing).** Pericardial pain is the sharp, stabbing one; ischaemic pain is usually pressure, tightness or heaviness, not affected by breathing or posture.
**Made worse by inspiration and lying supine.** Both press the inflamed layers together.
**Relieved by sitting up and leaning forward.** The heart falls away from the posterior parietal pericardium.
**Radiates to the trapezius ridge, or not at all.** The phrenic nerve (C3–5) shares segments with the skin over the trapezius; trapezius-ridge pain is close to specific for pericarditis.
mimic: Pericarditic vs ischaemic pain
Sharp, pleuritic, positional, to the trapezius ridge; versus pressure-like, exertional, to the arm or jaw, unaffected by breathing.
traps: “Pericarditis pain radiates to the left arm like angina”
The typical radiation is to the trapezius ridge.
decode: Pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward, radiating to the trapezius ridge? [pattern]
Acute pericarditis.
CVS-05.punch: Pericarditic pain is sharp, worse with breathing and lying flat, eased by leaning forward and felt at the trapezius ridge, because the phrenic nerve carries it.

CVS-06.intro: Step 2 continues with the only near-specific physical sign: two roughened layers rubbing as the heart moves. It is specific but often missed because it comes and goes.
why: **Present in more than 50% of cases.** ESC 2015 gives it in only up to a third (≤33%); it is evanescent, so repeated listening finds more.

**A high-pitched, scratchy sound, best heard with the diaphragm parasternally.** Lean the patient forward and listen at end-expiration. Up to three components (atrial systole, ventricular systole, early diastolic filling) because the heart moves three times per cycle.
**Hold the breath: a pleural rub disappears, a pericardial rub persists.** The heart keeps moving when breathing stops; the lungs do not.
mimic: Pericardial vs pleural rub
Persists with breath-holding and follows the heartbeat; versus disappears with breath-holding and follows respiration.
traps: “A large effusion abolishes the rub”
Not reliably; a rub can persist with an effusion.
decode: How do you tell a pericardial from a pleural rub at the bedside? [pattern]
Ask the patient to hold the breath: the pericardial rub persists.
CVS-06.punch: A rub is specific but heard in only about a third of patients. It persists when the patient holds the breath, because it follows the heart, not the lungs.

CVS-07.intro: Step 2 then shows how inflammation reaches the ECG. Inflamed epicardium injures the subepicardial myocardium all round the heart, so the injury current points towards the apex in most leads; inflamed atrial epicardium does the same to the PR segment.
why: **Up to 60% show widespread concave ST elevation and PR depression, except in aVR and V1, not corresponding to any one artery.** Not every patient has the classic changes: normal or atypical tracings are common, so a normal ECG does not exclude pericarditis.

**The two changes are diffuse concave ST elevation and PR depression; aVR and V1 are the exceptions.** PR depression is an atrial injury current; diffuse PR depression with diffuse ST elevation is what separates pericarditis from STEMI, though PR depression alone can occur in other conditions.
**In aVR (± V1): reciprocal ST depression and PR elevation.** aVR looks at the cavity from above right, opposite to the diffuse vector, so it shows the mirror image.

**Sinus tachycardia is common; the changes are static: ST elevation and T inversion do not coexist.** In the classic sequence (stage 1 ST elevation with PR depression, 2 normalisation, 3 T inversion, 4 normal) T waves invert only after the ST segment has returned to baseline; T inversion with ST still elevated suggests ischaemia.
mimic: PR depression of pericarditis vs atrial infarction
Diffuse and with diffuse ST elevation; versus localised with territorial changes (rare).
traps: “No ST elevation, so not pericarditis”
Classic changes appear in only up to 60%.
decode: ST depression with PR elevation in aVR and diffuse concave ST elevation elsewhere? [pattern]
Acute pericarditis.
CVS-07.punch: Diffuse inflammation gives a diffuse injury current: concave ST elevation and PR depression everywhere except aVR, which shows the mirror image. T waves invert only after the ST has settled.

CVS-08.sub: Pericarditis → ECG → Versus ischaemia and infarction
CVS-08.intro: Step 2 continues with the discrimination that matters most in the chest-pain room: thrombolysing pericarditis risks haemopericardium, and missing a STEMI is worse.
why: **Pericarditis: diffuse, concave, not in one territory; ischaemia: anatomical, convex.** Infarction follows a coronary artery; pericarditis follows the whole epicardium.

**Reciprocal ST depression absent in pericarditis (except aVR); present in ischaemia.** ST depression in leads facing away from an infarct (for example aVL in inferior STEMI) is the strongest pointer to STEMI.
**PR depression in pericarditis; none in ischaemia.**

**Pericarditis is static, changing over several weeks; ischaemia is dynamic, progressing to Q waves.** In STEMI, change is over minutes to hours, Q waves form and T waves invert while the ST is still raised.
**Electrical alternans is present with tamponade in pericarditis; absent in ischaemia.** It reflects a heart swinging in a large effusion (CVS-22).
mimic: Inferior STEMI vs pericarditis
ST elevation III greater than II with reciprocal depression in aVL; versus II with I and V-leads, no reciprocal change outside aVR.
traps: “Concave ST elevation excludes STEMI”
Early STEMI can be concave; reciprocal changes and territory decide, not shape alone.
decode: Which ECG feature best separates STEMI from pericarditis? [pattern]
Reciprocal ST depression (and territorial distribution, Q waves).
CVS-08.punch: Pericarditis is everywhere and static; ischaemia follows an artery, has reciprocal depression and evolves to Q waves. Reciprocal change is the single best discriminator.

CVS-09.sub: Pericarditis → ECG → Versus benign early repolarisation
CVS-09.intro: Step 2 ends with the commonest benign mimic: early repolarisation in young, fit people, which also gives concave ST elevation. The one real question gave an asymptomatic athlete.
why: **ST elevation limited to the precordial leads.** Pericarditis is more diffuse, including the limb leads.
**No PR depression.** PR depression points to pericarditis.
**Prominent T waves.** The ST segment is small relative to a tall T wave, which is the basis of the ratio in f.
**A ‘fish-hook’ appearance in V4.** A notch or slur at the J point.
**Seen in young men; needs no treatment.** It is stable over time, unlike the evolving changes of pericarditis.

**In V6, ST/T ratio below 0.25 = benign early repolarisation; above 0.25 = acute pericarditis.** ST elevation height divided by T-wave height in V6; a high ratio means the ST is out of proportion to the T wave.
mimic: Early repolarisation vs Brugada
J-point notch with concave ST in V3–V5; versus coved ST elevation with T inversion in V1–V2.
Early repolarisation vs LV aneurysm
Young, no history; versus persistent ST elevation with Q waves weeks after anterior MI.
traps: “Widespread concave ST elevation in a young man = myocarditis”
Myocarditis needs symptoms and a troponin rise; an asymptomatic athlete with J-point elevation and no reciprocal change has early repolarisation.
decode: Asymptomatic 29-year-old athlete, J-point elevation in V3–V5, concave ST, no reciprocal depression? [DocT GT]
Early repolarisation.
ST/T ratio in V6 of 0.3? [pattern]
Favours pericarditis (over 0.25).
CVS-09.punch: Early repolarisation is precordial, has no PR depression, a J-point notch and tall T waves in a well young man. An ST/T ratio in V6 above 0.25 favours pericarditis.

CVS-10.intro: Step 3 is how the diagnosis is made. The ESC 2015 rule is two of four; ESC 2025 has restructured it around the presentation, and both versions turn up in questions.
why: **Two of the four criteria are needed.** ESC 2025 now requires a compatible clinical presentation (typical pain) plus additional criteria; with one it is possible, with more it is definite.

**Pericarditic chest pain; pericardial rub; new widespread ST elevation or PR depression; new or worsening pericardial effusion.** Their frequencies explain why two are asked for: pain over 85%, ECG and effusion up to 60%, rub about a third.

**Supporting: raised CRP, ESR, WBC; pericardial inflammation on CT or CMR.** In ESC 2025 raised CRP and CMR oedema or late gadolinium enhancement have become criteria in their own right, not just support.
mimic: ESC 2015 vs ESC 2025 rule
Any 2 of 4; versus typical presentation plus additional criteria, with CRP and CMR promoted.
traps: “A raised troponin is a diagnostic criterion”
Troponin marks myocardial involvement (myopericarditis), not pericarditis (CVS-11).
decode: Pleuritic pain and a new effusion, normal ECG, no rub — does this meet the ESC 2015 criteria? [pattern]
Yes, two of four.
CVS-10.punch: ESC 2015: two of pain, rub, ECG change and effusion. ESC 2025 starts from the typical presentation and counts CRP and CMR inflammation as criteria.

CVS-11.intro: Step 3 continues with the first-line tests, each answering a different question: is it pericarditis, is there fluid, is the myocardium involved, and is the inflammation settling.
why: **ECG, chest X-ray, transthoracic echo, inflammatory and cardiac biomarkers.** The ECG and echo test criteria; the X-ray looks for lung or mediastinal causes and a big heart.

**At least 200–250 mL before the cardiac silhouette enlarges on CXR.** A normal heart size on X-ray does not exclude a dangerous acute effusion; 100–200 mL that arrives fast can cause tamponade (CVS-19).
**Raised troponin I or CK-MB means concomitant myocardial injury.** That is myopericarditis; it needs longer exercise restriction and is a minor predictor of poor prognosis (CVS-12).
**CRP and ESR support the diagnosis, monitor activity and monitor response to treatment.** Tapering is done only when CRP is normal (CVS-15).
mimic: Myopericarditis vs perimyocarditis
Mainly pericarditis with some myocardial injury; versus mainly myocarditis with pericardial involvement (falling LV function).
traps: “Normal heart size on CXR excludes tamponade”
The silhouette needs over 200 mL; acute tamponade can occur with less.
decode: Pericarditis with a raised troponin — what does it mean? [pattern]
Myopericarditis: concomitant myocardial injury.
CVS-11.punch: Echo, ECG, CXR and markers answer different questions. The X-ray stays normal until over 200 mL, troponin means the myocardium is involved, and CRP decides when to taper.

CVS-12.sub: Pericarditis → Triage → Predictors of poor prognosis
CVS-12.intro: Step 3 ends in triage: most patients go home on NSAID and colchicine, and these features pick out those who need admission and a search for a specific cause.
why: **Major: fever over 38 °C, subacute onset, large effusion (less likely post-viral), tamponade, no response to aspirin or NSAID after at least 1 week.** Each suggests a specific cause (TB, bacterial, neoplastic) or a complication. ESC 2025 defines a large effusion as over 20 mm on echo (CVS-23).

**Minor: myopericarditis, immunosuppression, oral anticoagulant therapy.** ESC 2015 and ESC 2025 both list a fourth, trauma. Reviews of ESC 2025 also count effusive-constrictive or incessant disease, signs of right heart failure and extensive pericardial late gadolinium enhancement on CMR as high-risk features.
mimic: High-risk vs low-risk pericarditis
Any major or minor predictor: admit and investigate; none: outpatient NSAID plus colchicine and review at 1 week.
traps: “Only three minor predictors”
ESC 2015 and 2025 list four: trauma is the one missing from the card.
decode: Which feature mandates admission in acute pericarditis? [pattern]
Any major predictor, for example fever over 38 °C, subacute onset, large effusion, tamponade or failure of 1 week of NSAID.
CVS-12.punch: Fever, subacute onset, a large effusion, tamponade or NSAID failure are the major predictors, with myopericarditis, immunosuppression, trauma and anticoagulation as minor ones: any one means admission.

CVS-13.sub: Pericarditis → Drainage → When pericardiocentesis is justified
CVS-13.intro: Step 3 decides who needs a needle. In ordinary viral pericarditis the fluid tells you little and the procedure carries risk; the balance changes when the fluid is the cause of shock or holds the diagnosis.
why: **Not justified in mild or moderate effusions: low diagnostic power; viral/idiopathic disease is self-limiting and needs only anti-inflammatory treatment; high procedural risk for the yield.** Small effusions also offer a small target, so the risk of puncturing the heart rises.

**Justified for tamponade, refractory effusion, or suspected bacterial or neoplastic pericarditis.** Tamponade is treated, purulent fluid must be drained, and cytology or culture changes management. The one real question was malignant tamponade: drain now by needle, consider a surgical window later for recurrence.
mimic: Pericardiocentesis vs surgical window
Fast, bedside, for tamponade; versus for recurrent malignant effusions, loculated or posterior fluid, or when tissue is needed.
traps: “A malignant effusion with hypotension needs a pericardial window first”
Haemodynamic compromise needs immediate needle drainage; a window is for recurrence.
decode: Breast cancer, dyspnoea, hypotension, effusion on echo — intervention? [Marrow]
Pericardiocentesis.
Small effusion in uncomplicated viral pericarditis — tap? [pattern]
No: low yield, self-limiting disease, high risk.
CVS-13.punch: Do not tap the routine viral effusion. Tap for tamponade, for refractory fluid, or when bacterial or malignant disease is suspected, and in malignant tamponade drain first, window later.

CVS-14.sub: Pericarditis → Aetiology → Western Europe vs Africa
CVS-14.intro: Step 1 ends with geography, because it sets the default diagnosis. In a low-TB country a first episode is treated as idiopathic; in a high-TB country, especially with HIV, TB must be excluded first.
why: **Idiopathic: 55% in Western Europe vs 13.7% in Africa.** A specific cause is found in most African cases (86.3%).

**Tuberculosis: under 1% in Western Europe vs 69.5% in Africa.** HIV drives this; ESC 2025 puts TB at about 70% of cases in endemic regions, which include India, and that is why TB is the classic cause of constriction here (CVS-18).
mimic: Idiopathic vs tuberculous effusion
Short illness, high CRP, small effusion, settles on NSAID; versus subacute, weight loss, fever, large effusion, often HIV.
traps: “Neoplastic pericarditis is much commoner in Europe”
It is about 9% in both settings; TB is the big difference.
decode: Commonest cause of pericarditis in sub-Saharan Africa? [pattern]
Tuberculosis.
CVS-14.punch: Most pericarditis is idiopathic in Western Europe but tuberculous in Africa; malignancy is about 9% in both, so in a TB-endemic setting TB is excluded first.

CVS-15.intro: Step 4 treats the inflammation. NSAID or aspirin controls pain and inflammation; colchicine is added to prevent recurrence (CVS-16). The one real question tested exactly that first-line choice and the dose.
why: **Aspirin 500–1000 mg every 6–8 h (1.5–4 g/day).** ESC 2015 and 2025 give 750–1000 mg every 8 h. Aspirin is preferred after MI or when antiplatelet treatment is needed anyway, because other NSAIDs can impair infarct healing.

**Ibuprofen 600 mg every 8 h (1200–2400 mg/day).** ESC 2025 gives 600–800 mg three times daily. Add gastric protection. Indomethacin 25–50 mg every 8 h works but reduces coronary flow, so it is avoided in coronary disease and the elderly.
**1–2 weeks for a first uncomplicated episode.**
**2–4 weeks to several months for recurrences.**
**CRP guides the length; taper every 1–2 weeks only when asymptomatic and CRP is normal.** Stopping while CRP is still raised is a common cause of early relapse.
mimic: Aspirin vs other NSAID
After MI or on antiplatelets; versus other patients.
traps: “Colchicine monotherapy is first-line”
43% missed this. Colchicine is added to aspirin or NSAID; on its own it does not control the acute inflammation.
“Prednisone 1–1.5 mg/kg”
High-dose steroid increases recurrence; steroids are second line at low dose (CVS-17).
decode: Young man, positional pleuritic pain, rub, diffuse ST elevation — first-line treatment? [DocT GT]
Ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily (with colchicine).
When can NSAID be tapered? [pattern]
Once asymptomatic and CRP has normalised.
CVS-15.punch: First line is aspirin or NSAID at full dose for 1–2 weeks, with colchicine. CRP, not the calendar, decides when to taper.

CVS-16.intro: Step 4 continues with the drug that halves recurrence. Recurrence affects 15–30% of patients after a first episode and about half after a recurrence without colchicine, so its job is to prevent the next episode, not to treat the pain.
why: **It concentrates in leucocytes and interferes with chemotaxis and degranulation.** It binds tubulin and blocks microtubule assembly in neutrophils, and so also dampens the inflammasome that drives IL-1 release, the same pathway anakinra blocks (CVS-18).

**0.5–0.6 mg twice daily; once daily if under 70 kg.** No loading dose, which only adds diarrhoea; ESC 2025 adds that the dose should be halved in some elderly patients and given once daily in severe renal impairment.

**Contraindicated with CrCl under 10 (reduced doses at CrCl 35–49 and 10–34); avoid in severe hepatobiliary dysfunction.** It is cleared by the kidney and by CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, so clarithromycin, ciclosporin and similar drugs raise levels to toxic ones.
mimic: Colchicine vs NSAID
Prevents recurrence over months; versus controls acute pain and inflammation over weeks.
traps: “Colchicine alone is enough first-line”
It is added to aspirin or NSAID, not used instead of it.
decode: First-line treatment of acute pericarditis? [DocT GT]
Aspirin or NSAID plus colchicine.
Colchicine duration after a recurrence? [pattern]
At least 6 months.
CVS-16.punch: Colchicine halves recurrence: 0.5 mg twice daily (once if under 70 kg), 3 months after a first episode and 6 after a recurrence, with doses cut in renal impairment.

CVS-17.intro: Step 4 then deals with steroids. They control symptoms fast but make the disease more likely to come back, especially at high dose, so they are kept for specific indications or failure of first-line treatment.
why: **Second line: only if aspirin, NSAID or colchicine are contraindicated, and after infection is excluded.** Specific reasons to use them earlier are autoimmune disease, pregnancy (NSAIDs are avoided after 20 weeks) and renal failure. ESC 2025 makes steroids as initial therapy without such an indication class III.
**Avoided in active infection (bacterial, TB).** They can spread infection; in TB they are only an adjunct to ATT (CVS-18).
**NSAID failure: chest pain still needing analgesia, fever, or worsening effusion despite at least 1 week of treatment.** This is also a major poor-prognosis predictor (CVS-12).

**Starting dose 0.25–0.50 mg/kg/day.** ESC 2015 and 2025 give prednisone 0.2–0.5 mg/kg/day, and say avoid 1 mg/kg. Taper slowly, especially below 10–15 mg/day, and only when asymptomatic with normal CRP.
mimic: Low-dose vs high-dose prednisone
0.2–0.5 mg/kg with slow taper; versus 1 mg/kg, which raises recurrence and side effects.
traps: “Steroids are first line for recurrence”
First line for acute AND recurrent disease is the same: aspirin or NSAID plus colchicine and exercise restriction.
decode: Pericarditis not settling after 1 week of NSAID and colchicine, infection excluded — next? [pattern]
Low-dose prednisone (0.2–0.5 mg/kg/day) added to colchicine.
CVS-17.punch: Steroids are second line, low dose (0.2–0.5 mg/kg), after infection is excluded, because they make recurrence more likely.

CVS-18.intro: Step 4 ends with the hard cases: disease that keeps coming back, and TB, where the danger is constriction. Both real questions were about constriction, the late end of this story.
why: **First: aspirin or NSAID + colchicine + exercise restriction; second: low-dose steroids; third: IV immunoglobulin, anakinra or azathioprine; fourth: pericardiectomy.** This is the 2015 ladder. ESC 2025 recommends IL-1 blockers (anakinra, rilonacept) for recurrent pericarditis with raised CRP that is corticosteroid-dependent and colchicine-resistant (reported as class I), and the ACC 2025 guidance uses them after failure of first-level therapy and/or steroids, especially with an inflammatory phenotype, so steroids need not come first; IVIG, azathioprine and hydroxychloroquine remain options for refractory, steroid-dependent disease. Recurrent pericarditis with a high CRP is an autoinflammatory, IL-1-driven disease, which is why these work.

**2 months of HRZE, then 4 months of HR.** Adjunctive steroids do not improve survival: in the IMPI trial (Mayosi, NEJM 2014, 1400 patients) prednisolone cut constriction (4.4% vs 7.8%) and hospitalisation but not the combined outcome of death, tamponade or constriction, and it raised HIV-associated cancers. ESC 2025 therefore suggests steroids only in HIV-negative patients.
**Pericardiectomy if not improving, or deteriorating, after 4–8 weeks of ATT.** By then fibrosis rather than active infection drives the constriction.

**Constriction in 50%; ATT reduces it to 17%.** The 50% is the rate without treatment; with ATT older series give 17–40%, so 17% is the best of that range. ESC 2025 says constriction affected up to 50% before effective TB therapy and 5–25% with contemporary treatment, and gives a 20–30% constriction risk for bacterial pericarditis overall, compared with under 1% for viral or idiopathic disease.
mimic: Constrictive pericarditis vs restrictive cardiomyopathy

Mitral inflow variation over 25%, septal bounce, septal e′ normal or high (annulus reversus), thick or calcified pericardium, near-normal BNP, discordant RV and LV pressures with breathing; versus little variation, low e′ (under 8 cm/s), thick myocardium, biatrial enlargement, high BNP, concordant pressures.
Chronic calcific vs transient constriction
Cured only by pericardiectomy; versus inflammatory, CMR late-enhancement positive, resolves with anti-inflammatory treatment.
traps: “High-dose diuretics are the definitive treatment of calcific constriction”
Diuretics only palliate congestion; pericardiectomy is the cure.
“Restrictive cardiomyopathy” for a TB patient with respiratory mitral variation
34% chose wrong: exaggerated respiratory variation of mitral inflow is the constrictive sign; restriction shows little.
“Dip-and-plateau and equal end-diastolic pressures separate constriction from restriction”
Both show them; discordant RV and LV systolic pressures with breathing are the discriminator.
decode: Prior cardiac surgery, ascites, hepatomegaly, oedema, pericardial calcification on CT — definitive treatment? [DocT GT]
Pericardiectomy.
Past TB, ascites, hepatomegaly, respiratory variation in mitral inflow, preserved EF — diagnosis? [DocT GT]
Constrictive pericarditis.
TB pericarditis worsening after 6 weeks of ATT? [pattern]
Pericardiectomy.
CVS-18.punch: Recurrence climbs the ladder from NSAID and colchicine to steroids or, now earlier, IL-1 blockers, then surgery. In TB the enemy is constriction: give ATT, and operate if there is no improvement after 4–8 weeks.

CVS-19.intro: Step 5 moves from inflammation to pressure. Tamponade is not a size of effusion; it is the point at which pericardial pressure exceeds the filling pressure of the heart. The one real question was the fastest version, a stab or gunshot wound.
why: **Haemodynamic decompensation when pericardial pressure compresses the heart; a medical emergency needing emergency decompression.** The right atrium and ventricle fill at the lowest pressure, so they are squeezed first, and output falls as the chambers cannot fill.

**Volume of fluid, rate of accumulation and compliance of the pericardium.** Rate matters most: 100–200 mL of blood in minutes can kill, while 1–2 L of slowly gathering fluid may be tolerated (CVS-20).

**Pericardial reserve volume: 200–250 mL.** The volume the sac takes before pressure climbs steeply; the same figure as the volume needed to enlarge the silhouette on X-ray (CVS-11), which is why acute tamponade often has a normal-sized heart on film.
mimic: Traumatic tamponade vs tension pneumothorax
Raised JVP and hypotension in both; equal air entry and a central trachea point to tamponade.
traps: “Pericardiocentesis is the definitive management of traumatic tamponade”

It is the bedside life-saving step offered in the recall, and the keyed answer; the definitive treatment is thoracotomy or sternotomy to repair the injury, and clotted blood often cannot be aspirated.
“Bilateral chest tubes” for penetrating trauma with muffled sounds and clear lungs
Clear lungs and Beck’s triad point to the pericardium, not the pleura.
decode: Gunshot to the left chest, BP 70/40, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds, normal lungs — definitive management? [NEET 2025 recall]
Urgent pericardiocentesis as keyed; true definitive care is surgical.
CVS-19.punch: Tamponade is pressure, not volume: it depends on how fast the fluid arrives in a sac with only about 200 mL to spare. Traumatic tamponade gets a needle as a bridge and a surgeon as the cure.

CVS-20.sub: Tamponade → Pathophysiology → Pressure-volume curve, last drop, interdependence
CVS-20.intro: Step 5 continues with the mechanism that explains every sign. Both real questions tested it: why the blood pressure falls on inspiration, and why intubation can kill.
why: **Acute: small reserve, so a small volume quickly exceeds pericardial stretch; chronic: the pericardium stretches and a much larger volume is tolerated.** The pressure-volume curve is flat, then very steep; slow accumulation shifts the steep part far to the right.

**Last drop effect: the final increment causes critical compression, and the first decrement during drainage gives the largest relative decompression.** On the steep part of the curve, small volume changes cause large pressure changes, so removing even 50 mL can sharply lower pericardial pressure and restore output.

**Less RV output, less LV preload; the RV cannot take venous return, pushes the septum towards the LV, LV volume and output fall, cardiac output drops and the patient becomes hypotensive.** Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart; inside a fixed sac the RV can only grow by pushing the septum left, so LV filling and stroke volume fall: this is pulsus paradoxus (CVS-22).
mimic: Pulsus paradoxus in tamponade vs in severe asthma
Septal shift in a fixed sac; versus large swings in intrathoracic pressure.
traps: “Inspiration pools blood in the lungs, reducing LV filling”
That happens normally and gives the small physiological fall; the exaggerated fall comes from septal shift.
“Enhanced adrenergic tone causes collapse after intubation”
The reverse: positive intrathoracic pressure cuts the venous return that keeps the right heart filling, and induction removes the compensating sympathetic tone.
decode: Large effusion, SBP falls 15 mmHg on inspiration — mechanism? [DocT GT]
Increased venous return to the right heart shifts the septum left and restricts LV filling.
Tamponade needing urgent airway — greatest risk of collapse after intubation? [DocT GT]

Positive intrathoracic pressure. Drain first under local anaesthesia, sitting up; if intubation cannot wait, keep spontaneous breathing, use ketamine, low PEEP and tidal volume, with the needle ready.
CVS-20.punch: The pressure-volume curve is flat then steep, so a little fluid kills and a little drained saves. In a fixed sac the right heart grows only at the left heart’s expense, which is why inspiration and positive pressure both cut output.

CVS-21.sub: Tamponade → Presentation → Acute, subacute, regional, low pressure
CVS-21.intro: Step 5 shows that tamponade wears four faces. The three real questions used the acute ones: a catheter-lab complication, a malignant effusion and blunt trauma.
why: **Acute: trauma or an invasive procedure; needs emergent decompression.** Cardiac perforation in the catheter or electrophysiology lab (trans-septal puncture, pacing, ablation) is now a common cause; the volume is small and the onset fast.
**Subacute: days to weeks, with chest pain, dyspnoea and chest heaviness.** Malignant, uraemic or idiopathic effusions; the sac has stretched, so the effusion is large before tamponade appears.

**Regional: localised effusion or haematoma.** Typical after cardiac surgery; a posterior clot can compress the left atrium or ventricle alone, the classical signs may be absent, and transthoracic echo can miss it, so TOE is used.

**Low pressure: hypovolaemia.** Pericardial and filling pressures are both low (for example after haemorrhage or dialysis), so the JVP is not raised; filling may improve output briefly, and pericardiocentesis still helps.
mimic: Tamponade vs massive haemothorax or tension pneumothorax after blunt trauma
Equal air entry, raised JVP, hypotension unresponsive to fluid; versus absent breath sounds on one side.
traps: “Check for pulsus paradoxus to confirm tamponade”
Echo confirms it and guides drainage; pulsus is unreliable in AF and tachypnoea (18% chose otherwise).
“Electrical alternans or pulsus paradoxus best confirms tamponade”
27% missed this: the catheter hallmark asked was equalisation of diastolic pressures (RA, RV diastolic, PA diastolic and wedge within a few mmHg); in practice the diagnosis is clinical plus echo.
decode: Hypotension, JVD and muffled sounds an hour after LARIAT with trans-septal puncture, in AF — next step to confirm? [DocT GT]
Echocardiogram.
Metastatic lung cancer, hypotension, JVD, RA collapse and plethoric IVC — which finding best confirms tamponade? [DocT GT]
Equalisation of diastolic pressures.
Blunt chest trauma, equal air entry, soft abdomen, hypotension despite fluids? [DocT GT; NEET 2024 recall]
Cardiac tamponade.
CVS-21.punch: Tamponade is acute after trauma or procedures, subacute with large malignant or inflammatory effusions, regional after cardiac surgery, and low-pressure in hypovolaemia. Echo confirms it, and equal diastolic pressures are its catheter signature.

CVS-22.sub: Tamponade → Signs → Beck’s triad, pulsus paradoxus, alternans
CVS-22.intro: Step 5 reaches the bedside, and this is the most-asked card in the deck (8 questions). Every sign is a direct reading of the physiology in CVS-20: low output, high venous pressure, fluid between heart and stethoscope, and septal shift with breathing.
why: **Beck’s triad: hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds.** Low output, venous pressure backing up behind a heart that cannot fill, and fluid damping the sounds. It is a picture of acute surgical tamponade; in slow medical tamponade the full triad is often absent.

**Breathlessness, tachycardia, pulsus paradoxus, electrical alternans.** Tachycardia keeps output up when stroke volume is fixed. Electrical alternans (beat-to-beat change in QRS height) means a large effusion with the heart swinging in it; together with low voltage it is highly suggestive. The lungs are clear, because the left heart is underfilled, not failing; Kussmaul’s sign (JVP rising on inspiration) belongs to constriction, not tamponade.

**Pulsus paradoxus: an inspiratory fall in cardiac output and blood pressure.** Defined as an inspiratory fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mmHg. On an arterial line, systolic and pulse pressure fall on inspiration while diastolic barely changes, because stroke volume is what falls. It can be absent despite tamponade with aortic regurgitation, atrial septal defect, a stiff or failing LV with high filling pressure, positive-pressure ventilation and regional tamponade, and it is hard to read in AF.
mimic: Tamponade vs left heart failure
Clear lungs; versus crackles and pulmonary oedema.
Tamponade vs constriction
Pulsus paradoxus prominent, Kussmaul absent, no pericardial knock; versus Kussmaul present, pulsus less common, knock.
Tamponade vs tension pneumothorax
Equal air entry; versus absent breath sounds and a deviated trachea.
traps: “Bibasilar crepitations support tamponade”
Tamponade has clear lungs; crackles point to LV failure.
“Loud S1 and opening snap”
That is mitral stenosis; tamponade muffles the sounds.
“Tension pneumothorax or massive haemothorax” after blunt trauma with equal air entry
Equal air entry removes both; fluid-resistant hypotension then means tamponade.
“Pulsus paradoxus means the diastolic pressure falls”
It is the systolic and pulse pressure that fall; diastolic hardly moves.
decode: Hypotension, tachycardia, high JVP, muffled sounds — which sign best supports tamponade? [DocT GT; Marrow]
Pulsus paradoxus over 10 mmHg.
Large effusion, SBP falls 15 mmHg on inspiration — mechanism? [DocT GT]
Inspiratory venous return to the RV shifts the septum left and restricts LV filling.
Post-viral pericarditis with electrical alternans; if untreated, what follows? [Marrow]
Beck’s triad: hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds.
Tamponade: arterial line change on inspiration? [Marrow]
Fall in systolic and pulse pressure.
CVS-22.punch: Beck’s triad, clear lungs and pulsus paradoxus are tamponade at the bedside: low output, high venous pressure, a muffled heart and an inspiratory fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mmHg from septal shift.

head: Sign
What it reflects
rows: Venous return cannot enter the compressed right heart
Fluid between heart and chest wall
Inspiratory septal shift reduces LV filling
Heart swinging in a large effusion

CVS-23.intro: Step 6 starts with the echo measurement. Size is measured as the end-diastolic echo-free space; it tells you how much fluid there is, not whether the heart is compressed.
why: **Large: over 20 mm.** Over 20 mm is a major poor-prognosis feature and an indication to drain in stable patients when chronic or symptomatic (CVS-12, CVS-27).
**Circumferential or loculated.** Loculated effusions (after surgery) can compress single chambers and are harder to reach with a needle.
mimic: Effusion vs epicardial fat pad
Fat is anterior only and moves with the heart; an effusion collects posteriorly first.
Pericardial vs pleural effusion
Pericardial fluid lies anterior to the descending aorta in the parasternal long axis; pleural fluid behind it.
traps: “A small effusion cannot cause tamponade”
A small fast bleed can; size is not physiology.
decode: Echo-free space 15 mm in diastole? [pattern]
Moderate effusion.
CVS-23.punch: Under 10 mm is mild, 10–20 moderate and over 20 large. Size measures fluid, not compression; tamponade is decided by collapse and haemodynamics.

CVS-24.sub: Tamponade → Echo → RA and RV collapse, IVC
CVS-24.intro: Step 6 continues with the echo signs that show the pressure. A chamber collapses when pericardial pressure exceeds its own pressure at that moment, so each sign appears at the time in the cycle when that chamber is at its lowest pressure. Three real questions tested timing, specificity and the view.
why: **RA collapse: late diastole and early systole; RV collapse: early diastole.** The RA is at its lowest pressure during atrial relaxation, the RV at the start of filling.

**RA collapse lasting more than 1/3 of the cardiac cycle: 94% sensitive, 100% specific for tamponade.** The figures are Gillam’s (Circulation 1983): any RA inversion was 100% sensitive but only 82% specific, and an inversion lasting over 0.34 of the cycle was 94% sensitive and 100% specific in that series. Brief RA inversion is common and non-specific; prolonged inversion is what counts. RA collapse is the earliest and most sensitive sign; LA collapse is late (or seen with a loculated posterior effusion).
**RV collapse is most evident in expiration.** In expiration venous return to the right heart falls, so RV pressure is lowest and the wall gives way.

**RV collapse is the more specific indicator, over 90%, and goes with a significant fall in cardiac output.** RV wall is thicker, so it collapses only at higher pericardial pressure. It is absent when the RV is hypertrophied or under high pressure (pulmonary hypertension).

**IVC plethora: 97% sensitive but non-specific, present in all states of high systemic venous pressure.** Its specificity is only about 40% (Himelman 1988; ESC 2025 quotes the same 97% and 40%). A normal, collapsing IVC makes tamponade very unlikely; a dilated one proves nothing on its own. It is best seen in the subcostal view, which also shows the effusion and the RA.
mimic: RA vs RV collapse
Earliest, most sensitive, late diastole; versus later, more specific, early diastole, worst in expiration.
traps: “RA collapse occurs late in tamponade”
False: RA collapse is the earliest sign; ‘late’ applies to its timing in the cycle (late diastole), not to the course of disease. LA collapse is the late one.
“Systolic RA collapse over 1/3 of the cycle is the most specific finding”

On the card’s own figure (100% specificity) this is defensible, but the DocT key and the exam convention name early diastolic RV collapse as the most specific single sign; choose RV collapse on exam day.
“Mitral E variation over 15% is diagnostic”
The cut-off is over 25% (CVS-25).
“A dilated IVC confirms tamponade”
It is sensitive, not specific.
decode: Best view for IVC collapse and RA filling in suspected tamponade? [DocT QBank, 72%]
Subcostal (long-axis) view.
Large effusion, rising vasopressors — which echo finding is most specific? [DocT GT]
Early diastolic RV collapse.
False statement about echo in tamponade? [Marrow]
‘RA collapse occurs late’: it is the earliest sign.
CVS-24.punch: Each chamber collapses when it is at its lowest pressure: the RA in late diastole and earliest, the RV in early diastole, in expiration, and more specifically. A plethoric IVC is sensitive but proves little alone.

CVS-25.intro: Step 6 turns interdependence into numbers. Doppler measures the flow into each ventricle with breathing; in tamponade the respiratory swing is exaggerated in opposite directions on the two sides.
why: **Tricuspid E wave peak velocity rises more than 40% on inspiration.** Inspiration fills the right heart.
**Mitral E wave peak velocity falls more than 25% on inspiration.** The septum moves left, so LV filling falls.

**On inspiration LVOT VTI falls more than 10% and RVOT VTI rises more than 10%: neither sensitive nor specific; the inspiratory septal bounce towards the LV is not specific either.** These changes are also seen in constriction, COPD and asthma. ESC 2025 quotes the inflow thresholds as ranges (mitral fall over 25–30%, tricuspid rise over 40–60%); the card gives the lower ends. With positive-pressure ventilation the pattern reverses, because inspiration then reduces venous return.
mimic: Tamponade vs constriction on Doppler
Both have exaggerated mitral variation (over 25%); constriction adds a preserved or high septal e′ and a thick pericardium (CVS-18).
traps: “Mitral E rises on inspiration”
Mitral falls, tricuspid rises.
decode: Doppler threshold for mitral inflow variation in tamponade? [pattern]
Fall of more than 25% on inspiration (tricuspid rises more than 40%).
CVS-25.punch: On inspiration the right side fills more and the left less: tricuspid E up more than 40%, mitral E down more than 25%. Positive-pressure ventilation reverses the timing.

CVS-26.intro: Step 6 then puts accuracy on the echo signs. The figures come from Mercé (1999), 110 patients with moderate or large effusions judged against clinical tamponade. The table is a lesson in trade-off: each extra sign you demand raises specificity and lowers sensitivity. Both real questions asked which test or sign confirms tamponade.
why: **Any collapse: 90% sensitive, 65% specific.** Good for ruling out: no collapse at all makes tamponade unlikely.
**RA collapse: 68% sensitive, 66% specific.** Brief RA inversion is common without tamponade; prolonged inversion (over 1/3 of the cycle, CVS-24) is much more specific.
**RV collapse: 60% sensitive, 90% specific.** Specific, so it rules in.
**Abnormal venous flow: 75% sensitive, 91% specific.** Hepatic and caval flow with blunted or reversed diastolic forward flow.
**Abnormal venous flow plus two collapses: 37% sensitive, 98% specific.** Almost certain when present, but missed in most.
mimic: Rule-out vs rule-in signs
Any collapse or IVC plethora (sensitive); versus RV collapse or combinations (specific).
traps: “Pulsus paradoxus or MRI to confirm tamponade after a procedure”
Echo is the confirming test and guides drainage; MRI and catheterisation waste time.
“Systolic RA collapse is the most specific sign”
Exam convention keys early diastolic RV collapse; the card’s 100% figure for prolonged RA collapse comes from one series (CVS-24).
decode: After LARIAT, hypotension, JVD, muffled sounds — next best step to confirm? [DocT GT]
Echocardiogram.
Most specific single echo finding for tamponade? [DocT GT]
Early diastolic RV collapse.
CVS-26.punch: The more signs you require, the more certain a positive becomes and the more cases you miss: any collapse rules out, RV collapse rules in, and venous flow plus two collapses is 98% specific.

CVS-27.intro: Step 6 ends with the procedure. In the unstable patient there is only one indication; in the stable one the question is whether fluid will cause trouble or holds the diagnosis. Both real questions were cardiac arrest.
why: **Unstable: tamponade.** Drain at once; in arrest, an effusion seen on POCUS at the rhythm check is treated as tamponade and drained during CPR, because compressions cannot fill a compressed heart.

**Stable: large effusion over 20 mm; chronic effusion over 3 months; symptomatic moderate-to-large effusion not responding to medical treatment; small effusion if TB, bacterial or neoplastic.** A large chronic idiopathic effusion can progress to tamponade without warning, and a small infected or malignant one holds the diagnosis.

**Subcostal, parasternal or apical.** Echo guidance chooses the site where fluid is deepest and closest; subcostal is the classic blind route and the one used during CPR; parasternal punctures stay close to the upper border of the rib and away from the internal thoracic artery.

**Absolute: aortic dissection; post-MI free-wall rupture.** Draining reduces the pressure that is holding the bleeding; both need surgery. ESC 2015 names only aortic dissection as the major contraindication and prefers surgery for free-wall rupture and traumatic haemopericardium.

**Relative: platelets under 50 × 10⁹/L, coagulopathy, anticoagulant therapy, severe pulmonary hypertension (the RV may fail after drainage).** ESC also lists small, posterior or loculated effusions. ESC 2025 advises removing under about 500 mL at a time; after drainage watch for pericardial decompression syndrome, paradoxical deterioration (pulmonary oedema or LV failure) after successful drainage.
mimic: Effusion vs dilated RV on POCUS in arrest
Fluid around the heart: drain; dilated RV without effusion: consider PE and thrombolysis.
traps: “Start thrombolytics” for an arrest with an effusion on POCUS

Half the cohort got this wrong. Thrombolysis is for a dilated RV; an effusion means drain, and resuscitative delivery still follows if there is no return of circulation by about 5 minutes with the fundus at or above the umbilicus.
“Pericardiocentesis for aortic dissection with haemopericardium”
Contraindicated; it can extend the bleed. Go to surgery.
decode: 29 weeks pregnant, collapse, POCUS at rhythm check shows effusion — next step? [DocT QBank, 50%]
Pericardiocentesis.
Tamponade arrest with alternans and JVD — next step after CPR? [Marrow]
Emergency pericardiocentesis.
CVS-27.punch: Tamponade is drained at once, in arrest during CPR. Do not needle dissection or free-wall rupture: they need surgery, because the pericardial pressure is holding the bleed.

spine: The sac and what inflames it
The pericardium is a stiff fibrous bag with a thin serous lining, and in the developed world most inflammation of it is viral or idiopathic, whereas in Africa it is mostly tuberculous.
Pain, rub and the ECG
Inflamed pericardium hurts sharply with breathing and lying flat, rubs against itself, and injures the epicardium under it, so the ECG shows diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression.
Diagnose, time and triage
The diagnosis rests on two of pain, rub, ECG and effusion, the time course names the form, and fever, subacute onset, a large effusion, tamponade or NSAID failure send the patient into hospital.
Damp the inflammation, stop recurrence
NSAID or aspirin plus colchicine is first line, steroids raise recurrence and are kept for failure or specific causes, and tuberculous pericarditis needs ATT to prevent constriction.
Tamponade: pressure beats filling

When fluid outruns the stretch of the sac, pericardial pressure exceeds right-heart filling pressure, the septum is pushed left on inspiration, and output falls: hypotension, high JVP, quiet heart, pulsus paradoxus.
Echo grades it, the needle relieves it
Echo sizes the effusion and shows right-sided collapse and a plethoric IVC; tamponade is drained at once, and the first small volume removed gives the largest gain.
CVS01.primer: The heart sits inside a sac whose outer fibrous layer barely stretches over minutes, so the pressure inside it depends on how fast fluid arrives, not only how much. The right heart fills at low pressure (a few mmHg), so it is the first chamber to be squeezed when pericardial pressure rises. Both ventricles share one septum inside one fixed sac, so whatever fills the right side on inspiration takes room from the left: this is ventricular interdependence. Inflammation of the sac (pericarditis) and fluid under pressure in it (tamponade) are the two halves of this deck.

CVS-28.intro: Step 1 starts with what the word means. Myocarditis is a tissue diagnosis, and the WHO definition says which tissue tests count.
why: **Inflammatory disease of the myocardium, diagnosed by established histological, immunological and immunohistochemical criteria.** The definition is pathological on purpose: chest pain, troponin and ECG changes are shared with many diseases, so only tissue proves inflammation. ESC 2025 still keeps biopsy as the reference standard but now also accepts a compatible presentation with confirmatory CMR as ‘definite’ myocarditis (CVS-42).

**Inflammatory infiltrates with myocyte degeneration and necrosis of non-ischaemic origin.** This is the Dallas histological criterion: the inflammatory cells must sit next to damaged myocytes, and the damage must not look like infarction (which is zonal and follows a territory).

**Inflammatory cardiomyopathy: myocarditis in association with cardiac dysfunction.** Inflammation plus a failing ventricle; ESC 2025 uses the term for chronic myocarditis with dysfunction and remodelling, the bridge to dilated cardiomyopathy (CVS-35).
mimic: Myocarditis vs inflammatory cardiomyopathy
Myocarditis is the inflammation; inflammatory cardiomyopathy is the same inflammation with ventricular dysfunction.
traps: “Myocarditis is diagnosed when troponin rises after a viral illness with normal coronaries”
That is clinically suspected myocarditis (CVS-44); the definition needs tissue (or, since ESC 2025, confirmatory CMR).
decode: [pattern] Myocarditis with LV dysfunction — WHO term?
Inflammatory cardiomyopathy.
CVS-28.punch: Myocarditis is a tissue diagnosis: inflammation next to non-ischaemic myocyte injury. Add ventricular dysfunction and it becomes inflammatory cardiomyopathy.

CVS-29.intro: Step 1 continues with counting. Ordinary histology (Dallas) misses patchy or low-grade inflammation, so immunohistochemistry stains and counts the immune cells per area.
why: **At least 14 leukocytes/mm² in the myocardium.** Staining for CD45 makes scattered leukocytes visible that light microscopy misses; a count, unlike a pattern, can be compared between pathologists.

**Including up to 4 monocytes/mm².** Macrophages normally live in the myocardium, so resident cells alone could reach a count; capping the monocyte/macrophage share at 4 makes sure most of the infiltrate is lymphocytic, the cell type of immune injury.

**7 or more CD3-positive T lymphocytes (per mm²).** T cells are the effectors of the adaptive phase (CVS-35); requiring them makes the count specific for active inflammation. These are the ESC 2013 immunohistochemical criteria; the Dallas criteria (1986) are the histological ones on CVS-28.
mimic: Dallas vs immunohistochemical criteria
Dallas: infiltrate plus non-ischaemic myocyte necrosis on H&E, insensitive because of sampling error. Immunohistochemical: ≥14 leukocytes/mm² with ≤4 monocytes and ≥7 CD3+ T cells/mm².
traps: “The Dallas criteria are the immunohistochemical counts”
Dallas is histological (infiltrate plus necrosis); the 14/4/7 counts are the ESC 2013 immunohistochemical criteria.
decode: [pattern] Immunohistochemical threshold for myocarditis on EMB?
≥14 leukocytes/mm², up to 4 monocytes/mm², with ≥7 CD3+ T cells/mm².
CVS-29.punch: Fourteen leukocytes per mm², no more than four of them monocytes, and at least seven CD3+ T cells: these are the immunohistochemical criteria, not Dallas, which is the older histological definition.

CVS-30.intro: Step 1 ends with the split that decides treatment. The same biopsy that proves inflammation is tested for viral genome by PCR.
why: **Viral: histological myocarditis with positive viral PCR.** The virus is still in the myocardium, so suppressing immunity would let it replicate; antiviral or supportive treatment is the route (CVS-45).

**Autoimmune: negative viral PCR, with or without serum cardiac autoantibodies.** The inflammation continues without a virus, so it is driven by the immune system itself, the group in which immunosuppression is considered (CVS-47).
**Viral and immune: both positive.** Virus present and autoantibodies present; this mixed group is not a candidate for immunosuppression until the virus is dealt with.
mimic: Autoimmune myocarditis vs viral myocarditis with autoantibodies
The PCR decides: autoantibodies with a positive PCR is viral-and-immune, not autoimmune.
traps: “Positive autoantibodies alone justify steroids”
Only if the viral PCR on biopsy is negative (CVS-43c).
decode: [pattern] Biopsy-proven lymphocytic myocarditis, PCR negative — subtype and therapy considered?
Autoimmune; immunosuppression may be considered.
CVS-30.punch: The PCR on the biopsy decides: positive means viral and no immunosuppression; negative means autoimmune, the only group where it is considered.

CVS-31.sub: Myocarditis → Epidemiology → Incidence, sudden death, outcome
CVS-31.intro: Step 1 sizes the problem. Most cases are mild and never biopsied, which is why every figure here is uncertain, as the card itself says.
why: **22 per 100,000 annually in western countries.** This is the Global Burden of Disease estimate; subclinical cases are missed, so the true figure is higher.

**1–5% of sudden cardiac death in athletes.** Exercise during active inflammation raises arrhythmia risk, the reason for exercise restriction after myocarditis (ESC 2025: initially 1 month, then individualised; AHA 2020: 3–6 months for competitive sport). Published figures vary widely with the population and the autopsy method: reviews of athlete series quote roughly 5–20%, while a recent UK community registry found myocarditis in only about 1% of all sudden cardiac deaths, so the card’s figure sits at the low end.

**8.6% of sudden cardiac death in young adults.** This is an autopsy figure (quoted in the Mayo Clinic review of viral myocarditis, 2009); autopsy series select the fatal end of the spectrum, and the ESC 2013 position statement gives a range of 2–42% across autopsy studies of young sudden death.

**10–40% of idiopathic cardiomyopathy.** Many ‘idiopathic’ dilated cardiomyopathies are the late phase of myocarditis (CVS-35, phase 3). The share depends on how inflammation is counted: ESC 2013 puts biopsy-proven myocarditis at 9–16% of adults with unexplained non-ischaemic DCM (and 46% of children with an identified cause); higher figures come from immunohistochemical inflammation or viral genome detection.

**79% transplant-free at 1 year; 56% at 5 years.** These come from 112 consecutive patients with biopsy-proven myocarditis (Magnani, Am Heart J 2006): once myocarditis is severe enough to be biopsied, outcome is poor. The Myocarditis Treatment Trial cohort (CVS-47) was similar, with mortality 20% at 1 year and 56% at 4.3 years. Biventricular dysfunction is the strongest adverse predictor.
traps: “Myocarditis is benign because most patients recover”
Mild cases do; biopsy-proven myocarditis with dysfunction has roughly half survival free of transplant at 5 years.
decode: [pattern] Proportion of sudden cardiac death in young adults due to myocarditis?
About 8.6% (autopsy series).
CVS-31.punch: About 22 per 100,000 a year, around one in twelve young sudden deaths, and a large share of ‘idiopathic’ DCM; once it causes dysfunction, only about half are alive without transplant at 5 years.

CVS-32.intro: Step 2 opens with the causes. Viruses dominate, but bacteria, fungi, parasites and protozoa all inflame the myocardium, and the three real questions test the breadth of this list rather than the detail.
why: **Viral: adenoviruses, enteroviruses (coxsackievirus), herpes viruses (HHV-6, EBV), HCV, HIV, influenza A, parvovirus B19.** Coxsackie B and adenovirus enter myocytes through the coxsackie-adenovirus receptor and lyse them directly; parvovirus B19 infects the endothelium of small vessels, so it injures the muscle indirectly. Influenza (and SARS-CoV-2) myocarditis can present with shock and a low ejection fraction in a patient whose lungs are clear (CVS-38).

**Bacterial: Borrelia, Mycobacterium, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, streptococcal species, Treponema pallidum.** Borrelia (Lyme carditis) typically causes AV block. Diphtheria and Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) belong here too: diphtheria toxin causes myocarditis with conduction block and is the leading cause of death in diphtheria.
**Fungal: Aspergillus, Candida, Coccidioides, Cryptococcus, Histoplasma.** Mostly in the immunocompromised, as part of disseminated infection.
**Parasitic: larva migrans, schistosomiasis.** Helminths provoke an eosinophilic infiltrate.

**Protozoal: Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas disease).** Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy causes conduction disease (right bundle branch block, AV block), apical aneurysm and ventricular arrhythmia; Toxoplasma is another protozoal cause in the immunocompromised.
mimic: Influenza myocarditis vs ACS
Influenza myocarditis: febrile illness, troponin rise, global dysfunction, clean lungs and, if done, normal coronaries; ACS: risk factors, territorial ECG changes and wall-motion defect.
Viral myocarditis vs bacterial endocarditis
Endocarditis is a valve infection: persistent bacteraemia, a vegetation and a new regurgitant murmur; myocarditis has none of these.
traps: “Influenza with hypotension and a low EF — ACS” (31% missed the key)
With no infiltrates and a confirmed influenza infection, the troponin and global dysfunction are influenza myocarditis; ACS needs an ischaemic story and territorial changes.
“Diphtheria or Q fever do not cause myocarditis”
Both do; diphtheria toxin myocarditis with heart block is the commonest cause of death in diphtheria, so ‘all of the above’ was right.
“EBV is the most likely virus after a flu-like illness”
EBV is a recognised cause, but the classic textbook answer for the commonest viral cause is coxsackie B (CVS-34).
decode: Confirmed influenza, hypotension, raised troponin, low EF, no infiltrates — diagnosis? [DocT GT, 69% right]
Influenza myocarditis: clean lungs exclude influenza pneumonia as the cause of shock; the heart is the failing organ.
Young man, flu-like illness, diffuse ST changes, raised troponin — most likely virus? [DocT GT, 85% right]
Coxsackie B.
Coxsackie, diphtheria, Q fever — which cause inflammatory myocarditis? [DocT GT, 89% right]
All of them.
CVS-32.punch: Almost any infection can inflame the heart: coxsackie B is the classic virus, influenza causes shock with clear lungs, diphtheria and Lyme cause heart block, and Chagas is the protozoal cause.

CVS-33.intro: Step 2 continues with the non-infectious causes. They matter because some are treated by stopping a drug and others by immunosuppression.
why: **Toxins: anthracyclines, cocaine, interleukin-2.** Direct myocyte toxicity or, for cocaine, catecholamine injury and vasospasm. Immune checkpoint inhibitors are now an important addition: their myocarditis is often fulminant and is treated with high-dose steroids.

**Hypersensitivity: cephalosporins, digoxin, diuretics, dobutamine, sulfonamides, tricyclic antidepressants.** A drug allergy with an eosinophilic infiltrate (CVS-43d); suspect it with rash, fever and blood eosinophilia, stop the drug, and give steroids. Dobutamine infused for days can itself cause it, a trap in the ICU patient whose heart worsens on inotropes.

**Immunological: Churg–Strauss, diabetes mellitus, inflammatory bowel disease, giant cell myocarditis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, sarcoidosis, SLE, Takayasu arteritis, thyrotoxicosis.** Most are systemic immune-mediated diseases that inflame the myocardium without a virus; giant-cell myocarditis, sarcoid and the vasculitis or connective-tissue forms are the group where immunosuppression has a role (CVS-47). Thyrotoxicosis and diabetes sit on the list as associations, not as indications for immune therapy.
mimic: Hypersensitivity vs giant-cell myocarditis
Hypersensitivity: drug exposure, rash, eosinophils, responds to stopping the drug. Giant-cell: young adult, rapidly progressive failure, VT and heart block, needs combined immunosuppression.
traps: “Worsening heart failure on dobutamine is always disease progression”
Prolonged dobutamine can cause eosinophilic hypersensitivity myocarditis.
decode: [pattern] Which drug used in the ICU can cause hypersensitivity myocarditis?
Dobutamine (also cephalosporins, sulfonamides, diuretics).
CVS-33.punch: Toxins injure directly, drugs cause an eosinophilic allergy that stops when the drug stops, and systemic immune diseases cause the virus-negative forms that immunosuppression can treat.

CVS-34.intro: Step 2 then shows that the viruses found in biopsies have changed with time and place, which is why exam answers and current biopsy series can disagree.
why: **1948 coxsackie B/A → 1950s enterovirus → 1990s adenovirus → 2000 parvovirus B19/HHV-6 → 2007 HCV/EBV; enterovirus myocarditis declining, non-enterovirus rising.** Part of the shift is real, and part reflects better PCR detection of genomes that persist in tissue.

**Japan: hepatitis C commoner, 4.4%.** In the Japanese multicentre survey (Matsumori 1998) HCV antibody was commoner in patients with heart muscle disease than in blood donors (2.4%), reaching 10.6% in HCM and 6.3% in DCM. HCV genome has also been found in the myocardium, so it is a real cardiotropic virus in Japan, not a chance finding.
**Europe: parvovirus B19 most common.** Parvovirus B19 is found in many biopsies, including those of people without heart disease, so its presence alone does not prove it caused the myocarditis.

**India: hepatitis E case reports; adenovirus loads significantly higher than in the normal population in DCM.** The Indian evidence is small series and case reports; a higher viral load in DCM hearts than in controls suggests a causal role but does not prove it, since low-level genomes are also found in normal hearts.

**Kandolf series (n 3219): 46% virus positive, 54% negative.** About half of biopsies carry no virus, the group in which autoimmune disease is considered (CVS-30). Even a positive PCR needs interpretation: low copy numbers of parvovirus B19 are common in hearts without myocarditis.
mimic: Classic textbook virus vs current biopsy virus
Exam questions on the ‘most likely viral cause’ expect coxsackie B; questions on current European biopsy data expect parvovirus B19 (and HHV-6).
traps: “Parvovirus B19 is the answer to ‘most likely viral cause’ in a young man after a flu-like illness”
The DocT key is coxsackie B (85% right); parvovirus B19 is the commonest genome in European biopsy series, a different question.
decode: Young man, flu-like illness, diffuse ST changes, raised troponin — most likely virus? [DocT GT, 85% right]
Coxsackie B, the classic enterovirus cause.
[pattern] Commonest virus in European endomyocardial biopsy series?
Parvovirus B19.
CVS-34.punch: Coxsackie B is the classic answer, but modern European biopsies most often show parvovirus B19 and HHV-6, and about half are virus-negative.

CVS-35.intro: Step 2 ends with the time course, which explains both the presentations and why treatment depends on timing.
why: **Phase 1, minutes–hours to 1–7 days: viral entry through CAR and DAF, innate immune activation, active replication and myocyte lysis.** The coxsackie-adenovirus receptor (CAR) with its co-receptor decay-accelerating factor (DAF) lets the virus in; damage now is direct viral lysis, so this is when antivirals would make sense and immunosuppression would be dangerous.
