**Phase 2, 1–4 weeks: adaptive immune response with cytokines, chemokines and T-cell-mediated clearance and myocardial injury.** T cells kill infected myocytes, and cross-reactive autoimmunity can injure uninfected ones; this is when the patient presents, 1–4 weeks after the viral illness (CVS-36).

**Phase 3, months to years: resolution (viral clearance, normal LV function) or dilated cardiomyopathy (chronic inflammation, fibrosis, remodelling).** Persistent virus or persistent autoimmunity keeps the injury going and the ventricle dilates; this is why some ‘idiopathic’ DCM is old myocarditis (CVS-31).
mimic: Phase 1 vs phase 2 injury
Phase 1: the virus lyses myocytes. Phase 2: the immune response does, which is what immune therapy targets once the virus is gone.
traps: “Steroids early in viral myocarditis limit the damage”
In phase 1 the virus is replicating; suppressing immunity can increase viral injury. Immunosuppression needs a virus-negative biopsy (CVS-43c).
decode: [pattern] Receptor used by coxsackie B virus to enter cardiomyocytes?
The coxsackie-adenovirus receptor (CAR), with DAF as co-receptor.
CVS-35.punch: Days of viral lysis, weeks of immune injury, then recovery or dilated cardiomyopathy; the phase decides whether the target is the virus or the immune response.

CVS-36.intro: Step 3 describes the commonest picture in a young adult: chest pain, ST changes and troponin, as if this were an infarct.
why: **Acute chest pain mimicking ACS, 1–4 weeks after a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection.** The delay matches phase 2 (CVS-35), when the immune response injures the myocardium; pain may be pleuritic when the pericardium is also inflamed.

**No angiographic evidence of CAD.** Clean coronaries (or CT coronary angiography) turn ‘ACS’ into MINOCA, whose commonest cause in the young is myocarditis; CMR then separates it from takotsubo and small infarcts.
**ST/T wave changes.** Often diffuse, without reciprocal depression (CVS-40), but they can mimic STEMI.
**With or without normal or regional/global LV and/or RV dysfunction on echo or CMR.** Wall-motion abnormalities do not follow coronary territories.

**With or without raised TnT/TnI.** Troponin reflects ongoing myocyte necrosis and is raised in most ACS-like cases; its height does not separate myocarditis from infarction, which is why the coronaries and CMR decide.
mimic: Myocarditis vs STEMI
Myocarditis: viral prodrome, young, diffuse ST change without reciprocity, normal coronaries, non-ischaemic LGE. STEMI: territorial change, reciprocal depression, an occluded artery.
traps: “Normal coronaries and raised troponin exclude a cardiac cause”
They point to myocarditis (or another MINOCA cause); CMR is the next test.
decode: [pattern] Young man, chest pain 2 weeks after diarrhoea, ST elevation, troponin up, normal angiogram — diagnosis?
Acute myocarditis (ACS-like presentation).
CVS-36.punch: A coronary-looking presentation one to four weeks after a viral illness, with clean coronaries: that is ACS-like myocarditis, and CMR is the next step.

CVS-37.intro: Step 3 continues with the second picture: heart failure arriving over weeks after an infection. The one real question gave a teenager with a flu-like illness, raised troponin and pulmonary oedema.
why: **New or progressive heart failure over 2 weeks to 3 months (DCM).** The window is the adaptive phase running into early remodelling; the ventricle may already be dilated.

**Impaired LV and/or RV systolic function, with or without increased wall thickness, with or without dilated LV/RV.** Thick walls with a normal-sized LV mean oedema in acute or fulminant disease; a dilated, thin ventricle means longer-standing disease.
**Symptoms after a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection.** The prodrome is the clue that separates it from other new cardiomyopathy.

**Non-specific ECG signs, bundle branch block, AV block (D/D diphtheria, Chagas) and/or ventricular arrhythmias (D/D giant cell, lymphocytic myocarditis).** AV block in myocarditis points to diphtheria, Chagas, Lyme or sarcoid; new VT with failure points to giant-cell myocarditis, and both are reasons to biopsy (CVS-43).
mimic: Myocarditis vs peripartum or tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy
Myocarditis: viral prodrome, troponin rise, non-ischaemic LGE with oedema on CMR. The others lack the inflammatory signal.
traps: “Pulmonary oedema with troponin in a teenager means MI”
After a flu-like illness, with no risk factors, it is acute myocarditis presenting as heart failure.
decode: Teenager, flu-like illness, raised troponin, pulmonary oedema — diagnosis? [Marrow]
Acute myocarditis: heart failure after a respiratory or GI infection.
[pattern] Heart failure over 6 weeks with new VT and heart block in a young adult — suspect?
Giant-cell myocarditis (or cardiac sarcoid); biopsy.
CVS-37.punch: New heart failure over weeks after a viral illness is myocarditis until proven otherwise; heart block or VT in that setting points to giant-cell myocarditis, sarcoid or Chagas and calls for biopsy.

CVS-38.intro: Step 3 ends at the two extremes: the patient who arrives in shock or arrest, and the one found by chance. The real question was the shock end, triggered by influenza.
why: **Life-threatening arrhythmia and aborted sudden death; cardiogenic shock; severely impaired LV function.** This is fulminant myocarditis (ESC 2025: myocarditis with cardiogenic shock). Diffuse oedema stiffens and stuns the whole ventricle at once, so output falls within hours; the walls look thick and the LV is not dilated. An older series (McCarthy, NEJM 2000) found excellent long-term survival after fulminant lymphocytic myocarditis; newer cohorts (Ammirati, Circulation 2017 and 2019) show that fulminant disease carries more death and transplant than non-fulminant, but ventricular function often recovers in those who are supported through the acute phase, which is why mechanical support as a bridge is worth it (CVS-46).
**Asymptomatic: troponin I raised, coronary angiogram normal, echo showing varying LV function.** Found during screening or after a viral illness; still needs CMR and follow-up because some progress.
mimic: Fulminant myocarditis vs septic cardiomyopathy

Septic cardiomyopathy: an infective source with vasodilatory shock and a dilated, recovering LV. Fulminant myocarditis: a viral prodrome, very high troponin, thick oedematous walls, low output and cold peripheries.
Fulminant myocarditis vs pulmonary embolism
PE: a dilated RV with a small LV, hypoxaemia and normal LV function. Myocarditis: global LV failure.
traps: “Influenza with hypotension and a low EF — ACS” (31% missed the key)
Influenza can cause fulminant myocarditis; global dysfunction after a viral illness with clean lungs is myocarditis, not plaque rupture.
decode: Confirmed influenza, hypotension, raised troponin, reduced EF, no pulmonary infiltrates — diagnosis? [DocT GT, 69% right]
Influenza myocarditis (life-threatening presentation).
CVS-38.punch: Fulminant myocarditis is cardiogenic shock from a thick, oedematous, stunned ventricle; it is more dangerous than non-fulminant disease but can recover, so support it. Influenza is a classic trigger.

CVS-39.intro: Step 4 starts with the blood tests. None proves myocarditis; each answers a narrower question.
why: **Inflammation: ESR, CRP, WBC, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-10.** They show that inflammation is present somewhere, not that it is in the heart; a normal CRP does not exclude myocarditis.

**Cardiac biomarkers: troponin / CK-MB.** Troponin shows myocyte injury, is raised in most cases and supports the diagnosis, but is not specific; a normal troponin makes acute myocarditis less likely.

**Viral serology: limited diagnostic value (HIV, hepatitis C).** Antibodies to common cardiotropic viruses are frequent in the population and do not show that the virus is in the heart, so ESC 2025 advises against routine serology; HIV and hepatitis C are the exceptions because they change management.

**Cardiac autoantibodies: no viral genome on EMB with positive autoantibodies = autoimmune myocarditis, which identifies the patient for immunosuppression.** The autoantibodies support an immune mechanism, but the negative viral PCR on tissue is the condition that makes immunosuppression safe (CVS-43c).
traps: “A positive coxsackie antibody titre confirms viral myocarditis”
Serology does not localise the virus to the heart; PCR on biopsy tissue does.
decode: [pattern] Role of viral serology in suspected myocarditis?
Limited; not routinely recommended except HIV and hepatitis C.
CVS-39.punch: Troponin shows injury, CRP shows inflammation, serology shows little; only a biopsy with negative viral PCR and positive autoantibodies identifies the patient for immunosuppression.

CVS-40.intro: Step 4 continues with the ECG: cheap and almost always abnormal in some way, but not specific and not sensitive enough to rule myocarditis out. The one real question tested exactly that.
why: **Role: a screening tool.** It is done in everyone, but its changes are non-specific and a normal ECG does not exclude myocarditis; it raises suspicion, it does not decide.
**Sinus tachycardia is the most common finding.** It reflects fever, pain and a falling stroke volume, and is the least specific finding of all.

**ST-T changes without reciprocation; LV strain; QRS and QT prolongation; AV conduction block and ventricular arrhythmias.** Inflammation is patchy and epicardial, so ST changes are diffuse without a reciprocal territory, as in pericarditis (CVS-08); fulminant disease may show low voltage from oedema. Block and VT suggest giant-cell myocarditis, sarcoid or Lyme (CVS-37).

**Bad prognosis: QTc >440 ms, ventricular arrhythmia, QRS >120 ms.** A wide QRS means inflammation and fibrosis in the conducting tissue and was an independent predictor of death or transplant in biopsy-proven myocarditis.
mimic: Myocarditis vs STEMI on the ECG
Myocarditis: diffuse ST change without reciprocity and often sinus tachycardia. STEMI: territorial elevation with reciprocal depression (CVS-08).
traps: “The ECG is sensitive for myocarditis”
False: it is often abnormal but non-specifically, and a normal ECG does not exclude it. Troponin is also more specific than sensitive, so CMR or biopsy confirms.
decode: Myocarditis statements — which is false? [Marrow]
‘The ECG is sensitive’: it is non-specific and insensitive, a screening test only.
[pattern] ECG features of poor prognosis in myocarditis?
QRS >120 ms, QTc >440 ms, ventricular arrhythmia.
CVS-40.punch: The ECG in myocarditis is usually abnormal but non-specific: sinus tachycardia and diffuse ST-T changes without reciprocity. It screens, it cannot exclude, and a wide QRS predicts a bad outcome.

CVS-41.intro: Step 4 adds echo, which cannot see inflammation but excludes other causes and finds the dangerous signs.
why: **Its primary role is to rule out other causes of heart failure.** Valve disease, hypertrophic or restrictive cardiomyopathy, tamponade and territorial wall-motion defects of infarction are all seen at the bedside.
**Regional or global LV and/or RV dysfunction.** In fulminant disease the walls are thick from oedema and the LV is not dilated; in subacute disease the LV is dilated.

**Done before EMB to exclude pericardial effusion and intracavitary thrombi.** Perforation is the main biopsy complication and a pre-existing effusion would hide or worsen it; a thrombus in the ventricle could embolise when the bioptome passes.
**RV dysfunction: poor prognosis.** Biventricular failure means more extensive disease and is the strongest predictor of death or transplant (ESC 2025, AHA 2020).

**Coronary angiography must be done to rule out ACS.** Echo cannot tell an infarct from myocarditis when dysfunction is regional; an angiogram (or CT coronary angiography in low-risk patients) excludes coronary disease, a condition of the diagnosis (CVS-44d).
traps: “Echo can confirm myocarditis”
It cannot characterise tissue; CMR or biopsy does (CVS-42, 43).
decode: [pattern] Echo finding of worst prognosis in myocarditis?
RV dysfunction (biventricular failure).
CVS-41.punch: Echo excludes other causes and an effusion before biopsy, and finds RV dysfunction, the worst prognostic sign; coronary angiography must still exclude ACS.

CVS-42.intro: Step 4 reaches the test that sees the tissue without a biopsy. The real question asked when CMR works best and what it can and cannot tell, and half the cohort got it wrong.
why: **Performed in symptomatic patients with clinical suspicion of myocarditis.** ESC 2025 makes CMR the non-invasive cornerstone and accepts a compatible presentation with positive CMR as definite myocarditis. Yield is highest when it is done after about the first week (ideally within 2–3 weeks), when oedema, hyperaemia and LGE are all present; very early or late scans miss oedema.

**Three markers of tissue injury: intracellular and interstitial oedema, hyperaemia and capillary leakage, necrosis and fibrosis.** These are the 2009 Lake Louise markers (T2 oedema, early gadolinium enhancement, LGE), two of three positive; sensitivity 67%, specificity 91%. The 2018 update needs one T2-based criterion (oedema) and one T1-based criterion (native T1, extracellular volume or non-ischaemic LGE), drops early enhancement, and is more accurate (sensitivity about 88%, specificity about 96%).

**Late gadolinium enhancement of myocardial pattern.** The pattern is non-ischaemic: patchy, subepicardial or mid-wall, typically inferolateral or septal, sparing the subendocardium. An infarct starts at the subendocardium and follows a territory, so the location separates the two; it does not name the virus or the type of myocarditis.
mimic: Myocarditis LGE vs infarct LGE
Myocarditis: subepicardial or mid-wall, patchy, inferolateral or septal. Infarct: subendocardial or transmural, in a coronary territory.
traps: “The location of LGE confirms a viral aetiology”
CMR cannot tell viral from non-viral or name the histology; that needs biopsy with PCR.
“CMR replaces endomyocardial biopsy”
Not when giant-cell, eosinophilic or fulminant myocarditis is suspected, or before immunosuppression; histology and PCR decide treatment.
“LGE extent does not predict events; LVEF does” (DocT’s explanation for rejecting option C)

DocT’s key is ‘sensitivity highest after 7 days’ and its explanation names LVEF, not LGE, as the prognostic marker. That is dated: LGE presence and extent, especially mid-wall septal LGE, independently predict events (ITAMY; ESC 2025). In a DocT paper pick ‘after 7 days’; in a newer paper LGE extent is also correct.
decode: Suspected myocarditis, subepicardial inferolateral LGE — which statement on CMR is correct? [DocT GT, 50% right]
Key: sensitivity highest after about 7 days from onset. LGE extent predicting events is also true by current evidence; LGE location does not identify the virus, and CMR does not replace biopsy.
[pattern] 2018 Lake Louise criteria for myocarditis?
One T2-based (oedema) plus one T1-based (T1 mapping, ECV or non-ischaemic LGE) criterion.
CVS-42.punch: CMR shows oedema and patchy subepicardial or mid-wall LGE; the 2018 Lake Louise criteria need one T2 and one T1 marker, yield is best after the first week, and the extent of LGE carries prognosis, but it cannot name the cause.

CVS-43.intro: Step 4 ends with the gold standard. Biopsy is invasive and samples only a few millimetres, so the questions are when to do it and what each pattern means.
why: **Gold standard for the diagnosis of myocarditis.** It is the only test that names the histological type and detects viral genome; its weakness is sampling error, because inflammation is patchy. Taking several samples from both ventricles, or guided by CMR or mapping, improves yield.

**It identifies the specific aetiology, so treatment can be tailored, and it is the basis for starting immunosuppression.** Giant-cell, eosinophilic and sarcoid myocarditis are treated with immunosuppression; lymphocytic viral myocarditis is not. ESC 2025 advises biopsy in acute heart failure or cardiogenic shock, malignant arrhythmia or conduction disease, LVEF <40%, extensive acute LGE, suspected giant-cell myocarditis or sarcoid, and failure to respond to treatment. The AHA (Cooper 2007) list is new unexplained heart failure under 2 weeks with haemodynamic compromise; 2 weeks to 3 months with a dilated LV and new ventricular arrhythmia, Mobitz II or complete block, or no response in 1–2 weeks; and heart failure with rash, fever or eosinophilia, connective-tissue disease, suspected infiltrative disease or suspected giant-cell myocarditis.
**Immunosuppression only after active infection has been ruled out by PCR on the biopsy.** Suppressing immunity while the virus replicates removes the defence that limits myocyte lysis (CVS-35).

**Lymphocytic: viral or autoimmune; neutrophilic: bacterial, fungal or early viral; eosinophilic: hypersensitivity or hypereosinophilic syndrome; granulomatous: sarcoidosis; giant cells: giant-cell myocarditis.** Giant cells with extensive myocyte necrosis and no well-formed granulomas mean giant-cell myocarditis; non-caseating granulomas with less necrosis mean sarcoid.
mimic: Giant-cell myocarditis vs cardiac sarcoid

Both cause VT and heart block. Giant-cell: younger, faster, diffuse necrosis with giant cells and no granulomas, worse survival. Sarcoid: non-caseating granulomas, extracardiac disease, slower course.
traps: “Giant-cell myocarditis gets supportive care, as viral myocarditis does”

It is the one myocarditis where combined immunosuppression (steroid plus cyclosporine, with or without azathioprine) is life-saving; refractory VT and shock are typical, so plan early mechanical support or transplant.
“Failure of EF to improve after optimal heart failure therapy is not an indication for EMB” (Marrow’s key)

The key is disputed. Marrow’s source table lists worsening EF despite therapy but not failure to improve. The AHA/ACC/ESC 2007 statement itself makes failure to respond to usual care within 1–2 weeks a Class I indication (heart failure of 2 weeks to 3 months with a dilated LV), ESC (CVS-45) sends LV dysfunction persisting after 3 months of therapy to biopsy, and ESC 2025 lists failure to respond. In Marrow’s question pick its key; in any guideline-based question it is an indication.
decode: Cardiogenic shock with refractory VT; biopsy shows multinucleated giant cells and extensive necrosis — management priority? [DocT GT]
High-dose combined immunosuppression and early consideration of mechanical support or transplant.
Indications for endomyocardial biopsy — which is incorrect? [Marrow]

Marrow keys ‘no EF improvement after optimal HF therapy’; refractory HF, new block or VT, eosinophilia, CTD, infiltrative disease and suspected giant-cell are the classic indications. By AHA 2007 and ESC, failure to respond is also an indication, so the key is disputed.
CVS-43.punch: Biopsy names the type and the virus, and only a virus-negative biopsy licenses immunosuppression; giant cells with necrosis mean giant-cell myocarditis, the form that needs immediate combined immunosuppression and early mechanical support.

Usual cause
Treatment it points to
rows: Combined immunosuppression; early MCS or transplant

CVS-44.sub: Myocarditis → Diagnosis → ESC clinically suspected myocarditis
CVS-44.intro: Step 4 pulls the tests together. Since most patients are never biopsied, ESC defined when myocarditis is clinically suspected, the trigger for further work-up.
why: **Acute chest pain (pericarditic or pseudo-ischaemic); new or worsening heart failure; subacute or chronic heart failure; palpitations or syncope; cardiogenic shock.** The three syndromes of CVS-36 to 38, with arrhythmia added.

**ECG/Holter/stress test features; raised troponin; functional and structural abnormalities on imaging; tissue characterisation by CMR.** Each criterion is a different kind of evidence: electrical, biochemical, mechanical and tissue.

**Diagnosis if >1 presentation AND >1 criterion, or >2 criteria.** The ESC 2013 wording is ‘≥1’ presentation with ‘≥1’ criterion from different categories, or, in an asymptomatic patient, ‘≥2’ criteria. One clinical feature with one objective test is enough to suspect it.

**In the absence of CAD or pre-existing heart disease.** Specifically no angiographic stenosis of 50% or more and no known cardiovascular or extracardiac cause that explains the picture. ESC 2025 now calls myocarditis definite when a compatible presentation is confirmed by CMR (2018 Lake Louise) or biopsy, and lower-certainty findings possible.
traps: “Two clinical presentations are needed”
One presentation with one diagnostic criterion is enough; two criteria are needed only when the patient is asymptomatic.
decode: [pattern] Asymptomatic patient — how many ESC criteria for clinically suspected myocarditis?
Two or more.
CVS-44.punch: One clinical presentation plus one objective criterion, or two criteria if asymptomatic, with coronary disease excluded: that is clinically suspected myocarditis, which CMR or biopsy then confirms.

CVS-45.intro: Step 5 turns the diagnosis into a route. The branch point is haemodynamics, because an unstable patient needs a tissue answer fast.
why: **First, exclude coronary artery disease where appropriate.** The commonest cause of troponin with dysfunction is still an infarct; angiography or CT coronary angiography removes it.
**Haemodynamically stable: cardiac MRI.** CMR confirms the diagnosis without risk, and most stable patients do well with supportive care.

**Haemodynamically unstable: EMB.** Shock or malignant arrhythmia raises the chance of giant-cell, eosinophilic or fulminant necrotising forms that need specific treatment within days; CMR is often impossible in such patients anyway.
**Normal LV function: supportive care.** Rest from exercise, symptom relief (ESC 2025: paracetamol, aspirin or NSAID, with colchicine if pericarditic symptoms) and follow-up.

**LV dysfunction: neurohormonal antagonists.** Standard heart-failure therapy (ACE inhibitor or ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor). If dysfunction persists despite 3 months of optimal therapy, biopsy; virus-negative lymphocytic myocarditis may then get immunosuppression, virus-positive antiviral therapy.
mimic: Stable vs unstable branch
Stable: CMR then heart-failure therapy. Unstable: biopsy because the histology changes treatment now.
traps: “Persistent LV dysfunction after 3 months of optimal therapy is never a biopsy indication” (Marrow’s key)
In the ESC route it is, and the AHA/ACC/ESC 2007 statement also counts failure to respond to usual care as an indication; Marrow’s key is disputed (CVS-43). Pick it only in Marrow’s own question.
decode: Indications for endomyocardial biopsy — which is incorrect? [Marrow]
Marrow keys ‘no EF improvement after optimal HF therapy’; by this ESC route (and by AHA 2007), persistent dysfunction despite therapy is an indication, so the key is disputed.
[pattern] Suspected myocarditis, haemodynamically stable, coronaries normal — next investigation?
Cardiac MRI.
CVS-45.punch: Exclude coronary disease, then branch: stable patients get CMR and heart-failure therapy, unstable ones get a biopsy, and dysfunction that persists 3 months on therapy goes to biopsy to decide on immune or antiviral treatment.

CVS-46.intro: Step 5 continues with the unstable patient, the ICU part of the deck. Both real questions are the same scenario: shock that keeps worsening on drugs.
why: **Class IV shock with normal BP: vasodilators.** If pressure is preserved, lowering afterload (nitrates, nitroprusside) lets a weak ventricle eject more.

**Cardiogenic shock with low BP: inotropes and vasopressors.** Norepinephrine to hold perfusion pressure, dobutamine or milrinone for output; they buy time but raise myocardial oxygen demand and arrhythmia risk in an inflamed heart.
**Increased filling pressures: diuretics.** To relieve congestion once perfusion is secured.

**Refractory shock: IABP, ECMO, VAD.** Fulminant myocarditis can recover fully if the patient survives the acute weeks, so mechanical support is a bridge to recovery. VA-ECMO is the most used (SCAI D–E, biventricular failure); an IABP may be a first bridge in less severe shock; a microaxial LV pump (Impella) unloads the LV, alone or with ECMO; durable VADs are for no recovery.

**No recovery within 4 weeks: cardiac transplantation.** The guidelines give no fixed number of weeks: ESC 2013 says transplantation should be deferred in the acute phase because recovery may occur, and considered when the patient cannot be weaned from drug and mechanical support; ESC 2025 says refractory cases may need long-term MCS or transplant. The tension is the same: waiting too long on temporary support risks multiorgan failure and device complications, transplanting too early removes a heart that might have recovered. Giant-cell myocarditis rarely recovers, so it reaches transplant or durable support sooner (AHA 2020).
mimic: Fulminant myocarditis vs AMI shock on MCS
In myocarditis the injured muscle can recover, so MCS is a bridge to recovery; in AMI shock, scar is permanent and the route to durable support or transplant is commoner.
traps: “Switch dobutamine to milrinone and add vasopressin”
Changing drugs does not fix refractory shock (CI 1.8, lactate 5 on two agents); the next step is VA-ECMO.
“Pulse methylprednisolone for biopsy-proven viral myocarditis in shock”
Immunosuppression with virus present can worsen it; steroids are for virus-negative immune forms (CVS-47).
“Repeat the biopsy to see if inflammation has resolved”
A deteriorating patient needs support now, not more histology.
decode: Biopsy-proven viral myocarditis, CI 1.8, lactate 5, on high-dose dobutamine and norepinephrine, worsening — next step? [DocT GT]
VA-ECMO: mechanical support for shock refractory to drugs.
Fulminant myocarditis, ventilated, shock despite maximal inotropes — next step? [Marrow]

Mechanical circulatory support as a bridge to recovery (Marrow keys LVAD). In practice the first device is temporary, usually VA-ECMO with or without a microaxial LV pump; a durable LVAD comes only if the heart does not recover.
CVS-46.punch: When fulminant myocarditis stays in shock on two vasoactive drugs, go to mechanical support, usually VA-ECMO, because the heart may recover; transplant or durable support is for the heart that cannot be weaned, the card’s ‘4 weeks’ being a rule of thumb rather than a guideline cut-off.

CVS-47.intro: Step 6 asks when to treat the immune response itself. The negative trial explains the caution; the ESC list says where it is still used.
why: **Myocarditis Treatment Trial (NEJM 1995): 111 patients with myocarditis and LVEF <45%, randomised to conventional therapy alone or with 24 weeks of immunosuppression.** Prednisone with cyclosporine or azathioprine did not improve LVEF or survival; it included virus-positive and virus-negative patients alike, since PCR was not used. Later virus-negative trials (TIMIC: prednisone plus azathioprine for 6 months) did improve LVEF.

**Worsening heart failure despite standard treatment; giant-cell or eosinophilic myocarditis, sarcoidosis; myocarditis with autoimmune disease.** These are the virus-negative immune forms. ESC 2025 says immunosuppressants and corticosteroids should not be used as initial therapy; it reserves them for biopsy-proven or highly suspected immune forms (giant-cell, eosinophilic, sarcoid, autoimmune), fulminant non-infectious myocarditis (IIa C) and refractory ventricular dysfunction (IIb C).

**Started only after active infection has been ruled out on EMB by PCR.** Suppressing immunity while a virus replicates removes the defence that limits myocyte lysis. Patient selection is the likely reason the unselected MTT was negative while the virus-negative TIMIC was positive (CVS-30, 43).
mimic: Myocarditis Treatment Trial vs TIMIC
MTT: unselected histological myocarditis, no benefit. TIMIC: virus-negative inflammatory cardiomyopathy, LVEF improved.
traps: “The Myocarditis Treatment Trial showed immunosuppression improves LVEF”
It did not; benefit appears only when patients are selected by a negative viral PCR.
decode: [pattern] Absolute precondition before immunosuppression in myocarditis?
Active infection excluded by PCR on endomyocardial biopsy.
CVS-47.punch: Unselected immunosuppression failed in the Myocarditis Treatment Trial; it works only in virus-negative immune forms, above all giant-cell and eosinophilic myocarditis, so a negative PCR on biopsy comes first.

CVS-48.intro: Step 6 ends with IVIG, the immune therapy whose evidence points in two directions by age.
why: **IVIG 2 g/kg.** The same immunomodulatory dose as in Kawasaki disease, given over one to two days; it neutralises antibodies, blocks Fc receptors and dampens cytokines.

**In recent-onset dilated cardiomyopathy IVIG does not augment the improvement in LVEF.** In the IMAC trial both arms improved by a similar amount, because many recent-onset cases recover on standard therapy anyway.
**In small series of acute paediatric myocarditis IVIG has been effective.** Better recovery of LV function and a trend to survival, but uncontrolled and small.

**ESC: no recommendation for IVIG in adult myocarditis.** The ESC 2013 position statement says IVIG was ineffective in the IMAC trial and gives no recommendation for its use; the ESC 2025 guideline summaries do not list it among the treatments of myocarditis, so adults do not receive it routinely.
traps: “IVIG is standard in adult myocarditis because it works in children”
Adult evidence (IMAC) was negative; ESC makes no recommendation.
decode: [pattern] Role of IVIG in adult myocarditis per ESC?
No recommendation; the controlled trial in recent-onset DCM showed no added LVEF benefit.
CVS-48.punch: IVIG 2 g/kg helped in small paediatric series but added nothing to LVEF recovery in the adult trial, so ESC gives no recommendation for adults.

spine: What counts as myocarditis

Myocarditis is inflammation of the heart muscle proven by tissue: an infiltrate with non-ischaemic myocyte injury, counted by immunohistochemistry, and split by viral PCR into viral, autoimmune or both.
Causes and the three phases

Viruses (now parvovirus B19 and HHV-6 more than coxsackie) cause most cases; the virus injures myocytes in days, the immune response that clears it injures them for weeks, and months later the heart either recovers or dilates.
Three ways it presents
It looks like an ACS with clean coronaries, like new heart failure after a viral illness, or like sudden arrhythmia and shock.
Building the diagnosis
ECG and troponin raise the suspicion, echo and angiography exclude other causes, CMR shows oedema and non-ischaemic scar, and endomyocardial biopsy proves it and names the type.
Route by haemodynamics
Stable patients go to CMR and heart-failure therapy; unstable ones go to biopsy, inotropes and, when shock is refractory, mechanical support as a bridge to recovery or transplant.
Immune therapy only when virus-negative
Immunosuppression helps only proven virus-negative immune forms (giant-cell, eosinophilic, sarcoid, autoimmune), so a negative PCR on biopsy comes first; IVIG has no adult role.
CVS02.primer: Troponin rises whenever myocytes die, whatever the cause, so a raised troponin with normal coronary arteries points away from plaque rupture and towards myocarditis, takotsubo or other non-ischaemic injury. Cardiac MRI (CMR) reads tissue: T2-weighted images show water (oedema), T1 mapping and extracellular volume show expanded interstitium, and late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) shows contrast trapped in dead or scarred muscle. Ischaemic scar starts at the subendocardium and follows a coronary territory; inflammatory scar is patchy, subepicardial or mid-wall. Endomyocardial biopsy takes small pieces of right-ventricular septum through a vein for histology, immunohistochemistry and viral PCR.

CS-01.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Introduction → Aetiology, sex, associations
CS-01.intro: Step 2 is who gets cardiogenic shock. This card gives the broad picture: the three big sources of a failing pump and the comorbidities that tip a weak heart into shock. It has not been asked directly; the numbers on CS-14 carry the exam weight.
why: **Acute coronary syndrome and its complications, acute-on-chronic heart failure, and de novo heart failure (one third of cases).** ACS is the classic cause because it kills muscle suddenly. Modern cardiac ICU registries now see more heart-failure-related shock than infarct shock (about 59% vs 27% in the 2024 SHARC-definition registry), and in those the de novo share was about 28% of heart-failure shock, close to the card’s one third.
**Men (younger) more than women.** Men have infarcts earlier, so they reach shock younger; women who develop it are older and have more comorbidity.

**Anaemia, renal dysfunction, metabolic syndromes, COPD.** Each lowers oxygen delivery or reserve: anaemia cuts oxygen content, renal failure adds fluid and acidosis, COPD adds hypoxaemia and right-sided load. They are also the triggers that decompensate chronic heart failure (CS-24).
mimic: De novo vs acute-on-chronic heart failure shock
De novo has no prior cardiomyopathy (often a first infarct or myocarditis); acute-on-chronic is a known weak heart pushed over by infection, anaemia, arrhythmia or renal failure.
traps: “AMI is still the cause in most cardiogenic shock”
True in older series and still the exam’s default (CS-14), but contemporary cardiac ICU data show heart-failure-related shock is now the larger group.
decode: Commonest cause of cardiogenic shock [pattern]
Acute MI with LV failure — the exam answer, even though modern registries show heart-failure shock overtaking it.
CS-01.punch: Most cardiogenic shock still begins with a coronary event, but a known failing heart decompensated by infection, anaemia or renal failure is now just as common.

CS-02.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Definitions → Shock, cardiogenic shock, clinical definition
CS-02.intro: Step 1 is drawing the line around cardiogenic shock. Shock is a mismatch of oxygen supply and demand at the tissue level; cardiogenic shock is that mismatch caused by the heart; and the clinical definition demands proof on both the bedside and the laboratory side. The one real question tests the opposite end: recognising when there is no shock at all.
why: **Shock: inadequate organ perfusion to meet the tissues’ oxygen demand.** It is defined by the tissues, not by the blood pressure: a normal pressure with a rising lactate is shock, and a low pressure with normal perfusion may not be.

**Cardiogenic shock: critical end-organ hypoperfusion and hypoxia due to a primary cardiac disorder.** The word ‘primary’ separates it from septic myocardial depression, where the heart is a casualty of another process (CS-12).

**Clinical definition: a cardiac disorder producing BOTH clinical AND biochemical evidence of tissue hypoperfusion.** Cold, clammy skin or confusion alone can be anxiety or cold; a lactate alone can be adrenaline or liver failure. Requiring both raises specificity, which is why modern definitions (ESC 2021, SCAI) pair signs with lactate.
mimic: Cardiogenic shock vs decompensated heart failure
Both have a low output and high filling pressures; only shock has hypoperfusion (lactate, oliguria, confusion) — the point tested on CS-05.
traps: “Wheezing, tachycardia 100 and breathless — must be some form of shock”
BP 130/80 and CVP 6 with no sign of hypoperfusion is no shock at all; 90% got this right.
decode: Asthmatic, wheeze, BP 130/80, HR 100, CVP 6: haemodynamic status? [DocT QBank]
Acute asthma without shock — normal pressure, normal CVP, no hypoperfusion (90%).
CS-02.punch: Shock is a tissue diagnosis; cardiogenic shock is that tissue failure caused by the heart and proven by both signs and biochemistry.

CS-03.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Definitions → SHOCK trial criteria
CS-03.intro: Step 1 continues with the trial definitions. The SHOCK trial (1999) set the classic research definition, and it is the only one of the three that demands measured haemodynamics, so it is the one quoted when a stem gives a wedge pressure and a cardiac index.
why: **SBP <90 mmHg for ≥30 min.** Thirty minutes excludes the transient dip of a vagal reaction or a drug bolus.
**Or support needed to keep SBP ≥90 mmHg.** A patient already on norepinephrine with a ‘normal’ pressure still qualifies, because the drug is hiding the shock.
**Plus end-organ hypoperfusion: urine output <30 mL/h or cool extremities.** These are the bedside proofs that the low pressure is starving organs.

**Haemodynamic: CI ≤2.2 L/min/m² AND PCWP ≥15 mmHg.** The low index proves the pump is failing; the raised wedge proves the ventricle is full, so the problem is not hypovolaemia. Many textbooks quote a split threshold (CI <1.8 without support, <2.2 on support), but the trial itself used ≤2.2 and ≥15.
mimic: Cardiogenic vs hypovolaemic shock on a PA catheter
Both have a low CI and high SVR; the wedge is high in cardiogenic and low in hypovolaemic shock.
traps: “A low cardiac index alone defines cardiogenic shock”
Hypovolaemic and obstructive shock also have a low index; it is the combination with a high wedge that points to the left ventricle.
decode: Shock with elevated PCWP — which type? [Marrow]
Cardiogenic: PCWP ≥15 with CI ≤2.2 (SHOCK criteria).
Which definition carries haemodynamic criteria? [pattern]
Only the SHOCK trial; IABP-SHOCK II and ESC are clinical (CS-07).
CS-03.punch: SHOCK is the definition with numbers from the catheter: CI ≤2.2 with a wedge ≥15, on top of 30 minutes of hypotension and hypoperfusion.

CS-04.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Definitions → IABP-SHOCK II criteria
CS-04.intro: Step 1, the second trial definition. IABP-SHOCK II (2012, n 600) used a purely clinical definition that could be applied at the cath-lab door without a PA catheter, and it added two things SHOCK did not: pulmonary congestion and a lactate threshold.
why: **SBP <90 mmHg for ≥30 min.** The same pressure and duration as SHOCK.
**Or catecholamines needed to keep SBP >90 mmHg.** ‘Catecholamines’ rather than ‘support’: the drug, not a device, defines the alternative.
**Plus pulmonary congestion.** This replaces the wedge pressure: crackles or oedema on the film stand in for PCWP ≥15 and exclude the dry, hypovolaemic patient.

**Plus impaired end-organ perfusion: altered mental status, cold/clammy skin and extremities, urine output <30 mL/h, lactate >2.0 mmol/L.** Any one of the four suffices. The lactate threshold is the definition’s distinctive feature (CS-07).
mimic: IABP-SHOCK II vs SHOCK definition
IABP-SHOCK II asks for congestion and allows lactate >2; SHOCK asks for CI ≤2.2 and PCWP ≥15.
traps: “IABP-SHOCK II showed the balloon pump saves lives”
It did not: 30-day mortality 39.7% vs 41.3%, which is why routine IABP is now class III in ESC 2023 and the 2025 ACC/AHA guideline.
decode: Which definition includes lactate >2 mmol/L? [pattern]
IABP-SHOCK II only.
CS-04.punch: IABP-SHOCK II defines shock clinically — hypotension, congestion and one of four perfusion markers including lactate above 2 — and the trial itself found the balloon pump useless.

CS-05.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Definitions → ESC heart failure definition
CS-05.intro: Step 1, the guideline definition. The ESC heart failure guideline defines shock by hypoperfusion and lists its clinical and laboratory signs; the one real question asks what separates shock from simple heart failure, and fewer than half got it.
why: **SBP <90 mmHg with adequate volume, plus clinical or laboratory signs of hypoperfusion.** This is the ESC 2016 wording: volume must be adequate so that hypovolaemia is excluded first. ESC 2021 (following the 2020 HFA position statement) defines cardiogenic shock by hypoperfusion from primary cardiac dysfunction and no longer requires hypotension, because compensatory vasoconstriction or drugs can keep the pressure up while the tissues starve — normotensive cardiogenic shock (CS-31).

**Clinical hypoperfusion: cold extremities, oliguria, mental confusion, dizziness, narrow pulse pressure.** These are the signs ESC 2021 lists, and the laboratory three in part c are its list too; only the hypotension requirement has gone. Each is the body diverting flow away from skin, kidney and brain; a narrow pulse pressure reflects a small stroke volume.
**Laboratory hypoperfusion: metabolic acidosis, raised lactate, raised creatinine.** Lactate is the most direct marker of anaerobic metabolism and is the one used to stage shock (SCAI C: ≥2 mmol/L).
mimic: Cardiogenic shock vs acute decompensated heart failure
Both have a low CI and a high PCWP; only shock has hypoperfusion, so the lactate separates them.
traps: “A cardiac index under 2.2 or a wedge over 18 separates shock from heart failure”
Decompensated heart failure has the same numbers; 46% picked lactate. Hypoperfusion defines shock; the catheter numbers only say the pump is the cause.
“ESC still requires SBP <90”
That is the 2016 wording on the card; ESC 2021 accepts hypoperfusion without hypotension.
decode: Post-MI, CI 1.9, PCWP 19, oliguria, raised lactate: which finding separates shock from isolated HF? [DocT GT]
Elevated lactate — hypoperfusion (46%).
CS-05.punch: What turns heart failure into cardiogenic shock is hypoperfusion — a raised lactate, oliguria, confusion — not a lower cardiac index.

CS-06.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Diagnosis → Three clinical criteria
CS-06.intro: Step 1 at the bedside: in practice the diagnosis rests on three things — persistent hypotension, no response to fluid and proven hypoperfusion. The one real question flips the CS-05 logic: here the shock is already established, and it asks what proves the heart is the cause.
why: **Persistent hypotension: SBP <90 mmHg.** Persistent means sustained (the trials used 30 minutes), not a single reading.
**No adequate response to volume resuscitation.** Fluid unresponsiveness separates the empty circulation (which recovers with fluid) from the failing pump (which does not, and may get worse).
**End-organ hypoperfusion, clinical AND biochemical.** As on CS-02, both are needed.
mimic: “Is this shock?” vs “Is this shock cardiogenic?”
The first is answered by hypoperfusion (lactate, CS-05); the second by a raised filling pressure (PCWP >15) with a low output.
traps: “Cold extremities or a narrow pulse pressure confirm cardiogenic shock”
They show hypoperfusion and a small stroke volume, which any low-output shock has; the raised wedge is what pins it on the left ventricle.
“Lactate 2 mmol/L confirms it”
A lactate of exactly 2 is borderline, and lactate does not tell you the cause.
decode: Anterior MI, SBP 86 for 40 min on norepinephrine, CI 1.8, PCWP 20, UO 20 mL/h: which finding confirms cardiogenic shock? [DocT GT]
PCWP >15 — the full ventricle proves a pump problem.
CS-06.punch: Hypoperfusion tells you it is shock; a high wedge with a low cardiac index tells you the heart caused it.

CS-07.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Definitions → The three compared
CS-07.intro: Step 1 side by side. Each definition adds one distinctive element, and examiners ask which one carries it. Not asked directly, but CS-03 to CS-06 questions turn on these differences.
why: **SHOCK trial: CI ≤2.2 and PCWP ≥15.** The only definition that needs a catheter.
**IABP-SHOCK II: pulmonary congestion required.** Congestion is its bedside substitute for a raised wedge.
**ESC HF: adequate volume first.** The ESC wording builds fluid adequacy into the definition (2016); ESC 2021 dropped the hypotension requirement (CS-05).
**Urine output <30 mL/h in SHOCK and IABP-SHOCK II; lactate >2.0 only in IABP-SHOCK II.** The two trials share the oliguria cut-off; only IABP-SHOCK II names a lactate.
mimic: SHOCK vs IABP-SHOCK II support clause
SHOCK: any support to keep SBP ≥90; IABP-SHOCK II: catecholamines to keep SBP >90.
traps: “Lactate >2 is part of the SHOCK definition”
It is not; SHOCK used urine output or cool extremities.
decode: Which definition requires pulmonary congestion? [pattern]
IABP-SHOCK II.
Which builds adequate volume into the wording? [pattern]
ESC HF guideline.
CS-07.punch: SHOCK has the catheter numbers, IABP-SHOCK II has congestion and lactate, and ESC has adequate volume.

CS-08.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Staging → SCAI stages A–E
CS-08.intro: Step 1 ends with severity. The SCAI classification (2019, updated 2022) grades shock from at-risk to extremis so that teams speak the same language and escalate on time; mortality climbs steeply with each stage. Not asked directly here, but the B–C boundary underlies CS-05.
why: **A — At risk: risk factors, no signs or symptoms (large AMI, prior infarct, acute or acute-on-chronic HF).** Normal exam and normal lactate.
**B — Beginning: relative hypotension or tachycardia WITHOUT hypoperfusion.** Lactate is normal; the patient is compensating.

**C — Classic: hypoperfusion needing an intervention beyond volume (inotrope, pressor, MCS or ECMO), typically with relative hypotension.** The 2022 update puts lactate at ≥2 mmol/L and the CI typically <2.2 here.
**D — Deteriorating: fails to respond to initial interventions; like C and getting worse.** Lactate stays high or rises and support escalates.
**E — Extremis: on multiple interventions, may be in cardiac arrest with ongoing CPR and/or ECMO.** The 2022 table adds lactate ≥8 and pH <7.2.

**Arrest (A) modifier: CPR, including defibrillation.** The 2022 update narrows it to arrest with coma (unresponsive to voice), because a brief arrest with prompt awakening does not carry the same risk; the update also adds a three-axis model (stage, phenotype and aetiology, risk modifiers such as age).
mimic: SCAI B vs C
B has hypotension or tachycardia with normal perfusion; C has hypoperfusion that needs more than fluid.
traps: “Hypotension defines stage C”
Hypoperfusion defines C; a hypotensive but well-perfused patient is B, and a normotensive hypoperfused one can be C.
decode: Post-MI, BP 88/60, HR 110, warm, lactate 1.4, good urine output: SCAI stage? [pattern]
B — hypotension without hypoperfusion.
Already on two pressors and a device, lactate rising: stage? [pattern]
D — failing initial support.
CS-08.punch: SCAI staging turns on hypoperfusion: B is low pressure without it, C is hypoperfusion needing more than fluid, D is failing that, E is collapse.

CS-09.intro: Step 2 needs a framework for causes. Six branches cover every way the heart can fail as a pump; the detail sits on CS-10 to CS-13. Not asked directly.
why: **Myocardial.** The muscle itself: infarction, cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, stunning (CS-10 to CS-12).
**Mechanical complication.** Papillary muscle, septal or free-wall rupture after infarction.
**Valvular, native or prosthetic.** Stenosis blocks forward flow; acute regurgitation volume-loads a ventricle that has not had time to dilate.
**Electrical.** Too fast (no filling time), too slow (too few beats) or uncoordinated.
**Extra-cardiac / obstructive.** Tamponade, constriction, massive PE: the heart is normal but cannot fill or eject.
**Other.** Toxins and hypothermia depressing the myocardium.
mimic: Obstructive vs cardiogenic
Many classifications keep obstructive shock separate; this framework folds it in because the final common path is a low cardiac output.
traps: “Tamponade is cardiogenic”
In the four-category physiological classification it is obstructive; this card files it under an extra-cardiac branch of cardiogenic shock (CS-13).
decode: Classify this cause of low-output shock [pattern]
Pick the branch by where the pump fails: muscle, structure, valve, rhythm, obstruction, other.
CS-09.punch: Every cardiogenic shock is muscle, mechanics, valve, rhythm, obstruction or toxin; asking which one points straight at the fix.

CS-10.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Aetiology → AMI: muscle loss and complications
CS-10.intro: Step 2’s commonest cause: myocardial infarction. How much muscle is lost decides whether shock follows. Not asked directly, but the mechanical complications return on CS-32 and CS-33.
why: **More than 40% loss of LV mass causes shock on its own.** Autopsy studies of fatal infarct shock found at least 40% of the LV destroyed, old and new together, which is why a second infarct in a scarred heart is so dangerous.

**Less than 40% loss causes shock only with an added arrhythmia or vasodilation.** A smaller infarct is tipped over by AF, VT or bradycardia (lost filling or rate) or by a systemic inflammatory response that drops SVR.
**Right ventricular infarction.** Usually with an inferior infarct; the RV cannot fill the LV, so the patient is hypotensive with clear lungs and a high JVP and needs preload, not diuretics (CS-31).

**Mechanical complications: papillary muscle rupture, ventricular septal rupture, free-wall rupture.** Usually within the first week (classically days 3–5, but in the reperfusion era often within the first 24 hours), typically after a first, late-presenting or unreperfused infarct; a new murmur or sudden collapse is the clue.
mimic: Papillary muscle rupture vs post-infarct VSD
Both give a new systolic murmur after MI; papillary rupture gives flash pulmonary oedema (often inferior MI), VSD gives a left-to-right shunt with an O₂ step-up in the RV.
traps: “Under 40% loss rules out cardiogenic shock”
Not if an arrhythmia or vasodilation is added: 30% loss plus fast AF is still cardiogenic shock.
decode: Inferior MI, hypotension, clear lungs, raised JVP [pattern]
RV infarction — give fluid, avoid nitrates and diuretics.
CS-10.punch: Lose 40% of the left ventricle and shock follows; lose less and it takes an arrhythmia, vasodilation, RV infarction or a rupture to get there.

CS-11.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Aetiology → Heart failure, cardiomyopathies, pregnancy, endocrine
CS-11.intro: Step 2, the non-infarct muscle causes. These are the stems where coronary angiography is normal or the history points elsewhere — drink, a stressor, pregnancy, a thyroid. Four real questions, and the alcohol one was missed by two thirds.
why: **Acute decompensated HF: chronic HF of known cause that decompensates, or acute HF as the first presentation.** These are the two heart-failure-related shock groups (CS-01).

**Chronic ischaemia, dilated cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, stress-induced (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy.** Alcoholic cardiomyopathy is a dilated cardiomyopathy: heavy drinking for years (often quoted as >80 g a day for >5 years) gives a large, poorly contracting ventricle, cold low-output failure that needs inotropes, partly reversible with abstinence. Takotsubo follows an emotional or physical stressor, usually in a post-menopausal woman: ST elevation or deep T inversion, a modest troponin rise, unobstructed coronaries and apical ballooning with a hyperkinetic base; it recovers over weeks. Its danger is dynamic LVOT obstruction, where inotropes make it worse (CS-33).

**Pregnancy-associated: peripartum cardiomyopathy, coronary artery dissection.** PPCM is LV systolic failure (EF <45%) late in pregnancy or the months after delivery. A better outlook is predicted at diagnosis by a less dilated ventricle (LVEDD under about 5.5–6 cm), EF above 30–35% (fractional shortening >20%), no troponin rise and no LV thrombus. Spontaneous coronary dissection is the commonest cause of MI in pregnancy.

**Endocrine: hypo- or hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma.** Thyroid storm gives high-output failure and fast AF; profound hypothyroidism a weak, slow heart; phaeochromocytoma a catecholamine cardiomyopathy that can look exactly like Takotsubo.
mimic: Alcoholic cardiomyopathy vs wet beriberi
Both in drinkers; beriberi is warm, high-output failure with low SVR that reverses within hours of thiamine, cardiomyopathy is cold, low-output and persists after thiamine.
Takotsubo vs anterior STEMI
Same ECG and chest pain; angiography shows open coronaries and a wall-motion abnormality beyond one coronary territory.
traps: “Alcoholic with Wernicke’s, hypotension after thiamine — neurogenic shock”

Wernicke’s has no cord lesion to cut sympathetic outflow; shock persisting after thiamine is alcoholic dilated cardiomyopathy (only 34% right). Sepsis from aspiration is the other popular wrong pick, but nothing in the stem suggests it.
“Takotsubo with hypotension — start dobutamine”
If the base is hyperkinetic and the outflow obstructed, inotropes increase the gradient; use fluid, phenylephrine and a beta-blocker.
decode: Chronic drinker, confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; hypotension persists after thiamine [DocT QBank]
Alcoholic cardiomyopathy causing cardiogenic shock (34%).
Woman, chest pain and ST elevation after sudden bereavement, clean coronaries [DocT GT PYQ; NEET 2024]
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.
Peripartum cardiomyopathy: favourable prognostic factors [Marrow]
All of the above — small LVEDD, EF >30–35%, no troponin rise, no thrombus.
CS-11.punch: When the coronaries are clean, think muscle: alcohol (persists after thiamine), stress (Takotsubo, beware the outflow tract), pregnancy and the endocrine glands.

CS-12.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Aetiology → Post-cardiotomy, LVOT, post-arrest, septic, contusion
CS-12.intro: Step 2, the remaining muscle causes — mostly hearts stunned by something else: bypass, arrest, sepsis or a blow. Two real questions: post-CABG low output and blunt cardiac injury.
why: **Post-cardiotomy shock: prolonged cardiopulmonary bypass, insufficient cardioprotection.** Ischaemia during cross-clamp and reperfusion injury stun the myocardium; output is lowest at about 6–12 hours after bypass. Cold, clammy, confused and oliguric in that window is low cardiac output syndrome. Treat by optimising preload and afterload, correcting potassium, magnesium and calcium, fixing rate and rhythm (epicardial pacing), then inotropes (dobutamine or milrinone), IABP or MCS if refractory, and always exclude tamponade and graft failure.
**Dynamic outflow tract obstruction.** A small, hyperdynamic ventricle (hypertrophy, Takotsubo, hypovolaemia, inotropes) pulls the mitral leaflet into the outflow tract (CS-33).
**Post-cardiac-arrest stunning.** Global ischaemia–reperfusion depresses the heart for 24–72 hours and usually recovers.
**Myocardial depression in septic shock or SIRS.** Cytokines and nitric oxide depress contractility; it is reversible and secondary, which is why it is not primary cardiogenic shock (CS-02).

**Myocardial contusion.** Blunt chest trauma bruises the muscle (usually the anterior RV). Screen with ECG and troponin: if either is abnormal, monitor for 24–48 hours for arrhythmia, and echo if unstable; normal ECG with normal troponin effectively excludes significant injury.
mimic: Low cardiac output syndrome vs tamponade after cardiac surgery
Both are cold and oliguric; tamponade has rising, equalising filling pressures, falling drain output and a clot on echo, and needs re-opening, not inotropes.
traps: “Post-CABG low output — start high-dose vasoconstrictors”
Raising SVR in a stunned ventricle lowers output further; optimise loading, rhythm and electrolytes, then inotropes (97% got this right).
decode: 8 h after on-pump CABG: confused, cold, clammy, oliguric — next? [DocT GT]
Optimise preload and afterload, correct electrolytes, inotrope if needed (97%).
Stable blunt chest trauma with PVCs on ECG — next? [Marrow]
Admit for 24–48 h cardiac monitoring.
CS-12.punch: Bypass, arrest, sepsis and trauma all stun the heart; treat the stunned ventricle by loading, rhythm and inotropes, and never miss tamponade after surgery.

CS-13.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Aetiology → Valvular, electrical, obstructive, other
CS-13.intro: Step 2’s last branches. Two Marrow questions test the edges of the classification: what counts as obstructive shock, and which lesions block forward flow.
why: **Native valve: stenosis, acute regurgitation, valvular obstruction.** Acute regurgitation is the deadly one: a normal-sized ventricle suddenly takes a large regurgitant volume, so filling pressures soar (CS-32).

**Prosthetic valve: obstruction (thrombus, pannus), leaflet failure or restriction, mechanical failure, dehiscence.** A new murmur or muffled clicks with shock in a patient with a prosthetic valve is valve thrombosis until shown otherwise.
**Electrical: atrial arrhythmia with rapid ventricular rate, VT, bradycardia.** A fast rate cuts filling time; a slow one cuts beats per minute.

**Extra-cardiac / obstructive: cardiac tamponade, constriction, pulmonary embolism.** The wider physiological list of obstructive shock also includes tension pneumothorax and aortic dissection, and ‘obstruction to forward flow’ includes critical AS, dynamic LVOT obstruction (HCM), mitral stenosis and LA myxoma.
**Other: toxidromes, hypothermic myocardial depression.** Beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers and other cardiotoxins; cold depresses contractility and rate.
mimic: Obstructive vs distributive (adrenal crisis)
Adrenal crisis is distributive (endocrine) shock with low SVR; obstructive shock has a high SVR and a low output from blocked filling or ejection.
traps: “Myocardial contusion obstructs forward flow”
Contusion reduces contractility; it belongs with the myocardial causes, not with AS, HCM, MS and tamponade.
decode: Which is NOT obstructive shock? [Marrow]
Adrenal crisis — distributive.
Cardiogenic shock from mechanical obstruction to forward flow [Marrow]
AS, HCM (dynamic LVOT), MS, tamponade — not contusion.
CS-13.punch: Valves, rhythm and obstruction are the non-muscle causes; obstruction means blocked filling or ejection, never a weak muscle and never adrenal crisis.

CS-14.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Epidemiology → AMI share, incidence, mortality
CS-14.intro: Step 2’s numbers. These are the classic figures quoted in older reviews; not asked directly, but the STEMI–NSTEMI swap is a standard trap.
why: **AMI accounts for 80% of cardiogenic shock.** This is the older, infarct-era figure (reviews quote 60–80%). In contemporary cardiac ICUs AMI shock is about 27% and heart-failure shock about 59% (2024 registry), so expect the classic figure in the exam but know it is changing.
**Cardiogenic shock complicates 5–10% of acute MI.** Most series give 5–8%.
**It is the leading cause of death after MI.** In-hospital death of infarct shock remains around 40–50% despite revascularisation.

**STEMI causes about twice as many cases as NSTEMI, but NSTEMI shock has the higher mortality.** NSTEMI patients are older, with more multivessel disease and comorbidity, and shock develops later, often after the window for early revascularisation.
**6- and 12-month mortality about 50%.** Most of the deaths happen in the first month; survivors have a reasonable long-term outlook.
**18.6% 30-day readmission (MI and CHF).** From the US Nationwide Readmissions Database; heart failure was the commonest cardiac reason, infection the commonest non-cardiac one.
mimic: Frequency vs mortality
STEMI more often causes shock; NSTEMI kills more of the shocks it causes.
traps: “NSTEMI causes more cardiogenic shock”
It is STEMI that causes more; NSTEMI only wins on mortality.
decode: Incidence of cardiogenic shock in AMI [pattern]
Commonest cause of death in hospitalised AMI [pattern]
Cardiogenic shock.
CS-14.punch: Shock complicates 5–10% of infarcts and kills about half; STEMI causes more of it, NSTEMI shock kills a larger share.

CS-15.intro: Step 3 begins with the pressure–volume loop, the picture of one heartbeat. Its width is stroke volume, its top-left corner sits on the end-systolic pressure–volume line (Emax, the slope that measures contractility), and its bottom edge is the diastolic filling curve. Not asked directly.
why: **Steady state: the green baseline loop on a steep Emax line.** A normal ventricle fills to about 120 mL, ejects about 70 mL and generates a systolic pressure of about 120 mmHg.

**Acute MI: Emax flattens (lost contractility) while the loop is drawn little changed.** Early on, compensation (sympathetic drive, a modest rise in filling) keeps stroke volume and pressure near baseline despite the weaker muscle.

**Cardiogenic shock: the loop shifts right on a flat Emax line.** End-systolic and end-diastolic volumes rise, the loop narrows (smaller stroke volume), its top falls (lower systolic pressure) and the end-diastolic point climbs the stiffer filling curve (high LVEDP, pulmonary congestion).
mimic: Lost contractility vs raised afterload on a PV loop
Lost contractility flattens the Emax slope; raised afterload makes the loop taller and narrower on the same slope.
traps: “A flatter Emax alone means shock”
Both MI and shock flatten Emax; the rightward shift and narrow loop mark shock (CS-16).
decode: Which PV loop shows cardiogenic shock? [pattern]
Shifted right, narrow, low, with a high end-diastolic pressure on a flat Emax.
CS-15.punch: In cardiogenic shock the loop slides right, narrows and sinks on a flattened Emax line: big, weak, high-pressure ventricle ejecting little.

CS-16.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Pathophysiology → Reading the PV loops
CS-16.intro: Step 3, the loops read in words. Contractility falls in both MI and shock; what changes once shock supervenes is the position of the loop. Not asked directly.
why: **Acute MI: contractility decreased; pressure and volume remain the same; loop position unchanged.** The weaker muscle is still compensated: heart rate, catecholamines and a little more filling hold stroke volume.

**Cardiogenic shock: contractility decreased; pressure and volume shifted right; loop shifted to the RIGHT.** Volumes rise as the ventricle dilates to use Frank–Starling, but the flat Emax means each beat ejects less and the systolic pressure falls, while filling pressure rises.
mimic: Cardiogenic shock vs hypovolaemia on a PV loop
Hypovolaemia shifts the loop LEFT (small volumes) with normal Emax; cardiogenic shock shifts it right with a flat Emax.
traps: “Lower contractility separates shock from MI”
Both have it; the rightward shift is the discriminator.
decode: PV loop with reduced Emax and rightward shift [pattern]
Cardiogenic shock (not uncomplicated MI).
CS-16.punch: Contractility falls in both; only shock drags the loop to the right.

CS-17.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Pathophysiology → The neurohormonal spiral
CS-17.intro: Step 3’s engine. A falling output is sensed by baroreceptors and kidneys, and the reflexes meant to defend blood pressure end up overloading the injured heart. The one real question asks which part of this response does the most damage.
why: **Myocardial injury → reduced cardiac output.** The starting point of the spiral.

**→ less carotid baroreceptor stimulation and less renal perfusion.** The baroreceptors sense lower pressure and stop restraining sympathetic outflow; the juxtaglomerular cells sense less flow and release renin.
**→ activation of the SNS and RAAS.**

**SNS: more heart rate and inotropy, and myocardial toxicity; inhibited by beta-blockers.** Tachycardia and inotropy raise oxygen demand in a heart already short of supply, and chronic catecholamine exposure injures myocytes.

**RAAS: angiotensin II vasoconstriction (more afterload) and aldosterone salt retention (more preload); inhibited by ACE inhibitors, ARBs, aldosterone antagonists and ADH antagonists.** Higher afterload raises wall stress and myocardial oxygen demand and lowers stroke volume; more preload raises LVEDP, pulmonary congestion and subendocardial ischaemia.

**Common end point: negative remodelling and worse LV function → heart failure; BNP and ANP oppose the vasoconstriction and fluid retention.** Natriuretic peptides are the counter-regulatory brake, which is why BNP rises with stretch (CS-22). In about a fifth of infarct shock a systemic inflammatory response adds vasodilation, so SVR is not always high.
mimic: Afterload vs preload harm in the spiral
Afterload (angiotensin II, catecholamines) raises wall stress and cuts stroke volume; preload (aldosterone, ADH) raises filling pressure and congestion.
traps: “Reduced oxygen extraction or capillary recruitment worsens the injury”
These are distractors; the direct harm of a persistently high SVR is a higher afterload, which raises myocardial wall stress and oxygen demand.
decode: Large anterior MI, shock, SVR stays high after reperfusion: what worsens myocardial injury? [DocT GT]
Increased cardiac afterload.
CS-17.punch: The reflexes that defend blood pressure raise afterload and preload on an injured heart, and that extra load is what drives the spiral.

CS-18.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Haemodynamic profiles → Forrester quadrants
CS-18.intro: Step 4 sorts the patient by perfusion and congestion. Forrester (1976) did this with a PA catheter after MI; the same quadrants (cold or warm, wet or dry) are now read at the bedside. Four real questions, mostly the ‘high CVP plus low BP’ pattern.
why: **Cold and wet: classic cardiogenic shock — CI down, SVRI up, PCWP up.** Low output, compensatory vasoconstriction and a congested left heart; about two thirds of infarct shock.
**Cold and dry: euvolaemic cardiogenic shock — CI down, SVRI up, PCWP normal.** Low output without congestion; these patients may tolerate small fluid boluses (CS-31).
**Warm and wet: vasodilatory cardiogenic or mixed shock — CI down, SVRI down or normal, PCWP up.** A failing heart plus inflammation or sepsis that drops vascular tone; needs norepinephrine.
**Warm and dry: vasodilatory shock, NOT cardiogenic — CI up, SVRI down, PCWP down.** The only quadrant with a high output; this is the profile of sepsis and other distributive states.
mimic: High-CVP shock: cardiogenic vs obstructive vs RV failure
All have a high CVP; a high wedge with a low CI and poor LV is cardiogenic, a low wedge with a high CVP is RV failure, PE or tamponade.
traps: “Thyrotoxicosis or AV shunts are the commonest cause of high-output hypotension”
They cause high output, but sepsis is by far the commonest (63% right).
decode: Prior MI, BP 80/50, HR 110, CVP 15 [DocT QBank]
Cardiogenic shock from LV dysfunction (88%).
Chronic HF, BP 90/50, CVP 18, low EF [DocT QBank]
Cardiogenic shock (93%).
Older patient, cold shock, high CVP, PCWP and SVR [Marrow]
Acute MI — classic wet and cold.
Commonest cause of high-output hypotension [DocT QBank]
Sepsis (63%).
CS-18.punch: Three Forrester quadrants have a low cardiac index and are cardiogenic; warm and dry has a high one and is not cardiogenic shock at all.

CS-19.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Haemodynamic profiles → Bedside correlates
CS-19.intro: Step 4 without a catheter. Congestion is heard, seen on the film and counted on lung ultrasound; perfusion is felt in the hands. Four real questions test recognising pulmonary oedema and acute heart failure from bedside clues.
why: **Wet: pulmonary congestion — dyspnoea and orthopnoea; CXR pulmonary oedema; lung ultrasound B lines.** B lines are vertical artefacts from thickened, fluid-filled interlobular septa; three or more per intercostal space in several zones on both sides with preserved sliding is interstitial oedema. An S3 with bibasal crackles adds weight: it is rapid early filling into a stiff, overfull ventricle with a high LVEDP — specific (about 90%) but insensitive.
**Dry: does NOT show signs of pulmonary congestion.** Clear lungs, A lines on ultrasound, no orthopnoea.

**Warm type: can present as hypertensive heart failure.** Perfusion is maintained and the pressure is high; the problem is afterload and redistribution of fluid into the lungs, treated with nitrates (CS-28).
mimic: Hypertensive acute heart failure vs aortic dissection
Both give chest pain with severe hypertension; pulmonary oedema with no pulse or BP differential and no widened mediastinum points to acute heart failure.
B lines vs pneumothorax
Pneumothorax abolishes sliding and B lines; oedema has many B lines with preserved sliding.
traps: “BP 200/120, chest pain, confusion and oedema — aortic dissection or AMI”
A normal ECG and pulmonary oedema make it acute (hypertensive) heart failure; 68% right.
“Oedema with CVP 18 is CKD fluid overload”
Possible, but in a hypertensive diabetic with breathlessness the expected answer is acute pulmonary oedema from LV failure (83%).
decode: HTN, diabetes, breathless, oedema, BP 100/60, CVP 18 [DocT QBank]
Acute pulmonary oedema due to left heart failure (83%).
BP 200/120, chest pain, disoriented, normal ECG, pulmonary oedema on CXR [DocT QBank]
Acute heart failure (68%).
CAD, crackles, S3, sinus tachycardia, no ST change [DocT QBank]
Congestive heart failure (89%).
Lung ultrasound >3 B lines per field, sliding preserved [DocT QBank]
Pulmonary oedema (86%).
CS-19.punch: Wet is crackles, oedema on the film and B lines on ultrasound; warm and wet with a high pressure is hypertensive heart failure.

CS-20.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Monitoring → Frequency and rationale
CS-20.intro: Step 4 continues once the patient is profiled: how closely to watch. These frequencies come from the AHA 2017 cardiogenic shock statement; not asked directly, but the CVP point recurs across shock questions.
why: **Telemetry, pulse oximetry, respiratory rate: continuous — arrhythmias, ventilatory failure and pulmonary oedema are common.**
**Critical care unit monitoring: 1:1 nurse-to-patient ratio — haemodynamic deterioration and multi-organ failure are common.**
**Arterial BP: continuous, until vasoactive drugs have been off for 12–24 h.** Cuff pressures are unreliable in vasoconstricted, low-output patients.

**CVP: continuous; a single value is unreliable, trends inform fluid status.** One CVP number depends on compliance, intrathoracic pressure and the RV, so it predicts fluid response poorly; the direction of change is more useful.

**Central venous oxygen saturation: every 4 h — trends track cardiac output.** With constant oxygen consumption and haemoglobin, a falling ScvO₂ means more extraction because delivery (output) has fallen.
**Urine output: hourly — renal perfusion and AKI.**

**PAC or non-invasive cardiac output monitor: selected use — early if not responding to initial therapy or the diagnosis is uncertain.** Routine PA catheters did not improve outcomes in unselected patients, but in refractory shock they separate LV, RV and mixed failure and guide devices.
mimic: ScvO₂ vs lactate
ScvO₂ falls when delivery falls relative to demand; lactate rises when tissues have already turned anaerobic.
traps: “A CVP of 8 means the patient is adequately filled”
A single CVP is unreliable; follow the trend and the response to a challenge.
decode: Which monitored variable is unreliable as a single value? [pattern]
CVP.
When is a PA catheter indicated in cardiogenic shock? [pattern]
Failure to respond to initial therapy or diagnostic uncertainty.
CS-20.punch: Watch continuously, trend the CVP and ScvO₂ rather than trusting single values, and bring in a PA catheter when the patient fails to respond.

CS-21.intro: Step 4’s laboratory rhythm, also from AHA 2017. Lactate is the test that drives decisions. Not asked directly.
why: **Complete blood count: every 12–24 h, more often if bleeding.** Devices, anticoagulants and antiplatelets make bleeding common.
**Electrolytes: every 6–12 h.** Diuretics and renal failure shift potassium and magnesium, and low levels provoke arrhythmias.
**Creatinine: every 12–24 h — renal perfusion and AKI.**
**Liver function: daily — congestive hepatopathy and hypoperfusion.** A sharp transaminase rise (‘shock liver’) signals hypoperfusion; cholestasis signals congestion.
**Lactate: every 1–4 h; clearance marks resolving hypoperfusion, failure to clear predicts death.** Lactate trajectory moves the SCAI stage from C to D (CS-08).
**Coagulation: every 4–6 h on anticoagulants until stable, otherwise daily.** Hepatic congestion alters drug handling and devices need anticoagulation.
mimic: Ischaemic hepatitis vs congestive hepatopathy
Ischaemic: transaminases in the thousands after a low-output episode, falling within days; congestive: raised bilirubin and ALP with a high CVP.
traps: “Lactate once a day is enough”
It is checked every 1–4 h because clearance (or its absence) is the earliest sign that treatment is working or failing.
decode: Which lab trend best predicts mortality in cardiogenic shock? [pattern]
Lack of lactate clearance.
CS-21.punch: Repeat lactate every few hours: its clearance is the clearest sign that perfusion is coming back.

CS-22.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Investigations → Echo, ECG, CXR, BNP, lactate
CS-22.intro: Step 4’s first tests. Echo tells you which part of the heart has failed, the ECG whether it is ischaemic, the film whether the patient is wet. Three real questions, and the Kerley-line item was missed by four in five.
why: **Echocardiography: LV and RV dysfunction, valvular abnormalities, chamber dimensions, response to therapy.** It also finds the causes that need a different treatment: tamponade, a ruptured papillary muscle or septum, LVOT obstruction.
**12-lead ECG: exclude arrhythmias and new ischaemia or infarction.** ST elevation or its equivalent sends the patient straight to the cath lab (CS-23).

**Chest X-ray: upper-lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, pleural effusion, cardiomegaly.** Kerley lines are thickened, oedematous interlobular septa — not swollen lymphatics, as first thought. B lines are short (about 1 cm) horizontal lines at the peripheral bases, perpendicular to the pleura; A lines are longer (2–6 cm) lines deep in the lung running towards the hila. Cardiogenic oedema also shows perihilar ‘bat-wing’ shadowing, peribronchial cuffing and a widened vascular pedicle (>70 mm); ARDS gives patchy peripheral opacities with a normal heart and pedicle and few effusions or septal lines.

**Pro-BNP elevated in cardiogenic shock; troponin I.** BNP rises with myocardial stretch or poor clearance, so it is also high in PE (RV strain), AF, renal failure, sepsis, ACS and old age. Obesity lowers it. Sacubitril raises BNP but not NT-proBNP, so NT-proBNP is the marker on an ARNI.
mimic: Cardiogenic oedema vs ARDS on CXR
Cardiogenic: big heart, upper-lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, effusions; ARDS: normal heart, peripheral patchy opacities, air bronchograms.
LV failure vs RV failure vs tamponade on echo
Poor LV with a dilated LV; dilated RV with septal flattening; effusion with diastolic RV collapse.
traps: “Kerley lines are swollen pulmonary lymphatics” (marked as true)
That is the false statement: they are oedematous septa. Only 19% chose it — most thought the A-line description was wrong, but A lines really are the deep lines running to the hila.
“All of these raise BNP — including hypothyroidism”
Hypothyroidism has no stretch mechanism and is the usual odd one out; obesity lowers BNP.
decode: All true about Kerley lines EXCEPT [DocT GT]
‘Represent swollen lymphatics’ — they are oedematous interlobular septa (19%).
CXR: cardiomegaly, bat-wing opacities, Kerley B lines [DocT GT]
Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
HF patient, hypotensive, echo shows poor LVEF: cause of shock? [DocT QBank]
Cardiogenic shock from acute left-sided failure (56%).
CS-22.punch: Echo finds the failing chamber and the surgical lesions; the film shows wetness, and Kerley lines are oedematous septa, not lymphatics.

CS-23.intro: Step 4’s invasive test. Angiography both diagnoses and treats when the cause may be ischaemic. Not asked directly, but CS-34 questions turn on it.
why: **Indication: acute RV or LV failure of suspected ischaemic aetiology.** ESC 2023 gives immediate angiography with PCI of the culprit a class I recommendation in ACS with shock, whatever the time since symptom onset.
**Assesses the coronaries, pressures, valves and structural lesions.** Right and left heart pressures, LVEDP and shunt runs are measured in the same sitting.
**Identifies contributors to the shock.** A septal rupture, severe MR or an unsuspected valve lesion changes the plan to surgery or a device.
mimic: Angiography first vs echo first
Echo at the bedside comes first to exclude tamponade and mechanical lesions; angiography follows immediately if ischaemia is suspected.
traps: “Stabilise for 24 h before angiography”
In infarct shock, delay costs lives; angiography is immediate (SHOCK, CS-35).
decode: Cardiogenic shock, suspected ischaemic cause: next step? [pattern]
Immediate coronary angiography with intent to revascularise.
CS-23.punch: Suspect ischaemia in cardiogenic shock and you go straight to the cath lab, which both finds and fixes the cause.

CS-24.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Management → Level of care, triggers, shock centres
CS-24.intro: Step 5 starts with where the patient is treated. Shock outcomes depend on volume and on having a team that can offer revascularisation and devices around the clock. Not asked directly.
why: **ICU admission for pulmonary oedema, cardiogenic shock, de novo acute heart failure.**

**Acute-on-chronic HF decompensates from intercurrent infection, anaemia or renal dysfunction.** Each raises demand or lowers delivery in a heart with no reserve; arrhythmia, ischaemia and stopping medication are the other triggers.
**ESC: a cardiac ICU is better than a general ICU; AHA does not advocate either.** The AHA 2017 statement prefers organisation (a shock team and hub) over the label on the unit.

**Regionalised care: centre volume over about 100 cases a year lowers in-hospital mortality; field diagnosis → bypass the nearest non-shock site → direct transfer to a hub shock centre, with the team mobilised after a doctor-to-doctor call.** The volume data come from a US national inpatient sample (Shaefi 2015): the highest-volume quartile of hospitals had lower adjusted in-hospital mortality than those treating 27 or fewer shock cases a year (about 37% vs 42%). Experience with devices, round-the-clock PCI and surgery, and a practised team are the likely reasons.
mimic: Hub vs spoke
The hub offers 24/7 PCI, MCS, cardiac surgery and a shock team; the spoke stabilises and transfers.
traps: “Which guideline recommends the CICU over the ICU — AHA”
It is ESC; AHA takes no position.
decode: Commonest triggers of acute-on-chronic decompensation [pattern]
Infection, anaemia, renal dysfunction (plus arrhythmia, ischaemia, non-adherence).
CS-24.punch: Shock is treated best in high-volume hub centres with a shock team; ESC prefers the cardiac ICU, AHA does not take sides.

CS-25.intro: Step 5’s map of treatment: every intervention targets one of the determinants of output — rate, rhythm, preload, afterload, contractility. Not asked directly, but CS-26 to CS-31 are this list applied.
why: **Rate: maintain normal sinus rhythm.** Too fast shortens filling, too slow cuts output; aim for a rate the ventricle can fill at.
**Rhythm: restore sinus rhythm.** The atrial kick supplies a large share of filling in a stiff ventricle; cardiovert unstable AF or VT.

**Preload: diuretics to lower it; renal replacement if diuretic-resistant.** In the wet patient, lowering LVEDP relieves congestion without much loss of output because the failing ventricle sits on the flat part of its Starling curve.
**Afterload: vasodilators such as NTG.** A failing ventricle is very sensitive to afterload, so small falls in SVR give large rises in stroke volume — if the pressure allows.

**Contraction: inotropes — sympathomimetics, inodilators, calcium sensitisers; MAP may fall with inotropes, so norepinephrine is used alongside.** Dobutamine, milrinone and levosimendan all vasodilate (CS-29).
mimic: Afterload reduction vs inotropy
Both raise stroke volume; vasodilators do it without raising oxygen demand, inotropes at the cost of more demand and arrhythmia.
traps: “Diuretics drop output in the wet failing heart”
On the flat part of the Starling curve, lowering preload relieves congestion with little loss of stroke volume — unless the patient is dry (CS-26 f).
decode: Inotrope started, MAP falls: next? [pattern]
Add norepinephrine (inodilators lower SVR).
