CS-25.punch: Treat cardiogenic shock by its determinants: fix rate and rhythm, lower preload and afterload where the pressure allows, and add an inotrope with norepinephrine behind it.

CS-26.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Management → ESC bedside profile algorithm
CS-26.intro: Step 5 at the bedside: the ESC warm/cold, wet/dry algorithm (ESC 2016) matches treatment to the profile from CS-18 and CS-19. Nine real questions, the most-asked management card, and three of DocT’s keys need care.
why: **Wet and warm, vascular type (hypertension predominates): vasodilator + diuretic.** The fluid has been redistributed into the lungs by a sudden afterload rise rather than gained; nitrates unload the ventricle fastest (CS-28).

**Wet and warm, cardiac type (congestion predominates): diuretic + vasodilator; ultrafiltration if diuretic-resistant.** Here the patient has gained fluid over days, so IV loop diuretic is the first-line treatment.

**Wet and cold, SBP <90: inotrope; vasopressor if refractory; diuretic once perfusion is corrected; MCS if no response to drugs.** Diuresing a hypoperfused patient lowers output further, so perfusion comes first. The AHA/SCAI and ACC/AHA 2025 teaching starts norepinephrine first in hypotensive shock and then adds dobutamine; ESC (2021) also prefers norepinephrine when a vasopressor is needed.
**Wet and cold, SBP ≥90: vasodilators + diuretics; inotrope only if refractory.** With an adequate pressure, unloading improves output without the costs of an inotrope.
**Dry and warm: compensated — adjust oral therapy.**

**Dry and cold: hypoperfused and hypovolaemic — fluid challenge; inotrope if still hypoperfused.** Wet is 95% of acute heart failure presentations, dry 5%. ESC 2021 now organises acute HF by four presentations (decompensated HF, acute pulmonary oedema, isolated RV failure, cardiogenic shock), but the profile logic is unchanged.
mimic: Wet-cold SBP <90 vs ≥90
Below 90: perfusion first (inotrope/pressor), diuretic later; at or above 90: vasodilator and diuretic.
traps: “SBP 95/60 with congestion — start norepinephrine”
95 is above 90 and perfusion is not described as failing; this is wet-warm and needs IV furosemide (73%).
“HFrEF, BP 85/50, HR 120: norepinephrine”

DocT keys dobutamine (58%), following the ESC algorithm; AHA/SCAI would start norepinephrine at this pressure. If the stem says low output and asks for the next drug, choose dobutamine; if it says shock with MAP <65 and offers norepinephrine, choose norepinephrine.
“Hypotension after diuresis — dopamine” (DocT key)

Outdated: SOAP II found more arrhythmias and, in the cardiogenic subgroup, higher mortality with dopamine. The patient was 120/80 before diuresis, so this is over-diuresis: hold the diuretic and reassess volume; if a drug is needed, norepinephrine (42% chose the keyed dopamine).
“Hypertensive pulmonary oedema — nitroprusside or morphine to lower preload”

Nitroglycerin is the first-line preload reducer (59%); nitroprusside is a potent balanced arterial and venous dilator that needs arterial-line titration and carries cyanide and thiocyanate risk, so it is kept for refractory hypertension or acute valve regurgitation, and morphine is no longer routine.
decode: IHD, orthopnoea, crackles, oedema, BP 130/85 [DocT QBank ×3]
IV furosemide (86%, 94%, 73% with LVEF 30%).
DCM, BP 85/60, HR 110, starting inotropic support [DocT QBank]
Dobutamine (75%).
HFrEF, BP 85/50, HR 120, next step [DocT QBank]
Dobutamine per DocT (58%); norepinephrine per AHA/SCAI if shock is explicit.
CHF at a picnic, SpO₂ 85%, BP 185/90: first-line preload reducer [DocT QBank]
Nitroglycerin (59%).
CS-26.punch: Read the profile: wet with a pressure gets diuretic and vasodilator, wet and cold gets perfusion first, dry and cold gets fluid — and dopamine is never the modern answer.

table.title: Which drug the stem wants
head: Stem
Exam answer
rows: Asks for an inotrope, SBP 85, low output
Shock, MAP <65 or SBP clearly <90, offered norepinephrine
Stop the diuretic, reassess volume; norepinephrine if a drug is needed

CS-27.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Supportive care → Ventilation, induction, renal support
CS-27.intro: Step 5’s supportive measures. Positive pressure is a treatment for the failing left ventricle, not just for the lungs, and examiners test exactly why. Five real questions.
why: **CPAP/NIV: more alveolar recruitment, less extravascular lung water, less work of breathing.** Recruiting flooded alveoli improves oxygenation; the pressure gradient pushes fluid back; unloading the respiratory muscles frees cardiac output for other organs.

**Etomidate preferred at induction because of the risk of haemodynamic collapse.** It has the least effect on SVR and contractility. Its cost is adrenal suppression: one dose blocks 11β-hydroxylase for 24–72 hours, and with azoles (ketoconazole) or enzyme inducers (phenytoin, rifampicin) it can produce critical-illness corticosteroid insufficiency.

**Positive pressure ventilation has a POSITIVE effect on LV function.** Raised intrathoracic pressure surrounds the LV and lowers its transmural pressure during systole, which is a fall in afterload; it also cuts venous return (preload), which helps the congested ventricle. On the right side it lowers RV preload and raises RV afterload. Removing it at a spontaneous breathing trial does the reverse and can cause weaning-induced pulmonary oedema.

**About 20% of cardiogenic shock need CRRT; consider it from KDIGO stage 2 or for life-threatening indications.** Continuous rather than intermittent therapy, because it removes fluid without the swings in pressure that a failing heart cannot tolerate.
mimic: PPV in cardiogenic vs hypovolaemic shock
In cardiogenic shock lowering preload and afterload helps; in hypovolaemic shock the loss of venous return drops output.
traps: “CPAP mainly reduces preload” (true?)
False: it reduces LV afterload as well as preload (Marrow keyed this as the false statement).
“NIV lowers afterload by lowering alveolar pressure or blocking RAAS”
It works by raising intrathoracic pressure and lowering LV transmural pressure.
“Hypertensive pulmonary oedema — loop diuretic and wait, or intubate now”
Nitrates plus NIV first (65%); diuretics are slow and the patient is redistributed, not overloaded; intubate if NIV fails or consciousness falls.
“Only etomidate caused the adrenal crisis”
Etomidate, ketoconazole and phenytoin all contribute — ‘all of the above’ (44%).
decode: ACPE: how does NPPV reduce LV afterload? [DocT GT]
Raises intrathoracic pressure, reducing LV transmural pressure in systole.
SBP 180, pink frothy sputum, SpO₂ 88%, alert [DocT GT]
Nitrates + NIPPV (65%).
Haemodynamic effects of PEEP [NEET 2024]
RV preload down, RV afterload up, LV afterload down.
Phenytoin, ketoconazole, etomidate; refractory shock responding to hydrocortisone [DocT GT]
All of the above (44%).
CS-27.punch: Positive pressure lowers LV afterload and preload, so in the failing left heart it is a treatment, not just a ventilation mode.

CS-28.intro: Step 5’s unloading drugs. In the warm, wet, hypertensive patient the fastest relief comes from reducing load, not from removing fluid. Five real questions, all on hypertensive acute pulmonary oedema (SCAPE).
why: **Loop diuretics: less circulating volume, mild venodilation, lower LVEDP and RVEDP.** The venodilation comes within minutes (before the diuresis); the volume effect takes hours.
**NIV: better oxygenation, less work of breathing, less LV wall stress.** Less wall stress is the afterload effect of CS-27.

**Vasodilators (nitroglycerin): veno-arterial dilatation, lower preload and LVEDP, lower afterload.** Venodilation dominates at low doses; high doses (as used in SCAPE) add arterial dilation. In sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary oedema (SBP often 180+), high-dose IV nitrates with NIV are first line, IV furosemide second; avoid nitrates if hypotensive, after phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and in RV infarction or severe AS. Morphine is no longer routine (more ventilation and deaths in registry data).
**Haemodialysis / haemodiafiltration / haemofiltration: lower volume and LVEDP/RVEDP, correction of electrolytes.**
mimic: SCAPE vs volume-overloaded ADHF
SCAPE: sudden, hypertensive, fluid redistributed — nitrates first; ADHF: days of weight gain, normal BP — diuretic first.
traps: “Hypertensive pulmonary oedema — furosemide alone”
Too slow and does not treat the afterload surge; nitroglycerin plus furosemide (NEET 2025).
“Morphine for the distressed patient in pulmonary oedema”
No longer routine; it is linked to more ventilation and mortality.
“Esmolol-triggered pulmonary oedema needs more beta-blockade”
After esmolol for amphetamine SVT, pulmonary oedema needs nitrates and diuretics.
decode: Acute HF with pulmonary oedema, BP 180/100 [NEET 2025]
NTG + furosemide.
SCAPE after CABG: drug of choice [NEET 2024]
Nitroglycerin.
Amphetamine, hypertensive SVT → esmolol → pulmonary oedema: next? [Marrow]
Nitrates and diuretics.
Wet-warm, BP 130/85: first line [DocT QBank]
IV furosemide (86%).
CS-28.punch: When the pressure is high and the lungs are wet, nitroglycerin and NIV unload the ventricle in minutes; the diuretic follows.

CS-29.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Drugs → Inotropes: receptors and net effect
CS-29.intro: Step 5’s inotropes, the most-asked card in the deck (15 questions). Every inotrope raises contractility by raising calcium availability or sensitivity, and every one in this table also vasodilates — which is why blood pressure falls and norepinephrine is so often added.
why: **Dobutamine: β1 (more contractility and heart rate) and β2 (arteriolar dilation); net effect ‘inodilation’.** β1 → Gs → adenylate cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A, which phosphorylates L-type calcium channels and ryanodine receptors (more systolic calcium: inotropy), phospholamban (releases SERCA2a: faster reuptake, lusitropy) and troponin I. Tachycardia is a dose-related direct β1 effect, not a reflex. Because β2 vasodilates, dobutamine can lower the pressure: a patient still hypotensive on it needs norepinephrine, not less dobutamine.

**Adrenaline: β1 (contractility and rate), α1 at higher doses (vasoconstriction), more lactate production.** The lactate is β2-driven aerobic glycolysis, not hypoperfusion, so it can mislead. In infarct shock adrenaline caused more refractory shock than norepinephrine (OptimaCC, 2018).

**PDE-3 inhibitors (milrinone): more myocardial cAMP and contractility, more vascular cAMP → vasodilation, especially pulmonary.** Acting below the receptor, milrinone works in a beta-blocked patient. It vasodilates more than dobutamine, so hypotension is its main effect, and it is renally excreted, so it accumulates in AKI or ESRD (reduce the rate, skip the load). DOREMI (2021) found no outcome difference from dobutamine.

**Levosimendan (calcium sensitiser): more contractility, reduced calcium flux, vascular K⁺-channel activation → vasodilation and lower afterload.** It binds troponin C and increases its calcium sensitivity without raising intracellular calcium, so oxygen cost and arrhythmia are lower; opening ATP-sensitive potassium channels dilates vessels. An active metabolite keeps it working for days.
mimic: Milrinone vs levosimendan
Milrinone: PDE-3 inhibition, more cAMP and calcium; levosimendan: troponin C sensitisation, no rise in calcium, K-ATP vasodilation.
Isoprenaline vs dobutamine
Isoprenaline is a pure β1+β2 agonist: big rate rise and diastolic fall, so myocardial ischaemia limits it; it is a bridge to pacing in bradycardia.
traps: “On dobutamine, HR 130 and still hypotensive — decrease dobutamine” (DocT key)

Disputed: cutting dobutamine slows the heart but does not raise the pressure; add norepinephrine (33% chose the key). If the stem stresses the tachyarrhythmia with an adequate BP, reduce the dose (77% did, correctly).
“Tachycardia on dobutamine is a reflex”
It is dose-related direct β1 chronotropy, the ‘toxic effect’ (66%).
“Serelaxin is an inotrope”
It is a relaxin-2 vasodilator; omecamtiv mecarbil is the myosin activator that raises stroke volume without raising cAMP, calcium or oxygen use.
“Milrinone hypotension is toxicity or bradycardia”
It is milrinone-induced vasodilation (88%).
decode: Inotrope after failed dobutamine: cAMP up, venodilation, faster relaxation — mechanism? [DocT GT]
PDE-3 inhibition (50%).
On high-dose norepinephrine, still low output — which inotrope? [DocT GT ×2]
Dobutamine (100%, 95%).
Dobutamine: intracellular mechanism of better contraction and relaxation [DocT GT]
Ryanodine receptor phosphorylation (via cAMP–PKA).
Which comorbidity prolongs milrinone? [Marrow] / milrinone false statement [NEET 2024]
End-stage renal disease; milrinone is a PDE-3 inhibitor that works downstream of the β receptor.
CS-29.punch: Every inotrope here also dilates vessels, so pressure falls: the answer to hypotension on an inotrope is norepinephrine, not a smaller dose.

CS-30.intro: Step 5’s decision tree. Low output with a low pressure starts an inotrope; the first branch is whether the right ventricle or the pulmonary circulation is the problem. Ten real questions, and two DocT keys are out of date.
why: **Entry: MAP <65 mmHg AND LVEF <40% or CI <1.8 L/min/m².** A low pressure with proof of a weak pump.
**Branch: RV dysfunction and/or raised pulmonary resistance?**

**No: begin dobutamine; if MAP stays <65 add norepinephrine, then vasopressin.** Dobutamine is the standard β-agonist inotrope for LV failure; norepinephrine restores the pressure that its β2 effect lowers.

**Yes: begin milrinone or levosimendan WITH norepinephrine; if MAP stays <65 add vasopressin.** Both lower pulmonary vascular resistance, which unloads the RV, but both dilate systemic vessels too, so norepinephrine starts with them. Vasopressin raises SVR without raising PVR (CS-31).
**If vasopressin fails: consider a mechanical support device.** Both arms converge there; SCAI D is the stage where MCS is considered.
mimic: Dobutamine vs milrinone first
Dobutamine for LV failure; milrinone or levosimendan when the RV or PVR is the problem, or the patient is on a beta-blocker.
traps: “BP 80/50 after fluids, which inotrope? — dopamine” (DocT key)

Outdated: SOAP II showed more arrhythmias and higher mortality in the cardiogenic subgroup. Norepinephrine for the pressure, dobutamine or milrinone for output (38% chose the keyed dopamine). Pick dopamine only if it is the sole vasoactive option.
“Still hypotensive on dobutamine — decrease dobutamine” (DocT key)
Add norepinephrine (MAP <65 → norepinephrine, as this card says); 33% chose the key.
“Hypotension on dobutamine — switch to milrinone”
Milrinone vasodilates more; the fix for pressure is norepinephrine (62% and 90%).
decode: HFrEF, BP 85/55 on dobutamine, BP falling [DocT QBank]
Add norepinephrine (90%).
End-stage HF on low-dose dobutamine, BP 80/50 after fluids [DocT QBank]
Add norepinephrine (62%).
BP 80/50 despite fluids, which drug to improve output? [DocT QBank]
DocT keys dopamine (38%); exam-day answer norepinephrine if offered.
Diltiazem overdose, low CI, normal SVR [Marrow]
Dobutamine — choose by phenotype after calcium and high-dose insulin.
CS-30.punch: Dobutamine for the failing left ventricle, milrinone or levosimendan with norepinephrine when the right side is failing, norepinephrine whenever MAP stays under 65, and a device when drugs fail.

CS-31.intro: Step 5 by phenotype, from the AHA 2017 statement. Each Forrester profile (CS-18) gets its own vasoactive choice. Not asked directly, but CS-26 and CS-30 questions draw on it.
why: **Classic wet and cold: norepinephrine first, then an inotrope once stable and after revascularisation; low CI, high SVR.** In SOAP II’s cardiogenic subgroup dopamine gave more arrhythmias and higher mortality, so it is not an equal choice.
**Euvolaemic cold and dry: as above, plus small fluid boluses; LVEDP may be low.**
**Vasodilatory warm and wet or mixed: norepinephrine, haemodynamics-guided; this subtype has a LOW SVR.** Often post-arrest or infarct shock with a systemic inflammatory response; look for sepsis.

**RV shock: fluid boluses; norepinephrine, dopamine or vasopressin; inotropes; inhaled pulmonary vasodilators — keep preload, lower PVR, treat bradycardia, keep AV synchrony; vasopressin raises SVR with neutral PVR.** The RV needs filling and a low afterload, and its coronary perfusion depends on systemic pressure, so a pressor that does not constrict the pulmonary bed is ideal.
**Normotensive shock: inotrope or vasopressor; SBP >90 with a relatively high SVR, so initial inotropy may be appropriate.** This is ESC 2021’s hypoperfusion-without-hypotension (CS-05).
mimic: RV shock vs LV shock
RV: clear lungs, high CVP, needs fluid and a low PVR; LV: congestion, needs diuresis and afterload reduction.
traps: “Diuretics and nitrates for RV infarction with hypotension”
They drop preload in a preload-dependent ventricle; give fluid, then norepinephrine or vasopressin.
decode: RV shock: which pressor does not raise PVR? [pattern]
Vasopressin.
Hypoperfused but SBP 100 with high SVR [pattern]
Normotensive cardiogenic shock — an inotrope may be first.
CS-31.punch: Match the drug to the phenotype: norepinephrine for the cold and hypotensive, an inotrope for the normotensive, fluid and a PVR-sparing pressor for the right ventricle.

CS-32.intro: Step 6 starts with valves, where each lesion has its own haemodynamic rules and a definitive fix. Five real questions: low-flow aortic stenosis three times, acute AR and acute MR once each — and the AR question was answered correctly by only one in five.
why: **Aortic stenosis: phenylephrine or vasopressin; if LVEF low, echo- or PAC-guided dobutamine; afterload-dependent; inotropy may not help if LVEF is preserved; definitive SAVR, balloon valvuloplasty, TAVR.** The fixed valve sets the outflow, so dilating vessels drops pressure without raising flow, and the hypertrophied ventricle depends on diastolic pressure for coronary perfusion. Symptomatic severe AS — including low-flow, low-gradient AS (valve area <1 cm² with a low gradient because the stroke volume is low) — needs urgent valve replacement, TAVI often preferred in the acutely ill elderly; balloon valvuloplasty is only a bridge (restenosis within months).

**Aortic regurgitation: dopamine, temporary pacing; a faster heart rate shortens diastole and lowers LVEDP; definitive SAVR.** Less diastolic time means less time to regurgitate. That is for the hypotensive patient. With pulmonary oedema and a normal pressure, nitroprusside is the bridge to surgery: it lowers afterload and the regurgitant volume. IABP is contraindicated (it augments diastolic pressure and the regurgitant jet), and β-blockers lengthen diastole.

**Mitral stenosis: phenylephrine or vasopressin, esmolol or amiodarone; preload-dependent; avoid chronotropes, slow the rate to lengthen filling, keep AV synchrony; definitive MVR or balloon valvuloplasty.** Flow across a narrow mitral valve needs time; fast AF can cause sudden oedema and shock.

**Mitral regurgitation: norepinephrine or dopamine, an inotrope, temporary MCS including IABP; afterload reduction lowers LVEDP; IABP reduces regurgitant fraction by lowering afterload and raising CI; definitive repair, replacement or edge-to-edge.** In an inferior STEMI, a new systolic murmur with flash pulmonary oedema and shock is posteromedial papillary muscle rupture (that muscle has a single blood supply); IABP is the bridge to surgery.
mimic: Acute AR vs acute MR
Both need afterload reduction; IABP helps MR and is contraindicated in AR.
AR vs MS heart rate
Raise it in AR to shorten diastole; slow it in MS to lengthen filling.
traps: “Acute AR with pulmonary oedema, BP 120/70 — norepinephrine, adrenaline or furosemide”
Raising afterload increases regurgitation; nitroprusside is the bridge (only 20% right).
“Inferior STEMI, new systolic murmur, oedema, BP 90/50 — norepinephrine or milrinone”
Norepinephrine raises afterload and the regurgitant fraction; milrinone drops the pressure; IABP unloads and perfuses (38% right).
“Low-flow AS — balloon valvuloplasty, diuresis or fluids”
Valvuloplasty is a bridge, diuresis or fluids leave the obstruction: urgent valve replacement (59–71%).
decode: 78-year-old, oedema, weak carotid upstroke, AVA 0.7 cm², low gradient [DocT GT ×3]
Urgent aortic valve replacement (71%, 59%, 61%).
IVDU, aortic vegetation, severe AR, pulmonary oedema, BP 120/70 [DocT GT]
Nitroprusside (20%).
Inferior STEMI, systolic murmur, pulmonary oedema, cold, BP 90/50 [DocT GT]
Intra-aortic balloon pump (38%).
CS-32.punch: Stenoses need pressure and time (pressors, slow rates), regurgitation needs unloading (vasodilators, IABP in MR but never in AR), and every valve shock needs the valve fixed.

CS-33.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Subtypes → Mechanical and electrical
CS-33.intro: Step 6, the lesions that make standard treatment harmful. LVOT obstruction is the one place where inotropes are contraindicated. One real question, on Takotsubo with outflow obstruction.
why: **Post-infarct VSD: treat as classic wet and cold; temporary MCS including IABP, which lowers the shunt fraction by lowering afterload and raising CI; surgical repair or percutaneous umbrella closure.** Lower systemic resistance means more blood goes out of the aorta rather than across the septum.

**Dynamic LVOT obstruction: fluid boluses, phenylephrine or vasopressin; AVOID inotropes and vasodilators; esmolol or amiodarone; RV pacing — raise preload and afterload, reduce inotropy and ectopy, keep AV synchrony.** A bigger, slower, less forceful ventricle with a higher aortic pressure keeps the mitral leaflet out of the outflow tract; inotropes and vasodilators make the cavity smaller and the gradient larger. Takotsubo with a hyperkinetic base is the classic ICU example.

**Bradycardia: chronotropes (atropine, isoprenaline, dopamine, dobutamine, adrenaline), temporary pacing; treat the cause.** Look for inferior ischaemia, drugs (beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, digoxin) and hyperkalaemia.

**Pericardial tamponade: fluid bolus, norepinephrine; pericardiocentesis or a surgical window is the definitive treatment.** Fluid and pressor only buy time; avoid positive pressure ventilation if possible, because it further limits filling.
mimic: LVOT obstruction vs LV pump failure
Both are cold and hypotensive; LVOTO has a small hyperdynamic LV, systolic anterior motion and a high outflow gradient, and gets worse with dobutamine.
traps: “Takotsubo with hypotension — dobutamine or norepinephrine”
With LVOT obstruction, phenylephrine (pure α) raises afterload without inotropy; dobutamine worsens the gradient.
decode: Takotsubo after near-drowning, hypotension with LVOTO: best vasopressor [Marrow]
Phenylephrine.
CS-33.punch: LVOT obstruction is the exception: fill it, constrict it with phenylephrine, slow it — and never give an inotrope.

CS-34.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Revascularisation → Stabilisation, anatomy, culprit vessel
CS-34.intro: Step 6’s decisive treatment in infarct shock: open the culprit artery. Two real questions, both asking what changes survival, and the device distractors pulled two thirds of the cohort away.
why: **Stabilisation and resuscitation: IV fluids, oxygenation and ventilation, reperfusion and revascularisation, fibrinolysis vs PCI, PCI strategy, antithrombotic drugs, CABG.** Fibrinolysis is for when primary PCI cannot happen in time; it works less well in shock because low pressure limits drug delivery to the clot.
**15% have left main lesions; more than 50% have triple-vessel disease.** Shock usually means extensive coronary disease, so non-culprit vessels can no longer compensate.

**Culprit-vessel mortality: left main 78.6%, saphenous vein graft 69.7%, circumflex 42.4%, LAD 42.3%, RCA 37.4%.** Left main occlusion threatens most of the LV; the RCA usually supplies less LV muscle. Circumflex and LAD are effectively equal.

**Default primary PCI; rarely, depending on resources, CABG ± PCI or emergent transplantation.** ESC 2023 gives immediate angiography and culprit PCI a class I recommendation, with emergency CABG if the anatomy is not suitable. Routine IABP is class III (ESC 2023, ACC/AHA 2025); the 2025 ACC/AHA guideline gives a microaxial pump (Impella) class 2a in selected STEMI shock after DanGer Shock (180-day death 45.8% vs 58.5%, at the cost of more bleeding, limb ischaemia and RRT), and routine VA-ECMO class 3 after ECLS-SHOCK (30-day death 47.8% vs 49.0%, more bleeding).
mimic: Revascularisation vs device support
Revascularisation treats the cause and saves lives (SHOCK); devices support the circulation while the cause is fixed.
traps: “Severe biventricular failure, EF 12%, VT — insert an LVAD or IABP first”
IABP and LV devices support one ventricle and fix nothing; with a large troponin rise and a likely ischaemic cause, urgent angiography comes first (37% right).
“High-dose dopamine, adrenaline or IABP improves survival in STEMI shock”
Only early reperfusion has proven survival benefit.
decode: Intubated, pressors, troponin 2.5, recurrent VT, EF 12% biventricular [DocT GT]
Urgent coronary angiography with intent to revascularise (37%).
Large anterior STEMI, BP 72/40, rising lactate: what most improves survival? [DocT GT]
Early coronary reperfusion.
CS-34.punch: In infarct shock, opening the culprit artery is the treatment that saves lives; drugs and devices only keep the patient alive until it is done.

CS-35.intro: Step 6’s founding trial. SHOCK (1999) is why infarct shock goes to the cath lab, even though its primary end point was negative. Not asked directly here, but CS-34 questions rest on it.
why: **Strong evidence for early revascularisation (PCI) in cardiogenic shock.** Early revascularisation meant PCI or CABG; well over a third of those revascularised had CABG, with similar survival.
**n = 302, MI complicated by cardiogenic shock, randomised.** Shock within 36 h of MI, randomised within 12 h of its onset; mostly STEMI with LV failure.
**Overall 30-day mortality was SIMILAR.** 46.7% vs 56.0% (p 0.11): a 9-point difference the trial was not large enough to prove; in patients under 75 it was significant (41.4% vs 56.8%).
**Revascularisation 50.3% vs medical therapy 63.1%.** These are the 6-month figures (p 0.027); at 1 year about 53% vs 66%.
**The 6-month and 1-year differences WERE significant.** The benefit persisted at 6 years: about 13 lives saved per 100 treated.

**Successful vs unsuccessful PCI: 35% vs 80% mortality.** The SHOCK PCI analysis (Webb 2003) gives one-year mortality of 39% if PCI succeeded vs 85% if it failed; by final flow, 38% with TIMI 3, 55% with TIMI 2 and 100% with TIMI 0–1. Either way, an open artery is what decides survival.
mimic: SHOCK vs CULPRIT-SHOCK
SHOCK: revascularise early (vs medical stabilisation); CULPRIT-SHOCK: revascularise the culprit only (vs all lesions).
traps: “SHOCK was negative, so early revascularisation is unproven”
The 30-day result missed significance, but 6-month and later survival was clearly better; it is a positive trial in practice.
decode: SHOCK trial: primary end point result [pattern]
No significant 30-day difference; significant benefit at 6 and 12 months.
CS-35.punch: SHOCK missed its 30-day end point but showed a lasting survival gain from early revascularisation, and success depends on actually opening the artery.

CS-36.intro: Step 6’s second question once the patient is on the table: open only the culprit or every lesion? CULPRIT-SHOCK (2017) answered it for shock. Not asked directly.
why: **n = 706; STEMI or NSTEMI with shock and an identifiable culprit lesion.** All had multivessel disease.
**Primary end point: death or renal failure needing dialysis at 30 days.**

**9.5% absolute risk reduction.** 45.9% culprit-only vs 55.4% immediate multivessel PCI (NNT 11), driven mainly by death. At 1 year the mortality gap (50.0% vs 56.9%) was no longer statistically significant, and the culprit-only group had more repeat revascularisation and heart-failure readmission.

**It contradicted widespread practice.** Guidelines had allowed multivessel PCI in shock; ESC now recommends culprit-only PCI at the index procedure in shock, with staged PCI of other lesions considered (IIa). Extra contrast, longer procedures and more ischaemia from multiple interventions in a failing heart are the likely reasons.
**Complete revascularisation benefit comes from NON-shock patients: DANAMI-3-PRIMULTI, PRAMI, CvLPRIT** (and later COMPLETE).
mimic: Shock vs stable STEMI
In shock, culprit only (CULPRIT-SHOCK); in haemodynamically stable STEMI, complete revascularisation (PRAMI, CvLPRIT, DANAMI-3-PRIMULTI, COMPLETE).
traps: “Complete revascularisation at the index PCI is preferred in shock”
Not in shock: culprit-only reduced 30-day death or dialysis by 9.5%.
decode: AMI shock with multivessel disease: PCI strategy [pattern]
Culprit lesion only, staged later if needed.
CS-36.punch: In cardiogenic shock open the culprit artery only; complete revascularisation belongs to stable patients.

topups.q: Chronic HF by LVEF — which drugs improve prognosis, and which only relieve symptoms?
a: - Classes: HFrEF ≤40% · HFmrEF 41–49% · HFpEF ≥50% (plus structural/diastolic abnormality or raised natriuretic peptides).

- HFrEF: four pillars started together, before discharge once stable after a decompensation — ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan beat enalapril in PARADIGM-HF) or ACEi/ARB, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor; each cuts death and HF admission.
- HFpEF/HFmrEF: SGLT2 inhibitor is the class I outcome drug (EMPEROR-Preserved, DELIVER); treat BP, AF and comorbidities.
- Loop diuretics relieve congestion in every class but do not change survival.
- No mortality benefit: digoxin (fewer admissions only), nitrates; IV inotropes (milrinone) raise mortality.
topups.src: DocT Heart Failure Q8; DocT Heart Failure Q14; DocT Heart Failure Q18; DocT Heart Failure Q19; DocT Heart Failure Q25; DocT GT AIM1 Q17

x.sub: Cardiogenic shock → After the shock → Chronic HF drugs by LVEF
x.intro: Step 5 ends where the shock does: the survivor goes home with heart failure, and the drugs that change survival are not the ones used in the ICU. The ejection fraction sorts the patient, and the exam asks which drugs prolong life and which only relieve symptoms. Six DocT questions, one of them answered correctly by fewer than a third.
why: **Classes: HFrEF ≤40%, HFmrEF 41–49%, HFpEF ≥50% (plus a structural or diastolic abnormality or raised natriuretic peptides).** The cut-offs are ESC 2021. A normal EF alone does not make the diagnosis; HFpEF needs objective evidence of raised filling pressure or a stiff ventricle, because breathlessness with a normal EF has many other causes.

**HFrEF: four pillars started together, before discharge once stable after a decompensation — ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan beat enalapril in PARADIGM-HF) or ACEi/ARB, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor; each cuts death and HF admission.** Each blocks a different limb of the spiral on CS-17: RAAS (ACEi, ARB, ARNI, MRA), the sympathetic system (β-blocker), and sodium and glucose handling (SGLT2 inhibitor), while neprilysin inhibition boosts the natriuretic peptides. Their benefits add up, so the old ‘start one, titrate, then add the next’ sequence has been replaced by starting all four quickly (ESC 2023: rapid up-titration after an admission, I-B).

**HFpEF/HFmrEF: an SGLT2 inhibitor is the class I outcome drug (EMPEROR-Preserved, DELIVER); treat BP, AF and comorbidities.** The benefit is mainly fewer HF admissions (with CV death in the composite); ESC 2023 made it class I-A. ACE inhibitors and β-blockers have no proven outcome benefit in HFpEF.
**Loop diuretics relieve congestion in every class but do not change survival.** They are the first treatment for the wet patient (CS-26) but not a prognostic drug.

**No mortality benefit: digoxin (fewer admissions only), nitrates; IV inotropes (milrinone) raise mortality.** Digoxin in DIG reduced HF admissions without changing death. Nitrates alone do not prolong life (hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate does, in ACE-inhibitor-intolerant and in self-identified Black patients). Chronic or repeated inotropes raise oxygen demand and arrhythmia: oral milrinone increased mortality (PROMISE), and IV milrinone gave no benefit with more hypotension and AF (OPTIME-CHF).
mimic: Prognostic vs symptomatic drugs
Prognostic: ARNI/ACEi/ARB, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor; symptomatic: diuretics, digoxin, nitrates.
HFrEF vs HFpEF treatment
HFrEF has four prognostic pillars; HFpEF has one (SGLT2 inhibitor) plus diuretics and comorbidity control.
traps: “HFrEF, EF 30%: which drug reduces mortality — ACE inhibitor (not β-blocker)” (DocT key)

Both reduce mortality (class I); DocT keys the ACE inhibitor because it is ‘typically started first’, which is outdated (only 30% chose the key). Choose ‘both’ or ARNI if offered; if forced, DocT’s key is the ACE inhibitor.
“HFpEF: diuretics improve symptoms and prognosis”
DocT keys diuretics (82% and 73%) because no SGLT2 inhibitor is offered; diuretics only treat symptoms. On a current paper, the prognostic drug is the SGLT2 inhibitor.
“IV milrinone reduces rehospitalisation”
It does not; ACE inhibitors and β-blockers do (87%).
decode: HFrEF stabilised after decompensation: which therapy improves long-term survival? [DocT GT]
Sacubitril/valsartan (90%).
HFrEF, EF 30%, stable: which drug reduces mortality? [DocT QBank]
DocT: ACE inhibitor (30%); really ACEi and β-blocker both.
HFrEF, EF 35%: what reduces rehospitalisation? [DocT QBank]
ACE inhibitors and β-blockers (87%).
HFpEF with congestion, BP 140/85 or 160/95 [DocT QBank ×2]
Diuretics as the least-wrong option (82%, 73%).
x.punch: In HFrEF four drugs — ARNI or ACEi, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor — all prolong life and start together; in HFpEF only the SGLT2 inhibitor changes outcome, and diuretics, digoxin and inotropes never do.

spine: Defining the shock
Cardiogenic shock is a primary cardiac problem with hypoperfusion proven clinically and biochemically, and SHOCK, IABP-SHOCK II, ESC and SCAI each draw that line slightly differently.
Who gets it and why
Acute MI with large muscle loss or a mechanical complication is the classic cause, but heart failure, valves, rhythm, obstruction and toxins fill the other branches.
The spiral of the failing pump
A weaker ventricle moves its pressure–volume loop to the right, and the sympathetic and renin systems that defend the pressure raise afterload and preload until they injure the heart further.
Profiling at the bedside
Cold or warm (perfusion) and wet or dry (congestion), confirmed by echo, lactate, wedge pressure and serial monitoring, sort the patient and choose the treatment.
Support the circulation
Unload congestion with nitrates, diuretics and positive pressure, add an inotrope for low output and norepinephrine for low pressure, and pick the drug by phenotype.
Fix the lesion behind it
Valve and mechanical lesions need their own haemodynamic rules and a definitive repair, and in AMI shock early culprit-vessel revascularisation is the only treatment proven to save lives.
CVS03.primer: Shock means the tissues get less oxygen than they need; in cardiogenic shock the reason is the heart itself, not the volume in the vessels or their tone. Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume, and stroke volume depends on preload (filling), afterload (the load the ventricle ejects against) and contractility. Blood pressure is cardiac output times systemic vascular resistance, so a failing heart can hold a normal pressure for a while by clamping down the vessels, which is why hypoperfusion, not hypotension, is the heart of every modern definition. The wedge pressure (PCWP) stands in for left-sided filling pressure, and the cardiac index is cardiac output divided by body surface area.

CS-37.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Mechanical circulatory support → Bridge strategies
CS-37.intro: Step 1 is why support is started at all: every device is a bridge, and the strategy names where the bridge leads. Not asked directly; it frames stems that describe a patient and ask what the support is for.
why: **Bridge to decision: uncertain suitability for transplant or long-term MCS; first goal haemodynamic stability so reversibility of organ failure and contraindications can be assessed.** The typical VA ECMO situation after a crash: neurology after arrest, kidneys and liver are unknown, so support first and decide later.
**Bridge to bridge: a provisional plan to move to long-term MCS once stabilised.** Typically ECMO or Impella now, a durable LVAD once organ function has recovered enough for surgery.
**Bridge to transplant: listed or known candidates, supported to prevent organ dysfunction until a donor heart is available.** Keeping the kidneys and liver intact keeps the patient transplantable.

**Bridge to recovery: potentially reversible myocardial dysfunction (e.g. myocarditis), supported until function allows weaning.** Fulminant myocarditis, stunning after reperfusion, takotsubo and post-cardiotomy failure are the classic settings.
mimic: Bridge to transplant vs destination therapy
Bridge to transplant expects a donor heart; destination therapy is a durable LVAD in a patient who will never be transplanted (CS-54, CS-55).
traps: “Bridge strategies are always short-term devices”
The card’s watch line says so, but in ESC terminology bridge to transplant is often a durable LVAD; the strategy is a destination, not a device class.
decode: Young man, fulminant myocarditis, VA ECMO placed: the strategy? [pattern]
Bridge to recovery — reversible myocardium.
Post-arrest, unknown neurology, on ECMO: the strategy? [pattern]
Bridge to decision.
CS-37.punch: The bridge is named by its far end: decision when the future is unknown, recovery when the heart may heal, transplant when a donor is awaited, bridge when a durable pump is next.

CS-38.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Mechanical circulatory support → Haemodynamic goals
CS-38.intro: Step 1, the goals. Every device is judged against the same three, and the devices differ mainly in the second one. Not asked directly.
why: **Maintenance of end-organ perfusion.** Flow and pressure to brain, kidney and gut; this is what stops the lactate rising and the patient sliding from SCAI C to D.

**Ventricular unloading — less ventricular volume, wall stress, myocardial work and oxygen consumption.** Wall stress rises with pressure and radius (Laplace), so emptying the ventricle cuts oxygen demand in an ischaemic, failing heart and may limit infarct size.
**Enhanced myocardial perfusion.** Coronary flow depends on aortic diastolic pressure minus LV end-diastolic pressure; raising the first (IABP) or lowering the second (unloading) both help.
mimic: Perfusion vs unloading
VA ECMO gives the most perfusion but raises afterload and can fail to unload (CS-52); Impella both perfuses and unloads.
traps: “More flow means a better-supported heart”
Flow serves the organs; the heart is helped only if the device also unloads it.
decode: Which haemodynamic goal does peripheral VA ECMO fail? [pattern]
Ventricular unloading.
CS-38.punch: Support has to do three things — perfuse the organs, unload the ventricle and feed the coronaries — and devices that do the first need not do the second.

CS-39.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Mechanical circulatory support → Percutaneous devices
CS-39.intro: Step 2 opens with the common ground: percutaneous devices can go in fast in the cath lab, and they share one list of complications that comes from large-bore arterial access, anticoagulation and blood passing through a pump. Not asked directly.
why: **Inserted percutaneously or surgically; the purely percutaneous route allows rapid deployment without specific surgical training.** An interventional cardiologist can place an IABP, Impella CP or peripheral ECMO in minutes, which matters when the shock is in the cath lab.

**Each device carries a profile of complications that may limit its success.** The choice is a trade between support and harm: in DanGer Shock the Impella saved lives but roughly quadrupled the composite of device-related adverse events (24.0% vs 6.2%).

**Limb ischaemia, bleeding, embolic phenomena (stroke), infection, haemolysis.** Limb ischaemia and bleeding scale with sheath size (7–8 Fr IABP vs 14 Fr Impella CP vs 15–25 Fr ECMO cannulae); stroke comes from clot on the device or in a stagnant aortic root; haemolysis from shear in rotary pumps, worst with Impella (CS-46).
mimic: Generic vs device-specific complication
Limb ischaemia, bleeding and pseudoaneurysm come with any femoral sheath; haemolysis is the one tied to the pump itself.
traps: “Percutaneous means low-risk”
Large-bore arterial access is the main source of harm; ECLS-SHOCK and DanGer Shock both had more bleeding and limb ischaemia with the device.
decode: Common complications of percutaneous MCS: all except? [pattern]
The five are limb ischaemia, bleeding, stroke, infection and haemolysis; anything else (e.g. neuropathy) is the odd one out.
CS-39.punch: Percutaneous devices go in quickly without a surgeon, but large sheaths, anticoagulation and pumps bring limb ischaemia, bleeding, stroke, infection and haemolysis.

CS-40.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Mechanical circulatory support → PV loops with devices
CS-40.intro: Step 3 is the pressure–volume loop. The card is a sketch; the words below are what the sketch should show, so each device can be drawn from its mechanism. Not asked directly, but CS-41 and CS-52 test the conclusions.
why: **IABP: the blue loop sits slightly lower and slightly wider than the green baseline, with a flatter Ea line.** Systolic deflation lowers the pressure the LV ejects against, so peak pressure falls, Ea falls and stroke volume rises a little; end-diastolic volume falls slightly. The change is small, matching the ‘modest’ effects on CS-43.

**pLVAD (Impella / TandemHeart): the loop moves left and shrinks.** End-diastolic volume and pressure fall because the device drains the ventricle (Impella) or the atrium (TandemHeart). With Impella the ventricle empties continuously, so the isovolumic phases disappear and the loop turns triangular; at high flow aortic pressure is held up by the pump while the LV’s own stroke volume falls.

**Peripheral VA ECMO: the loop moves right and up and narrows, with a steeper Ea.** Retrograde arterial flow raises aortic pressure, so the weak LV ejects less, end-systolic and end-diastolic volumes rise, and LVEDP climbs. In a very weak LV the aortic valve may stop opening and the loop collapses into a tall, narrow shape — the distended, unvented ventricle.
mimic: IABP vs pLVAD loop
IABP keeps the loop’s shape and nudges it down and wider; pLVAD shrinks it and shifts it left.
traps: “VA ECMO unloads the left ventricle because it bypasses the heart”
It unloads the right heart; for the LV it adds afterload, so the loop moves up and right.
decode: PV loop shifted rightward and upward with a steeper Ea after device insertion — which device? [pattern]
Peripheral VA ECMO.
CS-40.punch: Draw the IABP loop slightly lower and wider, the pLVAD loop smaller and shifted left, and the peripheral ECMO loop narrower, higher and shifted right.

CS-41.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Mechanical circulatory support → PV loop interpretation
CS-41.intro: Step 3, reading the loops: what each device does to stroke work and myocardial oxygen consumption, the two numbers that decide whether the heart itself is helped. Not asked directly.
why: **IABP: wider PV loop area, increased stroke volume.** ‘Wider’ is the stroke volume; because peak pressure also falls, the enclosed area (stroke work) and the pressure–volume area change little or fall modestly, which is why CS-43 lists a modest fall in stroke work and oxygen consumption.

**Impella / TandemHeart: smaller loop area, a significant fall in LV stroke work and myocardial oxygen consumption.** The pump does the work the ventricle used to do; lower volume and pressure shrink both the loop and the pressure–volume area. This is the mechanical basis for unloading.

**Peripheral ECMO: loop not unloaded; increased arterial elastance and stroke work, MVO2 unchanged or rising.** A higher afterload with a larger end-systolic volume enlarges the pressure–volume area, so oxygen demand stays the same or climbs while the organs are well perfused.
mimic: Loop width vs loop area
Width is stroke volume; area is stroke work. The IABP widens the loop but lowers its height.
traps: “A bigger loop on the IABP means more work for the heart”
The wider loop reflects a larger stroke volume at a lower pressure; oxygen consumption falls slightly, not rises.
decode: Device with greatest reduction in myocardial oxygen consumption? [pattern]
pLVAD (Impella or TandemHeart) — smallest loop and pressure–volume area.
CS-41.punch: The pLVAD shrinks the loop and the oxygen bill, the IABP widens it at a lower pressure for a modest gain, and peripheral ECMO leaves the LV working as hard or harder.

CS-42.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Mechanical circulatory support → IABP mechanism
CS-42.intro: Step 4 is the balloon pump, the most-asked card in this deck. Counterpulsation means the balloon does the opposite of the heart: it fills in diastole and empties in systole. Three Grand Test questions came from it — practicalities, timing errors and contraindications — and fewer than half got the practicalities right.
why: **Diastole: the balloon inflates, displacing blood volume, augmenting native stroke volume and enhancing coronary blood flow.** A 30–50 mL helium balloon in the descending aorta (tip about 2 cm below the top of the arch, beyond the left subclavian, ending above the renal arteries) inflates at aortic valve closure. The displaced blood raises aortic diastolic pressure (diastolic augmentation), and since the LV is perfused mainly in diastole, coronary pressure rises. Helium is used because its low density lets the balloon fill and empty within one beat.

**Systole: rapid deflation reduces LV afterload and increases LV stroke volume.** Collapsing the balloon just before the aortic valve opens leaves a space the LV ejects into, so end-diastolic aortic pressure (the pressure the LV must exceed) falls and the ventricle empties further for less work.

**Synchronised with the ECG.** The R wave triggers deflation and inflation follows at the T wave; the arterial pressure waveform (dicrotic notch) or a pacing spike can trigger instead. A regular rhythm is needed: in fast or irregular rhythms timing slips, so ‘requires an unstable rhythm’ is the reverse of the truth.
mimic: IABP vs Impella insertion
IABP: 7–8 Fr femoral sheath, femoral artery ≥4 mm. Impella CP: 14 Fr sheath, needs a larger vessel.
traps: “Usual sheath size is 13–14 Fr” (chosen by many; 46% got the question)
That is Impella CP and ECMO territory; the IABP goes through a 7–8 Fr femoral sheath, and the femoral artery must be over about 4 mm to avoid limb ischaemia.
“Implant beyond 2 weeks is safe”
Usual support is days; beyond 1–2 weeks limb ischaemia, infection and thrombocytopenia rise.
“Severe LV dysfunction or CAD contraindicates the IABP”

Those are its indications. The absolute contraindications are moderate–severe aortic regurgitation (diastolic inflation drives more blood back into the LV), aortic dissection and severe aorto-iliac disease (79% got this).
decode: IABP in cardiogenic shock: which is true — >2 weeks safe, femoral artery >4 mm, 13–14 Fr sheath, needs unstable rhythm? [DocT GT]
Femoral artery >4 mm (46%).
Inflation occurs before aortic valve closure: consequence? [DocT GT]
Increased LV workload — inflation against ejection raises afterload.
Contraindication to IABP after MI? [DocT GT]
Aortic regurgitation (79%).
CS-42.punch: The balloon inflates at the dicrotic notch to push blood into the coronaries and deflates just before systole to lower afterload; it needs a 7–8 Fr sheath, a regular rhythm and a competent aortic valve.

parts.q: Blood appears in the IABP gas line. What next?
parts.a: Balloon rupture: stop pumping, clamp the line and remove the balloon at once (helium embolism; clot inside can trap it); never reinsert the same balloon. A stationary balloon is thrombogenic, so never leave it switched off in situ.

CS-43.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Mechanical circulatory support → IABP effects
CS-43.intro: Step 4, what the balloon actually achieves. Every effect is modest, which is why it helps a borderline patient and fails a crashing one. Not asked directly; the comparison tables (CS-50, CS-51) carry these numbers into questions.
why: **Modest rise in SV and cardiac output.** The balloon moves only its own volume (30–50 mL) per beat and depends on the LV still ejecting; it adds no flow of its own.
**Modest fall in LVEDP, LV wall stress, stroke work and myocardial oxygen consumption.** Lower afterload lets the ventricle empty further, so end-diastolic pressure and wall tension fall slightly.
**Rise in diastolic BP with more coronary perfusion.** Coronary perfusion pressure is aortic diastolic pressure minus LVEDP, and the balloon raises the first and lowers the second.

**Up to 1 L/min more cardiac output, depending on balloon size and patient interaction.** ‘Interaction’ means heart rate, rhythm, aortic compliance and residual LV function; a stiff aorta, tachycardia or a nearly silent LV all shrink the gain.
**Decreases afterload; easily available and cost-effective.** It is the only device in the comparison table that lowers afterload (CS-51), and it is cheap, small-bore and familiar.
mimic: IABP vs Impella output
IABP adds 0.5–1 L/min and needs a beating LV; Impella CP adds up to about 3.5–4.3 L/min independent of LV ejection.
traps: “The IABP can support a heart in VF or asystole”
It augments only what the ventricle ejects; without ejection there is nothing to augment, unlike Impella or ECMO.
decode: Maximum increase in cardiac output with IABP? [pattern]
About 0.5–1 L/min (up to 1 L/min).
Which MCS device decreases afterload? [pattern]
IABP.
CS-43.punch: The IABP raises diastolic pressure and lowers afterload, but adds at most about 1 L/min and only to a heart that is still ejecting.

CS-44.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Mechanical circulatory support → IABP-SHOCK II trial
CS-44.intro: Step 4 ends with the evidence. IABP-SHOCK II (2012) is the trial that took the balloon pump off the routine list, and its derived risk score is what Marrow asked. CS-04 used its entry criteria as a definition; this card is its result.
why: **No difference in 30-day mortality, IABP vs no IABP.** 39.7% vs 41.3% (RR 0.96, p 0.69). The null result held at 12 months (52% vs 51%, RR 1.01) and 6 years (66.3% vs 67.0%), so it is not a short-follow-up artefact.
**AMI-related cardiogenic shock.** 600 patients at 37 German centres, all with planned early revascularisation (PCI in nearly all); most balloons (86.6%) went in after PCI.

**IABP is not routinely recommended in cardiogenic shock.** ESC 2023 ACS: routine IABP without mechanical complications class III; IABP for shock from a mechanical complication (VSD, papillary rupture) IIa. ACC/AHA 2025: routine IABP class 3 (no benefit).

**Major limitation: only mild to moderate cardiogenic shock was included.** The trial excluded the sickest (CPR >30 min, fixed dilated pupils, no intrinsic cardiac activity), and its 40% mortality was lower than registry figures, though 45% had been resuscitated, so ‘mild’ is the textbook shorthand. Other criticisms: open label, about 10% crossover, and IABP timing and escalation to LVADs left to the operator.
mimic: IABP-SHOCK II vs CULPRIT-SHOCK
IABP-SHOCK II tested the balloon (null); CULPRIT-SHOCK tested culprit-only PCI vs multivessel PCI (culprit-only won).
traps: “Prior MI is part of the IABP-SHOCK II score”
It is not; prior stroke is. The six are age, prior stroke, glucose, creatinine, post-PCI TIMI flow and lactate.
“IABP-SHOCK II proved the balloon is useless in all shock”
It showed no benefit from routine use in AMI shock; the most severe shock was not tested, and IABP keeps a IIa role for mechanical complications.
decode: IABP-SHOCK II score components: all except? [Marrow]
Prior MI.
IABP vs medical therapy in AMI cardiogenic shock — 30-day mortality? [pattern]
No difference (39.7 vs 41.3%).
CS-44.punch: IABP-SHOCK II found no survival benefit from the balloon in AMI shock at 30 days, 1 year or 6 years, so routine IABP is class III — with the caveat that the sickest patients were never tested.

CS-45.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Mechanical circulatory support → Impella mechanism
CS-45.intro: Step 2, the microaxial pump. Impella is a catheter-mounted motor that sits across the aortic valve and lifts blood out of the LV, which is why it unloads the ventricle directly. Not asked directly.
why: **Transvalvular axial flow pump placed across the aortic valve.** A small impeller spins at very high speed inside the catheter, like a ship’s propeller in a tube.
**Displaces blood directly from the LV into the ascending aorta.** Flow is antegrade and in series with the LV, so it lowers LV volume and pressure without raising afterload.

**Tip in the left ventricle.** The inlet sits in the LV cavity (about 3.5 cm below the aortic valve annulus for the 2.5 and CP) and the outlet in the aortic root; position is checked by echo, because a migrated inlet causes suction and haemolysis.

**Catheter diameter 9 Fr; peak flow up to 4.3 L/min.** These are Impella CP figures: 9 Fr catheter, 14 Fr pump head (so a 14 Fr sheath). The 2.5 gives 2.5 L/min; the 5.5 gives up to 5.5 L/min via axillary cutdown and is labelled for 14 days (CP for 4 days).
mimic: Impella vs TandemHeart
Impella drains the LV across the aortic valve; TandemHeart drains the left atrium through the septum.
traps: “The 9 Fr catheter means a 9 Fr sheath”
The pump head is 14 Fr for the CP; the sheath must fit the pump, not the catheter.
decode: Axial flow pump placed across the aortic valve? [pattern]
Impella.
CS-45.punch: Impella is an axial pump across the aortic valve that draws blood from the LV and delivers it to the ascending aorta — 2.5 to 5.5 L/min depending on the model.

CS-46.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Mechanical circulatory support → Impella effects
CS-46.intro: Step 5 is matching device to patient, and Impella’s contraindications and signature complication follow from its position across the valve and its spinning rotor. Two Grand Test questions: the contraindication (92% right) and the unique complication (39% right).
why: **Significant increase in cardiac output.** Up to 2.5–5.5 L/min by model, delivered whether or not the LV ejects. In DanGer Shock (STEMI shock, Impella CP) 180-day mortality fell from 58.5% to 45.8% (HR 0.74); ACC/AHA 2025 made a microaxial pump class 2a in selected STEMI with severe or refractory shock. ISAR-SHOCK (n 26) had shown better haemodynamics than IABP (cardiac index +0.49 vs +0.11) but the same mortality.
**Decrease in LVEDP, LV wall stress and myocardial oxygen consumption.** It empties the ventricle in series, so volume, pressure and oxygen demand all fall (CS-41).

**Contraindication: mechanical aortic valve.** The catheter must sit across the valve: it can jam a mechanical leaflet or be damaged by it. The label also lists LV mural thrombus (sucked into the pump and embolised), aortic stenosis with an orifice ≤0.6 cm², moderate–severe AR (the pump recirculates the regurgitant blood), severe peripheral arterial disease, ASD or VSD, significant RV failure, LV rupture and tamponade.

**Risk of haemolysis.** Shear from the rotor, made worse by suction when the LV is underfilled or the inlet is against the wall. Watch plasma free haemoglobin, urine colour and LDH; reposition under echo, give volume or lower the performance level.
mimic: Device-specific vs access complication
Haemolysis comes from the pump; pseudoaneurysm, bleeding and limb ischaemia come from any large femoral sheath.
traps: “Pseudoaneurysm or septicaemia is the unique Impella complication” (only 39% chose haemolysis)
Both happen with any femoral device; haemolysis is the one tied to the Impella rotor.
“Post-cardiotomy failure or acute myocarditis contraindicates Impella”
Those are labelled indications; severe aortic stenosis and a mechanical aortic valve are the bars (92% right).
decode: Cardiogenic shock with severe AS and prior mechanical AVR: contraindication to Impella? [DocT GT]
Severe aortic stenosis (92%) — and the mechanical valve itself.
Unique complication of Impella? [DocT GT]
Haemolysis (39%).
CS-46.punch: Impella raises output and unloads the LV, but it cannot cross a mechanical or tightly stenosed aortic valve, and its rotor shears red cells — haemolysis is its signature complication.

CS-47.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Mechanical circulatory support → TandemHeart
CS-47.intro: Step 2, the left-atrial bypass. TandemHeart takes oxygenated blood from the left atrium and pumps it into the femoral artery, which explains both its effects and its contraindications. One Grand Test question, answered by everyone.
why: **Drains oxygenated blood from the left atrium and returns it to the arterial circulation.** It bypasses the LV entirely, so the ventricle is unloaded from upstream.
**A paracorporeal circuit (next to the body).** The pump sits outside the body but close to it, unlike ECMO’s bedside console.

**Drainage via a femoral venous cannula passed by transseptal puncture into the LA.** A 21 Fr inflow cannula goes up the IVC and across the atrial septum; this is the only device needing a transseptal puncture, and the hardest to insert.
**Pump strapped to the leg; return via a femoral arterial cannula.** A 15–19 Fr arterial cannula sends flow retrograde up the aorta, which is why its afterload effect is +++ on CS-51.

**Significant rise in cardiac output; fall in LVEDP, LV wall stress, LV stroke work and myocardial oxygen consumption.** A centrifugal pump gives about 4–5 L/min. Draining the atrium lowers LV preload, so the LV does less work.
mimic: TandemHeart vs VA ECMO
TandemHeart drains oxygenated blood from the LA and needs no oxygenator; VA ECMO drains venous blood from the RA and oxygenates it.
traps: “TandemHeart helps isolated RV failure”
An LA-to-artery pump needs the right heart to deliver blood to the LA; in RV failure it cannot fill.
“VSD is fine with TandemHeart”
Dropping LA and LV pressure reverses the shunt right-to-left and causes hypoxaemia; VSD, severe PVD, LA thrombus and moderate–severe AR are contraindications.
decode: Not a contraindication to TandemHeart: PVD, LV failure, VSD, RV failure? [DocT GT]
LV failure — it is the indication (100%).
Device needing transseptal puncture? [pattern]
TandemHeart.
CS-47.punch: TandemHeart drains the left atrium through the septum and returns blood to the femoral artery, so it needs a working right heart, an intact septum and good femoral vessels.

CS-48.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Mechanical circulatory support → Venoarterial ECMO
CS-48.intro: Step 2, the full bypass. VA ECMO is the only device that adds an oxygenator, so it supports both heart and lungs, but its peripheral form pumps against the LV. Not asked directly.
why: **Blood drawn from the venous system, oxygenated, and pumped into the arterial circulation.** Peripheral: femoral vein to the right atrium, through a centrifugal pump and membrane oxygenator, back into the femoral artery and retrograde up the aorta at 4–6 L/min.

**Partial or complete support to the heart, and oxygenation of the blood.** It replaces right and left heart output and lung gas exchange, so it suits shock with arrest, biventricular failure or severe hypoxaemia (ECPR). ECLS-SHOCK (2023) found no 30-day mortality benefit from early routine use in AMI shock (47.8 vs 49.0%) with more bleeding, and ACC/AHA 2025 made routine VA-ECMO class 3.
mimic: VA vs VV ECMO
VA returns blood to an artery and supports the circulation; VV returns it to a vein and supports only gas exchange.
traps: “VA ECMO unloads the failing LV”
Retrograde flow raises afterload; the LV may distend and need venting (CS-52).
decode: MCS device that also provides oxygenation? [pattern]
VA ECMO.
CS-48.punch: VA ECMO takes venous blood, oxygenates it and pumps it into the arteries, so it supports both ventricles and the lungs — at the cost of LV afterload.

CS-49.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Mechanical circulatory support → Device mechanism and insertion
CS-49.intro: Step 2 in one table: what drives each device and how it goes in. The one linked question (an IABP practicalities question, also on CS-42) turns on insertion: the femoral artery has to be big enough.
why: **IABP: pneumatic; percutaneous via the femoral artery.** A console shuttles helium in and out of the balloon. Small 7–8 Fr sheath; femoral artery ≥4 mm; balloon sized to the patient’s height.

**TandemHeart: centrifugal, paracorporeal; percutaneous femoral artery and vein with transseptal puncture, or IJ vein with a trans-pulmonary route.** The femoral transseptal route is the left-sided set-up: LA blood to the femoral artery. The internal jugular route is the right-sided set-up: a dual-lumen cannula (ProtekDuo) placed through the right IJ drains the right atrium and returns blood into the pulmonary artery, so the same pump supports the RV.
**Impella: axial, transvalvular; percutaneous or peripheral surgical.** CP goes in percutaneously through the femoral artery; the 5.5 needs a surgical cutdown with a graft on the axillary artery.
**VA ECMO: centrifugal, extracorporeal; percutaneous or peripheral surgical.** Femoral cannulae are usually placed percutaneously; open cut-down is used when vessels are small or diseased.
**Surgical VAD: centrifugal, extracorporeal; central surgical access.** Cannulae go directly into the heart and great vessels through a sternotomy, so it needs a surgeon and an operating theatre.
mimic: Pneumatic vs rotary
Only the IABP is pneumatic and moves no blood of its own; all the others spin a rotor (axial in Impella, centrifugal in the rest).
traps: “An IABP needs a 13–14 Fr sheath”
That is the Impella CP; the IABP uses 7–8 Fr through a femoral artery of at least 4 mm (46% got this right).
decode: IABP: which is true — femoral artery >4 mm? [DocT GT]
Yes — minimum femoral artery size above 4 mm (46%).
Only axial-flow device? Only pneumatic device? [pattern]
Impella; IABP.
CS-49.punch: IABP is pneumatic, Impella axial, and the rest centrifugal; all but the surgical VAD can go in percutaneously, and TandemHeart alone needs a transseptal puncture.

CS-50.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Mechanical circulatory support → Ventricle supported and flow
CS-50.intro: Step 5 begins the comparison: which ventricle each device helps and how much flow it adds. Flow is the first filter when choosing a device for worsening shock. Not asked directly.
why: **IABP LV; TandemHeart LV or RV; Impella LV or RV; VA ECMO LV and RV; surgical VAD LV and/or RV.** TandemHeart and Impella have right-sided versions (an RA-to-PA circuit; Impella RP), but each configuration supports one side; only VA ECMO supports both at once from one circuit.

**Flow: IABP 0.5–1, TandemHeart 4, Impella 2.5–5, VA ECMO >5, surgical VAD >5 L/min.** The IABP only augments; the rotary pumps generate their own flow, rising with pump size from Impella 2.5 to 5.5 and up to full output with ECMO or a surgical VAD.
mimic: Biventricular support
VA ECMO supports both ventricles together; a surgical VAD can be an LVAD, RVAD or BiVAD.
traps: “Impella and TandemHeart give the same flow as ECMO”
They give 2.5–5 and about 4 L/min; only ECMO and surgical VADs exceed 5 L/min.
decode: Device providing the least flow? Device supporting both ventricles together? [pattern]
IABP (0.5–1 L/min); VA ECMO.
CS-50.punch: Flow climbs from under 1 L/min on the IABP to 2.5–5 on Impella, about 4 on TandemHeart and over 5 on VA ECMO and surgical VADs, and only VA ECMO supports both ventricles at once.

CS-51.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Mechanical circulatory support → Afterload, gas exchange and risk
CS-51.intro: Step 5, the costs: afterload, gas exchange and complications. The table follows from where each device returns its blood. Not asked directly.
why: **Afterload: IABP – (reduces); TandemHeart +++; Impella none; VA ECMO +++; surgical VAD none.** Retrograde femoral return (TandemHeart, peripheral ECMO) pushes against the LV; antegrade return into the ascending aorta (Impella, central VAD) does not; systolic deflation (IABP) lowers it.
**Gas exchange: none except TandemHeart possible and VA ECMO +++.** An oxygenator can be spliced into the TandemHeart circuit; ECMO has one by design.
**Limb ischaemia: IABP +, TandemHeart +++, Impella ++, VA ECMO +++, surgical VAD variable.** Risk tracks the arterial sheath size; ECMO needs a distal perfusion cannula to protect the leg.
**Haemorrhage: IABP +, TandemHeart +++, Impella +++, VA ECMO +++, surgical VAD ++.** Large-bore access plus full anticoagulation; in ECLS-SHOCK moderate or severe bleeding was 23.4% vs 9.6%.
mimic: Retrograde vs antegrade return
Retrograde (femoral artery) raises afterload; antegrade (ascending aorta) does not.
traps: “All pumps raise afterload because they add flow to the aorta”
Only retrograde femoral return raises it; Impella’s antegrade flow does not, and the IABP lowers it.
decode: Which device reduces afterload? Which has the lowest bleeding and limb risk? [pattern]
IABP for both.
CS-51.punch: Where the blood re-enters decides the afterload: the IABP lowers it, Impella and central VADs leave it, and femoral TandemHeart and ECMO raise it; the IABP is also the gentlest on limbs and bleeding.

CS-52.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Mechanical circulatory support → The ECMO paradox
CS-52.intro: Step 3’s key contrast: VA ECMO gives the most flow yet does the least for the left ventricle. Not asked directly, but it is the reasoning behind LV venting and behind the ‘ECPELLA’ combination.
why: **More flow: VA ECMO (>5 L/min) vs Impella 2.5–5 L/min.** ECMO can replace the whole cardiac output.

**Impella unloads and cuts stroke work significantly; VA ECMO fails to unload and increases stroke work (MVO2 unchanged or rising).** ECMO’s retrograde flow raises aortic pressure; a weak LV then ejects less, end-diastolic pressure rises, the aortic valve may stop opening, and the LV distends with pulmonary oedema and stasis thrombus. The fixes are venting: IABP, Impella (ECPELLA) or atrial septostomy.
**Arterial elastance increases on peripheral ECMO.** A steeper Ea line on the PV loop is the picture of the higher afterload (CS-40).
**Gas exchange: VA ECMO +++, the only device.** It is the only one built with an oxygenator; TandemHeart can have one added (CS-51).
mimic: ECMO with a distending LV vs recovering LV
Loss of pulsatility, a closed aortic valve and rising wedge pressure mean the LV needs venting; returning pulsatility means it is recovering.
traps: “The device with the highest flow best protects the ischaemic heart”
VA ECMO perfuses the body but raises LV afterload and oxygen demand; Impella offers less flow but unloads.
decode: Patient on peripheral VA ECMO develops pulmonary oedema and a non-opening aortic valve — mechanism? [pattern]
Raised afterload from retrograde flow, LV distension; vent the LV.
CS-52.punch: VA ECMO delivers the most flow and the only gas exchange, but its retrograde flow raises afterload so the LV works harder, while Impella delivers less flow and genuinely unloads.

CS-53.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Beyond temporary support → Indications for cardiac transplantation
CS-53.intro: Step 6 is where the bridge leads when the heart does not recover. Transplant is for end-stage disease of any of three kinds. Not asked directly.
why: **Advanced heart failure from ischaemic heart disease or dilated cardiomyopathy.** These two make up most adult transplants.

**Diastolic dysfunction from restrictive or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.** A stiff, small ventricle is poorly suited to an LVAD (there is little cavity to drain and the inflow cannula sucks down), so transplant is usually the only replacement.
**Heart failure from congenital heart disease.** Failing single-ventricle or systemic-RV circulations reach a point where only a new heart helps.
mimic: Transplant vs LVAD candidates
Dilated, ischaemic hearts can take either; restrictive or hypertrophic hearts with small cavities usually need transplant.
traps: “Restrictive cardiomyopathy is an LVAD indication”
A small, stiff cavity gives the pump nothing to drain; transplant is the option.
decode: Indications for cardiac transplantation: all except? [pattern]
The three are advanced ischaemic/dilated HF, restrictive/hypertrophic diastolic failure and congenital heart disease.
CS-53.punch: Transplant is for end-stage systolic failure (ischaemic or dilated), diastolic failure (restrictive or hypertrophic) and failed congenital hearts.

CS-54.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Beyond temporary support → Long-term MCS
CS-54.intro: Step 6, the durable pump. An implantable LVAD is the alternative when there is no heart to transplant or the patient cannot have one. Not asked directly.
why: **Implantable LVADs may be an alternative to heart transplantation.** As destination therapy for patients who are not candidates, or a bridge while they wait.

**The little data beyond 2 years suggests they are not as good as transplantation.** That was true of older pumps; MOMENTUM 3 now gives 5-year data for the HeartMate 3: survival 58.4% (vs 43.7% for the older axial HeartMate II). Transplant still does better, with a median survival of about 12.5 years in the ISHLT registry, so the card’s conclusion stands even though the data gap has closed.
mimic: Destination therapy vs bridge to transplant
Same pump; the difference is whether a donor heart is expected (CS-37).
traps: “A modern LVAD matches transplant survival”
Five-year LVAD survival is around 58%, well below transplant.
decode: LVAD vs transplant long-term outcome? [pattern]
LVAD inferior; transplant remains the better long-term option.
CS-54.punch: A durable LVAD is an alternative to transplant, not an equal: even the best pump gives about 58% survival at five years.

CS-55.sub: Cardiogenic shock → Beyond temporary support → Management algorithm
CS-55.intro: Step 6 ties the deck together: the AHA (2017) hub-and-spoke ladder that runs from drugs to a durable pump, with recovery and palliation as exits. Not asked directly.
why: **Spoke hospital → cardiogenic shock hub hospital.** Spokes stabilise and transfer; hubs offer 24/7 cath lab, MCS, surgery and transplant/LVAD services. Higher-volume centres have lower shock mortality.
**Rung 1, resuscitation and medical therapy: inotropes/vasopressors, mechanical ventilation, aetiology-specific medical therapy.** Norepinephrine for pressure, an inotrope for low output (CVS03).

**Rung 2, reperfusion for ACS only: PCI, CABG, fibrinolysis.** Only shock caused by infarction has a culprit to open. Early revascularisation was the first treatment shown to improve survival (SHOCK, at 6 and 12 months), and CULPRIT-SHOCK showed culprit-only PCI beats immediate multivessel PCI.

**Rung 3, temporary MCS: IABP, peripheral VAD, ECMO, implantable VAD.** Chosen by the flow and unloading needed (CS-50, CS-51); routine IABP and routine VA-ECMO are class 3 in ACC/AHA 2025, a microaxial pump 2a in selected STEMI shock.
**Rung 4, durable VAD: transplant or destination VAD.** For the heart that does not recover.
**Recovery and palliation are exits at every rung, in both directions.** A patient may wean at any rung, or the team may decide escalation no longer serves the patient.
mimic: Temporary vs durable MCS rung
Temporary devices bridge (days to weeks); durable VADs are destinations or long bridges to transplant.
traps: “Reperfusion is a step for every cardiogenic shock”
Only for ACS; shock from myocarditis or cardiomyopathy skips to temporary MCS.
decode: Which rung applies only to ACS? [pattern]
Reperfusion (PCI, CABG, fibrinolysis).
CS-55.punch: The ladder runs medical therapy, reperfusion for ACS only, temporary MCS, then transplant or a destination VAD, with recovery and palliation open at every rung.

spine: Why support the pump
Mechanical support buys time for a defined destination — recovery, a decision, a transplant or a durable pump — by keeping organs perfused, unloading the ventricle and feeding the coronaries.
How each device moves blood

The IABP is a pneumatic counterpulsation balloon, Impella an axial pump across the aortic valve, TandemHeart a centrifugal pump draining the left atrium, and VA ECMO a centrifugal circuit with an oxygenator.
What the loop shows
On the pressure–volume loop the IABP lowers pressure and modestly raises stroke volume, a pLVAD shrinks the loop and the work, and peripheral VA ECMO pushes it up and to the right.
The balloon pump
The IABP inflates in diastole and deflates just before systole, gives under 1 L/min, and IABP-SHOCK II showed no survival benefit, so routine use is now class III.
Matching the device to the patient
Flow, which ventricle is supported, afterload, gas exchange and the complication profile decide the device, and every device has anatomical contraindications.
Beyond temporary support
When the heart does not recover, the ladder ends in transplant or a destination LVAD, with palliation available at every rung.
CVS04.primer: Mechanical circulatory support (MCS) means devices that take over part of the heart’s pumping when drugs are not enough. Short-term devices (IABP, Impella, TandemHeart, VA ECMO) are inserted percutaneously or peripherally for days to weeks; durable LVADs are implanted surgically for months to years. On a pressure–volume loop, the width is stroke volume, the enclosed area is stroke work, and the total pressure–volume area (loop plus the triangle under the end-systolic line) tracks myocardial oxygen consumption. Arterial elastance (Ea) is the slope from end-diastolic volume to the end-systolic point and stands for afterload.

ECHO-01.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Why bedside echo
ECHO-01.intro: Step 1 is the case for echo at all. The numbers on this card come from a study in which cardiologists examined patients and then scanned them, and they show how much the stethoscope misses.
why: **Cardiac examination failed to detect 59% of overall cardiovascular findings.** In Spencer and colleagues’ study (JACC 2001; 36 patients, full echo as the gold standard), cardiologists’ physical examination missed 59% of findings; the same physicians with a small portable echo missed 29%. Murmurs, effusions and wall-motion defects are often silent at the bedside, more so in a ventilated, oedematous ICU patient.

**43% of MAJOR cardiovascular findings were missed.** The major-finding miss rate is lower than the overall rate because big abnormalities are more likely to make a sign; portable echo halved it to 21%.

**Intensivists achieve 77–93% agreement with cardiologists.** This is the source’s range; no single paper reporting it could be traced. Small studies of intensivists after focused training report agreement of this order for simple questions (in Melamed and colleagues’ 2009 hand-held study, 92% of normal and 80% of abnormal LV function correctly called against formal echo), which is why a yes-or-no answer on gross LV function or effusion can be acted on without waiting for a formal study.
mimic: Overall vs major miss rate
Overall 59%, major 43%: the larger figure belongs to the broader category.
traps: “59% of major findings were missed”
59% is the overall figure; major findings were missed 43% of the time.
decode: [pattern] What proportion of cardiovascular findings does clinical examination miss compared with echo?
59% overall, 43% of major findings.
ECHO-01.punch: Examination missed 59% of all findings and 43% of the major ones; trained intensivists agree with cardiologists 77–93% of the time, so focused echo belongs in the ICU examination.

ECHO-02.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → The TTE probe and frequency
ECHO-02.intro: Step 2 is the trade-off behind every probe choice: frequency against depth. The two DocT QBank questions are not about the heart at all; they test whether the rule can be applied to the pleura and the abdomen, and only about 60% got them right.
why: **Phased array probe.** Its small footprint fits between the ribs, and the beam is steered electronically from one point to fan out into a sector, so a wide image is made through a narrow window. The price is a narrow near field: structures just under the skin are poorly seen.

**Typical frequency range 1–5 MHz.** Cardiac views need an imaging depth of about 15–20 cm (the apical view reaches the atria), and only low frequencies reach that depth with enough echo left to image.

**A smaller frequency allows better delineation of DEEPER structures.** Attenuation, the energy lost as the beam travels, rises with frequency; a low-frequency beam loses less per centimetre and so returns usable echoes from depth. The cost is resolution, because a longer wavelength cannot separate two points close together.

**The orientation marker delineates the left or right side of the image.** The ridge or dot on the probe matches a marker on the screen, so the operator knows which side of the picture corresponds to which side of the probe; every standard view is defined by where the marker points (CVS05B).
mimic: Phased array vs curvilinear
Both are low frequency; the curvilinear has a wide footprint and near field (pleura, abdomen), the phased array a small footprint for rib spaces (heart).
Curvilinear vs linear for the pleura
Fluid and consolidation are deep: curvilinear. The pleural line and lung sliding are superficial: linear.
traps: “Phased array (2 MHz) is best for a pleural effusion” — the main wrong choice when 59% were right

It reaches the depth but has a narrow near field and sector; the curvilinear 4–5 MHz probe gives the wide, deep view of the costophrenic angle. The phased array is the second choice, used when the rib spaces are tight.
“Linear 10 MHz for the pleural cavity”
Excellent for the pleural line but it cannot see more than about 6 cm, so a moderate effusion and the lung beneath it are out of reach.
“5–10 MHz for a deep abdominal abscess” (60% right)
Higher frequency loses too much energy with depth; deep abdominal work needs 2–5 MHz.
decode: Ventilated patient, pleural effusion on POCUS — best probe? [DocT QBank]
Curvilinear 4–5 MHz (59% right).
Deep abdominal abscess — which frequency range gives optimal penetration? [DocT QBank]
2–5 MHz (60% right).
[pattern] Why does the cardiac probe use 1–5 MHz?
The heart is deep; low frequency attenuates less, at the cost of resolution.
ECHO-02.punch: Frequency buys resolution and costs depth: deep targets get low-frequency probes (phased array between ribs, curvilinear for pleura and abdomen), shallow ones the high-frequency linear.
