ECHO-03.intro: Step 3 turns echoes into a picture. B stands for brightness: each echo is drawn as a dot whose brightness follows its strength, placed at the depth its return time gives.
why: **A 2-dimensional cross-sectional view.** Many scan lines side by side build a slice through the heart, refreshed many times a second so that it moves.
**High reflectivity appears white.** A large impedance mismatch (pericardium, valve rings, calcium, bone) reflects most of the beam: hyperechoic.
**Low reflectivity (muscle) appears grey.** Myocardium scatters a moderate amount of sound: hypoechoic relative to the pericardium.
**No reflection (fluid) appears black.** Blood and effusion transmit sound with almost no echo: anechoic. This is why a pericardial or pleural effusion shows as a black stripe.
mimic: Anechoic fluid vs very dark muscle
Fluid is black and has no internal texture; poorly imaged muscle at too low gain is dark but speckled, and turning the gain up separates them (ECHO-13).
traps: “Muscle is hyperechoic”
Myocardium is grey; bright white is reserved for strong reflectors such as pericardium and calcium.
decode: [pattern] On 2D echo, how does a pericardial effusion appear?
Black (anechoic): fluid does not reflect.
ECHO-03.punch: B-mode draws echo strength as brightness: strong reflectors white, muscle grey, fluid black.

ECHO-04.intro: Still step 3: M-mode (motion mode) takes a single scan line from the 2D image and plots it against time. Because one line is sampled thousands of times a second, it times and measures fast movement better than the 2D picture.
why: **Detects and records RAPID MOVEMENTS.** The very high sampling rate along one line resolves the motion of valve leaflets and walls that 2D, at 30–60 frames a second, blurs.

**ECG or respiratory pressure waveforms are traced alongside.** The ECG marks end-diastole and end-systole for measurements; a respiratory trace lets the IVC or septal shift be timed against breathing.

**Calculates chamber dimensions, fractional shortening and ejection fraction.** LV diameters at end-diastole and end-systole give FS = (LVIDd − LVIDs)/LVIDd (normal above 25%; ASE/EACVI 2015 discourages its use). EF can be derived from these diameters (Teichholz), but ASE/EACVI 2015 advises against EF from linear measurements, because they assume a regular shape the ICU ventricle with regional defects does not have; the biplane method of disks (Simpson) on 2D is preferred.
mimic: M-mode vs 2D
M-mode: one line, superb time resolution, for timing and linear distances (TAPSE, MAPSE, IVC). 2D: the whole slice, for shape, regional motion and volumes.
traps: “M-mode EF is the recommended method”
It is possible but not recommended; current guidance prefers biplane Simpson’s from 2D.
decode: [pattern] Which echo mode measures TAPSE?
M-mode through the lateral tricuspid annulus in the apical 4-chamber view.
ECHO-04.punch: M-mode is one scan line plotted against time: unmatched for timing and linear distances, but the ejection fraction is better taken from 2D volumes.

ECHO-05.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → The Doppler principle
ECHO-05.intro: Step 4 changes what is being read. 2D uses the strength and timing of the echo; Doppler uses its frequency. The one Grand Test question sits one step earlier, on what makes an echo at all, and the card layer adds it.
why: **The observed frequency of a wave depends on the relative speed of the source and the observer.** A source moving towards the listener squeezes the waves together (higher pitch); moving away stretches them (lower pitch), as with a passing siren.

**Piezoelectric crystals convert electrical power to mechanical oscillations (sound waves).** A voltage makes the crystal vibrate and emit sound; the same crystal works in reverse when listening, turning returning sound into a voltage.
**Doppler echo uses reflection of ultrasound by MOVING RED BLOOD CELLS.** Red cells are the moving scatterers in blood; their echo is weak, but its frequency carries their speed.

**Doppler shift is the change in frequency between the emitted and the returning waveform.** Δf = 2 f₀ v cosθ / c, where f₀ is the transmitted frequency, v the velocity of the cells, θ the angle between beam and flow and c the speed of sound. The factor 2 is there because the cells first receive and then re-emit the sound while moving.

**The shift is determined by the velocity AND direction of blood flow, which gives haemodynamic information.** A positive shift means flow towards the probe, a negative shift flow away; the size gives velocity, and velocity gives pressure gradients (4V²) and stroke volume (VTI × LVOT area).
mimic: Acoustic impedance vs attenuation

Impedance (Z = density × speed of sound) is a medium’s resistance to sound and decides how much reflects at an interface. Attenuation is energy lost along the path with depth, and it rises with frequency.
Doppler shift vs echo amplitude
Doppler reads frequency (movement); 2D reads amplitude (structure).
traps: “Attenuation is the resistance to propagation of sound”
That is acoustic impedance. Attenuation is loss of energy with distance (absorption, scatter, reflection), which is why high frequencies do not reach deep.
“The piezoelectric effect is the resistance to sound”
It is the conversion between electrical and mechanical energy in the crystal.
decode: Which of the following is the resistance to propagation of sound? [DocT GT]
Acoustic impedance (Z = ρc); the size of the impedance mismatch decides reflection, hence gel and the blocking effect of lung and bowel gas.
[pattern] What does the Doppler shift depend on?
The velocity and direction of the red cells relative to the beam (and the transmitted frequency).
ECHO-05.punch: 2D reads how strong an echo is; Doppler reads how its frequency has changed, and that change gives the speed and direction of the red cells.

ECHO-06.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Doppler angle
ECHO-06.intro: Still step 4: the Doppler equation contains cosθ, so the machine only sees the part of the velocity that runs along the beam. This card is that one term turned into numbers.
why: **The USG beam must be PARALLEL to the direction of blood flow.** Only the component of flow along the beam changes the returning frequency. Cardiac Doppler is aligned, not angle-corrected (ASE: angle correction is not recommended): the angle is kept below about 20°, which is why gradients are taken from apical views where the beam runs with the blood (CVS05B).
**Cosine: 0° = 1, 30° = 0.87, 45° = 0.7, 60° = 0.5, 90° = 0.** The cosine is the fraction of true velocity that is measured; it falls slowly at first and then steeply.

**Measured velocity for a true 5 m/s: 5, 4.35, 3.5, 2.5 and 0 m/s.** Measured = true × cosθ, so 60° reads exactly half and 90° reads nothing. Because a gradient is 4V², the 30° reading (4.35 m/s) gives 76 mmHg instead of 100 mmHg: a severe aortic stenosis can be graded moderate.
**Error: 0° → 0%, 10° → 2%, 20° → 6%, 30° → 13%, 45° → 29%, 90° → 100%.** The error is 1 − cosθ; it stays under about 6% up to 20°, which is the working tolerance.
mimic: Doppler vs 2D angle
Doppler wants the beam parallel to flow; 2D wants it perpendicular to the structure for the sharpest edges.
traps: “Off-angle Doppler overestimates velocity”
Angle error always underestimates, because cosθ is never above 1.
decode: [pattern] True velocity 5 m/s, beam at 60° to flow — measured velocity?
ECHO-06.punch: The machine sees true velocity × cosθ: under 20° the error is small, at 60° it is half and at 90° there is no signal, so a misaligned beam always underestimates.

ECHO-07.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Pulse wave Doppler
ECHO-07.intro: Step 5 is the choice between Doppler modes, and pulse wave Doppler is the one that can say where the velocity comes from. The one linked DocT QBank question (57% right) turns on exactly that.
why: **The Doppler signal is analysed to depict velocity and direction of flow.** It is shown as a spectral trace: time on the x-axis, velocity on the y-axis, flow towards the probe above the baseline and away below.

**A SINGLE crystal transmits the ultrasound and receives it after a preset time delay.** The crystal sends a short pulse and then listens only at one moment; sound returning at that moment can only have come from one depth.

**The preset delay is a.k.a. the NYQUIST LIMIT.** That is the card’s wording, and it is wrong (FLAG): the delay sets the depth of the sample volume (range gating). The Nyquist limit is half the pulse repetition frequency, the highest velocity PW can show before aliasing (wrapping round to the other side of the baseline), usually about 1.5–1.7 m/s. The two are linked: a deeper sample needs a longer delay, so fewer pulses per second and a lower Nyquist limit.

**A ‘sample volume’ is placed over the 2-D image at the region of interest.** The small gate on the image (in the LVOT for VTI, at the mitral leaflet tips for E and A) is the only place the trace comes from.

**Used when flow disturbance must be LOCALISED, or blood velocity from a small region measured.** LVOT VTI for stroke volume, mitral inflow for diastolic function, a single point in a peripheral artery.
mimic: PWD vs CWD
PW: one site, low velocities, aliases above the Nyquist limit. CW: every depth along the beam at once, high velocities, no aliasing (ECHO-12).
traps: “Continuous wave Doppler for velocity and direction at a single site in the femoral artery” — the wrong choice when 57% were right
CW gives direction and velocity but cannot say from which depth; only PW localises to one site, and femoral velocities are low enough not to alias.
“The preset delay is the Nyquist limit” (the card’s own wording)
The delay sets depth; the Nyquist limit is PRF/2. In the exam, Nyquist limit means the maximum velocity before aliasing.
decode: Femoral artery: which Doppler mode best determines both flow direction and velocity at a single site? [DocT QBank]
Pulse wave Doppler (57% right).
[pattern] What is the Nyquist limit?
Half the pulse repetition frequency; above it PW aliases.
ECHO-07.punch: Pulse wave Doppler listens at one moment after each pulse, so it knows where the signal comes from; the price is a velocity ceiling, the Nyquist limit (PRF/2), which falls as the sample goes deeper.

ECHO-08.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Continuous wave Doppler
ECHO-08.intro: Still step 5: continuous wave Doppler gives up knowing where in exchange for measuring any speed.
why: **Good resolution of HIGH VELOCITIES.** Sending and receiving never stop, so there is no pulse repetition frequency and no Nyquist limit; jets of 4–6 m/s are recorded without aliasing.

**Localisation is LIMITED: the signal can originate at any point along the length or width of the beam.** With no timing gate, every moving scatterer along the line contributes; the trace shows the highest velocity anywhere on it, and the operator infers its origin from the anatomy.

**Measures velocities of regurgitation and systolic flow through the aortic valve.** TR peak velocity estimates PA systolic pressure (4V² + RAP); the AS jet gives peak and mean gradients; MR and AR jets are also traced by CW.
**2 crystals: one transmitting continuously, one receiving continuously.** One crystal cannot do both at once, so the jobs are split.
mimic: CW vs PW for aortic stenosis
The AS jet (above 4 m/s if severe) aliases on PW; CW records it whole. PW is used below the valve, in the LVOT.
traps: “CW tells you where along the beam a jet arises”
It cannot; that is the PW sample volume’s job.
decode: [pattern] Which Doppler mode measures the peak TR velocity?
Continuous wave.
ECHO-08.punch: Continuous wave Doppler never stops listening, so it has no velocity ceiling but cannot say where along the beam the fastest flow lies.

ECHO-09.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Colour flow imaging
ECHO-09.intro: Still step 5: colour flow imaging is pulse wave Doppler done at many sample points at once, each coded as a colour and laid over the 2D picture.
why: **Velocity and direction of blood flow as a colour map superimposed on the 2-D image.** Within a colour box, each pixel shows the mean velocity at that point.

**PULSE WAVE Doppler signals derive the image.** It is multigated PW, so it localises, and it has a Nyquist limit, shown at the ends of the colour bar; jets faster than that alias into a mosaic, which is itself a marker of turbulent high-velocity flow.
**Used to visualise and semi-quantitatively assess regurgitant jets and abnormal flows.** Jet area, vena contracta width and PISA come from colour; they grade severity in bands, not exact volumes.
**Higher velocities are shown in progressively LIGHTER shades of colour.** Dark red or blue is slow flow; pale, near yellow or cyan, is fast flow near the limit.
**BLUE = AWAY from the probe, RED = TOWARDS the probe; the source’s BART (Blue Away, Red Towards).** Colour shows direction relative to the beam, not to the heart.
mimic: Mosaic vs true flow reversal
A mosaic of colours in a jet is aliasing and turbulence; a clean change from red to blue across a straight vessel is the beam angle (ECHO-11).
traps: “Red means arterial, blue means venous”
Colour is direction relative to the probe; an artery flowing away is blue.
decode: [pattern] On colour Doppler, what does blue indicate?
Flow away from the probe.
ECHO-09.punch: Colour flow is pulse wave Doppler painted over the picture, so it localises but aliases; red is towards, blue away, and lighter shades are faster.

ECHO-10.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Tissue Doppler
ECHO-10.intro: Still step 5: tissue Doppler points the same pulse wave method at the heart wall instead of the blood.
why: **Measures velocities of TISSUE movement.** The filters are reversed: blood Doppler discards slow, strong signals (wall clutter); tissue Doppler keeps them and discards the fast, weak blood signal.
**These velocities are LOWER than blood velocities.** The annulus moves at centimetres per second (about 5–20 cm/s), blood at up to a metre or more per second.

**Assesses tricuspid and mitral annulus velocities.** At the mitral annulus, e′ reflects LV relaxation (reduced if septal ≤6 or lateral ≤7 cm/s in ASE 2025), and E/e′ estimates filling pressure (average >14 raised).

**Assesses RV systolic function.** The systolic velocity of the lateral tricuspid annulus, S′, below 9.5 cm/s indicates RV systolic dysfunction (ASE 2015); like TAPSE it is angle dependent and measures longitudinal function only.
mimic: S′ vs TAPSE
Both judge RV longitudinal function at the tricuspid annulus: S′ is a velocity (tissue Doppler, <9.5 cm/s abnormal), TAPSE a distance (M-mode, <17 mm abnormal).
traps: “Tissue velocities are higher than blood velocities”
They are much lower, but the signal is stronger.
decode: [pattern] Tricuspid annular S′ 8 cm/s — interpretation?
RV systolic dysfunction (<9.5 cm/s).
ECHO-10.punch: Tissue Doppler reads the slow, strong signal of the annulus: S′ for RV systolic function and e′ (with E/e′) for LV relaxation and filling pressure.

ECHO-11.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → The no-signal zone
ECHO-11.intro: Step 4’s cosine rule seen on the screen. A straight vessel crossing a sector image meets the diverging beam lines at different angles along its length, so one stretch of flow is coming towards the beam and another going away, though the blood never changes direction.
why: **At the centre the flow is perpendicular to the beam: 90°, cosine 0, no detectable Doppler shift. Where flow angles towards the probe it is RED; where it angles away it is BLUE.** The machine only sees the part of velocity along each beam line; where the line meets the vessel at right angles that part is zero, so the pixels are black, and on either side the sign of the cosine flips.
mimic: Angle colour change vs real reversal

Angle: colour changes at the point where the vessel is perpendicular to the beam, with a black gap between. Real reversal (as in AR in the descending aorta) changes colour in time across the cardiac cycle, not along the vessel.
traps: “The black centre is thrombus or no flow”
Flow is present; the beam meets it at 90°. Tilting the probe brings colour back.
decode: [pattern] Vessel across the beam shows red one end, blue the other and black in the middle — why?
The angle: cos 90° = 0 at the centre.
ECHO-11.punch: Same blood, same direction, different colours: the colour follows the beam angle, and where the angle is 90° the cosine is zero and there is no signal.

ECHO-12.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → PWD vs CWD
ECHO-12.intro: Step 5 in one table: every difference between the two spectral Doppler modes follows from one crystal timed against two crystals running continuously. The linked DocT QBank question (57%) rests on the localisation row.
why: **Crystals: PWD 1, CWD 2.** One crystal must stop transmitting to listen; two can share the work and never stop.

**PWD: one crystal transmits, then receives after a preset delay (Nyquist limit); CWD: one transmits continuously, one receives continuously.** The delay is what fixes the depth of the PW sample; the Nyquist limit is a separate quantity, PRF/2, the velocity ceiling (ECHO-07, FLAG).
**Localisation: PWD YES, at the sample volume; CWD LIMITED, signal from anywhere along the beam.** Timing the return pins the depth; continuous listening cannot.
**High velocities: PWD limited; CWD good resolution.** PW samples in pulses, so above the Nyquist limit it aliases; CW has no sampling limit.

**Uses: PWD for localising a flow disturbance and velocity from a small region; CWD for regurgitation velocities and systolic flow through the aortic valve.** Hence LVOT VTI and mitral inflow by PW, TR and AS jets by CW.
mimic: Colour vs PW
Colour flow is multigated PW, so it shares PW’s ability to localise and its aliasing.
traps: “CWD to measure velocity at a single site in the femoral artery”
CW cannot localise; PW is the answer (57% chose it).
decode: Which Doppler mode determines both flow direction and velocity accurately at a single site? [DocT QBank]
Pulse wave Doppler.
[pattern] Peak velocity of a 5 m/s AS jet — which mode?
Continuous wave; PW would alias.
ECHO-12.punch: Pulse wave knows where but not how fast; continuous wave knows how fast but not where. One crystal timed versus two running continuously explains every row.

ECHO-13.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Setting up
ECHO-13.intro: Step 6 closes the deck at the bedside: the settings that decide whether the views of CVS05B can be read at all.
why: **Optimal positioning: LEFT LATERAL position.** Turning the patient onto the left side brings the heart forward against the chest wall and moves lung out of the way, improving the parasternal and apical windows. The subcostal view is taken supine (CVS05B).

**Adjust the height of the patient bed and connect the ECG cables of the echo machine.** A comfortable working height steadies the probe hand; the ECG times systole and diastole for every measurement.

**2-D: adjust the gain knob until the picture is neither too dark nor too bright; depth knob so the structure of interest sits in the CENTRE of the screen.** Gain amplifies all returning echoes: too high fills the cavities with noise, too low hides endocardium. Too much depth wastes the image on structures behind the heart and lowers the frame rate.

**PWD and CWD: adjust baseline and scale so the entire waveform is seen.** Moving the baseline and raising the scale (for PW only up to the maximum pulse repetition frequency the depth allows) brings a clipped or wrapped trace back on screen, so peak velocity and VTI can be traced.
mimic: Gain vs depth
Gain changes brightness; depth changes how far down the image goes and how big the heart appears.
traps: “Turn the gain up until the cavities look grey”
Blood should be black; grey cavities mean too much gain.
decode: [pattern] Optimal patient position for parasternal and apical views?
Left lateral decubitus.
ECHO-13.punch: Left lateral position, ECG on, gain until the blood is black and the walls are clear, depth with the target in the centre, and Doppler baseline and scale so the whole waveform fits.

topups.q: Name the ultrasound probe manoeuvres.
a: - Slide — move across the skin; sweep — slide a long distance (track a vessel).
- ROCK (heel–toe) — tilt along the long axis with the contact point fixed.
- Fan/tilt — angle across the short axis, contact fixed.
- Rotate — turn on the spot (PLAX → PSAX); compress — press (vein compressibility).

- Probe choice: linear 5–15 MHz for superficial work (pleura, vascular access, ONSD, airway); curvilinear 2–5 MHz for abdomen, FAST and lung bases; phased array 1–5 MHz between ribs (heart, TCD). Higher frequency = better resolution, less depth.
topups.src: DocT Procedures, Techniques & POCUS Q19; DocT GT GT5 Q99

x.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Probe manoeuvres and probe choice
x.intro: Step 2 is about the probe, and this card adds how it is moved. Each manoeuvre changes one thing while the others stay fixed, which is what lets an operator find a view and then refine it without losing it; the last line repeats the frequency–depth rule that both Grand Test and QBank questions use.
why: **Slide: move across the skin; sweep: slide a long distance (track a vessel).** The whole probe changes position, so the window changes; a sweep follows a vein or artery along its course, for example a femoral vein before cannulation.

**ROCK (heel–toe): tilt along the long axis with the contact point fixed.** The beam swings within its own plane, towards or away from the marker, bringing a structure at the edge of the image towards the centre.

**Fan/tilt: angle across the short axis, contact point fixed.** The beam swings out of its plane, cutting successive slices; fanning through PSAX moves from the aortic to the mitral and papillary levels.

**Rotate: turn on the spot (PLAX → PSAX); compress: press (vein compressibility).** Rotation changes the plane at the same window, 90° clockwise from PLAX to PSAX; compression that flattens a vein fully excludes thrombus at that point.

**Probe choice: linear 5–15 MHz for superficial work (pleura, vascular access, ONSD, airway); curvilinear 2–5 MHz for abdomen, FAST and lung bases; phased array 1–5 MHz between ribs (heart, TCD). Higher frequency = better resolution, less depth.** Attenuation rises with frequency, so depth decides the frequency and the window decides the footprint (ECHO-02).
mimic: Rock vs fan
Rock moves the beam within its plane (in-plane); fan moves it across planes (out-of-plane). Both keep the contact point still.
Rotate vs fan
Rotation changes the plane’s orientation around the beam’s axis; fanning tilts the plane through the tissue.
traps: “Rotating the probe moves it to a new window”
Rotation keeps the window and changes the plane; sliding changes the window.
“Linear probe for a pleural effusion or the lung bases”
The linear probe is for the pleural line; deep fluid needs the curvilinear 2–5 MHz probe.
decode: [pattern] Which manoeuvre converts PLAX to PSAX?
Rotation, 90° clockwise, at the same window.
[pattern] Which probe for optic nerve sheath diameter or the cricothyroid membrane?
Linear, high frequency.
x.punch: Slide and sweep move the window, rock and fan swing the beam with the contact point fixed, rotate changes the plane, compress tests a vein; and depth decides the frequency.

spine: Why echo at the bedside
Physical examination misses much of what echo shows, and intensivists with focused training agree well with cardiologists, so echo is part of the ICU examination.
Probe, frequency and depth
Lower frequency penetrates deeper but resolves less, so the deep heart, seen between the ribs, needs a low-frequency phased array probe and superficial structures a high-frequency linear one.
Grey-scale pictures: B and M
B-mode turns echo strength into shades of grey to draw structure, and M-mode plots one line of it against time to time and measure fast movement.
Doppler shift and the angle
Moving red cells change the returning frequency in proportion to velocity times the cosine of the beam angle, so the beam must run parallel to flow and flow at 90° shows nothing.
Choosing the Doppler mode
Pulse wave Doppler tells where but not how fast, continuous wave tells how fast but not where, colour is pulse wave painted on the picture, and tissue Doppler reads the slow wall.
Getting a usable image
Position, gain, depth, baseline and scale decide whether the picture and the trace can be read at all.
CVS05A.primer: Ultrasound is sound above human hearing, sent into the body by a probe in pulses; the probe listens for the echoes, and the time each takes to return gives its depth, because sound travels at about 1540 m/s in soft tissue. Echoes arise wherever two tissues differ in acoustic impedance (density × speed of sound); air and bone reflect almost everything, which is why gel is needed and lung blocks the view. Higher frequency means a shorter wavelength and sharper detail but more energy lost per centimetre, so less depth. Doppler is a separate use of the same echoes: it reads the change in frequency caused by moving blood, not the strength of the echo.

ECHO-14.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → TTE planes
ECHO-14.intro: Step 1 starts with geometry: before any window or view, the heart is described in three planes at right angles to each other. Every named view lies in one of them, which is why the planes come first.
why: **Long axis: aortic root to LV apex.** The plane runs along the length of the LV, through the aortic valve and the apex. PLAX and the apical 3-chamber (apical long axis) view both lie in it, which is why both show the mitral and aortic valves together.

**Short axis: left mid-clavicle to the RIGHT hip.** The heart lies obliquely, its long axis running roughly from the right shoulder towards the left hip, so a plane at right angles to it runs from the left shoulder region down to the right hip. PSAX lies in it and cuts the LV as a circle.
**Four-chamber axis: apex to the base, perpendicular to the other two.** This plane cuts through both atria and both ventricles at once; the apical and subcostal four-chamber views lie in it.
mimic: Long axis vs short axis
Long axis shows the LV as an elongated chamber with the aortic root; short axis shows it as a ring.
traps: “The short axis runs from the left mid-clavicle to the left hip”
It crosses the body diagonally, to the RIGHT hip, because it is perpendicular to a long axis that points to the left hip.
decode: Which TTE plane runs from the aortic root to the LV apex? [pattern]
The long axis.
ECHO-14.punch: Three planes at right angles: long (root to apex), short (left shoulder to right hip, across it) and four-chamber (apex to base through all four chambers). Each view sits in one of them.

ECHO-15.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Probe positions
ECHO-15.intro: Still step 1: the windows are the places where the heart can be reached without lung or bone in the way. Each has a fixed landmark.
why: **Parasternal: 2nd to 4th intercostal space, LEFT sternal border.** Here the RV outflow and the heart touch the anterior chest wall beside the sternum, with no lung in between in most patients (more so in the left lateral position).

**Apical: 4th to 5th intercostal space, lateral.** The probe goes on the apex beat, usually around the 5th space near the mid-clavicular to anterior axillary line; turning the patient to the left brings the apex against the chest wall.
**Subcostal: below the xiphoid.** The beam passes through the liver, which is an acoustic window, so it works when lungs or chest wall block the parasternal and apical windows (ECHO-17).
**Right parasternal: 2nd to 4th intercostal space, RIGHT sternal border.** Used mainly to line the beam up with an aortic stenosis jet when the ascending aorta runs to the right.
**Suprasternal: suprasternal notch.** Shows the aortic arch and descending aorta (coarctation, dissection extending into the arch).
mimic: Parasternal vs right parasternal
Same 2nd–4th spaces, opposite side of the sternum.
traps: “The apical window is in the 2nd–4th space”
Apical is the only window defined by the 4th–5th space, laterally, at the apex beat.
decode: Probe at the left sternal border, 3rd intercostal space — which window? [pattern]
Parasternal.
ECHO-15.punch: Parasternal and right parasternal share the 2nd–4th spaces and differ by side; apical is the apex beat at the 4th–5th space; subcostal is under the xiphoid through the liver; suprasternal is the notch.

ECHO-16.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Marker dot directions
ECHO-16.intro: The last part of step 1: the marker dot on the probe matches a mark on the screen, so it decides which way the plane is cut and which side of the image is which. Get it wrong and the anatomy is mirrored or the wrong plane appears.
why: **Subcostal: LEFT shoulder.** The probe lies flat under the xiphoid with the plane in the four-chamber orientation, the marker towards the patient’s left.
**PLAX: RIGHT shoulder.** The LV long axis runs from right shoulder to left hip, so the marker points to the right shoulder to cut along it.
**PSAX: LEFT shoulder.** Turning the probe 90° clockwise from PLAX moves the marker from the right to the left shoulder and cuts across the LV (ECHO-23).
**Apical 4-chamber: LEFT shoulder.** With the marker to the patient’s left (cardiology convention), the left heart is displayed on the right of the screen.
**Apical 2-chamber: LEFT side of the NECK.** Rotating from A4C swings the marker up towards the neck, cutting a plane that misses the RV (ECHO-30).
mimic: Cardiology vs emergency-medicine convention

Emergency-medicine machines often put the screen marker on the other side, so the apical and subcostal marker points to the patient’s right; the image looks the same, only the probe is held differently.
traps: “PSAX marker points to the right shoulder”
Only PLAX does; PSAX is rotated 90° clockwise to the left shoulder.
decode: Probe marker towards the right shoulder at the left sternal edge — which view? [pattern]
PLAX.
ECHO-16.punch: Two exceptions to learn: PLAX is the only right-shoulder view and A2C the only neck view; subcostal, PSAX and A4C all point to the left shoulder.

ECHO-17.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Subcostal view
ECHO-17.intro: Step 2 begins with the window that still works in a ventilated, emphysematous or obese patient. One real question asks which view assesses IVC collapse and RA filling in suspected tamponade; about one in four missed it.
why: **SUPINE, with a relaxed abdomen.** Flexing the knees relaxes the rectus muscles so the probe can be pressed under the costal margin; no turning is needed, which suits a ventilated or unstable patient and the pulse check in cardiac arrest.
**Probe under the xiphisternum.** The liver is the acoustic window, so the beam reaches the heart without passing through lung.
**Marker dot towards the LEFT shoulder.** This gives the subcostal four-chamber view; rotating towards a cranio-caudal (north–south) orientation then brings in the IVC (ECHO-18).

**Useful in obesity, emphysema and chest wall deformity.** Hyperinflated lung (emphysema, high PEEP) gets between the heart and the chest wall and kills the parasternal and apical windows; the subcostal approach comes from below the lung.

**Assesses IVC variability, pericardial effusions and RV enlargement.** The RV free wall lies closest to the probe here, so a pericardial effusion and RA or RV diastolic collapse in tamponade are seen well, and the IVC is in the same window, which is why it is the view for tamponade physiology.
mimic: Subcostal vs apical 4-chamber in tamponade
Both show RA and RV collapse, but only the subcostal window also shows the IVC; A4C is the view for Doppler of mitral inflow variation.
traps: “Apical four-chamber best assesses IVC collapse and RA filling”
The IVC cannot be seen from the apex; the subcostal long axis is the answer (72% right).
decode: ICU patient, suspected tamponade — view for IVC collapse and RA filling? [DocT QBank]
Subcostal long axis.
Ventilated patient with COPD, no parasternal window — which view? [pattern]
Subcostal: supine, through the liver, below the lung.
ECHO-17.punch: Subcostal is the supine view through the liver, so it works when lung blocks the chest windows, and it shows the effusion, the RV and the IVC in one place.

ECHO-18.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → IVC technique
ECHO-18.intro: Step 2 continues with how to measure the IVC so the number means something. The one linked question (tamponade, which view) is answered by part a; the rest is technique that decides whether the RAP estimate in ECHO-19 is right.
why: **Subcostal approach, longitudinal view.** The IVC is followed in its long axis as it passes through the liver into the right atrium.
**North–south probe orientation.** From the subcostal four-chamber view the probe is rotated so the marker points to the head, cutting the IVC lengthways.

**The IVC lies slightly to the RIGHT of midline.** The aorta lies to the left; telling them apart matters, because a pulsatile, thick-walled aorta that does not change with breathing can be mistaken for a plethoric IVC. The IVC enters the RA and receives the hepatic veins; the aorta gives off the coeliac axis and SMA.
**Transducer below the xiphisternum, 1–2 cm to the right of midline.**

**M-mode line through the IVC 1 cm CAUDAL to its junction with the hepatic vein.** ASE (2015, and the 2025 right heart guideline) places the measurement just distal to the hepatic vein junction, about 0.5–3.0 cm from the RA ostium. The IVC’s diameter varies along its length and the vessel moves with the diaphragm, so only a fixed site gives numbers that can be compared with the reference bands and from one scan to the next.

**Measure the maximum and minimum diameter.** These give the collapsibility index, (max − min) ÷ max, used with the maximum diameter for RAP (ECHO-19). The line must cut the vessel at right angles through its centre: an off-centre cut underestimates the diameter, and the IVC moving with breathing can slide out of the M-mode line, so check on 2D.
mimic: IVC vs aorta
IVC: right of midline, thin wall, enters the RA, hepatic veins drain into it, changes with breathing. Aorta: left, thick wall, pulsatile, branches anteriorly.
traps: “Measure at the junction with the RA or at the diaphragm”
Measure about 1 cm caudal to the hepatic vein junction; elsewhere the diameter, and therefore the RAP estimate, changes.
decode: Which view assesses IVC collapse and RA filling? [DocT QBank]
Subcostal long axis.
Where is the IVC diameter measured? [pattern]
About 1 cm caudal to the hepatic vein junction, on M-mode or 2D, maximum and minimum.
ECHO-18.punch: Find the IVC to the right of midline in a north–south subcostal view, confirm it is not the aorta, and measure maximum and minimum about 1 cm below the hepatic vein junction.

ECHO-19.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → IVC and right atrial pressure
ECHO-19.intro: Step 2’s central card, and the most-asked in the deck (nine questions). The IVC is a floppy tube connected straight to the right atrium, so its size and whether it collapses on a sniff tell you the atrial pressure. Two questions were answered right by about half: one where the stem is set in a ventilated patient, and one RVSP calculation where most forgot to add the RAP.
why: **Normal RAP 0–5 (3) mmHg: IVC ≤2.1 cm with >50% collapse on sniff.** When RAP is low the IVC sits on the steep part of its compliance curve: it is small, and the fall in intrathoracic pressure on spontaneous inspiration (exaggerated by a sniff) empties it by more than half.

**Intermediate RAP 5–10 (8) mmHg: either ≤2.1 cm with <50% collapse, or >2.1 cm with >50% collapse.** Each pattern has one ‘normal’ and one ‘high’ feature, so the two cancel to a middle value. ASE’s rule (2010, kept in the 2025 right heart guideline): in this band look at the secondary indices; if none is present the estimate is moved down to 3, if they are present up to 15, and if doubt remains it stays at 8.

**High RAP 10–20 (15) mmHg: IVC >2.1 cm with <50% collapse; secondary indices RA enlargement, RV hypertrophy, hepatic vein S/D <1, tricuspid E/e′ >6.** A full IVC at high pressure is on the flat part of its compliance curve and cannot collapse. Hepatic vein flow turns diastolic-predominant because the stiff, high-pressure RA blunts systolic forward flow, and a high tricuspid E/e′ reflects raised RA pressure, as mitral E/e′ does for the LA (ECHO-40). In the ASE 2025 right heart guideline the secondary indices are RA enlargement, an interatrial septum bulging into the LA, restrictive right-sided filling, tricuspid E/e′ >6 and a hepatic vein systolic filling fraction <55% (S/D <1); RV hypertrophy is not among them, and they are used mainly to settle the intermediate band. ASE 2025 also adds a fifth band: IVC >2.5 cm with no respiratory variation means about 20 mmHg.
mimic: Plethoric IVC from tamponade vs from RV failure or volume overload
All three are dilated and non-collapsing; tamponade adds an effusion with RA/RV diastolic collapse and a small LV (GT2), RV failure adds a dilated RV.
Spontaneous breathing vs passive ventilation
Spontaneous inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure and the IVC collapses; positive-pressure inspiration raises it and the IVC distends. Sniff-collapse bands apply only to spontaneous breathing.
Large IVC with normal RAP
Trained athletes and some young patients have a large IVC with normal pressure; severe TR dilates it regardless; raised intra-abdominal pressure can make a small IVC look ‘empty’.
traps: “Ventilated patient, IVC 17 mm, >20% variation — tamponade or RV failure”

Only half got this right (49%, 54%). Both tamponade and RV failure give a dilated, fixed IVC. A 17 mm IVC is below 2.1 cm and it changes with each breath, so the RAP is low (key A). The stem’s ‘collapsibility’ is spontaneous-breathing language: in a passively ventilated patient the IVC DISTENDS on inspiration, and a distensibility index >18% predicts fluid responsiveness. ASE also warns that IVC collapse cannot estimate RAP reliably under positive pressure; the useful finding there is size, and the ASE 2025 right heart guideline states that an IVC ≤2.1 cm in an intubated patient accurately identifies RAP <10 mmHg, which fits this 17 mm IVC.
“RVSP = 4 × 3.5² = 49 mmHg”
Only 33% got this: 49 is the RV–RA gradient. RVSP = 4V² + RAP = 49 + 10 = 59 ≈ 60 mmHg (key B).
“Dilated IVC with minimal collapse means fluid responsiveness”
It means a high RAP (84% right); a full, fixed IVC is the least likely to respond to fluid (ECHO-20).
decode: Ventilated, IVC 17 mm with >20% ‘collapsibility’ — what does it suggest? [DocT QBank, DocT GT]
Low right atrial pressure.
TR peak 3.5 m/s, RAP 10 mmHg — RVSP? [DocT QBank]
Effusion, RA diastolic collapse, dilated non-collapsing IVC — haemodynamic profile? [DocT GT]
↓ LVEDA, ↑ IVC diameter, narrow pulse pressure, ↑ CVP.
Small IVC with >50% collapse after surgery; dilated IVC with minimal collapse in shock? [DocT GT, Marrow, NEET 2024]
Hypovolaemia (normal or low RAP); elevated RAP. Normal IVC = <2.1 cm with >50% collapse.
ECHO-19.punch: Small and collapsing is low RAP, large and fixed is high RAP, and one of each is the middle band. The sniff rule is for spontaneous breathing only: under positive pressure the IVC distends instead.

parts.q: How is RVSP estimated, and when does the TR velocity suggest pulmonary hypertension?
parts.a: RVSP = 4 × (peak TR velocity)² + RAP, and it equals PA systolic pressure if there is no pulmonary stenosis or RVOT obstruction. ESC/ERS 2022: peak TR velocity ≤2.8 m/s is low echo probability of PH, 2.9–3.4 m/s intermediate, >3.4 m/s high (combined with other RV, PA and RA/IVC signs).

ECHO-20.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → IVC and fluid responsiveness
ECHO-20.intro: Step 2 then asks a different question of the same vessel: not ‘what is the pressure?’ but ‘will the stroke volume rise with fluid?’. Three questions test it, and the cut-offs differ from the RAP table on purpose.
why: **Check the absolute number AND the variability (collapsibility) of the IVC with inspiration.** A diameter alone describes the pressure; variation with breathing shows that the vessel, and so the right heart’s filling, is on the steep part of its curve.

**LESS likely fluid responsive: >2 cm, <50% collapse.** A large, fixed IVC means a high RAP; the right heart is already on the flat part of the Frank–Starling curve, so more volume mostly raises venous pressure.

**MORE likely fluid responsive: <1 cm, >50% collapse. This only suggests: the IVC alone predicts modestly, worse in spontaneous breathing; confirm with PLR or VTI change.** Fluid responsiveness needs both ventricles to be preload-dependent, and the IVC reports only the right side. In spontaneous breathing the collapse depends on how hard the patient breathes (a vigorous inspiration collapses any IVC), and raised intra-abdominal pressure compresses it. In passively ventilated patients (tidal volume about 8 mL/kg or more, no breathing effort) the distensibility index, (max − min) ÷ min, >18% (Barbier 2004), or the respiratory variation (max − min) ÷ mean >12% (Feissel 2004), performs better; unlike pulse pressure variation, it does not need sinus rhythm. The test that settles it is a passive leg raise with a rise in LVOT VTI (or stroke volume) of about 10–15%.
mimic: RAP thresholds vs fluid-responsiveness thresholds
RAP uses 2.1 cm and 50%; fluid responsiveness uses <1 cm and >2 cm, leaving 1–2 cm unclassified.
Collapsibility vs distensibility
Collapsibility (÷ max) for spontaneous breathing; distensibility (÷ min, >18%) for passive ventilation.
traps: “Septic shock, 1 L given, IVC varies >50% — start noradrenaline (or do a PLR first)”

The key is another 500–1,000 mL bolus (76% right): the IVC already shows preload dependence and only 1 L of the initial 30 mL/kg has gone in. Noradrenaline may be started alongside if hypotension persists, but stopping fluid here is wrong; corticosteroids are for shock that persists on vasopressors.
“Dilated IVC with minimal collapse means fluid responsiveness”
It means a high RAP, the opposite (84% right).
“A 1.5 cm IVC predicts fluid responsiveness”
1–2 cm is the grey zone; neither threshold applies, so use PLR or VTI.
decode: Septic shock after 1 L, IVC >50% variation — next step? [DocT GT]
Another 500–1,000 mL crystalloid bolus.
Shock, dilated IVC with minimal collapse — indicates? [DocT GT]
Elevated right atrial pressure (not fluid responsiveness).
Ventilated patient, IVC 17 mm, >20% respiratory variation? [DocT GT]
Low RAP; in a ventilated patient read it as distensibility (>18% suggests responsiveness).
ECHO-20.punch: A tiny IVC that collapses suggests fluid will help and a large fixed one suggests it will not, but the IVC only hints; a PLR with a VTI rise of 10–15% decides.

ECHO-21.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Pleural view
ECHO-21.intro: Step 5 includes the pleura, because FATE is a heart-and-lung protocol by design (position 4). One real question asks what the sinusoid sign means, and the card layer adds the mirror-image and spine signs.
why: **Pleura appreciated in the MID-AXILLARY LINES BILATERALLY.** The probe sits above the diaphragm in the mid-axillary line, with liver or spleen as the landmark; fluid collects posteriorly and at the bases in a supine patient, so this low lateral position finds it.

**A transudative effusion is ANECHOIC.** Transudates have little protein or cells, so they return no echoes. The reverse does not hold: an anechoic effusion can still be an exudate, whereas complex, septated or diffusely echogenic effusions are exudates.

**Plankton sign: swirling, punctiform echoes in an effusion; may indicate infection or haemothorax.** The floating echoes are cells, protein and fibrin strands moving with breathing and the heartbeat, so the fluid is cellular (empyema, parapneumonic exudate, blood).
mimic: Effusion vs consolidation
Effusion: anechoic space with a sinusoid sign and the spine visible above the diaphragm. Consolidation: tissue-like (hepatised) lung, which does not move like fluid.
Effusion vs pneumothorax on M-mode
Effusion: sinusoid sign. Pneumothorax: barcode (stratosphere) sign and a lung point.
traps: “Sinusoid sign = pneumothorax or consolidation”
It is pleural effusion: on M-mode the lung line swings towards the pleural line on inspiration, tracing a sine wave; with the quad sign it confirms free fluid.
“Liver mirrored above the diaphragm means fluid”
The mirror image needs air-filled lung, so it means NO effusion at that spot; with an effusion the mirror image disappears and the spine becomes visible above the diaphragm (spine sign).
decode: ‘Sinusoid sign’ on ultrasound is characteristic of? [DocT GT PYQ]
Pleural effusion.
Swirling echoes within a pleural collection suggest? [pattern]
An exudate: infection (empyema) or haemothorax.
ECHO-21.punch: Scan the pleura in both mid-axillary lines: anechoic fluid with a sinusoid sign is free fluid, swirling echoes mean cells or blood, and an anechoic effusion is not proof of a transudate.

ECHO-22.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Parasternal long axis
ECHO-22.intro: Step 3 starts with the first chest-wall view. PLAX lies in the long-axis plane, so it shows the LV, mitral valve, LVOT, aortic valve and root in one picture, with the descending aorta behind the LA. Four questions test what it shows, how it separates pericardial from pleural fluid and its role in dissection.
why: **Transducer at the LEFT sternal edge, 2nd to 4th ICS.**
**Marker dot towards the RIGHT SHOULDER.** This lines the plane up with the LV long axis (ECHO-14, ECHO-16).

**Useful for assessing contractility, calculating EF, detecting RWMA and measuring LVOT diameter.** The beam crosses the septum and posterior wall at right angles, so M-mode measures wall thickness, cavity size, fractional shortening and EPSS here (ECHO-39); the anteroseptal and inferolateral walls show regional motion. The LVOT is measured in mid-systole, inner edge to inner edge, just below the aortic valve; because stroke volume = 0.785 × D² × VTI, a 1 mm error in the diameter becomes a large error in stroke volume. The same view shows the aortic root and proximal ascending aorta (dilatation, an intimal flap, AR).
mimic: Pericardial vs pleural effusion on PLAX
Pericardial fluid lies ANTERIOR to the descending aorta, between the aorta and the LA; pleural fluid lies posterior and lateral to it, because the pericardial reflection stops at the aorta.
PLAX vs PSAX at aortic valve level
PLAX shows the LVOT, aortic valve and root lengthways; PSAX AV level shows the valve in cross-section (Mercedes-Benz sign) and the pulmonary artery.
traps: “Best TTE view for aortic dissection is PSAX at the aortic valve”
PLAX is (75% right): it shows the root and proximal ascending aorta lengthways. TTE can still miss a dissection, so CT aortography or TEE confirms.
“Left 4th space, marker to the right shoulder shows the PA bifurcation or the IVC”
That is PLAX, which shows the LVOT and aortic valve (75% and 88% right); the PA bifurcation is PSAX at the aortic level, the IVC is subcostal.
“Fluid anterior to the descending aorta on PLAX is pleural”
It is pericardial.
decode: Left 4th ICS, marker to the right shoulder — which structure is best seen? [DocT QBank, DocT GT]
LV outflow tract and aortic valve.
Anechoic fluid anterior to the descending aorta on PLAX? [DocT GT]
Pericardial effusion.
Best echo view for aortic dissection and aneurysm? [DocT GT]
Parasternal long axis.
ECHO-22.punch: PLAX lies along the LV and aortic root: it measures the LVOT diameter, shows the root for dissection, and separates fluid by the descending aorta (in front pericardial, behind pleural).

ECHO-23.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Parasternal short axis
ECHO-23.intro: Step 3 continues: turn the probe from PLAX and the LV becomes a ring. Two questions ask what this view is best for, and about one in three chose a Doppler measurement instead of wall motion.
why: **Rotate the probe CLOCKWISE 90° from PLAX.** The plane turns from along the LV to across it.
**Transducer at the LEFT sternal edge, 2nd to 4th ICS.** The same spot as PLAX; only the rotation changes.

**Short-axis views from the aortic valve down to the LV apex.** Tilting the beam from base to apex gives successive slices (breadloafing, ECHO-24). At the mid-papillary level all three coronary territories are seen together: anterior and anteroseptal walls (LAD), inferior and inferoseptal (RCA), inferolateral (circumflex) and anterolateral (circumflex, often shared with the LAD), which is why this view is best for regional wall motion. The ring shape of the LV also shows septal flattening (a D-shaped LV) when the RV is overloaded.
mimic: Septal flattening in systole vs in diastole
Systolic flattening means RV pressure overload (PE, PH); diastolic flattening means RV volume overload.
traps: “PSAX is for LVOT gradient, stroke volume or RVSP”
Those need Doppler with the beam parallel to flow, from apical views (LVOT, TR); PSAX is for regional wall motion (61%, 67% right).
decode: Probe rotated 90° clockwise from PLAX, circular LV — primary advantage? [DocT QBank, DocT GT]
Evaluating LV regional wall motion.
D-shaped LV on PSAX in systole — what does it mean? [pattern]
RV pressure overload (PE, pulmonary hypertension).
ECHO-23.punch: PSAX is PLAX turned 90° clockwise from the same spot, marker to the left shoulder; it shows the LV as a ring, so all coronary territories and the septum’s shape are seen at once.

ECHO-24.intro: Still step 3: from the PSAX position the beam is tilted, not moved, to cut the heart in slices from base to apex.
why: **Change the angulation on the chest wall.** The probe stays at the same spot and is tilted from pointing at the right shoulder (base) towards the left hip (apex).
**Any number of short-axis views can be obtained.** Each degree of tilt gives a new slice.

**The standard four: aortic valve, mitral valve, LV papillary muscles, LV apex.** AV level shows the three cusps, RVOT and PA (ECHO-26); MV level the ‘fish-mouth’ mitral orifice; papillary level the mid-LV (ECHO-25); the apex the apical segments.
**Like cutting a loaf of bread into slices.**
mimic: Breadloafing (angulation) vs PSAX from PLAX (rotation)
Rotation turns the plane from long to short axis; angulation then moves the short-axis slice up and down the heart.
traps: “Only four short-axis views exist”
Any number can be obtained; four are standard.
decode: The four standard PSAX levels? [pattern]
Aortic valve, mitral valve, papillary muscles, apex.
ECHO-24.punch: Tilting the probe at the PSAX position slices the heart from aortic valve to apex; four slices are standard, but any number is possible.

ECHO-25.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → PSAX papillary level
ECHO-25.intro: Step 3’s workhorse slice, the one in the basic FATE set. One question asks its main advantage; the hypovolaemia questions in ECHO-36 are also read here (‘kissing’ papillary muscles).
why: **LV end-diastolic area.** A small end-diastolic area with end-systolic cavity obliteration means an underfilled LV (hypovolaemia), though a small, hyperdynamic cavity is also seen with low afterload and with a hypertrophied LV.
**Contractility.** Wall thickening and inward motion around the whole ring give a global impression of LV function.
**Detecting RWMA.** All three coronary territories are in one slice (ECHO-23).
**Detecting RV enlargement.** The normal RV is a crescent wrapped around the LV; when it dilates it becomes as large as or larger than the LV, and the septum flattens.
**IVS motion abnormalities.** Paradoxical septal motion follows cardiac surgery and LBBB; septal flattening reflects RV pressure (systolic) or volume (diastolic) overload.
mimic: ‘Kissing’ papillary muscles from hypovolaemia vs from low SVR
Both obliterate the cavity in systole; hypovolaemia has a small end-diastolic area and a small IVC, low SVR has a normal end-diastolic size (ECHO-36).
traps: “The main advantage of the circular LV view is measuring the LVOT gradient”
It is regional wall motion (67% right); gradients need apical Doppler.
decode: Circular LV after rotating 90° clockwise from PLAX — primary advantage? [DocT GT]
Evaluating LV regional wall motion.
Small LV with end-systolic cavity obliteration at the papillary level? [pattern]
Hypovolaemia (check the IVC), or low SVR if diastolic size is normal.
ECHO-25.punch: The mid-papillary slice gives LV filling, global and regional contraction, RV size and septal shape in one look, which is why it is the PSAX level in basic FATE.

ECHO-26.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → PSAX mitral and aortic levels
ECHO-26.intro: The basal slices of step 3: at the mitral and aortic levels the valves are seen in cross-section.
why: **Mitral valve level: measure the mitral valve AREA, assess regurgitant flow and look for vegetations.** Cut across the leaflet tips, the orifice is seen face-on as a ‘fish mouth’, so its area can be traced directly (planimetry), the reference method in mitral stenosis (severe at ≤1.5 cm²). Colour shows where along the coaptation line a regurgitant jet arises.

**Aortic valve level: structural abnormalities; the MERCEDES-BENZ sign is seen.** The three closed cusps form a ‘Y’ in diastole; a bicuspid valve shows a single closure line and an oval (‘fish-mouth’) opening in systole. The same slice shows the tricuspid and pulmonary valves, the RVOT, the pulmonary artery and the interatrial septum.
mimic: Tricuspid (Mercedes-Benz) vs bicuspid aortic valve
Three cusps and a Y-shaped closure line vs two cusps and a single closure line.
traps: “Mitral valve area is measured in A4C”
A4C gives inflow Doppler; the area is traced in PSAX at the mitral level (ECHO-33).
decode: View for planimetry of the mitral valve area? [pattern]
PSAX at the mitral valve level.
ECHO-26.punch: At the mitral level the orifice is traced for its area; at the aortic level the Mercedes-Benz sign shows three normal cusps.

ECHO-27.intro: Step 4: from the apex the beam runs along the long axis of the heart, parallel to blood moving through the atrioventricular valves. Three versions of one question ask which view grades TR and estimates RVSP; only about half got it in two of them.
why: **Transducer at the APEX of the heart.**

**Uses: chamber enlargement; detecting and quantifying regurgitant and stenotic lesions; RV and LV contractility; mitral and tricuspid INFLOW pattern.** All four chambers are side by side, so their relative size is judged directly (the RV is normally under two-thirds of the LV; RV/LV >1.0 is an ESC 2019 sign of RV dysfunction in PE). Mitral and tricuspid flow, including regurgitant jets, runs along the beam, so colour and CW Doppler measure them with little angle error; the TR peak velocity gives RVSP = 4V² + RAP. TAPSE and MAPSE are measured here on M-mode, and LV EF by the biplane method (with A2C). PW Doppler at the mitral leaflet tips gives E, A and deceleration time (ECHO-40).
mimic: A4C vs subcostal IVC for RVSP
A4C gives the TR velocity (the 4V² part); the subcostal IVC gives the RAP that is added to it.
traps: “Subcostal IVC view assesses TR severity and RVSP”
It gives only the RAP; the TR jet is measured in A4C (58%, 51%, 89% right).
“PLAX or A2C for TR”
In PLAX the TR jet runs across the beam; A2C contains no RV or tricuspid valve.
decode: Best view for TR severity and RVSP by Doppler? [DocT QBank, DocT GT ×2]
Apical four-chamber.
Where is TAPSE measured? [pattern]
A4C, M-mode through the lateral tricuspid annulus.
ECHO-27.punch: A4C lines the beam up with flow across both AV valves, so it is the view for inflow Doppler, regurgitant jets and the TR velocity behind RVSP, and the view where the four chambers are compared.

ECHO-28.intro: Step 4’s commonest error: an apical view that misses the true apex makes the LV look short and gives wrong volumes.
why: **The beam does NOT cut through the true apex but transects ABOVE and ANTERIOR to it.** The usual cause is a probe placed one rib space too high or too medial.

**Geometric DISTORTION of the LV image.** The LV appears shorter, so volumes are underestimated and EF misreported, and apical problems (apical wall motion abnormality, aneurysm, thrombus, Takotsubo) can be missed.
**Apex looks ‘ROUNDED’ instead of the normal ‘BULLET’ shape.** The fix is to move down and laterally until the LV is longest and the apex tapers.
mimic: Rounded apex from foreshortening vs from a real apical aneurysm
Foreshortening disappears when the probe is moved to the true apex; an aneurysm persists and bulges in systole.
traps: “A rounded apex is normal”
The normal apex is bullet-shaped; rounded means foreshortened.
decode: Apical view with a rounded LV apex — what is wrong? [pattern]
Foreshortening: the beam is above and anterior to the true apex.
ECHO-28.punch: If the apex looks round, the beam has missed it: move down and out until the LV is longest and bullet-shaped, or volumes and apical motion will be wrong.

ECHO-29.intro: Step 4 again: a small tilt from A4C brings the LVOT and aortic valve into the beam, parallel to systolic flow.
why: **Slight ANTERIOR angulation of the transducer, towards the chest wall.** Tilting, not rotating: the plane moves forward onto the LVOT.
**The fifth ‘chamber’ is the aortic valve and ascending aorta.** It is the outflow tract and root, not a cavity.

**Assesses LVOT velocities; detects and quantifies aortic regurgitation and stenosis.** PW Doppler just below the valve gives the LVOT VTI, which with the PLAX diameter gives stroke volume (ECHO-33) and, before and after a PLR, fluid responsiveness. CW through the valve gives the aortic stenosis peak velocity and gradient (severe at ≥4 m/s); the AR jet runs back along the beam.
mimic: A5C (angulation) vs A2C and A3C (rotation)
A5C is the only apical view made by tilting.
traps: “The fifth chamber is the coronary sinus or LA appendage”
It is the aortic valve and ascending aorta.
decode: View for LVOT VTI and aortic stenosis gradient? [pattern]
Apical five-chamber (or A3C).
ECHO-29.punch: Tilt forward from A4C and the aortic root appears as a ‘fifth chamber’: this is the view for LVOT velocity, VTI and aortic valve Doppler.

ECHO-30.intro: Step 4: rotate at the apex and the RV leaves the picture, leaving the LV and LA alone.
why: **Transducer at the APEX of the heart.**
**Marker dot towards the LEFT SIDE OF THE NECK.**

**Rotate the probe 90° from the apical 4-chamber.** Most texts describe about 60–90° counter-clockwise. Rotating on the apex gives the apical long-axis and two-chamber views, which show different LV segments.
**Focus on the LV WITHOUT ANY RV IMAGE.** A2C shows the anterior and inferior LV walls, which A4C does not, so A4C plus A2C give the biplane (Simpson’s) EF and full regional assessment.
mimic: A4C vs A2C
A4C: septum and lateral wall, with the RV. A2C: anterior and inferior walls, no RV.
traps: “A2C can assess the RV or TR”
There is no RV in the image.
decode: Apical view that shows the LV and LA without the RV? [pattern]
Apical two-chamber.
ECHO-30.punch: A2C is A4C rotated so the marker points at the neck: the RV disappears, and the anterior and inferior walls appear for biplane EF.

ECHO-31.intro: Step 4: the apical long axis is the PLAX plane seen from the apex, so the LVOT now runs along the beam.
why: **Transducer at the APEX of the heart.**

**Transducer turned CLOCKWISE by 60° from the A2C view.** This is the card’s wording. Standard texts rotate a further ~60° COUNTER-clockwise from A2C (about 120° from A4C), bringing the marker towards the right shoulder, the same plane as PLAX (see FLAGS).

**Mitral AND aortic valves in the SAME PLANE.** Because it lies in the long-axis plane (ECHO-14), the LVOT, aortic valve and mitral valve appear together, with the anteroseptal and inferolateral walls.

**Measure LVOT velocities.** The outflow tract runs along the beam, so PW and CW Doppler measure LVOT VTI, aortic stenosis velocity and dynamic LVOT obstruction (systolic anterior motion) with little angle error.
mimic: A3C vs PLAX
Same plane; PLAX measures the LVOT DIAMETER (beam perpendicular), A3C its VELOCITY (beam parallel).
traps: “A3C is obtained by tilting from A4C”
Tilting gives A5C; A3C is reached by rotation, taken from A2C on the card.
decode: Apical view with mitral and aortic valves in the same plane? [pattern]
Apical 3-chamber (apical long axis).
ECHO-31.punch: A3C is the long-axis plane seen from the apex: both left-sided valves in one picture and the LVOT lined up for Doppler.

ECHO-32.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Rotations compared
ECHO-32.intro: Step 4 summarised: each derived view comes from a reference view by a rotation or a tilt.
why: **PSAX: rotate clockwise, from PLAX, 90°.** Marker from right to left shoulder.
**A5C: angulate anteriorly, from A4C, no angle.** The only tilt.
**A2C: rotate, from A4C, 90°.** Usually counter-clockwise, about 60–90°.
**A3C: rotate clockwise, from A2C, 60°.** Card wording; standard texts rotate further counter-clockwise from A2C (see FLAGS on ECHO-31).
mimic: Rotation vs angulation
Rotation turns the plane around the beam axis; angulation tilts the beam to a different part of the heart in the same orientation.
traps: “A5C is a rotation from A4C”
It is the only angulation.
decode: Manoeuvre to go from PLAX to PSAX? [pattern]
Rotate 90° clockwise.
ECHO-32.punch: Three rotations and one tilt: PLAX → PSAX 90° clockwise, A4C → A5C tilt forward, A4C → A2C and then A2C → A3C by rotation.
