ECHO-33.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Which view measures what
ECHO-33.intro: Step 4’s rule in one table: diameters come from views where the beam is perpendicular to the structure, velocities from views where it is parallel to the flow.
why: **LVOT diameter: PLAX.** Axial resolution is best when the beam strikes the walls at right angles.
**LVOT velocities: A5C and A3C.** Doppler underestimates velocity by the cosine of the angle; under 20° the error is small. Stroke volume = 0.785 × D² (PLAX) × LVOT VTI (apical).
**Mitral valve area: PSAX, mitral valve level.** The orifice is seen face-on for planimetry.
**Mitral and tricuspid inflow pattern: A4C.** Inflow runs along the beam.
mimic: Diameter vs velocity
Perpendicular beam (PLAX) vs parallel beam (apical).
traps: “LVOT velocity is measured in PLAX”
In PLAX the flow runs across the beam; Doppler there reads near zero.
decode: Views needed to calculate stroke volume by echo? [pattern]
PLAX for LVOT diameter, A5C or A3C for LVOT VTI.
ECHO-33.punch: Measure size where the beam is perpendicular and velocity where it is parallel; that is why stroke volume needs two views.

ECHO-34.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Basic FATE views
ECHO-34.intro: Step 5: FATE (focus-assessed transthoracic echo, Jensen 2004) is a short protocol for the anaesthetist and intensivist, built from the views most likely to be obtainable.
why: **1 Subcostal 4-chamber, 2 Apical 4-chamber, 3 PLAX, 4 PSAX at papillary level, 5 Pleural scanning.** On the FATE card these are positions 1 to 4, with PLAX and PSAX together as position 3 and pleural scanning as position 4; the card says to scan in the most favourable sequence. Subcostal comes first because it works supine; pleural scanning is in the basic set because effusions are a common cause of breathlessness and low output.
mimic: FATE vs RUSH
FATE is a structured cardiac and pleural exam; RUSH adds the IVC, abdomen, aorta and leg veins to find the type of shock.
traps: “Pleural scanning is an extended view”
It is basic.
decode: Which PSAX level is in the basic FATE set? [pattern]
Papillary muscle level.
ECHO-34.punch: Basic FATE is subcostal, apical, parasternal long and short (papillary) and the pleura: a heart-and-lung exam from the start.

ECHO-35.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Extended FATE views
ECHO-35.intro: Step 5 continues: when the basic scan raises a question, the extended views answer it.
why: **1 Subcostal IVC, 2 A2C, 3 A3C, 4 A5C, 5 PSAX at mitral valve level.** These add filling (IVC), the LV segments missing from A4C (A2C, A3C), outflow Doppler (A5C, A3C) and the mitral valve (PSAX). The FATE card itself lists PSAX at both the mitral AND aortic levels among the extended views (see FLAGS).
mimic: Subcostal 4-chamber vs subcostal IVC
Same window: the 4-chamber view is basic, the IVC view is extended.
traps: “The IVC view is basic because subcostal is basic”
Subcostal 4-chamber is basic; the IVC view is extended.
decode: Which PSAX level is in the extended FATE set? [pattern]
Mitral valve level (the card also lists the aortic level).
ECHO-35.punch: Extended FATE adds the IVC, the other apical views and the basal PSAX: filling, all LV segments and Doppler.

ECHO-36.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Goals of FATE
ECHO-36.intro: Step 5’s core: what the FATE scan is for. Four questions test how its findings are read; one of them, a hyperdynamic LV with normal volume status, was got right by only 38%.
why: **Goal 1: exclude obvious pathology: pleural and pericardial effusions, valvular disease, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism.** These are the causes of instability that change management at once. In PLAX, fluid anterior to the descending aorta is pericardial and fluid behind it is pleural (ECHO-22).

**Goal 2: assess wall thickness and chamber dimensions: hypertrophy, relative LV/RV size, chamber enlargement.** A small LV with cavity obliteration suggests hypovolaemia; a dilated, thin-walled LV is chronic cardiomyopathy; a dilated RV with septal flattening points to PE or RV failure.

**Goal 3: assess contractility qualitatively: hyperdynamic, normal, mild, moderate or severe dysfunction.** Eyeballing in all views is quick and, in trained hands, agrees well with measured EF. A hyperdynamic LV means a small end-systolic volume: if the end-diastolic size is small too, the patient is hypovolaemic; if it is normal, afterload is low (sepsis, anaemia, liver failure, thyrotoxicosis).

**Goal 4: image the pleura bilaterally: a transudative effusion is ANECHOIC; the ‘plankton sign’ suggests infection or haemothorax.** A free-flowing effusion moves with a sinusoid sign on M-mode (ECHO-21).
mimic: Hyperdynamic LV: hypovolaemia vs low SVR
Hypovolaemia: small end-diastolic LV and a small, collapsing IVC. Low SVR: normal end-diastolic size and normal IVC, with an empty-looking LV only in systole.
Hypovolaemic vs cardiogenic vs obstructive oliguria
Small hyperdynamic LV with cavity obliteration vs dilated poorly contracting LV vs dilated RV with septal flattening.
traps: “Hyperdynamic LV with normal volume status = hypovolaemic shock”

Only 38% got this: the stem says volume status is normal, so the LV is not underfilled; it empties because the afterload is low (key A, low SVR). Raised pulmonary resistance gives a dilated RV, not a hyperdynamic LV.
“Anechoic dependent fluid with a sinusoid sign proves a transudate”

The key (simple transudative effusion, 61% right) is the best option, but it over-reads: the sinusoid sign proves free-flowing, low-viscosity fluid, and an anechoic effusion can be an exudate. Empyema and organised haemothorax damp the swing.
“Fluid anterior to the descending aorta on PLAX is pleural”
It is pericardial; the pericardial reflection stops at the aorta.
decode: Acute dyspnoea, hyperdynamic LV, normal volume status — haemodynamic state? [DocT QBank]
Low systemic vascular resistance.
Post-hypotension oliguria — echo finding of a prerenal, hypovolaemic cause? [DocT GT PYQ]
Hyperdynamic LV with near-complete cavity obliteration in systole.
Dependent anechoic pleural fluid moving sinusoidally — indicates? [DocT QBank]
Free-flowing simple effusion (keyed transudate).
Anechoic fluid anterior to the descending aorta on PLAX? [DocT GT]
Pericardial effusion.
ECHO-36.punch: FATE asks four things in order: is there an obvious lesion, are the chambers the right size and thickness, how well do they contract, and is there pleural fluid. A hyperdynamic LV is hypovolaemia only if it is also small in diastole.

ECHO-37.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → LV dimensions
ECHO-37.intro: Step 6 begins the numbers. These are the FATE-style textbook values measured on PLAX M-mode; ASE 2015 now gives sex-specific ranges, which differ at the upper ends.
why: **Internal diameter: end-systolic 2.0–4.0 cm, end-diastolic 3.5–5.6 cm.** ASE 2015 gives LVIDd 4.2–5.8 cm in men and 3.8–5.2 cm in women; LV size is now better described by indexed volumes.

**Diastolic wall thickness, septum and posterior wall: 0.6–1.2 cm.** ASE 2015: 0.6–1.0 cm in men and 0.6–0.9 cm in women; mildly abnormal (LVH) is 1.1–1.3 cm in men and 1.0–1.2 cm in women. The FATE card itself gives 6–10 mm.
**Systolic wall thickness, septum and posterior wall: 0.9–1.8 cm.** The wall thickens as it contracts; failure to thicken marks a regional abnormality.

**Fractional shortening 30–45%; ejection fraction 50–85%.** FS = (LVIDd − LVIDs) ÷ LVIDd, and EF is roughly twice FS. ASE 2015 normal LVEF is 52–72% in men and 54–74% in women; FS is valid only when the LV contracts evenly, because it samples one line.
mimic: Diastolic vs systolic wall thickness
0.6–1.2 cm vs 0.9–1.8 cm, identical for septum and posterior wall.
traps: “A septum of 1.2 cm is normal”
It is at the card’s upper limit but mildly thickened by ASE 2015 standards.
decode: Normal LV end-diastolic diameter? [pattern]
ECHO-37.punch: Card values: LVIDs 2–4, LVIDd 3.5–5.6, walls 0.6–1.2 in diastole and 0.9–1.8 in systole, FS 30–45%, EF 50–85%; current ASE ranges are sex-specific and tighter.

ECHO-38.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Other chamber dimensions
ECHO-38.intro: Step 6 continues with the other linear sizes, again older M-mode values that ASE 2015 has largely replaced.
why: **Left atrium: 2.0–4.0 cm.** A single antero-posterior diameter underestimates LA enlargement because the atrium grows mostly downwards and sideways; ASE 2015 uses the LA volume index (normal ≤34 mL/m²), which is also a marker of chronic raised filling pressure.
**Aortic root: 2.0–4.0 cm.** ASE 2015 mean at the sinuses is about 3.4 cm in men and 3.0 cm in women, best judged against body size and age.

**Right ventricle (systolic–diastolic): 0.7–2.3 cm.** This is the old M-mode RV dimension in PLAX. ASE 2015 (and the 2025 right heart guideline) measures the RV in an RV-focused A4C: basal diameter >4.1 cm or mid >3.5 cm is dilated.
mimic: LA diameter vs LA volume index
Diameter is quick but insensitive; volume index is the current standard.
traps: “A normal LA diameter excludes LA enlargement”
The LA can enlarge in other directions; check the volume.
decode: Normal LA and aortic root diameters? [pattern]
2.0–4.0 cm each (card).
ECHO-38.punch: LA, aortic root and LV end-systolic diameter all share 2.0–4.0 cm on the card, and RV 0.7–2.3 cm; current practice uses LA volume and RV-focused apical diameters.

ECHO-39.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Systolic function grading
ECHO-39.intro: Step 6’s grading table, from the FATE card, turns function into bands. The NEET 2024 recall asks where EPSS (the card’s MSS) is measured; the TR questions return to A4C, where TAPSE comes from.
why: **EF: normal ≥55%, mild 45–54, moderate 30–44, severe <30.** ASE 2015 grades slightly differently: normal 52–72% (men) and 54–74% (women), mildly abnormal 41–51 (men) / 41–53 (women), moderate 30–40, severe <30.
**FS: normal ≥25%, mild 20–24, moderate 15–19, severe <15.** EF is roughly twice FS.

**MSS (mitral–septal separation, EPSS): normal <10 mm, mild 7–12, moderate 13–24, severe >24.** In PLAX on M-mode, the anterior mitral leaflet’s early opening (E point) normally nearly touches the septum because a large stroke volume passes through a normal-sized LV. In a dilated, poorly contracting LV the leaflet opens less and the septum is further away. EPSS >7 mm is usually taken as reduced EF. It is unreliable when the anterior leaflet cannot open fully for another reason (mitral stenosis, or an AR jet striking the leaflet), which raises it falsely, and with asymmetric septal hypertrophy or a septal wall-motion abnormality.
**MAPSE: normal ≥11 mm, mild 9–10, moderate 6–8, severe <6.** Longitudinal fibres move the mitral annulus towards the apex in systole; the distance is measured on M-mode in A4C.

**TAPSE: normal ≥17 mm, mild 11–16, moderate 6–10, severe <6.** The RV contracts mostly longitudinally, so tricuspid annular motion in A4C reflects RV function; ASE 2015 takes <17 mm as dysfunction (mean about 24 mm), and the ASE 2025 right heart guideline grades it as mild 13–17, moderate 10–13 and severe ≤10 mm. ESC 2019 uses TAPSE <16 mm among the echo signs of RV dysfunction in PE, and TAPSE/sPAP <0.55 mm/mmHg supports PH (ESC/ERS 2022). TAPSE is angle-dependent and load-dependent, and falls after cardiac surgery even when RV function is preserved.
mimic: MSS vs the other indices
MSS runs the other way: high is bad.
MAPSE vs TAPSE
Same severe cut-off (<6 mm), different normals (≥11 vs ≥17).
traps: “EPSS is measured in A4C”
It is measured on PLAX M-mode (NEET 2024).
“TAPSE comes from PLAX”
EF, FS and MSS come from PLAX (FATE position 3); MAPSE and TAPSE come from A4C (position 2).
decode: Best view to measure EPSS? [NEET 2024]
Parasternal long axis; EPSS >7 mm suggests low EF.
TAPSE cut-off for RV systolic dysfunction? [pattern]
<17 mm (ASE 2015); <16 mm in ESC 2019 PE.
ECHO-39.punch: EF, FS and EPSS come from PLAX, MAPSE and TAPSE from A4C; EPSS rises as function falls, and TAPSE under 17 mm marks a failing RV.

ECHO-40.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Normal Doppler values
ECHO-40.intro: Step 6 ends with the Doppler numbers and the one equation of the chapter. Five questions link here: three on where the TR jet is measured, one RVSP calculation (33% right) and one asking the name of the equation (48% right).
why: **CW: peak pressure gradient = 4V²; normal AO <2 m/s, PA <1 m/s, TI <2.5 m/s.** The simplified Bernoulli equation: when blood accelerates through a narrow orifice, pressure energy becomes kinetic energy, and with blood’s density and unit conversions the gradient in mmHg is about 4 × V² (m/s). It ignores the velocity before the orifice, which is safe when that is under about 1 m/s. Applied to TR: RVSP = 4V² + RAP. Aortic velocity rises with stenosis (severe ≥4 m/s); ESC/ERS 2022 treats a TR velocity >2.8 m/s as raising the probability of pulmonary hypertension.

**PW: mitral inflow deceleration time 140–240 ms; max E <1.2 m/s; E/A >1 (age dependent).** PW at the mitral leaflet tips in A4C. E is early passive filling, driven by the LA–LV pressure difference and LV relaxation; A is atrial contraction. With age and impaired relaxation E falls, A rises and DT lengthens (E/A <1); when LA pressure is high E rises again and DT shortens (restrictive filling, E/A ≥2). Because a normal and a high-pressure pattern can look alike (pseudonormal), E/A is read with e′ and E/e′.

**TVI: E/e′ <8–10; IVC <20 mm; 50% inspiratory collapse is normal.** TVI here is tissue velocity imaging (tissue Doppler), not velocity–time integral. e′ is the speed of early diastolic mitral annular motion, a measure of relaxation that is fairly independent of load, so E/e′ tracks LA pressure. Current cut-offs: average E/e′ >14 indicates raised filling pressure (ASE/EACVI 2016, kept in the ASE 2025 update, which also uses TR ≥2.8 m/s, LA volume index >34 mL/m² and LA reservoir strain ≤18%). The IVC figure (<20 mm) is the FATE card’s; the ASE RAP table uses 2.1 cm (ECHO-19).
mimic: Bernoulli vs Laplace vs Poiseuille
Bernoulli converts velocity to a pressure gradient; Laplace relates wall tension to pressure and radius; Poiseuille relates laminar flow to pressure, radius and viscosity.
Mitral E/e′ vs tricuspid E/e′
Mitral <8 normal and >14 raised LA pressure; tricuspid >6 suggests raised RA pressure (ECHO-19).
traps: “RVSP = 4 × 3.5² = 49 mmHg”
That is the RV–RA gradient; add the RAP: 49 + 10 ≈ 60 mmHg (33% right).
“The pressure gradient between two chambers is calculated by Laplace’s law”
It is Bernoulli’s (48% right); Laplace is wall tension, and the ‘Dubois’ formula is body surface area.
“Subcostal IVC or PLAX for TR and RVSP”
The TR jet is measured in A4C, parallel to the beam (ECHO-27).
decode: Equation for the pressure gradient between two chambers? [DocT GT]
Bernoulli: ΔP = 4V².
TR 3.5 m/s, RAP 10 mmHg — RVSP? [DocT QBank]
≈60 mmHg.
Best view for TR severity and RVSP? [DocT QBank, DocT GT ×2]
Apical four-chamber.
ECHO-40.punch: Every CW velocity becomes a pressure by 4V², and adding the RAP to the TR gradient gives RVSP. Mitral E and A describe filling, and E/e′ (tissue Doppler) says whether the LA pressure is high.

topups.q: Shock on POCUS (RUSH: pump, tank, pipes) — which type?
a: - Pump: poor LV contraction with dilated chambers → cardiogenic; hyperdynamic LV → hypovolaemic or distributive.
- Tank: small IVC (<1.5 cm) collapsing >50% with 'kissing' papillary muscles → hypovolaemic (VTI rise >10–15% on PLR confirms responsiveness).
- Plethoric IVC + a cause → obstructive: effusion with RA/RV diastolic collapse (tamponade), RV > LV with D-shaped septum (PE), absent sliding (tension pneumothorax).
- Plethoric IVC + poor LV + bilateral B-lines → cardiogenic; normal/small IVC + hyperdynamic LV → early sepsis.
- Pipes: aortic aneurysm/dissection flap and leg-vein compression complete the scan.
topups.src: DocT Procedures, Techniques & POCUS Q32; DocT GT GT8 Q113; DocT GT AIM2 Q65

x.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Shock on POCUS (RUSH)
x.intro: Step 5 puts the views to work. FATE grades the heart; RUSH (pump, tank, pipes) is the shock protocol that adds the IVC, lungs, abdomen, aorta and leg veins to sort shock into its four types. Three Grand Test questions ask which type a set of findings fits.
why: **Pump: poor LV contraction with dilated chambers → cardiogenic; hyperdynamic LV → hypovolaemic or distributive.** A dilated, poorly contracting LV cannot generate output; a hyperdynamic one is either underfilled (hypovolaemia) or emptying against a low afterload (sepsis), and the tank decides which (ECHO-36).

**Tank: small IVC (<1.5 cm) collapsing >50% with ‘kissing’ papillary muscles → hypovolaemic; a VTI rise >10–15% on PLR confirms responsiveness.** A small collapsing IVC means low RAP (ECHO-19), and end-systolic cavity obliteration means an underfilled LV; the PLR test shows that stroke volume actually rises with preload (ECHO-20).

**Plethoric IVC plus a cause → obstructive: effusion with RA/RV diastolic collapse (tamponade), RV larger than LV with a D-shaped septum (PE), absent lung sliding (tension pneumothorax).** In all three the venous return is blocked before the LV, so the IVC is full and the LV small. The effusion compresses the low-pressure right chambers; in PE the pressure-loaded RV dilates (RV/LV >1.0) and flattens the septum; in tension pneumothorax the lung never touches the chest wall, so sliding disappears.

**Plethoric IVC + poor LV + bilateral B-lines → cardiogenic; normal or small IVC + hyperdynamic LV → early sepsis.** Raised left filling pressure pushes fluid into the interstitium (B-lines) and backs up to the IVC; in early sepsis venodilation keeps the IVC normal or small while the LV empties against low SVR.

**Pipes: aortic aneurysm or dissection flap, and leg-vein compression, complete the scan.** An abdominal aorta >3 cm is aneurysmal, and in a shocked patient one >5 cm is treated as rupture (haemorrhagic shock) until proved otherwise; a flap means dissection, which can bleed or cause tamponade. A non-compressible femoral or popliteal vein supports PE.
mimic: Hypovolaemic vs early distributive
Both hyperdynamic; hypovolaemia has a small collapsing IVC and small end-diastolic LV, early sepsis a normal LV size.
Obstructive vs cardiogenic with a plethoric IVC
Obstructive: small LV with a visible cause (effusion, dilated RV, no sliding). Cardiogenic: dilated poor LV with B-lines.
traps: “A plethoric IVC means cardiogenic shock”
It means a high RAP from any cause: tamponade, PE and tension pneumothorax also give it, so look for the cause before calling it the pump.
“A hyperdynamic LV means hypovolaemia”
Only with a small IVC and small end-diastolic LV; with a normal size it is low SVR.
decode: Shock, plethoric IVC, RV larger than LV with a D-shaped septum [pattern]
Obstructive shock from PE.
Shock, small IVC collapsing >50%, kissing papillary muscles [pattern]
Hypovolaemic shock.
x.punch: Pump, tank, pipes: a dilated poor LV with a full IVC and B-lines is cardiogenic, a full IVC with a small LV and a cause is obstructive, and a hyperdynamic LV is hypovolaemic only if the tank is empty.

topups.q: When is TEE the right tool — and when is it not?
a: - TEE: prosthetic and native valve detail, LA/LAA thrombus before cardioversion, aortic dissection, endocarditis (vegetation, abscess), guiding valvuloplasty, LAA occlusion and ASD/PFO closure, intra-operative monitoring.
- Pericardiocentesis is guided by TTE (subcostal/apical) — TEE sees the anterior pericardial space poorly.
- TEE is semi-invasive (sedation, oesophageal injury); TTE comes first in most ICU questions.

- In shock, the transgastric mid-papillary short-axis view gives LV size, systolic function and wall motion in all three coronary territories in one look; mid-oesophageal views give valves and chambers, upper-oesophageal views the great vessels.
topups.src: Marrow QB02-Q02; DocT GT CGT5 Q40

x.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → TEE vs TTE
x.intro: Step 1 is about windows, and TEE is the window from behind: the oesophagus lies right against the left atrium with no lung or rib in the way. Two questions ask when that advantage matters and when it does not.
why: **TEE: prosthetic and native valve detail, LA/LAA thrombus before cardioversion, aortic dissection, endocarditis (vegetation, abscess), guiding valvuloplasty, LAA occlusion and ASD/PFO closure, intra-operative monitoring.** Posterior structures (LA, appendage, mitral valve, thoracic aorta) are closest to the probe, so a higher-frequency, higher-resolution image is possible; the LAA is barely seen on TTE, and prosthetic valves cast shadows that hide the atrial side from the front.

**Pericardiocentesis is guided by TTE (subcostal or apical); TEE sees the anterior pericardial space poorly.** The needle enters from the front or below, where the fluid is closest to the skin; TTE shows that path, while the TEE probe looks from behind.

**TEE is semi-invasive (sedation, oesophageal injury); TTE comes first in most ICU questions.** It needs sedation or a protected airway and risks oesophageal and pharyngeal injury; oesophageal perforation, stricture, tumour and recent oesophageal surgery are contraindications, and varices a relative one.

**In shock, the transgastric mid-papillary short-axis view gives LV size, systolic function and wall motion in all three coronary territories in one look; mid-oesophageal views give valves and chambers, upper-oesophageal views the great vessels.** It is the TEE counterpart of the PSAX papillary level (ECHO-25), which is why it is the monitoring view in theatre and in the ICU.
mimic: TEE vs TTE for tamponade
TTE (subcostal) diagnoses it and guides the needle; TEE is needed only for loculated posterior collections, as after cardiac surgery.
traps: “TEE guides pericardiocentesis”
TTE does; TEE sees the anterior space poorly.
“TTE excludes LA appendage thrombus before cardioversion”
Only TEE shows the appendage reliably.
decode: TEE view for LV function and wall motion in all coronary territories in shock? [pattern]
Transgastric mid-papillary short axis.
Imaging to guide pericardiocentesis? [pattern]
TTE, subcostal or apical.
x.punch: TEE wins for posterior structures (LA appendage, prosthetic and mitral valves, thoracic aorta, endocarditis) because it looks from behind; for the front of the heart and the pericardial needle TTE is better and comes first.

topups.q: AR severity cut-offs and normal prosthetic-valve Doppler?
a: - AR vena contracta <0.3 mild / 0.3–0.6 moderate / >0.6 cm severe.
- AR regurgitant volume <30 / 30–59 / ≥60 mL; pressure half-time >500 / 200–500 / <200 ms.
- Normal prosthetic aortic valve: peak velocity ≤3 m/s, mean gradient ≤20 mmHg.
- Normal prosthetic mitral valve: peak velocity <1.9 m/s, mean gradient ≤5 mmHg.

x.sub: Cardiology → Echo in ICU → Valve echo numbers
x.intro: Step 6’s numbers extended to the valves: Marrow asks the aortic regurgitation severity cut-offs and what normal Doppler looks like across a prosthetic valve.
why: **AR vena contracta: <0.3 cm mild, 0.3–0.6 moderate, >0.6 cm severe.** The vena contracta is the narrowest part of the jet just below the valve, which reflects the size of the regurgitant orifice and is little affected by loading or by the jet’s spread.

**AR regurgitant volume <30 / 30–59 / ≥60 mL; pressure half-time >500 / 200–500 / <200 ms.** The more severe the leak, the faster aortic and LV diastolic pressures equalise, so the CW slope steepens and the half-time shortens. Half-time also shortens when LV diastolic pressure is high for other reasons, so it supports rather than decides severity.

**Normal prosthetic aortic valve: peak velocity ≤3 m/s, mean gradient ≤20 mmHg.** Every prosthesis is mildly stenotic compared with a native valve, so its normal gradient is higher; above these values, consider obstruction (thrombus, pannus) or patient–prosthesis mismatch, or high flow.

**Normal prosthetic mitral valve: peak velocity <1.9 m/s, mean gradient ≤5 mmHg.** Both figures rise with heart rate and flow, so they are read with the heart rate and with the VTI ratio across the valve.
mimic: Pressure half-time in AR vs in mitral stenosis
In AR a SHORT half-time means severe disease; in MS a LONG half-time means a tight valve (MVA ≈ 220 ÷ PHT).
traps: “A longer AR half-time means more severe AR”
The reverse: <200 ms is severe.
“Any mean gradient above 10 mmHg across a prosthetic aortic valve is obstruction”
Up to 20 mmHg is normal for a prosthesis.
decode: AR vena contracta 0.7 cm — severity? [pattern]
Severe (>0.6 cm).
Normal mean gradient across a prosthetic mitral valve? [pattern]
≤5 mmHg (peak velocity <1.9 m/s).
x.punch: Severe AR: vena contracta >0.6 cm, regurgitant volume ≥60 mL, half-time <200 ms. A normal prosthesis is mildly stenotic: aortic peak ≤3 m/s and mean ≤20 mmHg, mitral peak <1.9 m/s and mean ≤5.

spine: Planes, windows and the marker
The heart is imaged in three orthogonal planes from five windows, and the marker dot fixes which way the plane is cut, so every standard view is a window plus a plane plus a marker direction.
Subcostal window and the IVC
The subcostal window works supine when the chest windows fail, and the IVC’s size and its change with breathing estimate right atrial pressure well and fluid responsiveness only modestly.
Parasternal views: long and short
PLAX shows the LV, LVOT, aortic root and the relation of fluid to the descending aorta; rotating 90° clockwise gives PSAX slices, where all three coronary territories are seen together.
Apical views line the beam up
Apical views put the beam parallel to blood flow, so Doppler of mitral and tricuspid inflow, the LVOT and the TR jet comes from them, while diameters come from views where the beam is perpendicular.
FATE: sequence, goals, pleura
FATE strings the basic views and a bilateral pleural scan into one protocol that excludes obvious pathology, sizes the chambers and grades function by eye.
Numbers: size, function, Doppler
Normal dimensions and systolic grading bands turn pictures into numbers, and the Bernoulli equation turns a velocity into a pressure: RVSP = 4V² + RAP.
CVS05B.primer: Ultrasound images only what the beam can reach through soft tissue or fluid; air (lung) and bone block it, so the heart is seen through a few ‘windows’ where it touches the chest wall or can be reached from the abdomen. Two-dimensional images show structure best when the beam hits it at right angles, whereas Doppler measures velocity best when the beam runs parallel to the blood (the error grows with the cosine of the angle). The inferior vena cava is a compliant, valveless vein draining straight into the right atrium, so its size and its change with breathing follow right atrial pressure. CVS05A covered the physics and the basic principles; this deck is the views, the IVC, the FATE protocol and the normal numbers.

RVF-01.sub: RV failure → Introduction → Epidemiology, mortality and ICU settings
RVF-01.intro: Step 1 sets the size of the problem and what ‘failure’ means. The RV is uncommon as the primary cause of an acute heart failure admission but common as a complication in the ICU, and the one real question asked how true RV failure differs from mere RV dysfunction or a high CVP.
why: **2–9% of acute heart failure admissions to hospital.** Most acute heart failure is left-sided; isolated acute RV failure is a minority. The figure varies with how strictly RV failure is defined (RVF-02 gives 3–9%, which the card attributes to AHEAD).

**In-hospital mortality 5–17%.** This is higher than for many acute LV presentations because RV failure is usually driven by something else serious (massive PE, ARDS, RV infarct) and because a failing RV cannot be supported easily: fluid, vasodilators and positive pressure can each make it worse.

**ARDS, MI, pulmonary embolism, decompensated chronic lung disease, after cardiac surgery; worsening RV function directly affects ICU mortality.** Each of these either raises RV afterload suddenly (PE, ARDS, hypoxic and hypercapnic lung disease) or removes RV contractility (RV infarct, bypass stunning). The definition that decides questions: RV failure is RV dysfunction with limited RV filling, so the RV can only fill and deliver an adequate stroke volume to the LV at the cost of a high CVP and venous congestion.
mimic: RV failure vs RV dysfunction
Dysfunction is an abnormal RV on imaging with normal filling pressures; failure is dysfunction plus a high CVP and inadequate forward flow.
RV failure vs hypervolaemia
A high CVP with a normally contracting RV is volume, not failure; it falls with diuresis without improving output problems.
traps: “True RV failure is an elevated CVP with normal RV function”
That is volume loading. Failure needs the RV itself to be dysfunctional and unable to fill without a high CVP (69% chose correctly on DocT GT).
“Increased RV filling without decreased output defines failure”
If output is maintained, the RV is coping; failure is the point where more filling no longer buys more stroke volume.
decode: Septic shock, CVP 16, low CO, dilated poorly contracting RV — which best defines true RV failure? [DocT GT]
RV dysfunction with limited RV filling (69%).
Proportion of acute heart failure admissions due to acute RV failure / its in-hospital mortality [pattern]
2–9% (card’s AHEAD figure 3–9%); 5–17%.
RVF-01.punch: RV failure is not a high CVP and not a weak RV on echo alone: it is a dysfunctional RV that can fill only at a high venous pressure and still cannot deliver enough to the LV, and it carries an in-hospital mortality up to about one in six.

RVF-02.sub: RV failure → Introduction → AHEAD registry and HFpEF
RVF-02.intro: Step 1 again, with the registry figures that support the introduction. Never asked directly; the numbers matter only to recognise them in an option.
why: **AHEAD registry: 3–9% of acute heart failure admissions; in-hospital mortality of acute RV failure 5–17%.** These are the figures the card gives for AHEAD. In the literature the 3–9% range comes from several European registries (OFICA, ESC-HF pilot, RO-AHFS, EuroHeart Failure Survey II), the 2.2% lower end of the introduction’s range from the CHARITEM registry, and the 5–17% mortality from EuroHeart Failure Survey II. The spread reflects definition: some registries count only isolated right heart failure, others any acute RV failure.

**RV dysfunction in HFpEF: 14–40% across cohorts.** In HFpEF a stiff LV raises left atrial pressure, which is transmitted back to the pulmonary circulation (post-capillary PH, group 2, RVF-20). The RV then faces a raised afterload and fails in a sizeable minority, and when it does, prognosis worsens sharply.
mimic: Lower end from CHARITEM (2.2%) vs pooled European registries (3–9%); same mortality, 5–17%.
traps: “RV dysfunction is rare when LV function is normal”
Up to 40% of HFpEF patients have it, driven by post-capillary pulmonary hypertension.
decode: Prevalence of RV dysfunction in HFpEF [pattern]
RVF-02.punch: Acute RV failure is single-digit per cent of heart failure admissions with up to 17% in-hospital mortality, and a normal LV ejection fraction does not protect the RV: up to 40% of HFpEF patients have RV dysfunction.

RVF-03.sub: RV failure → Anatomy → Free wall, cavity, crista, fibres
RVF-03.intro: Step 2 starts with the shape of the pump, because almost every later behaviour of the RV follows from its thin wall. Not asked directly; the anatomy explains why TAPSE works and why the RV fails under pressure.
why: **Thin (2–3 mm), compliant free wall forming a hemi-ellipsoid that adheres to the LV.** A thin wall is cheap to perfuse and stretches easily, which suits a low-pressure circuit. By Laplace, wall stress rises with radius and pressure and falls with thickness, so a thin wall develops high stress as soon as pressure rises. On echo a free wall over 5 mm in diastole means hypertrophy, which implies chronic pressure load.

**Crescent-shaped cavity.** The RV wraps around the convex septum, so in cross-section it is a crescent. This shape gives a large surface for a small volume change, efficient for moving volume at low pressure, and makes RV volume hard to measure by 2D echo (no simple geometric formula fits).

**Crista supraventricularis: muscular ridge connecting the inflow and outflow tracts.** It separates the trabeculated inflow from the smooth infundibulum and contributes to the peristaltic sequence of contraction (RVF-04).

**Superficial circular fibres and deeper longitudinal fibres.** The LV has a third, middle circumferential layer; the RV does not, so RV ejection depends heavily on longitudinal shortening that pulls the tricuspid annulus towards the apex. That is why TAPSE, a single longitudinal measure, tracks RV function reasonably well.
mimic: RV vs LV wall layers
RV two layers, mainly longitudinal shortening; LV three layers with a dominant middle circumferential layer and radial thickening.
traps: “A thick RV free wall is normal in an adult”
Normal is 2–3 mm; over 5 mm on echo is RV hypertrophy and points to chronic pressure overload.
decode: Why is TAPSE a valid surrogate of RV systolic function? [pattern]
RV ejection is dominated by longitudinal fibre shortening.
RVF-03.punch: The RV is a 2–3 mm crescent that ejects mainly by longitudinal shortening, which makes it efficient at moving volume, easy to assess by TAPSE and defenceless against a sudden rise in pressure.

RVF-04.sub: RV failure → Physiology → Stroke work, circuit, peristalsis
RVF-04.intro: Step 2 continued: how the thin pump works against its low-pressure circuit. Not asked directly.
why: **RV stroke work is one quarter of the LV.** Both ventricles eject the same stroke volume, but the RV does it against a mean pressure of about 15 mmHg instead of about 90, so it does a fraction of the work with a fraction of the muscle.

**Highly compliant, low-resistance pulmonary circulation.** PVR is about a tenth of SVR, and the pulmonary bed can recruit and distend vessels, so flow can double with little rise in pressure in a healthy lung.

**Peristaltic contraction: free-wall area falls and longitudinal fibres shorten, starting at the inflow tract and moving towards the outflow tract.** Contraction sweeps from the inlet to the infundibulum with a delay of a few tens of milliseconds, squeezing blood forward like a peristaltic wave rather than a radial squeeze.

**Lower peak systolic pressure than the LV; exists at a higher steady-state volume.** RV systolic pressure is about 25 mmHg, and RV end-diastolic volume is normally a little larger than the LV’s, so the RV works on a flatter, high-volume portion of its pressure–volume relationship.
mimic: RV vs LV contraction
RV peristaltic, inflow to outflow, longitudinal; LV radial thickening with twisting.
traps: “The RV does about the same stroke work as the LV because it ejects the same stroke volume”
Stroke work is stroke volume × the pressure developed; with the same volume but a far lower ejection pressure, RV stroke work is about a quarter of the LV’s (some sources give a quarter to a sixth).
decode: RV stroke work relative to LV [pattern]
About one quarter.
RVF-04.punch: The RV moves the same volume as the LV against a sixth of the pressure, with a peristaltic inflow-to-outflow contraction, which is why it is a volume pump and not a pressure pump.

RVF-05.intro: Step 2’s last piece of normal physiology: the RV is perfused throughout the cardiac cycle, and losing that advantage is what turns pressure overload into ischaemia (RVF-15). Not asked directly.
why: **80% of the population: RV supplied by the right coronary artery; remaining 20%: the left coronary artery.** The 80/20 split follows coronary dominance: in most people the RCA gives the acute marginal branches to the free wall. The anterior RV wall and the moderator band also receive branches from the LAD in most people, which is one reason RV infarction is less complete and recovers better than LV infarction.

**Unlike the LV, RV perfusion occurs during both systole and diastole, giving oxygen delivery throughout the cardiac cycle.** Coronary flow depends on aortic pressure minus the pressure in the surrounding myocardium. LV systolic pressure equals aortic pressure, so the LV is perfused only in diastole. RV systolic pressure (about 25 mmHg) is far below aortic pressure, so flow continues in systole.

**Disrupted by pulmonary arterial hypertension.** When RV systolic pressure rises towards systemic, the systolic gradient disappears and the RV becomes diastole-dependent like the LV, while its wall stress and oxygen demand rise. Systemic hypotension narrows the gradient further, which is why keeping aortic pressure up (noradrenaline) protects a pressure-loaded RV.
mimic: RV vs LV coronary flow timing
RV: systole and diastole; LV: diastole only, because LV systolic pressure equals aortic pressure.
traps: “Like the LV, the RV is perfused only in diastole”
Only when RV pressure approaches systemic, as in severe PH; normally flow is continuous.
decode: Why is the RV at risk of ischaemia in severe PH with hypotension? [pattern]
Loss of systolic coronary flow plus a lower aortic driving pressure and higher wall stress.
RVF-05.punch: RV coronary flow runs through systole as long as RV pressure stays well below aortic pressure; pulmonary hypertension and hypotension remove that margin, and the RV becomes ischaemic.

RVF-06.sub: RV failure → RV vs LV → Structure
RVF-06.intro: Step 2 set side by side with the LV: each structural row is a consequence of one ventricle being built for volume and the other for pressure. Not asked directly.
why: **Morphology: RV complex and crescentic; LV bullet-shaped, ellipsoid.** A sphere-like LV generates pressure efficiently; a wrap-around crescent moves volume efficiently.

**Cross-section: RV semicircular, serpentine; LV circular.** In short axis the RV is a crescent hugging the septum; when it is pressure-loaded the septum flattens and the LV becomes D-shaped (RVF-10).

**Myocardium: RV thin and heavily trabeculated; LV thick, smooth-walled with fine trabeculations.** Coarse trabeculation and the moderator band are how the RV is identified on echo or in congenital disease, whatever its position.

**Pump: RV peristaltic-like from inflow to outflow, with bellows-like free-wall motion towards the septum; LV radial thickening and contraction.** The RV ejects by longitudinal shortening and by pulling the free wall in towards the septum; LV contraction also pulls the septum, so part of RV output comes from LV contraction.

**Flow: RV has no or minimal isovolumetric periods; LV has well-defined isovolumetric periods.** The PA opens almost as soon as the RV starts to contract, and flow coasts on after RV pressure falls (RVF-08).
mimic: Identifying the morphological RV
Coarse trabeculation, moderator band and a more apical tricuspid valve, not its position or wall thickness.
traps: “The RV has distinct isovolumetric contraction and relaxation like the LV”
Both phases are short or absent because the pulmonary circuit is low-pressure.
decode: Which feature distinguishes RV from LV flow? [pattern]
Minimal isovolumetric periods.
RVF-06.punch: The LV is a thick, smooth ellipsoid that squeezes radially with clear isovolumetric phases; the RV is a thin, trabeculated crescent that ejects peristaltically with almost none, because one faces 120 mmHg and the other 25.

RVF-07.sub: RV failure → RV vs LV → The numbers
RVF-07.intro: Step 2 in numbers. Not asked directly, but the ejection fraction row is the one most likely to appear: a normal RV ejection fraction starts lower than a normal LV one.
why: **End-diastolic thickness ≤3 mm vs ≤11 mm; volume 49–101 vs 44–89 (mL/m²); EF 40–68% vs 57–74%.** These are cardiac MRI-type normal ranges. The RV is slightly larger and ejects a smaller fraction of its volume because its crescent shape gives a big volume for a small inward movement. On echo the cut-offs differ: ASE 2015 calls a 3D RVEF under 45% abnormal and an RV wall over 5 mm hypertrophied, so ‘RVEF 45% is normal’ sits at the lower limit.
**Systolic pressure 25 vs 120 mmHg; coronary perfusion continuous vs diastolic.** The pressure difference explains the perfusion difference (RVF-05).
**RV tolerates volume overload better (compliance rises); LV tolerates pressure overload better.** Thin compliant muscle dilates; thick muscle generates pressure (RVF-12).
**P–V loop: RV trapezoidal; LV rectangular, with rapid rise and fall in pressure.** RVF-08 explains the shape.
mimic: RVEF 45% vs LVEF 45%
Low-normal for the RV; reduced for the LV.
traps: “An RVEF of 45% means RV systolic dysfunction”
The RV’s normal range starts at about 40–45%; the LV’s at about 55%.
decode: Normal RV systolic pressure and timing of RV coronary flow [pattern]
About 25 mmHg; continuous through the cycle.
RVF-07.punch: The RV is thinner (≤3 mm), slightly larger, works at 25 mmHg, is perfused continuously and has a lower normal ejection fraction than the LV, so one cut-off cannot be applied to both ventricles.

RVF-08.sub: RV failure → Physiology → The pressure–volume loop
RVF-08.intro: Step 2 ends with the loop that summarises the pump. Every difference in shape follows from the low-pressure circuit downstream, not from the muscle itself. Not asked directly.
why: **LV loop rectangular with parallel sides from well-defined isovolumetric contraction and relaxation, and sharp corners where systole and diastole begin and end.** The aortic valve opens only once LV pressure reaches about 80 mmHg, so the LV must spend a measurable time building pressure at constant volume, and the same in reverse at the end of systole.

**RV isovolumetric contraction is shorter: the pulmonary valve opens as soon as RV pressure exceeds the low PA pressure.** PA diastolic pressure is about 10 mmHg, so very little pressure needs to be built before ejection starts.
**End-systole is less well defined, so the RV loop looks almost triangular.** RV pressure peaks early and then falls while ejection continues, rounding off the upper left corner.

**Ejection continues despite falling RV pressure because of the momentum of blood in the low-pressure system, so isovolumetric relaxation is shortened or absent.** In a compliant, low-impedance bed, blood keeps moving forward after the RV has started to relax (the ‘hangout’ period). When PVR rises, momentum is lost early, the loop becomes rectangular like the LV’s, and an isovolumetric phase reappears: a sign of pressure overload.
mimic: Short isovolumetric contraction vs absent isovolumetric relaxation
The first because the PA opens early; the second because flow coasts on momentum.
traps: “The RV loop is triangular because RV muscle contracts differently”
It is the low-pressure, compliant circuit downstream that shapes it; raise PVR and it becomes rectangular.
decode: Why is RV isovolumetric relaxation absent? [pattern]
Ejection continues on blood momentum into a low-pressure bed.
RVF-08.punch: The RV loop is nearly triangular because the pulmonary valve opens early and blood keeps flowing after RV pressure falls; a rising PVR squares the loop off, which is what pressure overload looks like.

RVF-09.sub: RV failure → Mechanics → Preload tolerance and its limit
RVF-09.intro: Step 3 is the central asymmetry: the RV takes volume well and pressure badly. This card is the volume side and its limit. Not asked directly, but it is the reason a fluid bolus can harm a failing RV.
why: **The RV is tolerant of preload.** A compliant chamber accepts extra volume with little rise in pressure, as in an ASD or tricuspid regurgitation, which can be tolerated for decades.

**Low muscle mass lets the compliant RV dilate (up to a point) in the face of excess volume.** Thin muscle offers little resistance to stretch, so the chamber enlarges rather than its pressure rising.

**With ongoing distension, decompensation occurs and failure ensues.** Past a point, stretch increases wall stress (Laplace) and oxygen demand without more output, and the chamber meets the limit of the pericardium.

**Excess RV dilatation → tricuspid annulus dilates → TR → RA pressure rises → LV filling and function impaired.** The tricuspid annulus has little fibrous support, so it stretches with the RV; regurgitation adds more volume to the RV and raises venous pressure. Meanwhile the dilated RV pushes the septum into the LV (RVF-10), so LV preload and output fall. This is why fluid given to a dilated, failing RV can lower cardiac output.
mimic: Preload-responsive RV vs over-distended RV
The first increases output with fluid (e.g. early RV infarct); the second dilates, develops TR and compresses the LV, so output falls.
traps: “The RV tolerates preload, so keep giving fluid in RV failure”
Only up to a point; beyond it, TR and septal shift lower LV filling. Volume is given cautiously and stopped when CVP rises without output.
decode: Why can a fluid bolus worsen hypotension in RV failure? [pattern]
Annular dilatation and TR, plus septal shift reducing LV filling.
RVF-09.punch: The RV takes extra volume by dilating, but only up to a point: once the annulus stretches and the septum bows, more fluid raises venous pressure and lowers LV filling and output.

RVF-10.intro: Step 4 is where RV trouble becomes LV trouble. The two ventricles share a septum inside a pericardium that cannot stretch acutely, so a distended RV steals space from the LV. Both linked questions test this: pulsus paradoxus in tamponade, and a high left atrial pressure with a small LV.
why: **Pathological rises in RV filling pressure are transmitted to the interventricular septum.** The septum is a shared wall; its position is set by the pressure difference across it at each moment of the cycle.

**The RV is constrained by the pericardium, so the septum shifts leftwards and the LV becomes D-shaped.** With a fixed outer envelope, the only way the RV can enlarge is inwards, against the LV. A D-shaped LV in diastole means RV volume overload; persisting into systole means pressure overload.

**Cardiac output falls through lower LV distensibility, lower preload and lower ventricular elastance, impairing LV diastolic filling.** The LV now has less room and a stiffer apparent compliance, so its end-diastolic volume is low even though its diastolic pressure (and the left atrial and wedge pressures) is high. This is the trap: a raised wedge pressure here does not mean the LV is full.

**The same shift impairs RV contraction by distorting normal ventricular geometry.** The septum normally contributes to RV ejection (LV contraction pulls it); once it is flattened or bowed leftward, that contribution is lost.
mimic: Septal shift vs LV diastolic failure
Both give a high LA pressure; septal shift gives a small LV (low LVEDV), primary LV disease or aortic regurgitation a normal or large one.
Pulsus paradoxus in tamponade vs constriction
Tamponade: inspiration fills the RV, the septum bows left, LV output falls; constriction shows discordant RV/LV pressures but pulsus paradoxus is less common.
traps: “Inspiratory fall in BP in tamponade is from blood pooling in the lungs”
Pooling contributes little; the key is inspiratory RV filling pushing the septum into the LV inside a fixed pericardium.
“Aortic regurgitation causes a high LA pressure with a low LVEDV”
AR raises LVEDV. High LAP with a small LV comes from pulmonary hypertension, high PEEP or severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure through septal shift (Marrow ‘NOT a cause’ key).
decode: Large effusion, SBP falls 15 mmHg on inspiration — mechanism? [DocT GT]
Inspiration raises RV filling, the septum shifts left, LV filling falls.
High LAP + low LVEDV ‘diastolic dysfunction’ — which is NOT a cause: PH, high PEEP, severe AHRF, AR? [Marrow]
Aortic regurgitation.
RVF-10.punch: A fixed pericardium turns RV distension into LV compression: the septum shifts left, the LV becomes small but high-pressure, and output falls, which is why the wedge pressure misleads in RV failure and why inspiration drops the pulse in tamponade.

RVF-11.sub: RV failure → Mechanics → Afterload and impedance
RVF-11.intro: Step 3, the pressure side. RV afterload is more than PVR, and the RV handles any acute rise in it poorly. Not asked directly.
why: **RV afterload is the load the RV has to overcome during ejection.** In practice it is the pulmonary arterial input impedance plus wall stress.

**Influenced by PVR, PA distensibility and pulse wave reflections in the pulmonary bed; together called RV impedance.** PVR is the steady part; the pulsatile part depends on how stiff the proximal PAs are and how early reflected waves return. In PH, stiff arteries and early reflections can add a large load not visible in PVR (RVF-14).

**Less able to handle acute afterload changes because of its smaller muscle mass.** A thin wall cannot develop a high pressure quickly; a previously normal RV fails acutely at a mean PA pressure of around 40 mmHg. That is why a massive PE rarely produces a very high PA pressure: the RV fails first.

**So the RV is described as intolerant of afterload.** Chronic loading lets it hypertrophy and reach systemic pressures over years (as in idiopathic PAH or Eisenmenger); acute loading does not allow that time.
mimic: Acute vs chronic RV pressure load
Acute: thin RV, failure at mPAP around 40, little hypertrophy; chronic: hypertrophied RV can reach systemic pressures.
traps: “RV afterload equals PVR”
PVR is only the steady component; impedance adds PA stiffness and wave reflection.
decode: Massive PE in a previously well patient — why is the measured PA pressure only moderately raised? [pattern]
A non-hypertrophied RV cannot generate more than about 40 mmHg mean before failing.
RVF-11.punch: RV afterload is impedance, not just PVR, and a thin RV that has had no time to hypertrophy fails at pressures a chronically loaded RV would cope with.

RVF-12.sub: RV failure → Mechanics → Preload tolerant, afterload intolerant
RVF-12.intro: Step 3 in one table: the same anatomical fact, low muscle mass, gives opposite responses to the two kinds of load. The one linked question applies this to the definition of RV failure in septic shock.
why: **RV is preload tolerant: low muscle mass → compliant → dilates to accommodate volume.** Extra volume is absorbed by stretch with little pressure rise, up to the limit described in RVF-09.
**RV is afterload intolerant: low muscle mass → cannot generate pressure against a rising load.** Its contractile reserve is small, so stroke volume falls as soon as impedance rises (RVF-11).

**RV tolerates volume overload better; LV tolerates pressure overload better.** The LV’s thick wall keeps wall stress down at high pressure (Laplace: stress falls with thickness), so aortic stenosis or hypertension is tolerated for years; the thin RV has no such protection, but its compliance lets it absorb volume.

**On the curves, RV stroke volume falls steeply as mean PA pressure rises from 0 to 30 mmHg, while LV stroke volume declines only gently across 100–140 mmHg.** A modest PA rise, as in ARDS, high PEEP or a moderate PE, can halve RV output; the LV can absorb a 40 mmHg rise in aortic pressure with little loss. This is why lowering RV afterload (oxygen, correcting CO₂ and pH, lower plateau pressure, pulmonary vasodilators) improves output more than pushing preload.
mimic: RV failure vs a full but functioning RV
Failure: stroke volume does not rise with filling, CVP climbs; a functioning RV converts extra filling into output.
traps: “RV failure is increased RV filling without decreased output”
That is adaptation; failure is when filling rises (high CVP) and output does not (DocT GT, 69%).
“The RV is afterload tolerant because it already works against a low resistance”
Working at low resistance is exactly why it has little reserve when resistance rises.
decode: Septic shock, CVP 16, low CO, dilated hypokinetic RV — true RV failure? [DocT GT]
RV dysfunction with limited RV filling.
Stroke volume vs afterload curves: which ventricle falls steeply? [pattern]
The RV, over a mean PA pressure of 0–30 mmHg.
RVF-12.punch: Low muscle mass makes the RV stretch easily and push weakly: it absorbs volume but its stroke volume collapses with even a modest rise in PA pressure, so treating RV failure is mostly treating its afterload.

RVF-13.sub: RV failure → Mechanics → Contractility and afterload
RVF-13.intro: Step 3 continued: even in a normal RV, afterload rather than intrinsic contractility sets ejection fraction. Not asked directly.
why: **Afterload is the primary determinant of normal RV function.** RVEF is highly load-dependent, so a low RVEF often reflects a high PA pressure rather than weak muscle; contractility measured by end-systolic elastance is often preserved or raised early in PH.

**RVEF is inversely proportional to pulmonary artery pressure.** As PA pressure rises, RVEF falls almost linearly; this is why RV–PA coupling (TAPSE relative to PA systolic pressure) is a better index than TAPSE alone in PH.
**Antegrade flow from the pulmonary valve meets retrograde waves generated at the many bifurcations of the pulmonary tree.** Each branch point reflects part of the pressure wave back towards the RV.

**This reduces antegrade flow and raises peak PA systolic pressure.** In a compliant bed the reflections return late, in diastole; in stiff PH vessels they return early, during ejection, adding to the load the RV must overcome.
mimic: Low RVEF from afterload vs from myocardial disease
Afterload: RVEF improves when PA pressure falls (e.g. after thrombolysis, iNO); myocardial: it does not.
traps: “A low RVEF in PH means the RV muscle is failing”
RVEF falls with PA pressure even with preserved contractility; the coupling of the two matters.
decode: Main determinant of normal RV ejection [pattern]
Afterload; RVEF falls as PA pressure rises.
RVF-13.punch: For the RV, ejection fraction is a measure of load as much as of muscle: it falls as PA pressure rises and wave reflections return earlier, so judge the RV against the pressure it faces.

RVF-14.intro: Step 3’s measurement: PVR is the number used to grade RV afterload and to define pre-capillary PH (RVF-20), with one known blind spot. Not asked directly here, but the threshold appears in every PH definition question.
why: **PVR = (mPAP − PCWP) × 80 / CO.** The transpulmonary gradient (mPAP minus wedge) is the pressure drop across the lung vessels; dividing by flow gives resistance. Without the ×80 the result is in Wood units (mmHg·min/L); with it, dyn·s·cm⁻⁵. ESC/ERS 2022 defines a raised PVR as over 2 WU (160 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵); older teaching used 3 WU.

**Limitation: the impedance offered by the large pulmonary arteries is not reflected.** PVR is a steady-flow resistance; it ignores PA stiffness and wave reflection (RVF-11, 13). It also depends on an accurate wedge: if PCWP is overestimated, PVR is underestimated.
mimic: Wood units vs dyn·s·cm⁻⁵
Multiply Wood units by 80; 2 WU = 160, 3 WU = 240.
traps: “PVR = mPAP / CO”
Wedge pressure must be subtracted; otherwise a high left atrial pressure looks like pulmonary vascular disease.
decode: mPAP 35, PCWP 10, CO 5 — PVR? [pattern]
RVF-14.punch: PVR is the transpulmonary gradient divided by cardiac output, over 2 WU is raised by ESC 2022, and it misses the pulsatile load from stiff proximal pulmonary arteries.

RVF-15.sub: RV failure → Pathophysiology → The pressure-overload spiral
RVF-15.intro: Step 4 joins the pieces: wall stress, ischaemia, interdependence and shock form a loop that closes through coronary perfusion. Not asked directly, but every management step for acute RV failure aims at a link in this chain.
why: **RV pressure overload → raised RV wall tension and RV dilatation.** Higher pressure and a larger radius both raise wall stress (Laplace).

**Raised wall tension → raised oxygen demand; meanwhile coronary perfusion falls → arrhythmia, RV ischaemia, injury, inflammation → lower contractility.** Demand rises as supply falls: high intramural pressure removes systolic coronary flow (RVF-05) and systemic hypotension lowers the driving pressure. Troponin rises in PE for this reason.

**Lower contractility / RV dysfunction → lower RV output and altered systolic and diastolic interdependence.** The RV delivers less to the lungs and its dilatation pushes the septum into the LV (RVF-10).

**Both → lower LV preload → low cardiac output, hypotension, shock → further fall in coronary perfusion (the vicious circle); separately, TR/PR → RV volume overload → raised RA pressure and CVP → systemic congestion.** Forward failure and backward congestion run together: the gut, liver and kidneys get low flow and high venous pressure at once.

**Both limbs converge on organ dysfunction or failure.** Breaking the loop means raising aortic pressure (noradrenaline) to restore the coronary gradient, lowering RV afterload, avoiding over-filling, and supporting contractility.
mimic: Forward limb vs backward limb
Forward: low LV preload, low output, hypotension; backward: TR, high CVP, venous congestion of liver, kidney and gut.
traps: “In RV failure with hypotension, fluids first and vasopressors later”
Hypotension removes RV coronary perfusion; restoring aortic pressure early is part of breaking the spiral, and fluid can worsen dilatation.
decode: Why does systemic hypotension accelerate RV failure in massive PE? [pattern]
It lowers RV coronary perfusion while wall stress and oxygen demand are high.
RVF-15.punch: A pressure-loaded RV dilates, needs more oxygen, gets less, weakens, shrinks the LV and lowers aortic pressure, which starves it further; the loop is broken by restoring coronary perfusion pressure and lowering afterload.

RVF-16.sub: RV failure → Causes → Acute, by mechanism
RVF-16.intro: Step 5 lists what pushes the RV over. Sorting causes by mechanism tells you what to fix: contractility, volume or afterload. Not asked directly.
why: **Sepsis and LVAD support act by both reduced contractility and volume overload.** Sepsis depresses myocardium through cytokines and adds resuscitation fluid; it also raises PVR through hypoxia, acidosis and ARDS. An LVAD unloads the LV, which pulls the septum leftwards (lost septal contribution to RV contraction) while increasing venous return to the RV.

**RV infarction, myocarditis and perioperative injury or ischaemia (post-cardiotomy) act by reduced contractility.** RV infarction comes with a proximal RCA occlusion and typically presents with hypotension, raised JVP and clear lungs.
**Excess transfusion acts by volume overload.** Large volumes dilate the RV beyond its compliant range (RVF-09).

**Acidosis, hypoxia, PE, ARDS and positive-pressure ventilation act by pressure overload.** Hypoxia and acidosis cause pulmonary vasoconstriction; PE obstructs; ARDS adds vasoconstriction, microthrombi and remodelling; positive pressure compresses alveolar vessels when lung volume or PEEP is high, raising PVR. These are the causes the ICU can reverse.
mimic: RV infarct vs massive PE
Both give hypotension, high JVP and clear lungs; RV infarct shows inferior ST elevation and a normal PA pressure, PE shows a high PA pressure, RV/LV over 1 and McConnell’s sign.
traps: “Positive-pressure ventilation affects RV preload only”
It also raises RV afterload by compressing alveolar vessels; high PEEP and plateau pressures are a cause of acute RV failure.
decode: Which acute causes act by pressure overload? [pattern]
PE, ARDS, positive-pressure ventilation, hypoxia, acidosis.
RVF-16.punch: Acute RV failure is lost contractility (RV infarct, myocarditis, post-cardiotomy), extra volume (transfusion), both (sepsis, LVAD) or, most often in the ICU, raised afterload from PE, ARDS, the ventilator, hypoxia and acidosis.

RVF-17.sub: RV failure → Causes → Chronic, by mechanism
RVF-17.intro: Step 5, the chronic list. The two linked Marrow questions take two rows further: ARVC and its syndromes, and a patient with chronic RV strain who needs anticoagulation.
why: **RV cardiomyopathy and ARVC act by reduced contractility.** ARVC is a desmosomal disease (plakophilin-2 is the commonest gene) with fibrofatty replacement of the RV free wall, presenting in young people with ventricular arrhythmia of LBBB morphology, syncope or sudden death. Naxos disease is ARVC with woolly hair and palmoplantar keratoderma (recessive, plakoglobin); Carvajal syndrome has the same skin and hair with a dilated, LV-dominant cardiomyopathy (desmoplakin).

**Ebstein anomaly spans reduced contractility and volume overload.** The tricuspid leaflets are displaced apically, so part of the RV is ‘atrialised’ (less functional muscle) and the valve regurgitates (volume).

**Left heart disease and single ventricle span volume and pressure overload.** Left heart disease raises pulmonary venous pressure (post-capillary PH, pressure load) and is often accompanied by functional TR (volume); it is the commonest cause of chronic RV failure.

**PR, TGA and TR act by volume overload.** Regurgitant valves return blood to the RV each beat. In d-TGA after an atrial switch, and in congenitally corrected TGA, the RV is the systemic ventricle and its load is mainly pressure.

**Pericardial disease, PAH, CTEPH, pulmonary stenosis, left-sided valve disease and restrictive cardiomyopathy act by pressure overload.** PAH and CTEPH raise PVR; PS obstructs outflow; left valve disease and restrictive cardiomyopathy raise left atrial pressure, which the RV must pump against. CTEPH is suspected when dyspnoea persists over 3 months after PE; the V/Q scan is the screening test.
mimic: Naxos vs Carvajal
Both woolly hair and palmoplantar keratoderma; Naxos is RV-dominant ARVC, Carvajal LV-dominant dilated cardiomyopathy.
ARVC vs RVOT tachycardia
Both LBBB-morphology VT; ARVC has a structurally abnormal RV, epsilon waves and T inversion V1–V3; RVOT VT has a normal heart and a benign course.
traps: “The ARVC syndrome with woolly hair and keratoderma is Carvajal”
Carvajal (desmoplakin) gives the same hair and skin signs with a dilated, LV-dominant cardiomyopathy; the RV-dominant ARVC syndrome is Naxos (plakoglobin), Marrow’s key.
“Syncope, RV hypertrophy, TR murmur, raised troponin and CKD — wait for imaging”
Marrow keys a heparin infusion: treat suspected thromboembolism while the work-up (V/Q rather than contrast CT in CKD) proceeds.
decode: ARVC with sustained VT in a teenager: associated syndrome? [Marrow]
Naxos syndrome.
Syncope, RVH, TR murmur, raised troponin, CKD: next step? [Marrow]
Heparin infusion.
RVF-17.punch: Chronic RV failure is mostly pressure: left heart disease first, then PAH, CTEPH, stenoses and restrictive disease; the contractility causes are ARVC and RV cardiomyopathy, and the volume causes are regurgitant valves and shunts.

RVF-18.sub: RV failure → ICU settings → ARDS and RV-protective ventilation
RVF-18.intro: Step 5 in the commonest ICU setting. ARDS raises PVR, and the ventilator can add to it; the one linked question shows PEEP dropping the blood pressure because the RV could not cope.
why: **RV dysfunction occurs in 22–55% of ARDS.** The lower figure is acute cor pulmonale (dilated RV with septal dyskinesia) on TOE under protective ventilation (Mekontso Dessap 2016: 22%); wider definitions of RV dysfunction give higher figures.

**Survival is much higher in ARDS without RV dysfunction.** In the largest TOE cohort the excess mortality was concentrated in severe acute cor pulmonale (57% vs 42%); milder RV dysfunction carried less clear risk. RV dysfunction is a marker of a bad trajectory and a target, not only a bystander.

**Predisposing: hypoxia, hypercarbia, respiratory acidosis, high PEEP, positive-pressure ventilation raising PVR.** Hypoxia and acidosis constrict pulmonary vessels; high PEEP and plateau pressure over-distend alveoli and compress the capillaries around them. The validated risk score uses pneumonia as the cause, driving pressure ≥18 cmH₂O, P/F under 150 and PaCO₂ ≥48 mmHg.

**RV-protective ventilation: minimise plateau and driving pressures; lower PVR by improving PaO₂ and PaCO₂; prone positioning to unload the RV.** Prone positioning recruits dorsal lung at lower pressures, improves oxygenation and CO₂ clearance and reduces RV size; in severe ARDS with acute cor pulmonale it is used for the RV as much as for oxygenation. PEEP is titrated to recruit without over-distending: on echo, a rising RV/LV ratio or falling output after a PEEP increase means too much.
mimic: PEEP-induced hypotension from RV afterload vs from low preload
Afterload: RV dilates, septum flattens, CVP rises; preload: small, underfilled ventricles, falls with fluid.
traps: “Raising PEEP is least likely to help in severe ARDS or obesity”

Those are the patients who usually recruit, and in LV dysfunction PEEP lowers LV afterload and preload and may help; with RV dysfunction the extra PEEP raises PVR and drops output (DocT GT keys RV dysfunction).
“Prone positioning is only an oxygenation manoeuvre”
It also unloads the RV by lowering PVR and plateau pressure.
decode: Severe ARDS, P/F 85, PEEP 5→10, MAP falls 65→45 — setting where more PEEP is least likely to help? [DocT GT]
Right ventricular dysfunction.
Components of RV-protective ventilation [pattern]
Limit plateau and driving pressure, correct PaO₂ and PaCO₂, prone positioning.
RVF-18.punch: ARDS loads the RV through hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis and high airway pressures; RV-protective ventilation limits plateau and driving pressure, corrects the gases and uses prone positioning, and a fall in pressure after more PEEP signals an RV that cannot take it.

RVF-19.sub: RV failure → ICU settings → After cardiac surgery
RVF-19.intro: Step 5 after cardiac surgery, where the RV is stunned and loaded at the same time. The one linked question asks about gas embolism, the anaesthetist’s version of the same problem.
why: **Cardiopulmonary bypass → myocardial stunning.** The thin, anterior RV is the hardest chamber to protect: retrograde cardioplegia reaches it poorly because much of its venous drainage bypasses the coronary sinus, and it rewarms quickly because it lies uppermost in the open chest. Stunned RV muscle then meets a raised PVR.

**Air embolism.** Air entering the coronaries goes preferentially to the RCA because its ostium is anterior (uppermost in the supine patient), causing acute RV ischaemia; air in the venous circulation lodges in the RVOT and pulmonary arteries.
**Raised post-operative PVR.** Bypass triggers inflammation, protamine reactions, transfusion, hypoxia and atelectasis, all of which raise PVR.
**LVAD implantation.** Unloading the LV shifts the septum leftwards and increases venous return to the RV; RV failure after LVAD occurs in a sizeable minority and may need temporary RV support.
mimic: Venous gas embolism vs coronary air embolism
Venous: air lock in the RVOT, high PA pressure, falling ETCO₂; coronary: RV ischaemia with inferior ST elevation after bypass.
traps: “Left lateral head-down position (Durant) helps by improving venous return”

It is meant to hold the gas in the right atrium and RV apex, away from the RV outflow tract, relieving the air lock (a postulated mechanism with little outcome evidence); aspirate through a central line (Marrow).
decode: CO₂ embolism during laparoscopic cholecystectomy: purpose of left lateral head-down position? [Marrow]
Traps the embolus in the RV, away from the outflow tract.
RVF-19.punch: After cardiac surgery the RV is stunned by bypass, embolised by air, loaded by a raised PVR and destabilised by an LVAD; venous gas is managed by trapping it at the RV apex and aspirating it.

RVF-20.sub: RV failure → Pulmonary hypertension → Definition, group 1 and group 2
RVF-20.intro: Step 6 classifies the commonest chronic cause of RV pressure load. This is the most-asked card in the deck (seven questions): the haemodynamic definition, how a normal wedge pressure separates pre-capillary from post-capillary disease, and the young woman with Raynaud’s and right heart failure.
why: **Pulmonary hypertension: MAP >25 mmHg (mean PA pressure).** ESC/ERS 2022 now defines PH as mPAP over 20 mmHg at rest on right heart catheterisation; 25 was the pre-2018 cut-off. The definition then splits on wedge pressure and PVR: pre-capillary PH (PAH, groups 1, 3, 4, some 5) = mPAP over 20, PAWP 15 or less, PVR over 2 WU; isolated post-capillary PH = PAWP over 15, PVR 2 WU or less; combined post- and pre-capillary PH = PAWP over 15 and PVR over 2. Exercise PH is an mPAP/cardiac output slope over 3 mmHg/L/min.

**Group 1, pulmonary arterial hypertension: idiopathic; heritable (BMPR2, ALK-1, endoglin, unknown); drug and toxin induced; associated with connective tissue disease, HIV, portal hypertension, congenital heart disease, schistosomiasis, chronic haemolytic anaemia; pulmonary veno-occlusive disease / capillary haemangiomatosis; persistent PH of the newborn.** Group 1 is disease of the small pulmonary arteries themselves (intimal and medial proliferation, plexiform lesions), so the wedge is normal and PVR high. Systemic sclerosis is the classic associated disease: a young woman with Raynaud’s, exertional dyspnoea, a raised JVP, oedema and a loud P2 without orthopnoea or crackles has CTD-associated PAH. The 2022 list splits idiopathic PAH into vasoreactivity non-responders and acute responders, names methamphetamines and dasatinib as definite drug causes, renames PVOD/PCH ‘PAH with features of venous/capillary involvement’, and places chronic haemolytic anaemia in group 5. Exertional dyspnoea is the commonest symptom (the RV cannot raise output); fatigue, exertional angina and exertional syncope follow, with oedema late.

**Group 2, PH due to left heart disease (post-capillary): LV systolic dysfunction, LV diastolic dysfunction, valvular disease, congenital/acquired left heart inflow or outflow obstruction, congenital cardiomyopathy.** A high left atrial pressure is transmitted backwards, so the wedge is over 15 mmHg. It is the commonest cause of PH overall. In 2022 wording: heart failure with preserved, mildly reduced or reduced EF, valvular disease, and congenital or acquired conditions causing post-capillary PH. A raised PCWP or LVEDP therefore excludes PAH.
mimic: PAH (group 1) vs PH of left heart disease (group 2)
PAWP 15 or less vs over 15; left heart disease gives orthopnoea, crackles and LA enlargement.
CTD-associated PAH vs ILD-associated PH (group 3)
Both in systemic sclerosis; ILD gives crackles, restriction and fibrosis on CT; PAH has clear lungs and an isolated low DLCO.
PAH vs CTEPH
CTEPH needs a thromboembolic history or risk (APS), mismatched perfusion defects on V/Q, and a normal wedge too.
traps: “Young woman, Raynaud’s, JVD, oedema, loud P2 — left heart failure, ILD or CTEPH”
Raynaud’s points to systemic sclerosis and group 1 PAH; no orthopnoea or crackles argues against left heart failure and ILD, and nothing suggests VTE (only 54% and 68% on two DocT GTs).
“The RHC criterion for PAH is mPAP >25 mmHg” (DocT GT key)

That is the pre-2022 threshold. ESC/ERS 2022: mPAP over 20, PAWP 15 or less, PVR over 2 WU. If over 20 is offered, choose it; if only over 25 appears alongside a PCWP over 25 or LVEDP over 15, choose over 25, because a high wedge or LVEDP means group 2.
“PVR under 3 WU fits PAH”
PAH needs a raised PVR, now over 2 WU.
“A raised mPAP with a normal wedge means group 1 PAH”
A normal wedge only makes it pre-capillary (groups 1, 3, 4 or 5); with antiphospholipid syndrome the likely cause is recurrent PE (CTEPH, group 4) (Marrow).
“Syncope is the commonest symptom of PH”
Exertional dyspnoea is; syncope is a late, high-risk sign.
decode: Raynaud’s, exertional dyspnoea, JVD, oedema, loud P2 in a 42-year-old woman — diagnosis? [DocT GT ×4]
Pulmonary arterial hypertension (54–91%).
True statement on RHC in PAH: mPAP >25 / PCWP >25 / LVEDP >15 / PVR <3 [DocT GT]
mPAP >25 (76%); today mPAP >20.
Most common symptom of PH [DocT GT]
Exertional dyspnoea (76%).
APS, JVD, oedema, mPAP 28, PCWP 11 — likely cause? [Marrow]
Recurrent pulmonary embolism.
RVF-20.punch: PH is now mPAP over 20 mmHg; a wedge of 15 or less with a PVR over 2 WU makes it pre-capillary, and in a young woman with Raynaud’s and right heart failure that means group 1 PAH from systemic sclerosis, while a high wedge means left heart disease, group 2.
