PCA-48.sub: Neuroprognostication → Biomarkers → The NSE cut-off conflict
PCA-48.intro: Step 4, the number to quote. NSE thresholds vary with the assay, the timing and the population, so different sources give different figures. No question is linked; the exam number is the ERC one.
why: **Biomarkers section: 33 vs 47, from different studies.** 33 µg/L is the older AAN 2006 figure from the era before cooling, when it was set at days 1–3; later cohorts treated with temperature control needed higher thresholds to keep false positives near zero.

**Reasons for the discrepancy: different technique, other sources of the marker, kinetics not clear.** Assays differ between laboratories; red cells and platelets add NSE (haemolysis, PCA-47); and the peak timing varies between patients.
**ERC algorithm: NSE >60 at 48 h and/or 72 h.** This is the guideline figure in both 2021 and 2025.
**The unit: NSE is reported in micrograms per litre (µg/L), not mg/L.** A threshold printed in mg/L is out by a factor of a thousand.
mimic: High NSE vs normal NSE
NSE >60 µg/L at 48–72 h supports poor outcome; a normal NSE (around 17 µg/L or less) within 72 h supports a good outcome (AHA 2025, ERC–ESICM 2025).
traps: “NSE >33 µg/L at 24 h predicts poor outcome”
An older, pre-cooling figure; the current threshold is >60 µg/L at 48 and/or 72 h.
decode: [pattern] NSE threshold and timing in the ERC–ESICM algorithm
>60 µg/L at 48 h and/or 72 h.
PCA-48.punch: Quote NSE >60 µg/L at 48 and/or 72 hours as the guideline figure; older lower figures come from different assays and an era before temperature control.

PCA-49.intro: Step 4, imaging. CT shows swelling, MRI shows dying cells, and each has a window. The GT1o day-6 question (41% right) is keyed on MRI, and GT6 asks the MRI day window.
why: **MRI is more sensitive.** Diffusion-weighted imaging detects cytotoxic oedema (cells swelling as their ion pumps fail) before the tissue changes density on CT.

**DWI, measure ADC.** Restricted diffusion appears bright on DWI and dark on the ADC map; a low ADC confirms true restriction rather than T2 ‘shine-through’. AHA 2025 accepts extensive restricted diffusion or reduced ADC at 2–7 days.

**Hyperintensity in cortex and basal ganglia.** The cortex (especially occipital and the perirolandic areas), basal ganglia, thalamus and hippocampus have the highest metabolic demand and fail first. GT1o’s key is ‘MRI can assist, and the cortex is the most commonly affected area’.

**MRI at 2–7 days after arrest; early CT can show reduced grey-white ratio; if the first CT is normal and the patient is still unconscious, repeat at 72–96 h.** Before day 2 diffusion changes may not have appeared fully; after about a week the ADC pseudo-normalises and injury is underestimated. AHA 2025 and ERC–ESICM 2025 both use 2–7 days; ERC–ESICM 2021 said 2–5 days. The repeat CT at 72–96 h is ERC–ESICM 2025.
mimic: CT vs MRI after arrest
CT: early, quick, shows oedema and lost grey-white ratio, low sensitivity early. MRI: 2–7 days, more sensitive, shows cytotoxic injury.
traps: “EEG is the most accurate prognostic test” (GT1o option A)
No single test is ‘the most accurate’; bilateral absent N20 is the most specific one.
“No corneal responses at day 6 means no recovery” (option B)
Corneal absence alone is not enough: ERC needs absent pupillary AND corneal reflexes plus a second criterion.
“NSE can be used at day 6” (option C)

The guideline threshold is set for 48 h and/or 72 h; a day-6 value is outside the window the cut-off was validated for, and temperature control can alter NSE kinetics, so ‘not affected by cooling’ is also too strong.
“MRI immediately after arrest” or ‘days 2–5 only’ (GT6)

Too early shows nothing. DocT keys days 3–7 (69% right). The 2025 guidelines say 2–7 days; 2–5 days is ERC–ESICM 2021. Pick 2–7 if offered. With these four options, pick DocT’s 3–7 (inside the current 2–7 window); choose 2–5 only if the stem is explicitly framed on ERC–ESICM 2021.
decode: Post-arrest day 6, limited recovery: which is most correct? [DocT GT]
MRI can assist with prognosis, and the cortex is the most commonly affected region (41% right).
On what day is MRI brain advised after cardiac arrest? [DocT GT]
Key: days 3–7 (69% right); guideline window 2–7 days.
PCA-49.punch: CT is early and shows swelling; diffusion MRI at 2–7 days is more sensitive and shows restriction in the cortex and basal ganglia; repeat a normal early CT at 72–96 hours if the patient is still unconscious.

PCA-50.intro: Step 4, what the CT shows. Global hypoxia swells the grey matter until it looks like white matter. The Marrow hanging question tests what that means for management.
why: **Cerebral oedema: around 50% incidence.** Reported rates vary widely with how long after arrest the CT is done; early CT is often normal, which is why a negative first scan is repeated (PCA-49).

**Attenuation of the grey-white matter interface.** Grey matter (cortex, basal ganglia) uses more energy, so it swells first; its density falls towards that of white matter, the boundary fades and sulci and cisterns efface. A reduced grey-white ratio is the measurable form; ERC–ESICM 2025 uses a marked reduction, and repeats a normal early CT at 72–96 h if the patient is still unconscious.
mimic: Global anoxic injury vs focal stroke or haematoma
Anoxic injury is diffuse and symmetrical with no mass to remove; a focal lesion may have a surgical answer.
traps: “Neurosurgical consult” for diffuse loss of grey-white differentiation after hanging
There is no surgical target; the step is multimodal prognostication and counselling the family (Marrow).
decode: Hanging, GCS 3, CT loss of grey-white differentiation: diagnosis and step? [Marrow]
Anoxic brain injury; family education and prognostication, not surgery.
PCA-50.punch: Diffuse loss of grey-white differentiation on CT means global anoxic injury with nothing to operate on, so the response is prognostication and honest discussion with the family.

PCA-51.sub: Neuroprognostication → Monitoring → Matching changes to methods
PCA-51.intro: Step 3, the wider monitoring picture. Each post-arrest change in the brain has a tool that detects it; only EEG and SSEP are part of the guideline algorithm. No question is linked.
why: **Electrical phenomena (N20, SSEPs): EEG.** EEG and evoked potentials measure cortical function directly (PCA-45, PCA-46).
**ICP becoming high pressure: ICP monitoring.** Diffuse oedema after arrest can raise ICP, though invasive monitoring is rarely used here.
**Normoxia becoming hypoxia: brain oxygen monitoring.** Brain tissue oxygen (PbtO₂) or near-infrared spectroscopy shows whether supply meets demand.

**Balanced metabolism becoming metabolic imbalance: metabolic tracing.** After reperfusion, neurones shift towards anaerobic glycolysis and release excitatory glutamate; trends in glucose, lactate and glutamate (on microdialysis, or FDG-PET in research) track this. It is a research and neurocritical-care tool, not part of the prognostic algorithm.
**Mitochondrial function, measured by the lactate:pyruvate ratio: microdialysis.** A high lactate:pyruvate ratio with normal oxygen points to mitochondrial failure rather than lack of supply.
mimic: Raised lactate:pyruvate ratio: ischaemia vs mitochondrial dysfunction
Low pyruvate and low tissue oxygen mean ischaemia; normal or high pyruvate with adequate oxygen means mitochondrial failure.
traps: “Microdialysis measures oxygen”
It samples extracellular metabolites (lactate, pyruvate, glucose, glutamate); oxygen needs a PbtO₂ probe.
decode: [pattern] Monitoring method for mitochondrial dysfunction in brain injury
Cerebral microdialysis, lactate:pyruvate ratio.
PCA-51.punch: Each brain change has its monitor: EEG for electrical activity, ICP probes for pressure, oxygen probes for hypoxia and microdialysis for mitochondrial function through the lactate:pyruvate ratio.

PCA-52.intro: Step 5 opens the ERC algorithm. Four conditions must all be true before the six criteria are applied; each closes off a way a recoverable brain might be misjudged. No question is linked.
why: **Resuscitation from cardiac arrest.** The criteria were validated in post-anoxic coma; trauma, stroke and drug coma have different courses.
**Targeted temperature management and rewarming complete.** Cooling slows drug clearance and suppresses EEG and reflexes.
**Unconscious patient, M ≤5 at ≥72 hours (ERC–ESICM 2025; was M ≤3 in 2021).** Anyone not obeying commands now enters, so fewer patients are left out of a structured assessment.
**Without confounders.** Sedation, paralysis, hypothermia, severe hypotension, hypoglycaemia, and metabolic or respiratory derangements (PCA-43).
mimic: Algorithm entry vs brain death testing
Entry to prognosis needs some brainstem function; absence of all brainstem reflexes sends the patient to brain death testing instead (PCA-54).
traps: “Entry needs GCS motor ≤3”
That is 2021; 2025 is M ≤5.
decode: [pattern] Entry condition to the ERC–ESICM 2025 prognostication algorithm
Unconscious (M ≤5) at ≥72 h after ROSC, rewarmed, confounders excluded.
PCA-52.punch: The ERC algorithm applies only to a post-arrest patient who has been rewarmed, is still not obeying commands at 72 hours (M ≤5 since 2025) and has no confounders.

PCA-53.sub: Neuroprognostication → ERC algorithm → The six criteria
PCA-53.intro: Step 5’s core. Six independent signs, each with its own time, and two are needed. The GT1o day-6 question (41% right) tests this card: corneal absence alone, and EEG as ‘the best test’, were the wrong choices.
why: **No pupillary AND corneal reflex at ≥72 h.** Both together; the corneal reflex alone is too easily lost to opioids and paralysis. ERC–ESICM recommends a pupillometer when available.
**Bilaterally absent N20 SSEP at ≥24 h.** Specificity is not affected by time after ROSC (PCA-46); AHA 2025 says ≥48 h.
**Highly malignant EEG at >24 h (suppressed background ± periodic discharges, or burst suppression).** After 24 h, because earlier suppression may still be drug or cooling effect (PCA-45).
**NSE >60 at 48 h and/or 72 h.** In µg/L (PCA-48).
**Status myoclonus ≤72 h.** The only criterion defined by early appearance: continuous generalised myoclonus of at least 30 minutes within 72 h; record EEG during it.

**Diffuse and extensive anoxic injury on brain CT/MRI.** A marked reduction in grey-white ratio on CT (repeated at 72–96 h if the first scan was normal), or extensive diffusion restriction on MRI at 2–7 days (PCA-49).

**At least 2 required: yes, poor outcome likely; no, observe and re-evaluate.** Two independent signs make it very unlikely that one confounded test drives a withdrawal decision; ‘likely’, not ‘certain’.
mimic: Poor outcome ‘likely’ vs brain death
Two criteria give a probability that permits a WLST discussion; brain death is a declaration of death (PCA-56).
traps: “EEG is the most accurate test” (GT1o)
No single test decides; absent N20 is the most specific.
“Absent corneal responses at day 6 mean no recovery” (GT1o)
It needs pupillary absence too, and a second criterion.
decode: Day 6 after VF arrest and 24 h cooling, limited recovery: which statement is most correct? [DocT GT]
MRI can assist with prognosis, the cortex being most often affected (41% right).
PCA-53.punch: Poor outcome is likely when two of six criteria are met: absent pupillary and corneal reflexes at 72 hours, absent N20 from 24 hours, a highly malignant EEG after 24 hours, NSE above 60 at 48–72 hours, status myoclonus within 72 hours, or diffuse anoxic injury on imaging.

PCA-54.sub: Neuroprognostication → Algorithm → Route from the unresponsive patient
PCA-54.intro: Step 6 lays out the whole road from ROSC, of which prognostication is only one branch. Both Marrow questions sit on it: residual sedation, and donation after circulatory death.
why: **Unresponsive patient after ROSC: suspected neurological cause of arrest?** Subarachnoid haemorrhage, stroke or trauma can cause the arrest; finding it changes everything that follows.
**Yes: brain CT.** Before temperature control, to find a lesion that needs a different treatment.

**No: TTM, then unresponsive after rewarming, then exclude confounders, particularly residual sedation.** Temperature control goes to every comatose survivor; sedation delays the examination, not the cooling.
**All brainstem reflexes absent? Pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, cough.** These test the midbrain, pons and medulla in turn.

**Yes: brain death pathway. No: neuroprognostication, WLST at any time, then evaluate for organ donation; circulatory death at any time, then evaluate for organ donation.** AHA 2025 (COR 1): consider organ donation in every patient who meets brain death criteria and before planned WLST. Donation after circulatory death: the treating team withdraws treatment, circulatory death follows, a no-touch period of a few minutes, then retrieval; the donation team never leads the WLST decision.
mimic: Donation after brain death vs after circulatory death
Brain death donors are dead by neurological criteria with the heart beating; circulatory death donors die after planned WLST.
traps: “Comatose on propofol and fentanyl with pinpoint pupils: neither temperature control option is indicated yet” (Marrow key)

Disputed: AHA and ERC give temperature control to all comatose survivors. Sedation delays prognosis and brain death testing, not temperature control. If asked about starting temperature control, start it; if about prognosis, wait for sedation to clear.
“The donation team should lead the withdrawal discussion”
WLST is decided and carried out by the treating team; donation is raised separately.
decode: Post-OHCA on propofol/fentanyl, GCS 3T, pinpoint pupils: what next? [Marrow]
Key ‘neither TTM option yet’ (disputed); the real point is that sedation must clear before any neurological judgement.
Severe TBI, not brain dead, family requests withdrawal: management? [Marrow]
Offer donation after circulatory death.
PCA-54.punch: Suspect a neurological cause and scan first; otherwise control temperature, rewarm and clear sedation, then check the brainstem: all reflexes absent leads to brain death testing, some present to prognostication, and organ donation is considered on every branch.

PCA-55.intro: Step 6, the other road. When the whole brain including the brainstem has stopped working, the question is no longer outcome but death. Marrow asks which criteria can declare it.
why: **Signs of brain death: fixed dilated pupils, diabetes insipidus, cardiovascular changes.** Hypothalamic and posterior pituitary failure stops ADH release, so polyuria and hypernatraemia follow; loss of brainstem control causes a catecholamine surge, then vasoplegia and hypotension.
**CT: severe cerebral oedema and brainstem herniation.** This is the CT that turns the question from prognosis to brain death testing.

**Follow the World Brain Death Project recommendations.** The 2020 consensus: coma of known irreversible cause, absent brainstem reflexes and a positive apnoea test (no breathing when PaCO₂ reaches ≥60 mmHg with pH <7.30, or ≥20 mmHg above baseline in chronic CO₂ retainers), after prerequisites (core temperature ≥36 °C, systolic ≥100 mmHg or MAP ≥60 mmHg, no confounding drugs, at least five half-lives of the longest-acting sedative). Spinal reflexes may persist. EEG and blood-flow studies are ancillary, used when the clinical examination cannot be completed.
**Brain death confirmed according to local legislation.** The criteria are international; the declaration is local (in India, under the Transplantation of Human Organs Act, by a board of doctors).
mimic: Brain death vs locked-in syndrome
Locked-in patients are conscious with vertical eye movements and blinking preserved; a ventral pontine lesion, not loss of the whole brain.
traps: “An isoelectric EEG is required to declare brain death”
The diagnosis is clinical; EEG is ancillary. Marrow’s key (isoelectric EEG, absent brainstem reflexes, positive apnoea test) lists what can be used, not what is mandatory.
“Preserved spinal reflexes exclude brain death”
They may persist because the spinal cord is intact.
decode: Which criteria can be used to declare brain death? [Marrow]
Absent brainstem reflexes and a positive apnoea test in coma, with isoelectric EEG as an ancillary test.
PCA-55.punch: Brain death is a clinical diagnosis of coma, absent brainstem reflexes and a positive apnoea test once confounders are excluded; diabetes insipidus is one of its signs, EEG is ancillary and the declaration follows local law.

PCA-56.intro: Step 6’s summary: four findings, four routes. The difference between them is the point; no question is linked.
why: **Suspected neurological cause: brain CT first, not TTM first.** A bleed or stroke needs its own treatment.
**All brainstem reflexes absent: brain death determination.** This is a test for death, not a prognosis.
**Reflexes present, M ≤3 at ≥72 h, no confounders: ERC prognostication algorithm (the six criteria).** M ≤3 is the 2021 entry; ERC–ESICM 2025 uses M ≤5 (PCA-52).
**Fewer than 2 criteria met: observe and re-evaluate.** Indeterminate is not ‘good’; repeat examination and tests over the following days.
mimic: Brain death vs poor prognosis
Brain death is death; poor prognosis is a probability that allows a WLST discussion but is not death.
traps: “Fewer than two criteria means a good outcome”
It means not yet known; some of these patients recover, some do not.
decode: [pattern] Comatose at 72 h, brainstem reflexes present, one criterion met: next step?
Observe and re-evaluate; do not withdraw on one criterion.
PCA-56.punch: Neurological cause goes to CT first, absent brainstem reflexes to brain death testing, a patient not obeying commands at 72 hours to the six criteria, and fewer than two criteria to further observation.

spine: Wait, then exclude confounders
Prognosis is not judged before 72 hours, and only once temperature, sedatives, glucose and CO₂ have been corrected, because each of them can make a recoverable brain look dead.
No single test, zero false positives
A false prediction of poor outcome leads to withdrawal of care from someone who would have woken, so no test is used alone and the accepted false positive rate is close to zero.
Examination, EEG and SSEP
Absent pupillary and corneal reflexes at 72 hours, a highly malignant EEG after 24 hours and bilaterally absent N20 are the clinical and electrical signs of devastating injury.
Biomarkers and imaging
Serum NSE above 60 µg/L at 48–72 hours and diffuse anoxic injury on CT or diffusion MRI add evidence that sedatives cannot fake, but haemolysis and timing can.
The ERC algorithm
An unconscious patient at 72 hours without confounders who has two or more of the six criteria is likely to have a poor outcome; with fewer, observe and re-evaluate.
Brain death is a different road
If every brainstem reflex is absent the question is not prognosis but death by neurological criteria, which is declared under the World Brain Death Project rules and local law.
CVS07C.primer: After ROSC most comatose survivors who die in hospital die because life-sustaining treatment is withdrawn on a prediction of poor neurological outcome, so the prediction itself decides survival. Neuroprognostication is therefore about avoiding a false positive: calling poor outcome in a patient who would have recovered. ‘Comatose’ or ‘unconscious’ here means not obeying commands, a Glasgow Coma Scale motor score below 6. ‘Poor outcome’ in the studies means death, vegetative state or severe disability (CPC 3–5, or mRS 4–6).

ACLS-01.sub: BLS & ACLS → Chain of survival → The 2025 unified chain
ACLS-01.intro: Step 1 opens with the frame for everything that follows. The 2025 guideline collapsed the four 2020 chains into one, because the order of what saves a life is the same whatever the age or setting.
why: **Recognition and activation → high-quality CPR → defibrillation → advanced resuscitation → post-cardiac arrest care → recovery and survivorship.** The order is the order of time-dependence: nothing happens until someone recognises arrest and calls, CPR buys minutes of flow, a shock is the only treatment that ends VF, and drugs and airway come after. Recovery as a link (rehabilitation, psychological support) was added in 2020 and is kept.

**A single chain for adult and paediatric, in-hospital and out-of-hospital arrest.** Children arrest more often from hypoxia and adults more often from a primary cardiac rhythm, but the sequence of actions does not change, so one chain is taught.

**Prevention and preparedness sit before the chain.** Recognising deterioration in hospital, training lay rescuers and placing AEDs and naloxone in public prevent arrests or make the first links faster.

**It replaces the four separate 2020 chains (adult/paediatric × IHCA/OHCA); a separate newborn chain of care now exists.** The newborn chain runs from antenatal care to follow-up after birth, because newborn resuscitation is mostly about breathing at delivery, not arrest.
mimic: 2020 chains vs 2025 chain
2020: four chains split by age and setting. 2025: one universal chain plus a separate newborn chain of care.
traps: “Recovery was added as a new link in 2025”
Recovery was added in 2020; 2025 unified the chains.
decode: [pattern] How many links in the 2025 chain of survival, and which comes after post-arrest care?
Six; recovery and survivorship.
[pattern] To which populations does the 2025 chain apply?
All: adult and paediatric, in and out of hospital (newborns have their own chain of care).
ACLS-01.punch: One chain now covers every adult and child in or out of hospital: recognise, CPR, shock, advanced care, post-arrest care, recovery, with prevention and preparedness in front.

ACLS-02.sub: BLS & ACLS → BLS sequence → Recognition and the pulse check
ACLS-02.intro: Step 1 continues at the bedside: the first seconds decide whether compressions start at once or are delayed by checks. Both real questions test the same thing, that an unresponsive patient who only gasps and has no definite pulse gets compressions, not breaths or a rhythm check first.
why: **Ensure scene safety, then check responsiveness (call out, loud tap).** A rescuer injured by traffic, electricity or gas becomes a second patient; responsiveness is checked by voice and a firm tap because both take seconds and need no equipment.
**Activate EMS: in India 108 (ambulance) or 112 (unified emergency number).** In hospital this is the code team. The card’s source printed 109, which is neither number.

**Check the carotid pulse for no more than 10 seconds, together with breathing; no definite pulse = start CPR.** Even trained staff are poor at feeling a pulse in a collapsed patient: they miss weak pulses and imagine absent ones, and longer feeling does not help. The cost of compressing a patient who has a pulse is small; the cost of 30 seconds without flow is not. The sequence is C-A-B: compressions first, then airway and breaths, because in a sudden cardiac arrest the blood is still oxygenated and the problem is flow, and every delay to compressions lowers coronary perfusion.

**An agonal gasp is not normal breathing → start CPR.** Gasps are brainstem reflexes from a hypoxic brain and are common in the first minutes after collapse. Mistaking them for breathing is one of the commonest reasons lay rescuers and dispatchers delay CPR.
mimic: Agonal gasp vs normal breathing
Gasps are slow, irregular, effortful and ineffective; with no pulse they mean arrest. Regular breathing with a pulse means recovery position and watch.
traps: “Begin rescue breaths first” [CGT5 option]
In adult arrest compressions come first (C-A-B); breaths follow after 30 compressions.
“Check the rhythm first”
A monitor or AED is attached as soon as it arrives, but compressions start now, not after the rhythm is known.
decode: ICU collapse, unresponsive, occasional gasps, no definite pulse in 10 s — next action? [DocT GT]
Start CPR (compressions).
CPR sequence starts with? [Marrow]
Circulation: C-A-B.
ACLS-02.punch: Unresponsive, not breathing normally (gasps count as not breathing), no definite pulse in 10 seconds: start compressions at once, because flow is what is missing.

ACLS-03.sub: BLS & ACLS → High-quality CPR → Chest compressions
ACLS-03.intro: Step 2 is the part of resuscitation that produces flow. Every number here exists because coronary and cerebral perfusion during CPR is fragile: too slow, too shallow, too much leaning or too many pauses and it falls. The one real question checks that a school-age child is compressed at the same rate as an adult and to about 5 cm.
why: **Interlocked hands, palms over the lower half of the sternum, centre of the chest.** The heel of the lower hand is the contact point; pressing the lower half of the sternum compresses the ventricles most directly, while pressing lower risks the xiphisternum and liver.
**Rate 100–120/min.** Below 100 too little blood is moved per minute; above 120 the depth falls and the heart has too little time to fill between compressions.

**Depth at least 5 cm but not more than 6 cm; allow full recoil.** Deeper compressions move more blood up to about 5–6 cm; beyond 6 cm injuries rise without benefit. The upper limit is not new: 2020 and 2025 use the same words. Recoil matters because the chest’s re-expansion creates the negative pressure that draws venous blood back; leaning on the chest keeps intrathoracic pressure up and lowers coronary perfusion. In children the depth is at least one-third of the chest’s front-to-back diameter, about 4 cm in infants and 5 cm in children; adult values apply from puberty.
**Shoulders directly above the hands, elbows locked straight, using body weight.** The force then comes from the hips, not the arms, so depth is kept as the rescuer tires.

**Firm, flat surface; torso at about the level of the rescuer’s knees.** A soft mattress absorbs part of each compression; lowering the bed or using a step lets the rescuer stay above the chest. In obesity the technique is the same (AHA 2025 class 1).

**No advanced airway: 30:2.** In children with two rescuers the ratio is 15:2, because their arrests are more often hypoxic; one rescuer uses 30:2 at any age. Pauses for breaths or rhythm checks should be under 10 seconds.
mimic: Adult vs child compressions
Same rate (100–120). Adult depth 5–6 cm; child about 5 cm, infant about 4 cm (one-third AP diameter). Two-rescuer paediatric ratio 15:2, adult 30:2.
traps: “About 1 inch for a 7-year-old” (67% right)
One inch (2.5 cm) is too shallow even for an infant; a child is compressed about 2 inches (5 cm).
The rate is 100–120/min at every age.
decode: 7-year-old in arrest — rate and depth of compressions? [DocT QBank]
100–120/min, about 2 inches (5 cm).
[pattern] Adult compression depth and its upper limit?
At least 5 cm, avoiding more than 6 cm.
ACLS-03.punch: Push on the lower half of the sternum 5–6 cm (about 5 cm in a child, 4 cm in an infant) at 100–120/min, let the chest come fully back, and keep every pause under 10 seconds.

ACLS-04.sub: BLS & ACLS → High-quality CPR → Ventilation in 2025
ACLS-04.intro: Step 2 continues with the other half of CPR. In 2025 the guideline put breaths back in focus: rescuers often give too little or too much, and both harm. The one real question checks the rate once an advanced airway is in.
why: **Enough tidal volume to produce visible chest rise; no number is specified.** Chest rise is the only measure a rescuer can see; a fixed volume in mL cannot be judged with a bag.

**Avoid hypoventilation and hyperventilation.** Too little fails to oxygenate, which matters most in hypoxic arrests (children, drowning, opioids). Too much raises intrathoracic pressure, which cuts venous return and coronary perfusion, and inflates the stomach, raising the risk of regurgitation.
**30:2 is retained because it lets the rescuer watch for chest rise.** The pause for two breaths is when ventilation can be checked; recent studies found rescuers often ventilate inadequately.

**With an advanced airway, 1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min) with continuous compressions; respiratory arrest with a pulse, also 1 every 6 seconds.** Once the airway is secured, compressions no longer stop for breaths, and 10/min is enough because CPR moves only a fraction of normal cardiac output, so less CO₂ needs clearing. In children the advanced-airway rate is higher, 20–30/min.
**‘Rescue breaths’ is now simply ‘breaths’.** The 2025 text speaks only of breaths and ventilations.
mimic: Adult vs paediatric ventilation rate
Adult with advanced airway or with a pulse: 10/min (every 6 s). Child with advanced airway: 20–30/min; child with a pulse: every 2–3 s.
traps: “8–10/min, one every 6–8 seconds”
That is the 2010 wording; since 2015 it has been one breath every 6 seconds (10/min). Where options offer ‘1 every 5–6 s’, that is the closest.
“More breaths improve oxygenation during CPR”
Hyperventilation lowers venous return and coronary perfusion; it is a harm, not a safety margin.
decode: Ventilation rate during CPR after an advanced airway? [NEET 2024]
1 breath every 6 s (10/min); if offered, ‘1 every 5–6 s’.
ACLS-04.punch: Give each breath just enough for visible chest rise; with an advanced airway or a pulse that is one breath every 6 seconds, and more is harm, not safety.

ACLS-05.sub: BLS & ACLS → High-quality CPR → Mechanical CPR devices
ACLS-05.intro: Step 2 ends with the machine that promises perfect compressions. It does not beat good hands, so the guideline keeps it for situations where hands cannot work.
why: **Routine use is not recommended: RCTs have not shown better outcomes than well-performed manual compressions.** The large trials (LINC, PARAMEDIC, CIRC) found no survival benefit, partly because deploying the device interrupts compressions at the worst time, early in the arrest.

**High-quality manual CPR with minimal interruptions remains the gold standard.** Hands can start at once, whereas any device must be fetched and fitted, and every pause lets coronary perfusion pressure fall.

**May be considered where manual compressions are difficult, unsafe or impossible: prolonged transport, moving ambulances, hazardous or confined spaces.** Also during PCI or as a bridge to ECPR, where a person cannot stand at the chest.
**Only if interruptions during deployment and removal are strictly limited.** The pause to fit the device is where any advantage is lost.
traps: “Mechanical devices improve survival because compressions are consistent”
Consistency has not translated into survival in trials; the indication is safety and logistics.
decode: [pattern] Role of mechanical CPR devices in adult arrest per AHA 2025?
Not routine; consider only where manual CPR is impractical or unsafe, with minimal pauses to deploy.
ACLS-05.punch: Mechanical CPR is for when hands cannot do the job safely, such as a moving ambulance or the cath lab, not for routine arrests; good manual CPR is still the standard.

ACLS-06.sub: BLS & ACLS → Choking → The adult FBAO algorithm
ACLS-06.intro: Step 3 covers the emergencies that arrive before the heart stops. In choking the problem is the airway, and the sequence changes the moment the patient loses consciousness. The one real question tests that moment.
why: **Signs of severe obstruction: weak or absent cough, unable to speak, colour change (cyanosis), altered mental status, apnoea.** A patient who can cough forcefully and speak is still moving air; one who cannot is obstructed enough to die.
**Signs absent → encourage coughing and keep watching.** A forceful cough is more effective than any external manoeuvre, and slaps or thrusts can move a partial obstruction into a complete one.
**Signs present → activate the emergency response first.** Back blows and thrusts may fail, and a patient who becomes unresponsive will need CPR, suction and airway equipment within minutes.

**Responsive: repeated cycles of 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled or the patient becomes unresponsive; if expelled, keep monitoring.** Back blows came first in 2025 because in the evidence they relieved obstruction more often and caused fewer injuries; abdominal thrusts can injure the liver, spleen and stomach, which is why monitoring continues after success.

**Unresponsive → start CPR beginning with compressions; look in the mouth for a visible object before breaths.** Chest compressions generate airway pressures at least as high as abdominal thrusts, so they double as an obstruction-relief manoeuvre. Remove only what you can see; blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper and are classed as harmful.
mimic: Mild vs severe obstruction
Effective cough and speech: encourage coughing. Weak cough, no speech, cyanosis: back blows and thrusts. Unresponsive: CPR.
traps: “Unresponsive choking child: keep giving back blows and thrusts”
Once unresponsive, start CPR with compressions; check the mouth before breaths.
“Do a blind finger sweep”
It can impact the object further; remove only a visible object.
decode: 3-year-old choking on a peanut becomes unresponsive — next step? [Marrow]
Chest compressions (start CPR).
[pattern] Conscious adult, cannot speak, weak cough — first manoeuvre per AHA 2025?
5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, repeated.
ACLS-06.punch: Severe choking in a conscious adult: call for help, then cycles of 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts. The moment the patient becomes unresponsive it is CPR, starting with compressions.

ACLS-07.sub: BLS & ACLS → Choking → Children, infants and pregnancy
ACLS-07.intro: Step 3 continues with the groups whose bodies change the second manoeuvre. All now start with back blows; only what follows differs. The one real question is the pregnant patient.
why: **Adults and children: 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts, repeated.** A child’s abdomen can be encircled and the thrust raises intrathoracic pressure through the diaphragm. Back blows first is new in 2025 for children too; before, children received abdominal thrusts alone.

**Infants: 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts with the heel of one hand, repeated; abdominal thrusts are not recommended (abdominal organ injury).** An infant’s liver and spleen sit low and unprotected below a soft rib cage, so a thrust there injures them; a chest thrust raises intrathoracic pressure without that risk. Abdominal thrusts were not recommended in infants in 2020 either; what changed in 2025 is the hand. The heel of one hand matches the 2025 infant compression change, which dropped the two-finger technique because it did not reach adequate depth.

**Late pregnancy, or abdomen cannot be encircled: 5 chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts.** A gravid uterus pushes the abdominal contents up and a thrust would hit the uterus; in a very large abdomen the rescuer cannot get an effective grip. Chest thrusts are given over the lower sternum.
mimic: Second manoeuvre by group
Adults and children: abdominal thrusts. Infants, late pregnancy, abdomen too large to encircle: chest thrusts. First is back blows in all.
traps: “Third trimester: back blows then abdominal thrusts”
Abdominal thrusts are replaced by chest thrusts in late pregnancy.
“Start CPR immediately in a conscious choking patient”
CPR is for the unresponsive patient; while she is conscious it is back blows and thrusts.
decode: Third trimester, conscious, cannot speak, weak cough — immediate intervention? [DocT GT]
Cycles of 5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts.
ACLS-07.punch: Back blows first for everyone; then abdominal thrusts for adults and children, chest thrusts for infants (heel of one hand), late pregnancy and anyone whose abdomen cannot be encircled.

ACLS-08.sub: BLS & ACLS → Opioid overdose → Recognition and naloxone
ACLS-08.intro: Step 3 ends with the commonest reversible respiratory arrest. Opioids stop breathing first; the heart stops later from hypoxia, so the window for naloxone and breaths comes before the arrest. Both real questions offer flumazenil as the distractor.
why: **Slow or absent breathing, choking or gurgling sounds, extreme drowsiness or unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils, blue or grey skin, lips or nails.** Opioids act on μ receptors in the brainstem respiratory centre, so rate falls before anything else; gurgling is the unprotected airway; miosis is a μ-receptor effect on the Edinger–Westphal nucleus.
**Call for help: activate EMS.** Do not wait to see whether naloxone works before calling.

**Give naloxone: it reverses opioid effects rapidly and restores protective airway reflexes.** It is a competitive μ antagonist given intranasally, IM or IV. Its effect can wear off before that of a long-acting opioid such as methadone, so the patient is watched for re-sedation.

**Support breathing; in arrest naloxone is reasonable only if it does not interfere with standard resuscitation, including CPR with breaths.** Once the heart has stopped, the problem is hypoxic arrest, and naloxone cannot restart circulation; compressions and breaths do the work.
**At discharge, give an opioid antagonist and instruction in its use.** Survivors have a high risk of another overdose, and public naloxone access is now promoted alongside public AEDs.
mimic: Opioid vs benzodiazepine toxidrome

Opioid: pinpoint pupils, slow breathing, naloxone. Benzodiazepine: sedation with near-normal breathing and pupils; flumazenil is rarely used because it can precipitate seizures, especially in mixed overdoses or dependence.
traps: “Flumazenil” (86% right)
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines; pinpoint pupils and slow breathing point to opioids.
“Urine toxicology then sedation” / “gastric lavage”
Neither treats respiratory depression; naloxone and ventilation do.
“Intubate first”
In a patient breathing 6/min with a pulse, naloxone (with bag-mask support) usually makes intubation unnecessary.
decode: Unconscious, pinpoint pupils, RR 6/min, stable BP — next step? [DocT QBank]
Naloxone.
Known opioid user, altered, respiratory depression — initial step? [NEET 2025]
IV naloxone.
ACLS-08.punch: Opioid poisoning is a breathing arrest first: call for help, ventilate and give naloxone. In cardiac arrest naloxone is only an add-on and never delays CPR with breaths.

ACLS-09.sub: BLS & ACLS → Adult arrest algorithm → The shockable limb
ACLS-09.intro: Step 5 starts with the limb where the shock is the treatment. Every box puts defibrillation first and drugs second, because only a shock ends VF and the chance it works falls each minute. The one real question, VF after electrical injury, checks that the cause does not change this.
why: **Box 2 VF/pVT → box 3 shock.** Biphasic at the manufacturer’s dose (120–200 J) or the maximum if unknown; monophasic 360 J. Compressions resume immediately after the shock without a pulse check, because a heart that has just been defibrillated rarely pumps well enough to help for the first minute.
**Box 4: CPR for 2 minutes and obtain IV/IO access.** IV first (ACLS-19).

**Box 5 shock → box 6: CPR 2 min, epinephrine every 3–5 min, consider advanced airway and capnography.** Epinephrine enters after the second shock. Its α effect raises aortic diastolic pressure and coronary perfusion, which makes the next shock more likely to work; given before any shock it only delays defibrillation.

**Box 7 shock → box 8: CPR 2 min, amiodarone or lidocaine, treat reversible causes.** For VF/pVT that persists after shocks: amiodarone 300 mg then 150 mg, or lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg then 0.5–0.75 mg/kg. They improve ROSC and survival to admission but not clearly survival with good neurology.
**A non-shockable rhythm at any check sends you to box 10 or 11.**
mimic: Shockable vs non-shockable limb
Shockable: shock, CPR, shock, then epinephrine, then antiarrhythmic. Non-shockable: epinephrine as soon as possible, no shocks (ACLS-10).
traps: “VF after electrical injury: amiodarone first” (81% right)
VF from any cause is defibrillated at once; antiarrhythmics are for VF that persists after shocks.
“Magnesium” or “pacing” for VF
Magnesium is for torsades; pacing has no role in VF.
decode: VF shortly after high-voltage contact — immediate treatment? [DocT QBank]
Immediate defibrillation.
[pattern] At which point in VF arrest is epinephrine first given?
After the second shock (box 6).
ACLS-09.punch: In VF and pulseless VT the shock comes first and repeats every 2 minutes; epinephrine joins after the second shock and amiodarone or lidocaine after the third.

ACLS-10.sub: BLS & ACLS → Adult arrest algorithm → The non-shockable limb
ACLS-10.intro: Step 5 continues with the limb where no shock can help. With nothing to defibrillate, epinephrine is the only drug that raises coronary perfusion, so it is given as soon as possible. The one real question asks exactly that timing.
why: **Box 9 asystole/PEA → epinephrine as soon as possible.** In non-shockable arrest the chance of ROSC depends on coronary perfusion pressure, which epinephrine raises; observational data show worse outcomes with each minute it is delayed. AHA 2025 class 2a.
**Box 10: CPR 2 min, IV/IO access, epinephrine every 3–5 min, consider advanced airway and capnography.** Every second 2-minute cycle meets the 3–5 minute interval.
**Box 11: CPR 2 min, treat reversible causes.** PEA in particular is often a reversible cause in disguise: hypovolaemia, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, PE (ACLS-12).
**Box 12: no ROSC → box 10 or 11; ROSC → post-cardiac arrest care; consider whether to continue resuscitation. A shockable rhythm at any check → box 5 or 7.**
mimic: Epinephrine timing in the two limbs
Non-shockable: as soon as feasible. Shockable: after failed initial defibrillation (box 6).
traps: “Wait until after the second rhythm check”
That is closer to the shockable rule; in asystole epinephrine goes in as soon as feasible.
“Only after an advanced airway” / “only if ETCO₂ >20”
Neither airway nor capnography is a condition for epinephrine.
decode: Adult asystole — epinephrine timing? [DocT GT]
As soon as feasible.
ACLS-10.punch: In asystole and PEA there is nothing to shock, so epinephrine 1 mg goes in as soon as access allows and every 3–5 minutes after, while the reversible cause is hunted.

ACLS-11.sub: BLS & ACLS → Adult arrest algorithm → The CPR quality box
ACLS-11.intro: Step 2 returns in the algorithm’s side panel: the same compression rules, plus capnography to check that they are working.
why: **Push hard (at least 5 cm, not more than 6 cm) and fast (100–120/min), allow complete recoil.** See ACLS-03.

**Minimise interruptions; avoid excessive ventilation.** Each pause lets coronary perfusion pressure fall, and it takes several compressions to rebuild it; extra breaths raise intrathoracic pressure and cut venous return.
**Change compressor every 2 minutes, or sooner if fatigued.** Depth falls within 1–2 minutes even before the rescuer feels tired; the change is made at the rhythm check.
**No advanced airway: 30:2.** With one, a breath every 6 seconds with continuous compressions.

**Quantitative waveform capnography; if PETCO₂ is low or falling, reassess CPR quality.** In arrest, CO₂ delivered to the lungs depends on pulmonary blood flow, so ETCO₂ tracks the cardiac output CPR is producing. AHA 2025 suggests aiming for at least 10 mmHg, ideally 20 or more.
traps: “A low ETCO₂ during CPR means the tube is in the oesophagus”
A flat trace suggests that; a low but present waveform usually means poor compressions or low flow.
decode: [pattern] ETCO₂ falls from 18 to 8 mmHg during CPR — first action?
Reassess compression quality and change the compressor.
ACLS-11.punch: Push hard and fast with full recoil, change compressor every 2 minutes, and use waveform capnography as the live gauge: low or falling ETCO₂ means better CPR is needed.

ACLS-12.sub: BLS & ACLS → Adult arrest algorithm → Reversible causes
ACLS-12.intro: Step 5 turns to why the heart stopped. Many arrests, PEA above all, will not respond to CPR and drugs until the cause is fixed. Three real questions test the list, one through pregnancy and one through a ventilated patient with tension pneumothorax.
why: **Five H’s: hypovolaemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo/hyperkalaemia, hypothermia.** Each stops the heart by a different route: no preload, no oxygen for the myocardium, acid that depresses contractility and blunts catecholamines, potassium that destabilises the resting membrane, and cold that slows conduction and favours VF. In pregnancy the list widens (bleeding, magnesium toxicity, amniotic fluid embolism, pre-eclampsia), but the electrolyte disturbances that stop the heart are those of potassium, calcium and magnesium, not sodium. For suspected hyperkalaemic arrest, AHA 2025 says the effectiveness of IV calcium, bicarbonate and insulin–glucose is not well established (each 2b): they may be given but must not displace CPR, shocks and epinephrine.

**Five T’s: tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, pulmonary thrombosis, coronary thrombosis.** Tension pneumothorax and tamponade are obstructive: the heart cannot fill, so CPR moves nothing until the obstruction is released. Tension in an arrested, ventilated patient shows as absent breath sounds on one side, rising airway pressures and late tracheal deviation; it is decompressed at once (needle or finger thoracostomy) without imaging, then a chest drain. High PEEP and positive-pressure ventilation make tension more likely.
mimic: Obstructive vs metabolic causes in PEA
Narrow-complex, rapid PEA suggests a mechanical cause (tension, tamponade, hypovolaemia, PE); broad, slow PEA suggests a metabolic or toxic cause (hyperkalaemia, acidosis, sodium-channel blockers).
traps: “Hypocalcaemia or hypomagnesaemia is least likely to cause arrest in pregnancy” (49% right)

Hypocalcaemia prolongs the QT and low magnesium triggers torsades, so both can cause arrest (and magnesium sulphate toxicity in pre-eclampsia is a separate cause); hypernatraemia is the one that does not stop the heart.
“Thrombocytopenia” is an H or T (90% right)
Thrombosis (coronary and pulmonary) is on the list; thrombocytopenia is not.
“Get a chest X-ray to confirm tension”
In arrest, decompress on clinical signs; imaging wastes minutes.
decode: Which is NOT one of the H’s and T’s? [DocT QBank]
Thrombocytopenia.
Electrolyte disturbance LEAST likely to cause arrest in pregnancy? [DocT QBank]
Hypernatraemia.
Ventilated on PEEP 20, PEA, absent left breath sounds, tracheal shift — next? [Marrow]
Needle decompression, then chest drain.
ACLS-12.punch: Run through the H’s and T’s in every arrest, especially PEA: hypovolaemia, hypoxia, acid, potassium, cold; tension, tamponade, toxins, and clot in lung or coronary. Release a tension pneumothorax on clinical signs alone.

ACLS-13.sub: BLS & ACLS → After the rhythm check → Signs of ROSC
ACLS-13.intro: Step 6 asks how you know circulation has returned without stopping compressions to feel for it. The answer lies mostly in monitors already attached. The one real question asks the capnography sign.
why: **Return of a palpable pulse and measurable blood pressure.** The confirmation, but it needs a pause in compressions, so it is checked at the 2-minute rhythm check.

**Abrupt, sustained increase in PETCO₂, typically ≥40 mmHg.** When the heart starts pumping, pulmonary blood flow jumps and the CO₂ that built up in the tissues during low flow is washed into the lungs, so ETCO₂ rises suddenly, often above the normal 35–45. The 40 mmHg figure was the 2020 algorithm’s; AHA 2025 no longer prints it and says only that a sudden rise of more than 10 mmHg may indicate ROSC, which can occur below 40. A rise right after a bicarbonate dose is CO₂ released from the buffer, not ROSC.

**Spontaneous arterial pressure waves with an arterial line.** A waveform that appears between compressions, or a sudden rise in diastolic pressure at a rhythm check, shows that the heart is ejecting.
mimic: ETCO₂ for ROSC vs ETCO₂ for CPR quality
ROSC: an abrupt, sustained rise. CPR quality: aim at least 10, ideally 20 mmHg or more (ACLS-11).
traps: “A gradual ETCO₂ climb from 15 to 22 mmHg means ROSC”
A slow rise reflects better compressions; ROSC is a sudden step.
decode: During CPR, which ETCO₂ finding suggests ROSC? [Marrow]
A sudden, sustained rise.
[pattern] Value classically quoted for ROSC on capnography?
≥40 mmHg (2020 algorithm); AHA 2025: an abrupt rise of more than 10 mmHg.
ACLS-13.punch: ROSC announces itself on the monitors: an abrupt, sustained ETCO₂ jump or spontaneous arterial waves, confirmed by a pulse at the rhythm check.

ACLS-14.sub: BLS & ACLS → Arrest rhythms → Shockable and non-shockable
ACLS-14.intro: Step 4 is the question asked at every 2-minute check: can a shock help? Three real questions test it, two by asking which rhythm can never perfuse.
why: **Shockable: VT (monomorphic and polymorphic) and VF (fine and coarse).** A shock depolarises the whole myocardium at once, ending re-entrant or chaotic ventricular activity and letting the sinus node take over. VF can never produce output: the ventricles quiver without a coordinated contraction. VT can carry a pulse, so it is ‘shockable’ in the arrest sense only when pulseless; with a pulse it gets synchronised cardioversion or drugs.

**Non-shockable: PEA and asystole.** There is no chaotic activity to reset: in asystole there is no electrical activity, and in PEA the electrical activity is organised but the heart does not produce a pulse. Shocking either only interrupts CPR.

**AF, atrial flutter and SVT are not shockable arrest rhythms; they are cardiovertible rhythms that perfuse. Without a pulse, organised atrial activity is PEA.** A pulseless patient with AF on the monitor gets CPR and epinephrine; synchronised cardioversion is for the unstable patient who still has a pulse.
mimic: Defibrillation vs synchronised cardioversion
Defibrillation: unsynchronised, for VF, pulseless VT and polymorphic VT. Cardioversion: synchronised to the R wave, for perfusing tachycardias (AF, flutter, SVT, monomorphic VT with a pulse).
traps: “VT cannot support perfusion”
VT often carries a pulse; VF never does.
“AF with RVR is shockable in arrest”
If pulseless it is PEA; if it has a pulse it is cardioverted, not defibrillated.
decode: Maternal arrest, ECG for immediate defibrillation? [DocT QBank]
Pulseless VT (96% right).
Which rhythm cannot support perfusion? [DocT GT ×2]
VF (82% and 100% right).
ACLS-14.punch: Only VF and pulseless VT are shocked in arrest. VF never perfuses; VT may, so it is shockable only without a pulse; any organised rhythm without a pulse, AF included, is PEA.

ACLS-15.sub: BLS & ACLS → Arrest rhythms → Monomorphic VT
ACLS-15.intro: Step 4 continues with the regular broad-complex tachycardia. A single ventricular focus or re-entry circuit fires every beat, so every QRS looks the same. The real questions show it in arrest and as the classic ischaemic patient.
why: **Regular, broad-complex tachycardia.** The impulse starts in the ventricle and spreads muscle to muscle instead of through the His–Purkinje system, so the QRS is broad (usually more than 120 ms, often over 140).
**Uniform QRS complexes, each identical within a lead.** One focus or one circuit gives one path of activation.

**Exception: fusion and capture beats.** An atrial impulse occasionally gets through the AV node: if it captures the ventricles alone it gives a normal narrow beat (capture); if it meets the VT wavefront it gives a hybrid beat (fusion). Both prove AV dissociation and so prove VT. In a patient with ischaemic heart disease, a regular broad-complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise; treating it as SVT with verapamil can cause collapse.
mimic: VT vs SVT with aberrancy
VT: AV dissociation, fusion and capture beats, very broad QRS, extreme axis, concordance, a history of infarction. SVT with aberrancy: typical bundle-branch-block shape, P waves linked to QRS.
traps: “Wide QRS, no P waves, rate 150 in IHD = atrial flutter or AF” (88% right)
Flutter and AF are narrow unless aberrant, and AF is irregular; regular and broad in IHD is VT.
decode: IHD, chest pain, wide QRS, no P waves, rate 150 — diagnosis? [DocT GT]
Ventricular tachycardia.
Maternal arrest, broad regular rhythm, needs immediate defibrillation? [DocT QBank]
Pulseless VT.
ACLS-15.punch: Regular, broad and identical beats is monomorphic VT; fusion and capture beats break the uniformity and prove it, and in a patient with heart disease a broad tachycardia is VT until shown otherwise.

ACLS-16.sub: BLS & ACLS → Arrest rhythms → Polymorphic VT and torsades
ACLS-16.intro: Step 4’s most-asked card. Polymorphic VT is unstable by nature, and the treatment splits on two questions: is it sustained (shock) or recurring, and is the QT long (magnesium) or normal (ischaemia, lidocaine, amiodarone). Four real questions test that split, and one key is disputed.
why: **Multiple ventricular foci, so the QRS varies in amplitude, axis and duration.** Activation takes a different path each beat.
**Commonest cause: myocardial ischaemia or infarction.** Ischaemic polymorphic VT has a normal QT; it is treated by revascularisation, amiodarone or lidocaine, and magnesium does not help.

**Torsades de pointes: polymorphic VT in the setting of a long QT, with QRS complexes that twist around the baseline.** A prolonged QT reflects slow, uneven repolarisation; early afterdepolarisations then trigger beats, often after a pause (short–long–short sequence), especially with bradycardia and low potassium or magnesium. Drugs that block the potassium current (haloperidol, methadone, macrolides, sotalol, ondansetron) are the usual triggers. Magnesium 2 g IV suppresses the afterdepolarisations without shortening the QT and can be repeated; stop the offending drugs and correct potassium. If it keeps recurring despite magnesium, raising the heart rate by overdrive pacing or isoproterenol shortens the QT; amiodarone and sotalol lengthen the QT and are avoided.

**Polymorphic VT is shocked unsynchronised at high energy (defibrillation), never synchronised.** The QRS changes from beat to beat, so the synchroniser cannot find a consistent R wave and may fire on the T wave. AHA 2025 recommends an immediate unsynchronised shock at maximum energy for sustained polymorphic VT (class 1) and states that all forms of polymorphic VT are considered haemodynamically and electrically unstable; magnesium is for recurrences when the QT is long (2b) and is not recommended when the QT is normal.
mimic: Torsades vs ischaemic polymorphic VT
Torsades: long QT, pause-dependent, magnesium, avoid amiodarone. Ischaemic: normal QT, revascularise, amiodarone or lidocaine.
traps: “Synchronised cardioversion for polymorphic VT”
The synchroniser cannot track a changing QRS; it is always an unsynchronised shock.
“Recurrent torsades after magnesium, patient talking: go straight to pacing or cardioversion” (60% right)
Repeat magnesium first and stop methadone and haloperidol; pacing or isoproterenol if magnesium fails.
“Amiodarone for torsades”
It lengthens the QT further; it belongs to normal-QT polymorphic VT.
Disputed key: “polymorphic VT with a pulse → immediate unsynchronised shock” [CGT4]

The cardlayer note limits the shock to unstable or pulseless cases. AHA 2025 goes further: sustained polymorphic VT gets an immediate shock because all polymorphic VT is treated as unstable. Exam-day answer: sustained polymorphic VT, or any sign of instability → shock; a stable patient with long QT whose torsades recurs or stops on its own, and an option for magnesium → magnesium.
decode: Haloperidol + methadone, torsades converted with magnesium, recurs, patient alert — next? [DocT GT]
More magnesium (60% right).
ICU, polymorphic VT, QTc 540, stable — first-line drug? [DocT GT]
IV magnesium 2 g.
Polymorphic VT with a pulse — most critical action? [DocT GT; key disputed]
Unsynchronised shock (matches AHA 2025 for sustained polymorphic VT).
Critically ill, twisting polymorphic VT on the strip — diagnosis and treatment? [NEET 2025]
Torsades de pointes, magnesium sulphate.
ACLS-16.punch: Polymorphic VT that is sustained or unstable gets an unsynchronised shock at maximum energy. Torsades that recurs on a long QT gets magnesium, the QT drugs stopped and potassium corrected, then pacing if it keeps returning.

Answer
