ACLS-17.sub: BLS & ACLS → Arrest rhythms → Ventricular fibrillation
ACLS-17.intro: Step 4 closes the ventricular rhythms with the one that never perfuses. Thousands of small wavelets activate the ventricle in no order, so no beat ever happens. The one real question asks exactly that.
why: **Chaotic, irregular deflections of varying amplitude.** Multiple wandering re-entrant wavelets mean the trace never repeats.
**No identifiable P waves, QRS complexes or T waves.** There is no organised ventricular depolarisation, so there is no contraction and no output.
**Rate 150 to 500 per minute.** The deflections are wavelets, not beats, so the ‘rate’ only describes how fast the trace oscillates; no deflection produces a contraction.

**Amplitude falls with time: coarse VF becomes fine VF.** As the myocardium uses up its energy stores, the wavelets weaken. Fine VF marks a longer downtime and a worse outlook, but it is still shocked; good CPR and epinephrine can make it coarser and more likely to respond. Very fine VF can look like asystole, so check gain and two leads before calling asystole.
mimic: Fine VF vs asystole
Fine VF: low irregular waves, shock it. Asystole: flat; confirm in two leads at higher gain, do not shock.
traps: “Fine VF is too late to shock”
Fine VF is still shockable.
decode: Which rhythm cannot support perfusion? [DocT GT]
VF (100% right).
ACLS-17.punch: VF is chaos without a single QRS, so it never perfuses; it decays from coarse to fine as the minutes pass, and at any amplitude the treatment is a shock.

ACLS-18.sub: BLS & ACLS → Arrest rhythms → AF and atrial flutter
ACLS-18.intro: Step 4 ends with the two atrial rhythms that the card’s source wrongly called shockable (ACLS-14). Both real questions describe the same patient with an irregularly irregular tachycardia.
why: **Atrial fibrillation: an SVT of disorganised atrial activation, uncoordinated atrial contraction, multiple re-entry circuits.** With no organised P wave and the AV node receiving impulses at random, the ventricular response is irregularly irregular and the baseline shows fibrillatory waves. It is common in the elderly with hypertension and heart failure because stretched, fibrosed atria sustain the wavelets.

**Atrial flutter: an SVT with one macro-re-entrant circuit → rapid atrial activation but intermittent ventricular response.** Typical flutter circles the right atrium at about 300/min and gives sawtooth flutter waves in II, III and aVF; the AV node conducts only every second or third impulse, so the ventricular rate is often about 150 and regular.

**Both are forms of SVT; they commonly co-exist and are treated similarly** (rate control, anticoagulation by stroke risk, synchronised cardioversion when unstable, starting at at least 200 J in AF (class 2a) and 200 J in flutter (2b) per AHA 2025).
mimic: AF vs flutter vs AVNRT
AF: irregularly irregular, no P waves. Flutter: sawtooth waves, often regular at 150. AVNRT and AVRT: regular, narrow, abrupt onset, usually in younger patients.
traps: “Irregular tachycardia with absent P waves = atrial flutter”
Flutter has flutter waves and is usually regular; absent P waves with an irregularly irregular rhythm is AF.
decode: Elderly with hypertension and CHF, irregularly irregular tachycardia, fibrillatory baseline — arrhythmia? [DocT GT ×2]
Atrial fibrillation (79% and 88% right).
ACLS-18.punch: AF is many chaotic circuits with an irregularly irregular pulse; flutter is one circuit at about 300/min with block, often regular at 150. Both are SVTs, and with a pulse they are cardioverted, never defibrillated.

ACLS-19.sub: BLS & ACLS → Adult arrest algorithm → Vascular access
ACLS-19.intro: Step 5 asks how the drugs get in. 2025 reversed the momentum towards IO in adults after three trials, and removed the endotracheal route. The real questions test the IO fallback in trauma and the old ET rule.
why: **Attempt IV access first in adult cardiac arrest.** AHA 2025, class 1.

**IO is reasonable if IV attempts fail or are not feasible.** In haemorrhagic shock, after two failed peripheral attempts (or about 90 seconds), an IO needle in the proximal humerus or tibia gives drugs, fluids and blood within a minute, faster and safer than a central line in a collapsed patient. In a conscious patient IO infusion is painful, so 40 mg preservative-free 2% lidocaine is given slowly into the marrow first.

**A 2025 ILCOR review of three large RCTs found no significant outcome benefit with IO and lower odds of sustained ROSC (OR 0.89).** The three trials, all in out-of-hospital arrest comparing IO-first with IV-first, were PARAMEDIC-3 (UK), IVIO (Denmark) and Ko et al. (Taiwan). The Taiwanese trial was retracted in December 2025 for randomisation errors; ILCOR’s update with the two remaining trials gives the same answer, lower odds of sustained ROSC with IO (OR 0.89, 0.80–0.99) and no difference in survival or neurological outcome. Drugs from a tibial site may reach the central circulation more slowly. The card’s note doubts that ET drugs were removed: AHA 2025 does remove them, because ET drugs give low and unpredictable blood levels; ‘ET’ in the algorithm now means intubation only. The old rule (2–2.5 times the IV dose diluted in 5–10 mL) survives only in older question banks.
mimic: IV vs IO in arrest vs in trauma
Arrest (adult): IV first, IO if IV fails. Haemorrhagic shock with failed IV: IO next, not a central line.
traps: “Subclavian or IJ line after failed peripheral access” (81% right)
Slower and risks pneumothorax; IO is the next step. Central access is a 2b option only if IV and IO both fail.
Outdated key: “adrenaline can be given intratracheally” [Marrow]
True before 2025; AHA 2025 removed the ET route. Choose it only when no IV/IO option exists and the question is plainly pre-2025.
“IO first because it is faster”
In adult arrest, IO-first did not improve outcomes; IV is attempted first.
decode: Trauma, haemorrhagic shock, two failed IV attempts — next access? [DocT GT]
Intraosseous needle.
Adrenaline in CPR: true statement? [Marrow]
Keyed ‘can be given intratracheally’; outdated under AHA 2025.
ACLS-19.punch: In adult arrest try IV first and go IO if it fails; the endotracheal drug route is gone in 2025, and in a bleeding trauma patient with failed veins the IO comes before any central line.

ACLS-20.sub: BLS & ACLS → Ending resuscitation → Termination rules
ACLS-20.intro: Step 6 ends with the decision to stop. Termination rules exist so that EMS teams stop where survival is near zero and transport where it is not. Three real questions test which rule fits which system, and one asks about traumatic arrest.
why: **Universal TOR rule: all three of arrest not witnessed by EMS, no shock delivered, no ROSC.** Together they identify arrests with very low survival: the arrest had already lasted an unknown time before EMS arrived, the rhythm was never shockable, and nothing has worked.
**Reasonable in a tiered EMS system with both ALS and BLS professionals; prospectively validated there.** AHA 2025 class 2a.

**The rule used depends on EMS scope of practice: BLS, ALS and universal rules.** The BLS rule (for BLS crews where ALS is not available) uses the same three criteria; the ALS rule adds ‘not witnessed by a bystander’ and ‘no bystander CPR’, so it is stricter, because ALS crews can offer more. None is validated for trauma, overdose or in-hospital arrest.

**ETCO₂ must not be used in isolation to stop.** In an intubated patient, ETCO₂ under 10 mmHg after 20 minutes of ALS may be one part of a multimodal decision; in a non-intubated patient no ETCO₂ cut-off should be used (class 3, harm), because mask leak and ventilation make it unreliable.
**EMS systems should be prepared to stop on scene, with training in death notification.** Transport with ongoing CPR is dangerous for crews and seldom saves a patient who meets the rule.
mimic: BLS vs ALS vs universal rule
BLS and universal: not EMS-witnessed, no shock, no ROSC. ALS: those three plus not bystander-witnessed and no bystander CPR.
Medical vs traumatic arrest

TOR rules are for medical OHCA. In trauma, resuscitative thoracotomy is for penetrating injury with CPR under about 15 minutes (blunt under 10); with no cardiac activity on echo after about 20 minutes, stop.
traps: “The BLS rule is the four- or five-criterion rule”
The card’s note has it backwards: the BLS rule has the same three criteria as the universal rule; the ALS rule adds the bystander criteria.
“TOR rules apply to traumatic arrest if criteria are met”
They are not validated in trauma.
“An isolated ETCO₂ threshold rule”
ETCO₂ is never used alone to stop.
decode: Tiered BLS/ALS system, OHCA — which TOR rule? [DocT GT ×2]
Universal TOR rule.
Penetrating chest trauma, asystole, 25 min downtime — management? [Marrow]
Echo; no cardiac motion → stop.
ACLS-20.punch: In a tiered EMS system use the universal rule: not EMS-witnessed, no shock, no ROSC, all three, then stop on scene. Never stop on ETCO₂ alone, and the rules do not apply to trauma.

spine: One chain: recognise and act
Every arrest, adult or child, in or out of hospital, follows one six-link chain, and it starts with a 10-second check that sends an unresponsive, gasping, pulseless patient straight to compressions.
Compressions and breaths that work
Blood flows only while the chest is being pushed 5–6 cm at 100–120/min with full recoil and few pauses, and breaths are judged by visible chest rise, not by a number.
Choking and opioids: before arrest
Severe choking is back blows then thrusts until the patient collapses, when it becomes CPR; opioid poisoning is a breathing arrest that naloxone reverses, but never at the cost of CPR.
Name the rhythm, choose the limb
VF and pulseless VT are shocked; asystole and PEA are not, and any organised rhythm without a pulse, AF included, is PEA.
Shocks, drugs, access, causes
Shockable arrest gets shocks first and epinephrine only after they fail, non-shockable gets epinephrine at once, drugs go IV first, and the H’s and T’s are hunted throughout.
ROSC or stopping
Return of circulation shows as a pulse, a pressure wave or an abrupt ETCO₂ rise; when none comes, validated termination rules, never ETCO₂ alone, decide when to stop.
CVS08A.primer: Cardiac arrest is the loss of effective cardiac output; the brain loses consciousness within seconds and is injured within minutes, so every step is judged by how quickly it restores some flow. During CPR, coronary flow depends on the pressure difference between aorta and right atrium in the relaxation phase (coronary perfusion pressure), which builds over several compressions and collapses with every pause. Rhythms in arrest are sorted by one question, whether a shock can help (VF and pulseless VT) or not (asystole and PEA). The AHA 2025 guidelines, which this deck follows, kept the algorithm’s structure but changed choking, access and several BLS details.

ACLS-21.intro: Step 1 is getting enough current through the fibrillating heart. The energy rules are simple once the logic is clear: biphasic shocks are more efficient, so less energy is needed, and when in doubt the highest available dose is the safer error. The one real question tests whether pregnancy changes any of this.
why: **A device that delivers a therapeutic dose of electrical energy to the heart to force it to produce a more normal cardiac rhythm.** The shock depolarises a critical mass of myocardium simultaneously, ending the chaotic re-entry of VF; the sinus node or another pacemaker then has a chance to take over. It does not ‘restart’ an asystolic heart, which is why asystole is not shocked.

**Biphasic: follow the manufacturer’s recommendation (e.g. initial 120–200 J); if unknown, use the maximum available.** Biphasic waveforms reverse the current half-way through the pulse, which defibrillates at lower energy with less myocardial injury; AHA 2025 prefers biphasic over monophasic (2a). Devices differ (rectilinear, truncated exponential), so the effective dose is device-specific; if the setting is not known, the maximal dose may be considered (2b), because under-dosing a fibrillating heart costs more than the small risk of a high shock.

**Second and subsequent doses should be equivalent, and higher doses may be considered.** AHA 2025 tells you to follow the manufacturer’s fixed or escalating protocol (2a) and allows higher energy for later shocks (2b). A failed first shock suggests high transthoracic impedance or a hard-to-defibrillate substrate, so escalating where the device allows is reasonable.
**Monophasic: 360 J.** Monophasic current flows one way only and is less efficient, so the full 360 J is used for every shock.
mimic: Defibrillation vs synchronised cardioversion energy
Defibrillation uses the device’s maximum or recommended dose unsynchronised; cardioversion uses rhythm-specific lower doses timed to the R wave (ACLS-26).
traps: “Halve the dose, or avoid shocks, in pregnancy”
Transthoracic impedance is not meaningfully changed in pregnancy and little current reaches the fetus; standard adult doses are used without modification (81% got this).
“Only biphasic is acceptable”
Biphasic is preferred, but a monophasic device at 360 J is still recommended to treat VF; any defibrillator is better than delay.
decode: Third-trimester woman in VF — which statement on defibrillation is true? [DocT QBank]
Standard energy doses, no modification.
Biphasic device, manufacturer dose not known [pattern]
Use the maximum available energy.
ACLS-21.punch: Use the manufacturer’s biphasic dose or, if unknown, the maximum; monophasic is 360 J. Pregnancy changes nothing about the energy.

ACLS-22.intro: Still step 1, scaled to the child. Paediatric doses are weight-based because current needed rises with body size, and the ceiling stops a large child getting more than an adult.
why: **First shock: 2 J/kg.** AHA 2025 allows 2–4 J/kg for the first shock and teaches 2 J/kg for simplicity (2a).
**Second shock: 4 J/kg.** A failed first shock is followed by 4 J/kg (2b).

**Subsequent shocks: 4 J/kg.** AHA 2025 keeps 4 J/kg for refractory VF but adds that higher levels may be considered. ERC 2025 uses 4 J/kg for every shock, from the first, and for VF that persists after repeated shocks allows stepwise escalation to at most 8 J/kg (maximum 360 J).
**Maximum: 10 J/kg or the adult dose.** Whichever is reached first; in a 40 kg adolescent 10 J/kg would be 400 J, above most adult devices, so the adult dose is the ceiling.
mimic: Paediatric defibrillation vs paediatric cardioversion
Defibrillation starts at 2 J/kg; synchronised cardioversion for SVT with cardiopulmonary compromise starts at 0.5–1 J/kg, then 2 J/kg (AHA 2025 PALS, 2a). The ERC uses 1 J/kg, then 2 J/kg.
traps: “4 J/kg is the fixed ceiling”
AHA 2025 allows higher doses for refractory VF, up to 10 J/kg or the adult maximum; the card’s 2 → 4 → 4 is the default sequence, not a ban on going higher.
decode: Child in VF, first shock — energy? [pattern]
2 J/kg (2–4 J/kg acceptable).
Refractory paediatric VF after two shocks [pattern]
4 J/kg, may go higher, never above 10 J/kg or the adult dose.
ACLS-22.punch: Two, then four joules per kilogram, more only if refractory, and never beyond 10 J/kg or the adult dose.

ACLS-23.intro: Step 1 again: the energy only works if it crosses the heart. Pad position and size decide how much of the current takes that path rather than skirting it through the chest wall.
why: **Anterolateral or anteroposterior — both acceptable.** Each places the heart between the pads; trials have not shown one to be clearly better for VF, so the choice follows access (anteroposterior suits a pacing patient, a large breast or a device in the right pectoral area).
**Electrode diameter greater than 8 cm in adults.** Larger pads lower transthoracic impedance and spread current, so more of it reaches the myocardium with less skin burn.

**It might be reasonable to adjust the position of a bra rather than remove it.** Pads must touch skin and avoid underwire, but the delay and reluctance that come with removing clothing cost more; women receive bystander defibrillation less often, partly for this reason.
mimic: Anteroposterior vs vector change
Anteroposterior is an acceptable first-choice position; vector change is moving pads from anterolateral to anteroposterior after failed shocks (ACLS-24).
traps: “Anteroposterior is only for cardioversion”
Both positions are acceptable for defibrillation in 2025.
decode: Which pad positions are acceptable for adult defibrillation? [pattern]
Anterolateral or anteroposterior.
Female collapse, rescuer hesitant about clothing [pattern]
Adjust the bra, do not delay removing it.
ACLS-23.punch: Either position, pads over 8 cm, and move clothing rather than delay the shock.

ACLS-24.sub: ACLS → Refractory VF → Vector change, DSED, head-up CPR
ACLS-24.intro: The last part of step 1 is the patient whose VF survives three standard shocks. The new tools change where or how much current is delivered, and the guideline is cautious because the evidence is one trial.
why: **Vector change defibrillation: usefulness not established.** Moving the pads from anterolateral to anteroposterior sends current through a different path, which may capture myocardium the first vector missed (2b).
**Double sequential defibrillation (DSED): usefulness not established.** Two defibrillators fire in rapid sequence from two pad sets, delivering more energy along two vectors (2b).

**The basis is a single small RCT supporting both, with outstanding questions.** DOSE-VF (2022, n 405) found survival to discharge 13.3% with standard shocks, 21.7% with vector change and 30.4% with DSED, but it was small (405 of a planned 930, stopped early because of COVID-related staffing problems), and AHA 2025 notes the benefit held by intention-to-treat, not when patients were analysed by the treatment they actually received. ERC 2025 reads the same trial differently: it suggests considering a vector change (anteroposterior pads) after three failed shocks, but does not recommend routine DSED. One positive trial is not enough to call a therapy established.
**Head-up CPR is not recommended except in clinical trials.** No RCTs exist, only observational studies at serious risk of bias (3: No Benefit).
mimic: Refractory VF vs recurrent VF
Refractory VF never terminates despite shocks; recurrent VF terminates and then returns, which points to a trigger (ischaemia, electrolytes) rather than an energy problem.
traps: “DSED is the 2025 treatment for refractory VF”
It may be considered, but its usefulness is not established; the standard remains good CPR, standard shocks, adrenaline and amiodarone or lidocaine.
decode: Refractory VF after three shocks: 2025 status of DSED or vector change? [pattern]
May be considered; usefulness not established (one small RCT).
Head-up CPR in adult arrest [pattern]
Not recommended outside trials.
ACLS-24.punch: Vector change and DSED rest on one small positive trial, so both are ‘not established’; head-up CPR belongs only in trials.

ACLS-25.intro: Step 2 is the shock given to a heart that still has an organised rhythm. The whole difference from defibrillation is timing: a shock that lands on the T wave of a beating heart can cause the VF you are trying to avoid.
why: **Cardioversion is synchronised, delivered on the peak of the R wave; defibrillation has no synchronisation.** The device senses the R wave and fires a few milliseconds later, when the ventricle is fully depolarised and refractory, so the shock cannot strike the vulnerable period.

**Cardioversion: VT with a pulse, AF, flutter; defibrillation: VF and polymorphic VT.** Polymorphic VT has QRS complexes of varying shape, so the device cannot pick a reliable R wave; it may sense a T wave or fail to fire, which is why it is treated as VF.

**Synchronisation helps prevent the R-on-T phenomenon.** The relative refractory period on the upslope of the T wave is when parts of the ventricle are excitable and parts are not, the substrate for re-entry; a shock there can induce VF.
mimic: Synchronised vs unsynchronised mode on the same device
Sync must be switched on, and many devices drop it after each shock, so it must be reselected (ACLS-27).
traps: “Sync on the T wave or the P wave”
On the R wave; the T wave is exactly what sync avoids.
decode: Synchronised cardioversion — shock timed to which wave? [Marrow]
The R wave, to avoid R-on-T.
ACLS-25.punch: Synchronise on the R wave whenever there is an organised QRS; VF and polymorphic VT have none, so they get unsynchronised shocks.

ACLS-26.intro: Step 2 continues with how much energy the synchronised shock needs. The 2025 change is that AF and flutter both start at 200 J: starting low saves nothing and fails more often. Five questions test this, two of them still keyed to the older numbers.
why: **Atrial fibrillation: 200 J.** AHA 2025: an initial setting of at least 200 J is reasonable (2a). Pooled biphasic trials found 200 J gave over 90% cumulative success, more efficiently than starting low, with no extra myocardial injury. AF has many small wavelets spread across both atria, so it needs a large current to depolarise all the atrial tissue.

**Atrial flutter: 200 J.** Flutter is a single macro-re-entry circuit and is easier to terminate (50 J succeeds 50–75% of the time), but 200 J succeeds nearly always, so AHA 2025 suggests 200 J here too (2b).
**Narrow-complex tachycardia: 100 J.** Regular SVT (AVNRT, AVRT) is a small circuit through the node and terminates easily.
**Monomorphic VT: 100 J.** An organised ventricular circuit with a reliable R wave to sync on.

**Polymorphic VT: unsynchronised, high-energy shock (defibrillation).** AHA 2025 recommends an immediate unsynchronised shock for sustained polymorphic VT (1); sync cannot lock on. The rationale line on the card is the reason for higher starting doses: low-energy shocks provoked VF in AF and AF in flutter.
mimic: AHA 2025 vs ERC 2025 cardioversion energies

AHA: AF at least 200 J, flutter 200 J, narrow SVT and monomorphic VT 100 J. ERC 2025: maximum output for AF, 70–120 J for flutter and SVT, 120–150 J for VT with a pulse. The bank keys for this card follow AHA.
Polymorphic VT with a pulse vs torsades that self-terminates
Sustained polymorphic VT is shocked unsynchronised; recurrent self-terminating torsades with a long QT is treated with IV magnesium 2 g and removing QT-prolonging drugs.
traps: “Unstable AF: start at 120–200 J” (DocT CGT4 key)
That is the pre-2025 range; AHA 2025 starts AF at 200 J or more. Pick cardioversion; if both are offered, the 2025 answer is ≥200 J.
“Unstable AF: synchronised cardioversion at 100 J” (DocT QBank key)
Cardioversion is right, the energy is old; 100 J is for narrow regular SVT and monomorphic VT.
“Polymorphic VT with a pulse: synchronised 100 J or magnesium”

AHA 2025 recommends an immediate unsynchronised shock for sustained polymorphic VT (1) with no stability qualifier, because it regards every form of polymorphic VT, whatever the QT, as haemodynamically and electrically unstable. Magnesium is for torsades with a long QT and gives no benefit when the QT is normal.
decode: Unstable AF, 2025 initial energy? [DocT GT]
≥200 J biphasic.
BP 75/40, HR 180, regular broad QRS, no P waves [DocT QBank]
Synchronised cardioversion (81%); for monomorphic VT, 100 J.
Polymorphic VT with a pulse — most critical action? [DocT GT]
Immediate unsynchronised shock.
Septic ICU patient, new AF 155/min, BP falling to 90/60 [DocT GT]
Synchronised cardioversion; the key says 120–200 J, 2025 says ≥200 J.
ACLS-26.punch: AF and flutter now start at 200 J, narrow SVT and monomorphic VT at 100 J, and polymorphic VT is defibrillated. Low energies fail and can provoke the next arrhythmia.

table.title: 2025 synchronised cardioversion, adult

Energy
Why
rows: Multiple wavelets, need large atrial mass depolarised
Low energy works often, 200 J nearly always

ACLS-27.intro: Step 2 ends with doing the cardioversion safely. The questions test when to shock at once, that sedation is given whenever feasible, and the anticoagulation that follows AF cardioversion.
why: **Ventricular rate over 150/min: prepare for immediate cardioversion; generally not needed at 150 or below.** At rates under 150 a healthy heart is rarely made unstable by the rate itself, so instability below that suggests another cause (sepsis, bleeding, hypoxia) driving a compensatory tachycardia; shocking it will not help. The main 2025 algorithm says ‘typically ≥150/min’.

**At the bedside: oxygen saturation monitor, suction, IV line, intubation equipment.** Sedation can cause apnoea or aspiration, and the shock can cause bradycardia or VF, so airway and resuscitation equipment must be at hand.

**Prerequisites: consent, sedation/analgesia, rule out left atrial clot.** Sedate whenever feasible, even when unstable, unless it would dangerously delay the shock. LA clot matters in AF or flutter of 48 hours or more or unknown duration: restoring atrial contraction can expel it. Then anticoagulate for 3 weeks before (or exclude clot by TOE) and at least 4 weeks after, because the atria stay stunned after sinus rhythm returns. An unstable patient is cardioverted at once with heparin started alongside.

**Resynchronise after each cardioversion; if synchronisation is delayed and the patient is critical, go to unsynchronised shocks.** Many devices revert to unsynchronised mode after a shock. If the device cannot sense the R wave and the patient is deteriorating, a defibrillation-dose shock is safer than waiting.
mimic: Compensatory sinus tachycardia vs primary tachyarrhythmia
Rate under 150 with obvious sepsis, bleeding or fever: treat the cause; shocking a sinus tachycardia does nothing.
traps: “Mandatory intubation or an arterial line before cardioversion”
AHA 2025 asks for sedation whenever feasible; intubation and lines only delay the shock.
“Unstable new AF of 5 minutes after surgery: amiodarone or metoprolol first”
Hypotension with a rate of 167 is instability; synchronised cardioversion (87%).
“Anticoagulate 2 or 3 weeks after cardioversion”
At least 4 weeks after; 3 weeks is the time before.
decode: Post-thoracotomy, new AF 167/min, BP 73/34 [DocT GT]
Synchronised cardioversion.
Unstable flutter being prepared for cardioversion — what step is specifically recommended? [DocT GT]
Sedation whenever feasible.
After cardioversion of AF, anticoagulate for how long? [DocT GT]
4 weeks (78%).
Narrow irregular 140/min, BP 80/50 [NEET 2025]
Synchronised cardioversion; diltiazem, metoprolol and digoxin are for stable patients.
ACLS-27.punch: Shock at once when the rate is over about 150 and it is causing instability; sedate when you can, resynchronise every time, and anticoagulate for at least 4 weeks after cardioverting AF.

ACLS-28.sub: ACLS → Tachycardia algorithm → Stable or unstable
ACLS-28.intro: Step 3 opens with the only question that matters first in any tachycardia: is it causing the patient harm? Six questions test this, and the lowest score (30%) is a stable patient whom many chose to shock.
why: **Unstable: hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischaemic chest discomfort, acute heart failure.** Each means the rate is cutting cardiac output or coronary flow: diastole shortens, the ventricle fills less and the myocardium is starved. The tachycardia must also be the cause of the instability, which is why the rate is usually 150 or more.

**Unstable → synchronised cardioversion; adenosine may be considered only if the rhythm is regular and narrow.** Electricity works in seconds and does not depress the heart. A regular narrow rhythm is likely nodal re-entry, which adenosine ends almost instantly, so it may be tried while the defibrillator is readied.
**Stable → 12-lead ECG and IV access, then assess the QRS.** With time to spare, the 12-lead defines the rhythm before any drug is chosen.

**Narrow: QRS under 0.12 s; wide: QRS 0.12 s or more.** A narrow QRS means the ventricles are activated through the His–Purkinje system, so the origin is above the ventricles; a wide QRS is VT until proved otherwise.
mimic: Symptomatic but stable vs unstable
Palpitations, light-headedness with a normal BP and mentation is stable; hypotension, confusion, chest pain or pulmonary oedema is unstable.
traps: “Recurrent palpitations, no chest pain or breathlessness, AF on ECG: sedate and cardiovert at 100 J”
He is stable; stable AF gets rate control (diltiazem or a β-blocker). Only 30% chose diltiazem.
“Unstable WCT: intubate first” (Marrow key)
Unstable tachycardia gets synchronised cardioversion; intubation delays it. Marrow keyed the airway only because cardioversion was not offered: pick cardioversion if it is there.
“Child with SVT that recurs after adenosine and becomes unstable: give diltiazem or amiodarone”
Synchronised cardioversion (0.5–1 J/kg, then 2 J/kg); verapamil and diltiazem cause collapse in infants.
decode: BP 75/40, HR 180, regular broad QRS [DocT QBank]
Synchronised cardioversion (81%).
Adolescent SVT recurs 30 s after adenosine, now unstable [DocT QBank]
Synchronised cardioversion (90%).
Stable regular narrow 180/min, vagal failed [DocT GT ×2]
IV adenosine (76% and 100%).
Stable intermittent palpitations, AF [DocT QBank]
Diltiazem — rate control (30%).
ACLS-28.punch: Instability caused by the tachycardia means a synchronised shock, with adenosine allowed only for a regular narrow rhythm; stability buys time for a 12-lead and a decision by QRS width.

ACLS-29.intro: Step 3, narrow branch. A stable regular narrow tachycardia is almost always a re-entry circuit using the AV node, so the treatment is a sequence of ever-stronger nodal blocks. Nine questions test this, and half the cohort skipped the vagal manoeuvre.
why: **Regular: vagal manoeuvres first.** A vagal surge slows AV-nodal conduction and can break a circuit that runs through the node (AVNRT, AVRT). The modified Valsalva (strain, then lie flat with legs raised) converts about 43% versus 17% for the standard one (REVERT). Carotid sinus massage is supine, on ECG, one side for 5–10 s, and contraindicated with a carotid bruit or prior TIA or stroke.

**If ineffective: adenosine, then β-blockers or calcium channel blockers.** Adenosine (ACLS-31) blocks the node for seconds and ends most nodal re-entry; if the rhythm persists or returns, a longer-acting nodal blocker (diltiazem, verapamil or a β-blocker) is used.

**Irregular: β-blockers or calcium channel blockers.** An irregular narrow tachycardia is AF, flutter with variable block, atrial tachycardia with variable block or multifocal atrial tachycardia; the node is not part of the circuit, so adenosine cannot end it, and the goal is rate control (ACLS-33).

**2025: synchronised cardioversion for unstable narrow-complex tachycardia, and for a stable one that persists despite vagal manoeuvres and drugs, or when they are contraindicated.** Electricity is the end of the sequence, not the start, in a stable patient.
mimic: AVNRT vs AVRT vs flutter 2:1

AVNRT: young woman, P hidden in the QRS or pseudo-r′ in V1; orthodromic AVRT: P after the QRS with RP over 70 ms; flutter 2:1: rate about 150, saw-tooth waves seen when adenosine slows the ventricles.
traps: “Stable SVT 180/min: adenosine first”
Vagal manoeuvres first (only 50% chose Valsalva); adenosine comes when they fail.
“Stable regular narrow 180/min after failed vagal: cardiovert or amiodarone”
Adenosine is next (76%).
“AVRT is a cause of irregular narrow tachycardia”
AVNRT and AVRT are always regular; irregular means AF, flutter or atrial tachycardia with variable block, or MAT.
decode: Stable, HR 180, narrow [DocT QBank]
Valsalva manoeuvre (50%).
Stable regular narrow, vagal failed [DocT GT ×2, Marrow]
Adenosine 6 mg, then 12 mg.
Young woman, no structural disease, stable narrow 170/min — diagnosis? [DocT GT]
AVNRT (67%).
Contraindication to carotid sinus massage [DocT GT]
Carotid bruit.
ACLS-29.punch: Stable regular narrow tachycardia is broken at the AV node: vagal manoeuvre, then adenosine, then a β-blocker or calcium channel blocker, and a shock only if all fail. Irregular narrow tachycardia needs rate control, not adenosine.

ACLS-30.intro: Step 3, wide branch. A regular wide tachycardia in a patient with heart disease is VT about 80% of the time (over 90% after MI), so every choice here is made as if it were VT. Six questions test this.
why: **Adenosine only if the rhythm is regular and monomorphic, for treatment or diagnosis.** If it is SVT with aberrancy, adenosine ends it or reveals the atrial rhythm; VT is usually unaffected, and a regular monomorphic VT rarely deteriorates from a brief nodal block (2b).

**Procainamide, amiodarone or sotalol.** All three act on the ventricle as well as the atria (2b). With decompensated heart failure, amiodarone is the usual choice: procainamide and sotalol are negatively inotropic and hypotensive, and the algorithm says to avoid procainamide in CHF. PROCAMIO (2017, 74 patients, stable regular WCT) found procainamide ended more tachycardias than amiodarone within 40 minutes (67% vs 38%) with fewer major cardiac adverse events (9% vs 41%), and the advantage held in structural heart disease; it was small and open-label and excluded patients with poor haemodynamic tolerance.
**Do not give verapamil or diltiazem.** If the rhythm is VT, these depress the myocardium and dilate vessels without touching the ventricular circuit, and collapse follows (3: Harm).

**Do not give adenosine for unstable, irregularly irregular or polymorphic WCT.** Unstable WCT needs a shock; an irregular wide rhythm may be pre-excited AF, where nodal block sends all conduction down the accessory pathway; polymorphic VT can degenerate (3: Harm).
**2025: synchronised cardioversion for unstable WCT, and for stable WCT when drugs are ineffective or contraindicated.**
mimic: VT vs SVT with aberrancy
AV dissociation, fusion and capture beats, QRS over 160 ms, a northwest axis and precordial concordance favour VT.
Irregular wide tachycardia vs VT
Irregularly irregular, varying QRS shapes, very fast (up to 300): pre-excited AF (ACLS-33).
traps: “Stable monomorphic VT in a heart failure patient on metoprolol: adenosine or verapamil”
Amiodarone (76–78%); verapamil is harm, adenosine does not treat VT, and cardioversion is for instability.
“Stable regular WCT: immediate defibrillation or cardioversion”
Antiarrhythmic infusion first; electricity when it fails or the patient becomes unstable.
decode: IHD, chest pain, wide QRS, absent P, 150/min — diagnosis? [DocT QBank, DocT GT]
Stable regular WCT, 2025 algorithm next step [DocT GT]
Antiarrhythmic infusion.
Decompensated HF, stable monomorphic VT 160/min [DocT GT ×2]
IV amiodarone.
ACLS-30.punch: Treat any wide tachycardia as VT: no verapamil or diltiazem, adenosine only when regular and monomorphic, amiodarone when the heart is weak, and a shock when drugs fail or the patient is unstable.

ACLS-31.intro: Step 3 relies on adenosine for both treatment and diagnosis. It works for seconds because it is cleared almost at once, which explains how it must be given and why it fails in some patients.
why: **First dose 6 mg rapid IV push, followed by a saline flush.** Adenosine’s half-life is under 10 seconds (uptake into red cells and endothelium), so it must reach the heart as a bolus: a large proximal vein, a fast push and a 20 mL flush.

**Second dose 12 mg if required.** Used when 6 mg fails. Start at 3 mg via a central line, after heart transplant (denervated, supersensitive) or with dipyridamole or carbamazepine, which potentiate it; theophylline and caffeine antagonise it.

**Converts AVNRT, AVRT and many atrial tachycardias.** It acts on A1 receptors in the AV node, opening potassium channels and blocking conduction for a few seconds; any circuit that uses the node is broken.

**Diagnostic: blocks the AV node, unmasking atrial flutter or fibrillation.** When the node is not part of the circuit, the atrial rhythm continues while ventricular beats pause, showing flutter waves (often about 300/min) or fibrillation.

**Can cause severe bronchospasm in asthma.** Adenosine receptors in the airway (mainly A2B and A3 on mast cells, which release bronchoconstrictor mediators, plus A1 on smooth muscle) narrow an already hyper-reactive airway; most patients also feel a brief flush, chest tightness and a sense of doom.
mimic: Flutter 2:1 vs AVNRT after adenosine
Flutter: rate slows and saw-tooth waves appear, then the tachycardia returns; AVNRT: the rhythm terminates.
traps: “Adenosine terminates the SVT, it recurs and the child is unstable: give more adenosine or diltiazem”
Repeating adenosine buys another 30 s; synchronised cardioversion (90%).
“Central line: still 6 mg”
3 mg via a central line; it reaches the heart undiluted.
decode: Adenosine 6 mg via central line reveals saw-tooth waves at 300/min [DocT GT]
Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction.
Stable SVT, adenosine 6 mg failed [Marrow]
Adenosine 12 mg.
Only access is an IJ line — adenosine dose? [Marrow]
3 mg.
ACLS-31.punch: Adenosine lasts seconds, so give it fast with a flush, 6 then 12 mg (3 mg centrally); it ends nodal re-entry, unmasks flutter and AF, and is avoided in asthma.

ACLS-32.sub: ACLS → Tachycardia drugs → Procainamide, amiodarone, sotalol
ACLS-32.intro: Step 3 needs a dose for each of the three wide-complex antiarrhythmics. Each endpoint or bar comes from the drug’s own toxicity, and the one real question tests why sotalol is barred by a long QT.
why: **Procainamide 20–50 mg/min until the arrhythmia is suppressed, hypotension ensues, the QRS widens by over 50% or 17 mg/kg is given; maintenance 1–4 mg/min; avoid with prolonged QT or CHF.** It is a class Ia sodium-channel blocker: QRS widening means toxic conduction slowing, hypotension comes from its ganglion-blocking and negative inotropic effect, and its metabolite NAPA prolongs the QT.

**Amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes, repeat if VT recurs; maintenance 1 mg/min for the first 6 hours.** It blocks potassium, sodium and calcium channels and β-receptors, with little negative inotropy at these doses, which is why it is the choice in poor LV function (then 0.5 mg/min for the next 18 hours).

**Sotalol 100 mg (1.5 mg/kg) over 5 minutes; avoid with prolonged QT.** Sotalol is a β-blocker with class III potassium-channel (IKr) block, so it lengthens repolarisation and the QT; a prolonged QT is the substrate for torsades. Its β-block also makes it negatively inotropic. Note that sotalol remains in the AHA 2025 guideline text (2b) but has been dropped from the 2025 tachyarrhythmia algorithm, which lists only adenosine, procainamide and amiodarone doses.
mimic: Procainamide vs amiodarone choice
Preserved LV function: procainamide works faster; poor LV function or heart failure: amiodarone.
traps: “Sotalol’s main adverse effect is bradycardia or hypotension”
These occur, but the serious one is QT prolongation and torsades from potassium-channel block.
decode: Adverse effect of sotalol is due to? [NEET 2024]
QT prolongation from potassium-channel (class III) block.
Procainamide infusion: when do you stop? [pattern]
Arrhythmia suppressed, hypotension, QRS +50% or 17 mg/kg given.
ACLS-32.punch: Procainamide is stopped by QRS widening, hypotension or 17 mg/kg; amiodarone is 150 mg then 1 mg/min; sotalol and procainamide are barred by a long QT because both prolong repolarisation.

ACLS-33.sub: ACLS → Tachycardia algorithm → AF/flutter with RVR
ACLS-33.intro: Step 3’s most-asked card (13 questions). In AF the problem is too many atrial impulses reaching the ventricle, so the treatment is AV-nodal block, unless the ventricle is failing (decompensated heart failure, hypotension) or the node is bypassed (pre-excitation). Several keys here are disputed.
why: **IV β-blocker or non-dihydropyridine CCB for acute rate control without pre-excitation.** Both slow AV-nodal conduction (Class 1); diltiazem is 0.25 mg/kg over 2 min. In the ICU with labile BP, esmolol suits best: onset 2–3 min, half-life about 9 min (red-cell esterases), so it can be switched off. Never give IV verapamil or diltiazem soon after a β-blocker: additive nodal block and negative inotropy can cause asystole. Carvedilol has no IV form.

**IV amiodarone is useful for rate control in critically ill patients without pre-excitation.** It slows the node with little drop in BP or contractility (2a), so it fits septic shock on vasopressors or a failing ventricle; it may also convert to sinus rhythm.

**Pre-excited AF/flutter: avoid digoxin, β-blockers, non-DHP CCBs and IV amiodarone.** The accessory pathway has no decremental conduction; blocking the node leaves the pathway to carry atrial impulses at up to 300/min, which can become VF (3: Harm). It looks like an irregular, very fast wide tachycardia with varying QRS shapes. Treat with cardioversion if unstable, procainamide or ibutilide if stable.

**LV systolic dysfunction with decompensated HF: avoid non-DHP CCBs and IV β-blockers.** Both are negative inotropes; in a ventricle already failing they can precipitate cardiogenic shock (3: Harm). Use amiodarone or digoxin for rate and treat the congestion.

**Conversion of AF/flutter of over 48 hours in non-anticoagulated patients risks thromboembolism.** Clot forms in the stagnant left atrial appendage; restoring contraction can dislodge it (ACLS-27). For AF under 48 h when rhythm control is wanted, ibutilide 1 mg over 10 min (repeat once; torsades risk), flecainide only without structural disease, amiodarone with it.
mimic: Pre-excited AF vs polymorphic VT
Both are irregular and wide; pre-excited AF has a known WPW pattern, rates up to 300 and QRS shapes that vary beat to beat without the twisting of torsades.
traps: “HFrEF, AF 130/min, worsening dyspnoea: IV β-blocker” (DocT key, 39%)
Disputed key: worsening dyspnoea means decompensated HF, where IV β-blockers are 3: Harm. Use amiodarone or digoxin and IV diuretics; the card is right.
“WPW with AF: only verapamil is contraindicated” (DocT key, 54%)
Every nodal blocker is contraindicated, including adenosine, esmolol and IV amiodarone, so the item has no single right option; verapamil is the classic answer.
“Septic shock, new AF 140, BP 102/65: diltiazem or oral amiodarone”
An IV β-blocker (keyed, 42–56%); IV amiodarone is equally defensible. Diltiazem worsens vasopressor-dependent hypotension; oral amiodarone is too slow.
“Stable symptomatic AF: IV ibutilide” (Marrow key)
The AHA stable irregular pathway is rate control. Pick rate control if offered; pick ibutilide only if the stem asks to restore sinus rhythm in AF under 48 h.
decode: Septic shock, severe LV dysfunction, AF 170 — least suitable? [DocT GT]
Verapamil.
Post-op AF with labile BP, fastest-onset titratable drug? [DocT GT]
Esmolol.
Irregular wide 280/min, varying QRS [DocT GT]
AF with WPW.
Diltiazem contraindicated with? [Marrow]
Low EF, after a β-blocker, pre-excited AF — all.
ACLS-33.punch: Slow the node with a β-blocker or diltiazem, unless the ventricle is failing (amiodarone or digoxin), BP is labile (esmolol or amiodarone) or a pathway bypasses the node (no nodal blocker at all: procainamide, ibutilide or a shock).

table.title: Rate control in AF with RVR: the setting decides

Use
Avoid
rows: Procainamide or ibutilide; shock if unstable
All nodal blockers incl. IV amiodarone

parts.q: Which IV β-blockers are used for atrial tachyarrhythmias?
parts.a: Esmolol, metoprolol, atenolol and propranolol; carvedilol has no IV form.

ACLS-34.intro: Step 4 is the hours after ROSC, when the brain is exposed to secondary injury from low pressure, abnormal gases and fever. The questions test whether the old 32–34 °C answer still stands.
why: **MAP ≥65 mmHg; avoid hypotension.** The brain after arrest has impaired autoregulation, so flow follows pressure; AHA 2025 dropped the old SBP target because the trials used MAP (1). Higher MAP targets (BOX, NEUROPROTECT) did not improve outcome.

**SpO₂ 90–98% (PaO₂ 60–105 mmHg); 100% FiO₂ until SpO₂ can be measured reliably.** Hypoxia worsens brain injury, and hyperoxia adds free-radical injury on reperfusion, so FiO₂ is titrated down once the saturation reads reliably.
**PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg.** Low CO₂ constricts cerebral vessels and lowers flow to an ischaemic brain; high CO₂ raises ICP. Hyperventilation is to be avoided.

**Temperature control for at least 36 hours in patients unresponsive to verbal commands; goal 32–37.5 °C.** TTM (33 vs 36 °C) and TTM2 (33 vs normothermia with fever prevention, ≤37.5 °C) showed no difference in survival or neurological outcome, so AHA 2025 accepts any deliberate target in this range. The essential element is preventing fever, which worsens injury. ERC–ESICM 2025 recommend actively preventing fever (target 37.5 °C or less) for 36–72 hours in patients who remain comatose (the 2021 version said 37.7 °C or less for at least 72 hours).

**Coronary angiography before discharge in survivors with suspected cardiac cause, especially an initial shockable rhythm, unexplained LV dysfunction or severe ischaemia.** Emergent angiography is for persistent ST elevation; without it, immediate angiography did not help (COACT, TOMAHAWK).
mimic: Temperature control vs therapeutic hypothermia
Hypothermia is one strategy (32–34 °C); temperature control includes normothermia with active fever prevention.
traps: “Target temperature after VF arrest is 32–34 °C” (DocT key, 57%)
That is the 2002–2010 answer. AHA 2025: 32–37.5 °C for at least 36 h, any rhythm. If only one range fits the question, pick it, but know 32–34 is historical.
decode: Post-arrest TTM — what should be avoided? [DocT GT]
Fever, hypoxia and hyperventilation — all (100%).
VF arrest, ROSC, comatose, stable — modality? [Marrow]
Targeted temperature management (temperature control).
ACLS-34.punch: After ROSC keep MAP 65 or more, SpO₂ 90–98%, PaCO₂ 35–45, and control temperature at 32–37.5 °C for at least 36 hours; preventing fever is what matters, not how cold.

ACLS-35.intro: Step 5 begins with the slow rhythm where the problem is the pacemaker itself: the sinus node fires slowly or the junction takes over. The P wave tells you which.
why: **Sinus bradycardia: normal PR interval; physiological, drug-induced or pathological (hypoxia, MI, raised ICP, hypothyroidism).** Every P is sinus and conducts normally; the node is just slow. Vagal tone (athletes, sleep), β-blockers and CCBs, hypoxia, inferior MI (vagal and nodal artery), Cushing’s reflex in raised ICP and hypothyroidism all slow it. Treat only if it causes symptoms.

**Junctional bradycardia: P waves inverted, absent or after the QRS; narrow QRS; from hyperkalaemia, SA exit block or severe sinus bradycardia.** When the sinus node fails, the AV junction escapes at 40–60/min. The atria are activated backwards, so the P is inverted in II, III and aVF and may be hidden in or follow the QRS. The ventricles are activated normally, so the QRS is narrow.
mimic: SA exit block type II vs sinus pause
Exit block type II: constant PP with a pause that is an exact multiple (usually twice) of the PP; a sinus pause bears no fixed relation to the PP.
SA exit block type I vs type II
Type I: PP intervals shorten progressively, then a pause shorter than two PP; type II: constant PP then a sudden double-length pause.
traps: “Constant PP with a pause equal to two PP intervals is a sinus arrest”
An exact multiple means the impulse fired but failed to exit the node: SA exit block type II (75%).
decode: Elderly, syncope, regular 40/min with normal P and QRS [DocT QBank]
Sinus bradycardia (92%).
Constant PP with a pause equal to two PP [DocT GT]
SA exit block Mobitz II.
ACLS-35.punch: A normal P before each QRS means sinus bradycardia; an inverted, absent or late P with a narrow QRS means the junction has taken over because the sinus node failed.

ACLS-36.intro: Step 5’s core: where along the conduction system is the impulse being blocked? Seven questions test this; two keys are disputed and the lowest score is 22%. The answer always comes from the level of block: AV node (vagal, benign, atropine-responsive) or below it (His–Purkinje, unstable, needs pacing).
why: **First degree: PR over 200 ms, 1:1 conduction; can be normal, drugs, inferior MI, myocarditis; usually no treatment.** Every beat conducts, just slowly through the node; it is not a true block and an asymptomatic patient is discharged.

**Mobitz I (Wenckebach): progressive PR lengthening then a dropped QRS; atropine if symptomatic; can progress to complete block.** The AV node tires with each beat (decremental conduction) until one fails. The block is nodal, so the QRS is usually narrow; atropine and exercise speed conduction and improve it, carotid massage worsens it. Seen in inferior MI and with high vagal tone.

**Mobitz II: fixed PR, random dropped QRS; necessitates treatment — cardiologist and transvenous pacing.** The block is below the node (His–Purkinje): all-or-none failure, often a wide QRS and a sudden risk of complete block. Atropine speeds the sinus rate without helping His–Purkinje conduction, so it can make the ratio worse; carotid massage may paradoxically improve it.

**Complete heart block: no P–QRS relationship, constant independent P–P and R–R; asymptomatic: pads, monitor, admit; symptomatic: pace.** A narrow escape (40–60) means a junctional pacemaker below a nodal block; a wide, slow escape (20–40) is ventricular and unreliable.

**Some blocks cannot be differentiated, e.g. 2:1 block: you cannot tell whether the PR lengthens.** With every other beat dropped, there is no run of conducted beats to compare. Use the clues: a narrow QRS, a vagal setting (sleeping athlete) or improvement with atropine favours nodal block; a wide QRS or anterior MI favours infranodal block.
mimic: Mobitz II vs blocked PACs
Blocked PACs come early and deform the T wave; in Mobitz II the non-conducted P is on time.
traps: “Anterior MI with second-degree block: Mobitz I, benign, give atropine” (DocT key)

Key is wrong: block after anterior MI is infranodal (LAD supplies the His–Purkinje system), does not respond to atropine and needs immediate transvenous pacing. On exam day pick the option that places the block in the His bundle or Purkinje fibres and paces.
“Sleeping athlete with 2:1 block: His bundle or bundle branch”
Vagal setting with a narrow QRS: AV node (only 42% chose it).
“Asymptomatic first-degree block: admit or observe”
Discharge (only 39% chose it).
“Septic, HR 34, CHB, BP 80/50: permanent pacemaker”
Atropine is keyed first (22%); prepare TCP at once because infranodal CHB often fails atropine. A permanent pacemaker comes after stabilisation.
decode: Progressive PR lengthening then a dropped beat [NEET 2025]
Mobitz I (Wenckebach).
Type I (nodal) block — feature NOT seen? [Marrow]
Worsening with atropine.
HF patient, ECG with long PR, all conducted [DocT QBank]
First-degree AV block (71%).
ACLS-36.punch: The level of block decides everything: nodal block (narrow QRS, vagal, inferior MI) is benign and helped by atropine; infranodal block (wide QRS, anterior MI, Mobitz II) progresses and needs pacing.

ACLS-37.intro: Step 6 turns reading into treatment. The algorithm runs atropine, then pacing or an adrenergic infusion, then transvenous pacing. Eight questions test it, with low scores (22–43%) where atropine meets an infranodal block, and old doses in two keys.
why: **Symptomatic: hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischaemic chest discomfort, acute heart failure.** The same five features as the tachycardia algorithm: the slow rate is no longer maintaining output. AHA 2025 defines the bradyarrhythmia as typically under 50/min.
**If absent, monitor and observe.** An asymptomatic slow rate is watched, the cause sought.

**Atropine 1 mg bolus, repeat every 3–5 min, maximum 3 mg.** Atropine blocks vagal (muscarinic) input to the sinus and AV nodes, so it works in sinus bradycardia and nodal block; it does little for infranodal block or a transplanted heart, and in those it must not delay pacing. 3 mg is full vagal blockade; more adds nothing. AHA moved from 0.5 mg to 1 mg in 2020; ERC 2025 still gives 500 micrograms, repeated every 3–5 minutes to 3 mg.

**If atropine is ineffective: transcutaneous pacing, or dopamine infusion, or adrenaline infusion.** These are listed as equals. Pacing bypasses the conduction problem; dopamine and adrenaline raise the rate and contractility through β₁ receptors (ACLS-38). In unstable Mobitz II or wide-complex CHB, pacing is the reliable bridge.

**If still ineffective: transvenous pacing and expert consultation; 2025: temporary transvenous pacing is reasonable in refractory unstable bradycardia.** It is more reliable than transcutaneous capture, and comes with more complications (2a).
mimic: Bradycardia with a pulse vs asystole
Pacing helps bradycardia with a pulse; routine pacing in established arrest is not recommended (ACLS-39).
traps: “Unstable Mobitz II (septic, BP 75/40): atropine first” (43% chose TCP)
Atropine rarely helps infranodal block and must not delay pacing; DocT keys transcutaneous pacing.
“Post-CABG pericarditis, HR 33, 3 mg atropine given, waiting for pacing: norepinephrine or isoproterenol”
Dopamine (35%); the algorithm names dopamine or adrenaline. More atropine is pointless after 3 mg.
“Atropine dose 0.5 mg” (Marrow key)
0.5 mg is the pre-2020 AHA dose and is still the ERC dose, so it is not wrong, but AHA 2020 and 2025 give 1 mg every 3–5 min, max 3 mg. Pick 1 mg if offered.
“Pacing fails: dopamine or adrenaline?” (NEET 2025 keys dopamine)
AHA lists them as equals, and ERC 2025 uses isoprenaline (5 mcg/min) or adrenaline (2–10 mcg/min) as its second-line drugs; pick dopamine for this recall, adrenaline if dopamine is not offered.
decode: HR 28, BP 80/50, confused, wide-QRS Mobitz II, atropine 1 mg failed [DocT GT]
Transcutaneous pacing.
Post-ACS/stent, HR 42 — first drug? [NEET 2025]
Atropine.
Mobitz I, BP 80/60, HR 45 [Marrow]
IV atropine 1 mg.
Unstable sinus bradycardia with pauses [Marrow]
Atropine and arrange temporary pacing.
ACLS-37.punch: Symptomatic bradycardia: atropine 1 mg to a total of 3 mg, then pacing or dopamine or adrenaline, then transvenous pacing. With an infranodal block, go to pacing without waiting for atropine to fail.

ACLS-38.intro: Step 6 needs two infusion doses. The units differ, and that difference is the trap.
why: **Dopamine 5–20 mcg/kg/min, titrate to response, taper slowly.** At these doses dopamine stimulates β₁ receptors (rate, contractility) and, higher up, α₁ receptors (vasoconstriction); stopping suddenly can drop the BP.
**Adrenaline 2–10 mcg/min, titrate to response.** A fixed adult rate in mcg/min, not mcg/kg/min: 2–10 mcg/min in 70 kg is about 0.03–0.14 mcg/kg/min, β-predominant, raising rate and output.
mimic: Bradycardia adrenaline vs post-ROSC adrenaline
Bradycardia: 2–10 mcg/min as a fixed adult rate; post-ROSC vasopressor: 0.1–0.5 mcg/kg/min, which is 7–35 mcg/min in a 70 kg adult.
traps: “Adrenaline 2–10 mcg/kg/min”
That is about 70 times the dose in a 70 kg adult; the bradycardia dose is per minute, not per kg.
decode: Dopamine dose in the bradycardia algorithm [pattern]
5–20 mcg/kg/min.
Adrenaline infusion for bradycardia [pattern]
2–10 mcg/min.
ACLS-38.punch: Dopamine is per kilogram (5–20 mcg/kg/min); adrenaline is per minute (2–10 mcg/min). Mixing the units is a seventy-fold error.

ACLS-39.intro: Step 6’s bridge: pacing through the chest wall until a transvenous wire or the cause is fixed. The card layer adds that pacing has no place in an established arrest.
why: **Used in haemodynamically unstable bradycardias.** It is a bridge (2b) to transvenous pacing or to correction of the cause, and the immediate choice in unstable high-degree block when IV access is not yet available.
**Narcotics and benzodiazepines for sedation and analgesia; obtain consent.** The current stimulates chest-wall muscles and is painful in a conscious patient.
**Set the pacer to 60–80 bpm.** Enough to restore output without excess demand on an ischaemic heart.

**Current output over 2 mA above the level at which capture is observed.** Electrical capture is a wide QRS and broad T after each spike; mechanical capture must be confirmed by a femoral pulse or arterial trace (the carotid can be confused with muscle twitch). Threshold drifts, so a margin above it prevents loss of capture.
mimic: Pacing in bradycardia vs in arrest
Pacing with a pulse can save the patient; routine pacing in established asystole or PEA does not improve ROSC or survival (3: No Benefit).
traps: “Electrical capture confirms effective pacing”
Only a palpable femoral pulse or arterial waveform confirms mechanical capture.
decode: Transcutaneous pacing rate and output [pattern]
60–80/min; just above the capture threshold (by about 2 mA).
Routine pacing in asystolic arrest? [pattern]
Not recommended.
ACLS-39.punch: Pace unstable bradycardia at 60–80/min, a little above capture, with sedation, and confirm with a pulse; do not pace an established arrest.

ACLS-40.intro: Step 6 ends with what to treat alongside the drugs. Each cause is reversible, and one question tests which drug combination adds up to bradycardia.
why: **Myocardial ischaemia or infarction.** Inferior MI (the RCA supplies the sinus and AV nodes in most people) causes vagal and nodal bradycardia; anterior MI causes infranodal block (ACLS-36).

**Drugs and toxins: calcium channel blockers, β-blockers, digoxin.** All slow nodal conduction, and their effects add; digoxin raises vagal tone and slows the node directly. Each has a specific treatment: calcium and high-dose insulin for calcium channel blockers, glucagon and high-dose insulin for β-blockers, digoxin-specific Fab fragments for digoxin.
**Hypoxia.** A late, ominous cause, especially in children; correcting oxygenation is the treatment.
**Electrolyte abnormality, e.g. hyperkalaemia.** High potassium depolarises cells and slows conduction at every level; calcium stabilises the membrane while potassium is lowered.
mimic: Drug-induced vs structural (sick sinus) bradycardia
Drug-induced resolves when the drug is stopped or reversed; degenerative sinus node disease does not (Top-up).
traps: “The β-blocker alone explains bradycardia in a patient on metoprolol and digoxin”
Digoxin is the synergistic culprit; both slow the AV node.
decode: Metoprolol for AF, now symptomatic bradycardia — synergistic culprit? [Marrow]
Digoxin.
ACLS-40.punch: Ischaemia, nodal-blocking drugs, hypoxia and hyperkalaemia are all reversible, so they are sought and treated at the same time as atropine, not after it fails.

topups.q: Irregular pulse; ECG shows early, wide (>120 ms), bizarre QRS with no preceding P wave — diagnosis and ICU approach?
a: - Ventricular premature beats: premature wide QRS, T wave opposite the QRS, full compensatory pause.
- PACs differ: premature abnormal P wave, narrow QRS, incomplete pause.
- ICU causes: low K/Mg, ischaemia, hypoxia, catheter/wire irritation, inotropes — treat the cause, not the beats; couplets or R-on-T in ischaemia warn of VT/VF.

x.sub: ACLS → Tachyarrhythmia → Premature ventricular beats
x.intro: Step 3 sorts rhythms by QRS width, and the single early wide beat is the smallest version of that question. In the ICU the beat matters less than what is irritating the ventricle.
why: **Ventricular premature beats: premature wide QRS, T wave opposite the QRS, full compensatory pause.** The beat starts in ventricular muscle and spreads cell to cell, not through the Purkinje system, so the QRS is wide and repolarisation runs the opposite way. It does not reset the sinus node, so the next sinus beat comes on time: the pause makes up the lost interval exactly.

**PACs differ: premature abnormal P wave, narrow QRS, incomplete pause.** An atrial beat conducts normally through the ventricles (narrow QRS) and resets the sinus node, so the pause is shorter than compensatory.

**ICU causes: low K/Mg, ischaemia, hypoxia, catheter or wire irritation, inotropes — treat the cause, not the beats; couplets or R-on-T in ischaemia warn of VT/VF.** Suppressing ectopy with antiarrhythmics does not improve outcome (CAST showed harm after MI); correcting potassium and magnesium, withdrawing a wire from the ventricle and reducing catecholamines does.
mimic: VPB vs PAC with aberrant conduction
An aberrant PAC has a premature P before it and usually an RBBB shape with an incomplete pause.
traps: “Frequent VPBs in the ICU: start amiodarone or lidocaine”
Look for the cause first: electrolytes, ischaemia, a central line or PA catheter tip in the RV, inotropes.
decode: Irregular pulse, early wide bizarre QRS without a preceding P [DocT]
Ventricular premature beats.
x.punch: An early wide beat without a P, followed by a full compensatory pause, is a VPB; in the ICU fix the potassium, magnesium, oxygen, wire or inotrope that is causing it.

topups.q: Elderly patient on no drugs: sinus bradycardia with pauses — cause, what to exclude, and fix?
a: - Sick sinus syndrome: idiopathic degenerative fibrosis of the SA node is the commonest cause in the elderly; may coexist with AV-nodal disease and AF (tachy–brady).
- Exclude reversible causes first: β-blocker, CCB, digoxin, hypothyroidism, hyperkalaemia, hypothermia, raised ICP.
- Symptomatic → permanent pacemaker; atropine or transcutaneous pacing only as a bridge if unstable.

x.sub: ACLS → Bradycardia → Sick sinus syndrome
x.intro: Step 5 reads where the slow rhythm starts. In an elderly patient on no drugs, sinus slowing with pauses usually means the node itself is failing.
why: **Sick sinus syndrome: idiopathic degenerative fibrosis of the SA node is the commonest cause in the elderly; may coexist with AV-nodal disease and AF (tachy–brady).** Fibrosis replaces pacemaker cells, so the node fires slowly, pauses or fails to exit; the same atrial disease predisposes to AF, and pauses often follow its termination.

**Exclude reversible causes first: β-blocker, CCB, digoxin, hypothyroidism, hyperkalaemia, hypothermia, raised ICP.** Each slows the node and mimics intrinsic disease (ACLS-40); a pacemaker is not indicated until they are excluded.
**Symptomatic → permanent pacemaker; atropine or transcutaneous pacing only as a bridge if unstable.** Pacing treats the brady side and allows rate-controlling drugs for the tachy side.
mimic: Sick sinus vs drug-induced sinus bradycardia
Drug-induced resolves when the drug is stopped; fibrosis does not.
traps: “Tachy–brady syndrome: give a β-blocker for the AF without pacing”
The β-blocker deepens the pauses; pace first, then control the rate.
decode: Elderly, on no drugs, sinus bradycardia with pauses — cause and fix? [DocT GT]
Degenerative SA node fibrosis; exclude reversible causes, then permanent pacemaker if symptomatic.
x.punch: Sick sinus syndrome is a fibrosed SA node, often with AF; exclude drugs, thyroid and potassium, then pace if symptomatic.

topups.q: Pacemaker leads — unipolar vs bipolar?
a: - Unipolar: tip electrode is the cathode and the can is the anode, so the circuit spans the chest wall → large spike, more myopotential/EMI oversensing and pocket muscle stimulation.
- Bipolar: tip + ring electrode ~10 mm proximal → small local circuit, less oversensing; the standard today (so 'unipolar is better' is false).
- One lead per paced chamber; RA lead usually in or near the appendage.

x.sub: ACLS → Pacing → Unipolar vs bipolar leads
x.intro: Step 6 ends with pacing, and the lead configuration explains the ECG spike size and why some pacemakers oversense.
why: **Unipolar: the tip is the cathode and the can is the anode, so the circuit spans the chest wall → large spike, more myopotential and EMI oversensing, pocket muscle stimulation.** A wide circuit acts as a large antenna: it picks up pectoral muscle activity and electromagnetic interference (diathermy), which can inhibit pacing.

**Bipolar: tip plus a ring electrode about 10 mm proximal → small local circuit, less oversensing; the standard today, so ‘unipolar is better’ is false.** The small spike can be hard to see on the ECG, but sensing is more reliable.
**One lead per paced chamber; the RA lead usually sits in or near the appendage.** A dual-chamber device has an atrial and a ventricular lead; CRT adds a coronary sinus lead for the LV.
mimic: Large vs small pacing spike
A large spike suggests a unipolar configuration; a tiny or invisible one, bipolar.
traps: “Unipolar leads are better”
Bipolar leads sense more reliably and are the standard.
decode: Pacemaker leads — which statement is true? [DocT GT]
Bipolar has a small local circuit and less oversensing; unipolar is not better.
x.punch: Unipolar pacing uses the can as the anode, so it gives a large spike and oversenses muscle and diathermy; bipolar keeps the circuit at the tip and is the standard.

spine: Defibrillation: dose and delivery

An unsynchronised shock depolarises enough myocardium at once to stop fibrillation, so what matters is enough current through the heart: the right energy, large pads in either position, and nothing that delays the first shock.
Synchronised cardioversion

In an organised rhythm with a pulse the shock is timed to the R wave so it never lands on the vulnerable T wave, and in 2025 AF and flutter start at 200 J because low energies fail and can provoke VF.
Tachycardia: unstable, then QRS
Instability sends any tachycardia to the shock; a stable one is sorted by QRS width and regularity, which decides whether vagal manoeuvres, adenosine, nodal blockers or antiarrhythmics are safe.
After ROSC: the targets
After ROSC the brain is protected by avoiding the second hits: hypotension, hypoxia, hyperoxia, abnormal CO₂ and fever, with temperature control for at least 36 hours.
Reading the slow rhythm
Where the block lies (sinus node, AV node or below it) is read from the P–QRS relationship and the QRS width, and the level of block predicts whether it will progress and whether atropine can help.
Treating the bradycardia
Symptomatic bradycardia gets atropine, then pacing or an adrenergic infusion, then transvenous pacing, while the reversible cause (ischaemia, drugs, hypoxia, potassium) is treated alongside.
CVS08B.primer: Electrical therapy works by depolarising a large mass of myocardium at once so the sinus node can take over again. A shock that lands during the T wave (the vulnerable period, when cells are partly repolarised) can itself start VF, which is why shocks in a patient with an organised rhythm are synchronised to the R wave and shocks in VF cannot be. The AHA tachycardia and bradycardia algorithms both start with the same question: is the rhythm causing hypotension, altered mentation, shock, ischaemic chest pain or acute heart failure? CVS08A covered BLS, the cardiac arrest algorithm and arrest drugs; this deck covers the shocks, the rhythms with a pulse and the care after ROSC.

ACLS-41.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → Airway management in arrest
ACLS-41.intro: Step 1 starts with getting air in. The airway is opened by the simplest manoeuvre that works and escalated only when needed, because every more complex device costs compression time. Four real questions test the ladder, its order with a cervical spine at risk, the weakness of bag-mask ventilation and when a supraglottic airway beats a tube.
why: **Head tilt–chin lift; adjuncts OPA / NPA.** In the unconscious patient the tongue and epiglottis fall back against the posterior pharynx; lifting the mandible pulls the tongue forward. An oropharyngeal airway suits the patient with no gag (it provokes vomiting otherwise); a nasopharyngeal airway is tolerated by a semi-conscious patient. AHA 2025 prefers the OPA when a basal skull fracture or severe coagulopathy is suspected, because a nasal tube can enter the cranium or cause brisk bleeding.

**Definitive airway: ETT / supraglottic airway / i-gel / Combitube.** These are the advanced airways of ACLS. Strictly, a definitive airway (the ATLS term) is a cuffed tube in the trachea; a supraglottic device sits above the cords and does not fully protect against aspiration (FLAG). For arrest outcomes the choice matters little: AHA 2025 accepts either a supraglottic airway or a tube, and prefers the supraglottic airway where intubation success is low, because it goes in faster with fewer pauses in compressions.

**Ladder: compression-only CPR → mouth-to-mouth → bag-mask (basic) | supraglottic airway → tracheal intubation (advanced).** The border lies after the bag-mask: every step beyond it is a device inserted into the pharynx (supraglottic airway) or the trachea (tube). Bag-mask ventilation is the step most often done badly; its main limitation is gastric inflation, because pharyngeal pressures above about 20 cmH2O open the oesophageal sphincter, the stomach fills, the diaphragm is splinted and regurgitation follows. Slow breaths over 1 second, just enough to see the chest rise, and a two-person grip reduce it.

**2025: in head and neck trauma, if the airway cannot be opened with a jaw thrust and an adjunct, a trained rescuer should open it with head tilt–chin lift.** The jaw thrust without head extension stays the first choice (class 1) because it moves the cervical spine least. But a hypoxic arrest kills in minutes, while worsening a cord injury by some neck extension is uncommon, so patency wins. The full trauma sequence the NEET recall asked is: suction first, then jaw thrust (or chin lift), then OPA/NPA, then a cuffed tube with manual in-line stabilisation, then a surgical airway if intubation fails.
mimic: Advanced airway vs definitive airway
ACLS calls any SGA or tube ‘advanced’; ATLS reserves ‘definitive’ for a cuffed tube below the cords.
Jaw thrust vs head tilt–chin lift
Jaw thrust first in suspected spinal injury; head tilt–chin lift only when the thrust and an adjunct fail.
traps: “The key limitation of bag-mask ventilation is tracheal injury or that it needs two rescuers”
It is gastric inflation; two rescuers make it better but are not required.
“In OHCA intubation is always the preferred advanced airway”
Where the system’s intubation success is low, a supraglottic airway is preferred; outcomes are similar.
“Advanced airway first, then suction and basic manoeuvres”
The ladder runs from simple to complex: clear the airway, open it, add an adjunct, then a device.
decode: EMS system with low intubation success — preferred advanced airway in OHCA? [DocT GT]
Supraglottic airway.
Key limitation of bag-valve-mask ventilation? [DocT GT]
Gastric inflation (100%).
Correct airway sequence with cervical spine control [NEET 2025]
Suction → jaw thrust/chin lift → OPA/NPA → cuffed ETT ± RSI or surgical airway.
Chin lift, Guedel, supraglottic device — which is not used to maintain the airway? [NEET 2025]
None: all are used.
ACLS-41.punch: Go up the ladder only as far as you need: the jaw thrust protects the neck, but a closed airway is the more urgent threat, and an SGA placed quickly beats a tube placed slowly.

ACLS-42.intro: Step 1 continues with how much to breathe for the patient. The aim is enough oxygen with as little rise in intrathoracic pressure as possible, because each over-sized breath cuts the venous return that compressions depend on. Only 31% chose the right answer to the question on what protects cerebral perfusion.
why: **100% FiO2 initially.** During CPR the cardiac output is a fraction of normal, so oxygen delivery is limited by flow, and the only lever left on oxygen content is a high inspired fraction. AHA 2025 says the maximal feasible FiO2 is reasonable.

**Waveform capnography to confirm and monitor ET tube placement.** A sustained waveform over several breaths means CO2 is coming from the lungs; an oesophageal tube gives a few falling breaths then nothing. Seeing the tube pass the cords, chest movement and breath sounds all mislead. A chest X-ray shows depth (tip 2–5 cm above the carina) but cannot exclude oesophageal placement.

**Keep the maximal feasible FiO2 throughout CPR; titrate only after ROSC (SpO2 90–98%).** There is no saturation target during arrest: pulse oximetry is unreliable without a pulse, and hypoxia is the greater danger. Hyperoxia becomes a concern only once flow returns. AHA 2025 then titrates to SpO2 90–98% with PaO2 60–105 mmHg (2020 used 92–98%); ERC–ESICM 2025 uses SpO2 94–98% with PaO2 75–100 mmHg.
**EtCO2 goal: at least 10 mmHg, ideally 20 or more.** These are the values AHA 2025 quotes for adjusting compressions; ACLS-43 covers what to do when it is low.

**Advanced airway in place: 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 breaths/min) with continuous chest compressions.** Before an advanced airway the ratio is 30:2, with each breath over 1 second and just enough volume to see the chest rise (about 500–600 mL). Hyperventilation raises intrathoracic pressure, which reduces venous return and so coronary and cerebral perfusion; it also lowers PaCO2, constricting cerebral vessels.
mimic: Intra-arrest oxygen vs post-ROSC oxygen
During CPR: maximal FiO2, no target. After ROSC: titrate to SpO2 90–98%.
Tube in the trachea vs tube at the right depth
Waveform capnography confirms the first; the chest X-ray confirms the second.
traps: “Deliver 10 breaths per minute” with a bag-mask (chosen often; only 31% right)
10/min applies once an advanced airway is in; with a bag-mask it is 30:2. The answer that protects perfusion is avoiding hyperinflation.
“Increase the tidal volume to 900 mL”
Too large: it raises intrathoracic pressure and inflates the stomach; visible chest rise is enough.
“Chest X-ray is the best way to verify the tube” (NEET 2025 key)

The X-ray checks depth only; waveform capnography confirms tracheal placement. If capnography is offered, choose it; if the stem has already shown CO2 and asks for ‘proper position’, the keyed X-ray stands.
“Titrate oxygen to 92–98% during CPR”
There is no intra-arrest saturation target; titration begins after ROSC.
decode: Bag-mask CPR — which action best preserves cerebral perfusion? [DocT GT]
Avoid hyperexpansion during breaths (31%).
Intubated during CPR — ventilation rate? [DocT GT]
1 breath every 5–6 seconds (AHA: every 6 s).
Cords seen, colorimetric CO2 positive, breath sounds equal — best verification of proper position? [NEET 2025]
Chest radiograph (depth); waveform capnography if offered.
ACLS-42.punch: Give all the oxygen you can, but in small slow breaths: in arrest the danger is not too little ventilation but too much pressure in the chest, and capnography, not the stethoscope, tells you the tube is in the trachea.

ACLS-43.intro: Step 1 ends with feedback. During arrest the CO2 reaching the alveoli depends on how much blood is pushed through the lungs, so the capnograph becomes a flow meter for compressions. Both real questions show a low or falling value and ask what to do.
why: **Low or flat trace (around 5–10 mmHg) → improve chest compressions; EtCO2 reflects pulmonary blood flow and therefore compression quality.** With ventilation fixed, ETCO2 falls only when less blood reaches the lungs: a tired compressor, shallow or slow compressions, or leaning. A gradual fall from 18 to 7 with no rhythm change is the classic tiring compressor; rotate and push harder. Hyperventilation lowers ETCO2 too, which is why a constant ventilation rate is needed before reading the number.

**Abrupt sustained rise (typically ≥40 mmHg) → ROSC.** When the heart restarts, output jumps and the CO2 that has built up in the tissues is washed to the lungs at once, so the value rises suddenly, often above normal. A rhythm and pulse check confirms it. A bolus of sodium bicarbonate also raises ETCO2 briefly, a known false signal.

**Compression depth: good 2–2.4 inches (5–6 cm); bad <2 inches (<5 cm).** Depth sets stroke volume during CPR. Too deep (over 6 cm) adds injury without benefit. AHA 2025 keeps the rate at 100–120/min with full recoil.
mimic: Falling ETCO2 in CPR vs falling ETCO2 under anaesthesia
In arrest it means less flow (fix compressions); under anaesthesia with a pulse it can also mean hyperventilation, PE or a leak.
traps: “ETCO2 8 mmHg — give bicarbonate or increase the ventilation rate”
Bicarbonate is not routine and more breaths lower ETCO2 further; improve compressions.
“ETCO2 8 mmHg — terminate resuscitation”

A low value alone is never a reason to stop; AHA 2025 allows ETCO2 under 10 after 20 minutes of ALS in an intubated patient only as one factor among several, and never in a non-intubated patient (ACLS-20).
decode: Intubated PEA, persistent ETCO2 8 mmHg despite correct ventilation [DocT GT]
Reassess and improve CPR quality.
ETCO2 falling from 18 to 7 over minutes, rhythm unchanged [DocT GT]
Reassess CPR quality (the compressor is tiring).
ACLS-43.punch: During arrest the capnograph measures flow, not breathing: a low or falling number means push better, and a sudden jump means the heart has started.

ACLS-44.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → Circulation targets during CPR
ACLS-44.intro: Step 1 also asks how you know compressions are perfusing the heart. Both real questions ask which parameter best predicts ROSC, and only 53–58% chose coronary perfusion pressure; the rest picked numbers that are easy to see but do not reach the myocardium.
why: **Monitor CPR quality via EtCO2.** ETCO2 reports flow through the lungs, and with an arterial line the diastolic pressure reports what is left for the coronaries; AHA 2025 suggests using either when feasible. Both are surrogates for coronary perfusion pressure.
**EtCO2 goal >10 mmHg.** AHA 2025 text puts it as at least 10, ideally 20 or more (ACLS-42).

**Arterial diastolic BP: no adult target in AHA 2025; ERC 2025 suggests ≥30 mmHg.** The heart is perfused in the release phase, so coronary perfusion pressure is aortic diastolic minus right-atrial diastolic pressure; animal and human studies found that ROSC is rare below about 15 mmHg. The arterial diastolic pressure is its bedside proxy. AHA 2020 used ‘under 20 mmHg, improve CPR’; AHA 2025 says adult data are inadequate to set any number. ERC 2025, as a pragmatic physiology-guided approach, aims for a diastolic pressure of ≥30 mmHg with an arterial line and an ETCO2 of ≥25 mmHg.

**Attach monitor / defibrillator • obtain IV/IO access • use drugs appropriately.** The shock decides shockable rhythms, so the defibrillator comes first; access follows without stopping compressions.
mimic: Coronary perfusion pressure vs systolic pressure during compressions
Systolic peaks show the push; diastolic pressure minus right-atrial pressure shows what reaches the myocardium.
traps: “Systolic or peak arterial pressure during compressions best predicts ROSC”
The coronaries fill in diastole; systolic peaks can be high while the heart is not perfused.
“A palpable femoral pulse means compressions are effective”
The femoral vein lies next to the artery and transmits pressure waves; a felt pulse may be venous and says nothing about coronary flow.
decode: Pulseless, high-quality CPR — which parameter best correlates with ROSC? [DocT GT ×2]
Coronary perfusion pressure (58% and 53%).
ACLS-44.punch: The heart in arrest is fed only between compressions, by the gap between aortic diastolic and right-atrial pressure; ETCO2 and the arterial diastolic pressure are the two windows on that gap.

ACLS-45.intro: Step 2 begins with the one vasopressor left in the algorithm. Epinephrine’s α effect constricts the periphery and raises aortic diastolic pressure, which lifts coronary perfusion pressure (ACLS-44). Six questions test its timing, dose, preparation, its use in pregnancy and the end of vasopressin; the dilution question was answered right by only 34%.
why: **Non-shockable: administer epinephrine as soon as possible.** In asystole or PEA there is no shock to deliver, and the chance of ROSC falls with every minute before the first dose, so the drug goes in as soon as access exists (AHA 2025, 2a).
