**Shockable: reasonable to administer after initial defibrillation attempts have failed.** Here the treatment that works is the shock; epinephrine raises myocardial oxygen demand and can make VF harder to terminate. AHA gives it after the second shock; ERC after the third.

**Adult: 1 mg IV/IO every 3–5 minutes.** It is the same in pregnancy: no dose change and no other first-line vasopressor. The 1 mg is 10 mL of 1:10,000 (0.1 mg/mL). In India it is often prepared by drawing 1 mL of the 1:1000 ampoule (1 mg/mL) and diluting to 10 mL. 1:1000 undiluted is the IM anaphylaxis strength (0.5 mL = 0.5 mg); 10 mL of it would be a tenfold overdose. High-dose epinephrine has no benefit.
**Paediatric: 0.01 mg/kg (0.1 mL/kg of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration), max 1 mg, every 3–5 min.** The weight-based dose reaches the adult dose at 100 kg.

**2025: vasopressin alone, or with epinephrine, offers no advantage as a substitute for epinephrine.** Vasopressin acts on V1 receptors rather than α receptors, which seemed attractive in an acidotic circulation, but trials of vasopressin alone or added to epinephrine showed no better survival, so the algorithm was simplified to one drug (AHA 2020 and 2025, 3: No Benefit). Adding vasopressin with methylprednisolone in in-hospital arrest raised ROSC in trials but not survival.
mimic: 0.1 mg/mL (IV in arrest, 10 mL for 1 mg) vs 1 mg/mL (IM in anaphylaxis, 0.5 mL).
Epinephrine timing in VF vs asystole
VF: after failed shocks. Asystole/PEA: as soon as feasible.
traps: “10 mL of 1:1000” or “1 mL of 1:1000” as the IV arrest preparation (34% right)
The arrest dose is 1 mg as 10 mL of 1:10,000; 10 mL of 1:1000 is 10 mg.
“Phenylephrine, noradrenaline or dopamine as first-line in maternal arrest” (54% right)
Pregnancy changes the position and the access route, not the drugs: epinephrine 1 mg every 3–5 min.
“Wait for the second rhythm check, or for an advanced airway, before epinephrine in asystole”
Give it as soon as feasible; neither the airway nor ETCO2 gates it.
“Vasopressin is first line for shockable rhythms or superior after long down-times”
It offers no advantage over epinephrine.
decode: Asystole — when is epinephrine given? [DocT GT]
As soon as feasible.
1 mg every 3 minutes — correct volume and concentration? [DocT GT]
Maternal arrest — first-line vasopressor and dose? [DocT QBank ×2]
Epinephrine 1 mg IV every 3–5 min (54%, 95%).
Vasopressin in the 2025 guideline? [DocT GT] [Marrow]
No advantage over epinephrine; not in the algorithm.
ACLS-45.punch: Epinephrine is the only arrest vasopressor: 1 mg of 1:10,000 every 3–5 minutes, straight away when there is no shock to give, after the shocks when there is.

ACLS-46.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → Antiarrhythmics in refractory VF/pVT
ACLS-46.intro: Step 2 continues with the drugs for VF that keeps coming back after shocks. They do not restart the heart; they make the next shock more likely to hold. Both questions test that amiodarone and lidocaine are alternatives, one in a pregnant patient where the key is disputed.
why: **Amiodarone (class III), adult: first 300 mg bolus, second 150 mg.** In ALPS (2016, shock-refractory OHCA) survival to discharge was 24.4% with amiodarone, 23.7% with lidocaine and 21.0% with placebo, not significantly different; in the prespecified bystander-witnessed subgroup both drugs did better than placebo (about 28% vs 23%), which suggests the drugs help when given early. AHA 2025 gives them a weak 2b recommendation. ERC gives amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock and 150 mg after the fifth.
**Paediatric: 5 mg/kg bolus, may repeat up to 3 total doses.** Weight-based, unlike the fixed adult doses.
**Lidocaine, adult: first 1–1.5 mg/kg, second 0.5–0.75 mg/kg.** The maximum is 3 mg/kg. ERC uses fixed doses instead: 100 mg, then 50 mg.

**Class: the card labels amiodarone class III; lidocaine, the drug just above in the question, is class Ib.** Amiodarone is class III because its main action is potassium-channel block, which prolongs repolarisation and refractoriness, although it also blocks sodium and calcium channels and β receptors. Lidocaine blocks fast sodium channels with rapid on–off kinetics, so it acts mainly on ischaemic, depolarised tissue, which is why it suits ischaemic VF.
mimic: Amiodarone vs lidocaine in arrest
Equal outcomes in ALPS; the algorithm reads ‘amiodarone or lidocaine’, never both in sequence as a rule.
traps: “Lidocaine + magnesium is wrong for eclamptic maternal VF” (key: amiodarone + magnesium, 67% right)
AHA lists amiodarone or lidocaine, so lidocaine + magnesium is equally correct; fetal thyroid risk is irrelevant in arrest. With both pairs offered, pick the keyed amiodarone pair.
“Procainamide infusion for refractory VF”
Procainamide is an option for stable VT with a pulse; in arrest its benefit is uncertain (ACLS-47).
decode: Three shocks and two doses of epinephrine, still VF — preferred antiarrhythmic strategy? [DocT GT]
Either amiodarone or lidocaine; equivalent survival to discharge.
Eclampsia, status epilepticus, then VF arrest at 30 weeks — drug pair? [DocT QBank]
Amiodarone + magnesium (keyed; lidocaine + magnesium equally valid).
ACLS-46.punch: After failed shocks give amiodarone 300 then 150 mg, or lidocaine 1–1.5 then 0.5–0.75 mg/kg; they are alternatives with equal outcomes, and pregnancy does not change them.

ACLS-47.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → Drugs of uncertain or no benefit
ACLS-47.intro: Step 2 also lists the drugs that were tested and found wanting. Each was given because it made physiological sense, and each failed to improve survival when trialled. The exam asks which ones are out and what single job magnesium keeps.
why: **β-blockers, bretylium, procainamide, sotalol for defibrillation-unresponsive VF/pVT: uncertain benefit.** The evidence is a few small studies. β-blockade in electrical storm makes sense (it blunts the catecholamine drive), but has not been shown to improve survival in arrest (AHA 2025, 2b).
**Vasopressin: no advantage, alone or combined with epinephrine.** See ACLS-45.

**IV calcium for arrest from suspected hyperkalaemia: effectiveness not well established; must be weighed against detracting from CPR, defibrillation and epinephrine.** Calcium stabilises the cardiac membrane against a high potassium, which is why it is used with a pulse; in arrest the trials of routine calcium showed no benefit and a signal of harm, so AHA 2025 makes routine calcium a 3: No Benefit and leaves it a weak 2b where hyperkalaemia is suspected. It does keep a clear place in arrest on a magnesium infusion (ACLS-52) and in calcium-channel-blocker toxicity.

**Intra-arrest magnesium: did not improve ROSC, survival or neurological outcome regardless of rhythm, and not useful for monomorphic VT. It retains its role in torsades de pointes.** Torsades arises from early afterdepolarisations in a long QT; magnesium suppresses them by blocking the calcium current that triggers them, without needing to correct a low serum level. The dose is 2 g IV (NEET 2024).
mimic: Torsades vs monomorphic VT
Torsades (twisting axis, long QT) responds to magnesium; monomorphic VT does not.
Calcium with a pulse vs calcium in arrest
With a pulse, hyperkalaemic ECG changes are a clear indication; in arrest its effect is not established.
traps: “Cocaine-related arrest with polymorphic VT — β-blocker”
The keyed answer is magnesium for torsades (70% right). Cocaine more often causes a wide-QRS VT from sodium-channel block, which takes bicarbonate (TOX-07).
“Bretylium is back on the shelf, so it is recommended again”
It returned to the market without new evidence; its benefit is uncertain.
decode: Indication for MgSO4 in cardiac arrest? [NEET 2024]
Torsades de pointes (2 g IV).
Polymorphic VT after cocaine, collapse — best immediate management? [DocT QBank]
IV magnesium (torsades).
Vasopressin as substitute or adjunct to epinephrine? [DocT GT]
No advantage.
ACLS-47.punch: Outside epinephrine and one antiarrhythmic, nothing routine survives in the arrest algorithm: magnesium is kept only for torsades, and calcium only for a specific cause.

ACLS-48.intro: Step 2 ends with a drug that left the arrest algorithm long ago but remains first line in another. Atropine blocks vagal (muscarinic) slowing of the sinus and AV nodes, so it works only where the block is in or above the node. Only 22% chose it for unstable complete heart block in the ICU.
why: **Used only for the symptomatic bradycardia algorithm.** In asystole the problem is not vagal tone, and trials found no benefit, so it was removed in 2010.

**1 mg × 3 times (maximum 3 mg), repeated every 3–5 minutes.** AHA moved from 0.5 mg to 1 mg in 2020; doses under 0.5 mg can cause paradoxical slowing. If it fails, go to transcutaneous pacing or an epinephrine or dopamine infusion. It rarely works in Mobitz II or complete block below the node (typical of anterior MI, wide QRS escape) or in a transplanted (denervated) heart; there go straight to pacing.
mimic: Nodal vs infranodal block
Narrow QRS escape, inferior MI, Mobitz I: atropine often works. Wide QRS escape, Mobitz II, anterior MI: pace.
traps: “Unstable complete heart block — permanent pacemaker or cardioversion” (only 22% right)
Atropine first while pacing is prepared; a permanent device comes after stabilisation, and cardioversion is for tachycardia.
“Bradycardia after stenting — dopamine or noradrenaline first”
Atropine first; infusions are the second line.
“Atropine 0.5 mg” (an older dose still in some explanations)
AHA now uses 1 mg every 3–5 min, maximum 3 mg.
decode: HR 34, BP 80/50, complete heart block, good contractility — next step? [DocT GT]
Atropine (22%), with pacing ready.
Post-ACS/stenting bradycardia, HR 42 — drug to start? [NEET 2025]
Atropine.
ACLS-48.punch: Atropine belongs to bradycardia, not arrest: 1 mg every 3–5 minutes to 3 mg, and if the block is below the node, pace.

ACLS-49.intro: Step 3 is who does what. The resuscitation triangle is the three people around the patient whose work keeps flow going; no real question is linked, but stems ask who rotates and how often.
why: **Compressor: assesses the patient, does 5 cycles of compressions, alternates with the AED/monitor role.** Compression quality falls within about 2 minutes as the rescuer tires, often before he notices.

**AED / monitor / defibrillator: brings and operates the device, alternates with the compressor, places the monitor where the team leader can see it.** Swapping these two at the rhythm check means the change happens in a pause that already exists.

**Airway: opens the airway, gives bag-mask ventilation, inserts adjuncts.** Ventilation is a separate job so that breaths are given at the right rate and size while the other two keep compressions and shocks going; only the compressor and AED roles are set to swap.
**Compressor and AED roles alternate every 5 cycles or 2 minutes, earlier with fatigue; no one leaves the triangle except for his or her own safety.**
mimic: Triangle roles vs leadership roles
The triangle keeps the patient perfused; the leader, medications and recorder roles (ACLS-50) run the decisions around it.
traps: “The compressor changes only when he feels tired”
Fatigue degrades compressions before it is felt; swap every 2 minutes.
decode: How often should compressors rotate? [pattern]
Every 2 minutes (5 cycles), at the rhythm check.
ACLS-49.punch: Swap the compressor every 2 minutes at the rhythm check, because quality fades before the rescuer knows it.

ACLS-50.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → Leadership roles and team composition
ACLS-50.intro: Step 3 continues with the three roles that surround the triangle. No real question is linked; the likely ask is the leader’s duties and what the recorder tracks.
why: **Team leader: every team must have a defined leader; assigns roles, makes treatment decisions, gives feedback, assumes responsibility for roles not assigned.** The leader stays hands-off where possible so he can see the whole scene and think ahead to the next rhythm check.
**IV/IO / medications: an ACLS provider role; starts IV/IO access, gives medications.**

**Time / recorder: records the time of interventions and medications, announces when next due, records the frequency and duration of compression interruptions.** Pauses are the commonest hidden failure in CPR, which is why they are timed.
**2025: in-hospital code teams should comprise ALS-trained members with clearly defined roles and simulation-based training; an ALS-level clinician present is beneficial in OHCA.**
mimic: Leader vs recorder
The leader decides; the recorder keeps time and prompts the next drug or rhythm check.
traps: “The leader performs the most skilled task himself, such as intubation”
The leader directs and covers unassigned roles; doing a task narrows his view.
decode: Who records the frequency and duration of interruptions in compressions? [pattern]
The timer/recorder.
ACLS-50.punch: One named leader decides, the recorder times every drug and pause, and the 2025 guideline asks for ALS-trained teams that practise by simulation.

ACLS-51.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → Arrest in pregnancy: principles
ACLS-51.intro: Step 4 opens the special circumstances with pregnancy. From about 20 weeks the uterus compresses the inferior vena cava and aorta when the woman lies supine, so CPR on her back produces even less output than usual. Three questions test that and the airway.
why: **Priorities: high-quality CPR and relief of aortocaval compression.** Compressions need venous return to fill the heart; a gravid uterus on the vena cava removes much of it.

**Continuous manual left lateral uterine displacement.** Pushing the uterus up and to the left lifts it off the vena cava while the woman stays flat, so compressions stay effective. A tilted board was used before, but tilting reduces compression force; AHA 2025 makes manual displacement class 1. It needs a second rescuer, which is the answer to the NEET recall.

**A difficult airway is common in pregnancy; use the most experienced provider; ETT or SGA; waveform capnography to confirm and monitor.** Airway oedema, breast tissue, a full stomach with a lax oesophageal sphincter and a lower functional residual capacity with higher oxygen demand mean she desaturates fast and aspirates easily. A cuffed tube protects the airway best, so it is the preferred device when an expert can place it.
**1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min) with continuous compressions once the advanced airway is in; team planning with obstetric, neonatal, emergency, anaesthesia, intensive care and arrest services.**
mimic: Manual uterine displacement vs left lateral tilt
Displacement keeps her flat for good compressions; tilt weakens them.
traps: “Half-dose epinephrine in pregnancy” or “avoid intubation until ROSC”
Drug doses are unchanged and the airway is secured early by the most experienced person.
“The second rescuer is needed for perimortem caesarean or defibrillation”
The second pair of hands is for continuous uterine displacement.
decode: 28 weeks, arrest in ICU — most critical ACLS modification? [DocT QBank]
Manual left uterine displacement (97%).
Preferred airway device in maternal arrest? [DocT QBank]
Endotracheal tube (92%).
Why is a second rescuer essential? [NEET 2025]
Uterine displacement.
ACLS-51.punch: In maternal arrest the uterus is the obstruction: push it left by hand while compressions continue, and let the most experienced person secure an airway that is both difficult and at risk of aspiration.

ACLS-52.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → Maternal arrest interventions and causes
ACLS-52.intro: Step 4 continues with what the maternal algorithm adds. Each addition answers a feature of pregnancy: the vena cava is blocked, the patient may be on magnesium, and the causes differ. Six questions test these, and two keys are disputed.
why: **Maternal: airway management • 100% O2, avoid excess ventilation • place IV above the diaphragm.** With the vena cava compressed, a drug given in a leg may not reach the heart; AHA 2025 recommends upper-limb IV or IO access.

**If receiving IV magnesium, stop it and give calcium chloride or gluconate.** Magnesium toxicity causes loss of reflexes, respiratory depression, conduction block and arrest; calcium antagonises its effect on the membrane. Hypermagnesaemia is the electrolyte cause to suspect when a woman on a magnesium infusion becomes bradycardic and arrests. Seizure prophylaxis can resume after ROSC.

**Obstetric: continuous lateral uterine displacement • detach fetal monitors • prepare for resuscitative delivery.** Fetal monitors are removed because they slow the move to delivery and interfere with defibrillation; the fetus is best served by restoring the mother’s circulation.

**Aetiologies A–H: anaesthetic complications, bleeding, cardiovascular, drugs, embolic, fever, general non-obstetric causes (H’s and T’s), hypertension.** Haemorrhage is the commonest single cause of maternal arrest, so PEA in pregnancy is treated as hypovolaemia first (wide-bore access above the diaphragm, massive transfusion, uterotonics, obstetrician to theatre). Drugs include magnesium toxicity and local anaesthetic toxicity; embolic includes amniotic fluid and pulmonary embolism.
mimic: Magnesium in eclampsia vs magnesium in arrest
Before arrest it is the treatment; once she arrests on an infusion it is a suspected cause: stop it and give calcium.
traps: “Give magnesium promptly as part of ACLS in eclampsia-related arrest” (DocT key, 68% chose it)
The algorithm says stop magnesium and give calcium; magnesium for seizures resumes after ROSC. If she was already on magnesium, choose calcium.
“Continue the magnesium infusion to prevent seizures, or delay changes until ROSC”
Stop it now and give calcium.
“Hypokalaemia or hypercalcaemia” for bradycardic arrest on the ICU (61% right)
On magnesium the suspect is hypermagnesaemia.
“Attach fetal monitors”
They are detached.
decode: PEA in pregnancy — commonest reversible cause? [DocT QBank]
Hypovolaemia from obstetric haemorrhage (81%).
Pregnant, bradycardia then arrest in ICU — electrolyte? [DocT QBank]
Hypermagnesaemia (61%).
Arrest on IV magnesium for pre-eclampsia, CPR and displacement under way — next? [DocT GT]
Stop magnesium, give IV calcium.
Maternal arrest — which is NOT indicated? [Marrow]
Attaching fetal monitors.
ACLS-52.punch: The maternal algorithm adds three things: access above the diaphragm because the vena cava is blocked, calcium because magnesium may be the cause, and delivery because the uterus is the obstruction.

ACLS-53.intro: Step 4 turns to delivery during arrest. Emptying the uterus relieves aortocaval compression, increases venous return and removes the fetus’s and placenta’s oxygen demand, so it is a manoeuvre for the mother first. Four questions test the timing, the evidence and the incision; two are poorly answered because they ask about trials.
why: **2025 term: resuscitative delivery, replacing ‘perimortem caesarean delivery’.** The new name says what it is for: maternal resuscitation, not fetal salvage.

**Preparation should begin at the recognition of cardiac arrest.** It is indicated when the fundus is at or above the umbilicus (about 20 weeks) and standard resuscitation has not restored circulation (class 1). The team, kit and operator are gathered from the first minute so that the clock is not lost.

**Goal: complete delivery by 5 minutes.** This comes from Katz, Dotters and Droegemueller (1986), the ‘4-minute rule’: start by 4 minutes, deliver by 5. It is a goal from case series, not a trial result. It is done where she lies, through a vertical midline incision from just above the symphysis to the umbilicus, with CPR and displacement continuing.
**Purpose: improve both maternal and fetal outcomes.** In case reviews (Katz 2005, Einav 2012) ROSC often followed delivery; earlier delivery was linked to better survival of both.

**ECPR is reasonable in pregnant or peripartum patients not responding to standard resuscitation (55% survival in the ELSO registry, 87% of 57 patients); a massive transfusion protocol with a balanced strategy, with tranexamic acid, for suspected amniotic fluid embolism (both class 1).** AHA 2025 gives the figures precisely: the 55% is survival among 42 obstetric patients given ECLS for cardiac arrest in the ELSO registry (for ECPR itself the registry figure was 29%), and the 87% is 30-day survival among 57 patients cannulated for arrest in pregnancy or within 24 hours of delivery. Pregnant patients are young, with reversible causes, which is why extracorporeal support does well. In AFE the typical sequence is sudden collapse with right heart failure, then consumptive coagulopathy and massive bleeding; AHA 2025 also supports VA-ECMO and inhaled pulmonary vasodilators.
mimic: Resuscitative delivery vs ordinary emergency caesarean
One is done at the bedside during CPR to resuscitate the mother; the other is done in theatre for maternal or fetal indications.
traps: “The HELP trial studied maternal arrest and perimortem caesarean” (DocT key; 14% right)

No such trial exists; the evidence is Katz 1986/2005 and Einav 2012. If Katz or a case series is offered, choose it; otherwise eliminate MOMS (fetal spina bifida surgery), ALPS (late-preterm steroids) and PROWESS (drotrecogin alfa in sepsis).
“After 20 minutes of failed CPR”, “only after fetal demise” or “after ROSC”
Prepare at recognition and deliver by 5 minutes if there is no ROSC.
“Supra-umbilical or xiphoid incision” (45% right)
Vertical midline from just above the symphysis to the umbilicus.
decode: Timing of perimortem delivery at 34 weeks [DocT QBank]
Within 5 minutes of arrest if no ROSC (92%).
Origin of the ‘4-minute rule’ [DocT QBank]
Katz et al (54%).
Landmark for the incision [DocT QBank]
Just above the symphysis pubis, vertical midline (45%).
ACLS-53.punch: Resuscitative delivery is a manoeuvre for the mother: start preparing when the arrest is recognised, deliver by 5 minutes, and if that fails, extracorporeal support is reasonable.

ACLS-54.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → The unresponsive LVAD patient
ACLS-54.intro: Step 4 includes a patient whose circulation does not depend on a beating heart. A continuous-flow LVAD pumps without pulsatility, so most patients have no palpable pulse while perfusing well. No real question is linked; the likely ask is how to judge perfusion and when to compress.
why: **Adequate perfusion if any of: normal skin colour and temperature, normal capillary refill, MAP >50 mmHg, PETCO2 >20 mmHg. Patients may not have a palpable pulse.** The MAP is read with a Doppler or arterial line, because a cuff may not register non-pulsatile flow. Current durable LVADs give continuous flow, so most patients have no pulse at all; its absence is not a sign of arrest.
**Adequate → do not perform external chest compressions; assess and treat non-LVAD causes; monitor perfusion.** If the pump is moving blood, compressions add nothing.

**Impaired → perform external chest compressions, assess LVAD function if a second rescuer is available, continue BLS/ALS, transport and contact the VAD centre.** AHA 2025 makes compressions class 1 here: the fear of dislodging the cannula is theoretical, while hypoperfusion is lethal.

**Restart checks: alarms • the LVAD hum • driveline connected? • power source connected? • replace the system controller?** A disconnected driveline, a flat battery or a failed controller are faults that can be fixed at the bedside in seconds, which is why they are checked before anything else.

**Non-LVAD causes: dysrhythmia, haemorrhage/hypovolaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, overdose, RV failure, sepsis, stroke.** The pump depends on RV output to fill it, so RV failure or a ventricular arrhythmia that stops the RV can starve it.
mimic: No pulse with an LVAD vs no pulse in arrest
With an LVAD it is expected; perfusion is judged by MAP, PETCO2, skin and capillary refill.
traps: “Never compress the chest of an LVAD patient”
Compress whenever perfusion is impaired; the risk of dislodgment is outweighed.
decode: Unresponsive LVAD patient, no pulse, MAP 60, PETCO2 25 — compress? [pattern]
No; perfusion is adequate, look for non-LVAD causes.
ACLS-54.punch: In an LVAD patient the pulse means nothing: judge perfusion by MAP over 50 or PETCO2 over 20, and if it is impaired, compress without delay.

ACLS-55.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → Asthma, hypothermia and hyperthermia
ACLS-55.intro: Step 4 ends with the most-asked card in the deck: eleven questions, almost all on temperature. Cold and heat both kill, but in opposite ways: cold protects the brain and makes the heart unresponsive, so rewarming comes before drugs; heat injures every minute, so cooling speed is everything.
why: **Asthma: ECLS may be reasonable; volatile anaesthetics may be considered; survival 83.5–100% in observational studies.** Refractory asthma kills by gas trapping and hypercapnia, not by a damaged lung, so taking over gas exchange buys time for bronchodilators to work. Volatile agents relax bronchial smooth muscle directly.

**Hypothermia: ECLS for rewarming; prognostication scores (HOPE, ICE) to guide initiation; may rewarm with ECLS if core <28 °C even without arrest.** Below 28 °C the heart is prone to VF on handling. ECLS rewarms the core at 1.5–5 °C/h while supporting the circulation. HOPE estimates survival (under 10% predicts death) and is better than a potassium threshold alone; potassium above 12 mmol/L suggests cell lysis from asphyxia or death before cooling, and is non-survivable. Grades and rewarming: mild 32–35 °C passive external (dry, insulate; shivering rewarms); moderate 28–32 °C active external (forced air, warmed IV fluid); severe under 28 °C or unstable, active internal (ECLS, or thoracic or peritoneal lavage). The cold myocardium does not respond to shocks or drugs, and drugs accumulate: AHA 2025 now says defibrillate once and defer further shocks and epinephrine until 30 °C; ERC allows up to three shocks, withholds adrenaline below 30 °C and doubles its interval at 30–35 °C.

**Hyperthermia: ice water immersion (1–5 °C) preferred; cool as rapidly as possible, at least 0.15 °C/min.** Heat stroke (core over 40 °C with CNS dysfunction) damages cells in proportion to time above the critical temperature, so the outcome depends on how fast the core falls. Water conducts heat far better than air, which is why immersion beats fans, blankets and cold IV fluid. If ice water is not available, AHA 2025 accepts tepid water at 8–17 °C or tarp-assisted ice water; where immersion is not possible at all (frail elderly, ICU), evaporative cooling with ice packs is the fallback. Antipyretics do nothing because the set-point is normal, and dantrolene has no role outside malignant hyperthermia. AHA 2025 stops active cooling at 38.6 °C, because the core keeps falling after removal.
mimic: Hypothermic arrest vs normothermic arrest
Cold: rewarm, limit shocks and defer drugs below 30 °C, continue CPR long. Normothermic: standard ALS.
Heat stroke vs fever
Heat stroke has a normal set-point and needs physical cooling; fever responds to antipyretics.
traps: “Cool exertional heat stroke to at least 36 °C to prevent rebound” (DocT key; 78% chose it)
The key is wrong: stop cooling at about 38.6–39 °C (AHA 2025: 38.6 °C), because the core falls further after removal. Choose ‘stop at 39 °C’ if offered.
“Cooling blankets and fans” or “cold IV fluid alone” for heat stroke (59% right)
Ice-water immersion is fastest.
“Passive rewarming is wrong for mild hypothermia — use active external” (47% right)
Stable mild hypothermia needs only passive external rewarming.
“Give antiarrhythmics for VF at 29 °C” (53% right)

Continue CPR and withhold antiarrhythmics until above 30 °C; lidocaine does not work in a cold heart. ‘Defibrillate once and proceed with active rewarming’ is not wrong either (AHA 2025 allows one shock, ERC up to three), but the keyed answer is ‘continue CPR and withhold antiarrhythmics’.
“AHA is more permissive than ERC on shocks and drugs in hypothermia”
That was AHA 2020; AHA 2025 defers further shocks and epinephrine below 30 °C, close to ERC.
decode: Hot day, core 41 °C, confused — initial step? [DocT QBank ×2]
Ice-water immersion (59%, 88%).
Core 29 °C, VF — next step? [DocT QBank]
Continue CPR, withhold antiarrhythmics until above 30 °C (53%).
Core 30 °C, Osborn waves, wide QRS — strategy? [DocT QBank]
Active internal rewarming with gentle handling (83%).
Pulseless in snow — which test decides continuing CPR? [Marrow]
Serum potassium (over 12 mmol/L is non-survivable).
ACLS-55.punch: Cold protects the brain and paralyses the heart, so rewarm (by ECLS when severe) and hold drugs and repeated shocks below 30 °C; heat injures every minute, so immerse in ice water at 0.15 °C/min and stop at about 38.6 °C.

table.title: Accidental hypothermia: grade and rewarming
head: Grade
Core
Rewarming
rows: Passive external: dry, insulate, warm room
Active external (forced air) + warmed IV fluid
Active internal: ECLS first, lavage if unavailable

parts.q: Which conduction site does hypothermia depress first? [Marrow]
parts.a: The sinoatrial node: sinus bradycardia comes first, then atrial fibrillation, Osborn (J) waves and a long QT; VF risk is highest below 28 °C.

ACLS-56.intro: Step 5 is what happens once the heart restarts. Most deaths after ROSC come from brain injury and recurrent shock, so the algorithm first protects oxygen delivery, then sorts patients by whether the brain is working. No real question is linked to this card.
why: **Initial stabilisation: airway • oxygenation and ventilation (SpO2 90–98%, PCO2 35–45) • haemodynamics (MAP ≥65).** FiO2 stays at 100% until the saturation can be read reliably. Both hypoxia and hyperoxia, and both low and high CO2, injure the reperfused brain (low CO2 constricts cerebral vessels). ERC–ESICM 2025 targets 94–98% and MAP over 60–65.
**Early diagnostics: 12-lead ECG; consider CT (head to pelvis) and/or ultrasound.** The ECG finds the coronary cause; CT finds bleeding, PE, aortic dissection or injury from CPR.

**Assess the patient off sedation and neuromuscular blockade, if able → follows commands?** Sedation can make an awake brain look comatose, which would push a patient wrongly into the coma arm and later into a false poor prognosis.

**No or unsure: the same, plus a deliberate temperature-control strategy, EEG and appropriately timed multimodal prognostication.** Temperature is held between 32 and 37.5 °C for at least 36 hours (AHA 2025), with fever prevented; EEG detects seizures that are often non-convulsive; prognostication is consolidated at least 72 hours after normothermia and stopping sedation (AHA 2025; ERC–ESICM counts 72 hours from ROSC), using several tests together, because sedatives and cooling slow the recovery of brain function and an early single test misleads.

**Emergency cardiac intervention for persistent ST elevation, cardiogenic shock, recurrent or refractory ventricular arrhythmias, severe myocardial ischaemia.** Without these, early angiography after arrest without ST elevation did not improve survival (COACT, TOMAHAWK).
mimic: Follows commands vs does not
Awake: critical care and angiography as needed. Not awake or unsure: add temperature control, EEG and delayed multimodal prognostication.
traps: “Prognosticate at 24 hours on a single test”
Wait at least 72 hours after normothermia and sedation are off, and use several tests.
decode: Post-ROSC targets for SpO2, PaCO2 and MAP? [pattern]
What decides entry to temperature control and EEG? [pattern]
Not following commands off sedation.
ACLS-56.punch: After ROSC, stabilise oxygen, CO2 and pressure, find the cause, then ask one question off sedation: does the patient follow commands? A ‘no’ brings temperature control, EEG and prognostication at 72 hours.

ACLS-57.intro: Step 6 leaves arrest for the patient who may arrest next. In ACS the ECG sorts patients in minutes into those who need reperfusion now and those who need a troponin pathway. The one real question, a T-wave inversion with pain, was answered right by only 44%.
why: **Prehospital: support ABCs and monitor ECG • obtain and evaluate a 12-lead ECG • consider IV access, oxygen, aspirin, nitrate, morphine • transfer to an emergency PCI-capable facility.** A prehospital ECG lets the cath lab be activated before arrival. Oxygen only if SpO2 is under 90%; giving it to normoxic patients does not help (AVOID, DETO2X).

**ED concurrent assessment in <10 minutes: vitals, 12-lead ECG, targeted history, hs-cTn, electrolytes, coagulation, CXR and TTE, call cardiology.** The ECG within 10 minutes is the step that decides everything that follows.

**Chew aspirin 162–325 mg; nitroglycerin spray; IV morphine if discomfort is not relieved by nitroglycerin.** Chewing gives faster absorption. Nitrates are avoided in hypotension, RV infarction and after a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor. Morphine delays absorption of oral P2Y12 inhibitors, so it is kept for pain that nitrates do not settle.

**ST elevation or new LBBB → suspicious for STEMI → consult cardiology: do not delay reperfusion.** ACC/AHA no longer treat a new LBBB alone as diagnostic (Sgarbossa criteria help); ESC 2023 manages any bundle branch block with ongoing ischaemic symptoms as a STEMI equivalent.

**Non-ST elevation → suspicious for UA/NSTEMI → hs-cTn on arrival (0 h); positive + clinical presentation: CCU or monitored bed; negative: chest pain unit, recheck hs-cTn at 1 h or 3 h, with ECG monitoring.** The rule-out depends on the assay; ESC 2023 uses 0/1 h or 0/2 h algorithms. Immediate angiography in NSTE-ACS is only for very high risk (shock, refractory pain, arrhythmia, mechanical complication).
mimic: STEMI vs NSTE-ACS first hour
STEMI: reperfusion without delay. NSTE-ACS: monitor, aspirin, troponin, risk-stratify.
traps: “T inversion with pain — call the cath lab for immediate PCI”
That is for STEMI or very-high-risk NSTE-ACS; first monitor, oxygen if hypoxic, aspirin.
“Two sublingual nitrates and observe” or “CXR then aspirin, clopidogrel and heparin”
The immediate step is monitor, oxygen if needed and aspirin; dual antiplatelets and anticoagulation follow assessment.
decode: New chest pain, lateral T inversion — most immediate step? [DocT GT]
Monitor, oxygen if needed, aspirin (44%).
ACLS-57.punch: In suspected ACS the 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes splits the road: ST elevation goes straight to reperfusion, the rest get aspirin, monitoring and a repeat high-sensitivity troponin.

ACLS-58.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → Stroke algorithm time goals
ACLS-58.intro: Step 6 ends with the stroke clock. Brain tissue in an ischaemic penumbra dies by the minute, so the algorithm sets fixed targets from the door. No real question is linked; the usual ask is the door-to-needle time and what is checked first.
why: **10 minutes: immediate general assessment and stabilisation — ABCs, oxygen if hypoxic, IV access and labs, check glucose, neurological screen, activate the stroke team, order emergent CT or MRI, 12-lead ECG.** Hypoglycaemia mimics stroke and is excluded by a bedside glucose first.

**25 minutes: neurological assessment by the stroke team — history, time of onset or last known normal, NIH Stroke Scale.** The time last known normal sets the lysis window (within 4.5 hours, later only with imaging selection). The 2026 AHA/ASA guideline also aims for imaging within 25 minutes of arrival.
**45 minutes: CT interpretation — does it show haemorrhage?** A bleed excludes lysis and goes to neurology or neurosurgery.

**60 minutes: give rtPA if still a candidate; no anticoagulants or antiplatelets for 24 hours.** The 2026 AHA/ASA guideline endorses either tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (maximum 25 mg, single bolus) or alteplase 0.9 mg/kg within 4.5 hours. Blood pressure must be under 185/110 to lyse and is kept under 180/105 for 24 hours after.
**3 hours: begin the post-rtPA stroke pathway — aggressive monitoring, BP per protocol, admit to stroke unit or ICU.**
**Not a fibrinolytic candidate → administer aspirin.** Once haemorrhage is excluded.
mimic: Time of onset vs time last known normal
For a stroke found on waking, the clock starts when the patient was last seen well, not when found.
traps: “Start aspirin with lysis”
No antiplatelets or anticoagulants for 24 hours after a lytic.
decode: Door-to-needle goal for lysis? [pattern]
60 minutes.
Door-to-CT interpretation goal? [pattern]
45 minutes.
ACLS-58.punch: Stroke runs on a door clock (10, 25, 45, 60 minutes), and the time last known normal decides whether the 60-minute needle is still possible.

topups.topic: Echo at the CPR pulse check
topups.q: Focused echo at a CPR pulse check — what does each finding mean, and true vs pseudo-PEA?
a: - Effusion with RV diastolic collapse = tamponade → pericardiocentesis during CPR.
- Dilated RV with a D-shaped LV = massive PE → lysis; small hyperdynamic 'kissing' ventricles = hypovolaemia → volume or blood.
- No cardiac motion = true PEA (CPR + adrenaline; poor prognosis); coordinated motion without a pulse = pseudo-PEA — profound shock where fluids/vasopressor may restore a pulse, better survival.

- AHA 2025: POCUS may be used by experienced operators to find a reversible cause only if it does not lengthen pauses (subxiphoid or TEE views, <10 s); not routine, not a replacement for pulse checks and not a sole reason to stop. CTPA, MRI or CXR mean leaving the resuscitation.
topups.src: DocT Cardiac Arrest & Resuscitation in Pregnancy Q14; DocT GT GrandT1 Q24; DocT GT GT5 Q147; DocT GT CGT4 Q126

x.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → Echo at the CPR pulse check
x.intro: Step 1 is about feedback during CPR, and a few seconds of echo at the pulse check is the most direct feedback there is: it shows whether the heart is moving and whether a reversible cause is visible. Four Grand Test questions ask what each picture means and how true PEA differs from pseudo-PEA.
why: **Effusion with RV diastolic collapse = tamponade → pericardiocentesis during CPR.** The RV is the thinnest, lowest-pressure chamber, so it collapses first when pericardial pressure rises; it cannot fill, so nothing reaches the LV. Draining even a small volume restores filling, which is why it is done without stopping CPR.

**Dilated RV with a D-shaped LV = massive PE → lysis; small hyperdynamic ‘kissing’ ventricles = hypovolaemia → volume or blood.** In PE the pressure-loaded RV dilates and pushes the septum into the LV, flattening it into a D. In hypovolaemia the chambers are underfilled and the walls touch in systole. Note that the RV also dilates in any arrest of a few minutes, as blood pools on the venous side, so RV dilatation alone is not proof of PE.

**No cardiac motion = true PEA (CPR + adrenaline; poor prognosis); coordinated motion without a pulse = pseudo-PEA, profound shock where fluids or vasopressor may restore a pulse, better survival.** In pseudo-PEA the heart is ejecting, but too little to feel; it behaves like severe shock, so treating its cause (volume, vasopressor, tamponade, PE) can restore a pulse. True cardiac standstill carries a very low chance of ROSC.

**AHA 2025: POCUS may be used by experienced operators to find a reversible cause only if it does not lengthen pauses (subxiphoid or TEE views, under 10 s); not routine, not a replacement for pulse checks and not a sole reason to stop. CTPA, MRI or CXR mean leaving the resuscitation.** Studies found that echo lengthened pauses, often beyond 10 seconds, and that what is seen as ‘standstill’ varies between observers; hence the weak 2b. TEE avoids interrupting compressions altogether.
mimic: True PEA vs pseudo-PEA
No motion: standard ALS, poor prognosis. Motion without pulse: treat as profound shock.
PE vs prolonged arrest on echo
Both dilate the RV; a clot in transit, a D-shaped LV before arrest or a DVT supports PE.
traps: “Send the patient for CTPA during CPR to confirm PE”
Imaging outside the room means leaving the resuscitation; decide on the bedside echo and the clinical picture.
“No cardiac motion on echo — stop resuscitation”
Echo is not a sole reason to stop.
decode: PEA, effusion with RV diastolic collapse on subxiphoid view [pattern]
Tamponade: pericardiocentesis during CPR.
PEA, coordinated cardiac motion, no palpable pulse [pattern]
Pseudo-PEA: treat as profound shock; better prognosis.
x.punch: Echo at the pulse check asks two questions in under 10 seconds: is the heart moving, and is there a fixable cause (fluid, a dilated RV, empty ventricles)? It informs, but never alone ends, the resuscitation.

topups.q: Drowning — the insult, the first resuscitation step, and why observe the 'well' patient?
a: - The insult is hypoxia: 5 rescue breaths, then CPR (ERC); no Heimlich; fresh vs salt water does not change management.
- Post-hypoxic cerebral oedema builds over hours and peaks at 24–72 h, so an alert patient can deteriorate later.
- Observe at least 6–8 h; ARDS can also appear late.

- Pulseless after long submersion: start CPR if submerged <60 min (cold water protects the brain); hypothermic → continue CPR with active rewarming (ECLS if available) — 'not dead until warm and dead'.
topups.src: DocT Pediatric Critical Care Q5; DocT GT GT4 Q27

x.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → Drowning
x.intro: Step 4 includes the arrest caused by water. In drowning the heart stops because of hypoxia, not a primary arrhythmia, so the order of resuscitation changes: oxygen comes first. Two questions test this and why a patient who looks well must be watched.
why: **The insult is hypoxia: 5 rescue breaths, then CPR (ERC); no Heimlich; fresh vs salt water does not change management.** The heart arrests after the oxygen runs out, so breaths treat the cause; AHA 2025 also requires CPR with breaths, not compression-only, from trained rescuers (class 1). Abdominal thrusts delay ventilation and cause vomiting; little water is aspirated. The old idea that fresh water causes haemolysis and salt water pulmonary oedema did not hold in humans at the volumes aspirated.
**Post-hypoxic cerebral oedema builds over hours and peaks at 24–72 h, so an alert patient can deteriorate later.**
**Observe at least 6–8 h; ARDS can also appear late.** Aspirated water washes out surfactant and inflames the alveoli, so hypoxaemia can emerge hours after rescue.

**Pulseless after long submersion: start CPR if submerged under 60 min (cold water protects the brain); hypothermic → continue CPR with active rewarming (ECLS if available).** Rapid cooling lowers cerebral oxygen demand before the brain becomes hypoxic, which is why children recovered from icy water have survived intact after long submersion. The 60-minute figure is the card’s; the published decision guide (Tipton and Golden 2011, used by UK rescue services) depends on water temperature: in water above 6 °C resuscitate if submerged under 30 minutes, in water at 6 °C or below under 90 minutes; beyond that survival is unlikely. In outcome studies short submersion (minutes) does well and submersion beyond about 25 minutes does poorly. The rewarming rules of hypothermia then apply (ACLS-55).
mimic: Drowning arrest vs cardiac arrest on land
Drowning is hypoxic: breaths first. Sudden cardiac arrest on land is usually arrhythmic: compressions and shock first.
traps: “Abdominal thrusts to clear water from the lungs”
They delay ventilation and risk aspiration; start rescue breaths.
“Alert after rescue — discharge”
Observe for 6–8 hours; lung injury and cerebral oedema can appear late.
decode: Child pulled from a pool, not breathing — first step? [pattern]
Five rescue breaths, then CPR.
Alert after near-drowning — disposition? [pattern]
Observe at least 6–8 h for delayed lung injury.
x.punch: Drowning stops the heart through hypoxia, so give breaths first, ignore the type of water, watch the ‘well’ patient for hours, and do not stop a cold patient’s CPR until he is warm.

topups.q: How do you confirm a perioperative reaction was anaphylaxis?
a: - Serum mast-cell tryptase 15 min–3 h after onset (peak 1–2 h), plus a baseline >24 h later.
- A rise above 1.2 × baseline + 2 ng/mL confirms mast-cell activation; a normal value does not exclude anaphylaxis (asthma does not raise it).
- Refer for skin testing at 4–6 weeks (NMBAs, cefazolin, chlorhexidine, latex).

x.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → Confirming anaphylaxis with tryptase
x.intro: Step 4 includes anaphylaxis, and after the event comes the question of proof. Tryptase is stored in mast cell granules and released when they degranulate, so a rise above the patient’s own baseline confirms that mast cells fired. One Grand Test question asks how and when to measure it.
why: **Serum mast-cell tryptase 15 min–3 h after onset (peak 1–2 h), plus a baseline more than 24 h later.** Tryptase peaks at about 1–2 hours and has a half-life of about 2 hours, so a late sample misses the rise. The baseline later is the patient’s own reference, because some people (mastocytosis) run high values.

**A rise above 1.2 × baseline + 2 ng/mL confirms mast-cell activation; a normal value does not exclude anaphylaxis (asthma does not raise it).** Basophil-driven or some food reactions release little tryptase. Acute asthma does not degranulate mast cells systemically, which is why tryptase separates anaphylactic bronchospasm from an asthma attack.

**Refer for skin testing at 4–6 weeks (NMBAs, cefazolin, chlorhexidine, latex).** Mast cells need weeks to restock after degranulation, so earlier testing gives false negatives. In the UK audit (NAP6) antibiotics were the commonest perioperative cause, followed by neuromuscular blockers, chlorhexidine and patent blue dye.
mimic: Tryptase vs histamine
Histamine peaks and clears within minutes, so it is impractical; tryptase stays up for hours.
traps: “A normal tryptase rules out anaphylaxis”
It confirms when raised but does not exclude when normal.
“Skin test the next day”
Wait 4–6 weeks for mast cells to recover.
decode: Hypotension and bronchospasm after induction — investigation to confirm anaphylaxis? [pattern]
Serum tryptase at 1–2 h, with a baseline after 24 h.
x.punch: Tryptase proves that mast cells fired: take it at 1–2 hours, compare it with the patient’s own baseline (1.2 × baseline + 2), and refer for skin tests after 4–6 weeks.

topups.q: Anaphylaxis — first drug, dose, route and site?
a: - IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL; child 0.01 mg/kg) into the anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis): faster, higher peak than deltoid or SC; repeat every 5 min.
- Refractory after 2 IM doses → IV adrenaline infusion; on β-blockers add glucagon.
- Antihistamine and steroid are adjuncts that never replace adrenaline; confirm with tryptase at 1–2 h.

x.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → Anaphylaxis: first-line adrenaline
x.intro: Step 4 ends with the first drug for anaphylaxis. Adrenaline treats every limb of the reaction: α vasoconstriction reverses vasodilatation and leak, β1 supports the heart, and β2 opens the bronchi and stabilises mast cells. The question asks the dose, route and site; it also shares a number with the arrest dose (ACLS-45).
why: **IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL; child 0.01 mg/kg) into the anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis): faster, higher peak than deltoid or SC; repeat every 5 min.** Thigh muscle is well perfused, so absorption is quick; subcutaneous fat is poorly perfused and adrenaline constricts its own vessels there. The IM route is safe without monitoring; IV boluses are for anaesthetists and intensivists with monitoring, in 50 µg steps, because a 1 mg IV bolus in a patient with a pulse can cause VT or a hypertensive crisis.

**Refractory after 2 IM doses → IV adrenaline infusion; on β-blockers add glucagon.** Two failed IM doses mark refractory anaphylaxis, which needs a titrated infusion and fluids for the leak. β-blockade blunts adrenaline’s cardiac and bronchial effects; glucagon raises cyclic AMP through its own receptor, bypassing the β receptor. If the patient arrests, standard ALS with 1 mg IV every 3–5 min replaces the IM dose (AHA 2025).

**Antihistamine and steroid are adjuncts that never replace adrenaline; confirm with tryptase at 1–2 h.** Antihistamines treat skin features only; steroids work over hours and have not been shown to prevent a biphasic reaction.
mimic: 0.5 mg IM of 1:1000 vs 1 mg IV of 1:10,000
Anaphylaxis with a pulse vs cardiac arrest.
traps: “Subcutaneous or deltoid adrenaline”
The anterolateral thigh gives the fastest, highest peak.
“Hydrocortisone and chlorphenamine first, adrenaline if they fail”
Adrenaline is first; the others are adjuncts.
decode: Anaphylaxis — first drug, dose and site? [pattern]
IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh.
x.punch: Anaphylaxis gets 0.5 mg of 1:1000 adrenaline into the thigh muscle, repeated at 5 minutes; after two doses start an infusion, and only in arrest switch to the 1 mg IV arrest dose.

spine: Airway, breaths and quality feedback
Open the airway with the least neck movement, ventilate just enough to see the chest rise, and use ETCO2 and diastolic pressure to tell you whether your compressions are making flow.
Drugs that help, and drugs that do not

Epinephrine is the only vasopressor, timed by rhythm, amiodarone or lidocaine follow failed shocks, and almost everything else (vasopressin, magnesium, calcium, atropine) has no routine place in arrest.
The team runs the code
Six defined roles around a leader keep compressions going, rotate the tiring compressor every 2 minutes and record every drug and pause.
Arrest in special circumstances
Pregnancy, an LVAD, asthma and extremes of temperature change the algorithm because the cause, the circulation or the heart’s response to drugs is different.
After ROSC: stabilise, then branch
Oxygenate to 90–98%, keep MAP 65 or more, find the cause, then ask whether the patient follows commands off sedation; that answer decides temperature control, EEG and prognostication.
Peri-arrest pathways: ACS and stroke
Chest pain and stroke run on clocks: an ECG in 10 minutes decides reperfusion, and a scan read by 45 minutes decides lysis by 60.
CVS08C.primer: During CPR the heart is perfused only in the release phase of each compression, by the gap between aortic diastolic and right-atrial pressure (coronary perfusion pressure); anything that raises intrathoracic pressure or interrupts compressions shrinks that gap. End-tidal CO2 during arrest is set by pulmonary blood flow, so it reads out cardiac output, not ventilation. Drugs only matter if they raise that perfusion pressure (epinephrine) or stop a recurring arrhythmia; most others were tested and dropped. CVS08A and CVS08B covered the BLS sequence and the core algorithms; this deck adds the drugs, the team, the special situations and what follows ROSC.

ACLS-59.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → AHA 2025 adult BLS changes
ACLS-59.intro: Step 1 is the bystander’s part of the story. Most adult BLS numbers (rate, depth, 30:2) did not move in 2025; what changed is how the chain is drawn, the order of choking manoeuvres, how a breath is judged and which devices are discouraged. No real question has been linked yet, so this is the short version.
why: **One unified six-link chain for all ages and settings.** 2020 drew separate chains for in- and out-of-hospital arrest and for adults and children. 2025 merges them into one: recognition and emergency activation, high-quality CPR, defibrillation, advanced resuscitation, post-cardiac arrest care, and recovery and survivorship. The 2025 systems-of-care text names prevention and preparedness as the missing link but chose not to add it yet. The steps are the same whoever collapses and wherever, so one chain is easier to teach and to remember under stress.

**Choking: back blows first — 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts (chest thrusts in infants and late pregnancy).** 2020 AHA taught abdominal thrusts alone for a choking adult; 2025 (class 1) alternates 5 back blows with 5 abdominal thrusts, as ERC already did. Back blows are simple and safe and often clear the object; abdominal thrusts generate more pressure but can injure viscera. Chest thrusts replace abdominal thrusts in late pregnancy and when the rescuer cannot encircle the abdomen. Once the patient is unresponsive, start CPR; blind finger sweeps are harmful.

**Tidal volume = enough for visible chest rise; avoid hypo- and hyperventilation.** A bystander cannot measure volume, so chest rise is the target (about 500–600 mL in an adult). Both too little and too much are now graded 3: Harm, because excess volume raises intrathoracic pressure, cuts venous return and inflates the stomach.

**Routine mechanical CPR not recommended.** ‘Not for routine use’ was already the 2020 position; 2025 grades it 3: No Benefit (B-R), because the large trials of piston and band devices showed no survival gain over good manual CPR. New is a 2b allowance where manual compressions are hard or dangerous (a moving ambulance, the cath lab, a bridge to ECPR), with pauses kept short during deployment.

**Firm surface; torso at the level of the rescuer’s knees; same technique in obesity.** With the chest at knee height the rescuer’s shoulders sit over the sternum and body weight does the work (class 1); a firm surface helps when it does not delay compressions (2a). In obesity the technique is unchanged (class 1); more force may be needed to reach depth (2b).

**Head tilt–chin lift permitted in trauma if jaw thrust plus adjunct fails.** Jaw thrust without head extension stays first (class 1). If it and an adjunct cannot open the airway, a trained rescuer should use head tilt–chin lift (also class 1), because hypoxic death is more certain than a worsened cord injury (see ACLS-41).

**Pads: anterolateral OR anteroposterior, >8 cm; a bra may be ADJUSTED rather than removed. ‘Rescue breaths’ retired → ‘breaths’.** Either pad position is reasonable (2a); the 8 cm is the pad diameter, not a distance from an implanted device. Moving a bra rather than removing it (2b) is new: women receive bystander defibrillation less often, and undressing a stranger in public is a known barrier. On wording, the 2025 BLS text and Highlights simply speak of ‘breaths’ and ‘ventilation’ (FLAG: an explicit retirement of ‘rescue breaths’ could not be confirmed).
mimic: Adult choking vs infant choking
Adult and child: back blows then abdominal thrusts. Infant: back blows then chest thrusts; never abdominal thrusts.
Mechanical CPR routinely vs in selected settings
Routine use is 3: No Benefit; in transport, the cath lab or as a bridge to ECPR it may be considered (2b).
traps: “2025: a choking adult gets abdominal thrusts first”
That is the 2020 AHA teaching. 2025 starts with 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, repeated.
“Pads must be placed more than 8 cm from a pacemaker”
The >8 cm in the card is pad size; the 2025 BLS text makes no distance rule.
decode: [pattern] Conscious adult with severe airway obstruction — first manoeuvre per AHA 2025?
5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, alternating.
[pattern] Which 2025 BLS statement is correct — routine mechanical CPR, visible chest rise, separate paediatric chain?
Visible chest rise defines the breath; mechanical CPR is not routine; the chain is now single.
ACLS-59.punch: Adult BLS kept its numbers; 2025 changed the order of choking manoeuvres, defined a breath by what you can see, and moved further against devices that add nothing to good hands on a firm surface at knee height.

ACLS-60.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → AHA 2025 adult ALS changes
ACLS-60.intro: Step 2 moves to the professional team. 2025 ALS is mostly about routes, timing and energy, and about saying no to new techniques whose evidence is thin. The two DocT Grand Test questions asked which termination-of-resuscitation rule a tiered EMS system uses and the first cardioversion energy for unstable AF.
why: **IV FIRST, IO if IV fails or is not feasible.** 2020 said attempting IV first was ‘reasonable’ (2a), with IO ‘may be considered’ (2b); 2025 makes IV first a class 1 recommendation (LOE A), with IO as the 2a fallback and central access (2b) only for trained operators. The change came from the 2024 randomised trials (PARAMEDIC-3, IVIO) and their meta-analysis: IO gave no survival benefit and slightly lower odds of sustained ROSC. One proposed reason is slower or less reliable drug delivery from a tibial IO in a low-flow state.

**Epinephrine AFTER failed initial defibrillation in shockable rhythms; vasopressin offers no advantage.** In VF the shock is the treatment, and early epinephrine adds myocardial oxygen demand and arrhythmia without making the shock work; in a non-shockable rhythm it is the only treatment, so it goes in as soon as feasible (both 2a). Two things moved from 2020. For shockable rhythms 2020 said epinephrine after failed shocks ‘may be reasonable’ (2b); 2025 says ‘is reasonable’ (2a). Vasopressin went from ‘may be considered but offers no advantage’ (2b) to 3: No Benefit, alone or with epinephrine.

**β-blockers, bretylium, procainamide, sotalol: UNCERTAIN BENEFIT in defibrillation-unresponsive VF/pVT.** This is a new 2b statement: there are small studies (esmolol in electrical storm, bretylium historically) but no trial showing survival. Amiodarone or lidocaine (2b) remain the only antiarrhythmics with a recommendation, based on ALPS.

**First-shock energy ≥200 J preferable for cardioversion of AF AND flutter.** AHA 2025: at least 200 J biphasic for AF (2a), 200 J for flutter (2b), escalating if the shock fails. Trials of high versus low starting energy found more first-shock success without more harm; a failed low-energy shock only means another shock under more sedation. This replaces the older ladder of 120–200 J for AF and 50–100 J for flutter (ACLS-64). The DocT key ‘>200 J biphasic’ matches; ‘360 J monophasic’ is the defibrillation dose, not a cardioversion step.

**Vector change and DSED: usefulness NOT established; head-up CPR NOT recommended outside trials.** After three or more failed shocks, changing pad position (vector change, new topic) and double sequential defibrillation (AHA calls it DSD) are both 2b ‘usefulness not established’. DOSE-VF (2022) favoured both, but it was one small trial stopped early, so the class did not rise. Head-up CPR, tested only within device bundles, is 3: No Benefit outside research.

**Universal TOR rule in tiered EMS systems; ETCO2 not to be used in isolation.** The universal rule (2a) applies the old BLS rule’s three criteria to every crew: arrest not witnessed by EMS, no shock delivered, and no ROSC before transport. 2020 used separate BLS and ALS rules; a tiered system now uses the one universal rule. ETCO2 <10 mmHg after 20 minutes in an intubated patient may be one factor, never the sole reason, and never in a non-intubated patient (see ACLS-43).

**Synchronised cardioversion for STABLE wide-complex tachycardia when vagal and drug therapy fail or are contraindicated; temporary TRANSVENOUS PACING for bradycardia refractory to medical therapy.** Cardioversion remains class 1 for unstable wide-complex tachycardia and is now also recommended for the stable patient once drugs fail. Transvenous pacing is reasonable (2a) for persistent unstable bradycardia despite drugs, accepting its infection and pneumothorax risk. For this algorithm bradycardia means a rate typically below 50/min, as the 2020 algorithm already said; 60/min is the ECG definition.
mimic: Universal TOR vs ALS TOR rule
The universal rule uses three criteria for every crew; the ALS rule adds two more and so stops fewer resuscitations.
Cardioversion energy vs defibrillation energy
Cardioversion of AF starts at ≥200 J synchronised; defibrillation is the device dose (120–200 J biphasic) or 360 J monophasic.
traps: “In a tiered system use the ALS TOR rule, since paramedics are present”
AHA 2025 recommends the single universal rule for tiered systems.
“An ETCO2 threshold alone can end resuscitation”
No: ETCO2 is one factor in an intubated patient and is never used in isolation.
“Unstable AF: start at 50 or 100 J”
Those are the old flutter and narrow-regular figures; 2025 says at least 200 J for AF.
“IO is equivalent and can be first line in arrest”
2025 makes IV first a class 1 recommendation; IO only if IV fails or is not feasible.
decode: Tiered EMS with BLS and ALS crews — which rule to consider TOR in OHCA? [DocT GT]
Universal TOR rule.
Haemodynamically unstable AF — preferred initial energy for synchronised cardioversion per 2025? [DocT GT]
≥200 J biphasic.
[pattern] Refractory VF — which 2025 statement on DSED or vector change is correct?
Usefulness not established (2b).
ACLS-60.punch: ALS 2025 favours the simple and proven: IV before IO, epinephrine timed by rhythm, a full-energy first cardioversion, one TOR rule, and no endorsement for double shocks, vector change or head-up CPR until better trials arrive.

table.title: Termination-of-resuscitation rules in OHCA
head: Rule
Criteria to consider stopping
rows: Not witnessed by EMS + no shock delivered + no ROSC
The three, plus not witnessed by a bystander and no bystander CPR

ACLS-61.sub: Cardiology → Post-cardiac arrest care → AHA 2025 changes
ACLS-61.intro: Step 3 follows the patient into the ICU. The post-arrest numbers changed more than any others in 2025, mostly because large trials (TTM2, BOX and the MAP-target trials) showed that more aggressive targets did not help. Both DocT Grand Test questions test temperature control: its duration and its range.
why: **MAP ≥65 mmHg; four RCTs showed no benefit from higher targets. Temporary MCS may be considered in refractory post-arrest cardiogenic shock.** MAP ≥65 is class 1. Four trials (over 1,000 OHCA patients) compared MAP targets around 65–70 with higher ones and found no difference in survival or neurological outcome, so the separate systolic target of 2020 (SBP ≥90) was dropped. Temporary MCS is 2b for highly selected refractory shock; routine use is 3: No Benefit because it added bleeding and ischaemic harm without survival gain.

**Temperature control for AT LEAST 36 HOURS, goal 32–37.5 °C (was ≥24 h at 32–36 °C).** TTM2 (2021) found no difference between 33 °C and normothermia with active fever prevention, so the range now runs up to 37.5 °C and both strategies count as temperature control (32–37.5 °C, class 1). Strictly, that wider range first appeared in the AHA 2023 focused update; the 2025 change is that the range is now joined to a 36-hour minimum. The minimum duration is 36 hours (2a), because the fever that follows early rewarming is linked to worse outcomes. Rewarm no faster than 0.5 °C/h (2b). ERC–ESICM 2025 frames the same idea as active fever prevention (≤37.5 °C) for 36–72 hours; the ‘>37.7 °C for 72 hours’ wording is their 2021 version.

**SpO2 90–98% (PaO2 60–105 mmHg); PCO2 35–45 unchanged. Avoid glucose <70 and >180 mg/dL.** Give 100% oxygen until saturation can be measured reliably (1), then titrate to 90–98% (2a); 2020 used 92–98%. BOX (2022) compared a PaO2 target of 68–75 with 98–105 mmHg and found no difference, so the lower floor is safe, and hyperoxia is avoided. PaCO2 35–45 (1) keeps cerebral blood flow normal; TAME showed no benefit from mild hypercapnia. Glucose: avoid the extremes (2b), with no tighter target. ERC–ESICM 2025 keeps 94–98%.

**HEAD-TO-PELVIS CT and echocardiography / POCUS may be reasonable after ROSC.** Both are new 2b statements. CT finds the cause (subarachnoid haemorrhage, pulmonary embolism, dissection) and the injuries of CPR (rib and sternal fractures, liver tears, pneumothorax), with a yield near 30%. Echo finds tamponade, RV strain, regional wall motion loss and LV failure that change treatment. A 12-lead ECG as soon as feasible stays class 1.

**Do NOT treat myoclonus WITHOUT an EEG correlate.** New: 3: No Benefit, because there is no evidence that non-epileptic myoclonus adds brain injury, and suppressing it needs sedatives that cloud the neurological examination. Myoclonus should prompt an EEG (1); clinical seizures are treated (1), non-convulsive seizures reasonably (2a), and prophylaxis is not given (3).

**Prognostication now includes predictors of FAVOURABLE outcome; NEUROFILAMENT LIGHT CHAIN added as a biomarker.** See ACLS-70 for the detail: a continuous EEG background without discharges, normal NSE or a withdrawal motor response now support a good outcome, and NfL joins NSE as a marker of poor outcome.

**Structured assessment and referral for emotional distress in SURVIVORS AND CAREGIVERS before discharge.** Anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress are common in both, so 2025 asks for a structured screen and referral after stabilisation and before discharge; the chain’s last link, recovery, starts in hospital.
mimic: Temperature control vs therapeutic hypothermia
Temperature control is the umbrella (32–37.5 °C); hypothermia (32–34 °C) is one way of doing it.
AHA vs ERC–ESICM post-ROSC oxygen
traps: “Temperature control for at least 24 hours” (2020)
2025 says at least 36 hours.
“Strict hypothermia at 32–34 °C for 72 hours”
Neither the range nor the duration: any target within 32–37.5 °C for at least 36 hours.
“Avoid temperature control unless seizures develop”
Protocolised temperature control is class 1 for every patient who does not follow commands after ROSC.
“Temperature control goal 32–35 °C is a component of post-arrest care”
That range belongs to no guideline; 2025 is 32–37.5 °C, so this is the option that is not a component, while MAP ≥65, PCO2 35–45 and EEG in the non-commanding patient all are.
decode: Comatose after OHCA — most appropriate temperature strategy per 2025? [DocT GT]
Temperature control for at least 36 hours.
Which is not a component of post-arrest care — MAP ≥65, PCO2 35–45, temperature 32–35 °C, EEG if not following commands? [DocT GT]
Temperature 32–35 °C.
[pattern] 2025 post-ROSC oxygen target?
ACLS-61.punch: Post-arrest care in 2025 is less aggressive in its targets but longer and broader in its reach: oxygen down to 90%, MAP 65, any temperature from 32 to 37.5 °C held for 36 hours, and imaging and prognosis that look for every cause and every chance.

ACLS-62.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → AHA 2025 special circumstances changes
ACLS-62.intro: Step 4 covers arrests where the standard algorithm needs adjusting. In each case the reason is physiological: the uterus compresses the cava, the LVAD replaces the pulse, the opioid stops breathing, the cold heart ignores shocks. The one linked DocT QBank question, answered correctly by 53%, is hypothermic VF at 29 °C.
why: **Pregnancy: ‘RESUSCITATIVE DELIVERY’ replaces ‘perimortem caesarean delivery’; prepare from recognition, complete by 5 min; ECPR reasonable; balanced massive transfusion for amniotic fluid embolism.** The new term says why it is done: emptying the uterus relieves aortocaval compression and improves the mother’s circulation, even when the fetus cannot survive. Preparation starts as soon as arrest is recognised, so that delivery, classically begun at 4 minutes, is complete by 5 minutes. ECPR in pregnant or peripartum arrest is new and judged reasonable, and suspected amniotic fluid embolism gets a balanced massive transfusion protocol (1) for its consumptive coagulopathy (detail in ACLS-52 and ACLS-53).

**LVAD: new algorithm — compressions if perfusion impaired, assess device simultaneously.** Most LVAD patients have no palpable pulse, so pulselessness cannot define arrest. Perfusion is judged by MAP (>50), ETCO2 (>20), skin colour and capillary refill; if it is impaired, start compressions (1) while another rescuer checks the device for a reversible fault.

**Opioid: new algorithm; PUBLIC ACCESS NALOXONE recommended alongside public access defibrillation; take-home naloxone at discharge.** Opioid arrest is respiratory first, and naloxone in lay hands can stop it before the heart stops. The 2025 systems-of-care chapter says public policies should allow lay rescuers to possess and use naloxone with immunity from civil and criminal liability for good-faith use (1), and that naloxone distribution programmes can be beneficial (2a); it describes public-access naloxone as naloxone stationed in public places, like AED cabinets. The special-circumstances chapter adds that every patient treated for overdose should leave with naloxone and teaching (1). In arrest, naloxone may be reasonable (2b) but must not delay CPR or calling for help (1), because a stopped heart cannot carry the drug to its receptors. 2020 already had opioid-emergency algorithms; 2025 redraws them.

**Asthma: ECLS and volatile anaesthetics may be considered.** Both are new: ECLS for life-threatening asthma refractory to standard treatment (2a, survival 83–100% in observational series) and volatile agents for bronchodilatation (2b). In arrest, remember dynamic hyperinflation: disconnect and decompress the chest.

**Hypothermia: ECLS rewarming; HOPE and ICE scores to guide it.** ECLS both restores flow and rewarms at 1.5–5 °C/h. The HOPE survival probability (below 10% predicts death) and the ICE score are better validated than a single potassium value for choosing who goes on ECLS. For the cold heart AHA 2025 now says: defibrillate once, then defer further shocks and epinephrine until the core is at least 30 °C (both 2b). ERC 2025 allows up to 3 shocks below 30 °C, then withholds shocks, adrenaline and antiarrhythmics until above 30 °C, and doubles the drug interval at 30–35 °C. The cold myocardium does not respond, and drugs accumulate and then act all at once on rewarming.

**Hyperthermia: ICE WATER IMMERSION (1–5 °C), cooling ≥0.15 °C/min.** Ice-water immersion (2a) cools fastest; tepid water (8–17 °C) is the fallback. Cool at least 0.15 °C per minute and stop at 38.6 °C to avoid overshoot; dantrolene has no place outside malignant hyperthermia.

**Hyperkalaemia: IV calcium effectiveness NOT WELL ESTABLISHED.** 2025 (2b) says there is no good evidence that calcium improves survival in hyperkalaemic arrest, in adults or children; it is still often given for a known high potassium, but it is no longer a firm recommendation (ACLS-63 notes this against the H’s and T’s).
mimic: Hypothermic arrest AHA 2025 vs ERC 2025
AHA: one shock, then defer shocks and epinephrine to ≥30 °C. ERC: up to three shocks, then withhold to >30 °C.
Resuscitative delivery vs perimortem caesarean
Same operation; the new name says it is for the mother’s circulation, done by 5 minutes.
traps: “29 °C VF: give antiarrhythmics now” or “rewarm to 36 °C before anything”
Below 30 °C drugs are withheld while CPR and rewarming continue; you do not wait for 36 °C to defibrillate or give drugs.
“AHA is more permissive: standard shocks and vasopressors below 30 °C” (DocT note)

That was the 2020 AHA position. AHA 2025 also defers further shocks and epinephrine until ≥30 °C after one shock, so keyed C (continue CPR, withhold drugs until >30 °C) is right, and ‘defibrillate once and rewarm’ is also defensible under AHA 2025.
“IV calcium is a class 1 treatment for hyperkalaemic arrest”
2025 downgrades it: effectiveness not well established (2b).
decode: 29 °C, VF after cold-water immersion — next step? [DocT QBank, 53%]
Continue CPR and withhold antiarrhythmics until the core is above 30 °C.
[pattern] Arrest in late pregnancy — new term and time goal?
Resuscitative delivery, completed by 5 minutes, prepared from recognition.
ACLS-62.punch: Each special circumstance changes the algorithm for a physiological reason, and in 2025 that reasoning is written into the names and new algorithms: deliver for the mother, judge the LVAD by perfusion, give naloxone early, and in the cold, stop shocking and dosing until the heart can respond.

ACLS-63.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → What AHA 2025 did not change
ACLS-63.intro: Step 6 begins with what stayed the same, because a transition-year question can be built on an unchanged number. Most arrest drug doses and the CPR numbers carried over; the twist is that some of them now rest on a different reason. No real question is linked yet.
why: **30:2 — but the rationale changed: it lets the rescuer SEE CHEST RISE and confirm adequate ventilation, not to protect compression fraction.** 2025 (2a) keeps 30:2 before an advanced airway because the pause for two breaths is the only moment the rescuer can watch the chest rise and know the breath went in; during continuous compressions with asynchronous breaths that cannot be seen. Most studies found no outcome difference from continuous compressions, so the ratio is justified by ventilation quality, not survival.

**Rate 100–120/min (depth now has a 6 cm ceiling).** Rate is unchanged (2a). The depth of at least 5 cm with deeper than 6 cm to be avoided was already the 2020 wording, so the ceiling is not new (FLAG; ACLS-64 itself calls depth unchanged).
**Epinephrine 1 mg every 3–5 min.** Same dose and interval; only its timing by rhythm is restated (ACLS-60). High-dose epinephrine still has no benefit.
**Amiodarone 300 then 150 mg; lidocaine 1–1.5 then 0.5–0.75 mg/kg.** Unchanged in the 2025 algorithm, either drug for VF/pVT after failed shocks (2b).
**Monophasic 360 J.** Unchanged; biphasic remains the manufacturer’s dose (120–200 J) or the maximum available if unknown.

**Atropine 1 mg × 3, max 3 mg, bradycardia only.** The 2025 bradycardia algorithm keeps 1 mg every 3–5 minutes to a 3 mg total; it has no place in arrest. Avoid it after heart transplantation (denervated heart), where pacing, dopamine or epinephrine are used.

**5 H’s and 5 T’s — though IV calcium for hyperkalaemia is now downgraded.** The list is unchanged: hypovolaemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion, hypo-/hyperkalaemia, hypothermia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, pulmonary and coronary thrombosis. Hyperkalaemia stays on it, but calcium as its arrest treatment is now 2b (ACLS-62).
mimic: Same ratio; the 2025 reason is seeing chest rise, not compression fraction.
traps: “2025 changed the compression depth to 5–6 cm”
The 5 cm minimum and the 6 cm ceiling were both in 2020; depth did not change.
decode: [pattern] Why does AHA 2025 keep 30:2 before an advanced airway?
The pauses let the rescuer see chest rise and confirm ventilation.
[pattern] Which of these changed in 2025 — epinephrine dose, amiodarone dose, post-ROSC SpO2, monophasic energy?
Post-ROSC SpO2; the rest are unchanged.
ACLS-63.punch: The drug doses, the rate, the ratio and the reversible causes all survived 2025; what a viva will probe is that 30:2 now rests on seeing the chest rise, and that calcium for hyperkalaemia lost its firm footing.

ACLS-64.intro: Step 6 continues with the numbers that moved. In a transition year the old figure is still keyed in many question banks, so each row has two defensible answers depending on the guideline the question was written to. No real question is linked yet; ACLS-60 and ACLS-61 carry the reasons.
why: **Cardioversion, AF: 120–200 J → ≥200 J.** AHA 2025 (2a): start at at least 200 J biphasic and escalate. The 120–200 J (biphasic; 200 J monophasic) figure comes from the 2010 algorithm, carried unchanged through 2015; the 2020 algorithm only said to use the device’s recommended energy, although the 2020 text already noted that 200 J or more gives better first-shock success.
**Cardioversion, flutter: 50–100 J → 200 J.** AHA 2025 (2b): 200 J may be reasonable. Flutter usually converts at low energy, but a failed shock just means another, so the start moved up.
**Compression depth: ≥5 cm, avoid >6 cm → unchanged.** Kept as a control row: it is the number examiners assume changed.
**Post-ROSC SpO2: 92–98% → 90–98%.** The floor dropped after BOX showed lower oxygen targets were safe; ERC–ESICM 2025 stays at 94–98%.
**Temperature duration: ≥24 hours → ≥36 hours.** The 36 hours is the minimum (2a).

**Temperature range: 32–36 °C → 32–37.5 °C.** Widened after TTM2 to include normothermia with fever prevention; the wider range was first written into the AHA 2023 focused update, so a 2024 question may already use it.

**Vascular access: IV first, weaker recommendation (algorithm box: IV/IO) → IV first (class 1), IO if IV fails.** 2020 called IV first ‘reasonable’ (2a) and IO ‘may be considered’ if IV failed (2b); 2025 makes IV first class 1 and IO the 2a fallback.
mimic: 2025 post-ROSC SpO2 vs 2020
90–98% now; 92–98% before. An option of 94–98% is ERC.
traps: “Temperature control 32–36 °C for 24 hours” offered as current
That is the 2020 figure; current AHA is 32–37.5 °C for at least 36 hours.
decode: [pattern] Give the old and new temperature control target after cardiac arrest.
[pattern] Which number did not change in 2025: depth, SpO2, AF energy, temperature?
Depth.
ACLS-64.punch: Five rows moved and one did not: know each pair, and read the question’s date and source to decide which figure the examiner is keying.

ACLS-65.intro: Step 5 turns to children. The 2025 paediatric changes improve compression technique, push epinephrine earlier when there is no shockable rhythm, and give blood pressure targets in centiles. The one linked DocT QBank question, answered correctly by 67%, asks the rate and depth for a 7-year-old.
why: **The TWO-FINGER technique for infants is NO LONGER RECOMMENDED → use the HEEL OF ONE HAND or the TWO THUMB-ENCIRCLING HANDS technique.** Two fingers rarely reach the target depth (one-third of the chest, about 4 cm) and tire quickly; the heel of one hand or the encircling thumbs (both class 1) give deeper, more consistent compressions. The heel of one hand is the choice when the rescuer cannot encircle the chest.
**Pauses in chest compressions should be LESS THAN 10 SECONDS.** New: a number for what was before ‘minimise interruptions’, matching the adult figure.

**Non-shockable rhythm: epinephrine AS EARLY AS POSSIBLE (best outcomes when <3 min).** Most paediatric arrests are asphyxial and non-shockable, so epinephrine is the main drug that can restore circulation. Registry data show lower odds of ROSC and survival with each minute of delay. 2020 said ‘within 5 minutes of starting compressions’ (2a); 2025 says ‘as early as possible’ (2a).

**Invasive arterial monitoring: target DBP ≥25 mmHg in INFANTS, ≥30 mmHg in CHILDREN ≥1 year.** Diastolic pressure during CPR drives coronary perfusion; these values were associated with survival in the paediatric observational data. In 2020 the figures sat only in the supporting text, under a recommendation to use diastolic pressure to judge CPR quality (2b); 2025 makes them an explicit target (2b) when an arterial line is already in place. AHA 2025 gives no diastolic target for adults (ERC 2025 uses ≥30 mmHg).

**Post-arrest: maintain systolic and mean BP above the 10th percentile for age.** 2020 used SBP above the 5th centile; 2025 raises the floor and adds MAP, because post-arrest hypotension in children predicts death.

**FBAO: children 5 back blows + 5 ABDOMINAL thrusts; infants 5 back blows + 5 CHEST thrusts (heel of one hand) — abdominal thrusts no longer recommended in infants.** For the child the change is back blows first (before 2025 AHA used abdominal thrusts). For the infant the change is the heel-of-hand chest thrust in place of two fingers; abdominal thrusts were never recommended in infants because the liver and spleen are unprotected below the costal margin (FLAG on ‘no longer’). Blind finger sweeps are harmful at any age.
mimic: Infant vs child FBAO
Both start with 5 back blows; the infant gets chest thrusts, the child abdominal thrusts.
Infant depth vs child depth
Both one-third of the AP diameter: about 4 cm in infants, about 5 cm in children.
traps: “7-year-old: depth about 1 inch” (chosen by many; 67% right)
1 inch is too shallow for anyone; a child needs about 2 inches (5 cm), an infant about 1.5 inches (4 cm).
“Children get a slower rate of 90–100/min”
Rate is 100–120/min at every age.
“ETCO2 below 20 mmHg means stop”
ETCO2 ≥20 is associated with better outcomes, but no ETCO2 cut-off alone should end resuscitation; children have survived below 20.
