decode: 7-year-old in arrest, PT teacher starts CPR — rate and depth? [DocT QBank, 67%]
100–120/min, about 2 inches (5 cm).
[pattern] Which infant compression technique is no longer recommended in 2025?
Two fingers.
ACLS-65.punch: Paediatric CPR 2025 is about effective pressure: real depth from the heel of a hand or two thumbs, short pauses, early epinephrine in the asphyxial arrest, and blood pressure kept above the 10th centile once the heart restarts.

ACLS-66.sub: Neonatology → Neonatal resuscitation → The newborn chain of care
ACLS-66.intro: Step 5 continues with the newborn, who for the first time has a chain of its own. Newborn arrest is almost never cardiac: the problem is lungs full of fluid that have not been aerated, so the chain is built around ventilation. No real question is linked yet.
why: **1. Prevention → 2. Recognition and activation → 3. Initial steps → 4. Ventilation → 5. Advanced resuscitation → 6. Postnatal care → 7. Recovery.** Prevention covers antenatal care and having a trained team at high-risk births; initial steps are warmth, positioning, clearing the airway if needed, drying and stimulating; ventilation is effective positive-pressure breaths; advanced resuscitation is intubation, compressions, epinephrine and volume.

**For the first time in resuscitation guidelines, a dedicated newborn chain addresses the unique physiological and developmental needs of neonates.** The adult and paediatric chain starts from collapse and ends with defibrillation and post-arrest care; a newborn’s problem is transition from fetal to air-breathing circulation. Effective ventilation alone corrects most newborn bradycardia, so it has its own link ahead of advanced resuscitation.
mimic: Newborn chain vs unified adult–paediatric chain
Seven links built around ventilation vs six links built around CPR and defibrillation.
traps: “The newborn uses the same chain of survival as children”
2025 gives the newborn a separate seven-link chain of care.
decode: [pattern] Which link comes immediately before advanced resuscitation in the newborn chain of care?
Ventilation.
ACLS-66.punch: The newborn chain puts ventilation in its own link because in the newborn effective breaths are the resuscitation; compressions and drugs come only if ventilation has failed.

ACLS-67.sub: Neonatology → Neonatal resuscitation → Umbilical cord management
ACLS-67.intro: Step 5 continues at the cord. Leaving the cord intact lets placental blood top up the newborn’s volume during transition, and 2025 strengthens this for preterm babies. No real question is linked yet.
why: **Term, not requiring immediate resuscitation: DEFERRED CORD CLAMPING for at least 60 SECONDS — improves haematologic indices and iron status.** About 60 seconds lets placental blood transfer; the benefit at term is iron stores and haemoglobin in infancy, not survival, so the wording is ‘can be beneficial’ (2a).

**Preterm <37 weeks, not requiring immediate resuscitation: deferred cord clamping for at least 60 seconds is RECOMMENDED — reduces mortality.** Meta-analyses show lower mortality than with immediate clamping, so the class is higher (1). The extra volume steadies the circulation of a preterm baby during transition.

**Non-vigorous term and late preterm ≥35 weeks: INTACT CORD MILKING may be reasonable.** New (2b): a non-vigorous baby cannot wait 60 seconds unresuscitated, and milking the intact cord gives a quicker transfer. It is not used below 28 weeks, where cord milking was linked with more severe intraventricular haemorrhage (PREMOD).

**Because clamping is deferred 60 s, the target oxygen saturation table now STARTS AT 2 MINUTES (65–70%), not 1 minute.** A reliable reading is rarely obtained in the first minute when the baby is still on the cord. The table then rises: 3 min 70–75%, 4 min 75–80%, 5 min 80–85%, 10 min 85–95%.
mimic: Deferred clamping at term vs preterm
Term: better iron (2a). Preterm: lower mortality (1).
traps: “Target saturation at 1 minute is 60–65%”
The 2025 table starts at 2 minutes (65–70%).
decode: [pattern] Preterm 32 weeks, breathing well — cord management?
Defer clamping for at least 60 seconds.
[pattern] Non-vigorous 36-week newborn — cord option?
Intact cord milking may be reasonable.
ACLS-67.punch: The cord is left alone for at least a minute because placental blood helps the transition; the preterm baby gains the most (lower mortality), which is why its recommendation is the stronger one.

ACLS-68.intro: Step 6 includes the new standalone ethics chapter. It sets the default (start CPR), when not to, who decides that treatment is futile, and how family and donation fit in. The two DocT Grand Test questions test autonomy; on the first only 20% chose correctly.
why: **Beneficence • non-maleficence • respect for autonomy • justice.** These are coequal: none automatically wins. Autonomy is the right of a capable patient to accept or refuse; it allows the doctor to persuade with honest argument and evidence, but not to coerce (a credible threat) or manipulate, and it does not oblige the doctor to give whatever is asked for. A refusal shields the doctor only if the patient was properly informed. Advance directives and surrogate decisions extend autonomy to the patient who can no longer speak.

**POLST = Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment — portable orders giving clear guidance on patient wishes regarding resuscitation and advanced interventions.** Unlike an advance directive, these are medical orders, signed by a clinician, that travel with the patient between home, ambulance and hospital. The 2025 chapter calls them ‘portable orders for life-sustaining treatment’, and the US POLST programme now uses POLST as a name (portable medical orders); the classic expansion on the card is what exams use.

**Default is to INITIATE CPR, except: serious risk of physical harm to the professional, objective signs of irreversible death, or an advance directive declining treatment.** Starting is the default because withholding needs certainty that rarely exists at the moment of collapse. The exceptions are narrow: rescuer safety, signs incompatible with life (decapitation, rigor mortis, decomposition, dependent lividity), and the patient’s own documented refusal.

**Family presence during CPR reduces complicated grief and improves psychological outcomes — institutions should have policies supporting it.** Families who watch see that everything was done; studies show less post-traumatic stress and no worse team performance.

**Determinations of no realistic benefit should rely on an INSTITUTIONAL COMMITTEE or ETHICS CONSULTANT, not an individual clinician, to limit bias and moral distress.** Clinicians are not obliged to give non-beneficial treatment even when a surrogate asks, but a single doctor’s judgement is open to bias, so the decision is shared.

**Organ donation should be considered in ALL post-arrest patients who progress to death by neurological criteria or for whom WLST is planned — decided BEFORE and INDEPENDENTLY of the donation discussion.** Separating the decision to withdraw from the offer of donation protects the patient from any suspicion that care was withdrawn for organs.
mimic: Persuasion vs coercion
Persuasion uses legitimate argument (respects autonomy); coercion uses a credible threat (violates it).
POLST vs advance directive
POLST is a clinician-signed medical order; an advance directive is the patient’s own statement.
traps: “Respect for autonomy means doing whatever the patient wants” (often chosen; 20% right)
Autonomy is a right to refuse and to choose among reasonable options, not a right to demand non-beneficial treatment.
“If a patient refuses, the doctor can never be liable”
Only an informed refusal protects; risks that were not explained still carry liability.
“Persuading a patient violates autonomy”
Persuasion by legitimate argument is allowed; coercion and manipulation are not.
decode: Which is true of respect for autonomy — coercion by threat, persuasion by argument, do whatever the patient wants, refusal removes liability? [DocT GT, 20%]
Persuasion by a legitimate argument.
Which principle supports advance directives and surrogate decisions? [DocT GT]
Autonomy.
ACLS-68.punch: The 2025 ethics chapter starts CPR by default, stops only for danger, certain death or the patient’s own refusal, and protects every hard decision by sharing it: with the family, with a committee, and apart from donation.

ACLS-69.intro: Step 6 ends with how CPR is taught. The 2025 education chapter strengthens what improves skill (feedback) and rejects anything that delays real compressions. No real question is linked yet.
why: **Feedback devices are RECOMMENDED (Class 1) during CPR training for both health care professionals AND lay rescuers.** Real-time feedback on depth, rate and recoil corrects errors a trainee cannot feel; the evidence is now level A, stronger than in 2020.

**VR: may be reasonable for KNOWLEDGE acquisition; VR should NOT be used to teach CPR SKILLS.** Knowledge 2b; skills 3: Harm, because without a real manikin there is no resistance to push against, and trainees learn the wrong depth and force.

**Cognitive aids: may be reasonable for HEALTH CARE PROFESSIONALS; NOT recommended for LAY RESCUERS — they delayed the start of CPR.** Professionals (2a) gain adherence; lay users (3: No Benefit) delayed calling and starting compressions by 30–70 seconds in trials.

**Start CPR training in children YOUNGER THAN 12 YEARS. Also: rapid-cycle deliberate practice, teamwork competencies, gamified learning, scripted debriefing.** Younger children may not yet reach adult depth, but the guideline’s reason for early training (class 1) is to increase willingness and self-confidence to act in later years.
mimic: VR for knowledge vs VR for skills
Knowledge 2b; skills 3: Harm.
traps: “Cognitive aids help lay rescuers perform better CPR”
They delayed calling and compressions; not recommended for lay rescuers.
decode: [pattern] Class of recommendation for feedback devices in CPR training, 2025?
Class 1, for professionals and lay rescuers.
ACLS-69.punch: CPR teaching in 2025 favours whatever trains the hands (feedback devices, practice) and rejects whatever puts a step between the rescuer and the first compression.

ACLS-70.sub: Post-cardiac arrest care → Neuroprognostication → AHA 2025 additions
ACLS-70.intro: Step 3 ends with prognosis, where 2025 made the assessment two-sided. Until 2020 every test looked only for signs of a poor outcome; now the guideline also lists signs of a good one. The two DocT Grand Test questions ask what NfL means and when to decide.
why: **The section now includes predictors of FAVOURABLE outcome, not only of poor outcome.** A continuous EEG background, a normal NSE (<17 µg/L at 24–72 h) and a withdrawal or better motor response (each 2b) may support a good outcome. Preserved pupillary or corneal reflexes do not (3: No Benefit), because many patients with them still do badly.

**NEUROFILAMENT LIGHT CHAIN (NfL) added as a serum biomarker.** NfL is a structural protein of large myelinated axons, so a raised serum or CSF level means axonal injury; it rises after any axonal damage, including repeated mild head injury in boxers. After arrest, high NfL (or NSE) within 72 hours may support a poor outcome (2b) when combined with other tests; no threshold is set and assays differ. NSE marks neuronal cell bodies, S-100B and GFAP mark glia.

**A continuous EEG background WITHOUT DISCHARGES within 72 h supports a FAVOURABLE prognosis, when interpreted with other tests.** A continuous, reactive background with no epileptiform discharges indicates a functioning cortex. This is the reverse of the poor-outcome EEG signs (burst suppression or suppression without sedation at ≥72 h).

**Treatment to suppress myoclonus WITHOUT an EEG correlate is NOT recommended — no evidence it contributes to secondary brain injury.** 3: No Benefit; get an EEG to separate it from seizures (ACLS-61e).

**Multimodal approach with delayed impressions: consolidate at ≥72 hours after NORMOTHERMIA and discontinuation of sedatives (class 2a).** No single sign decides (1), impressions are delayed (1), and the assessment is consolidated at least 72 hours after normothermia and off sedation (2a). The 72-hour rule was already in 2020; 2025 restates it. Hypothermia slows drug clearance and itself depresses reflexes, so an early examination during cooling overestimates injury.
mimic: NfL vs NSE vs S-100B/GFAP
Axons vs neuronal cell bodies vs glia.
Favourable vs unfavourable EEG
Continuous background without discharges vs burst suppression or suppression off sedation.
traps: “Day 2 of cooling, absent corneal reflexes: withdraw” (83% right)
Hypothermia and sedation confound the examination; wait at least 72 hours after normothermia.
“Send NSE now to guide immediate prognosis”
No single marker decides, and none is acted on before 72 hours.
“Raised NfL means glial scarring or BBB closure” (69% right)
NfL is axonal; glial injury is marked by S-100B and GFAP.
decode: Amateur boxer with raised CSF NfL — what does it suggest? [DocT GT, 69%]
Axonal injury.
Post-arrest, cooled, day 2: absent corneal reflexes, no pain response — next step in prognostication? [DocT GT, 83%]
Wait at least 72 hours before deciding.
ACLS-70.punch: Prognostication in 2025 waits at least 72 hours after normothermia, combines several tests, and now looks for signs of recovery as well as of damage, so it can argue for continuing as well as for stopping.

spine: BLS: simpler, ventilation-aware CPR
Adult BLS 2025 keeps the core numbers but unifies the chain, puts back blows first in choking, defines a breath by visible chest rise and drops gadgets that do not help.
ALS: IV first, fewer gadgets
ALS 2025 makes IV the first route, times epinephrine by rhythm, raises cardioversion energy and declines to endorse vector change, double shocks or head-up CPR.
Post-arrest: longer, warmer, two-sided
After ROSC the targets moved: SpO2 90–98%, MAP 65 or more, temperature control 32–37.5 °C for at least 36 hours, and prognostication now looks for good signs as well as bad.
Special circumstances get algorithms
Pregnancy, LVADs, opioids, asthma, cold, heat and hyperkalaemia each change the algorithm because the cause, the circulation or the response to drugs is different.
Children and newborns

Paediatric CPR loses the two-finger technique and gains early epinephrine and centile-based blood pressure targets, while the newborn gets its own chain of care built around ventilation and cord management.
Constants, old numbers, ethics, teaching
Most drug doses and the 30:2 ratio stayed, five numbers moved, and two new chapters set the ethical defaults and how CPR should be taught.
CVS08D.primer: AHA guidelines grade each statement by Class of Recommendation (1 = should / is recommended, 2a = is reasonable, 2b = may be considered, 3: No Benefit or 3: Harm) and by level of evidence; a ‘change’ can be a new number, a new topic, or the same advice moved up or down a class. The 2025 Guidelines for CPR and ECC (Circulation, October 2025) are the first full rewrite since 2020, and the European Resuscitation Council published its own 2025 guidelines with some different figures (for example post-ROSC SpO2 94–98%). Question banks written before late 2025 still carry 2020 numbers, so in a transition year you must know both the old and the new figure and which guideline a question is keyed to. CVS08A to CVS08C cover the algorithms themselves; this deck is the change log.

ACLS-71.sub: Cardiology → BLS → Lay-rescuer sequence in adult collapse
ACLS-71.intro: Step 1 is the opening minute of an out-of-hospital arrest, where survival is decided by how fast compressions start. The card gives the adult sequence; the one real question tests the exception, a drowned child, where the arrest is hypoxic and breaths come first.
why: **Check scene safety, then responsiveness: tap the shoulders and shout.** A rescuer who becomes a second casualty helps no one; the shake and shout separate the sleeping or intoxicated from the unresponsive.

**If unresponsive: shout for help, call EMS on speakerphone, send someone for an AED.** AHA 2025 (class 1) tells a lone rescuer with a mobile phone to call and start CPR at once; on speaker the dispatcher can coach compressions while they are given. In an adult, a witnessed sudden collapse is usually VF, and survival falls with every minute without a shock, so the AED is fetched early.

**Check breathing and pulse simultaneously, for no more than 10 seconds; a lay rescuer need not check a pulse at all.** The pulse check is for health care professionals (class 1, ≤10 s); even they miss or imagine pulses, so a long search wastes perfusion time. AHA 2025 tells the lay rescuer to assume arrest in anyone unresponsive and not breathing normally.

**No normal breathing and no definite pulse within 10 seconds: begin compressions. Agonal gasping is not breathing.** Gasps come from the brainstem in the first minutes of arrest and fade with time; AHA 2025 quotes them in up to 40–60% of out-of-hospital arrests (the card’s ‘up to 40%’ is the lower figure). They are the commonest reason bystanders wait, which is why dispatchers are trained to treat ‘breathing strangely’ as arrest.
mimic: Call first (adult, witnessed collapse) vs care first (child, drowning, asphyxia)

The adult is probably in VF and needs the defibrillator; the hypoxic arrest needs oxygen, so a lone rescuer without a phone gives about 2 minutes of CPR with breaths before leaving to call (AHA; ERC says 1 minute). With a phone, call on speaker and start at once. A child’s witnessed sudden collapse is the exception: it is likely arrhythmic, so call and fetch the AED first.
traps: “Abdominal thrusts to drain water from the drowned child’s lungs”
Little water is aspirated, and thrusts delay ventilation and cause regurgitation. Start CPR with rescue breaths (ERC: 5 initial breaths, then 30:2).
“High-flow oxygen and watch for spontaneous breathing”
An unresponsive child with no breathing is in arrest; oxygen by mask moves no air into apnoeic lungs. Ventilate and compress.
“Gasping means the patient is breathing, so wait”
Agonal gasps are a sign of arrest, not of adequate breathing.
decode: A 5-year-old pulled from a pool, unresponsive, not breathing — best initial management? [DocT GT]
CPR with a focus on rescue breathing (91% right): drowning is a hypoxic arrest.
Bystander sees an adult collapse — first action after confirming unresponsiveness? [pattern]
Call for help and EMS (speakerphone) and send for an AED, then check breathing and start compressions.
ACLS-71.punch: An unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally gets a call, an AED and compressions, with no pulse hunt by a lay rescuer; a drowned or asphyxiated patient, or a child, needs breaths early because oxygen, not a shock, is what is missing.

ACLS-72.intro: Step 2 starts when the AED reaches the patient. Every action is arranged so that compressions stop only for analysis and the shock.
why: **Switch on, attach the pads while compressions continue, stop only for analysis, deliver one shock if advised, resume compressions at once, reanalyse after 2 minutes.** Even when a shock ends VF, the stunned myocardium usually produces little or no output for the first minute or so (often a brief PEA or asystole), so a pulse check finds nothing and only costs perfusion. Two minutes of compressions both perfuses the myocardium and lets the rhythm declare itself. AHA 2025 prefers a single shock to stacked shocks (2a) because three shocks in a row lengthen the interruption, and today’s biphasic shock succeeds first time often enough that a second immediate shock adds little.
mimic: AED single shock vs old three stacked shocks

Single shock then 2 minutes of CPR is current; up to three stacked shocks survive only in the monitored, witnessed VF in the cath lab or after cardiac surgery, where the defibrillator is already attached (ERC).
traps: “Check the pulse straight after the shock to see if it worked”
Resume compressions immediately; the check comes at the next 2-minute analysis.
decode: What follows a delivered AED shock? [pattern]
Immediate compressions for 2 minutes, no rhythm or pulse check.
ACLS-72.punch: The AED pauses the chest twice only, to analyse and to shock; everything else, from pad placement to the post-shock period, happens with compressions running.

ACLS-73.sub: Cardiology → BLS → Pause and compression-fraction targets
ACLS-73.intro: Step 2 puts numbers on the pauses. The real question asked which statement about shocks was false, and only 36% chose correctly: survival falls as the perishock pause lengthens, it does not rise.
why: **Pre-shock pause as short as possible (AHA 2025, class 1); ERC 2025 says under 5 seconds; charge while compressions continue.** Charging takes several seconds; if done during compressions, the hands come off only for the final ‘clear’ and the shock. In 815 shockable out-of-hospital arrests (Cheskes 2011), a pre-shock pause of 20 seconds or more, against under 10, roughly halved the odds of survival to discharge (OR 0.47), and each extra 5 seconds cost about 18%; a perishock pause of 40 seconds or more, against under 20, did the same (OR 0.54).

**Post-shock pause as short as possible: resume compressions immediately, no rhythm or pulse check (AHA 2025, class 2a).** See ACLS-72: the post-shock heart is stunned and needs perfusion, not inspection. In the Cheskes data the post-shock pause alone was not independently linked to survival; the recommendation rests on the total perishock interruption and on physiology.

**Compression fraction at least 60% (AHA 2025, class 2b, a minimum); good teams exceed 80%, which is not a guideline target.** Compression fraction is the share of the resuscitation during which compressions are being given. It is a measure of how few and how short the pauses are.

**Rhythm checks every 2 minutes, timed with the compressor change.** AHA does not fix the interval in a recommendation, but 2 minutes matches the cycle of the algorithm and the point at which a compressor’s depth begins to fall, so one pause does two jobs.
mimic: Pre-shock pause vs perishock pause
Pre-shock is last compression to shock; perishock is pre-shock plus post-shock, from the last compression before to the first after.
traps: “The perishock pause is directly proportional to survival”
It is inversely related: the longer the pause, the lower the survival (a perishock pause of 40 seconds or more, against under 20, OR 0.54). This was the false statement (36% right).
“Repeated shocks hardly change impedance, so this must be the false one”
True as written: successive shocks lower transthoracic impedance only slightly, about 8% or less, which is one reason stacked shocks add little.
“Rescue shocks are not effective early in VF”
They are most effective when VF has lasted only 1–2 minutes, before the myocardium is depleted; true statement, so not the answer.
decode: Which is false about defibrillation: brief VF responds well; lowest effective energy; repeated shocks lower impedance ≤8%; perishock pause directly proportional to survival? [DocT GT]
The last: the perishock pause is inversely related to survival.
Minimum chest compression fraction in adult CPR? [pattern]
At least 60% (2b).
ACLS-73.punch: Coronary perfusion pressure falls within seconds of stopping and takes many compressions to rebuild, so every second of pause before or after a shock lowers the chance that the shock works; that is why the target is ‘as short as possible’.

ACLS-74.intro: Step 1 also sets how the compressions are given. Each target exists because blood flow in CPR depends on how deeply the chest is squeezed and how fully it refills.
why: **Rate 100 to 120 per minute.** Faster than 120 shortens each release phase, so the heart fills less and depth tends to fall (AHA 2025, 2a).

**Depth at least 5 cm, not more than 6 cm.** Deeper compressions eject more blood (class 1); beyond 6 cm, observational data show more injuries with no added survival, so the upper limit protects without costing flow.
**Full recoil; do not lean on the chest.** The heart fills and the coronaries perfuse during release; residual leaning keeps intrathoracic pressure up and lowers coronary perfusion.

**30:2 for one or two rescuers in an adult; with an advanced airway, continuous compressions and one breath every 6 seconds.** Once the airway is secured, breaths no longer need a pause; 10 a minute is enough because cardiac output during CPR is low.

**Untrained bystander: continuous compression-only CPR.** In a witnessed adult cardiac arrest the blood is still oxygenated for the first minutes, so compressions matter more than breaths, and bystanders are more willing to start.
mimic: Adult 30:2 vs child/infant 15:2 (two rescuers)
Children arrest from hypoxia more often, so two rescuers give more breaths; a single rescuer uses 30:2 at any age beyond the newborn.
traps: “Compression-only CPR is fine for a child or a drowning victim”
In asphyxial arrest ventilation is the treatment; AHA 2025 prefers conventional CPR with breaths in children.
decode: Adult compression rate and depth? [pattern]
100–120/min, 5–6 cm, full recoil.
ACLS-74.punch: Push at least 5 cm, at 100–120 a minute, and let the chest come all the way up; compressions alone suffice for a witnessed adult cardiac arrest, but not when hypoxia caused the arrest.

ACLS-75.sub: Cardiology → BLS → AED in special situations
ACLS-75.intro: Step 2 ends with the situations that tempt a rescuer to hold the shock. In each, the problem is the contact between pad and skin or between current and device, and it is fixed in seconds.
why: **Water or sweat: move the patient clear of standing water and dry the chest; rain or a wet surface alone is not a contraindication.** Water on the chest gives the current a path across the skin between the pads instead of through the heart.

**Hairy chest: press the pads firmly; if they will not stick, shave or rip off a first set of pads and apply a second.** Air under the pad raises impedance and can cause burns or a ‘check pads’ message.

**Pacemaker or ICD: pad at least 8 cm from the device, or anteroposterior; never withhold the shock.** Current passing through the generator can damage it or travel down the lead and burn the myocardium at its tip; moving the pad avoids that. Have the device checked afterwards.
**Medication patch: remove it and wipe the skin.** The patch backing can block current and cause arcing and burns.

**Child under 8 with no paediatric pads: use adult pads, anteroposterior.** AHA 2025 recommends a paediatric attenuator but allows an AED without one when nothing else is available; VF untreated is far more dangerous than an adult dose. Anteroposterior placement stops the large pads touching each other on a small chest.
traps: “An implanted ICD is a reason not to use the AED”
Shock, with the pad moved away from the device.
decode: AED use in a 5-year-old with no paediatric pads? [pattern]
Use adult pads, anteroposterior; do not delay the shock.
ACLS-75.punch: Water, hair, devices, patches and small chests are interface problems: correct the contact and shock, because no one of them outweighs untreated VF.

ACLS-76.sub: Cardiology → Newborn resuscitation → Initial steps and the golden minute
ACLS-76.intro: Step 3 changes patient: the newborn arrests because the lungs have not opened, not because of an arrhythmia, so the first minute is about warmth and air.
why: **Initial steps, about 30 seconds: warmth, sniffing position, clear secretions only if obstructing, dry, stimulate; then assess breathing and heart rate.** Newborns lose heat fast through wet skin, and cold raises oxygen use and worsens acidosis, so drying and warming are resuscitation. A newborn’s large occiput flexes the neck on a flat surface and narrows the airway, so the head is brought to neutral or slight extension (sniffing). AHA 2025 makes routine oral, nasal or tracheal suctioning ‘No Benefit’; suction only a blocked airway.

**Golden minute: initial steps, reassessment and, if needed, PPV all by 60 seconds of life.** AHA 2025 (class 1) says ventilation should begin within 60 seconds in an apnoeic or gasping baby. Most depressed newborns respond to ventilation alone; delay prolongs hypoxia and bradycardia.
mimic: Non-vigorous baby with meconium: old tracheal suction vs current PPV
Go straight to PPV; intubate and suction only if the trachea is obstructed (AHA 2025, 2a).
traps: “Suction the trachea of every non-vigorous meconium-stained baby before ventilating”
Removed; it delays the ventilation that works.
decode: Limp apnoeic term newborn — by when must PPV start? [pattern]
Within 60 seconds of birth (the golden minute).
ACLS-76.punch: A newborn is resuscitated through the lungs: warm, open, dry, stimulate, and ventilate within the first minute.

ACLS-77.intro: Step 3’s decisions rest on the heart rate, because in a newborn bradycardia is the read-out of hypoxia and rises when the lungs are ventilated.
why: **Below 100/min, or apnoea or gasping: start PPV.** AHA 2025 (class 1). A slowing newborn heart is a hypoxic heart, so ventilation is the treatment.

**Below 60/min after 30 seconds of effective PPV: start compressions, secure the airway, FiO2 1.0.** AHA 2025 (class 1) says ‘despite 30 seconds of ventilation’; effective means chest rise. An advanced airway makes ventilation reliable during compressions, and 100% oxygen is given while compressing (2b).
**Above 100/min with spontaneous breathing: PPV may stop.** A rising heart rate is the best sign that ventilation is working.
mimic: Under 100 vs under 60
Under 100 starts ventilation; under 60 after effective ventilation adds compressions.
traps: “Heart rate 50 at birth: start compressions first”
Ventilate first; compressions start only if the rate stays under 60 after 30 seconds of effective PPV.
decode: Newborn heart rate 80, gasping — next step? [pattern]
PPV.
ACLS-77.punch: Under 100 means ventilate; under 60 despite proven ventilation means compress; a rate rising above 100 says the ventilation has worked.

ACLS-78.sub: Cardiology → Newborn resuscitation → Ventilation corrective steps
ACLS-78.intro: Step 3 also covers the commonest failure: PPV that does not move the chest. Until the chest rises, the baby has not been ventilated, whatever time has passed.
why: **Mask reseal, reposition the head, suction mouth then nose, open the mouth, increase pressure in steps, then an alternative airway (ETT or laryngeal mask).** The order goes from the commonest and simplest cause of failure (mask leak, poor position) to the more invasive. Compressions are considered only after chest rise is achieved and 30 seconds of effective PPV have still left the heart rate below 60.
traps: “No chest rise after 30 seconds of PPV and heart rate 50: start compressions”
Correct the ventilation first; 30 seconds of PPV without chest rise does not count.
decode: PPV for 30 seconds, chest not moving — first corrective step? [pattern]
Adjust the mask to reseal it, then reposition the head.
ACLS-78.punch: No chest rise means no ventilation; fix the mask, position, airway and pressure before the heart is blamed.

ACLS-79.intro: Step 3 reaches compressions only after effective ventilation has failed. The ratio favours breaths because the cause is still asphyxia.
why: **3:1.** AHA 2025 (2b). More breaths per compression than in any other age group, because the lungs are the problem.
**120 events a minute: 90 compressions and 30 breaths.** One cycle of 3 compressions and 1 breath every 2 seconds.
**Two-thumb encircling technique, lower third of the sternum, one third of the AP diameter.** The two-thumb technique produces higher pressures and less fatigue than two fingers (2b).
**100% oxygen once compressions begin.** AHA 2025 (2b), then wean to saturation targets after recovery.

**Reassess the heart rate every 60 seconds.** A shorter interval interrupts compressions before they can raise coronary perfusion; AHA 2025 recommends ECG monitoring for an accurate rate during compressions (class 1).
mimic: Newborn 3:1 vs child 15:2
3:1 in the newborn (asphyxia); 15:2 for two rescuers beyond the newborn period, or in a newborn whose arrest is cardiac.
traps: “Newborn compressions at 15:2 like a child”
3:1 unless the arrest is known to be cardiac.
decode: Newborn compressions: ratio and events per minute? [pattern]
3:1, 90 compressions + 30 breaths = 120 events.
ACLS-79.punch: Newborn compressions run at 3:1, 120 events a minute, two thumbs at a third of the chest depth, with 100% oxygen and a heart-rate check each minute.

ACLS-80.sub: Cardiology → Newborn resuscitation → Adrenaline and volume
ACLS-80.intro: Step 3 ends with drugs, used only when ventilation and compressions together have not lifted the heart rate.
why: **Heart rate still below 60 after at least 60 seconds of compressions with effective PPV and 100% oxygen.** AHA 2025 (class 1) ties adrenaline to optimised ventilation and compressions; given earlier it treats the wrong problem.

**IV via umbilical venous catheter, or IO: 0.01–0.03 mg/kg (0.1–0.3 mL/kg of 1:10,000).** Confirmed in AHA 2025 (class 1). The umbilical vein is the quickest large vein at delivery; IO is acceptable if it fails (2a).
**Tracheal 0.05–0.1 mg/kg (0.5–1 mL/kg of 1:10,000).** AHA 2025 (2a), only while access is obtained; absorption from fluid-filled newborn lungs is unreliable, so the dose is higher.
**Every 3 to 5 minutes while the heart rate stays below 60.** AHA 2025 (2b), preferably intravascular; give the IV dose as soon as access is obtained, whatever the interval since a tracheal dose.
mimic: IV 0.01–0.03 vs tracheal 0.05–0.1 mg/kg
The tracheal dose is about ten times higher because little is absorbed.
traps: “Give the tracheal dose and delay the umbilical line”
Tracheal adrenaline is a holding measure; access is not delayed for it.
decode: Newborn heart rate 40 after 60 s of 3:1 CPR with 100% oxygen — dose of IV adrenaline? [pattern]
0.01–0.03 mg/kg of 1:10,000 via the umbilical vein; 10 mL/kg saline or blood if there is no response and blood loss is suspected.
ACLS-80.punch: Adrenaline comes last in newborn resuscitation, after proven ventilation and a minute of compressions, at 0.01–0.03 mg/kg IV; no response, think of blood loss and give volume.

ACLS-81.sub: Cardiology → ECMO → VA vs VV configuration
ACLS-81.intro: Step 4 is the choice of circuit, decided by one question: does the heart need support or only the lung? The two real questions test the consequence of that choice: arrest on VV ECMO is treated with ordinary CPR, and the commonest VA circuit is femoro-femoral.
why: **VA: gas exchange and circulation.** Blood is drained from the venous side and pumped, oxygenated, into an artery, so the circuit does the heart’s work as well as the lung’s.

**VA cannulation: femoral vein to femoral artery peripherally; right atrium to aorta centrally.** Femoral cannulation is quick at the bedside or during CPR; central cannulation is used after cardiac surgery, through the open chest, and gives antegrade flow.
**VA bypasses both the lungs and the heart.** That is why the native lungs and LV can be failing while the body is perfused, and why blood stagnating in the heart and lungs is a hazard (ACLS-84).
**VA indication: cardiogenic shock and cardiac arrest.**
**VV: gas exchange only.** Drained blood is oxygenated and returned to the venous side, so it reaches the right heart already oxygenated.

**VV cannulation: femoro-jugular, or a dual-lumen cannula in the right internal jugular.** Drainage and return are both venous, so no artery is needed; the dual-lumen cannula drains from both venae cavae and returns towards the tricuspid valve from a single neck site, which limits recirculation and lets the patient mobilise.
**VV: blood still traverses the lungs; the native heart does all the work.** Blood pressure and flow are entirely the patient’s own.
**VV indication: severe isolated respiratory failure.** Hypoxaemia with an adequate cardiac output takes VV; add shock and it becomes VA.
mimic: Arrest on VV vs arrest on VA ECMO
On VV the circuit gives no flow to the body, so standard ACLS with compressions; on VA the circuit itself is the circulation.
traps: “Arrest on VV ECMO: urgent conversion to VA” (the main wrong choice, 69% right)
VV gives no circulatory support, so the immediate step is chest compressions; conversion to VA is a later decision.
“Defibrillate the asystole at 200 J”
Shocks are for VF/pVT only; treat the cause, here hyperkalaemia.
“Epinephrine only, avoid compressions because of the cannulas”
Compressions are needed; the cannulas are not a reason to withhold CPR on VV.
decode: Patient on VV ECMO for ARDS, hyperkalaemia, VT then asystole — immediate next step? [DocT GT]
Start chest compressions (standard ACLS); VV ECMO gives no circulatory support.
Image of cannulation — which type? [DocT GT]
Peripheral VA femoro-femoral (83% right); a femoral vein drainage cannula with a femoral artery return cannula.
ACLS-81.punch: Ask what is failing: lung alone takes VV, which still needs a beating heart; heart as well takes VA, which replaces it. Arrest on VV is therefore an ordinary arrest.

ACLS-82.sub: Cardiology → ECPR → Configuration, selection, timing, exclusions
ACLS-82.intro: Step 5 applies VA ECMO to a heart that has stopped. The trials show it helps only when the right patient reaches the circuit quickly, with a fix waiting. The one real question tested the Surugadai criteria, and only 42% saw that a core temperature under 35 °C is not an exclusion.
why: **Venoarterial, always.** With no cardiac output, blood returned to a vein would sit in a still heart; only arterial return perfuses the body.

**Candidate: witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, initial shockable rhythm or another reversible cause, younger with few comorbidities, and a definitive treatment ready (PCI, thrombectomy, rewarming).** Each criterion shortens the no-flow time or predicts a heart and brain that can recover. AHA 2025 makes ECPR reasonable ‘in select patients when provided within an appropriately trained and equipped system of care’ (2a) but sets no fixed criteria; ELSO’s 2021 interim guideline uses age under 70, witnessed arrest, a shockable rhythm, no-flow under 5 minutes and low-flow under 60 minutes, and states these are consensus, not validated.

**Low-flow time as short as possible; most target cannulation within 60 minutes of arrest.** Neurologically intact survival falls steeply with each minute of conventional CPR. ARREST (30 patients, refractory VF, a mobile cath-lab system) showed survival to discharge of 43% vs 7% and stopped early; Prague OHCA (264 patients) gave 31.5% vs 22.0% good neurological survival at 180 days (not significant); INCEPTION (160 randomised, 134 analysed, 10 Dutch centres) gave 20% vs 16% at 30 days (not significant). The benefit appears only in fast, experienced systems.

**Exclusions: unwitnessed arrest, long no-flow time, terminal illness, severe aortic regurgitation, uncontrolled bleeding.** Aortic regurgitation lets retrograde ECMO flow fill the LV; bleeding forbids the heparin the circuit needs; aortic dissection is also an exclusion.
mimic: Hypothermia 30–35 °C vs below 30 °C (Surugadai)
Mild to moderate hypothermia is a protective, reversible state and favours ECPR; only a core temperature under 30 °C is listed as an exclusion.
traps: “Core temperature under 35 °C excludes ECPR” (42% right)
In the Surugadai criteria, as DocT quotes them, the exclusions are presumed non-cardiac cause, ROSC within 10 minutes of arrival, core temperature under 30 °C and pregnancy; 30–35 °C is not excluded.
“ROSC within 10 minutes is a reason to cannulate”
It is an exclusion: the patient no longer has a refractory arrest.
decode: Surugadai ECPR criteria — all are exclusions EXCEPT: non-cardiac cause, ROSC <10 min, core <35 °C, pregnancy? [DocT GT]
Core temperature <35 °C (the exclusion is <30 °C).
Which ECPR candidate does best? [pattern]
Young, witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, refractory VF, flow within 60 minutes, PCI ready.
ACLS-82.punch: ECPR is VA ECMO started in a refractory arrest so that a reversible cause can be fixed; it works only when the patient is well chosen and on the circuit within about an hour.

ACLS-83.sub: Cardiology → ECMO → Cardiogenic shock on VV ECMO
ACLS-83.intro: Step 4 explains why a VV circuit cannot rescue a failing heart: it adds oxygen to the venous blood but nothing to the pump that delivers it.
why: **Reconfigure to VA or VAV; no change in pump flow or sweep corrects falling cardiac output on VV.** Oxygen delivery is cardiac output times oxygen content; VV raises content, but if the native heart cannot pump, delivery falls and lactate rises. Pump flow and sweep act on oxygenation and CO2, which are not the failing step. VAV adds an arterial return limb to the VV circuit, so lung and heart are both supported. First exclude causes that VV itself can create or hide (tamponade, RV failure from high PEEP or acidosis, hypovolaemia) on echo.
mimic: VV recirculation vs heart failure on VV
Recirculation lowers patient saturation with a high drainage saturation; heart failure gives low pressure and rising lactate with adequate saturation.
traps: “Increase ECMO flow to improve the shock on VV”
More VV flow only adds oxygenated blood to the venous side; it does not raise cardiac output.
decode: VV ECMO for ARDS, now cardiogenic shock with rising lactate despite inotropes — next? [pattern]
Convert to VA (or VAV).
ACLS-83.punch: On VV ECMO the patient’s own heart delivers every litre; when it fails, the circuit must change to VA or VAV, because no setting on a VV circuit adds flow.

ACLS-84.sub: Cardiology → ECMO → Complications of peripheral VA ECMO
ACLS-84.intro: Step 6 follows from the plumbing: femoral VA ECMO returns blood up the aorta, against the heart. The three real questions test the two complications that arise from it and their fixes.
why: **Differential hypoxaemia (Harlequin, north-south): a recovering heart ejects blood from failing lungs into the aortic root and upper body, while ECMO flow supplies the lower body; monitor the right hand; treat by improving native oxygenation or converting to VAV.** The two streams meet at a ‘mixing zone’ in the aorta; when the LV recovers, it pushes the zone towards the abdomen, and the coronaries, brain and right arm receive the deoxygenated native output. The right subclavian comes off the brachiocephalic trunk, the first branch of the arch, so the right radial is the first site to show the native output’s low saturation; the femoral side reads high. Raising sweep FiO2 does nothing, because the ECMO blood is already fully oxygenated (left foot 99%). VAV adds a return cannula in the internal jugular, so oxygenated blood enters the right heart, passes the failing lungs and is ejected oxygenated by the LV.

**LV distension: retrograde aortic flow raises afterload on a ventricle that cannot eject, so it never unloads; treat by venting (IABP, Impella, atrial septostomy).** A non-ejecting LV still fills: the venous cannula never drains all the return, so some blood crosses the lungs, and bronchial and Thebesian flow and any aortic regurgitation add to it; pressure rises, the aortic valve stops opening (flat arterial trace, loss of pulse pressure), left atrial pressure rises and pulmonary oedema follows, with a risk of thrombus in the stagnant LV. Lowering ECMO flow and adding an inotrope are the first steps; an Impella pulls blood out of the LV directly (ECPELLA, ACLS-85).

**Distal limb ischaemia: prevented by a distal perfusion cannula at cannulation.** The arterial cannula occludes most of the femoral artery, so the leg beyond it depends on collaterals. A cool, pale, pulseless foot needs an antegrade distal perfusion cannula into the superficial femoral artery at once; heparin, elevation or thrombectomy do not address a cannula blocking the vessel.
mimic: Harlequin vs global hypoxaemia
Harlequin: right hand low, foot high; global: both low, a circuit or oxygenator problem.
LV distension vs good LV recovery
Distension: no pulse pressure, closed aortic valve, rising LA and PA pressures; recovery: rising pulse pressure with an opening valve.
traps: “Harlequin: increase ECMO pump flow”
More flow moves the mixing zone a little closer to the aortic root but raises LV afterload and does not oxygenate the native output; VAV is the definitive fix.
“Harlequin: increase sweep FiO2 to 1.0”
The circuit blood is already saturated; the deoxygenated blood comes from the native lungs.
“Harlequin: convert to VV”
The patient still needs circulatory support for cardiogenic shock; VV removes it.
“Cool pulseless leg: raise heparin, elevate, or thrombectomy”
Place an antegrade distal perfusion cannula.
decode: Femoral VA ECMO, right hand SpO2 84%, left foot 99%, TRALI — best intervention? [DocT GT]
Convert to VAV with a return cannula in the internal jugular vein.
Femoral VA ECMO, right radial severe hypoxaemia, femoral gases good — modification? [DocT GT]
Add a venous return cannula (VAV).
Six hours after right femoral arterial cannulation, cold pale pulseless foot — next step? [DocT GT]
Immediate antegrade distal perfusion cannula into the superficial femoral artery.
ACLS-84.punch: Peripheral VA ECMO pumps blood backwards up the aorta: the upper body gets whatever the native lungs and heart send, the LV pushes against the circuit, and the cannulated leg loses its inflow. Put a sensor on the right hand, a vent on the LV and a cannula into the distal leg.

ACLS-85.sub: Cardiology → Mechanical support → IABP, Impella, VA ECMO
ACLS-85.intro: Step 6 closes with the ladder of devices. Each adds more flow, but only one empties the LV, which explains why devices are combined. The real question asked which device works without cardiac synchrony, and the key is narrower than the truth.
why: **Mechanism: IABP inflates in diastole and deflates in systole; Impella is a microaxial pump from LV to aorta; VA ECMO is full cardiopulmonary support.** The IABP is triggered from the ECG or arterial trace, so a fast irregular rhythm or no rhythm defeats it; the Impella and ECMO are continuous-flow pumps that run regardless of rhythm, even in VF.

**Flow: IABP about 0.5 L/min; Impella 2.5–5 L/min by device; VA ECMO 4–6 L/min or more.** The IABP only augments native output and needs some (most sources give 0.5–1 L/min); the Impella’s output depends on the model (2.5 about 2.5 L/min, CP about 3.5–4, 5.0/5.5 about 5–5.5); ECMO can provide a full cardiac output and gas exchange.

**LV workload: IABP modestly lowers afterload; Impella directly unloads the LV; VA ECMO increases LV afterload and may need a vent.** The Impella removes blood from the LV, lowering its volume, wall stress and oxygen use; retrograde ECMO flow does the opposite (ACLS-84). Evidence: IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit, and the 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline lists routine IABP as no benefit (3); ECLS-SHOCK (420 patients) found no fall in 30-day mortality with early VA ECMO in infarct-related shock (47.8 vs 49.0%) and more bleeding; DanGer Shock (360 STEMI-shock patients) found lower 180-day mortality with Impella CP (45.8 vs 58.5%) at the cost of more bleeding, limb ischaemia and RRT, and microaxial support is now 2a in selected patients.
mimic: IABP vs continuous-flow devices
Only the IABP needs a native rhythm and output; Impella, TandemHeart and VA ECMO do not.
traps: “Only the Impella works despite an irregular rhythm” (keyed answer)
Only the IABP needs synchrony; TandemHeart and VA ECMO are equally rhythm-independent, and ECMO even supports VF. On the exam pick the keyed Impella if offered, as the classic contrast to the IABP.
“VA ECMO unloads the LV because it gives the most flow”
It raises LV afterload; most flow, least unloading.
decode: Refractory shock with rapid AF — device that does not need cardiac synchrony? [DocT GT]
Impella CP as keyed; strictly, TandemHeart and VA ECMO also qualify, only the IABP does not.
Rank IABP, Impella, VA ECMO by flow, and say which unloads the LV [pattern]
IABP < Impella < VA ECMO; Impella unloads, ECMO loads.
ACLS-85.punch: Flow rises from IABP to Impella to VA ECMO, but only the Impella empties the LV and only the IABP depends on the rhythm; ECMO’s full flow loads the ventricle, which is why it is sometimes paired with an Impella.

spine: Recognise, call, compress
An unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally is in arrest until proved otherwise, so call, send for the AED and start hard, fast compressions with as few pauses as possible.
Shock early, pause little
The AED goes on while compressions continue; the only pauses allowed are analysis and one shock, because coronary perfusion pressure collapses within seconds and the next shock depends on it.
The newborn needs ventilation first
Neonatal arrest is asphyxial, so warming, opening the airway and effective positive-pressure ventilation fix most babies; compressions and adrenaline follow only when proven ventilation fails.
Lung or heart: VV or VA
VV ECMO only oxygenates and needs the patient’s own heart to deliver the blood; VA ECMO also replaces the pump, so shock or arrest decides VA.
ECPR buys time for a fix
VA ECMO during refractory arrest works only in a selected patient, cannulated within about an hour, with a reversible cause that can be treated straight away.
Retrograde flow and the device ladder
Peripheral VA ECMO pumps blood backwards up the aorta, which explains Harlequin hypoxaemia, LV distension and leg ischaemia, and why an LV-unloading Impella is sometimes added.
CVS08E.primer: During CPR the heart is perfused only between compressions, by the gap between aortic diastolic and right-atrial pressure; it takes many compressions to build that gap and seconds to lose it. A defibrillator works best on a heart that has just been perfused. A newborn, unlike an adult, rarely arrests from a rhythm problem: the lungs have to open at birth, and failure to breathe causes the bradycardia. ECMO drains venous blood, oxygenates it and returns it either to a vein (VV, lung support only) or to an artery (VA, lung and circulation).

AD-01.intro: Step 1 is who tears. The typical patient is an older hypertensive man, and the timing follows the body’s own pressure peaks. There is no linked question; the card is the profile behind every vignette in this deck.
why: **Males, 5th to 7th decades.** In IRAD about 65% are men and the mean age is about 63; younger patients (under 40) point to Marfan syndrome, a bicuspid valve, pregnancy or cocaine.

**Higher during the daytime, peak 8 to 10 am.** Blood pressure, heart rate and catecholamines surge after waking, which raises wall stress at the time a weak media is most likely to give way (ESC 2024 puts the peak at 8–9 am).
**Most common in winter.** Cold raises sympathetic tone and blood pressure; ESC 2024 notes a January peak in the Northern Hemisphere.

**Ascending aorta involvement.** Untreated type A dissection kills about 1–2% per hour in the first 48 hours through rupture into the pericardium, coronary occlusion and acute aortic regurgitation (AD-12).
mimic: Dissection vs ACS in a hypertensive man in the morning
Both peak in the morning in the same patient; pain that is maximal at onset and moves to the back, with a pulse deficit, points to dissection (AD-15).
traps: “Dissection is a disease of young men with Marfan syndrome”
Most patients are hypertensive men in their 60s; Marfan explains the minority who are young.
decode: Which segment carries the highest mortality? [pattern]
Ascending aorta (type A).
Circadian or seasonal peak of dissection [pattern]
Morning (about 8–10 am) and winter.
AD-01.punch: Dissection strikes older hypertensive men, in the morning and in winter, when pressure surges; involvement of the ascending aorta is what kills fastest.

AD-02.intro: Step 1 continues with what weakens the wall. Two kinds of factor combine: things that raise the stress on the media (hypertension above all) and things that make the media weaker (connective-tissue disease, age). The one real question asks what Marfan patients die of.
why: **Hypertension: the most common predisposing factor.** Present in about three quarters of patients. Years of high pressure raise wall tension (Laplace) and damage the medial vasa vasorum, so the media degenerates.

**Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.** Marfan (fibrillin-1) and vascular Ehlers-Danlos (type III collagen) build a structurally weak media; dissection or rupture of the aorta is the leading cause of death in Marfan syndrome. Mitral valve prolapse is commoner in Marfan but rarely fatal.

**Atherosclerosis (changes vessel-wall structure), hyperlipidaemia, gene mutation, infectious disease, smoking.** Atherosclerosis causes penetrating ulcers more than classic dissection; genetic aortopathies (Loeys-Dietz, familial thoracic aortic disease) and aortitis weaken the wall directly.
**Elderly men: males, 5th to 7th decades.** Age itself thins and fragments the elastic media (AD-03).
mimic: Marfan: dissection vs mitral valve prolapse
MVP is the commonest cardiac finding; aortic dissection or rupture is the commonest cause of death.
traps: “Mitral valve prolapse or heart failure is the commonest cause of death in Marfan”
MVP is commoner but far less lethal; aortic dissection or rupture kills most Marfan patients, which is why their aortic root is replaced early.
decode: Most common cause of death in Marfan syndrome [Marrow]
Rupture of aortic dissection.
Most common predisposing factor for dissection [pattern]
Hypertension.
AD-02.punch: Hypertension is the commonest cause because it loads the media for years; connective-tissue disorders make the media weak from birth, and in Marfan the aorta, not the mitral valve, is what kills.

AD-03.intro: Step 1 ends at the microscope: the common pathway of every risk factor is a media that has lost its elastic structure. Not asked; a short card.
why: **Cystic medial necrosis.** Pools of mucoid (proteoglycan) material replace smooth muscle cells; despite the name there are no true cysts and no necrosis of the classic kind. It is the classic lesion of Marfan syndrome but also appears with age and hypertension.
**Elastin fragmentation.** Broken elastic lamellae mean the media can no longer spread the stress of each beat, so it splits along a plane.
**Fibrosis.** Scar replaces elastic tissue, making the wall stiff rather than strong.
**Medionecrosis.** Loss of smooth muscle cells in the media, often from vasa vasorum ischaemia in long-standing hypertension.
mimic: Medial degeneration vs atherosclerosis
Dissection starts in a degenerate media; atherosclerosis is an intimal disease that causes penetrating ulcers and aneurysms.
traps: “Cystic medial necrosis means cysts in the aortic wall”
It is mucoid degeneration with loss of elastic fibres and smooth muscle; there are no true cysts.
decode: Characteristic histology of the aortic wall in Marfan/dissection [pattern]
Cystic medial necrosis with elastin fragmentation.
AD-03.punch: Every risk factor ends in the same media: fragmented elastin and lost smooth muscle (cystic medial necrosis), which splits instead of stretching.

AD-04.intro: Step 2 begins with the tear itself. Once blood enters the wall, the false lumen it creates is what causes every later complication. Not asked directly, but each complication card builds on this sequence.
why: **Tear in the intima.** Usually in the right lateral wall of the ascending aorta a few centimetres above the valve, or just beyond the left subclavian, where the wall stress is highest.
**Blood dissects through the media, creating a false lumen.** Pulsatile flow drives a column of blood along the weak plane, antegrade and sometimes retrograde.

**Outer one-third of the media, where the vasa vasorum run.** The plane lies in the outer media, so the outer wall of the false lumen is thin; that is why the false lumen can rupture outward into the pericardium, pleura or mediastinum. A bleed from the vasa vasorum without an intimal tear is an intramural haematoma.
**Double-barrelled aorta: a true lumen and a false lumen.** The intimal flap that separates them is what CT and echo look for (AD-17).

**False lumen compresses the true lumen → impaired flow → malperfusion syndrome.** The false lumen often carries higher pressure, so it bulges into the true lumen (dynamic obstruction) or extends into a branch and occludes it (static obstruction) (AD-05).
mimic: Classic dissection vs intramural haematoma
Dissection has an intimal tear and a flap with flow in two lumens; IMH is crescentic wall thickening with no flap and no flow.
traps: “The false lumen lies between intima and media”
The plane is within the media, in its outer third.
decode: Layer in which the cleavage plane forms [pattern]
The media (outer third).
AD-04.punch: An intimal tear lets blood split the outer media; the false lumen then either ruptures outward through its thin wall or squeezes the true lumen and its branches, and that is the whole disease.

AD-05.intro: Step 2: when the false lumen compresses or extends into a branch, the organ supplied by that branch fails, and the presentation follows the branch. Not asked directly, but malperfusion turns a dissection into a ‘complicated’ one (AD-13) and drives the GT pairing question on AD-09.
why: **Coronary: MI or acute coronary syndrome.** When a coronary is involved it is usually the right ostium, giving an inferior ST-elevation pattern (AD-15). Only type A can do this.
**Cerebral: stroke or stroke-like symptoms.** Extension into the innominate or left carotid; again a type A (or arch) feature.
**Spinal cord: paraplegia or paraparesis.** Intercostal arteries arising from the false lumen lose flow; the artery of Adamkiewicz (T8–T12) is the critical one (AD-28).
**Renal: oliguria and acute kidney injury.** The left renal artery often arises from the false lumen (AD-07).
**Visceral: gut ischaemia, with abdominal pain and lactic acidosis.** Coeliac or superior mesenteric involvement; ESC 2024 gives mesenteric malperfusion a mortality of 65–95%.
**Limb: numbness, weakness or pain.** Iliac or subclavian compression gives a pulse deficit and an inter-arm or arm-leg pressure difference.
mimic: Coronary or cerebral vs visceral or renal malperfusion
Coronary and cerebral need the ascending aorta or arch (type A); visceral, renal and leg need the descending or abdominal aorta (DeBakey I or III).
traps: “Mesenteric malperfusion causes early abdominal tenderness”
Pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen with rising lactate is the early picture; peritonism is late.
decode: New paraplegia in a descending dissection — which artery? [pattern]
Artery of Adamkiewicz (intercostals T8–T12).
Dissection with rising lactate and abdominal pain [pattern]
Mesenteric malperfusion: the coeliac or SMA is compromised.
AD-05.punch: Each branch the false lumen squeezes gives its own syndrome, and which syndromes are possible depends on which part of the aorta is dissected.

AD-06.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Propagation and dP/dt
AD-06.intro: Step 2 asks what makes the tear spread. The answer, the steepness of each pressure upstroke, is why the drug order in AD-19 matters. The one real question is a type A dissection with a heart rate of 112, and a third of the cohort chose something other than a beta-blocker.
why: **Shear stress, a function of pressure over time, dP/dt.** Each systole drives a pressure wave into the flap; the faster pressure rises, the harder the column of blood pushes into the plane of the dissection and the further it travels. Mean pressure alone does not capture this.

**Influenced more by heart rate than by mean arterial pressure.** A faster heart means more upstrokes per minute and a steeper upstroke (more contractility, shorter ejection time). Halving the rate halves the number of pushes into the tear.

**Lowering the heart rate is critical to reduce propagation.** Hence a beta-blocker first, to HR about 60, before any vasodilator. A vasodilator alone lowers pressure but triggers baroreflex tachycardia and a stronger contraction, which raises dP/dt.
mimic: Dissection vs other hypertensive emergencies

In most hypertensive emergencies the target is the pressure; in dissection it is dP/dt, so the heart rate is controlled first and the pressure is lowered much further and faster (SBP <120 within the first hour).
traps: “Start nitroprusside: the BP of 182/93 is the problem” (38% of the cohort chose something other than esmolol)
Nitroprusside alone causes reflex tachycardia and raises dP/dt; it is added only after the beta-blocker.
“Get a TEE or consult cardiology first”
CT has already made the diagnosis; more imaging or a consult only delays anti-impulse therapy and surgery.
decode: Type A on CT, HR 112, BP 182/93, AR murmur — next best step? [DocT GT]
Start an esmolol infusion (62%), then arrange surgery.
Which variable most influences propagation? [pattern]
Heart rate (dP/dt), more than MAP.
AD-06.punch: A dissection spreads with every steep upstroke, so the heart rate is lowered first; a vasodilator given alone makes the heart beat faster and harder, and the tear spreads.

AD-07.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → True vs false lumen
AD-07.intro: Step 2: telling the lumens apart matters because TEVAR has to land in the true lumen and because the branches arising from the false lumen are the ones at risk. The real question asks how echo separates them; nearly half of the cohort picked a feature of the false lumen.
why: **True lumen is anteromedial.** In the descending aorta the false lumen usually spirals along the outer (left posterolateral) curve. Position helps on CT but is not reliable; flow and behaviour through the cardiac cycle are better.
**Coeliac, superior mesenteric and right renal arteries.** These usually stay with the true lumen.
**Left renal artery, often from the false lumen.** That is why left kidney malperfusion and AKI are common in type B and DeBakey I dissections.
mimic: Which lumen is larger?
The false lumen usually is; a small lumen is not proof it is false.
traps: “The false lumen is usually smaller” or “expands in systole” (56% right)
Both describe the true lumen in reverse: the false lumen is usually larger and is compressed in systole.
“Cobwebs are seen in the true lumen”
Cobwebs (strands of residual media) are a feature of the false lumen.
decode: Descending dissection — most helpful echo feature for the true lumen? [DocT GT]
Colour Doppler flow in phase with the cardiac cycle, systolic expansion (56%).
Which renal artery usually arises from the false lumen? [pattern]
Left.
AD-07.punch: The true lumen expands and fills forward in systole; the false lumen is larger, slower, has cobwebs, and often feeds the left renal artery.

table.title: Echo: true vs false lumen
head: Feature
True lumen
False lumen
rows: Systolic, forward, in phase with the cardiac cycle
Slow, delayed or reversed; spontaneous contrast or thrombus

AD-08.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → IRAD time classification
AD-08.intro: Step 3 begins with time, because risk of death and rupture falls steeply after the first days. Not asked directly; the trap is that IRAD and ESC use different time bands.
why: **Hyperacute: onset to 24 hours.** The highest mortality: untreated type A dies at about 1–2% per hour in the first 48 hours.
**Acute: 2 to 7 days.** Risk is still high; most early deaths happen in the first week.
**Subacute: 8 to 30 days.** The flap is still mobile, so TEVAR can still reshape the aorta.
**Chronic: beyond 30 days.** The flap stiffens and the false lumen thickens, so remodelling after TEVAR is less likely.

**Consider acute and unstable up to 14 days from onset.** This matches the ESC 2024 bands: hyperacute <24 h, acute 1–14 days, subacute 15–90 days, chronic >90 days. The ESC ‘subacute’ window (14–90 days) is the one in which TEVAR for uncomplicated type B is considered (AD-27).
mimic: IRAD subacute vs ESC subacute
8–30 days in IRAD; 15–90 days in ESC 2024, the window used for elective TEVAR.
traps: “Acute means the first 7 days, so a 10-day dissection is stable”
It is still treated as acute and unstable up to 14 days.
decode: Dissection 3 weeks old — which IRAD phase? [pattern]
Subacute (8–30 days).
AD-08.punch: IRAD splits time at 24 hours, 7 days and 30 days, ESC at 24 hours, 14 days and 90 days; either way, treat the first two weeks as unstable.

AD-09.intro: Step 3: DeBakey classifies by where the dissection starts and how far it extends. Both real questions were answered badly (12% and 38%), because each needs you to work out which branches and complications are anatomically possible.
why: **Type I: ascending AND descending aorta.** Starts in the ascending aorta and runs at least to the arch, usually beyond. Every complication is possible: coronary, cerebral, AR, tamponade, visceral, renal, spinal and limb.
**Type II: ascending aorta ONLY.** Confined proximal to the innominate artery. It can cause AR, tamponade and coronary occlusion, but it cannot reach the mesenteric or renal arteries.

**Type III: descending aorta ONLY.** Starts beyond the left subclavian. IIIa stops above the diaphragm (descending thoracic only); IIIb extends below it into the abdominal aorta. Both are Stanford B. It cannot cause AR, tamponade or coronary occlusion (unless it extends backwards into the arch).
mimic: DeBakey IIIa vs IIIb
IIIa is limited to the thoracic descending aorta; IIIb extends below the diaphragm.
DeBakey II vs Stanford A
All DeBakey II is Stanford A, but Stanford A also includes DeBakey I.
traps: “A dissection of the descending thoracic aorta is DeBakey III” (bare III, or IIIb; 38% right)
With the subdivision offered, thoracic-only is IIIa; IIIb goes below the diaphragm.
“Which pairing is NOT correct?” — only one option looks wrong (12% right)

Two are wrong: DeBakey II (ascending only) cannot cause high lactate, high INR and AKI from visceral malperfusion, and DeBakey III (descending only) cannot cause a new AR murmur. DocT keys A (the DeBakey II pairing); pick A.
decode: Dissection of the descending thoracic aorta — DeBakey type? [DocT GT]
IIIa (38%).
Which complication–classification pairing is wrong? [DocT GT]
Visceral malperfusion with DeBakey II (12%); AR with DeBakey III is also wrong.
AD-09.punch: DeBakey I is everywhere, II is ascending only, III is descending only (IIIa thoracic, IIIb below the diaphragm), and each type can cause only the complications its segment supplies.

AD-10.intro: Step 3: Stanford simplifies DeBakey to the one question that decides treatment: is the ascending aorta involved? The one real question is the GT pairing question shared with AD-09.
why: **Type A: involves the aorta proximal to the left subclavian origin.** Strictly, type A is any involvement of the ascending aorta, wherever the tear starts; an arch-only dissection is non-A non-B (AD-11).
**Type B: involves the aorta distal to the left subclavian origin.** Without ascending involvement.
**DeBakey I and II = Stanford A; DeBakey III = Stanford B.** DeBakey adds extent; Stanford keeps only what changes management.
**Deciding feature: is the ascending aorta involved?** If yes, the risks are tamponade, coronary occlusion and AR, which only surgery fixes, so type A is a surgical emergency (AD-12).
mimic: Stanford A from a descending tear
A tear in the descending aorta that extends backwards into the ascending aorta is still type A.
traps: “Elevated troponin cannot occur in Stanford A”
It can: the flap can occlude a coronary ostium. Troponin with Stanford A is a correct pairing.
decode: Pairing of complications with Stanford and DeBakey types [DocT GT]
Troponin rise with Stanford A and hemiplegia with DeBakey I are correct pairings.
AD-10.punch: Stanford asks only whether the ascending aorta is involved, because that is what decides between the operating theatre and the ICU.

AD-11.intro: Step 3 ends with the classification the 2024 ESC guideline adopted. It keeps Stanford’s logic but adds where the entry tear is and whether organs are ischaemic, because both change the operation. Not asked yet.
why: **T = Type of dissection; E = Entry tear location; M = Malperfusion (carries prognostic and therapeutic weight).** E0 means no entry seen; E1 entry in the ascending aorta (zone 0), E2 in the arch, E3 in the descending aorta. M0 none, M1 coronary, M2 supra-aortic, M3 spinal, visceral, renal or limb, each marked + if clinically symptomatic.
**Type A, Type B, non-A non-B.** ESC 2024 defines non-A non-B as dissections limited to the arch, or retrograde from the descending aorta into the arch, without involving the ascending aorta.

**Arch involvement WITHOUT ascending involvement: unclassifiable in Stanford, now non-A non-B.** These behave between A and B: they rarely need emergency sternotomy but often need arch or hybrid repair.
mimic: Non-A non-B vs type B
Type B stays distal to the left subclavian; non-A non-B involves the arch without the ascending aorta.
traps: “TEM replaced the need to assess malperfusion clinically”
M is graded with a + sign for clinical signs, so the bedside picture is part of the class.
decode: Classification used by ESC 2024 with a non-A non-B category [pattern]
TEM (type, entry, malperfusion).
AD-11.punch: TEM keeps Stanford’s A and B, adds non-A non-B for arch-only dissection, and records the entry tear and malperfusion because they decide the operation.

AD-12.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Management and mortality by type
AD-12.intro: Step 6 starts with the decision between theatre and ICU. The numbers invert between types: surgery saves type A and harms uncomplicated type B. The real question is the same type A vignette as AD-06, testing what comes before the surgeon arrives.
why: **Preferred: SURGERY for type A, MEDICAL for type B.** Type A kills by tamponade, coronary occlusion and AR, which no drug fixes. Uncomplicated type B rarely ruptures early, and an operation on the descending aorta carries the risks of paraplegia, renal failure and a thoracotomy.

**Medical mortality: ~50% for type A, ~15% for type B.** ESC 2024 gives about 50% within 48 hours for untreated type A (1–2% per hour); IRAD 2000 gave 58% for medically treated type A and 10.7% for type B.

**Surgical mortality: 15–20% for type A, ~30% for type B.** ESC 2024 quotes 17–25% perioperative mortality for type A; IRAD 2000 gave 26% for type A and 31.4% for surgically treated type B. Surgery in type B is usually reserved for complicated cases, which partly explains the high figure; TEVAR has largely replaced it (AD-27).
mimic: Type A: drug first or surgery first?
Both: start anti-impulse therapy at once and go to surgery; drugs are a bridge, not the treatment.
traps: “Type A on CT — order a TEE” or “consult cardiology” before treatment (62% right)
The diagnosis is made; esmolol starts now and the surgeon is called.
“Surgery improves survival in all dissections”
Open surgery roughly doubles mortality in uncomplicated type B; medical therapy (then TEVAR if complicated or high risk) is preferred.
decode: Type A on CT, tachycardic, hypertensive — next best step? [DocT GT]
Start esmolol (62%), with urgent surgery.
Mortality of medically treated type A in the first 48 h [pattern]
About 50%, 1–2% per hour.
AD-12.punch: Type A goes to theatre because its killers are mechanical and mortality without surgery is about 50%; uncomplicated type B stays on drugs because surgery there roughly doubles mortality.

AD-13.intro: Step 3: ‘complicated’ is the label that moves a type B dissection from medical treatment to TEVAR (AD-27). Not asked directly.
why: **Rupture or impending rupture.** Blood outside the aorta (haemothorax, mediastinal or periaortic haematoma) or rapid expansion.
**Intractable pain.** Pain that persists or recurs despite full analgesia and anti-impulse therapy means the dissection is still extending.
**Malperfusion syndrome.** Organ or limb ischaemia from the false lumen (AD-05).
**Cardiac tamponade.** Rupture into the pericardium, a type A feature (AD-25).

**Severe aortic valve insufficiency.** Also type A. ESC 2024 also counts rapid aortic expansion, paraplegia, periaortic haematoma and uncontrolled hypertension; ‘high-risk’ uncomplicated type B (commonly cited features: aorta >40 mm, false lumen >20 mm, entry tear >10 mm) is a separate group that may get TEVAR in the subacute phase.
mimic: Complicated vs high-risk uncomplicated type B
Complicated (rupture, malperfusion, intractable pain) → TEVAR now (I, B); high-risk uncomplicated (large aorta or false lumen, large entry tear) → consider TEVAR at 14–90 days (IIa, B).
traps: “Hypertension alone makes a dissection complicated”
Only refractory hypertension despite full therapy is counted, and it signals ongoing extension.
decode: Type B with leg ischaemia or rising lactate — management? [pattern]
Complicated → TEVAR.
AD-13.punch: Rupture, intractable pain, malperfusion, tamponade or severe AR makes a dissection complicated, and in type B that means TEVAR rather than drugs alone.

AD-14.intro: Step 4 is recognition at the bedside. The signs follow the anatomy: pain from the tearing wall, pressure differences from compressed branches, a diastolic murmur from a disrupted valve, and shock from tamponade or rupture. The linked real question shows a classic picture and asks for the imaging test, where DocT’s key is outdated (AD-17).
why: **Sudden-onset severe ‘ripping’ or ‘tearing’ chest pain, back pain radiating to the chest.** The key feature is that the pain is maximal at onset (85% abrupt in IRAD); only about half call it tearing, and sharp is the commonest word. Anterior chest pain suggests type A, back or abdominal pain type B; about 6% have no pain.
**HIGH blood pressure.** Typical of type B; type A patients are more often normotensive or hypotensive because of tamponade, AR or rupture.

**Difference between arms >20 mmHg (also radial pulse deficit).** The flap compresses the subclavian or innominate; a pulse deficit is seen in only about 15%, so its absence does not exclude dissection. Measure the pressure in both arms before giving thrombolysis.

**Diastolic murmur: aortic insufficiency.** Heard in about a third. The flap dilates the root, tears the commissures or prolapses through the valve. A murmur at the right sternal border points to root dilatation, as in the vignette.
**Low BP, muffled heart sounds.** Rupture into the pericardium; with raised JVP this is Beck’s triad.

**LATE sign (also collapse or syncope; focal neuro deficit → limb weakness, paraesthesia).** Hypotension means tamponade, rupture, severe AR or coronary occlusion, and it carries the worst prognosis. Syncope (about 9%) often means tamponade or carotid involvement.
mimic: Dissection vs ACS pain
Dissection: maximal at onset, tearing or sharp, moving to the back, pulse or pressure asymmetry. ACS: builds over minutes, pressing, with no asymmetry.
traps: “TEE is the preferred test” for a stable patient with BP 205/110 (DocT key; 40% chose it)
The key is outdated: ESC 2024 makes ECG-gated CT neck to pelvis first line (I, C). For a stable patient choose CT; TEE is for the unstable or for the theatre.
“No pulse deficit, so no dissection”
Pulse deficits are present in only about 15%.
decode: Tearing pain to the jaw, BP 205/110, diastolic murmur, widened mediastinum — preferred test? [DocT QBank]
CT angiography (DocT keys TEE, 40%).
Hypotension in dissection: early or late? [pattern]
Late, and ominous (tamponade, rupture, AR).
AD-14.punch: Pain maximal at onset with a pressure difference or a new diastolic murmur means dissection; high BP is usual, and hypotension means the aorta has ruptured into the pericardium or the valve has failed.

AD-15.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Dissection mimicking ACS
AD-15.intro: Step 4: the commonest misdiagnosis, and the one with the worst consequence, because the treatment for ACS can kill a dissection patient. Not asked directly here, but the GT question on AD-17 is built on this overlap.
why: **Misdiagnosed as ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROME; consider dissection once ACS is ruled out.** Both happen in older hypertensive men with severe chest pain, and most dissection ECGs are abnormal.

**Non-specific ST-T changes and T-wave inversion, especially when the dissection involves the coronary artery origins.** In IRAD, 41% had non-specific ST-T changes and 15% ischaemic changes, but only about 3% a new infarct pattern. When it happens, it is usually the right coronary ostium, so an inferior STEMI.
**Coronary origin involvement → true myocardial injury, mimicking MI.** Troponin also rises from hypotension, tachycardia and LVH strain, so a positive troponin does not exclude dissection.

**THROMBOLYSIS given for a presumed MI can be catastrophic.** Lysis or heparin turns the false lumen into a bleeding cavity and can cause tamponade. Aortic dissection is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis (MI-53), and the pressure in both arms is checked before lysis.
mimic: Inferior STEMI from RCA occlusion vs from type A dissection
Look for a pressure or pulse difference, AR murmur, widened mediastinum or effusion on bedside echo; image the aorta before lysis or the catheter lab.
traps: “Normal troponin excludes dissection” or “raised troponin confirms ACS”
Troponin is often normal in dissection and can be raised by it; it does not separate the two.
decode: Inferior STEMI with BP difference between arms — next step? [pattern]
Image the aorta (CT) before thrombolysis or anticoagulation.
AD-15.punch: Dissection imitates ACS, usually through the right coronary, and the treatment for ACS can kill it, so check both arms and look at the aorta before lysis.

AD-16.intro: Step 4: the bedside tests raise or lower suspicion but never settle it. The one real question asks which chest X-ray sign is seen.
why: **Widened mediastinum: 50%.** IRAD found a widened mediastinum in about 62% and an abnormal aortic contour in about 50%. Other signs: a double or irregular aortic contour, displacement of intimal calcification more than 5 mm inside the outer aortic wall (calcium sign; some texts use 1 cm), and a left pleural effusion.
**Falsely reassuring → missed diagnosis.** About 12% of chest X-rays are completely normal (IRAD). ESC 2024: an X-ray and ECG are done to exclude other causes, and normal findings must not delay CT.

**Leukocytosis or thrombocytopenia (platelet consumption).** The false lumen is a large thrombogenic surface; platelets and fibrinogen are consumed and D-dimer rises. A D-dimer under 500 ng/mL makes acute dissection unlikely (ESC 2024).
**Gut ischaemia: compromised coeliac or superior mesenteric arteries.** Lactate rises with mesenteric malperfusion, or with shock; a rising lactate after repair calls for repeat CT (AD-26).
mimic: Widened mediastinum: dissection vs traumatic aortic injury
Trauma: deceleration injury at the isthmus; dissection: spontaneous pain in a hypertensive patient. Both go to CT.
traps: “A normal chest X-ray excludes dissection”
About one in eight are normal.
decode: Feature of dissection on chest X-ray [Marrow]
Abnormal aortic contour (also a widened mediastinum, calcium sign).
Low-risk patient with D-dimer <500 ng/mL [pattern]
Dissection unlikely.
AD-16.punch: The X-ray shows a widened mediastinum or abnormal contour in about half to two thirds, is normal in one in eight, and can never rule dissection out; only CT does that.

AD-17.intro: Step 4 ends with the test that decides. Four real questions ask which test to choose and what it shows, and the choice depends on one thing: whether the patient can safely go to the scanner. DocT’s QBank key is outdated, and its GT question shows how an effusion leads people into a lethal step.
