why: **TTE: shows severe AR if the root or valve is involved; may miss the dissection.** It sees the root, valve, pericardium and LV well but only parts of the aorta. Its role is the first bedside look: an effusion, AR or a dilated root in a patient with chest pain means type A until proved otherwise.

**TEE: superior to TTE, sees nearly all the aorta (blind spot: distal ascending aorta and proximal arch, behind the trachea); useful if CT is contraindicated or the patient cannot be transported.** It shows an undulating flap separating the lumens, colour flow in both lumens, entry and exit tears, false-lumen stasis or thrombus, and intramural haematoma (crescentic wall thickening without a flap). ESC 2024 recommends it to guide peri-operative management (I, C): in theatre it confirms the entry tear, valve mechanism and coronary involvement.

**CT aortogram: the DEFINITIVE test, whole aorta; preferred over routine contrast CT chest or CT pulmonary angiography.** ESC 2024 first-line test: ECG-gated contrast CT from neck to pelvis (I, C), sensitivity 100% and specificity 98%. ECG gating removes motion artefact at the root that can mimic a flap; neck to pelvis shows the extent, the branches and malperfusion.
**MR angiography: detailed but slow, unsuitable for unstable patients.** It is used for follow-up and when contrast or radiation must be avoided.
mimic: Stable vs unstable suspected dissection
Stable → CT; too unstable to move → TEE in the ED or theatre (with bedside TTE first). The same split applies to PE: stable → CTPA, unstable → bedside echo.
CT aortogram vs CTPA
A CTPA times contrast for the pulmonary arteries and can miss the aorta; a suspected dissection needs an aortic (ECG-gated) protocol.
traps: “TEE is the preferred investigation” for a stable patient with BP 205/110 (DocT key; 40% chose it)
The key is outdated. ESC 2024 makes CT first line; TEE is for the unstable, CT contraindication, or in theatre. If the patient is stable and CT is offered, pick CT.
“Pericardiocentesis” or “coronary angiography” for chest pain, BP 200/89, negative troponin and an effusion (24% right)

The effusion with a normal troponin and hypertension points to type A dissection; pericardiocentesis can restore pressure and speed rupture, and coronary angiography delays surgery. Image the aorta with CT, then go to theatre.
“TEE sees the whole aorta”
The trachea hides the distal ascending aorta and proximal arch.
decode: Stable, tearing pain, BP 205/110, AR murmur, wide mediastinum — preferred test? [DocT QBank]
CT angiography (DocT keys TEE; 40%).
Chest pain, BP 200/89, troponin negative, moderate effusion on POCUS — next step? [DocT GT]
Contrast CT of the chest (24%), not pericardiocentesis.
CT angiogram with an intimal flap and two lumens [DocT QBank]
Aortic dissection (68%).
TEE findings of dissection [Marrow]
All: flap, flow in both lumens, entry and exit tears, false-lumen thrombus, IMH.
AD-17.punch: If the patient can go to the scanner, ECG-gated CT from neck to pelvis is the test; TEE is for the patient who cannot be moved and for the theatre; and an effusion with chest pain and hypertension is dissection until CT says otherwise.

AD-18.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Stabilisation and targets
AD-18.intro: Step 5 begins anti-impulse therapy: pain, heart rate and pressure, in that order, because each drives dP/dt. The one real question tests the drug sequence, which is covered in AD-19.
why: **Opioid (morphine): cuts sympathetic drive → prevents tachycardia and further shear stress (dP/dt).** Pain releases catecholamines that raise heart rate and contractility; analgesia is part of reaching the targets (ESC 2024: adequate pain control, I, C). Persistent pain despite analgesia means the dissection is still extending (AD-13).
**HR <60 bpm.** ESC 2024: HR ≤60 b.p.m. (I, B). The 2022 ACC/AHA guideline gives 60–80 b.p.m. (class 1, C-LD). In the exam, ‘about 60’ fits both.

**SBP <120 mmHg.** Both guidelines; ACC/AHA adds ‘or the lowest BP that maintains end-organ perfusion’ (class 1, C-LD), and most protocols aim to reach it within about the first hour. ESC 2024 accepts a higher pressure when an organ is malperfused. Heart rate first, then pressure.

**Arterial and central lines: avoid rapid BP fluctuations.** An arterial line, ideally in the arm with the higher pressure (the other arm may be reading a compressed subclavian), allows titration of short-acting infusions beat to beat; a central line is for vasoactive drugs.
mimic: ESC vs ACC/AHA heart-rate target
ESC 2024: ≤60; ACC/AHA 2022: 60–80. Same SBP target, below 120.
traps: “Labetalol alone is wrong because it is not esmolol”
Labetalol is an acceptable first-line agent (it blocks β and α1); the key prefers esmolol then nicardipine because it follows the beta-blocker-before-vasodilator rule.
“Put the arterial line in the arm with the lower pressure”
Use the arm with the higher reading; the lower one may reflect a compressed branch and underestimate the true pressure.
decode: Type B, BP 210/115, HR 102 — initial drugs? [DocT GT]
Esmolol followed by nicardipine (59%).
HR and SBP targets in acute dissection [pattern]
HR about 60 (ESC ≤60; ACC/AHA 60–80), SBP <120 mmHg.
AD-18.punch: Treat the pain, slow the heart to about 60, then bring the systolic below 120, watching an arterial line in the arm with the higher pressure.

AD-19.intro: Step 5’s core: five real questions all test one rule, beta-blocker before vasodilator. Each distractor is a drug that lowers pressure without slowing the heart, or a slow route of giving the right drug.
why: **IV BETA-BLOCKERS: labetalol (α1 + β1 + β2), esmolol (short-acting β1, infusion), metoprolol (small boluses).** Beta-blockade lowers heart rate and contractility, so dP/dt falls before pressure does. Esmolol is preferred when the patient may not tolerate beta-blockade (asthma, borderline pressure, AR) because it wears off in about 10–20 minutes. Labetalol alone can reach both targets, since it also vasodilates; ESC 2024 calls IV labetalol the usual first choice, with esmolol an option.

**Non-dihydropyridine CCB (diltiazem); ACE inhibitor also considered.** ESC 2024 (IIa, B) and ACC/AHA 2022 (2a, B-NR): an IV non-DHP calcium blocker for rate control if beta-blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated. Diltiazem and verapamil slow the sinus and AV nodes; dihydropyridines do not.
**Nitroglycerin or sodium nitroprusside.** Nicardipine (a dihydropyridine) is the other common choice and the one used in the DocT keys.
**ONLY after or with a beta-blocker, to block reflex tachycardia.** Once the rate is controlled, the vasodilator takes the systolic below 120.

**Reflex tachycardia ↑ dP/dt → propagation.** Vasodilation drops the pressure, the baroreflex speeds the heart and strengthens contraction, and the shear on the flap rises even though the cuff reading has fallen.
mimic: Diltiazem vs nicardipine
Diltiazem (non-DHP) slows the heart and replaces a beta-blocker; nicardipine (DHP) only vasodilates and must follow one.
traps: “IV nitroprusside alone” or “nicardipine infusion alone” (76–83% right)
Monotherapy with a vasodilator causes reflex tachycardia; it is used only after a beta-blocker.
“Oral metoprolol”
Right class, wrong route: the targets must be reached within the hour, so IV.
“Sublingual nitroglycerin then an ACE inhibitor”
Uncontrolled, with no rate control; neither is first line.
“Labetalol alone is wrong” (GT4/GT5; 59–83% right)
Labetalol alone is acceptable; DocT keys esmolol then nicardipine, so pick that when both are offered.
decode: First-line drug to limit propagation [DocT GT]
IV esmolol (76%).
Type A, BP 180/100 — first-line agent? [DocT GT]
Esmolol infusion (73%).
Type B, BP 210/115, HR 102 — initial pharmacological management? [DocT GT ×2]
Esmolol followed by nicardipine (59%, 83%).
Dissection with arm BP difference on CTA — next step? [Marrow]
Esmolol.
AD-19.punch: Every dissection drug question has the same answer: an IV beta-blocker first (or diltiazem if one cannot be given), and a vasodilator only once the heart rate is controlled.

AD-20.intro: Step 5: the doses of the drugs that come first. The one real question asks only which drug to start, but the doses show why esmolol is the safest titratable choice.
why: **Esmolol (β1): bolus 500 mcg/kg over 1 min, then 50 mcg/kg/min, titrated up to 300 mcg/kg/min.** Red-cell esterases clear it with a half-life of about 9 minutes, so its effect stops within about 20 minutes, which makes it the safest choice if AR, asthma or low pressure might make beta-blockade risky.

**Labetalol bolus: 20 mg over 2 min, then 20–80 mg every 10 min.** The label gives repeat doses of 40–80 mg every 10 minutes, to a cumulative maximum of 300 mg. Its β:α ratio is about 7:1 IV, so it slows the heart and dilates the arteries.
**Labetalol infusion: load 20 mg, then 1–2 mg/min.** Its half-life is 5–8 hours, so it is harder to reverse than esmolol.
**Metoprolol: 5 mg over 2 min, repeated every 5 min, up to 3 doses.** Bolus-only control is less smooth, which is why it ranks behind the infusions.
mimic: Esmolol vs labetalol
Esmolol: pure β1, minutes-long, infusion; labetalol: β plus α1, hours-long, boluses or infusion.
traps: “Oral metoprolol to limit propagation”
Too slow; the IV route is needed to reach targets within the hour.
decode: First-line IV agent to limit propagation [DocT GT]
IV esmolol (76%).
Esmolol loading dose [pattern]
500 mcg/kg over 1 minute, then 50 mcg/kg/min.
AD-20.punch: Esmolol is the easiest beta-blocker to titrate because a 500 mcg/kg load and a 50–300 mcg/kg/min infusion wear off within minutes; labetalol (ESC 2024’s usual first choice) and IV metoprolol work equally well but last much longer.

AD-21.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Second-line doses and vasodilator toxicity
AD-21.intro: Step 5 ends with the vasodilators and the most-asked card in the deck: seven questions, six of them on what each drug does to the body with prolonged use. The key fact is the chemistry: nitroprusside carries cyanide, nitroglycerin carries nitrite.
why: **Diltiazem (non-DHP): 0.25 mg/kg over 2 min, then 5–10 mg/h, up to 15 mg/h.** It is the rate-controlling alternative when a beta-blocker is contraindicated.
**Nicardipine (DHP): 5 mg/h, increased by 2.5 mg/h every 5–15 min, max 15 mg/h.** A pure arterial dilator with no effect on the heart rate, so it follows the beta-blocker.

**Nitroprusside: 0.3 mcg/kg/min, max 10 mcg/kg/min (no more than 10 min at max); cyanide toxicity, unsuitable for prolonged use.** Each molecule releases five cyanide ions. Rhodanese uses thiosulfate to turn cyanide into thiocyanate, which the kidney excretes. Two toxicities follow. Cyanide comes early, at high doses (above about 2 mcg/kg/min) or when thiosulfate runs out: cells cannot use oxygen, so there is lactic acidosis, a high venous oxygen saturation, confusion and tachycardia. Thiocyanate builds up later, after 48–72 hours or in renal failure (toxic above about 60 mg/L on a serum level), causing confusion, psychosis and seizures. Stop the infusion and give hydroxocobalamin or sodium thiosulfate.

**Nitroglycerin: 5 mcg/min, increased by 5 mcg/min every 3–5 min (ceiling commonly quoted as 200 mcg/min).** Mostly a venodilator at low doses. Prolonged use causes headache, reflex tachycardia, tachyphylaxis within 24 hours, methaemoglobinaemia (its nitrite oxidises haemoglobin) and inhibition of platelet aggregation, but never cyanide toxicity.
mimic: Cyanide vs thiocyanate toxicity from nitroprusside
Cyanide: early, high dose, lactic acidosis and high venous saturation. Thiocyanate: late (48–72 h) or renal failure, neurotoxic, no lactic acidosis.
Hydroxocobalamin vs cyanocobalamin
Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to become cyanocobalamin, which is the harmless end product, not the antidote.
traps: GrandT1 keys “nitroglycerin” for confusion, tachycardia, acidosis and almond breath after a high-dose infusion (16% right)
The key is wrong: that is cyanide from nitroprusside, as the GT3 and AIM2 repeats and DocT’s own explanation say. Pick nitroprusside.
“Cyanide toxicity is a side effect of prolonged nitroglycerin” (41–43% right)
Nitroglycerin causes methaemoglobinaemia, headache, tachycardia and inhibited platelet aggregation; cyanide belongs to nitroprusside.
“Give thiocyanate” or “cyanocobalamin” for nitroprusside toxicity (39% right)
Thiocyanate is the toxic product, cyanocobalamin is what hydroxocobalamin becomes; the antidotes are sodium thiosulfate and hydroxocobalamin. Methylene blue treats methaemoglobinaemia.
“Urinary thiocyanate confirms it” (58% right)
Serum thiocyanate is the proper test, but among the four options it is still the best answer; an ABG shows acidosis but does not confirm the cause.
decode: 72 h of high-dose nitroprusside, altered sensorium, lactic acidosis — confirmatory test? [DocT QBank]
Thiocyanate level (58%).
Nitroprusside for 32 h in renal failure, confusion, acidosis — prevention/treatment? [DocT GT]
Sodium thiosulfate (39%).
Nitroglycerin drip for a day — least likely side effect? [DocT GT ×2]
Cyanide toxicity (41%, 43%).
High-dose infusion, confused, tachycardic, almond breath — drug? [DocT GT]
Nitroprusside (DocT keys nitroglycerin, 16%).
Most critical thing to monitor with prolonged nitroprusside [DocT GT]
Cyanide toxicity (95%).
Nitroglycerin infusion dose in hypertensive emergency [NEET 2024]
Start 5 mcg/min, titrate by 5 mcg/min every 3–5 min.
AD-21.punch: Nitroprusside carries five cyanides per molecule, so high doses or long infusions (especially in renal failure) cause lactic acidosis and confusion treated with thiosulfate or hydroxocobalamin; nitroglycerin carries nitrite, so it causes methaemoglobinaemia, never cyanide.

AD-22.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Type A repair
AD-22.intro: Step 6: type A goes to open surgery because the problems are at the root, where stents cannot yet land safely. Not asked directly.
why: **Proximity to the aortic root and involvement of the coronary origins makes endovascular repair challenging.** A stent graft needs a healthy landing zone; the ascending aorta is short, close to the valve and the coronaries, and moves with each beat.

**Resect the diseased segment → replace with a synthetic graft.** At minimum, the entry tear in the ascending aorta is removed and the graft is sewn to the reconstructed root and to the arch; ESC 2024 recommends an open distal anastomosis (under circulatory arrest, AD-23) to improve survival and false-lumen thrombosis (I, B).

**Valve involved, aortic insufficiency, or dilated root >55 mm → simultaneous aortic valve replacement.** ESC 2024 and ACC/AHA 2022: when the leaflets are normal, resuspension of the valve is preferred over replacement; root replacement with a valved conduit is for root destruction, a root aneurysm or a genetic disorder such as Marfan (I, B).
**Midline sternotomy.** On cardiopulmonary bypass, often with axillary artery cannulation so that perfusion goes into the true lumen.
mimic: AR in type A: resuspend vs replace
Normal leaflets with commissural detachment → resuspend; destroyed root, aneurysm or connective-tissue disorder → root replacement.
traps: “AR in type A always means valve replacement”
Most AR in type A is from commissural detachment with normal leaflets and is fixed by resuspension.
decode: Why type A is not treated with a stent graft [pattern]
Root and coronary ostia: no safe landing zone.
AD-22.punch: Type A is repaired openly through a sternotomy, replacing the ascending aorta with a graft and resuspending the valve unless the root itself is destroyed or diseased.

AD-23.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Hypothermic circulatory arrest
AD-23.intro: Step 6: repairing the arch means stopping flow to the brain, and cold is what makes that survivable. The one real question uses a different temperature scale altogether, and nearly half of the cohort mixed the two.
why: **Surgery on the aortic root or arch needs temporary arrest of the cerebral circulation.** No clamp can be placed on the arch without stopping flow to its branches, and the open distal anastomosis is sewn in a bloodless field.

**↓ Cerebral metabolic rate and oxygen consumption → protects neurons.** Cerebral metabolic rate falls by about 6–7% per °C; at about 18 °C the brain tolerates roughly 30–40 minutes of arrest, longer with selective cerebral perfusion (AD-24).

**Profound ≤14 °C, deep 14.1–20 °C, moderate 20.1–28 °C, mild 28.1–34 °C.** These are the 2013 international consensus grades for circulatory arrest. With antegrade cerebral perfusion many centres now use moderate hypothermia, which reduces bleeding and bypass time.
mimic: 30 °C: surgical vs accidental scale
On the surgical scale 30 °C is mild; on the accidental scale it is moderate. A TTM or ED stem uses the accidental scale.
traps: “30 °C during TTM is mild hypothermia” (55% right)
Clinical and accidental scales call 28–32 °C moderate; the surgical scale (mild 28.1–34 °C) applies only to circulatory arrest in theatre.
“Below 14 °C is deep hypothermia”
By the 2013 consensus, ≤14 °C is profound; deep is 14.1–20 °C.
decode: Post-arrest TTM, core falls to 30 °C — grade? [DocT GT]
Moderate (55%).
Temperature range of deep hypothermic circulatory arrest [pattern]
AD-23.punch: Arch surgery stops cerebral flow, so the brain is cooled to cut its oxygen use; know which scale the question uses, because 30 °C is mild in theatre and moderate everywhere else.

AD-24.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Cerebral perfusion during arch surgery
AD-24.intro: Step 6: cold alone buys limited time, so the brain is also perfused during the arrest. Not asked directly.
why: **Retrograde: through the SUPERIOR VENA CAVA.** Cold oxygenated blood is pumped backwards up the SVC into the cerebral veins at low pressure (about 25 mmHg). It cools the brain evenly and flushes air and debris out of the arch vessels, but delivers limited oxygen and can cause cerebral oedema.

**Antegrade: via a balloon-tipped catheter or axillary artery cannulation.** Blood flows forwards into the arch vessels, either through the right axillary artery (with the innominate clamped) or through cannulas placed directly into the vessel ostia. It gives physiological flow and allows longer, warmer arrests, which is why it is now the commoner choice.
mimic: Retrograde vs antegrade cerebral perfusion
Retrograde: SVC, venous route, mainly cooling and de-airing; antegrade: arterial route, real nutrient flow, longer safe arrest.
traps: “Retrograde perfusion goes through the carotids backwards”
It goes through the SVC and the cerebral veins.
decode: Route of retrograde cerebral perfusion [pattern]
Superior vena cava.
AD-24.punch: Retrograde perfusion goes up the SVC and mainly cools and de-airs; antegrade perfusion goes through the axillary artery or ostial balloon catheters and actually feeds the brain.

AD-25.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Tamponade in type A
AD-25.intro: Step 6: tamponade in type A is a rupture into the pericardium, and the clot in the pericardium is all that stops it bleeding. Not asked directly here, but the AD-17 GT question shows why pericardiocentesis is a trap.
why: **SLOW drainage, avoiding rapid haemodynamic change that worsens the dissection.** The pericardial pressure is holding back the bleeding; drop it suddenly and the systemic pressure rises, so the false lumen ruptures freely.

**Drain 30–40 mL, then wait for haemodynamic improvement.** Small volumes restore filling and cardiac output; the aim is a pressure just enough to perfuse. ESC 2024 allows an emergency pericardial puncture only as a temporary life-saving measure before transfer to theatre.
**Avoid COMPLETE drainage; it destabilises the dissection.** Full drainage restores full pressure into the false lumen.
**Maintain balance → expedite transfer to theatre.** The definitive treatment is surgical repair; drainage is a bridge.
mimic: Tamponade from dissection vs from other causes
Routine tamponade: drain completely (CVS-27). Type A dissection: drain small volumes only if surgery is delayed, and go to theatre.
traps: “Pericardiocentesis is the next step for an effusion with chest pain”
If dissection is possible, image the aorta; drainage of a haemopericardium from type A can cause fatal rupture.
decode: Type A with tamponade, surgery delayed — how to drain? [pattern]
Controlled drainage of small volumes (30–40 mL), not complete.
AD-25.punch: In type A tamponade the pericardium is holding back a rupture, so drain only enough to perfuse and get the patient to theatre.

AD-26.intro: Step 6: after repair, the false lumen may still be perfusing parts of the aorta, so every organ that was at risk before is still at risk. Not asked directly.
why: **Visceral: malperfusion, abdominal compartment syndrome; repeat CT if lactate rises.** Persistent malperfusion is not always relieved by proximal repair, and ischaemic gut and large-volume resuscitation raise intra-abdominal pressure.
**Pulses: check all four limbs for deficits.** A new deficit means the false lumen is still compressing a branch.
**Neurological: embolic events and stroke.** Air, debris and cerebral malperfusion during arch surgery; spinal cord ischaemia after descending repair (AD-28).
**Coagulation: coagulopathy (platelet consumption), treated with blood products.** Consumption in the false lumen, bypass, hypothermia and dilution all add up.
**Renal: AKI; wine-coloured urine = haemolysis.** Red cells are damaged by bypass and by flow through stent grafts or a partly thrombosed false lumen; free haemoglobin is toxic to the tubules.
mimic: Wine-coloured urine: haemolysis vs rhabdomyolysis
Both are dipstick-positive for blood without red cells; pink plasma and high free Hb point to haemolysis, a very high CK to rhabdomyolysis (limb ischaemia).
traps: “Once the ascending aorta is replaced, malperfusion resolves”
Distal false-lumen flow can persist; a rising lactate needs a repeat CT.
decode: Rising lactate after type A repair [pattern]
Persisting mesenteric malperfusion: repeat CT.
AD-26.punch: After repair, keep looking for the old complications: lactate for the gut, four pulses for the limbs, neurology for the brain and cord, platelets and urine colour for consumption and haemolysis.

AD-27.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Type B: medical vs TEVAR
AD-27.intro: Step 6: type B splits by whether it is complicated. Not asked directly, but the notes contradict themselves, and the population resolves it.
why: **MEDICAL: anti-impulse therapy.** Beta-blocker to HR about 60, SBP below 120, analgesia, then oral beta-blockers after 24 hours if the gut works (ESC 2024).

**TEVAR (2024 ESC I/B with favourable anatomy); open surgery the alternative.** For complicated type B (rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain or hypertension, rapid expansion), TEVAR is first line (I, B).

**Favourable anatomy → TEVAR in the SUBACUTE phase (IIa/B).** ESC 2024: in selected uncomplicated patients with high-risk features (aorta >40 mm, false lumen >20 mm, entry tear >10 mm), TEVAR between 14 and 90 days (the ESC subacute phase, not IRAD’s 8–30 days, AD-08) improves aortic remodelling.
**Stent graft seals the entry tear → false lumen obliterates over time.** Covering the entry stops flow into the false lumen, which thromboses and shrinks while the true lumen expands.

**Only if unsuitable for endovascular repair (higher morbidity and mortality): midline sternotomy or posterolateral thoracotomy, often on CPB.** Open descending repair carries more paraplegia, renal failure and death.
mimic: Uncomplicated vs complicated type B
Uncomplicated: drugs (± TEVAR later if high risk); complicated: TEVAR now.
traps: “The primary treatment of type B is TEVAR”
Only when complicated or high-risk; uncomplicated type B is medical first.
decode: Type B with malperfusion or rupture [pattern]
TEVAR (I, B).
Uncomplicated type B with an aorta of 45 mm [pattern]
Medical, then consider TEVAR at 14–90 days (IIa, B).
AD-27.punch: Uncomplicated type B is treated with drugs, complicated type B with TEVAR at once, and high-risk uncomplicated type B with TEVAR in the subacute window; open surgery is the fallback.

AD-28.sub: Cardiology → Aortic dissection → Spinal cord protection
AD-28.intro: Step 6: covering or replacing the descending aorta can cut off the intercostal supply to the cord, so cord perfusion pressure is protected from both sides. Not asked directly, but the top-up on spinal drain anticoagulant holds comes from a TEVAR stem.
why: **Hypothermia, distal aortic perfusion, CSF drainage.** Hypothermia lowers cord oxygen demand; distal (left heart) bypass keeps the lower body perfused while the aorta is clamped; CSF drainage lowers the pressure opposing cord blood flow.
**15 mL/h.** Protocols usually cap drainage at about 15–20 mL/h; draining faster risks intracranial hypotension and subdural haematoma.

**CSF pressure <10 mmHg; <5 mmHg if signs of paraplegia.** Spinal cord perfusion pressure is MAP minus CSF pressure (or CVP if higher). Protocols typically keep it at about 10 mmHg (range 8–12) and drain further if a deficit appears, while raising the MAP (often above 80–100 mmHg; ESC 2024 recommends a higher MAP in spinal ischaemia).

**Intercostal vessels T8–T12 → artery of Adamkiewicz.** The great radicular artery feeds the anterior spinal artery, which supplies the anterior two thirds of the lower thoracic and lumbar cord; reattaching its intercostal origin preserves the anterior spinal circulation.
**Hb >10 g/dL, cardiac index >2.5 L/min/m².** Oxygen delivery to a cord with marginal collateral flow depends on both.
mimic: Raising MAP vs lowering CSF pressure
Both raise cord perfusion pressure; they are used together.
traps: “Drain the CSF as fast as possible when paraplegia appears”
Drain to target but within the hourly limit; rapid drainage causes subdural haematoma.
decode: New leg weakness after TEVAR — immediate steps? [pattern]
Raise MAP, drain CSF to <10 (lower if needed), keep Hb and cardiac index up.
AD-28.punch: Cord perfusion pressure is MAP minus CSF pressure, so protect the cord by keeping the MAP high and draining CSF to below 10 mmHg at no more than about 15 mL/h, with good Hb and cardiac output.

AD-29.intro: Step 6 closes the deck by listing every way dissection kills; each one traces back to rupture or malperfusion (step 2). Not asked directly.
why: **~120 mmHg: protects the surgical sites.** Systolic pressure is kept near 120 after type B repair to protect the anastomoses and stent seal and to limit stress on any residual false lumen, while keeping the spinal cord and kidneys perfused.

**Stroke (impaired cerebral perfusion); spinal cord involvement (paraplegia or hemisensory loss); MI (coronary compromise); cardiac tamponade (aortic root involvement); severe aortic regurgitation; AKI; gut ischaemia.** The first five come from the ascending aorta and arch (type A); spinal, renal and gut ischaemia come from the descending and abdominal aorta. Rupture underlies tamponade, and every other item is malperfusion or valve failure.
mimic: Type A vs type B complications
Type A: tamponade, AR, MI, stroke. Type B: paraplegia, AKI, gut and limb ischaemia.
traps: “Tamponade and AR can complicate a type B dissection”
Only if it extends back into the ascending aorta, which makes it type A.
decode: Commonest cause of death in type A [pattern]
Rupture into the pericardium (tamponade).
AD-29.punch: Every complication of dissection is either rupture or malperfusion, and the segment involved decides which ones can happen.

topups.q: Minimum anticoagulant stop times before neuraxial or spinal-drain placement (ASRA 2018)?
a: - Aspirin alone: no hold; clopidogrel 5–7 days.
- Enoxaparin prophylactic 12 h, therapeutic 24 h; IV UFH 4–6 h with a normal aPTT.
- Apixaban, rivaroxaban: 72 h.
- Dabigatran: 120 h (5 days) by default (72 h only if CrCl >80 and no other risk) — the longest hold.

x.sub: Cardiology → Aortic repair → Spinal drain and anticoagulant holds
x.intro: Step 6 protects the spinal cord, and a lumbar CSF drain is one of the tools (AD-28). A drain is a neuraxial catheter, so it carries the same risk of spinal haematoma as an epidural, and the same ASRA stop times apply. The Grand Test question asks which drug history makes a drain most dangerous after TEVAR; only 30% picked dabigatran.
why: **Aspirin alone: no hold; clopidogrel 5–7 days.** Aspirin on its own does not measurably raise the risk of spinal haematoma. Clopidogrel blocks the P2Y12 receptor irreversibly, so platelet function returns only as new platelets are made, over 5–7 days.

**Enoxaparin prophylactic 12 h, therapeutic 24 h; IV UFH 4–6 h with a normal aPTT.** LMWH has a predictable half-life, so the interval scales with the dose. IV heparin wears off within hours, but the aPTT confirms it.
**Apixaban, rivaroxaban: 72 h.** At least five half-lives (apixaban about 12 h, rivaroxaban about 5–9 h); ASRA 2018 does not adjust this hold for renal function.

**Dabigatran: 120 h (5 days) by default (72 h only if CrCl >80 and no other risk), the longest hold.** Dabigatran is cleared about 80% by the kidney, so its half-life lengthens as renal function falls. ASRA gives 72 h for CrCl ≥80, 96 h for 50–79 and 120 h for 30–49, and advises against a neuraxial procedure below 30. Stopped only 4 days earlier, it is the one drug in the question whose hold may not have been met.
mimic: Dabigatran vs factor Xa inhibitors
Xa inhibitors: 72 h for everyone; dabigatran: 72–120 h depending on CrCl, 120 h if renal function is unknown or impaired.
traps: “Apixaban stopped 3 days before” (70% chose a wrong option)
Three days is the full 72-hour hold, so it is compliant.
“Enoxaparin prophylaxis 14 hours before”
The prophylactic interval is 12 hours, so 14 hours is safe.
“Aspirin the morning of surgery”
Aspirin alone does not need to be stopped.
decode: TEVAR for contained rupture, paraparesis on day 1, spinal drain — which drug history carries the highest haematoma risk? [DocT GT]
Dabigatran stopped 4 days before (30%): under the 120-hour default hold.
Minimum dabigatran hold before neuraxial catheter with normal renal function [pattern]
72 h if CrCl ≥80 and no other risk; otherwise up to 120 h.
x.punch: A spinal drain follows the neuraxial rules: no hold for aspirin, 12/24 h for LMWH, 72 h for apixaban and rivaroxaban, and up to 120 h for renally cleared dabigatran, the longest and the one most often under-held.

spine: A weak media meets pressure
Dissection happens when a medial layer weakened by age, hypertension or a connective-tissue disorder gives way under years of high pressure, most often in older hypertensive men.
The false lumen does the damage

Blood entering through an intimal tear splits the outer media, and the pressurised false lumen squeezes the true lumen and its branches, so every complication is either rupture outward or malperfusion inward, driven by dP/dt.
Naming it by site and time
Whether the ascending aorta is involved (Stanford A or B, DeBakey I–III, TEM) and how long since onset decide the risk and the treatment, more than anything else.
Recognising it, then imaging

Sudden severe pain with a pulse or pressure difference, a new AR murmur or a widened mediastinum points to it, ACS is the commonest misdiagnosis, and an ECG-gated CT of the whole aorta confirms it when the patient is stable.
Anti-impulse therapy first
Before any vasodilator, an IV beta-blocker brings the heart rate to about 60 and the systolic pressure below 120, because slowing the heart is what lowers dP/dt and stops the tear propagating.
Repair by type, protect the organs
Type A goes to open surgery, uncomplicated type B stays medical and complicated type B gets TEVAR, and the brain, spinal cord, gut and kidneys are protected around the repair.
CVS09.primer: The aortic wall has three layers: the intima facing the blood, the thick elastic media that gives the aorta its strength and recoil, and the adventitia outside. The aorta is divided at the left subclavian artery into a proximal part (ascending aorta and arch) and a distal part (descending thoracic and abdominal aorta), and almost every classification of dissection turns on which side of that line the tear lies. The force that splits the wall is not the mean pressure alone but how steeply pressure rises with each beat (dP/dt), which depends on contractility and heart rate. Acute aortic syndrome covers classic dissection, intramural haematoma and penetrating ulcer; this deck is mostly about classic dissection.

MI-01.intro: Step 1 is the distinction on which every later card rests. Troponin tells you that myocytes are damaged; it does not tell you why. Infarction is one specific cause of that damage: ischaemia.
why: **Acute myocardial INJURY (abnormal biomarkers, troponin) + evidence of acute myocardial ISCHAEMIA.** The injury must be acute (a rise and/or fall, with at least one value above the 99th centile), and the ischaemia must be shown by symptoms, new ischaemic ECG change, new Q waves, new imaging loss of myocardium or wall motion, or thrombus. Without both halves it is not MI.

**Myocardial cell death resulting from prolonged ischaemia.** The pathologist’s definition is the end state: necrosis with the time course of ischaemia (MI-02). The clinical definition is how that death is recognised in a living patient.

**Myocardial INJURY only - not infarction.** A troponin rise alone is the starting point of a differential (MI-03, MI-04), not a diagnosis; myocarditis, sepsis, PE or renal failure raise it without any coronary event.
mimic: Acute MI vs acute non-ischaemic injury
Both have a dynamic troponin; only MI has ischaemic evidence (symptoms, ECG, imaging, thrombus).
traps: “Raised troponin in a septic patient = NSTEMI”
It is myocardial injury until ischaemic evidence is found (MI-12).
decode: Raised troponin, no ischaemic symptoms or ECG change: diagnosis? [pattern]
Myocardial injury, not MI.
MI-01.punch: Troponin defines injury; injury that is acute and ischaemic defines infarction.

MI-02.sub: ACS → Pathology → Cellular course of ischaemic injury
MI-02.intro: Step 2 is what happens inside the wall after the artery closes. The subendocardium dies first because it is the most vulnerable layer, and necrosis then advances toward the epicardium; this wavefront is why the ECG divides infarcts into subendocardial (NSTEMI) and transmural (STEMI), which is what the one real question tests.
why: **↓cellular glycogen, relaxed myofibrils, sarcolemmal disruption.** Without oxygen the myocyte switches to anaerobic glycolysis and burns its glycogen; ATP falls, so the myofibrils relax and contraction stops within about a minute; failing membrane pumps and calcium overload then disrupt the sarcolemma, which is the point at which troponin leaks out.

**As early as 15-20 minutes after ischaemia onset.** The Fourth Universal Definition puts these first ultrastructural changes ‘as early as 10–15 min’ after the onset of ischaemia (see FLAGS); in animal models irreversible injury of the subendocardium follows at about 20–40 minutes.

**ENDOCARDIUM → EPICARDIUM.** The subendocardium is compressed hardest during systole, has the highest oxygen demand and sits at the far end of the perfusion line from the epicardial arteries, so it is the first to be starved. Over several hours the necrosis spreads outward. A partially occluded artery or a short occlusion leaves a subendocardial infarct (NSTEMI); a sustained complete occlusion makes it transmural (STEMI), which is why ST elevation marks full-thickness injury.

**Timely reperfusion therapy.** Opening the artery stops the wavefront where it is, so the salvaged outer wall is proportional to how early flow returns. Collateral flow and ischaemic preconditioning slow the wave and widen the window.
mimic: NSTEMI vs STEMI by pathology
NSTEMI: subendocardial (non-transmural) necrosis, partial occlusion; STEMI: transmural necrosis, complete occlusion.
Anterior subendocardial ischaemia vs posterior STEMI
Both give ST depression in V1–V3; posterior STEMI has tall R waves, upright T waves and ST elevation ≥0.5 mm in V7–V9 (MI-22).
traps: “ST depression in V1–V3 with raised troponin is always NSTEMI (subendocardial)”

Marrow keys subendocardial injury, but depression confined to V1–V3 may be a posterior STEMI (transmural): if the stem gives tall R in V1–V2 or ST elevation in V7–V9, pick posterior STEMI; otherwise NSTEMI.
“Necrosis starts at the epicardium, next to the occluded artery”
It starts in the subendocardium, farthest from the epicardial arteries, and moves outward.
decode: ST depression V1–V3 + positive biomarkers: mechanism of injury? [Marrow]
Subendocardial (non-transmural) ischaemic injury; exclude posterior STEMI.
In which direction does ischaemic necrosis spread? [pattern]
Endocardium to epicardium, over hours.
MI-02.punch: Myocytes stop contracting in about a minute, show structural damage in 10–20 minutes, and die from the subendocardium outward over hours; reperfusion is what stops the wave.

MI-03.sub: ACS → Definition → Ischaemic causes of a troponin rise
MI-03.intro: Step 1 continues with the ischaemic branch of a troponin rise. The Fourth Universal Definition (Table 1) divides it into one coronary event and a list of supply–demand imbalances; the split is what separates type 1 from type 2 MI (MI-05).
why: **Atherosclerotic plaque disruption with thrombosis.** Rupture or erosion exposes thrombogenic plaque and a thrombus narrows or occludes the artery. This is type 1 MI.

**Reduced perfusion: coronary spasm or microvascular dysfunction, coronary embolism, coronary artery dissection, sustained bradyarrhythmia, hypotension or shock, respiratory failure, severe anaemia.** Each lowers oxygen delivery to the myocardium without a plaque event: flow falls (spasm, embolism, dissection, slow rate, low pressure) or the oxygen content of the blood falls (hypoxaemia, anaemia). Under UDMI 2018 these are type 2 mechanisms; UDMI 2026 moves spasm, embolism and dissection to primary MI (MI-11).

**Increased O2 demand: sustained tachyarrhythmia, severe hypertension ± LVH.** Tachycardia raises demand and shortens diastole, when the left ventricle is perfused; hypertension and a hypertrophied wall raise wall tension and demand.
mimic: Plaque thrombosis vs supply–demand imbalance
Thrombus on angiography or intracoronary imaging means plaque disruption (type 1); a clear acute stressor with no thrombus means imbalance (type 2).
traps: “Coronary embolism and SCAD are type 1 because they are coronary”
In UDMI 2018 they are supply-side type 2 causes; only in 2026 are they primary MI.
decode: Septic shock, troponin rising, ST depression, no thrombus at angiography: mechanism? [pattern]
Supply–demand imbalance (reduced perfusion, hypotension); type 2 / secondary MI.
MI-03.punch: One cause is the plaque; everything else that starves or overworks the myocardium is supply–demand imbalance.

MI-04.intro: Step 1 ends with the troponin rises that have nothing to do with coronary ischaemia. Two real questions come from this list: Takotsubo after an emotional shock, and a troponin rise after stroke. In both the wrong answer is to treat the troponin as an ACS.
why: **Cardiac: heart failure, myocarditis, cardiomyopathy (any type), Takotsubo, coronary revascularisation, other cardiac procedures, catheter ablation, defibrillator shocks, cardiac contusion.** Wall stress and stretch (heart failure), inflammation (myocarditis), catecholamine toxicity (Takotsubo) and direct trauma (procedures, ablation, shocks, contusion) all damage the membrane without coronary occlusion.

**Systemic: sepsis or infection, chronic kidney disease, stroke or SAH, PE or pulmonary hypertension, infiltrative disease (amyloid, sarcoid), chemotherapy, critical illness, strenuous exercise.** Sepsis injures myocytes through cytokines and hypotension; CKD gives a chronic, stable elevation (reduced clearance plus structural heart disease), so the delta matters more than the value; stroke and SAH release a catecholamine surge (especially insular strokes); PE strains and injures the right ventricle. Most are chronic or acute injury, not MI, unless ischaemic evidence appears.
mimic: Takotsubo vs anterior STEMI
Takotsubo has unobstructed coronaries and apical ballooning that crosses territories; it is a diagnosis made at angiography.
Stroke-related troponin vs NSTEMI
A neurogenic troponin rise usually has no ischaemic symptoms and follows the stroke; NSTEMI has an ischaemic picture.
traps: “ST elevation after bad news = inferior MI”
With unobstructed coronaries and an emotional trigger it is Takotsubo; treat LVOT obstruction with fluids, phenylephrine and beta-blockers, not inotropes.
“Troponin up after alteplase for stroke: start DAPT for NSTEMI”

It is usually neurogenic injury; no antiplatelet for 24 h after alteplase. Marrow keys 21-day DAPT for a wake-up stroke given alteplase: 21-day DAPT is for minor stroke (NIHSS ≤3) or high-risk TIA without lysis, and wake-up stroke needs MRI mismatch before lysis. If minor and not lysed, pick DAPT; after alteplase, pick ‘no antiplatelet for 24 h’.
decode: Woman, chest pain after her son’s death, ST elevation, no obstructive lesion [DocT GT · PYQ]
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.
Stroke treated with alteplase, troponin raised: cause and drug plan [Marrow]
Stroke-related myocardial injury; hold antiplatelets 24 h after alteplase, statin now.
MI-04.punch: Heart failure, myocarditis, Takotsubo, sepsis, CKD, stroke and PE all raise troponin without a coronary event; treat the cause, not the number.

MI-05.intro: Step 3 opens with the 2018 classification by mechanism, set beside the syndromic labels used at the bedside. The two real questions here are the syndromic ones: chest pain, no ST elevation, troponin raised.
why: **Type 1: Atherothrombotic - STEMI and NSTEMI, significant CAD.** The classic ACS; it can present with or without ST elevation (MI-06).

**Type 2: O2 supply/demand mismatch, usually without significant CAD.** The trigger is an acute stressor, not a plaque event (MI-07). Many patients with type 2 MI do have fixed coronary disease that the stress unmasks, which the 2018 definition allows and the 2026 definition makes a criterion (MI-12; see FLAGS).
**Type 3: Sudden cardiac death before biomarkers obtained.** Defined so that a fatal MI is not lost from the statistics for want of a blood sample (MI-08).
**Type 4: PCI-related.** Subdivided into 4a (procedural), 4b (stent thrombosis) and 4c (restenosis), with troponin multiples (MI-09).

**Type 5: CABG-related.** A higher troponin multiple, because cardiac surgery itself releases troponin (MI-09). Syndromically, **STEMI vs NSTE-ACS** is decided by the ECG; within NSTE-ACS, **NSTEMI** has a troponin rise and **unstable angina** does not. With high-sensitivity assays much of what was called unstable angina is now detected as NSTEMI, so UA is becoming less common (ESC 2023).
mimic: NSTEMI vs unstable angina
Same pain and ECG; only troponin above the 99th centile with a rise/fall separates them.
NSTEMI vs STEMI
Persistent ST elevation (or an equivalent) decides STEMI; T inversion or ST depression with troponin is NSTEMI.
traps: “Lateral T inversion with troponin up = unstable angina”
Unstable angina by definition has no troponin rise; raised troponin makes it NSTEMI (71% right).
“T-wave inversion means STEMI”
Only persistent ST elevation (or an equivalent) is STEMI.
decode: Woman with risk factors, chest pain, lateral T inversion, troponin raised [DocT QBank, 71%]
NSTEMI.
Smoker, 40 min crushing pain, no ST elevation, troponin raised on repeat [DocT GT AIM1, 85%]
NSTEMI.
MI-05.punch: The ECG separates STEMI from NSTE-ACS, troponin separates NSTEMI from unstable angina, and the mechanism gives the type number.

MI-06.intro: Step 3 continues with the type that is ‘ACS’ in the everyday sense. The criteria are the general MI rule plus one criterion unique to type 1: a visible thrombus.
why: **Atherothrombotic CAD, precipitated by plaque disruption (rupture or erosion).** Rupture of a thin fibrous cap or erosion of the endothelium over a plaque exposes thrombogenic material, and thrombus forms on it.
**Rise and/or fall of cTn with at least one value above the 99th percentile URL.** The dynamic change proves the injury is acute; one high value alone could be chronic.

**At least one of: symptoms of acute myocardial ischaemia; new ischaemic ECG changes; new pathological Q waves; imaging evidence of new loss of viable myocardium or new RWMA; coronary thrombus on angiography, intracoronary imaging or autopsy.** The first four are shared with type 2; thrombus is the type 1-specific criterion, because it proves the plaque mechanism directly.
mimic: Type 1 vs type 2 at angiography
Thrombus or a ruptured plaque points to type 1; a clean or fixed-stenosis artery with a clear stressor points to type 2.
traps: “Q waves are needed to diagnose type 1 MI”
Any one of the five supporting criteria is enough; symptoms alone with a dynamic troponin suffice.
decode: Which criterion is specific to type 1 MI? [pattern]
Coronary thrombus on angiography, intracoronary imaging or autopsy.
MI-06.punch: Type 1 is a dynamic troponin over the 99th centile plus one ischaemic criterion, and only type 1 counts a thrombus as proof.

MI-07.sub: ACS → Classification → Type 1 vs type 2 MI
MI-07.intro: Step 3 turns to the commonest classification problem in ICU: is the MI the plaque or the stress? The one real question is a hypertensive patient with chest pain, a normal ECG and a small troponin rise, and the cohort split between NSTEMI, unstable angina and dissection.
why: **Type 1: plaque disruption with thrombosis; Type 2: supply-demand mismatch WITHOUT atherothrombotic plaque disruption.** In type 1 the artery is the problem; in type 2 the artery may be normal or fixed-narrowed, and the problem is a stressor that lowers supply or raises demand beyond what it can deliver. Treatment follows: antithrombotics and revascularisation for type 1, correction of the stressor for type 2.

**Acute GI bleed: precipitous fall in haemoglobin.** Oxygen content falls and tachycardia raises demand; anticoagulating this patient as a type 1 ACS would worsen the bleed. Other common ICU examples: septic shock, rapid AF, hypoxaemia, a hypertensive surge.

**Coronary thrombus: type 1 lists thrombus as a criterion; type 2 requires NO coronary thrombus on angiography, intracoronary imaging or autopsy.** Thrombus is the direct evidence of a plaque event; its absence, with a credible stressor, is what makes the label type 2.
mimic: Type 2 MI vs non-ischaemic injury
Type 2 still needs ischaemic evidence (symptoms, ECG, imaging); a troponin rise in sepsis without it is injury.
Hypertensive NSTEMI vs aortic dissection
Check BP in both arms, pain character and mediastinum before antithrombotics.
traps: “Normal ECG and only slightly raised troponin = unstable angina”
Any troponin above the 99th centile with a rise/fall plus ischaemic symptoms is NSTEMI, even with a normal ECG (68% right). With BP 180/110 and no prior CAD, think type 2 from a hypertensive surge.
“Severe hypertension and chest pain: aortic dissection”
Possible, and must be excluded before antithrombotics, but the stem gives nothing specific (no tearing pain or arm BP difference); NSTEMI is the keyed answer.
decode: BP 180/110, chest pain, normal ECG, troponin slightly raised [DocT QBank, 68%]
NSTEMI (consider type 2 from the hypertensive surge; exclude dissection).
Upper GI bleed, Hb 6, ST depression, troponin rising [pattern]
Type 2 MI (secondary MI in 2026 if CAD or new RWMA is shown); transfuse, no anticoagulation.
MI-07.punch: Type 1 is the plaque and gets antithrombotics; type 2 is the stressor and gets the stressor fixed; a thrombus decides between them.

MI-08.intro: Step 3 continues with the patient who dies before the troponin can be measured. Type 3 exists so that these deaths are counted as MI in registries and trials.
why: **Cardiac death with symptoms suggesting ischaemia, without biomarker data.** The troponin criterion cannot be met because the patient died before a sample was taken or before troponin had time to rise.
**Ischaemic symptoms + new ischaemic ECG changes or VF.** VF in the first hours of an occlusion is the commonest mechanism of sudden death in acute MI.

**Death before blood samples could be taken; MI may be found at autopsy.** Fresh thrombus or early necrosis at post-mortem confirms it. UDMI 2026 removes type 3 as a separate type: a fatal MI is assigned primary, secondary or procedure-related by its setting or post-mortem findings, and where no biomarkers or imaging exist MI may still be presumed from an ischaemic presentation with new ischaemic ECG changes or pathological Q waves (MI-10).
mimic: Type 3 MI vs type 1 MI with death after sampling
If a troponin was obtained and rising before death, it is type 1 (or 2); type 3 has no biomarker data.
traps: “Type 3 MI is the silent MI found on later imaging”
Type 3 is death before biomarkers; silent MI is a prior MI found on ECG or imaging.
decode: Collapse in VF after 20 min of chest pain, died before bloods: MI type? [pattern]
Type 3 (UDMI 2018); classified by setting or autopsy in 2026.
MI-08.punch: Type 3 is the ischaemic cardiac death without a troponin, and 2026 folds it back into the other categories.

MI-09.sub: ACS → Classification → Procedure-related MI (types 4 and 5, UDMI 2018)
MI-09.intro: Step 3 ends with MI caused by the treatment. This is the most-asked card in the deck: three real questions, and in the hardest only 23% of the cohort answered correctly. Every PCI and every CABG releases some troponin, so the definition sets a higher bar and demands a second, independent sign that a real infarct occurred.
why: **Type 4a: normal baseline, cTn >5 × 99th URL within ≤48 h of the procedure.** Small rises from side-branch trauma and microembolisation are expected after PCI; the multiple is set so that only a large rise counts. Any rise above the 99th centile but without the further evidence is ‘procedural myocardial injury’.

**Raised but stable (≤20% variation) or falling baseline: post-procedure rise >20% and the value still >5× (PCI) or >10× (CABG).** If troponin is already high from the presenting ACS, a further 20% rise is the minimum that a new event produces beyond analytical and biological variation.

**4b = stent or scaffold thrombosis; 4c = restenosis.** 4b is diagnosed with the type 1 criteria plus angiographic or autopsy proof of thrombus in the stent; 4c is focal or diffuse in-stent restenosis or a complex lesion with a troponin rise, no other culprit. UDMI 2026 moves these to procedure-related if within 30 days and primary MI after 30 days (MI-10).
**Type 5: cTn >10 × 99th URL within ≤48 h of CABG.** Cardiac surgery itself (handling, cardioplegia, cannulation) causes more troponin release than PCI, so the bar is higher.

**Plus new ischaemic evidence: new ischaemic ECG change, new Q waves, imaging loss of viable myocardium or new RWMA, or an angiographic flow-limiting complication (dissection, vessel or side-branch occlusion, thrombus, lost collateral flow, distal embolisation).** This is the half that people forget. For type 5 the 2018 list is narrower: new pathological Q waves, angiographic new graft or native-vessel occlusion, or imaging loss of viable myocardium/RWMA; new ST-T change alone does not count after CABG, because pericarditis and surgery make it common (see FLAGS). Isolated new Q waves meet type 5 even if troponin is rising but below 10×.
mimic: Type 4a MI vs procedural myocardial injury
Both can exceed 5×; only 4a has new ECG, Q-wave, imaging or angiographic evidence.
Type 4b vs type 1 after PCI
Thrombus inside the stent is 4b; a new plaque rupture elsewhere is type 1.
traps: “hs-cTn 6× URL after elective PCI, asymptomatic, ECG and echo normal = type 4a MI”
The troponin bar is met but no ischaemic evidence is present, so it is myocardial injury without infarction (only 23% right).
“Any troponin above the 99th centile after PCI is periprocedural MI”
That defines procedural injury; MI needs >5× (PCI) or >10× (CABG) plus evidence.
decode: Elective PCI, normal baseline, hs-cTn 6× URL, no ECG or wall motion change: classify [DocT GT2, 23%]
Myocardial injury without infarction.
MI from stent thrombosis on angiography or autopsy [Marrow]
Type 4b (2018); 2026: procedure-related ≤30 days, primary >30 days.
Post-CABG inferior MI, cTn >10× URL [Marrow]
Type 5.
MI-09.punch: After PCI it takes more than 5× the 99th centile, after CABG more than 10×, within 48 hours, and always a second sign; troponin alone is procedural injury.

Type 5 (CABG)
