parts.q: Mechanism of ventricular arrhythmia 24–72 h after MI? [DocT GT ×4]
parts.a: Abnormal automaticity of partly depolarised ischaemic myocytes and Purkinje fibres, driven by catecholamines and low K⁺/Mg²⁺; AIVR is enhanced normal automaticity; late monomorphic VT is scar re-entry.

MI-59.intro: Step 2 as a class list. No real question is linked; the testable ends are the Class I treatments (beta-blocker, revascularisation) and the Class III ‘prophylactic antiarrhythmics’.
why: **IV beta-blocker for polymorphic VT / VF: I, B.** Polymorphic VT during an MI is ischaemic and catecholamine-driven; a beta-blocker removes the trigger. ESC 2022 also recommends beta-blockers to prevent VA, and ESC 2023 words this row ‘IV beta-blocker and/or amiodarone’ for polymorphic VT/VF (I, B).
**Prompt complete revascularisation for recurrent VT / VF: I, C.** Ongoing ischaemia keeps the substrate unstable; ESC 2022 calls urgent reperfusion the most important therapy.

**IV amiodarone for recurrent polymorphic VT: I, C; for recurrent VT despite repeated cardioversion: IIa, C.** Amiodarone blocks potassium, sodium and calcium channels and has a beta-blocking effect, so it lengthens refractoriness and suppresses recurrence with little negative inotropy. The card follows the 2017 STEMI list. ESC 2023 merges it into the beta-blocker row (‘IV beta-blocker and/or amiodarone’, I, B), while the 2022 VA guideline says IV amiodarone ‘should be considered’ for recurrent haemodynamically relevant VA (IIa).

**Transvenous overdrive pacing: IIa, C; RF ablation then ICD for recurrent VT / VF / storm: IIa, C.** Pacing faster than the VT suppresses it; ablation works best when the VF is triggered each time by the same Purkinje PVC.
**Lidocaine if the above fail: IIb, C.** A sodium-channel blocker that acts best on ischaemic, partly depolarised tissue; third line.

**Prophylactic antiarrhythmics: III, B; treating asymptomatic, irrelevant VAs: III, C.** Prophylactic lidocaine reduced VF in old trials but did not reduce, and tended to increase, mortality, partly through bradycardia and asystole; class IC drugs given for post-MI ectopy increased death (CAST).
mimic: Electrical storm vs single VT episode
Storm is three or more sustained episodes in 24 hours: sedation, beta-blocker, amiodarone, revascularise, then pacing or ablation.
traps: “Prophylactic lidocaine after MI”
Class III: fewer VF episodes, but no fall in deaths and a trend to more.
decode: Recurrent polymorphic VT on day 1 of STEMI — first measures? [pattern]
IV beta-blocker, correct K⁺/Mg²⁺, urgent angiography and revascularisation; amiodarone next.
Prophylactic antiarrhythmic after MI — class? [pattern]
III (harmful).
MI-59.punch: Treat the cause first: an IV beta-blocker and an open artery are Class I, amiodarone, pacing and ablation come next, lidocaine last, and prophylactic antiarrhythmics are Class III.

MI-60.sub: Cardiology → ACS → AV block after MI
MI-60.intro: Step 3: the level of the block follows the artery. Both real questions are about the inferior–anterior split; one has a wrong key and the other has two true options.
why: **Proximal block: 1st degree, Mobitz I; RCA (inferior MI); usually transient, resolves with reperfusion; pacemaker not typically needed.** The RCA supplies the AV node in most people, and inferior MI adds vagal (Bezold–Jarisch) tone and adenosine release at the node. Nodal block has a narrow junctional escape at 40–60/min that keeps the patient perfused, responds to atropine and usually recovers within days. Inferior MI can also cause complete heart block at the node; it behaves the same way and still usually resolves.

**Distal block: 3rd degree; LAD (anterior MI); life-threatening; pacemaker often required.** Septal branches of the LAD supply the His bundle and bundle branches, so block here means a large septal infarct. Mobitz II or new bifascicular block warns of it; the escape is wide and slow (under 40/min) and unreliable. Atropine works on the node only and may worsen infranodal block by speeding the atrial rate.

**Bradycardia / high-grade block with haemodynamic intolerance: IV positive chronotropes (epinephrine, vasopressin and/or atropine) — I, C; temporary pacing if they fail — I, C; urgent angiography if no prior reperfusion — I, C.** Drugs buy minutes, the pacing wire gives a dependable rate, and reopening the artery treats the cause. AHA 2025 ACLS doses: atropine 1 mg every 3–5 minutes to 3 mg, then epinephrine infusion or pacing. ESC 2023 adds that a permanent pacemaker is recommended only if high-degree block persists at least 5 days after MI (I, C), and pacing is not recommended once the block has resolved (III, B), because most post-MI block recovers.
mimic: Mobitz I vs Mobitz II after MI
Mobitz I (progressive PR lengthening) is nodal, inferior and benign; Mobitz II (fixed PR, sudden dropped beat) is infranodal, anterior and needs pacing.
Narrow vs wide escape in complete block
Narrow escape at 40–60/min means a junctional pacemaker above the block (inferior); wide at under 40/min means a ventricular pacemaker below it (anterior).
traps: DocT GT keys “Mobitz I, benign, resolves with atropine” for block after an ANTERIOR MI
The key contradicts its own explanation. Block after anterior MI is infranodal (LAD, His–Purkinje), does not respond to atropine and needs pacing: choose the His–Purkinje/transvenous pacing option.
“Anterior MI most commonly produces 2nd and 3rd degree block”
Only 15% got this question right. Inferior MI causes more AV block of every degree, including complete block; anterior block is rarer but far more dangerous.
Two true options: “AV block transiently develops in 10–25%” and “inferior MI most commonly produces 1st and 2nd degree block”
Both are true; the key is the transient-block statement, so pick it when both appear.
“Anterior MI gives a narrow-complex escape”
Anterior block is below the His bundle, so the escape is wide.
decode: Anterior MI with this ECG (block) — level and management? [DocT GT]
His–Purkinje; transvenous pacing (key says Mobitz I/atropine, which is wrong).
True statement about AV block in acute MI? [DocT GT]
Transient AV block occurs in 10–25% (keyed); the inferior-MI statement is also true.
Inferior MI, complete heart block, narrow escape at 50/min, BP 70 — sequence? [pattern]
Atropine/epinephrine, then temporary pacing; reperfuse if not already done.
MI-60.punch: Inferior MI blocks the AV node: narrow escape, atropine works, it recovers. Anterior MI blocks the His–Purkinje system: wide escape, atropine fails, pace. If haemodynamics fail, chronotropes then a pacing wire then the cath lab, all Class I.

MI-61.sub: Cardiology → ACS → Acute heart failure in ACS
MI-61.intro: Step 4 starts with the pump. Lost myocardium gives either congestion with a blood pressure, or low output with hypotension; the three real questions test the first-line move in each.
why: **Diuretics, vasodilators, NIV.** In pulmonary oedema with a good or high blood pressure the problem is often redistribution into the lungs under high afterload, not excess total water. IV nitroglycerin reduces preload at low dose and afterload at high dose, works in minutes and is titratable; CPAP/NIV recruits flooded alveoli and lowers LV afterload. Loop diuretics help the overloaded but act more slowly.

**Vasopressor for hypotension (norepinephrine); inotrope for output (dobutamine).** Norepinephrine raises perfusion pressure with less tachycardia and arrhythmia than dopamine (SOAP II, worse in the cardiogenic subgroup) and less refractory shock than epinephrine after MI (OptimaCC). Dobutamine is added when output stays low once pressure is restored. ESC grades both only IIb, because no inotrope or pressor has been shown to improve survival.

**Longer stay, more mechanical ventilation, more RRT.** ESC 2023 links acute HF in ACS with renal failure, respiratory failure, pneumonia and death; Killip class rises with each step (I no HF; II S3 or rales <50% of the fields; III frank pulmonary oedema; IV shock), and so does mortality.

**Pulmonary congestion; cardiogenic shock / low output / hypotension.** The first is ‘wet and warm’, the second ‘wet and cold’. Both need emergency echo and angiography (ESC 2023), because a mechanical complication or an occluded artery may be the cause.
mimic: Hypertensive pulmonary oedema (SCAPE) vs cardiogenic shock
High BP: nitrates and NIV, avoid pressors. Low BP and cold periphery: norepinephrine, then inotrope, revascularise; nitrates are contraindicated.
traps: “Loop diuretic and wait” in BP 180/100 pulmonary oedema
Too slow and aims at the wrong problem; 65% chose nitrates with NIV.
“Intubate now” in an alert patient with SpO₂ 88%
Try NIV first; intubate for NIV failure, exhaustion or a falling GCS.
IV hydralazine or labetalol for hypertensive pulmonary oedema
Hydralazine is unpredictable and causes reflex tachycardia; labetalol’s beta-blockade depresses a failing LV (94% chose nitroglycerin).
“Dopamine” as the first vasopressor in post-MI shock
76% chose norepinephrine. Dopamine causes more arrhythmia and was associated with higher mortality in cardiogenic shock.
decode: Pink frothy sputum, BP 180/100, SpO₂ 88%, alert — next step? [DocT GT]
Nitrates and NIV.
Hypertensive pulmonary oedema, BP 210/120 — initial drug? [DocT GT]
IV nitroglycerin.
Post-MI cardiogenic shock — first-line vasopressor? [DocT GT]
Norepinephrine.
MI-61.punch: Congestion with a pressure gets nitrates and NIV (diuretic if overloaded); low output and hypotension gets norepinephrine first and dobutamine for output, then the artery opened. Each Killip class up raises mortality.

parts.q: Killip class III vs IV? [Marrow line]
parts.a: III is frank pulmonary oedema (rales over more than half the lung fields); IV is cardiogenic shock.

MI-62.sub: Cardiology → ACS → Cardiogenic shock in STEMI (ESC)
MI-62.intro: Step 4 in classes. All three real questions ask the one thing that saves life in post-MI shock: opening the artery, by PCI even when the patient looks too sick.
why: **Immediate PCI; emergency CABG if unsuitable / PCI fails: I, B.** Shock is a large ischaemic territory failing; only reperfusion stops it. In the SHOCK trial early revascularisation did not reach significance at 30 days but saved about 13 lives per 100 at 6 months. CULPRIT-SHOCK then showed that PCI of the culprit artery only, with any other lesions staged later, beat immediate multivessel PCI (ESC 2023: culprit-only at the index procedure, Class I).

**Arterial line, immediate Doppler echo, early heart-team repair of mechanical complications, O₂ / ventilation by gases: I, C.** The echo separates LV failure from RV infarction, tamponade, VSR and acute MR, each of which changes treatment.
**Fibrinolysis if PPCI not possible <120 min (mechanical cause excluded): IIa, C.** Lysis works poorly at low perfusion pressure, but is better than no reperfusion when the lab is far.

**IABP for shock from mechanical complications: IIa, C.** Deflating just before systole lowers afterload, which reduces the regurgitant or shunt fraction and improves forward flow while awaiting surgery.

**PA catheter (IIb, B), ultrafiltration (IIb, B), inotropes / vasopressors (IIb, C), short-term MCS (IIb, C).** Each can be used but none has shown a survival benefit; ESC 2023 keeps short-term MCS at IIb, C, while ACC/AHA 2025 makes a microaxial flow pump IIa in selected STEMI shock (MI-63).
**Routine IABP: III, B.** IABP-SHOCK II (n 600) found no mortality benefit at 30 days, 1 year or 6 years.
mimic: Shock from LV pump failure vs from a mechanical complication
Pump failure: PCI ± MCS, no routine IABP. Mechanical complication (new murmur, tamponade): IABP is IIa as a bridge to surgery.
Inferior STEMI shock with clear lungs
Think RV infarction: fluids, avoid nitrates, reperfuse.
traps: “Immediate fibrinolysis” when PCI is available in 75 minutes
Within 120 minutes primary PCI wins, and in shock even more so.
“Routine IABP” in STEMI shock
Class III since IABP-SHOCK II; only for mechanical complications.
“Multivessel PCI at the index procedure” in shock (the notes call it IIa)
CULPRIT-SHOCK: culprit-only first; stage the rest.
decode: STEMI with cardiogenic shock, door-to-balloon 75 min — reperfusion strategy? [DocT GT]
Primary PCI.
Treatment of choice: STEMI with cardiogenic shock? [Marrow]
Revascularisation with PCI (I, B); routine IABP III.
Inferior STEMI with shock — next step? [Marrow]
Primary PCI.
MI-62.punch: In STEMI shock open the culprit artery now (PCI, or CABG if not feasible), echo immediately and fix any mechanical lesion; routine IABP is Class III, and drugs, PA catheters and MCS are only IIb.

parts.q: Who gets shock after MI, and what predicts death? [Marrow line]
parts.a: Older age, anterior MI, multivessel disease, prior MI, diabetes, prior HF; a first posterior or inferior infarct with shock suggests a mechanical complication or RV infarction. Lactate >2 mmol/L and admission glucose independently predict death.

MI-63.intro: Step 4 through the trials. No real question is linked; the pattern is ‘which device improved survival in AMI shock’, and only one did, in one population.
why: **IABP-SHOCK II (n 600): no 30-day mortality benefit (39.7% vs 41.3%).** The balloon adds only about 0.5 L/min, too little for a failing LV; no benefit at 1 or 6 years either.

**ECLS-SHOCK (n 420): VA-ECMO — no 30-day benefit (47.8% vs 49.0%).** Full flow, but retrograde aortic flow raises LV afterload, and bleeding and vascular complications rose; most patients had been resuscitated from arrest before randomisation.

**DANGER-SHOCK (n 360, STEMI shock): Impella CP — 180-day death 45.8% vs 58.5%, HR 0.74, NNT 8.** The microaxial pump takes blood from the LV and ejects it into the aorta, so it unloads the ventricle while adding flow. The population was narrow: STEMI with LVEF <45%, lactate ≥2.5 mmol/L and SBP <100 mmHg or a vasopressor; comatose out-of-hospital arrest survivors (GCS <8), severe RV failure and mechanical complications were excluded. 360 were randomised and 355 analysed.

**More bleeding, limb ischaemia, RRT (safety composite RR 4.7).** The safety composite (severe bleeding, limb ischaemia, haemolysis, device failure, worsening aortic regurgitation) was 24.0% vs 6.2%; RRT was a separate outcome (41.9% vs 26.7%). A large-bore arterial sheath and pump haemolysis cost kidneys and limbs, so the benefit needs selection and an experienced centre.

**Microaxial flow pump reasonable (IIa) in selected AMI shock; routine IABP / VA-ECMO not recommended.** ACC/AHA 2025 words the pump recommendation for STEMI with severe or refractory shock (2a, B-R), mirroring the DanGer Shock population, and gives routine IABP and routine VA-ECMO 3: No Benefit. ESC 2023, written before DanGer Shock, still gives short-term MCS IIb, C.
mimic: Impella vs VA-ECMO
Impella unloads the LV; VA-ECMO gives full flow but raises LV afterload and may need venting.
traps: “IABP-SHOCK II showed benefit in resource-limited settings” (notes)
It showed no benefit anywhere; the notes are wrong.
decode: Which MCS device reduced mortality in STEMI cardiogenic shock in an RCT? [pattern]
Impella CP (DanGer Shock).
ECLS-SHOCK result? [pattern]
No 30-day mortality benefit from routine VA-ECMO; more bleeding.
MI-63.punch: IABP and VA-ECMO did not reduce death in AMI shock; Impella CP did, in carefully selected non-comatose STEMI shock, at the price of more bleeding, limb ischaemia and RRT.

MI-64.intro: Step 5 is the most asked card in the deck (seven real questions). Necrotic muscle is softest before collagen is laid down, so the wall, septum or papillary muscle can tear in the first days to a week; the presentation and the echo tell you which, and the stem’s wording (‘next’ vs ‘definitive’) decides between a bridge and surgery.
why: **Presents: free wall — sudden pain + collapse, EMD; VSR — rapid AHF / shock, days 1–7; papillary — sudden pulmonary oedema ± shock.** Free wall rupture fills the pericardium in minutes, so the rhythm continues without output (PEA). VSR shunts left to right, flooding the lungs and starving the systemic circulation. Papillary rupture flails a mitral leaflet and the LV empties into a small, non-compliant left atrium.

**Finding: haemopericardium, tamponade; new loud systolic murmur (VSR); murmur not always obvious, posteromedial muscle (papillary).** The posteromedial muscle depends on one artery (the PDA, usually from the RCA), so it ruptures after inferior or posterior MI; the anterolateral has a dual supply. In acute MR the LA pressure rises so fast that the murmur may be short and soft, so a quiet heart with flash pulmonary oedema still means echo. Echo also shows the VSR jet, and a step-up in oxygen saturation from right atrium to pulmonary artery confirms the shunt.

**Manage: free wall — pericardiocentesis (bridge) → wall repair + patch; VSR — IABP bridge → surgery, percutaneous closure; papillary — diuretic, vasodilator / inotrope ± IABP → MVR / repair.** The IABP lowers afterload, which cuts the regurgitant and shunt fraction and raises forward flow without the extra afterload a vasopressor adds. Surgery is the definitive treatment for all three (ESC 2023: surgery preferred, IABP IIa, C while awaiting it; ACC/AHA 2025: short-term MCS as a bridge, 2a).

**Mortality: free wall 75–80%; VSR early surgery 20–40%; papillary 20–25%.** **Free wall rupture <1%; risk — older age, no reperfusion, late lysis.** For VSR the card’s figure is optimistic: registry operative mortality is about 54% when repair is within 7 days (MI-65). ESC 2023 puts all mechanical complications at 0.27% of STEMI with 42.4% in-hospital mortality; late lysis can turn an ischaemic infarct haemorrhagic and weaken it further.
mimic: VSR vs papillary muscle rupture
Both give a new systolic murmur and shock. VSR is loud with a thrill at the left sternal edge and an O₂ step-up; papillary MR is apical, often soft, with severe pulmonary oedema. Echo decides.
Free wall rupture vs post-MI pericarditis effusion
Rupture gives sudden tamponade and PEA; pericarditis gives a small effusion and pleuritic pain.
traps: “Norepinephrine” for inferior STEMI with a systolic murmur, pulmonary oedema and shock
Only 38% chose IABP. A pressor raises afterload and worsens the regurgitant flow; the IABP lowers afterload and supports coronary perfusion, and is IIa for mechanical complications.
“Valve replacement” as the ‘next’ step for papillary rupture with pulmonary oedema
Only 44% chose IABP. When IABP is offered and the stem says ‘next’, stabilise first; surgery is definitive.
“Diuretics and observe” or “vasodilator and reassess in 48 hours” for partial papillary rupture with hypotension
62% chose urgent mitral surgery. Without an IABP option, the answer is urgent surgery; medical therapy alone is fatal.
“Pulmonary embolism” or “LV systolic dysfunction” for dyspnoea with a new apical holosystolic murmur after posterior MI
69% chose acute MR; a new apical murmur with crackles and a preserved BP is papillary dysfunction until echo says otherwise.
decode: PEA / sudden hypotension days after a large STEMI, echo shows tamponade or haemopericardium — cause? [DocT GT ×2]
LV free wall rupture.
Post-MI flash pulmonary oedema, papillary muscle rupture on echo — next step? [DocT GT] [Marrow]
IABP if offered as the next step; otherwise urgent mitral repair/replacement.
Posterior MI with new apical holosystolic murmur and crackles — mechanism of dyspnoea? [DocT GT]
Acute mitral regurgitation.
Inferior STEMI, murmur, pulmonary oedema, cold and hypotensive — intervention? [DocT GT]
Intra-aortic balloon pump.
MI-64.punch: Sudden PEA with tamponade is free wall rupture; a new murmur with shock is VSR or papillary rupture, sorted by echo. Lower afterload with an IABP as the next step and send for surgery as the definitive one; avoid pressors that raise afterload.

New loud holosystolic murmur, thrill, shock, O₂ step-up RA→PA

MI-65.intro: Step 5 narrowed to the septum. No real question is linked; the testable point is the timing trade-off — early surgery sews into friable necrotic muscle, late surgery risks death while waiting.
why: **Anterior or posterolateral MI (per notes).** Anterior MI (LAD) tears the apical septum, usually a simple defect; inferior MI (RCA/PDA) tears the basal inferior septum, a more complex defect often with RV infarction and a worse outcome. The usual pairing in guidelines and reviews is anterior and inferior.

**Early surgery: high mortality (20–40%) — for refractory symptoms.** The necrotic edges hold sutures poorly before scar forms, so early repair carries higher mortality and residual leaks; a patient in refractory shock has no other option. The card’s figure is low: in the STS registry operative mortality was 54% when repair was within 7 days of MI and 18% after that, partly because the sickest are operated on first.

**Late surgery: risk of rupture extension and death while waiting — if responding to therapy.** Delaying lets the edges fibrose and improves repair, but the defect can enlarge; this route is only for those stable on IABP or MCS and drugs.
**Percutaneous closure.** A septal occluder device, used in selected anatomy, as a bridge or for residual defects after surgery.
mimic: Apical (anterior MI) vs basal (inferior MI) VSR
Apical is simpler to repair; basal is complex and carries a worse prognosis.
traps: “Wait 4–6 weeks for every VSR”
Only if the patient is stable; in refractory shock operate now despite the risk.
decode: Post-MI VSR in refractory shock despite IABP — timing of surgery? [pattern]
Emergency surgery.
Post-MI VSR stable on support — strategy? [pattern]
Delayed surgery (or percutaneous closure) once the edges have scarred.
MI-65.punch: Early VSR repair is a dangerous operation on soft tissue and is reserved for those who cannot wait; delayed repair is safer for the stable, provided the defect does not extend.

MI-66.intro: Step 5 at the slow end. Instead of tearing, a transmural scar can thin and bulge, and it shows on the ECG as an ST elevation that never settles. The one real question (46% right) tests the Q wave, the permanent part of the scar.
why: **<5% of AMI; anteroseptal / apical LV.** Large anterior transmural infarcts without timely reperfusion; with prompt PCI aneurysm has become uncommon.

**Persistent ST elevation; Q waves.** The akinetic scar keeps the ST segment raised for weeks after the event, and the dead myocardium leaves Q waves. With no new pain and no new troponin rise, this is a fixed scar, not a new infarct (MI-27).

**LV thrombus (apex) → systemic embolism → long-term oral anticoagulation.** Stasis in the akinetic apex forms thrombus (over 9% after anterior STEMI). ESC 2023 says OAC (warfarin or a NOAC) ‘should be considered for 3–6 months’, guided by repeat echo or CMR, rather than indefinitely.
**Large aneurysm, recurrent thromboembolism, mural / apical thrombus.** Aneurysmectomy is also considered for refractory heart failure or ventricular arrhythmias arising from the aneurysm.
mimic: True aneurysm vs pseudoaneurysm

A true aneurysm is a wide-necked bulge of scar that rarely ruptures; a pseudoaneurysm is a contained free wall rupture with a narrow neck, walled by pericardium, and needs surgery because it ruptures.
Old MI vs acute MI on ECG
Q waves without ST elevation mean an old, healed infarct; ST elevation with symptoms or rising troponin is acute; persistent ST elevation with Q waves weeks later is aneurysm.
traps: “Acute coronary syndrome” for Q waves in I, aVL and V5 with exertional dyspnoea
Only 46% chose old MI. Q waves are permanent scar; acute ischaemia needs ST or T changes and a matching story.
“Re-infarction — reperfuse” for ST elevation weeks after an anterior MI
Persistent ST elevation with deep Q waves and no new troponin rise is aneurysm.
decode: Known CAD, fatigue, ECG with Q waves in I, aVL, V5 — diagnosis? [DocT QBank]
Old (lateral) myocardial infarction.
ST elevation still present 6 weeks after an anterior MI — cause? [pattern]
LV aneurysm.
MI-66.punch: Persistent ST elevation with Q waves weeks after an anterior MI is an aneurysm, not a new infarct; its danger is apical thrombus and embolism, treated with oral anticoagulation (ESC: 3–6 months), and surgery is for the large or embolising aneurysm.

parts.q: What makes a Q wave pathological? [DocT QBank]
parts.a: The classic definition is at least 40 ms wide or deeper than 25% of the following R wave, in two or more contiguous leads. The Fourth Universal Definition uses a lower bar: Q ≥30 ms and ≥1 mm deep (in V2–V3, any Q over 20 ms or a QS complex) in two contiguous leads.

MI-67.intro: Step 6 starts with grading the risk. No real question is linked; GRACE is tested through its cut-off of 140 and through the contrast with TIMI (MI-69).
why: **Background: age, history of heart failure, history of AMI. Admission / stay: heart rate, systolic BP, ST depression, serum creatinine, elevated cardiac enzymes, no in-hospital PCI.** These are the nine variables of the post-discharge (6-month) nomogram. The original in-hospital GRACE model uses eight: age, heart rate, systolic BP, creatinine, Killip class, cardiac arrest at admission, ST deviation and raised enzymes. Each variable is weighted, so age and haemodynamics count far more than any single item.
**6-month mortality after ACS.** The current calculator (GRACE 2.0) also gives in-hospital and 1-year figures.

**GRACE >140 = high risk (early invasive, MI-43; discharge threshold, MI-32).** In NSTE-ACS, GRACE >140 is one of the high-risk features that call for angiography within 24 hours; below 140, with a negative rule-out and no pain, early discharge is acceptable.
mimic: GRACE vs Killip
Killip is a bedside HF class (one of GRACE’s in-hospital inputs); GRACE combines many variables into a mortality estimate.
traps: “GRACE predicts 14-day events”
That is TIMI; GRACE predicts death, here at 6 months.
decode: NSTEMI, GRACE 160, stable — timing of angiography? [pattern]
Early invasive, within 24 hours.
MI-67.punch: GRACE weights nine variables into the risk of death at 6 months; above 140 the patient is high risk and goes for angiography within 24 hours.

MI-68.intro: Step 6 with the simpler tool. No real question is linked; the test is usually the variables, especially aspirin use, which surprises people.
why: **Age ≥65, ≥3 CAD risk factors, known CAD (stenosis ≥50%), aspirin in the last 7 days, ≥2 rest-angina episodes in 24 h, ST deviation, elevated cardiac markers.** Aspirin use counts because an ACS that breaks through aspirin marks a more aggressive, more thrombotic disease.
**Death, new / recurrent MI, or urgent revascularisation through 14 days.** A short-term composite, not mortality at 6 months.

**0–1 → 4.7%; 2 → 8.3%; 3 → 13.2%; 4 → 19.9%; 5 → 26.2%; 6–7 → 40.9%.** The risk climbs steeply with each point, which is why higher scores were linked to greater benefit from enoxaparin and an early invasive approach.
mimic: TIMI UA/NSTEMI score vs TIMI STEMI score
The STEMI score is a different, weighted tool for 30-day mortality; the seven one-point items are the UA/NSTEMI score.
traps: “Aspirin use lowers the TIMI score”
It adds a point.
decode: Which is a TIMI UA/NSTEMI variable — aspirin in the last 7 days, heart rate, creatinine? [pattern]
Aspirin in the last 7 days.
MI-68.punch: TIMI gives one point for each of seven items, aspirin use included, and predicts death, MI or urgent revascularisation at 14 days, from 4.7% at 0–1 points to 40.9% at 6–7.

MI-69.intro: Step 6 as a comparison. No real question is linked; the classic slip is giving TIMI the 6-month figure that belongs to GRACE.
why: **GRACE: weighted points → nomogram; TIMI: 1 point each (0–7).** Weighting makes GRACE more accurate, which is why ESC prefers it; TIMI is quicker at the bedside.
**GRACE: mortality at 6 months; TIMI: death / MI / urgent revasc at 14 days.**
**GRACE: ESC risk group (>140), discharge in 0/3 h algorithm; TIMI: UA / NSTEMI stratification.**
mimic: Mortality endpoint vs composite endpoint
GRACE predicts death alone; TIMI predicts a composite of death, MI and urgent revascularisation.
traps: “TIMI predicts 6-month mortality” (the notes)
6 months and mortality belong to GRACE; TIMI is a 14-day composite.
decode: Score preferred by ESC for NSTE-ACS risk, with cut-off? [pattern]
GRACE, >140 high risk.
MI-69.punch: GRACE is weighted, nine variables, death at 6 months and the ESC tool; TIMI is seven one-point items and a 14-day composite.

spine: Watch the first two days

After reperfusion the patient stays on a monitor for 24–48 hours because the early killers are arrhythmia and re-occlusion, and an echo before discharge sets the LVEF that decides the drugs and the device.
Ventricular arrhythmias by timing
Early VT/VF comes from ischaemia and is treated by reperfusion, potassium, magnesium and a beta-blocker; AIVR at reperfusion is benign; antiarrhythmics are never given prophylactically.
AV block by territory
Inferior MI blocks the AV node, which recovers; anterior MI blocks the His–Purkinje system, which does not respond to atropine and needs pacing.
Pump failure and shock

Lost myocardium causes congestion or low output; shock is treated by opening the culprit artery first, then drugs, with routine IABP and VA-ECMO of no benefit and Impella helping only selected STEMI shock.
Mechanical complications

Around days 1–7 the necrotic wall can tear — free wall, septum or papillary muscle — and present as sudden collapse or sudden pulmonary oedema with a new murmur; the answer is echo, a bridge and surgery.
Risk scores and lifelong drugs

GRACE (nine weighted variables, death at 6 months, >140 high risk) and TIMI (seven one-point items, 14-day events) grade the risk; a high-dose statin and 12 months of DAPT go to everyone, and beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor and MRA follow the LVEF.
CVS10D.primer: Once the artery is open, the infarct still threatens the patient in three ways. Electrically, ischaemic and then scarred myocardium fires abnormally or blocks conduction; mechanically, necrotic muscle softens over the first days and can tear; and as a pump, lost myocardium leaves too little forward output. Coronary anatomy predicts most of it: the RCA supplies the AV node in most people, LAD septal branches supply the His bundle and bundle branches, and the posteromedial papillary muscle depends on a single artery. ESC classes read as I ‘recommended’, IIa ‘should be considered’, IIb ‘may be considered’, III ‘not recommended’; CVS10C covered reperfusion itself.

MI-70.intro: Step 2 is the rebuilt definition. No real question is linked yet (the definition is three months old); the card is a translation table, and the testable point is why each old element went.
why: **Types 1–5 → primary / secondary / procedure-related.** The numbers mixed mechanism (type 1 plaque, type 2 supply–demand) with setting (4 and 5 procedures) and outcome (3 death). The 2026 scheme sorts by setting only: an acute coronary event, an outside stress, or a procedure.

**Type 3 → removed; classify fatal MI by setting / autopsy.** Type 3 was a death before troponin could be drawn; it told you nothing about cause. The death is now filed under whichever setting the history or post-mortem shows.

**>5× / >10× URL → no troponin multiples; complication and/or imaging evidence.** Troponin rises after almost every PCI and every CABG, so a multiple of the URL could not separate a real infarct from expected procedural injury. Procedure-related MI now needs an identifiable complication (side-branch loss, dissection, graft failure, no-reflow) with ischaemia and injury, and the same criteria apply to PCI and surgery.

**48 h window → 30 days.** Early stent thrombosis and graft failure happen within the first month, after the 48 hours had closed; 30 days captures them as procedure-related. Beyond 30 days the event is new disease and counts as primary MI (MI-71).

**One 99th URL → sex-specific 99th URL.** Women have lower normal troponin concentrations, so a single cut-off set largely on men under-recognised injury in women; the 2026 task force calls sex-specific limits necessary.

**MINOCA = infarction → MINOCA = injury, a working diagnosis.** Most patients labelled MINOCA turn out to have myocarditis, Takotsubo or a non-cardiac cause. The label now means ‘injury with non-obstructive coronaries, cause not yet found’; once a cause is proven the patient is reclassified (primary, secondary, procedure-related or a non-MI diagnosis).
mimic: UDMI 2018 type 2 vs UDMI 2026 secondary MI
Type 2 accepted supply–demand ischaemia on symptoms or ECG; secondary MI needs obstructive CAD on coronary assessment or a new wall-motion defect / loss of viability on imaging.
traps: “PCI-related MI: troponin >5 × URL within 48 h”
That is UDMI 2018 type 4a. Under UDMI 2026 there is no multiple and the window is 30 days; read which definition the stem assumes (watch line).
decode: [pattern] Which UDMI 2018 element was abolished outright in 2026?
Type 3 (fatal MI), and the troponin multiples for PCI and CABG.
[pattern] Time window for procedure-related MI under the 2026 definition?
30 days after the percutaneous or surgical cardiac procedure.
MI-70.punch: UDMI 2026 classifies MI by setting, not by number: no type 3, no 5× or 10× multiples, a 30-day procedural window, sex-specific 99th percentiles, and MINOCA demoted to injury until proven otherwise.

MI-71.sub: Cardiology → ACS → Classifying cases under UDMI 2026
MI-71.intro: Step 3 puts the new definition to work. Both real questions are stent thrombosis presenting as STEMI, one hours after PCI (48% right) and one at two months; the classification changes with the clock, the treatment does not.
why: **Stent thrombosis, day 10 → procedure-related MI (≤30 days).** It is a complication of the procedure inside the 30-day window. Classification aside, a new ST rise in the stented territory is a STEMI and goes straight back to the lab.

**Stent thrombosis, 6 months → PRIMARY MI (>30 days).** After 30 days stent thrombosis, restenosis and graft failure are treated as de novo coronary disease and filed as primary MI. The NEET 2025 stem (stent 2 months earlier) is therefore a primary MI.

**SCAD → PRIMARY MI.** Primary MI now covers every acute coronary pathology, not only plaque rupture: SCAD, vasospasm and coronary embolism are included. In 2018 SCAD sat under type 2 (supply), which is why it is the trap. SCAD affects mainly young and middle-aged women, often peripartum, and many have fibromuscular dysplasia, so renal, iliac and cerebral arteries are screened (Marrow line).

**GI bleed + known obstructive CAD + new RWMA → SECONDARY MI.** The bleed (anaemia, hypotension) is the outside stress; obstructive CAD without an acute coronary lesion and a new wall-motion defect each confirm secondary MI. The treatment is the bleed and the haemoglobin, not antithrombotics.

**Sepsis, no ischaemic evidence → myocardial INJURY, not MI.** Troponin rises in sepsis from inflammation, tachycardia and hypotension; without obstructive CAD or a new wall-motion defect there is no proof that ischaemia caused it. In 2018 many such cases were called type 2 MI.
**Non-obstructive coronaries, cause unknown → MINOCA, a working diagnosis.** Next comes the search for the cause, with CMR first (ESC 2023 I, B), then reclassification.
mimic: Secondary MI vs myocardial injury
Both follow an outside stress; secondary MI needs obstructive CAD or a new RWMA/loss of viability, injury has neither.
SCAD vs atherothrombotic primary MI
Both are primary MI; SCAD is a young woman, often peripartum or with FMD, few risk factors, and is usually managed conservatively unless flow is lost.
traps: “Intravenous nitroglycerin” or “transthoracic echo” first for new chest pain and ST elevation after PCI
Only 48% chose urgent repeat angiography. New ST elevation in the stented territory is acute stent thrombosis, a STEMI; nitrates, observation or echo only delay reperfusion.
“Thrombolysis” for stent thrombosis with ST elevation
Stent thrombus is platelet-rich and responds poorly to lysis; load DAPT, anticoagulate and send for primary PCI. Heparin alone or a beta-blocker is not reperfusion.
“SCAD is a supply–demand (secondary) MI”
That was 2018 type 2; in 2026 SCAD is an acute coronary pathology, a primary MI.
“Sepsis with a troponin rise is a secondary MI”
Not without ischaemic proof (obstructive CAD or a new RWMA); it is injury.
decode: New chest pain and ST elevation in the stented territory hours after PCI — next step? [DocT GT]
Urgent repeat coronary angiography (acute stent thrombosis).
DES 2 months ago, anterior ST elevation, suspected stent thrombosis — immediate management? [NEET 2025]
DAPT with urgent PCI; under UDMI 2026 it is a primary MI (>30 days).
[pattern] Septic shock, troponin rise, normal coronaries, no wall-motion change — UDMI 2026 label?
Myocardial injury, not MI.
MI-71.punch: File stent thrombosis by the clock (≤30 days procedure-related, later primary), file SCAD as primary, demand secondary MI to show obstructive CAD or a new RWMA, and treat every stent thrombosis with ST elevation as a STEMI: DAPT and the cath lab, not lysis.

UDMI 2026

MI-72.intro: Step 4: the antiplatelet rules after PCI. No real question is linked; the testable change is which drug is dropped early, and that ESC and ACC/AHA drop different ones.
why: **Aspirin + oral P2Y12 for at least 12 months — default.** ACC/AHA 2025 gives DAPT for at least 1 year (1, A) in patients not at high bleeding risk, because stent thrombosis and new plaque events cluster in the first year.

**Tolerating DAPT → switch to TICAGRELOR MONOTHERAPY ≥1 month after PCI (to reduce bleeding).** Class 1, A. Once the stent is covered, aspirin adds bleeding more than protection on top of a potent P2Y12 inhibitor; ticagrelor-alone trials (TWILIGHT, ULTIMATE-DAPT) cut bleeding without more ischaemic events. Lesser options are 2b: switching ticagrelor or prasugrel to clopidogrel after 1 month, or single antiplatelet therapy after 1 month if bleeding risk is high.

**Ticagrelor or prasugrel; clopidogrel if these cannot be used.** Class 1 for PCI in STEMI and NSTE-ACS, for fewer MACE and stent thromboses; ACC/AHA names no preference between the two, whereas ESC 2023 prefers prasugrel for patients going to PCI (IIa, B; ISAR-REACT 5). Clopidogrel is for those who cannot take them (prior stroke for prasugrel, oral anticoagulation, high bleeding risk).

**NSTE-ACS with angiography delayed >24 h → clopidogrel or ticagrelor.** It is 2b (‘may be considered’). Routine pretreatment before early angiography is not advised: the anatomy may send the patient to CABG, and prasugrel is not used before the anatomy is known. ESC 2023 also gives pretreatment beyond 24 hours IIb.
mimic: ESC 2023 vs ACC/AHA 2025 at the end of DAPT

ESC: 12 months of DAPT, then usually aspirin alone; single antiplatelet therapy, preferably a P2Y12 inhibitor, after 3–6 months ‘should be considered’ (IIa) if event-free and not high ischaemic risk, and aspirin or P2Y12 monotherapy after 1 month ‘may be considered’ (IIb) only in high bleeding risk; de-escalation in the first 30 days is not recommended. ACC/AHA: can drop aspirin at 1 month and continue ticagrelor alone.
traps: “After 1 month of DAPT, continue aspirin alone” as the ACC/AHA bleeding-reduction option
The Class 1 option keeps ticagrelor and drops aspirin (watch line).
decode: [pattern] ACS, PCI, tolerating ticagrelor-based DAPT, worried about bleeding — ACC/AHA 2025 option at 1 month?
Stop aspirin, continue ticagrelor alone (1, A).
[pattern] NSTE-ACS, angiography planned at 48 h — P2Y12 before the lab?
Clopidogrel or ticagrelor may be considered (2b); not prasugrel.
MI-72.punch: Default DAPT is 12 months with prasugrel or ticagrelor; ACC/AHA 2025 lets the patient drop aspirin and stay on ticagrelor alone from 1 month, whereas ESC keeps aspirin at the end.

MI-73.sub: Cardiology → ACS → Beta-blockers after MI without reduced EF
MI-73.intro: Step 6 starts with the drug whose old rule (everyone after MI) came from the pre-reperfusion era. No real question is linked; four recent trials answer whether reperfused patients with good LVEF still need it.
why: **REDUCE-AMI: LVEF ≥50% → no benefit.** 5,020 patients with obstructive CAD, 95% treated by PCI: death or MI 7.9% vs 8.3% (HR 0.96) over a median 3.5 years. With a small infarct and a normal ventricle there is little arrhythmic or remodelling substrate for the drug to act on.

**REBOOT (~8,000): LVEF >40%, no HF → no benefit overall; signal at 40–49%.** 8,505 patients: death, reinfarction or HF admission HR 1.04 (0.89–1.22). A prespecified sex analysis suggested more events with beta-blockers in women, mainly those with preserved EF, and none in men; it is hypothesis-generating, not a reason to withhold the drug when LVEF is reduced.

**BETAMI-DANBLOCK (~5,500): LVEF ≥40% → fewer events (14.2% vs 16.3%).** 5,574 patients, HR 0.85 (0.75–0.98), median follow-up about 3.5 years. Unlike REDUCE-AMI it included patients with mildly reduced EF (40–49%), where the benefit is concentrated; like the other trials it was open-label.

**LVEF 40–49% (4 trials) → 25% relative reduction in death / MI / HF (10.7% vs 14.4%).** The pooled analysis of 1,885 patients with mildly reduced EF from REBOOT, BETAMI, DANBLOCK and CAPITAL-RCT gave HR 0.75 (0.58–0.97). The benefit lies where the ventricle is damaged; it fades as LVEF normalises.
mimic: Starting vs stopping

REDUCE-AMI and REBOOT ask whether to start after a reperfused MI with good LVEF; ABYSS asks whether to stop years later: interruption (LVEF ≥40%, MI a median 2.9 years before) failed non-inferiority (23.8% vs 21.1%), mostly CV admissions, with no quality-of-life gain.
traps: “A long-term beta-blocker improves outcome in every post-MI patient”

Proven long-term benefit is for LVEF ≤40% (I, A in both guidelines) and, from the 2025 pooled data, 40–49%; at LVEF ≥50% REDUCE-AMI and REBOOT show none. The guidelines predate REBOOT: ESC 2023 gives routine beta-blockers regardless of LVEF IIa, and ACC/AHA 2025 still advises starting an oral beta-blocker within 24 hours in all ACS without contraindications (1, A), mainly against reinfarction and arrhythmia, leaving the duration in preserved EF open.
decode: [pattern] Reperfused STEMI, LVEF 58%, no HF — does a long-term beta-blocker improve outcome?
No clear benefit (REDUCE-AMI, REBOOT).
[pattern] Post-MI LVEF 45% — beta-blocker?
Yes: mildly reduced EF benefits (pooled analysis, HR 0.75).
MI-73.punch: After a reperfused MI the beta-blocker earns its place when LVEF is below 50% and has no proven benefit when LVEF is preserved; stopping one years later has not been shown to be safe (ABYSS).

MI-74.sub: Cardiology → ACS → Revascularisation, imaging, access and shock (ACC/AHA 2025)
MI-74.intro: Step 5 is what is done to the arteries. No real question is linked; the testable point is that complete revascularisation reverses in shock, and that devices help only in a narrow group.
why: **Recommended (I), index or staged; not in cardiogenic shock (culprit-only, CS-36).** Non-culprit lesions in a stable patient cause later MI, so treating them cuts MACE (COMPLETE): Class 1 in selected stable STEMI and in NSTE-ACS without left main disease or a plan for CABG. In shock routine non-culprit PCI at the index procedure is 3: Harm in both, because the extra contrast and time raised death or renal replacement in CULPRIT-SHOCK.

**Class 1 to guide PCI.** 1, A for stenting the left main or complex lesions: IVUS or OCT shows stent under-expansion and malapposition that angiography misses, the causes of stent thrombosis and restenosis.

**Radial preferred.** 1, A: fewer bleeds, fewer vascular complications and lower death than femoral, because the radial artery is superficial and compressible (the femoral retroperitoneal bleed is the Top-up).

**Reasonable (IIa) in selected patients — DANGER-SHOCK (MI-63).** 2a, B-R in STEMI with severe or refractory LV-dominant shock: DanGer Shock cut 180-day death (45.8% vs 58.5%) but with more bleeding, limb ischaemia and renal failure, and it excluded comatose cardiac-arrest survivors and RV shock.
**Not recommended (III).** Routine IABP or VA-ECMO is 3: No benefit (IABP-SHOCK II, ECLS-SHOCK: no survival gain). VA-ECMO raises afterload on a failing LV; it is a rescue tool, not routine.

**Transfer to shock centres (Class 1).** Shock outcomes are better where the team, round-the-clock PCI, mechanical support and cardiac surgery are all available, so the sickest patients are moved to such a hub early. Some guideline summaries (Cleveland Clinic) report this as a Class 1 recommendation, but the classed shock statements in the ACC/AHA 2025 text are about revascularisation and devices; the hub-and-spoke model with early transfer of refractory shock to a Level 1 shock centre comes from the ACC 2025 concise clinical guidance on cardiogenic shock, which carries no class (see FLAGS). The exam answer is still a centre with shock expertise.
mimic: Stable multivessel ACS vs multivessel ACS in shock
Stable: treat all significant lesions, at the index procedure or staged. Shock: culprit only at the index procedure.
ACC/AHA 2025 vs ESC 2023 classes

ESC 2023: complete revascularisation is recommended (I) in stable STEMI, at the index PCI or within 45 days, but only ‘should be considered’ (IIa) in NSTE-ACS; intravascular imaging ‘should be considered’ (IIa). ACC/AHA 2025 makes both Class 1.
traps: “Complete revascularisation at the index procedure in cardiogenic shock”
3: Harm (CULPRIT-SHOCK); the notes’ shock table is outdated here (watch line).
“Impella for every AMI shock”
Only selected STEMI LV shock (DanGer criteria), at the price of more complications.
decode: [pattern] STEMI in shock, three-vessel disease — what to stent at the index procedure?
The culprit only.
[pattern] AMI shock — routine IABP?
No (3: No benefit, IABP-SHOCK II).
MI-74.punch: Treat all significant lesions in the stable patient but only the culprit in shock, image complex lesions, go radial, and reserve a microaxial pump for selected STEMI shock; routine IABP and VA-ECMO bring no survival benefit.

MI-75.intro: Step 1 is how fast an NSTEMI can be ruled in or out. No real question is linked; the trap is that three sources give three intervals and the stem tells you which one it wants.
why: **ESC 2023: 0 h / 1 h (preferred) or 0 h / 2 h — I, B.** A high-sensitivity assay measures troponin in most healthy people, so a small change over an hour separates an evolving infarct from stable chronic injury; assay-specific cut-offs (e.g. a very low hs-cTnT <5 ng/L at 0 h, if pain began more than 3 hours earlier) give rule-in and rule-out at 1 or 2 hours, and an inconclusive result gets a further test at 3 hours.

**Notes (older ESC): 0 h / 3 h — MI-32.** It used the 99th percentile at presentation and 3 hours; ESC 2023 keeps it only as an alternative where the 1 h or 2 h algorithms are not available, with no class, because it balances safety and speed less well.

**AHA 2025 ACLS: recheck at 1 h OR 3 h — ACLS-57.** The course algorithm leaves the interval to the local assay; the AHA/ACC chest pain guideline gives 1–3 hours for high-sensitivity and 3–6 hours for conventional troponin.
mimic: High-sensitivity vs conventional troponin repeat
High-sensitivity: 1–2 hours (ESC) or 1–3 hours (AHA/ACC); conventional: 3–6 hours.
traps: “ESC recommends 0 h / 3 h” in an ESC-framed question
ESC 2023 wants 0 h / 1 h or 0 h / 2 h; 3 h is a fallback (watch line).
decode: [pattern] Per ESC 2023, preferred repeat interval for hs-cTn in suspected NSTE-ACS?
1 hour (0 h / 1 h), or 2 hours (0 h / 2 h).
MI-75.punch: ESC 2023 repeats hs-cTn at 1 or 2 hours; the 3-hour schedule survives as a fallback in ESC and in the AHA ACLS algorithm, so answer by the source the stem names.

MI-76.sub: Cardiology → ACS → Lipids, rehabilitation and anaemia (ACC/AHA 2025)
MI-76.intro: Step 6 ends with the long-term prescriptions. No real question is linked; the testable points are the two LDL thresholds with different classes and the haemoglobin of 10.
why: **High-intensity statin for all.** 1, A, regardless of baseline LDL-C (atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg), because the benefit tracks the absolute LDL-C reduction and ACS patients are at the highest risk.

**LDL-C ≥70 mg/dL → add ezetimibe / PCSK9 inhibitor / inclisiran / bempedoic acid (I).** 1, A on a maximally tolerated statin; each further fall in LDL-C lowers events (IMPROVE-IT, FOURIER, ODYSSEY OUTCOMES).

**LDL-C 55–69 mg/dL (IIa).** 2a, B-R. 55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) is the ESC goal, so the American guideline has moved towards it without making it a mandate. The ESC 2025 focused update keeps the goals and adds earlier combination: intensify during the index admission if already treated (I, C); start statin plus ezetimibe in hospital if the goal looks unreachable with statin alone (IIa, B).
**Fasting panel at 4–8 weeks after starting or changing therapy.** 1, C-LD: by then the statin effect is complete, so the result decides whether to add a non-statin agent.

**Refer before discharge (I); home-based if centre unavailable.** Referral before discharge is 1, A, because patients referred later often never attend; home-based rehabilitation is a reasonable alternative (2a).

**Transfusion to maintain Hb 10 g/dL may be reasonable.** 2b, B-R in ACS with anaemia and no active bleeding. Anaemia lowers oxygen delivery to an ischaemic myocardium; in MINT, a liberal target (≥10 g/dL) gave fewer 30-day deaths or MIs than restrictive (7–8 g/dL), 14.5% vs 16.9% (RR 1.15 for restrictive, P 0.07), so the difference fell short of significance and the class is only 2b. This is an exception to the general ICU threshold of 7 g/dL, which was never tested in acute MI.
mimic: Hb threshold: ACS vs general ICU
ACS with anaemia: aiming for 10 g/dL may be reasonable (MINT). General ICU: transfuse below 7 g/dL (TRICC).
traps: “LDL-C 60 mg/dL on maximal statin: adding ezetimibe is Class 1”
55–69 mg/dL is 2a (reasonable); Class 1 begins at ≥70 mg/dL (watch line).
“Restrictive transfusion (Hb 7) in acute MI with anaemia”
ACS is the exception: Hb 10 g/dL may be reasonable.
decode: [pattern] Post-ACS on atorvastatin 80 mg, LDL-C 82 mg/dL — next step?
Add a non-statin agent (1, A).
[pattern] NSTEMI, Hb 8.2 g/dL, no bleeding — transfusion target?
Hb 10 g/dL may be reasonable (2b, MINT).
MI-76.punch: High-intensity statin for all, add a non-statin agent at LDL-C ≥70 (Class 1) and consider one at 55–69 (2a), recheck at 4–8 weeks, refer to rehab before discharge, and in ACS anaemia aim for Hb 10, not 7.

topups.q: Hypotension with back/flank pain hours after femoral-access PCI, no visible groin haematoma?
a: - Retroperitoneal haematoma: high puncture above the inguinal ligament; women, obesity, anticoagulation.
- Diagnose with CT abdomen/pelvis; resuscitate, stop/reverse anticoagulation.
- Covered stent or embolisation (or surgery) if ongoing bleeding.

x.sub: Cardiology → PCI complications → Retroperitoneal bleed after femoral access
x.intro: Step 5 says go radial, and this is the main reason: a femoral puncture above the inguinal ligament can bleed into the retroperitoneum, where nothing can be compressed and nothing shows at the groin. The question is a patient who becomes hypotensive hours after PCI with a clean groin.
why: **Retroperitoneal haematoma: high puncture above the inguinal ligament; women, obesity, anticoagulation.** Above the ligament the external iliac artery lies behind the peritoneum with no femoral head behind it to press against, so blood tracks up into the retroperitoneal space instead of forming a visible groin haematoma. Women and patients at extremes of body size (low body weight is the classic risk; in obesity the ligament is hard to locate and punctures land high), full anticoagulation, GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors and large sheaths add to the risk.

**Diagnose with CT abdomen/pelvis; resuscitate, stop/reverse anticoagulation.** Back, flank or lower abdominal pain with hypotension, tachycardia and a falling haemoglobin after femoral access is this until proved otherwise; CT of the abdomen and pelvis shows the haematoma, and a contrast phase shows whether it is still bleeding. Ultrasound of the groin is often normal and does not exclude it. Fluids and blood, stop the heparin (protamine if needed) and weigh stopping antiplatelets against the stent-thrombosis risk with the cardiologist. Most stop with these measures.

**Covered stent or embolisation (or surgery) if ongoing bleeding.** Persistent instability or contrast leaking on CT means an active arterial bleed; an endovascular covered stent across the puncture or embolisation of a branch seals it, and open repair is the fallback.
mimic: Retroperitoneal bleed vs groin haematoma or pseudoaneurysm
A groin haematoma or pseudoaneurysm is visible or palpable at the groin (a pseudoaneurysm pulsates with a bruit, diagnosed by duplex); a retroperitoneal bleed has a quiet groin, back pain and shock.
Retroperitoneal bleed vs vagal reaction after sheath removal
Vagal: bradycardia and hypotension at sheath pull, settles with atropine and fluids. Bleed: tachycardia, falling Hb, hours later.
traps: “No groin haematoma, so the access site is not the cause”
A high puncture bleeds backwards into the retroperitoneum; the groin is typically normal.
“Hypotension after PCI: give inotropes for pump failure”
Check the haemoglobin and CT first; after femoral access the first cause to exclude is bleeding.
decode: Hypotension with back/flank pain hours after femoral-access PCI, no visible groin haematoma [Marrow]
Retroperitoneal haematoma: CT abdomen/pelvis, resuscitate, stop or reverse anticoagulation; covered stent or embolisation if it continues.
x.punch: Shock with back or flank pain after femoral PCI and a normal groin is a retroperitoneal bleed from a high puncture: CT, blood, stop the heparin, and seal it with a covered stent or embolisation if it keeps bleeding; radial access prevents it.

spine: Ruling in faster: troponin timing
ESC 2023 repeats high-sensitivity troponin at 1 or 2 hours, not 3; the 3-hour schedule survives only as a fallback and in the AHA ACLS algorithm.
The definition was rebuilt
UDMI 2026 drops numbered types, troponin multiples for procedures and the 48-hour window, uses sex-specific limits, and calls MINOCA an injury until a cause is found.
Classifying the case

A troponin rise is sorted by setting: an acute coronary event is primary MI, an outside stress on obstructive CAD or a new wall-motion defect is secondary MI, a complication within 30 days of a procedure is procedure-related, and anything without ischaemic proof is injury.
Antiplatelets: dropping aspirin early
ACC/AHA 2025 keeps 12 months of DAPT as the default with prasugrel or ticagrelor, but lets the patient drop aspirin and stay on ticagrelor alone from one month to cut bleeding.
The artery, the access and shock

Treat every significant lesion in stable patients, image complex ones, go radial, but in shock open only the culprit, use a microaxial pump only in selected STEMI shock, and never IABP or VA-ECMO routinely.
After the ward: beta-blocker, lipids, rehab

Beta-blockers help when LVEF is below 50% and not clearly above it; LDL-C at or above 70 mg/dL on a maximal statin mandates another agent, rehab is referred before discharge, and Hb 10 g/dL may be a reasonable target.
CVS10E.primer: This deck is a list of changes, so the old rule and the new one are learnt side by side and the exam question decides which it wants. ACC/AHA grade recommendations 1 (recommended), 2a (reasonable), 2b (may be reasonable) and 3 (No benefit or Harm); ESC grades I, IIa (should be considered), IIb (may be considered) and III. The Fourth Universal Definition (2018) sorted MI into types 1–5; the Fifth (2026, published August 2026) replaces them, so older keys still use the types. American guidance gives LDL-C in mg/dL: 70 mg/dL is about 1.8 mmol/L and 55 mg/dL about 1.4 mmol/L, the ESC goal.

CAR-01.sub: Cardiology → Tachyarrhythmias → Unstable AF: synchronised cardioversion
CAR-01.intro: The deck starts with the first fork of every tachycardia algorithm: is the patient unstable? Here fast AF has produced hypotension, crackles and hypoxaemia, so the rhythm is the cause of the shock and the question is how fast you can remove it.
why: **Unstable tachycardia = synchronised cardioversion NOW. Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion; do not wait for TOE or 3 weeks of anticoagulation — give heparin, but shock first.** At 160/min the ventricle has too little diastole to fill, the atrial kick is gone, and output falls; the rise in left atrial pressure gives the crackles. A drug takes minutes to work and every rate-control drug (diltiazem, metoprolol) is a negative inotrope or vasodilator that lowers the pressure further; a shock works in one beat. The thrombo-embolic rules (3 weeks of anticoagulation or TOE to exclude left atrial thrombus) exist to protect stable patients from an elective procedure; in shock the risk of waiting is greater than the risk of a stroke, so heparin is started and the patient is shocked. Synchronisation times the shock to the R wave so it does not fall on the T wave and induce VF.

**Biphasic energies (AHA 2025): flutter 200 J may be reasonable (COR 2b; older 50–100 J); AF ≥200 J (COR 2a; older 120–200 J); other narrow regular (SVT) 100 J (algorithm; older 50–100 J); monomorphic VT with pulse 100 J; polymorphic VT/VF unsynchronised = defibrillate.** AHA 2025 raised the starting energy for AF because the first shock succeeds more often at higher energy, and repeated failed shocks add nothing but delay; energy is then increased if the shock fails. Polymorphic VT cannot be synchronised (the machine cannot find a consistent R wave), so it is treated as VF.
mimic: Unstable vs stable AF
Unstable (hypotension, pulmonary oedema, ischaemia, altered mentation): cardiovert now. Stable: rate control, and anticoagulation rules (CAR-05b) before any elective cardioversion.
Sepsis-driven AF vs AF causing the shock

In septic shock new AF is often a consequence; still, if the AF itself drops the pressure (BP falling with the onset of AF), the algorithm answer is cardioversion. Amiodarone is the stable or post-shock option.
traps: “IV diltiazem or metoprolol to control the rate first”
Both lower the BP further; with hypotension and crackles they can precipitate arrest. Only 48% chose cardioversion on the mini test.
“Heparin, then delayed cardioversion” or “TOE first”
Thrombus rules apply to stable patients. In shock you anticoagulate and shock in the same minute.
“Synchronised cardioversion at 100 J” for AF (DocT QBank key)
Cardioversion is the right choice and the key stands among its options; but AHA 2025 starts AF at ≥200 J. If the stem offers 200 J, take it.
“Amiodarone 150 mg bolus” in unstable post-operative AF (GT2o)
A drug is the stable-patient path; with BP 73/34 the answer is synchronised cardioversion (87% got it).
decode: Irregular tachycardia 140, BP 70/40, basal crackles — first-line? [DocT QBank, 80% right]
Synchronised cardioversion; not heparin, diltiazem or metoprolol.
Post-thoracotomy new AF 167/min, BP 73/34, onset 5 min ago [DocT GT, 87%]
Synchronised cardioversion; amiodarone and procainamide are for stable patients.
Septic ICU patient, new AF 155, BP down to 90/60 [DocT GT]
Immediate synchronised cardioversion (the key quotes 120–200 J, the pre-2025 AF range).
CAR-01.punch: If the rate is causing the shock, cardiovert now with heparin on board and skip the TOE; AHA 2025 starts AF at 200 J or more and synchronises every shock except for polymorphic VT and VF.

CAR-02.sub: Cardiology → Tachyarrhythmias → Stable SVT: vagal, adenosine, verapamil
CAR-02.intro: Once the patient is stable, the question becomes which part of the conduction system the rhythm uses. A regular narrow tachycardia at 180 with no visible P waves is usually a circuit through the AV node, so anything that briefly blocks the node will break it — and anything it does not break reveals itself.
why: **Vagal manoeuvres (modified Valsalva).** Vagal tone slows AV-nodal conduction and can interrupt a circuit that runs through the node. In REVERT the modified Valsalva (strain against 40 mmHg for 15 s semi-recumbent, then lie flat with the legs raised to 45° for 15 s) converted about 43% vs 17% with the standard manoeuvre; the leg raise adds venous return, which increases the vagal reflex after the strain. Carotid sinus massage is an alternative: supine, on ECG, one side only (right first) for 5–10 s, never with a carotid bruit or a recent TIA or stroke, because pressure can dislodge plaque.

**Adenosine 6 mg rapid push + flush; then 12 mg (may repeat 12 mg once).** Adenosine acts on A1 receptors in the AV node, opening potassium channels and blocking conduction for a few seconds; its half-life is under 10 seconds, so it must reach the heart as a bolus, through a proximal vein with a fast flush. AHA 2025 notes that 1 mg may be enough via a central line or after heart transplant (the drug reaches the heart undiluted, and denervated receptors are supersensitive); dipyridamole and carbamazepine potentiate it, theophylline and caffeine blunt it. Warn the patient of a brief sense of doom, flushing and chest tightness.

**IV verapamil (or diltiazem) — adenosine can trigger bronchospasm.** Adenosine acting on A1/A2B receptors in the airways can provoke bronchospasm in asthma; a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker blocks the node through L-type calcium channels instead, with no airway effect. It is safe only with a normal ventricle and no pre-excitation (CAR-03, CAR-04).

**AVNRT — re-entry within the AV node (slow + fast pathways); P hidden in the QRS.** In typical (slow–fast) AVNRT the impulse goes down the slow pathway and up the fast one, so atria and ventricles are activated at the same time and the retrograde P wave is buried in, or just after, the QRS (pseudo-S in II, III, aVF; pseudo-r′ in V1). AVRT uses an accessory pathway, needs a longer loop and shows a separate retrograde P in the ST segment; a delta wave in sinus rhythm gives it away.
mimic: AVNRT vs AVRT vs atrial tachycardia
AVNRT: P hidden or just after QRS. AVRT: P clearly in the ST segment, delta wave between attacks. Atrial tachycardia: a distinct P before each QRS, unaffected by blocking the node.
Adenosine terminates vs adenosine unmasks
Node-dependent rhythms (AVNRT, AVRT) stop. Atrial flutter and atrial tachycardia continue in the atria; ventricular slowing reveals flutter waves at about 300/min.
traps: “Asthmatic with SVT — adenosine”
Verapamil (or diltiazem) instead; only 7% chose it on the mini test.
“Stable SVT — adenosine 6 mg first”
Vagal manoeuvres come first in a stable patient (only 50% in DocT QBank; 93–98% when asked plainly).
“Re-entry via an accessory pathway” for retrograde P inverted in II, III, aVF at 180/min
That P-wave picture is typical AVNRT, re-entry within the node (42% right in AIM1).
“Take a deep breath before straining” (Marrow false statement)
The manoeuvre is a sustained strain (40 mmHg for 15 s), not a deep inspiratory effort.
decode: Stable narrow-complex tachycardia 180–190/min — first step? [DocT QBank 50%; DocT GT 93–98%]
Vagal manoeuvres.
Regular 180, narrow, inverted P in II, III, aVF — mechanism? [DocT GT AIM1, 42%]
Re-entry within the AV node (AVNRT).
Adenosine 6 mg slows the rate and reveals sawtooth waves at 300/min [DocT GT]
Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction.
Carotid sinus massage — important contraindication? [DocT GT, 100%]
Carotid bruit (or prior TIA/stroke).
CAR-02.punch: Stable regular narrow tachycardia: modified Valsalva, then adenosine 6 then 12 mg as a fast push, verapamil if asthmatic; AVNRT hides its P wave in the QRS, and anything adenosine slows but does not stop is atrial.

CAR-03.sub: Cardiology → Tachyarrhythmias → WPW and pre-excited AF
CAR-03.intro: The AV node is the brake that protects the ventricles from fast atrial rhythms. In WPW a second, unbraked connection exists, and every rule about nodal blockers flips when AF runs down it.
why: **Short PR, delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke), wide QRS.** The accessory pathway conducts without the nodal delay, so part of the ventricle is activated early (short PR, under 120 ms) and slowly through muscle (the slurred delta wave); the rest arrives through the normal system and the QRS is a fusion, hence wide.

**Adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, β-blockers, digoxin — blocking the AV node sends every AF beat down the accessory pathway → VF.** The node and the pathway compete for each atrial impulse; block the node and the pathway, which has a short refractory period and no decremental brake, takes all of them, at rates up to 300/min, which can degenerate into VF. Verapamil and digoxin also shorten the pathway’s refractory period. AHA 2023 and 2025 add IV amiodarone to the harmful list (COR 3), because its early effect is mainly nodal.

**Unstable → cardioversion. Stable → procainamide (or ibutilide).** These drugs slow conduction or prolong refractoriness in the accessory pathway itself, so the ventricular rate falls without removing the competition. Definitive treatment is catheter ablation of the pathway.

**Flecainide (class Ic) — blocks conduction in the accessory pathway.** A sodium channel blocker slows conduction in pathway tissue; ESC lists flecainide or propafenone as alternatives for pre-excited AF, and it is used to prevent AVRT. It is contraindicated with structural or ischaemic heart disease (CAST: excess deaths after MI). Its commonest dose-related non-cardiac effect is blurred vision, with dizziness (Marrow).
mimic: Pre-excited AF vs VT
Pre-excited AF: irregularly irregular, broad complexes that vary in width beat to beat, rates up to 250–300 in a young person. VT: regular, uniform complexes.
Orthodromic AVRT vs pre-excited AF in WPW
Orthodromic AVRT is regular and narrow (down the node, up the pathway): vagal manoeuvres and adenosine are allowed. The ban on nodal blockers applies to pre-excited AF (irregular and broad).
traps: “Verapamil is THE contraindicated drug” (DocT GT AIM1 Q36 / GT4 Q56, 45–54%)
Verapamil is the classic answer to pick, but adenosine, esmolol and IV amiodarone in the same options are also harmful (AHA class 3); the item has more than one correct option.
“AV nodal dual pathway” for delta waves and short PR (GT4, 39%)
Dual nodal pathways cause AVNRT and leave a normal ECG between attacks; a delta wave means an accessory AV pathway.
decode: Delta wave, short PR, wide QRS in sinus rhythm — underlying abnormality? [DocT GT, 39% and 90%]
Accessory AV pathway.
Known WPW, AF with rapid response — contraindicated drug? [DocT GT ×2, 45–54%]
Verapamil (but adenosine, esmolol and IV amiodarone are also harmful).
PR 100 ms and slurred QRS after rate control [DocT QBank, 77%]
WPW syndrome.
Blurred vision during PSVT treatment — which drug? [Marrow]
Flecainide.
CAR-03.punch: In pre-excited AF block the pathway, never the node: cardiovert if unstable, procainamide or ibutilide if stable, and no adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, β-blocker, digoxin or IV amiodarone.

CAR-04.sub: Cardiology → Tachyarrhythmias → AF rate control with low EF
CAR-04.intro: Still in the stable tachycardia branch, the next variable is the ventricle. With an ejection fraction of 30% the output depends on the contractility left, so the drug that slows the rate must not also weaken the heart.
why: **Verapamil, diltiazem — negatively inotropic; precipitate decompensation.** Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers block L-type calcium channels in myocardium as well as in the node, so they reduce contractility; ESC advises against them when LVEF is below 40%. They should also not follow an IV β-blocker (additive block and hypotension), and they are banned in pre-excited AF (Marrow: diltiazem contraindicated in all three).

**Dronedarone — ↑ mortality in NYHA IV, recent decompensation, or permanent AF.** ANDROMEDA (recently decompensated, severe HF) and PALLAS (permanent AF) were stopped early for excess deaths, stroke and heart failure.

**β-blocker (if not decompensated), digoxin, amiodarone.** A β-blocker is the long-term rate-control drug in HFrEF, but IV β-blockade in a patient who is acutely decompensated (wet, borderline pressure) can tip him into shock. Digoxin slows the node by raising vagal tone without negative inotropy, and amiodarone slows the rate with little effect on contractility; both are the acute choice when the patient is congested. Dobutamine speeds AV conduction and can provoke a fast ventricular rate in AF; giving digoxin first prevents it (Marrow).
mimic: Compensated vs decompensated HFrEF with AF
Compensated: β-blocker. Decompensated (wet, low pressure): IV amiodarone or digoxin for rate, diuretic for congestion; no IV β-blocker or calcium channel blocker.
traps: “Beta-blocker therapy” for AF 130 in HFrEF admitted with worsening dyspnoea (DocT QBank key, 39%)
Disputed key: the patient is decompensating, so an IV β-blocker is avoided now; amiodarone or digoxin for rate and IV diuretic for congestion. A β-blocker is right once he is compensated.
“Dronedarone is fine for rhythm control in severe HF”
It raises mortality in NYHA IV, recent decompensation and permanent AF; only 12% got it on the mini test.
“Verapamil is acceptable rate control with EF 30%”
It is not recommended (only 24% got it); see CAR-27b.
decode: Septic shock, AF 170, severe LV dysfunction, borderline BP — least suitable IV rate-control drug? [DocT GT]
Verapamil.
HFrEF, AF with RVR, worsening dyspnoea, BP 110/70 [DocT QBank, 39%]
Key: β-blocker; if decompensated, amiodarone or digoxin.
Low-EF AF developed RVR on dobutamine — what would have prevented it? [Marrow]
Digoxin before dobutamine.
CAR-04.punch: With a weak ventricle, rate-control drugs must not depress contractility: no verapamil or diltiazem, no dronedarone in NYHA IV; use digoxin or amiodarone when decompensated, and a β-blocker once compensated.

CAR-05.sub: Cardiology → Tachyarrhythmias → AF anticoagulation and rate vs rhythm
CAR-05.intro: AF kills mostly through stroke, not through the rate. This card asks which anticoagulant, when it is safe to cardiovert, and whether controlling rhythm rather than rate changes the stroke risk.
why: **Warfarin (INR 2–3; mechanical mitral 2.5–3.5). DOACs are contraindicated; aspirin is inadequate.** Moderate–severe rheumatic mitral stenosis stagnates blood in a large left atrium, and a mechanical valve adds a thrombogenic surface; DOAC trials excluded both, and in mechanical valves dabigatran (RE-ALIGN) caused more thrombosis and more bleeding than warfarin. For non-valvular AF the risk score decides: ESC 2024 uses CHA₂DS₂-VA (sex removed); in CHA₂DS₂-VASc, which the question tests, male sex scores 0 and the other items are heart failure 1, hypertension 1, age ≥75 2, diabetes 1, stroke/TIA 2, vascular disease 1, age 65–74 1, female sex 1.

**3 weeks of anticoagulation, or TOE to exclude LA thrombus — then 4 weeks after.** Thrombus forms in the left atrial appendage after about 48 hours of AF, and a successful cardioversion can dislodge it; after cardioversion the atrium is stunned and contracts poorly for weeks, so anticoagulation continues for at least 4 weeks whatever the stroke score. ESC 2024 now sets the line at 24 hours: without prior anticoagulation or a TOE, early cardioversion is not advised once AF has lasted 24 hours or more (ACC/AHA 2023 keeps 48 hours).

**No difference in mortality, stroke or quality of life; rate control → fewer rehospitalisations.** In AFFIRM and RACE most strokes occurred in patients whose anticoagulation was stopped or subtherapeutic, so anticoagulation, not rhythm, decides stroke risk; rhythm control cost more admissions for cardioversion and drug toxicity. EAST-AFNET 4 (2020) later found that early rhythm control within a year of diagnosis lowered cardiovascular events, which is why current guidelines offer it earlier.
mimic: Valvular vs non-valvular AF
Valvular (moderate–severe MS or mechanical valve): warfarin only. Bioprosthetic valves, other native valve disease: DOACs allowed.
traps: “Male sex scores a point in CHA₂DS₂-VASc”
Female sex scores 1, male 0 (Marrow).
“Dabigatran is acceptable in rheumatic MS with AF” (CAR-27c)
Warfarin; only 36% chose it on the mini test.
“Rhythm control reduces stroke”
AFFIRM/RACE: no difference; rate control’s only win was fewer readmissions (24% right).
decode: AF stroke-risk score does NOT include which factor? [Marrow]
Male sex.
[pattern] AF of unknown duration, stable, planned cardioversion
3 weeks of anticoagulation or TOE, then 4 weeks after.
CAR-05.punch: Rheumatic MS or a mechanical valve means warfarin, never a DOAC; stable AF over 48 h needs 3 weeks of anticoagulation or a TOE before cardioversion and 4 weeks after; rate versus rhythm does not change stroke.

CAR-06.sub: Cardiology → Tachyarrhythmias → Torsades, long QT and Brugada
CAR-06.intro: The last rhythm decision in step 1 is the QT. Polymorphic VT on a long QT is a repolarisation disease, so the drugs that treat ordinary VT make it worse; Brugada is a sodium-channel disease that kills at rest.
why: **Magnesium sulphate 2 g IV; overdrive pacing or isoprenaline if recurrent; defibrillate if pulseless.** Torsades starts from early after-depolarisations during a prolonged plateau, driven by L-type calcium current; magnesium suppresses them even when serum magnesium is normal. Raising the heart rate (pacing at 90–110 or isoprenaline) shortens the QT and removes the pauses that trigger it. AHA 2025 gives magnesium as COR 2b. Correct potassium to the high-normal range.

**Amiodarone, procainamide, sotalol — all prolong QT further.** Any class Ia or III drug lengthens repolarisation. In drug-induced torsades the treatment is to stop the drug (e.g. levofloxacin, and hold dofetilide until the QTc is normal); because the cause is reversible, no ICD is needed (Marrow).

**SCN5A loss of function (sodium channel). Coved ST elevation ≥2 mm with a NEGATIVE T in V1–V2.** Less sodium current in the right ventricular outflow epicardium lets the transient outward current dominate, producing the coved ST and the substrate for phase-2 re-entry. The type 1 pattern may be spontaneous or unmasked by fever or a sodium channel blocker (ajmaline, flecainide, procainamide challenge); a saddle-back ST with a positive T is not diagnostic.

**At rest, sleep, fever. Treat fever aggressively; ICD for survivors.** High vagal tone and fever both reduce sodium current further, so VF strikes at night. An ICD is indicated after arrest and also after arrhythmic syncope (Marrow); quinidine (blocks the transient outward current) if an ICD is refused or for recurrent shocks, and isoprenaline for an electrical storm.
mimic: Torsades (long QT) vs polymorphic VT with a normal QT
Long QT: magnesium, pacing, stop QT drugs. Normal QT (usually ischaemia): treat ischaemia, amiodarone or β-blocker; urgent angiography.
Brugada vs CPVT
Brugada: sodium channel, death at rest or in sleep, coved ST in V1–V2. CPVT: RyR2 calcium leak, death on exercise or emotion, normal resting ECG, bidirectional VT (CAR-07).
traps: “Positive T wave in the right precordial leads” as a Brugada feature
The type 1 pattern has a negative T; only 57% knew it.
“Quinidine gives the greatest reduction in sudden death” for a Brugada arrest survivor
An ICD does; quinidine is the adjunct.
“ICD for drug-induced polymorphic VT”
Remove the cause; ICD only when there is no reversible cause.
decode: Survivor of nocturnal arrest, normal heart, coved ST V1–V3 — greatest reduction in sudden death? [DocT GT]
ICD implantation.
On IV amiodarone for AF, sudden syncope, torsades — which correction? [DocT GT, 91%]
IV magnesium sulphate.
Brugada with recurrent syncope — best therapy? [Marrow]
ICD.
Polymorphic VT on levofloxacin + dofetilide [Marrow]
Stop levofloxacin, hold dofetilide until the QTc normalises; no ICD.
CAR-06.punch: Torsades is treated with magnesium, a faster rate and removal of QT-prolonging drugs; Brugada is SCN5A with coved ST and a negative T in V1–V2, kills at rest or with fever, and needs an ICD after arrest or arrhythmic syncope.

CAR-07.intro: Digoxin closes step 1 because it causes both fast and slow rhythms at once. The questions test the ECG, the antidote and the one laboratory value that predicts death.
why: **Down-sloping ‘reverse tick’ ST in V4–V6, short QT, PAT with block, bidirectional VT, any brady/AV block.** The reverse tick and short QT are digoxin effect (at therapeutic levels too); toxicity shows as rhythms. Digoxin inhibits Na-K ATPase, raising intracellular sodium and so calcium (delayed after-depolarisations and ectopy), while raising vagal tone slows the SA and AV nodes; fast atria with a blocked node give atrial tachycardia with block, and alternating ventricular foci give bidirectional VT.
**Peaked T waves — that is hyperkalaemia.** Digoxin flattens or inverts T waves and shortens QT; a peaked T means the potassium is high, which itself is a marker of severe acute poisoning (part d).

**Digoxin-specific Fab: life-threatening arrhythmia, K above 5–5.5 in acute toxicity, end-organ damage.** Fab fragments bind digoxin with higher affinity than Na-K ATPase, pulling it off the pump within 30–60 minutes; a typical empirical dose is about 10 vials in acute poisoning and fewer in chronic. Bradycardia can be bridged with atropine while Fab is given (Marrow); calcium is not needed for the hyperkalaemia because Fab corrects it, and it is avoided unless the potassium is immediately life-threatening.

**Hyperkalaemia (acute poisoning blocks Na-K ATPase) — predicts death.** With the pump blocked, potassium cannot enter cells, so serum K rises in proportion to the poisoning. In the pre-Fab era (Bismuth 1973) a K above 5.5 mmol/L carried a very high mortality, a stronger predictor than the ECG or the digoxin level. In chronic toxicity it is the reverse: HYPOkalaemia (diuretics) increases digoxin binding and toxicity.
mimic: Bidirectional VT: digoxin toxicity vs CPVT

Digoxin: older patient on digoxin, GI symptoms, hyperkalaemia. CPVT: young, exercise- or emotion-triggered syncope, RyR2 or calsequestrin mutation; β-blockers (nadolol) first line, flecainide added, ICD reserved.
traps: “High-degree AV block or a digoxin level >1 ng/mL portends a poor prognosis”
Potassium >5.5 does (only 29% got it). The level is drawn too early in acute poisoning to mean much.
“Calcium gluconate first for K 5.8 on digoxin”
Fab is the treatment (71% right); it corrects the potassium and the arrhythmia together.
“Beta-blockers are contraindicated” in exercise-induced bidirectional VT
That is CPVT, where β-blockers are first line; this was the ‘except’ answer (42%).
decode: Digoxin, K 5.8, slow ventricular response with PVCs, confusion — initial step? [DocT QBank, 71%]
Digoxin-specific antibody fragments.
Acute digoxin overdose — which feature portends a poor prognosis? [DocT GT, 29%]
Serum potassium >5.5 mmol/L.
Young man, exercise syncope, bidirectional VT — all true EXCEPT [DocT GT, 42%]
‘β-blockers contraindicated’ (they are first line).
Drug of choice for severe digoxin toxicity [DocT GT PYQ]
Digoxin immune Fab.
CAR-07.punch: Digoxin toxicity shows as ectopy plus block, bidirectional VT or atrial tachycardia with block; peaked T means hyperkalaemia, a K above 5.5 in acute poisoning predicts death, and Fab is the answer.

CAR-08.sub: Cardiology → Bradycardia → Atropine, chronotropes and pacing
CAR-08.intro: Step 2 turns to slow rhythms. Atropine is the first drug only because most symptomatic bradycardia is vagal and above the His bundle; the card teaches the doses and where that assumption fails.
