why: **Atropine 1 mg IV, repeat every 3–5 min.** Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors at the SA and AV nodes, lifting vagal tone. The 1 mg dose replaced the old 0.5 mg; doses below 0.5 mg can cause paradoxical slowing.
**3 mg total.** At about 0.04 mg/kg the vagus is fully blocked, so more atropine adds only anticholinergic toxicity.

**Dopamine 5–20 µg/kg/min, or adrenaline 2–10 µg/min, or transcutaneous pacing.** If atropine fails the problem is not vagal, so the next step acts directly on β₁ receptors or bypasses conduction with pacing. They are alternatives; while pacing is being set up, start an infusion. Isoprenaline is a direct β-agonist used in some settings (e.g. denervated heart) but is not in the AHA algorithm.

**Mobitz II / complete heart block with wide QRS (infranodal), and the transplanted heart (denervated).** Below the AV node the His–Purkinje system has little vagal innervation, so atropine cannot help and can worsen the conduction ratio by speeding the sinus rate. A transplanted heart has no vagal supply: atropine, glycopyrrolate and indirect agents such as ephedrine fail, and atropine can even provoke high-grade block; use isoprenaline, adrenaline or pacing. Sinus node dysfunction early after transplant (up to half of patients) comes from surgical injury to the donor node and usually settles within weeks to 3 months.
mimic: Vagal (nodal) vs infranodal bradycardia
Nodal: narrow QRS, sinus brady or Mobitz I, responds to atropine. Infranodal: Mobitz II or CHB with wide escape, go straight to pacing.
traps: “Administer more atropine” after three 1 mg doses (GT2o, 35%)
3 mg is the maximum; next is dopamine or adrenaline while pacing comes.
“Isoproterenol” or “noradrenaline” while waiting for pacing (GT2o)
Dopamine is the algorithm answer; noradrenaline adds afterload with little chronotropy.
“Adrenaline 2–10 µg/kg/min”
It is 2–10 µg/min (34% right); dopamine is the one dosed per kg.
decode: Post-CABG pericarditis, HR 33, BP 62/36, three doses of atropine, waiting for TCP [DocT GT, 35%]
Dopamine infusion.
Heart transplant 3 years ago, intraoperative bradycardia — best drug? [Marrow]
Isoprenaline (direct-acting).
CAR-08.punch: Atropine 1 mg every 3–5 min to 3 mg, then dopamine 5–20 µg/kg/min, adrenaline 2–10 µg/min or pacing; atropine is useless below the node and in the denervated heart.

CAR-09.sub: Cardiology → Bradycardia → Pacing decisions and paediatric bradycardia
CAR-09.intro: Once atropine is set aside, the question is how quickly to pace. The level of the block decides it in adults; in children the cause (hypoxia) changes the whole response.
why: **Permanent pacemaker — His–Purkinje disease, high risk of complete block and sudden death.** Mobitz II (constant PR, sudden dropped beat) is infranodal; it progresses unpredictably to complete heart block with a slow, unreliable ventricular escape. With symptoms and no reversible cause (drugs, ischaemia, hyperkalaemia) it needs a permanent pacemaker.

**Pacing (transcutaneous now, transvenous next); chronotropes as a bridge.** In an unstable infranodal block transcutaneous pacing is the immediate step; it is uncomfortable and capture must be confirmed by a pulse, so transvenous pacing follows. Atropine rarely helps and must not delay pacing; dobutamine is not the rescue.

**Start CPR and give adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO (max 1 mg).** In children bradycardia is usually the last stage of hypoxia; heart rate below 60 with poor perfusion despite good oxygenation and ventilation behaves as an impending arrest, so compressions start. Adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg is 0.1 mL/kg of 0.1 mg/mL. Atropine (0.02 mg/kg) is only for increased vagal tone or primary AV block.
mimic: Adult vs child bradycardia with poor perfusion
Adult: atropine, chronotropes, pacing. Child: oxygenate and ventilate first; if HR still <60 with poor perfusion, CPR and adrenaline.
traps: “Transvenous pacemaker placement” as the initial intervention for unstable Mobitz II (GT4, 43%)
Transcutaneous pacing first, as the bridge; transvenous takes time.
“Atropine” for unstable Mobitz II
It acts on the node, not below it.
“Atropine or dopamine” for the child with HR 46 and poor perfusion
CPR and adrenaline (22% right).
decode: Septic ICU patient, syncope, Mobitz II on strip, BP 75/40 — initial intervention? [DocT GT, 43%]
Transcutaneous pacing.
CAR-09.punch: Symptomatic Mobitz II needs a permanent pacemaker and, if unstable, transcutaneous pacing now; a child with HR below 60 and poor perfusion despite oxygen and ventilation gets CPR and adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg.

CAR-10.sub: Cardiology → Devices → ICD and CRT in heart failure
CAR-10.intro: The long-term end of step 2: which patients with a weak heart get a device. The ICD prevents arrhythmic death; CRT treats the electrical delay that makes the ventricle contract out of step.
why: **LVEF ≤35%, NYHA II–III, on GDMT ≥3 months, more than 40 days after MI (90 after revascularisation).** These criteria come from MADIT-II and SCD-HeFT; three months of therapy lets the EF recover first, and early ICDs after MI (DINAMIT, IRIS) did not lower mortality because early deaths are often non-arrhythmic. NYHA IV patients are excluded unless they are CRT candidates, since they die of pump failure. A survivor of VF/VT arrest without a reversible cause is a different decision: a secondary-prevention ICD, whatever the EF (AVID, CIDS, CASH: ICD beat amiodarone).

**QRS width — LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms (plus EF ≤35%).** Left bundle branch block makes the septum contract before the lateral wall, wasting work; pacing both ventricles resynchronises them. Benefit is greatest with LBBB and QRS ≥150 ms (class I); between 130 and 149 ms it is weaker; under 130 ms CRT does not help and may harm (EchoCRT).
**Echo mechanical dyssynchrony, tissue Doppler, or EF alone.** Trials selecting by echo measures (PROSPECT, EchoCRT) failed: the measures were unreproducible and narrow-QRS patients did not benefit.
mimic: Primary vs secondary prevention ICD
Primary: no prior event, EF ≤35% on optimal therapy, >40 days after MI. Secondary: survived VF/VT arrest or haemodynamically unstable VT with no reversible cause, regardless of EF.
traps: “Amiodarone for secondary prevention” after a resuscitated arrest with EF 30%
ICD evaluation; ICD beats amiodarone on mortality (71% right in GT3).
“Echo dyssynchrony selects for CRT”
QRS width does (26% right).
decode: Resuscitated OHCA, no MI, LVEF 30% — next step to reduce long-term mortality? [DocT GT, 71%]
Refer for ICD.
Dilated cardiomyopathy, QRS 180 ms, LBBB — diagnosis? [DocT QBank, 84%]
HFrEF (the CRT candidate).
CAR-10.punch: Primary-prevention ICD needs EF ≤35% on 3 months of therapy and more than 40 days after MI; arrest survivors get one regardless of EF; CRT is chosen by QRS width (LBBB ≥150 ms), not by echo.

CAR-11.intro: Step 3 starts at the collapse. The BLS sequence is built around one physiological fact: coronary perfusion during arrest exists only while someone is compressing, so every step is ordered to get compressions and a shock going and keep them going.
why: **Scene safe → check responsiveness → shout for help, activate the emergency system, send for the AED → then check breathing and pulse together, ≤10 s → no pulse: CPR 30:2, attach the AED as soon as it arrives.** Help and the AED come before the pulse check because the commonest early shockable rhythm needs a defibrillator, and a lone rescuer cannot fetch it later without stopping CPR. Pulse checks by professionals are unreliable, so the check is limited to 10 seconds; gasping (agonal breathing) is not normal breathing and counts as arrest.

**Pulse but abnormal breathing → 1 breath every 6 s, recheck pulse every 2 min.** That is 10 breaths a minute, enough to oxygenate without raising intrathoracic pressure and cutting venous return; consider naloxone if opioids are suspected. If the pulse is lost, start CPR.

**‘No shock advised’ → resume CPR immediately for 2 min. No pulse check.** After any analysis or shock, compressions resume at once; a pause to feel for a pulse lowers coronary perfusion pressure, which takes many compressions to rebuild, and a rhythm that has just changed rarely produces a palpable pulse in the first seconds anyway.
mimic: Respiratory arrest vs cardiac arrest
Definite pulse, gasping: rescue breathing 1 every 6 s. No definite pulse in 10 s: CPR 30:2.
traps: “Begin 30:2” when a definite pulse is present with gasping
Rescue breathing only, 1 breath every 6 s (CGT2, CGT5).
“Check pulse first” or “repeat shock” after one shock for VF
Resume CPR for 2 minutes (CGT5).
“Check breathing and pulse, then shout for help”
Help and AED first (63% right on the mini test).
decode: Unresponsive, definite carotid pulse, only gasping — next step? [DocT GT]
1 breath every 6 s, reassess pulse every 2 min.
Collapse in ICU, apnoeic with gasps, no definite pulse in 10 s [DocT GT]
Start CPR.
AED shows VF, one shock delivered — next action? [DocT GT]
Resume CPR for 2 min.
CAR-11.punch: Shout and send for the AED before checking breathing and pulse for 10 s; with a pulse but abnormal breathing give 1 breath every 6 s, and after any analysis or shock resume CPR straight away for 2 minutes.

CAR-12.intro: The numbers of CPR follow the cause of arrest: adults usually arrest from a cardiac rhythm with oxygen still in the blood, children usually from hypoxia.
why: **30:2, one or two rescuers.** In adult arrest the blood is still oxygenated for the first minutes, so compressions matter more than breaths.

**One rescuer 30:2; two rescuers 15:2 (pre-pubertal).** Paediatric arrest is mostly asphyxial, so with two rescuers the extra breaths are worth the extra pauses; a lone rescuer keeps 30:2 to limit the time changing between tasks.
**Continuous compressions; adult 1 breath every 6 s, child/infant every 2–3 s.** With an advanced airway compressions no longer pause; AHA 2025 gives 20–30 breaths/min for infants and children.
**Heel of one hand, or two-thumb encircling — the two-finger technique was removed.** Two fingers rarely reach one third of the chest depth (about 4 cm in infants).
**Attach immediately; paediatric pads/attenuator if available, else adult pads (not touching).** AHA 2025: an attenuator is preferred under 8 years, but a standard AED is better than none.
traps: “8-year-old, one healthcare provider — 15:2”
One rescuer is 30:2 at any age; 15:2 needs two rescuers (71% right).
decode: [pattern] Infant arrest, two rescuers — ratio and technique?
15:2, two-thumb encircling (or heel of one hand); not two fingers.
[pattern] Child with advanced airway in CPR — ventilation rate?
1 breath every 2–3 s (20–30/min) with continuous compressions.
CAR-12.punch: Adults 30:2 whatever the number of rescuers; children 30:2 alone and 15:2 with two; with an airway 1 breath every 6 s in adults and every 2–3 s in children; the two-finger infant technique is gone.

CAR-13.intro: Drugs come after compressions and shocks in the arrest algorithm, and their timing differs by rhythm for a reason: in VF the shock is the treatment, in PEA and asystole there is nothing to shock.
why: **Adrenaline 1 mg after the 2nd shock, every 3–5 min. Amiodarone 300 mg, then 150 mg (or lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg, then 0.5–0.75).** AHA 2025 words it as adrenaline ‘after initial defibrillation attempts have failed’ (2a), and amiodarone or lidocaine as COR 2b (ALPS: survival to admission higher, no significant difference in survival to discharge). Lidocaine, a class Ib drug, acts only on ventricular tissue: its sodium-channel block depends on the long ventricular action potential, so it is useless in AF (Marrow).

**Adrenaline 1 mg as soon as possible, every 3–5 min. No shock, no amiodarone.** Adrenaline’s α effect raises aortic diastolic pressure and so coronary perfusion pressure; in non-shockable arrest earlier adrenaline is linked to more ROSC and survival (PARAMEDIC-2, all rhythms: better 30-day survival, but more survivors with severe neurological disability).
**Adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg; amiodarone 5 mg/kg; lidocaine 1 mg/kg.** Amiodarone may be repeated up to three doses in children.

**CPR quality (depth, rate, recoil, pauses under 10 s) and standard shocks. Vector change / double sequential defibrillation: usefulness not established (AHA 2025, COR 2b; one trial, DOSE-VF).** DOSE-VF (2022) found more survival to discharge with double sequential (30.4%) and vector change (21.7%) than standard shocks (13.3%), but it was a single, small trial, so AHA 2025 left both at 2b. Vasopressin, routine calcium and routine bicarbonate add nothing (COR 3).
mimic: Shockable vs non-shockable: when adrenaline
Shockable: after the second shock (failed initial defibrillation). Non-shockable: as soon as possible.
traps: “Shock or amiodarone” in PEA at 76/min with no pulse
Adrenaline 1 mg (61% right); PEA is never shocked.
“No amiodarone available — procainamide”
Lidocaine is the alternative (65%).
“Paediatric lidocaine 0.1 mg/kg”
decode: AF on ECG — which drug cannot be used? [Marrow]
Lignocaine (class Ib, ventricular only).
CAR-13.punch: Shockable: adrenaline 1 mg after the second shock and amiodarone 300 then 150 mg or lidocaine; non-shockable: adrenaline as soon as possible; in refractory VF CPR quality matters most, and double sequential shocks remain unproven (2b).

CAR-14.sub: Cardiology → Arrest → Special circumstances: the extra drug
CAR-14.intro: In some arrests the standard algorithm cannot work because a drug or toxin blocks the pathway that adrenaline uses. Each extra drug here bypasses or removes that block.
why: **Glucagon 1–5 mg IV — plus fluids. Not IM adrenaline in arrest; not sugammadex as monotherapy.** Glucagon acts on its own G-protein receptor and switches on adenylate cyclase directly, raising cAMP even when β-receptors are blocked; it is given slowly (it causes vomiting) and can be followed by an infusion. In arrest, adrenaline is IV, not IM. Sugammadex does not treat rocuronium anaphylaxis by itself. In β-blocker poisoning glucagon is the classic drug of choice, but many toxicologists now put high-dose insulin first, as the calcium channel blocker consensus does (St-Onge, Crit Care Med 2017).

**Calcium, high-dose insulin, vasopressors; lipid emulsion if refractory.** Calcium overcomes the channel block in part; high-dose insulin (1 U/kg bolus, then infusion, with glucose) restores myocardial carbohydrate use, which the poisoned heart depends on; lipid emulsion is reserved for refractory cases.

**20% lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg bolus.** Then 0.25 mL/kg/min, repeat the bolus for persistent instability, to a maximum of about 12 mL/kg. Lipid pulls lipophilic bupivacaine out of the heart and supplies fatty acids. Run standard ALS alongside, with smaller adrenaline doses (≤1 µg/kg); propofol is not a substitute.

**Naloxone — but never ahead of compressions.** In an opioid arrest the heart has stopped from hypoxia; naloxone may help a patient with a pulse but does not restart a heart, so CPR and ventilation come first.
mimic: Glucagon vs high-dose insulin in β-blocker or CCB poisoning
Glucagon bypasses the β-receptor; high-dose insulin is the stronger inotrope in both and is first line in the calcium channel blocker consensus.
traps: “More adrenaline or noradrenaline” for β-blocker shock unresponsive to catecholamines
Glucagon (37% right on the mini test); catecholamines need the receptor that is blocked.
“Epinephrine or bicarbonate” as drug of choice in bupivacaine arrest
Lipid emulsion.
decode: Chronic β-blocker, profound bradycardia and shock despite fluids and catecholamines — DOC? [DocT GT PYQ]
Glucagon.
Seizures then bradycardia and arrest after bupivacaine nerve block — DOC? [DocT GT PYQ]
Lipid emulsion.
CAR-14.punch: Glucagon bypasses β-blockade by activating adenylate cyclase directly; CCB poisoning needs calcium and high-dose insulin; local anaesthetic arrest needs 20% lipid 1.5 mL/kg; naloxone never comes before compressions.

CAR-15.sub: Cardiology → Post-ROSC → Targets for the comatose survivor
CAR-15.intro: After ROSC the heart has restarted, but the outcome is decided by the brain. Every target on this card protects a brain that has lost autoregulation and is primed for secondary injury.
why: **MAP ≥65, SBP ≥90 mmHg.** Without autoregulation, cerebral flow follows pressure, so hypotension adds ischaemia. AHA 2025 now gives only MAP ≥65 mmHg (COR 1) and has dropped the SBP target; no particular vasopressor is recommended. Higher MAP targets (BOX, NEUROPROTECT) did not improve outcome.

**SpO₂ 90–98% (PaO₂ 60–105); PaCO₂ 35–45.** 100% oxygen until saturation can be measured reliably, then titrate down: hypoxaemia kills neurons, while hyperoxia adds free radicals at reperfusion. Low CO₂ constricts cerebral vessels and reduces flow; high CO₂ raises ICP. Pulse oximetry can overestimate in darker skin.

**32–37.5 °C, any rhythm, any location; at least 36 h (2025); rewarm no faster than 0.5 °C/h; prevent fever.** TTM-2 found no difference between 33 °C and normothermia with active fever prevention, so the range is wide; what matters is avoiding fever, which increases neuronal death. It applies to every patient who does not follow commands, including PEA, asystole and in-hospital arrest. Rewarming is slow because a fast rise raises cerebral metabolic demand while oxygen delivery is still fragile, and causes vasodilatory hypotension and rebound hyperkalaemia as potassium moves out of cells. An automated device at about 0.25 °C/h takes about 16 hours for 4 °C; manual rewarming takes about 24 hours (Marrow).

**Seizure ≥10 min continuous, or seizures for ≥20% of any 60 min.** This is the ACNS 2021 definition of electrographic status epilepticus. AHA 2025: prompt EEG in all who do not follow commands; treat clinical seizures; no routine prophylaxis. Status epilepticus persisting at or beyond 72 h, burst suppression off sedation, bilaterally absent pupillary and corneal reflexes at ≥72 h, absent N20 SSEPs and high NSE support a poor outcome, only in a multimodal assessment at least 72 hours after normothermia.

**STEMI, or cardiogenic shock / suspected coronary cause — not everyone.** Emergent angiography for ST elevation (COR 1); reasonable for shock, recurrent ventricular arrhythmias or ongoing ischaemia (2a). For comatose patients without these, COACT and TOMAHAWK found no benefit from immediate angiography over a delayed approach (COR 3).
mimic: Post-arrest rewarming vs accidental hypothermia afterdrop
Post-arrest: slow rewarming to protect the brain. Afterdrop (core temperature falling as cold peripheral blood returns) belongs to accidental hypothermia.
traps: “Strict 32–34 °C” or “PEA excluded from temperature control”
Outdated: 32–37.5 °C for all comatose patients, any rhythm (GT4 Q60).
“36 °C for 12 h”
At least 36 hours of temperature control (the GT4 miss).
“Slow rewarming prevents a fall in potassium and post-rewarming diuresis”
Rewarming RAISES potassium; the main reason is cerebral metabolic demand outstripping delivery (only 45% chose that).
“No upper-limb motor response always means a poor outcome”
Absent or extensor arm response is of uncertain value; arms weak with legs moving may be a watershed (man-in-a-barrel) injury, and a short arrest can recover fully.
decode: Rationale for slow controlled rewarming after therapeutic hypothermia [DocT QBank, 45%]
Rapid rewarming abruptly raises cerebral metabolic demand → secondary brain injury.
Post-arrest coma: finding most specific for poor prognosis [Marrow]
Status epilepticus during active cooling (with other signs, at ≥72 h).
Rewarming 33 → 37 °C with ice packs, no automated device — timeframe? [Marrow]
About 24 hours.
Revived after 20 min arrest — NOT true [Marrow]
‘No upper-limb motor response always means poor outcome’.
CAR-15.punch: After ROSC keep MAP ≥65, SpO₂ 90–98% and PaCO₂ 35–45, control temperature at 32–37.5 °C for at least 36 h in every comatose patient, rewarm at ≤0.5 °C/h, and take only STEMI or shock straight to the lab.

CAR-16.intro: When neither the heart nor CPR can maintain flow, ECMO takes over. The configuration follows which organ has failed: VV supports the lungs and relies on the patient’s heart; VA replaces the heart as well.
why: **VA-ECMO. (‘Arteriovenous ECMO’ is not a mode.)** In refractory arrest there is no cardiac output to carry blood oxygenated in a vein, so blood must be returned into the arterial tree. ECPR is usually femoro-femoral, started within about 60 minutes of collapse in selected witnessed arrests.
**VV-ECMO.** Blood is drained from and returned to the venous system; the native heart pumps the oxygenated blood through the lungs and body.

**VA-ECMO — the only percutaneous device giving full heart + lung support (up to ~7 L/min).** Biventricular failure and fulminant myocarditis need both ventricles replaced, and VA-ECMO is the fastest route; it works in any rhythm, even VF.

**Convert to VA (or V-AV).** If cardiogenic shock develops on VV, the heart can no longer move the oxygenated blood; adding an arterial return cannula (V-AV) or converting to VA provides circulatory support.

**↑ LV afterload → LV distension, pulmonary oedema → vent the LV (Impella, IABP).** Retrograde arterial flow up the aorta pushes against the aortic valve. A weak LV that cannot open it distends, its wall stress and oxygen demand rise, pulmonary oedema worsens and the stagnant blood can clot; an Impella or IABP unloads it. Routine VA-ECMO in infarct-related shock did not lower 30-day mortality in ECLS-SHOCK (47.8% vs 49.0%) and caused more moderate or severe bleeding (23.4% vs 9.6%) and vascular complications (11.0% vs 3.8%).
mimic: VV vs VA
VV: lungs only, heart must work, no haemodynamic support. VA: heart and lungs, but raises LV afterload.
traps: “ECPR uses VV-ECMO” (CAR-27h)
VA; with no cardiac output, venous return of oxygenated blood goes nowhere (GT4 Q72 lost).
“VA-ECMO lowers LV afterload”
It raises it (43% right).
decode: Severe ARDS with cardiogenic shock after MI — preferred device? [DocT GT, 88%]
VA-ECMO.
CAR-16.punch: Lungs alone: VV; heart failing, or arrest: VA (or convert VV to V-AV); VA-ECMO’s cost is a higher LV afterload, so the LV may need venting with an Impella or IABP.

CAR-17.sub: Cardiology → ACS → STEMI without on-site PCI: pharmaco-invasive strategy
CAR-17.intro: Step 4 begins with the commonest ACS decision outside a PCI centre. Primary PCI is better than lysis only if it can be done quickly; the card gives the time limit and what follows lysis.
why: **If PCI cannot happen within 120 min of diagnosis → lyse (within 10 min of diagnosis; door-to-needle ≤30 min).** Beyond about 120 minutes of delay the advantage of PCI over lysis is lost to the extra myocardium that dies waiting (ESC 2023). Lysis works best early, when the thrombus is fresh and fibrin-poor, and is given within 12 hours of symptom onset. ESC targets the bolus within 10 minutes of the diagnostic ECG; the AHA target is door-to-needle within 30 minutes.

**Transfer for angiography 2–24 h after lysis (mini test: 3–24 h). Not before 2–3 h (bleeding peak).** Lysis opens the artery in about half to two thirds of patients but leaves the ruptured plaque, so routine early angiography prevents re-occlusion; within the first hours the lytic state makes arterial puncture and PCI more likely to bleed and gave no benefit (facilitated PCI).

**Below 50% ST resolution at 60–90 min, ongoing pain or instability → immediate rescue PCI.** ST resolution is the bedside marker of tissue reperfusion; failure to resolve by half means the artery is probably still closed. Repeat lysis is not effective.
mimic: Rescue PCI vs pharmaco-invasive PCI
Rescue: lysis failed, go now. Pharmaco-invasive: lysis worked, angiography in 2–24 h.
traps: “Transfer for PCI regardless of delay” when door-to-balloon is 160 min
Lyse first (77% right); ‘regardless of delay’ applies to cardiogenic shock (CAR-18a).
“1 h” or “48 h” for angiography after successful lysis
2–24 h; the mini test answer was 12 h (34% right).
decode: Anterior STEMI, door-to-balloon expected 160 min — best initial management? [DocT QBank, 77%]
Immediate thrombolysis before transfer.
Anterior STEMI 1 h, nearest PCI centre 150 km away [NEET 2025 recall]
Thrombolysis.
CAR-17.punch: If PCI cannot happen within 120 minutes of diagnosis, lyse within 10 minutes, then transfer for angiography at 2–24 h, or go for rescue PCI at once if ST elevation has not fallen by half at 60–90 minutes.

CAR-18.sub: Cardiology → ACS → STEMI with cardiogenic shock
CAR-18.intro: Shock changes the reperfusion rule of CAR-17: lysis needs a perfusion pressure to reach the clot, so the priority becomes mechanical revascularisation. The card then chooses the vasoactive drug by the blood pressure and by any β-blockade.
why: **Immediate transfer for PCI/CABG, whatever the delay. Culprit-only PCI (CULPRIT-SHOCK).** In the SHOCK trial early revascularisation improved long-term survival; lytics work poorly at low perfusion pressure. CULPRIT-SHOCK found culprit-only PCI better than immediate multivessel PCI (death or renal replacement at 30 days 45.9% vs 55.4%). ESC 2023 adds that fibrinolysis should be considered (IIa) if primary PCI is not possible within 120 minutes and mechanical complications are excluded; lysing and transferring are not exclusive.

**Dobutamine — low output without frank hypotension.** Dobutamine is a β₁ inotrope with β₂ vasodilation, so it raises output but can drop the blood pressure; it needs a pressure to start from. ESC also places an inotrope first in wet-cold patients with borderline pressure.

**Noradrenaline first, then add the inotrope.** Below SBP 90 (MAP <65) coronary and organ perfusion depend on pressure; noradrenaline raises it with less tachycardia and fewer arrhythmias than dopamine (SOAP II, worse outcome with dopamine in its cardiogenic subgroup) or adrenaline (OptimaCC: more refractory shock).

**Milrinone — PDE3 works downstream of the blocked β-receptor.** Milrinone inhibits phosphodiesterase III, so cAMP rises without needing the β-receptor; it also increases calcium reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum (lusitropy) and dilates veins and arteries, so it lowers the BP. Levosimendan also keeps working under β-blockade, by sensitising troponin C to calcium and opening K-ATP channels.

**Not routinely (IABP-SHOCK II: no mortality benefit).** 30-day mortality 39.7% vs 41.3%, with no difference at 6 years. Of the devices, only the Impella CP has improved survival in STEMI shock (DanGer Shock: 180-day death 45.8% vs 58.5%), at the cost of more moderate or severe bleeding (21.8% vs 11.9%), limb ischaemia (5.6% vs 1.1%) and renal replacement (41.9% vs 26.7%) (CAR-26).
mimic: Milrinone vs levosimendan vs dobutamine

Dobutamine: β₁ agonist, blunted by β-blockers. Milrinone: PDE3, raises cAMP beyond the receptor. Levosimendan: calcium sensitiser, no cAMP. Both of the latter work in β-blocked patients and both vasodilate.
traps: “Lyse because the PCI centre is 3.5 h away”
With shock, transfer for revascularisation (only 9% right); ESC allows lysis as a bridge if PCI is beyond 120 min.
“Dopamine” as the inotrope for BP 80/50 in ADHF (DocT QBank key, 38%)
Outdated: dopamine caused more arrhythmias and deaths in cardiogenic shock (SOAP II). Noradrenaline for the pressure, dobutamine for the output.
“Start a vasopressor such as noradrenaline” for HFrEF at SBP 85 (DocT QBank keys dobutamine, 58%)
DocT follows ESC (inotrope first with borderline SBP); this card follows AHA/SCAI (noradrenaline below SBP 90). Low output with borderline SBP: dobutamine. Shock with MAP <65: noradrenaline first.
“Selective β₁ stimulation” or “troponin C sensitisation” for the drug that improves CO, venodilates and enhances SR calcium reuptake (GT2, 50%)
PDE3 inhibition, raising cAMP: milrinone.
decode: Large anterior STEMI, BP 72/40, rising lactate — intervention with the strongest survival impact? [DocT GT]
Early coronary reperfusion.
On dobutamine, BP keeps falling (85/55) [DocT QBank, 90%]
Add a vasopressor such as noradrenaline.
ADHF on chronic β-blocker, CO low despite high-dose dobutamine [DocT GT]
Levosimendan.
STEMI with shock, PCI centre door-to-balloon 75 min [DocT GT]
Primary PCI.
CAR-18.punch: STEMI with shock goes for revascularisation of the culprit whatever the delay; dobutamine if the pressure holds, noradrenaline first if it does not, milrinone or levosimendan if β-blocked, and no routine IABP.

CAR-19.intro: Not every infarct shock is a failing left ventricle. In an inferior STEMI with clear lungs and a high JVP, the right ventricle has stopped pushing, and the treatment is nearly the opposite of LV failure.
why: **RV infarction; ST elevation in V4R.** The right coronary artery usually supplies the RV; a proximal occlusion causes inferior STEMI with RV involvement. ST elevation ≥1 mm in V4R is the most sensitive ECG sign and fades within hours; echo shows a dilated, hypokinetic RV.

**Cautious crystalloid bolus while arranging primary PCI.** A stunned RV moves blood through the lungs only if it is filled at a higher pressure; without that the LV is underfilled and output falls. Fluid is given in small boluses, because an over-distended RV bulges the septum into the LV and lowers output again.

**Nitrates, diuretics, morphine, β-blockers — all drop preload.** Venodilation or diuresis removes the filling pressure the RV depends on; a sudden collapse after sublingual nitrate is the classic presentation.

**Dobutamine; keep AV synchrony (pace if heart block).** Inferior infarcts often cause AV block; losing atrial contraction removes a large part of RV filling, so sequential pacing helps more than ventricular pacing alone.
mimic: RV infarct vs LV cardiogenic shock
RV: clear lungs, high JVP, Kussmaul sign, preload-dependent, give fluid. LV: crackles, high PAWP, avoid fluid.
traps: “Medication-related adverse reaction” for collapse to 60/30 after nitrate in inferior STEMI
The nitrate unmasked a preload-dependent RV infarct: cardiogenic shock (46% right; the distractor also drew about 46%).
decode: Inferior STEMI given aspirin, nitrate and morphine; BP falls from 160/90 to 60/30 [DocT QBank, 46%]
Cardiogenic shock (RV infarction).
CAR-19.punch: Inferior STEMI with hypotension, clear lungs and a high JVP is RV infarction: confirm with V4R, give cautious fluid, avoid nitrates, diuretics and morphine, use dobutamine and keep AV synchrony while PCI is arranged.

CAR-20.sub: Cardiology → ACS → Antithrombotics, nitrates and troponin
CAR-20.intro: Four separate ACS decisions sit on this card, each tested by a different trap: the anticoagulant when nobody is reperfused, the IV P2Y12 inhibitor, the nitrate ban, and troponin in kidney disease.
why: **Fondaparinux (OASIS-6) — less death/re-MI, no extra major bleeding. Not alone during primary PCI (catheter thrombosis).** Fondaparinux is an indirect factor Xa inhibitor given once daily; in STEMI patients without primary PCI it lowered death or re-infarction without more bleeding. It does not inhibit thrombin at the catheter tip, so if the patient goes to PCI a bolus of UFH is added. ESC 2023 recommends fondaparinux (class I) in NSTE-ACS when early angiography is not planned, advises against it during primary PCI (class III) and gives it IIa alongside streptokinase; it has no separate class for unreperfused STEMI, so the card’s answer rests on OASIS-6.

**Cangrelor — onset seconds, offset ~1 h.** Cangrelor is the only IV P2Y12 inhibitor: reversible, half-life 3–6 minutes, platelet function back within about an hour. Morphine and vomiting delay gut absorption of oral P2Y12 inhibitors, and IV cangrelor bypasses the gut. It is also the bridge when DAPT must stop for urgent surgery after a recent stent (BRIDGE).
**No nitrates within 24 h (sildenafil) / 48 h (tadalafil) — profound hypotension.** Both nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors raise cGMP in vascular smooth muscle; together they cause severe vasodilation.

**Chronically raised; diagnose MI by a rise and/or fall (dynamic change), not a single value.** Chronic kidney disease and chronic myocardial injury raise baseline troponin; the Fourth Universal Definition requires a rise and/or fall with at least one value above the 99th percentile, plus clinical evidence of ischaemia.
mimic: Cangrelor vs GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors
Cangrelor blocks P2Y12, reversible, offset about an hour. Eptifibatide and tirofiban block GP IIb/IIIa; abciximab binds platelets for days.
traps: “Enoxaparin or UFH” as the best anticoagulant when no reperfusion is given
Fondaparinux (23% right).
“Tirofiban or eptifibatide” as IV P2Y12 bridging
Cangrelor (35% right on the mini test; 80% in GT2).
“A single troponin above the 99th percentile in CKD 4 = MI”
A dynamic rise and/or fall is needed (GT3 lost).
decode: Recent stent, on DAPT, septic shock needing urgent surgery — IV antiplatelet bridge? [DocT GT, 80%]
Cangrelor infusion.
CAR-20.punch: No reperfusion: fondaparinux; IV P2Y12: cangrelor (also the surgical bridge); no nitrates within 24 h of sildenafil or 48 h of tadalafil; in CKD diagnose MI by a troponin rise and/or fall.

CAR-21.sub: Cardiology → Anticoagulation → Reversal agents and doses
CAR-21.intro: Bleeding on an anticoagulant is the most-asked single topic in the deck after shock profiles. Each drug has its own reversal because each works at a different point in the cascade.
why: **Dabigatran → idarucizumab 5 g IV: specific, immediate. Side effects: delirium, fever, constipation, hypoKALAEMIA.** Idarucizumab is a humanised antibody fragment that binds dabigatran about 350 times more tightly than thrombin, reversing it within minutes (given as 2 × 2.5 g). Its listed adverse effects include hypokalaemia, delirium, constipation, pyrexia and pneumonia; hyperkalaemia is not one.

**Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban) → andexanet alfa; or 4F-PCC 50 U/kg. Ciraparantag = investigational.** Andexanet is a decoy factor Xa that binds the drug. In ANNEXA-I (2024, ICH) it gave better haemostatic efficacy than usual care (67.0% vs 53.1%) but more thrombotic events (10.3% vs 5.6%; ischaemic stroke 6.5% vs 1.5%), and US sales ended in December 2025 after an FDA safety warning on thrombosis; 4F-PCC is now the usual choice where andexanet is unavailable. INR does not measure Xa inhibitor effect, and vitamin K does nothing for a DOAC.

**Warfarin + major bleed → 4F-PCC (25–50 U/kg by INR) + vitamin K 10 mg IV. FFP only if no PCC.** PCC supplies factors II, VII, IX and X (plus proteins C and S) in a small volume and corrects the INR in minutes; FFP needs large volumes, thawing and hours. Typical PCC dosing is 25 U/kg for INR 2–4, 35 for 4–6 and 50 above 6. Vitamin K takes 6–12 hours but prevents the INR rebounding once PCC wears off. Without bleeding: INR 4.5–10, hold 1–2 doses (low-dose oral vitamin K only if bleeding risk is high); INR above 10, oral vitamin K 2.5–5 mg.

**Heparin (UFH) → protamine 1 mg per 100 U given in the last 2–3 h (max 50 mg): full reversal.** Protamine is a basic protein that binds acidic heparin; UFH’s half-life is about 60–90 minutes, so only recent units are counted.

**Enoxaparin → protamine 1 mg per mg if dose <8 h ago; 0.5 mg/mg if 8–12 h: only ~60% reversal; none after 12 h.** Protamine binds the long chains that carry anti-thrombin activity; LMWH’s short chains, which carry the anti-Xa activity, escape, so reversal is partial.
mimic: Specific vs non-specific reversal
Specific: idarucizumab (dabigatran), andexanet (Xa inhibitors), protamine (heparins). Non-specific: PCC (warfarin; Xa inhibitors where andexanet is unavailable).
traps: “Factor VII is not in PCC” (GT7 key, 59%)
Outdated: modern 4-factor PCC contains II, VII, IX and X; only the old 3-factor PCC lacks VII.
“FFP + vitamin K” for warfarin ICH (Marrow key, recent stroke)

Marrow argues PCC is prothrombotic and PCC trials excluded recent MI/stroke; AHA/ESO still prefer 4F-PCC + IV vitamin K for life-threatening bleeding. Pick FFP only if the stem stresses a recent thrombotic event and asks for the ‘safest’ agent.
“Delay endoscopy until the INR is normal” or “FFP” for melaena at INR 2.8 (AIM1, 53%)
PCC (with vitamin K) and do not delay endoscopy.
“Hyperkalaemia is an adverse effect of idarucizumab”
Hypokalaemia is; hyperkalaemia is the ‘not seen’ answer (45%).
“Protamine after enoxaparin given 14 h ago”
None after 12 h; 1 mg/mg within 8 h, 0.5 mg/mg at 8–12 h (INI-SS lost, 35%).
decode: Dabigatran, massive GI bleed or ICH — reversal? [DocT QBank / GT ×5, 86–87%]
Idarucizumab.
Rivaroxaban or apixaban bleed — specific reversal? [DocT QBank / GT, 75–94%]
Andexanet alfa; or 4F-PCC (aPCC also keyed).
Warfarin, life-threatening bleed or ICH, INR 4–10 [DocT QBank / GT ×6]
4F-PCC + IV vitamin K.
Mechanical mitral valve, INR 8.4, no bleeding, CKD, aspirin [DocT GT]
Hold 1–2 doses + oral vitamin K 2–2.5 mg.
CAR-21.punch: Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g; Xa inhibitors: andexanet or 4F-PCC 50 U/kg; warfarin with major bleeding: 4F-PCC plus IV vitamin K 10 mg; heparin: protamine 1 mg per 100 U; enoxaparin: protamine, partial and none after 12 h.

CAR-22.sub: Cardiology → Vasopressors → Phenylephrine, vasopressin, methylene blue
CAR-22.intro: Shock pharmacology ends with what to add or switch when noradrenaline is not enough, or is causing harm. Each answer depends on which receptor or pathway the drug uses.
why: **Phenylephrine — pure α1, no β1 chronotropy (INI-SS key).** If noradrenaline’s β₁ effect drives a tachyarrhythmia, a pure α-agonist keeps the vascular tone without stimulating the heart; the reflex from the rise in pressure may even slow the rate. It can lower cardiac output by raising afterload, so it is a specific-situation drug, not first line.

**When noradrenaline reaches 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min.** Surviving Sepsis 2021 suggests adding vasopressin in this range rather than escalating noradrenaline. Septic shock causes a relative vasopressin deficiency, and V1 receptors still work when adrenergic receptors are down-regulated by acidosis and high catecholamine levels.

**Inhibits endothelial and inducible NO synthase and downstream soluble guanylate cyclase → less cGMP → vasoconstriction.** Vasoplegia (bypass, liver transplant, sepsis) is driven by NO → sGC → cGMP → smooth-muscle relaxation, plus K-ATP channel opening; methylene blue blocks it at two points. Other rescue agents: vasopressin, angiotensin II (ATHOS-3) and hydroxocobalamin (scavenges NO and H₂S). Angiotensin I is an inactive precursor needing ACE and is not a vasopressor drug.
mimic: Angiotensin II vs angiotensin I
Angiotensin II is the licensed vasopressor (ATHOS-3); angiotensin I is the precursor.
traps: “Methylene blue raises NO synthase activity” or acts on adrenergic receptors
It inhibits NOS and sGC; only 7% picked the correct statement.
“Angiotensin I raises MAP in vasoplegia”
It is the LEAST likely (17% right): an inactive precursor, not a drug.
“Noradrenaline” for flutter or AF with RVR in septic shock or stroke
Phenylephrine avoids β-stimulation (31% right in INI-SS).
decode: Liver-kidney transplant, vasoplegia on high-dose noradrenaline — LEAST likely to raise MAP? [DocT GT, 17%]
Angiotensin I.
Ischaemic stroke, MAP 58 after fluids, AF with RVR — preferred vasopressor? [DocT GT]
Phenylephrine, to avoid β-stimulation.
CAR-22.punch: When noradrenaline drives a tachyarrhythmia switch to pure α phenylephrine; add vasopressin at 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min; methylene blue inhibits NO synthase and guanylate cyclase, and angiotensin I is not a vasopressor.

CAR-23.sub: Cardiology → Pulmonary embolism → ESC risk classes and treatment
CAR-23.intro: Step 5 opens with the decision that most PE questions test: who gets lysis. The ESC classes are built around one fact — death in PE comes from RV failure, and only established haemodynamic failure justifies the bleeding risk of systemic lysis.
why: **High: SBP below 90 (or fall ≥40, or pressors) / arrest → systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2 h).** ESC 2019 defines high risk as cardiac arrest, obstructive shock (SBP <90 or vasopressors with end-organ hypoperfusion) or persistent hypotension (SBP <90 or a fall ≥40 mmHg for more than 15 minutes, not from another cause). The RV is already failing, so dissolving the clot is worth the bleeding risk; an accelerated 0.6 mg/kg over 15 min (max 50 mg) is the alternative, used in arrest. Surgical or catheter embolectomy if lysis is contraindicated or fails.

**Intermediate-high: normotensive + RV dysfunction AND troponin → anticoagulate, monitor; rescue lysis if decompensates.** In PEITHO, tenecteplase in this group reduced decompensation (1.6% vs 5.0%) but did not change mortality (1.2% vs 1.8%) and caused haemorrhagic stroke in 2.0% vs 0.2% and major bleeding in 11.5% vs 2.4%. So these patients are anticoagulated (usually LMWH) in a monitored bed and lysed only if they become hypotensive.
**Intermediate-low: one or neither of RV / troponin; PESI III–V → anticoagulate on ward.**

**Low: sPESI 0 → early discharge, DOAC.** The AHA/ACC 2026 PE guideline renames these groups as categories A–E (C1–C3 by RV and troponin, D incipient failure, E hypotension or arrest); systemic lysis is harmful up to C2, unclear in C3 and reasonable in E. The rule is the same: hypotension, not imaging or biomarkers, earns lysis.
mimic: Intermediate-high vs high risk
Both have a strained RV and raised troponin; only high risk has hypotension or shock. BP 96/58 is still intermediate-high.
traps: “RV strain + troponin with BP 96/58 → lysis”
Anticoagulate and monitor (INI-SS correct; GT4 Q26 you chose lysis).
decode: APS, saddle PE, hypotensive, RV hypokinesis despite heparin [Marrow]
rtPA (alteplase 100 mg over 2 h).
CAR-23.punch: In PE hypotension decides lysis: high risk (shock, SBP <90 or arrest) gets alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours; intermediate-high (RV strain plus troponin, normotensive) gets anticoagulation and monitoring, with rescue lysis only if it decompensates.

CAR-24.sub: Cardiology → Pulmonary embolism → D-dimer, subsegmental PE, Daniel score
CAR-24.intro: Three diagnostic points around PE severity: how to read a D-dimer in older patients, what to do with a tiny clot, and how the ECG scores RV strain.
why: **Age × 10 µg/L (FEU) if above 50 years.** D-dimer rises with age, so a fixed 500 µg/L cut-off excludes few older patients; ADJUST-PE showed the age-adjusted cut-off safely rules out PE in more of them (only in low or intermediate clinical probability).

**Clinical surveillance, no anticoagulation (repeat leg ultrasound).** CHEST 2021 suggests surveillance over anticoagulation for isolated subsegmental PE with no proximal DVT and low recurrence risk; anticoagulate if cancer, immobility, poor reserve or a positive leg scan.

**Daniel ECG score: HR >100 = 2; incomplete RBBB = 2; complete RBBB = 3; T inversion in all of V1–V4 = 4; S1Q3T3 (complete) = 2; score ≥10 = severe pulmonary hypertension.** Each item reflects RV pressure overload; the full score also adds points for the depth of T inversion in each of V1–V3 and for each part of S1Q3T3, to a maximum of 21. A score ≥10 suggests systolic PA pressure above about 50 mmHg.
traps: “Anticoagulate every subsegmental PE”
Isolated, no DVT, low risk: surveillance (only 17% right).
decode: [pattern] HR 118, incomplete RBBB, T inversion V1–V4 — Daniel score?
[pattern] 70-year-old, low pretest probability — D-dimer cut-off?
CAR-24.punch: Use an age × 10 µg/L D-dimer cut-off above 50, watch isolated low-risk subsegmental PE with repeat leg scans, and add the Daniel ECG points (tachycardia 2, RBBB 2 or 3, T inversion V1–V4 4) to grade RV strain.

CAR-25.sub: Cardiology → Haemodynamics → Shock profiles on a PA catheter
CAR-25.intro: This is the most-asked card in the deck (30 questions). Four numbers name the shock: RAP (right filling), PAWP (left filling), cardiac output and SVR. Each type of shock starts with one failure, and the other numbers follow from the body’s response to it.
why: **Hypovolaemic: RAP ↓, PAWP ↓, CO ↓, SVR ↑.** Too little volume: both filling pressures fall, output falls, and sympathetic vasoconstriction raises SVR. A child may stay normotensive by tachycardia and high SVR until late.

**Cardiogenic (LV): RAP ↑/N, PAWP ↑, CO ↓, SVR ↑.** The pump fails: blood backs up behind the LV (high PAWP, pulmonary oedema), output falls, SVR rises. Low output means more oxygen extraction, so ScvO₂ is low and the peripheries are cold.

**Distributive (early): RAP ↓/N, PAWP ↓/N, CO ↑, SVR ↓.** Vessels dilate first; output rises to compensate, so the skin is warm, the pulse pressure wide and the ScvO₂ normal or high. Sepsis is the commonest cause of high-output hypotension; others are liver failure, anaphylaxis, thyrotoxicosis, AV fistula, beriberi. Neurogenic shock is distributive too, but with bradycardia and low CO from lost sympathetic tone.

**Obstructive — PE: RAP ↑, PAWP ↓/N, CO ↓, SVR ↑.** The block lies between the right heart and the left: pressure piles up behind it (high RAP) while the left atrium is starved (low PAWP). High RAP with low PAWP means obstruction before the left heart.

**Obstructive — tamponade: RAP ↑, PAWP ↑ (equal), CO ↓, SVR ↑.** Fluid around the heart compresses all four chambers, so the diastolic pressures equalise (RAP = RV diastolic = PAWP); the LV is small, the IVC plethoric, the pulse pressure narrow. A massive pleural effusion (tension hydrothorax) behaves the same way: high CVP with obstructive shock, treated by drainage.
mimic: Hypovolaemic vs obstructive PE
Both have low PAWP and high SVR; RAP separates them — low in hypovolaemia, high in PE.
Cold low-flow vs warm distributive
Cold, low ScvO₂: low output (cardiogenic, hypovolaemic). Warm, wide pulse pressure, normal or high ScvO₂: distributive.
traps: “Hypovolaemic” for RAP 14, PAWP 6, high SVRI (GT4 Q75)
Hypovolaemia would make both pressures LOW; high RAP with low PAWP is obstructive.
“Septic shock” for cold peripheries, oliguria and LOW ScvO₂, CVP 10 (DocT QBank key, 60%)
Disputed key: low ScvO₂ with cold peripheries means low output, i.e. cardiogenic; only early unresuscitated sepsis gives a low ScvO₂.
“Cirrhosis with portal hypertension” as the cause of CVP 22 (DocT QBank / GT6 key)

Wrong physiology: portal pressure sits upstream of the liver, and cirrhosis is hyperdynamic with a normal-low CVP. CVP 22 means right-heart failure or volume overload — ‘AKI with fluid overload’ is the physiological answer.
“Acute PE” for CVP 18, BP 140/90, acute respiratory failure in a smoker (DocT key, 27–44%)

Ambiguous item: a normal BP makes it at most intermediate-risk PE, and COPD with cor pulmonale fits equally. Pick PE if the stem gives SBP <90 or RV strain with a clear chest; COPD if wheeze and chronic hypercapnia.
“Pulsus paradoxus” or “electrical alternans” as what best confirms tamponade (GT2, 73%)
On a catheter, equalisation of diastolic pressures.
decode: BP 80/50 with CVP 15 after MI; CVP 18 with low EF [DocT QBank / GT, 88–100%]
Cardiogenic shock.
Septic shock: MAP 60, SvO₂ 80%, CO high, SVR low [DocT GT ×3, 84–100%]
Distributive.
Large effusion on X-ray, BP 85/55, CVP 15–18 [DocT QBank, 79–85%]
Obstructive shock from massive pleural effusion.
Hypovolaemic vs cardiogenic by CVP, PCWP, CI, SVR [NEET 2025 recall]
Hypovolaemic ↓↓↓↑; cardiogenic ↑↑↓↑.
CAR-25.punch: Read RAP against PAWP first: both low is hypovolaemia, PAWP high is LV failure, RAP high with PAWP low is PE, all equal is tamponade; then CO and SVR separate warm distributive shock from the cold low-output kinds.

parts.q: Need EVLW and continuous cardiac output — which monitor? (INI-SS, lost)
parts.a: Transpulmonary thermodilution with pulse-contour analysis (e.g. PiCCO); a PA catheter gives intermittent CO and PAWP but not extravascular lung water.

CAR-26.sub: Cardiology → Mechanical support → Devices by flow
CAR-26.intro: The deck ends with machines that take over the pump. They differ in how much flow they add, which ventricle they support, and whether they need the heart’s own rhythm.
why: **IABP: LV, ~0.5–1 L; ↓ afterload, ↑ coronary perfusion; no routine benefit in shock.** The balloon inflates in diastole (raising coronary perfusion) and deflates before systole (lowering afterload). It needs a regular rhythm or pressure trigger to time this, so a very irregular rhythm degrades it; IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit.

**Impella CP: LV, ~3.5–4 L; pulls blood LV → aorta; can vent the LV on VA-ECMO.** A microaxial pump across the aortic valve unloads the LV directly and works independently of the rhythm. DanGer Shock (2024): in STEMI with shock, routine Impella CP lowered 180-day death (45.8% vs 58.5%) but increased moderate or severe bleeding, limb ischaemia and renal replacement.
**Impella RP / TandemHeart RA–PA: RV, ~4 L; right-sided support.** For isolated RV failure (RV infarct, after LVAD, PE) blood is moved from the right atrium or IVC to the pulmonary artery.

**VA-ECMO: heart + lungs, up to ~7 L; biventricular failure, ECPR, fulminant myocarditis.** The only device that gives full circulatory and respiratory support and keeps working even in VF; it raises LV afterload (CAR-16e).
mimic: Rhythm-dependent vs rhythm-independent devices
Only the IABP needs synchrony; Impella, TandemHeart and VA-ECMO are continuous-flow.
traps: “Impella CP” as the only device that supports without cardiac synchrony (CGT6 key)
Disputed: TandemHeart and VA-ECMO are also continuous-flow and rhythm-independent; only the IABP needs synchrony.
“Impella gives the highest flow with LV support”
VA-ECMO does (23% right).
decode: Refractory cardiogenic shock, recurrent fast AF — device effective without synchrony? [DocT GT]
Key: Impella CP (TandemHeart and VA-ECMO also correct).
CAR-26.punch: IABP adds under 1 L/min and needs a regular rhythm, Impella CP about 3.5–4 L and improved survival in STEMI shock (DanGer Shock), and VA-ECMO gives up to 7 L with full heart and lung support.

CAR-27.intro: The sweep checks nine statements, one from each part of the deck. Each turns on a single detail from an earlier card.
why: **False — negatively inotropic; avoid with EF below 40%** (CAR-04a).
**False — hyperkalaemia; digoxin = reverse tick, short QT** (CAR-07b).
**False — resume CPR for 2 min straight away** (CAR-11c).
**False — VA; the heart must be bypassed** (CAR-16a).
traps: “Every tachycardia drug is safe if the patient is stable”
Stability lets you use a drug, but the node (WPW), the ventricle (low EF) and the airway (asthma) still decide which one.
decode: [pattern] True/false on arrhythmia, arrest and PE rules
Mark each statement on its own before reading the options.
CAR-27.punch: Most errors here come from applying a default to the exception: no adenosine in asthma, no verapamil with low EF, no DOAC in rheumatic MS, no pulse check after analysis, no VV for ECPR, no lysis without hypotension.

topups.q: Hypertensive emergency: define it, how fast to lower, with what, and the exceptions?
a: - BP ≥180/120 + acute organ damage (encephalopathy, ICH/stroke, ACS, pulmonary oedema, dissection, AKI/TMA, eclampsia) = emergency → ICU + IV titratable drug; no organ damage = urgency → oral drugs over 24–48 h.
- Lower MAP by ≤25% in the 1st hour → 160/100–110 over the next 2–6 h → normal over 24–48 h (autoregulation is reset upward; fast drops cause watershed ischaemia).

- Drugs by organ: encephalopathy/stroke → labetalol, nicardipine or clevidipine; acute pulmonary oedema → IV nitroglycerin + loop diuretic + NIV (avoid labetalol/β-blockers in decompensated HF); renal failure → fenoldopam, nicardipine or clevidipine (no prolonged nitroprusside: cyanide/thiocyanate); avoid nitroprusside with raised ICP; oral drugs are too slow.

- Go faster: dissection SBP <120 and HR <60 within 20 min (β-blocker first); severe pre-eclampsia SBP <160 within 1 h; phaeochromocytoma α before β. Ischaemic stroke: treat only if >185/110 (before lysis) or >220/120.
- Clonidine withdrawal: restart clonidine; if organ damage, phentolamine or labetalol — never an unopposed pure β-blocker.

- Why it spirals: an abrupt BP rise injures the endothelium (lost NO, fibrinoid necrosis) and activates RAAS → more vasoconstriction; malignant hypertension's pressure natriuresis and RAAS surge cause volume depletion, hypokalaemia, polyuria and weight loss.
