x.sub: Cardiology → Vascular emergencies → Hypertensive emergency
x.intro: Step 4 deals with emergencies where the cardiovascular drugs are chosen by the organ at risk, and the hypertensive emergency (asked 15 times in the DocT tests) is the clearest case. The number alone does not make the emergency; acute organ damage does, and that also decides how fast and with what the pressure comes down.
why: **BP ≥180/120 + acute organ damage (encephalopathy, ICH/stroke, ACS, pulmonary oedema, dissection, AKI/TMA, eclampsia) = emergency → ICU + IV titratable drug; no organ damage = urgency → oral drugs over 24–48 h.** What separates the two is new organ injury, because that is what the pressure is doing now; a high reading without injury carries no short-term benefit from rapid lowering and the risk of overshoot.

**Lower MAP by ≤25% in the 1st hour → 160/100–110 over the next 2–6 h → normal over 24–48 h (autoregulation is reset upward; fast drops cause watershed ischaemia).** In chronic hypertension the cerebral and renal autoregulation curves shift to the right, so a ‘normal’ pressure is below the lower limit for that patient and flow falls; stroke, blindness and renal infarction follow over-rapid correction. The 2017 AHA guideline gives a fall in SBP of no more than 25% in the first hour.

**Drugs by organ: encephalopathy/stroke → labetalol, nicardipine or clevidipine; acute pulmonary oedema → IV nitroglycerin + loop diuretic + NIV (avoid labetalol/β-blockers in decompensated HF); renal failure → fenoldopam, nicardipine or clevidipine (no prolonged nitroprusside: cyanide/thiocyanate); avoid nitroprusside with raised ICP; oral drugs are too slow.** The drug is chosen for what it does to the injured organ: titratable IV agents allow precise control; nitroglycerin lowers preload in pulmonary oedema; nitroprusside dilates cerebral vessels (raising ICP) and accumulates cyanide and, in renal failure, thiocyanate.

**Go faster: dissection SBP <120 and HR <60 within 20 min (β-blocker first); severe pre-eclampsia SBP <160 within 1 h; phaeochromocytoma α before β. Ischaemic stroke: treat only if >185/110 (before lysis) or >220/120.** In dissection the force driving the tear (dP/dt) matters, so the heart rate is controlled first with an IV β-blocker (esmolol, labetalol) and only then a vasodilator, to avoid reflex tachycardia. In phaeochromocytoma an unopposed β-blocker leaves α-vasoconstriction unchecked. In ischaemic stroke the penumbra depends on pressure: lower only for lysis (<185/110, kept <180/105 after) or above 220/120 (by about 15% in 24 h). AHA 2022 ICH guidance targets SBP about 140, avoiding falls below 130.

**Clonidine withdrawal: restart clonidine; if organ damage, phentolamine or labetalol — never an unopposed pure β-blocker.** Stopping clonidine releases a catecholamine surge, like a phaeochromocytoma; a pure β-blocker would leave α-vasoconstriction unopposed and push the pressure higher.

**Why it spirals: an abrupt BP rise injures the endothelium (lost NO, fibrinoid necrosis) and activates RAAS → more vasoconstriction; malignant hypertension’s pressure natriuresis and RAAS surge cause volume depletion, hypokalaemia, polyuria and weight loss.** These patients are often volume-depleted, which is why a vasodilator can drop the pressure abruptly and why diuretics are avoided unless there is pulmonary oedema.
mimic: Hypertensive emergency vs urgency
Emergency: acute organ damage, IV drug in ICU, ≤25% in the first hour. Urgency: no damage, oral drugs over 24–48 h.
Dissection vs other emergencies
Dissection: SBP <120 and HR <60 within about 20 minutes, β-blocker first. Others: gradual reduction.
traps: “Lower the BP to normal within the first hour”
No more than 25% in the first hour; normal over 24–48 h. Exceptions are dissection, severe pre-eclampsia and phaeochromocytoma.
“Nitroprusside for hypertensive encephalopathy with raised ICP” or for days in renal failure
Nitroprusside raises ICP and accumulates cyanide/thiocyanate; nicardipine, clevidipine or labetalol instead.
“Labetalol for hypertensive acute pulmonary oedema”
IV nitroglycerin, loop diuretic and NIV; β-blockers worsen decompensated HF.
“Esmolol alone” for clonidine withdrawal or phaeochromocytoma crisis
Never an unopposed β-blocker: α-blockade first (phentolamine) or labetalol.
decode: [pattern; topic asked 15× in DocT GT] BP 220/130 with headache, confusion or papilloedema — target in the first hour?
Lower MAP by no more than 25%, then 160/100–110 over 2–6 h.
[pattern] Hypertensive emergency with acute aortic dissection — target and first drug?
SBP <120 and HR <60 within about 20 min; IV β-blocker first.
[pattern] Hypertensive pulmonary oedema — drug?
IV nitroglycerin with a loop diuretic and NIV.
[pattern] Ischaemic stroke, candidate for lysis — BP threshold?
Treat if above 185/110; keep below 180/105 after lysis.
x.punch: A hypertensive emergency is high BP with acute organ damage: lower by no more than 25% in the first hour with a titratable IV drug chosen for the organ, except dissection, pre-eclampsia and phaeochromocytoma, which need faster or different control.

topups.topic: First rhythm in sudden cardiac arrest
topups.q: First recorded rhythm in sudden cardiac arrest — which is commonest?
a: - Overall out-of-hospital arrest: asystole/PEA now outnumber VF (VF ~20–25% and falling).
- Witnessed collapse in the young or athletes: VF/VT is classic (HCM, channelopathy, commotio cordis) — the earlier the rhythm is recorded, the likelier VF.
- Late sudden death weeks after MI: asystole ~50%, PEA ~20% as first rhythm (Tintinalli).

x.sub: Cardiology → Arrest → First recorded rhythm
x.intro: Step 3 starts at the collapse, and the first rhythm recorded decides whether a shock can help. Which rhythm is ‘commonest’ depends on who has arrested and how quickly the monitor goes on.
why: **Overall out-of-hospital arrest: asystole/PEA now outnumber VF (VF ~20–25% and falling).** VF degenerates into asystole within minutes if untreated, so a late first recording finds asystole; fewer arrests are also caused by acute coronary occlusion now, and more by non-cardiac causes (respiratory, overdose).

**Witnessed collapse in the young or athletes: VF/VT is classic (HCM, channelopathy, commotio cordis) — the earlier the rhythm is recorded, the likelier VF.** A sudden arrhythmic death in a structurally abnormal or electrically unstable heart starts as VT or VF; a bystander-witnessed arrest with an AED on early catches it before it decays.

**Late sudden death weeks after MI: asystole ~50%, PEA ~20% as first rhythm (Tintinalli).** Late after infarction, deaths are often from pump failure, re-infarction or bradyarrhythmia rather than primary VF, which is why early ICDs after MI did not lower mortality (CAR-10).
mimic: Commonest first rhythm overall vs in the young
Overall OHCA: non-shockable (asystole/PEA). Young, witnessed, early AED: VF.
traps: “VF is the commonest first rhythm in all cardiac arrest”
It was in older series and remains so in witnessed arrests with early monitoring; in OHCA overall, asystole and PEA now outnumber it.
decode: [Marrow QB22] Commonest first recorded rhythm in sudden cardiac arrest?
Depends on the stem: OHCA overall → asystole/PEA; witnessed collapse in a young person → VF.
[Marrow QB22] First rhythm in sudden death weeks after MI?
Asystole (about half), then PEA.
x.punch: In out-of-hospital arrest overall the first rhythm is now usually asystole or PEA, with VF in only about a fifth; a witnessed collapse in a young person, recorded early, is classically VF.

topups.q: Hypertensive emergency (end-organ damage), no stroke or dissection: fundus grades and how fast to lower?
a: - Keith-Wagener-Barker: I narrowing; II AV nipping; III haemorrhages, exudates, cotton-wool; IV = III + papilloedema (malignant).
- Lower MAP 10–20% (≤25%) in the first hour, then to 160/100 over 2–6 h, normal over 24–48 h.
- Exceptions: aortic dissection (SBP <120 in 20 min), pre-eclampsia (<160/110, aim 140–150/90–100), ischaemic stroke and ICH have their own targets.

x.sub: Cardiology → Vascular emergencies → Hypertensive emergency: fundus and targets
x.intro: This short companion to the hypertensive-emergency card covers the two things it is asked on. The fundus shows whether the pressure has already damaged small vessels, and the targets say how fast to bring it down once there is organ damage.
why: **Keith–Wagener–Barker: I narrowing; II AV nipping; III haemorrhages, exudates, cotton-wool; IV = III + papilloedema (malignant).** Grades I–II are chronic arteriolar thickening. Grade III is acute endothelial injury: haemorrhages, leaking exudates, and cotton-wool spots, which are nerve-fibre infarcts. Grade IV adds disc swelling from raised pressure and ischaemia. Papilloedema with this picture is the classic sign of malignant hypertension and counts as organ damage.

**Lower MAP 10–20% (≤25%) in the first hour, then to 160/100 over 2–6 h, normal over 24–48 h.** Chronic hypertension shifts cerebral and renal autoregulation to higher pressures. A fast return to ‘normal’ pressure therefore drops below that patient’s lower limit and causes watershed ischaemia (stroke, blindness, renal infarction).

**Exceptions: aortic dissection (SBP <120 in 20 min), pre-eclampsia (<160/110, aim 140–150/90–100), ischaemic stroke and ICH have their own targets.** In dissection the shear force propagating the tear is the danger, so the heart rate is controlled first with an IV β-blocker and the SBP is brought down fast. In pre-eclampsia placental flow depends on pressure, so the aim stops at about 140–150/90–100. In ischaemic stroke, BP is lowered only above 185/110 before lysis or above 220/120 otherwise, to protect the penumbra; in ICH the SBP target is about 140, avoiding falls below 130 (AHA 2022).
mimic: Grade III vs grade IV retinopathy
Both have haemorrhages, exudates and cotton-wool spots; only grade IV has papilloedema (malignant hypertension).
traps: “Bring the BP to normal within the first hour”
No more than 25% in the first hour; dissection is the main exception that is lowered fast.
“Grade IV = haemorrhages and exudates”
That is grade III; grade IV needs papilloedema.
decode: [pattern; DocT and Marrow] Hypertensive emergency with papilloedema, no stroke or dissection — fundus grade and first-hour target?
Grade IV (malignant); lower MAP by 10–20%, at most 25%, in the first hour.
x.punch: Papilloedema on top of haemorrhages and exudates is grade IV, malignant hypertension. Lower the MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour, except in dissection, pre-eclampsia, ischaemic stroke and ICH, which have their own targets.

spine: Fast rhythms: shock or drug

An unstable tachycardia gets synchronised electricity at once; a stable one is sorted by whether it uses the AV node, and the drug is chosen by the node, the accessory pathway, the strength of the ventricle and the QT.
Slow rhythms and devices
Atropine works only where the vagus acts, so infranodal block and the denervated heart go straight to chronotropes and pacing; long term, EF and QRS width choose the ICD and CRT.
Arrest and after ROSC

Survival comes from uninterrupted good compressions and early shocks, with drugs secondary; after ROSC the care protects the brain: MAP ≥65, normal oxygen and CO₂, temperature control, angiography for ST elevation.
ACS, shock and the drugs
Time to PCI decides lysis or transfer, shock is revascularised and supported with noradrenaline and inotropes, and every anticoagulant has its own reversal agent.
PE, profiles and support
In PE hypotension, not RV strain or troponin, decides lysis; on a PA catheter the RAP–PAWP pairing with CO and SVR names the shock; support devices are ranked by flow.
HY2.primer: ‘Unstable’ in any arrhythmia algorithm means the rate itself is causing hypotension, altered mentation, ischaemic chest pain, acute heart failure or shock; that, not the rate number, sends the patient to electricity. The AV node conducts decrementally (the faster it is driven, the slower it conducts), which protects the ventricles; an accessory pathway has no such brake, and drugs that slow the node act only on rhythms that pass through it. In arrest, coronary perfusion pressure (aortic diastolic minus right atrial pressure) is generated only by compressions and collapses within seconds of a pause. On a PA catheter, RAP (or CVP) reflects right-sided filling and PAWP left-sided filling; with cardiac output and SVR (MAP = CO × SVR) these four numbers separate the four kinds of shock.

IE-01.sub: Infective endocarditis → Recognition → Organism by setting
IE-01.intro: Step 1 starts with the organism, because the setting predicts it before cultures return and the organism then sets the tempo, the complications and the regimen. The bank question behind this card gives a rheumatic valve with five days of fever and shock, and only a fifth of the cohort chose S. aureus.
why: **Acute (days, sepsis, new severe regurgitation, Janeway lesions) → S. aureus: commonest overall (~30%), also on rheumatic or damaged valves.** S. aureus binds both normal and damaged endothelium through surface adhesins and destroys a leaflet within days. The tempo outweighs the substrate: a rheumatic valve does not make it streptococcal when the course is five days and the patient needs pressors.

**IVDU, right-sided (tricuspid) → S. aureus; less often Pseudomonas, Candida.** Skin flora is injected straight into the venous return to the tricuspid valve; contaminated water and diluents bring Pseudomonas and Candida.

**Subacute on a damaged native valve after dental work → viridans streptococci.** They need a ready-made fibrin–platelet nidus on an abnormal valve and are not destructive, so they cause weeks of low-grade fever, not shock.

**Elderly after a GU or GI procedure → enterococci (E. faecalis); S. gallolyticus (bovis) → colonoscopy.** S. gallolyticus bacteraemia is linked to colonic neoplasia, so the colon is examined even without bowel symptoms.

**Early prosthetic valve (<12 months) → CoNS, S. aureus, Gram-negatives, Candida.** These are acquired around the operation or in hospital and live in biofilm on the sewing ring. After 12 months the spectrum returns to that of native-valve IE.

**Blood culture-negative → prior antibiotics (commonest); HACEK, Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella, Tropheryma.** These are fastidious or intracellular organisms that grow slowly or not at all in routine bottles, so they are found by serology, PCR or valve tissue (IE-15).
mimic: S. aureus vs viridans streptococci
Days, shock and a newly destroyed valve vs weeks of low-grade fever on an already abnormal valve.
Early vs late PVE
Under 12 months: hospital organisms (CoNS, S. aureus, Gram-negatives, Candida); later: the native-valve spectrum.
traps: “Rheumatic valve, so viridans streptococcus” (DocT GT2o Q124: only 20% chose S. aureus)
The predisposition tells you where IE settles, not which organism. Five days of fever, Janeway lesions, a newly severe MR and rising pressors are the S. aureus tempo.
“CoNS in the blood after valve surgery is a contaminant”
On a prosthetic valve within a year it is a leading cause, and Duke-ISCVID counts CoNS as a typical organism when intracardiac prosthetic material is present.
decode: Rheumatic MS, 5 days of fever, plantar lesions, newly severe MR, rising pressors: most likely organism? [DocT GT2o Q124, 20%]
S. aureus: an acute, destructive course whatever the substrate.
Fever and positive cultures 3 weeks after valve replacement: likely organism? [pattern]
CoNS or S. aureus (early PVE).
IE-01.punch: The tempo names the organism: days and destruction mean S. aureus, weeks on a damaged valve mean viridans streptococci, and the first year after valve surgery means hospital organisms.

IE-02.sub: Infective endocarditis → Recognition → Right-sided IE and the work-up
IE-02.intro: Step 1 continues with recognition: the drug user with fever, a murmur and lung shadows. The DocT question behind this card was answered well (85%); the teaching point is why its ‘four sets’ is still the only sensible option, and what the work-up order is.
why: **Right-sided (tricuspid) IE; infiltrates = septic pulmonary emboli; new AV block = suspect perivalvular extension.** Tricuspid vegetations shed into the pulmonary arteries and give multiple peripheral nodules that often cavitate, so the lung picture is the valve’s embolic shadow, not a primary pneumonia. New AV block means infection may have spread into the annulus near the conduction tissue, or that the aortic valve is involved as well (IE-06); TEE answers both.

**3 sets of blood cultures before antibiotics; TTE first, TEE if TTE negative, prosthetic valve or device, or complication suspected; repeat TTE/TEE in 5–7 days if still suspected; PET-CT or cardiac CT for an equivocal prosthetic valve; then empirical IV antibiotics.** ESC 2023 asks for at least three sets, 10 mL each, from a peripheral vein at 30-minute intervals: the bacteraemia is continuous, so separate sets prove persistence and three catch nearly all cases. TEE is advised even after a positive TTE because TTE misses abscess and perforation, except for good-quality TTE of isolated right-sided native IE. A stable patient can wait for cultures; a septic one is treated as soon as they are drawn.
mimic: Septic emboli vs pneumonia
Multiple peripheral, often cavitating nodules in a drug user with a murmur vs a single lobar consolidation.
traps: “Four sets of blood cultures” (DocT Specific Cardiac Diseases Q9 key)
ESC 2023 says at least three sets; the keyed option is still right because it is the only one that pairs cultures, echo and antibiotics.
“Start antibiotics first, culture later”
Prior antibiotics are the commonest cause of culture-negative IE; in a stable patient cultures always come first.
decode: IVDU, fever 3 days, murmur, bilateral infiltrates, first-degree block: next step? [DocT Specific Cardiac Diseases Q9, 85%]
Blood cultures, TTE, antibiotics; the monospot, NSAID-for-pericarditis and isoniazid options ignore the murmur.
Suspected IE, TTE negative, suspicion still high: next? [pattern]
TEE; if negative, repeat TTE/TEE in 5–7 days.
IE-02.punch: In a febrile drug user with a murmur, lung infiltrates are tricuspid emboli and new AV block is spread into the annulus; culture three times before antibiotics, then image TTE first and TEE next.

IE-03.intro: Step 2 is proof. The 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria turn the bedside picture into ‘definite’, ‘possible’ or ‘rejected’; the bank questions test the thresholds (how many sets, which organism, how to count), not the list.
why: **Major: typical organism in ≥2 sets, non-typical (e.g. E. coli) in ≥3; Coxiella phase I IgG >1:800; Bartonella IgG ≥1:800; positive PCR; imaging (vegetation, abscess, perforation, pseudoaneurysm, fistula, new dehiscence on echo or cardiac CT; PET-CT uptake >3 months after surgery; new regurgitation on echo); IE seen at operation.** The typical organisms are so specific for IE that two sets are enough; anything else needs three to exclude contamination or another source. With intracardiac prosthetic material, ISCVID also counts CoNS, Corynebacterium striatum/jeikeium, Serratia, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Cutibacterium, M. chimaera and Candida as typical. PET-CT within 3 months of surgery is only minor, because healing tissue around the sewing ring takes up FDG too.

**Minor: predisposition (prosthesis, prior IE, RHD, IVDU, CIED, HCM, congenital), fever >38 °C, vascular, immunological, microbiology not meeting major.** ISCVID words the valve predisposition as ‘more than mild regurgitation or stenosis of any cause’, which is why rheumatic MS/MR counts. A culture that fails the major threshold is not discarded; it becomes a minor criterion (IE-04).

**Definite = 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor; possible = 1 major + 1 minor, or 3 minor.** Definite can also be pathological (organisms or active IE in a vegetation, valve or embolus). ‘Rejected’ needs a firm alternative diagnosis, resolution (or no IE at surgery or autopsy) after under 4 days of antibiotics, or failure to reach ‘possible’.
mimic: Duke-ISCVID 2023 vs modified Duke (2000)
2023 adds cardiac CT and PET-CT as major imaging, the surgical criterion, PCR, and CIED/HCM/IVDU predispositions; the arithmetic for definite and possible is unchanged.
PET-CT major vs minor
More than 3 months after implantation: major; within 3 months: minor.
traps: “Worsening of a known murmur is a major criterion”
Only new regurgitation on echo is major; worsening of existing regurgitation does not count, and a new murmur on auscultation is minor and only when echo is unavailable.
“Any organism in two sets is major”
Two sets only for typical organisms; E. coli and other rare causes need three.
decode: Count majors and minors and classify (definite, possible, rejected) [DocT GT6 Q3; worked in IE-04]
2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor = definite.
Which imaging became a major criterion in 2023? [pattern]
Cardiac CT, and [18F]FDG PET-CT more than 3 months after surgery.
IE-03.punch: Two sets for a typical organism, three for a rare one; a culture that fails as major still counts as minor; definite is two major, one major plus three minor, or five minor.

IE-04.sub: Infective endocarditis → Diagnosis → Worked Duke-ISCVID case
IE-04.intro: Step 2 applied to the bank’s own case, where about half the cohort (54%) followed a key that miscounts. The parts follow the table’s rows.
why: **Major (imaging): 10 mm vegetation on TEE.** A mobile vegetation on echo is a major criterion on its own.

**Micro major? No: E. coli is non-typical → needs ≥3 sets.** Two of three is not enough because non-HACEK Gram-negatives rarely cause IE, and the stem’s pyuria offers a urinary source that can seed the blood transiently.

**Minor 1, 2, 3: rheumatic MS/MR (predisposition), fever >38 °C, and a positive culture not meeting major.** The failed microbiology criterion drops to minor instead of disappearing; that is the step the key misses.
**Total: 1 major + 3 minor = DEFINITE IE.** ‘Rejected’ would need an alternative diagnosis that explains everything; a urinary infection does not explain a 10 mm mobile vegetation.
mimic: E. coli in 2 sets vs viridans streptococci in 2 sets
E. coli: minor only; viridans streptococci: major (typical), making this 2 major.
traps: “Possible endocarditis” (DocT GT6 Q3 key; 54% chose it)
By Duke-ISCVID this is definite (1 major + 3 minor). The key looks wrong; answer ‘definite’ unless that option is absent.
“E. coli is never a cause of endocarditis”
Non-HACEK Gram-negatives cause about 2% of IE; being rare is why E. coli needs three sets, not a reason to exclude it.
decode: RHD, AF, fever on and off for 2 months, dental extractions, E. coli in 2 of 3 sets, 10 mm mobile vegetation on TEE: what is true? [DocT GT6 Q3, 54%]
Definite IE (1 major + 3 minor), despite the key.
Same case with viridans streptococci in 2 sets [pattern]
2 major = definite.
IE-04.punch: The vegetation is one major; RHD, fever and the E. coli cultures that fail as major are three minors; one major plus three minor is definite.

IE-05.sub: Infective endocarditis → Complications → Emboli and immune phenomena
IE-05.intro: Step 3: what the vegetation does once it is there. It throws fragments into the circulation and keeps releasing antigen into the blood; the bank questions give the embolic or immune picture and ask for the one diagnosis behind it.
why: **Brain (~20–40%): stroke, multiple ring-enhancing abscesses at the grey–white junction, mycotic aneurysm → ICH/SAH; spleen: infarct or abscess; lung: septic emboli from right-sided IE; also limbs, kidney, mesentery, coronary.** Left-sided fragments go wherever arterial flow takes them, and the brain is the commonest symptomatic target; emboli lodge where arteries narrow, at the grey–white junction. An infected embolus in a distal artery weakens its wall and forms a mycotic aneurysm, which can bleed.

**Embolic risk: vegetation >10 mm (>30 mm very high), mobile, mitral (anterior leaflet), S. aureus, Candida, prior embolism; highest before and in the first 2 weeks of antibiotics.** Effective therapy sterilises and organises the vegetation, so risk falls steeply after two weeks; that is why surgery to prevent embolism is decided early (IE-08).

**Immune complications: immune-complex GN (red-cell casts, low complement), Osler nodes, Roth spots, arthritis, positive RF.** Continuous antigen release forms circulating immune complexes that deposit in glomeruli (consuming complement), skin and retina.
mimic: Osler nodes vs Janeway lesions
Painful pulp nodules (immunological minor) vs painless palmar or plantar macules (vascular minor).
IE vs systemic vasculitis
Fever, a murmur, positive cultures and emboli point to IE; vasculitis does not make vegetations.
traps: “Vasculitis” for IVDU + apical murmur + stroke + red-cell casts (Marrow QB25-Q28)
Septic emboli and immune-complex GN from left-sided (mitral) IE explain every finding.
“Tuberculoma or glioma” for multiple ring-enhancing lesions in a febrile heroin user (DocT Substance-Related (Part 1) Q18, 87%)
Multiple lesions with acute fever and hemiparesis are septic embolic abscesses; tuberculoma is subacute and usually single or few.
decode: IVDU, fever, apical murmur, stroke, red-cell casts: cause? [Marrow QB25-Q28]
Septic emboli from IE.
RHD, fever, arthralgia, confusion: suspect? [Marrow QB23-Q12]
Acute infective endocarditis.
IV heroin, fever, altered sensorium, hemiparesis, multiple ring-enhancing lesions [DocT Substance-Related (Part 1) Q18, 87%]
Brain abscesses from septic emboli of IE.
IE-05.punch: A fever with emboli in several beds plus nephritis is one disease: the vegetation throws fragments and immune complexes, most dangerously in the first two weeks.

IE-06.sub: Infective endocarditis → Complications → New heart block = root abscess
IE-06.intro: Step 3 also covers spread beyond the leaflet. Two bank questions give new heart block in endocarditis and offer ‘continue antibiotics’ or ‘wait 6 weeks’. The parts follow the card’s bullets.
why: **New AV block = perivalvular (aortic-root) abscess eroding the conduction system near the AV node/His bundle.** The His bundle runs under the membranous septum, beneath the commissure between the non-coronary and right coronary cusps, so infection spreading from the aortic annulus there blocks conduction. New block in aortic IE is a specific marker of abscess, though many abscesses never cause it.
**TEE to define abscess, fistula, pseudoaneurysm.** TTE misses about half of root abscesses; ESC 2023 asks for repeat imaging (TEE, or cardiac CT) whenever a new complication is suspected.

**Urgent surgery (within 3–5 days): locally uncontrolled infection; antibiotics cannot sterilise an abscess.** A pus cavity has no blood supply, so drugs do not reach it and fever persists. ESC 2023 makes this a Class I urgent indication, native or prosthetic.

**Temporary pacing as needed; daily ECG in aortic IE to catch it early.** Mobitz II and complete block are infranodal and unstable. ESC 2023 also advises epicardial pacing at surgery when complete block is present with a predictor that it will persist.
mimic: Root abscess vs drug-induced AV block
Abscess: aortic IE, still febrile, progressive block; drugs (beta-blocker, digoxin, calcium-channel blocker): no fever, no new echo lesion.
traps: “Continue antibiotics alone” or “delay surgery 6 weeks” (DocT CGT6 Q118; Marrow QB25-Q10)
Heart block with an abscess and persistent fever is uncontrolled infection: urgent surgery, Class I.
decode: Aortic IE, day 3 of correct antibiotics, new Mobitz II: next step? [Marrow QB25-Q10]
Surgical referral (root abscess).
PVE, complete heart block, periannular abscess on TEE, still febrile: management? [DocT CGT6 Q118]
Urgent valve surgery.
IE-06.punch: In aortic endocarditis, new AV block means the infection has burrowed into the root beside the His bundle; image it with TEE and send for urgent surgery, because no antibiotic reaches an abscess.

IE-07.sub: Infective endocarditis → Complications → Acute severe AR: the bridge
IE-07.intro: Step 3’s haemodynamic face: a valve destroyed in days. Only a fifth of the cohort chose the right drug in the bank question. The parts follow the card’s bullets.
why: **Afterload reduction: nitroprusside (± dobutamine if hypotensive) to raise forward flow.** How much blood leaks back depends on the pressure behind the valve in diastole; lowering SVR lets more stroke volume go forward and lowers LV end-diastolic pressure and pulmonary pressure. A BP of 120/70 allows it, and nitroprusside can be titrated minute to minute.
**Keep HR relatively fast (shorter diastole = less regurgitant time).** Bradycardia lengthens diastole and the time for backflow.

**Avoid IABP (contraindicated in AR), beta-blockers, pure vasoconstrictors (norepinephrine raises regurgitation).** The balloon inflates in diastole and pushes more blood back through the open valve; beta-blockers remove the compensating tachycardia; vasoconstrictors raise the pressure driving the leak.
**HF from acute valve destruction with shock or oedema = emergency surgery (<24 h).** ESC 2023 times this regardless of how long antibiotics have run; drugs only buy hours.
mimic: Acute vs chronic AR
Acute: normal-sized stiff LV, high LVEDP, early mitral closure, tachycardia, little widening of pulse pressure; chronic: dilated compliant LV, wide pulse pressure, tolerated for years.
traps: “Norepinephrine or epinephrine” because the patient is sick (DocT GT2o Q60: only 20% chose nitroprusside)
Raising afterload pushes more blood back into the LV; the blood pressure here does not need support.
“Furosemide”
It eases congestion but does not increase forward flow; the leak is the problem.
decode: IVDU, aortic vegetation, severe AR, pulmonary oedema, SpO2 85%, BP 120/70, awaiting surgery: next step? [DocT GT2o Q60, 20%]
Nitroprusside.
Acute severe AR in shock: IABP as a bridge? [pattern]
No, contraindicated; emergency surgery.
IE-07.punch: In acute severe AR, unload the aorta (nitroprusside), keep the heart rate up, never use a balloon pump or a vasoconstrictor, and get the valve replaced within 24 hours.

IE-08.sub: Infective endocarditis → Surgery → ESC 2023 indications by timing
IE-08.intro: Step 4: when antibiotics are not enough. ESC 2023 groups indications by reason (heart failure, uncontrolled infection, embolism) and timing (emergency <24 h, urgent 3–5 days, non-urgent during the same admission). The parts follow the table’s rows.
why: **Emergency (<24 h): HF with cardiogenic shock or pulmonary oedema from severe acute regurgitation, obstruction or fistula.** This is a mechanical failure that no drug can fix, so the length of antibiotic treatment does not matter (IE-07).

**Urgent (3–5 days): HF without shock; locally uncontrolled infection (abscess, pseudoaneurysm, fistula, enlarging vegetation, new AV block).** ESC 2023 defines ‘urgent’ as 3–5 days (2015 said only ‘within a few days’). Walled-off infection is not reached by antibiotics (IE-06).

**Urgent: fungal or multiresistant organism; persistent bacteraemia despite correct antibiotics and source control.** Fungal and multiresistant IE are surgical because medical cure is rare (IE-15). ESC 2023 grades persistent positive cultures for more than a week, after metastatic foci are controlled, as ‘should be considered’ (IIa).

**Urgent: vegetation ≥10 mm + ≥1 embolic event on antibiotics (Class I).** Also Class I: a vegetation ≥10 mm with any other surgical indication. Embolic risk is highest early (IE-05), so the decision cannot wait for the course to finish.

**Urgent (IIa): vegetation ≥10 mm + severe valve disease and low risk; vegetation ≥30 mm; S. aureus or non-HACEK Gram-negative PVE.** Only the last is still IIa in ESC 2023 (‘should be considered’, IIa C): these organisms rarely clear from prosthetic material. The vegetation rows are 2015 wording. In 2023 a vegetation ≥10 mm with any other surgical indication, which takes in severe valve disease, was upgraded to Class I; the separate 30 mm cut-off was dropped; and an isolated vegetation ≥10 mm without embolism or severe dysfunction, in a low-risk patient, ‘may be considered’ (IIb B; 2015 set this at >15 mm, IIb C).
mimic: Left- vs right-sided IE surgery
Tricuspid IE is usually medical; ESC 2023 operates for RV failure from acute severe TR, recurrent pulmonary emboli needing ventilation, residual vegetation >20 mm, or left-sided involvement.
traps: “Add a second antibiotic” for MRSA aortic IE with a splenic embolus on day 2 (Marrow QB25-Q24)
Embolism with a vegetation is a surgical question: cardiothoracic opinion now.
“Finish 6 weeks of antibiotics before operating”
Emergency and urgent timings run from the indication, not the course; operating on active infection is accepted.
decode: MRSA aortic IE, splenic lesion on day 2: next step? [Marrow QB25-Q24]
Cardiothoracic surgery consult for septic embolus.
Mechanical mitral valve, candidaemia, EF 35%: next step? [Marrow QB25-Q35]
Antifungal plus early surgery (IE-15).
Which IE indication needs surgery within 24 h? [pattern]
Refractory pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock from valve failure.
IE-08.punch: Operate within 24 hours for shock or oedema from a failed valve, within 3–5 days for heart failure, uncontrolled infection or a ≥10 mm vegetation that has embolised; antibiotics do not change those clocks.

IE-09.intro: Step 4’s hardest call: the brain has been hit, and the operation needs full heparin and bypass. The answer depends on whether there is blood in the brain. The parts follow the card’s numbered points.
why: **Any neuro symptom → CT/MRI brain ± CT/MR angiography (mycotic aneurysm, haemorrhage).** ESC 2023 recommends brain imaging in every symptomatic patient, because ischaemia and haemorrhage lead to opposite surgical timing.

**No thrombolysis; thrombectomy may be considered for large-vessel occlusion.** Septic emboli inflame and weaken the arterial wall, so a lytic converts infarcts into bleeds; thrombectomy removes the clot without a systemic lytic.

**Ischaemic stroke/TIA, no haemorrhage, not comatose + a surgical indication → operate without delay.** ESC 2023 Class I: bypass rarely turns a bland infarct into a bleed, while recurrent emboli and heart failure kill if surgery waits.

**Intracranial haemorrhage → usually postpone surgery ≥4 weeks; earlier only if HF or uncontrolled infection forces it, weighing neuro prognosis.** Full heparinisation during bypass readily enlarges an existing bleed.
**Coma or severe neurological damage → defer.** Surgery adds risk without a meaningful neurological outcome to gain.

**ICH → stop all anticoagulation; ischaemic stroke on a mechanical valve → switch warfarin to UFH for 1–2 weeks; do not start aspirin or anticoagulants to prevent emboli.** Antithrombotics do not reduce IE emboli but do raise bleeding; UFH is short-acting and reversible if a bleed appears. ESC 2023 stops antiplatelets and anticoagulants in major bleeding (I C), but with a mechanical valve it restarts UFH as soon as possible after a haemorrhage, after team discussion (IIa C), because valve thrombosis is the other risk. The fixed ‘1–2 weeks’ of UFH after ischaemic stroke comes from ESC 2015; 2023 frames it as replacing the oral anticoagulant with closely monitored UFH.
**Large or ruptured mycotic aneurysm → endovascular or neurosurgical repair, ideally before valve surgery.** Securing it first stops bypass heparin from making it bleed.
mimic: Ischaemic vs haemorrhagic stroke in IE
Ischaemic without coma: operate if indicated, without delay; haemorrhage: usually wait ≥4 weeks.
traps: “Wait 2–4 weeks after any stroke”
ESC 2023: a non-haemorrhagic stroke without coma does not delay indicated surgery (Class I).
“Thrombolyse an IE stroke inside the window”
Contraindicated: septic arteritis bleeds.
decode: IE with acute ischaemic stroke, no haemorrhage on CT, an indication for surgery: timing? [pattern]
Without delay.
IE with intracerebral haemorrhage, haemodynamically stable: timing? [pattern]
Postpone surgery for about 4 weeks.
CT shows intraparenchymal bleed layering in the ventricles: most expected complication? [DocT Stroke (Part 2) Q16, 67%]
Hydrocephalus; mycotic aneurysm is a cause to look for in IE, not the expected complication.
IE-09.punch: Image the brain first: an ischaemic stroke without coma does not delay surgery, a haemorrhage usually delays it about four weeks, and IE strokes are never thrombolysed.

IE-10.intro: Step 5 begins before the organism is known: the regimen follows the setting, the same split as IE-01. The parts follow the table’s rows.
why: **Community NVE or late PVE (≥12 months): ampicillin + ceftriaxone, or ampicillin + (flu)cloxacillin + gentamicin.** This covers streptococci, enterococci (ampicillin + ceftriaxone act together, IE-13), HACEK (ceftriaxone) and, with cloxacillin, MSSA. ESC 2023 grades it IIa.
**Penicillin allergy: vancomycin + ceftriaxone.** The ESC 2023 table lists cefazolin or vancomycin with gentamicin (IIb) for this group; see FLAGS.

**Early PVE (<12 months) or healthcare-associated: vancomycin (or daptomycin) + gentamicin + rifampicin (rifampicin only for PVE).** Vancomycin covers MRSA and CoNS; rifampicin penetrates biofilm on prosthetic material but, given alone into a high inoculum, selects resistance, so ESC 2023 adds it after 3–5 days of effective therapy.
**Culture-negative early PVE (AHA): vancomycin + gentamicin + cefepime + rifampicin.** Cefepime adds the hospital Gram-negatives that the ESC early-PVE regimen leaves to gentamicin.

**Narrow to organism-specific therapy once cultures return.** In stable patients a later step-down to oral therapy is allowed: in POET (left-sided IE with streptococci, E. faecalis, S. aureus or CoNS, after ≥10 days IV) oral was non-inferior (composite 9.0% vs 12.1% at 6 months) and better at a median of 3.5 years. ESC 2023 asks for a TEE showing no progression before the switch.
mimic: Early vs late PVE regimen
Early: vancomycin-based with rifampicin and Gram-negative cover; late: the community native-valve regimen.
traps: “Vancomycin + ceftriaxone” 4 weeks after mechanical AVR with negative cultures (DocT CGT5 Q56)

Ceftriaxone misses Pseudomonas and many hospital Gram-negatives, and the pair has neither gentamicin nor rifampicin; early PVE needs MRSA, CoNS, biofilm and resistant Gram-negative cover: vancomycin, cefepime, gentamicin, rifampicin (AHA 2015).
“Rifampicin from day 1”
Added after 3–5 days, once the bacteraemia is controlled, or resistance emerges.
decode: Fever and heart failure 4 weeks after mechanical AVR, cultures negative after antibiotics: broadest recommended empirical cover? [DocT CGT5 Q56]
Vancomycin, cefepime, gentamicin, rifampicin.
Which IE patients may step down to oral antibiotics? [pattern]
Stable left-sided IE after ≥10 days IV with no complication on TEE (POET).
IE-10.punch: Empirical cover follows the setting: ampicillin plus ceftriaxone for community and late prosthetic IE, vancomycin-based with gentamicin and later rifampicin for early prosthetic IE.

IE-11.sub: Infective endocarditis → Antibiotics → Viridans streptococci and S. gallolyticus
IE-11.intro: Step 5 by organism, starting with oral streptococci. The questions turn on the penicillin MIC and the kidneys; two near-identical bank questions give different keys.
why: **Penicillin-susceptible (MIC ≤0.125 mg/L): penicillin G, amoxicillin or ceftriaxone 2 g once daily, 4 weeks NVE, 6 weeks PVE (2-week beta-lactam + gentamicin only for uncomplicated NVE with normal kidneys).** A beta-lactam alone kills these strains reliably; the 2-week option trades two weeks of drug for aminoglycoside risk.

**Relatively or fully resistant (MIC >0.125–2 mg/L): same beta-lactam 4 weeks + gentamicin for the first 2 weeks (PVE 6 weeks).** The beta-lactam damages the cell wall so the aminoglycoside gets in, which restores killing of less-susceptible strains. AHA 2015 uses three bands: ≤0.12, >0.12 to <0.5 (relatively resistant) and ≥0.5 (treat as enterococcal IE).

**Renal risk or elderly: ceftriaxone monotherapy 4 weeks (AHA: acceptable for MIC >0.12 to <0.5); avoids gentamicin.** This needs a ceftriaxone-susceptible isolate; killing stays good with once-daily dosing and no kidney toxicity.
**Beta-lactam allergy: vancomycin 4 weeks (6 weeks PVE).** Vancomycin kills more slowly and is nephrotoxic, so it is kept for patients who cannot take a beta-lactam.
mimic: Ceftriaxone alone vs vancomycin in CKD
Ceftriaxone for the non-allergic patient; vancomycin only when beta-lactams cannot be given.
traps: “Vancomycin” for S. mitis MIC 0.3 with CKD 4 (DocT CGT6 Q119 key)
Wrong for a non-allergic patient; its twin CGT5 Q55 correctly keys ceftriaxone monotherapy. Vancomycin is only the answer if ceftriaxone is not offered.
“Penicillin + gentamicin” for MIC 0.3 with CKD 4
Standard for the MIC, but gentamicin is unsafe in CKD 4.
decode: 71-year-old, native aortic IE, S. mitis penicillin MIC 0.3, CKD 4: preferred strategy? [DocT CGT5 Q55]
Ceftriaxone monotherapy.
S. gallolyticus IE: what else must be done? [pattern]
Colonoscopy.
IE-11.punch: For oral streptococci, the MIC decides whether gentamicin is added and the kidneys decide whether it can be; ceftriaxone alone is the gentamicin-free choice, and vancomycin is for allergy only.

IE-12.sub: Infective endocarditis → Antibiotics → S. aureus regimens
IE-12.intro: Step 5 for the commonest and most lethal organism. The DocT question behind this card offers vancomycin because it ‘covers everything’; for MSSA that is the wrong reason.
why: **MSSA native valve: (flu)cloxacillin 12 g/day in 4–6 doses (oxacillin/nafcillin) or cefazolin 6 g/day in 3 doses, 4–6 weeks; no gentamicin.** Beta-lactams kill MSSA faster than vancomycin, and MSSA treated with vancomycin fails and kills more often. ESC 2023 does not recommend aminoglycosides in staphylococcal native-valve IE: no benefit, more kidney injury.

**MRSA or true penicillin anaphylaxis: vancomycin 30–60 mg/kg/day (AUC 400–600) or daptomycin 10 mg/kg/day, 4–6 weeks.** ESC uses the high daptomycin dose (10 mg/kg) and advises a second agent with it (for example cloxacillin or fosfomycin) to prevent resistance. Daptomycin is inactivated by surfactant, so it fails in alveolar pneumonia; septic pulmonary emboli from right-sided IE are not a contraindication.

**Prosthetic valve: anti-staphylococcal agent + rifampicin (≥6 weeks) + gentamicin 2 weeks.** Rifampicin is the drug that acts in biofilm; it starts after 3–5 days of effective therapy to avoid resistance.

**Uncomplicated right-sided MSSA in IVDU: 2 weeks of (flu)cloxacillin can suffice.** ESC conditions: MSSA with a prompt clinical response, vegetation <20 mm, no metastatic infection, no left-sided or prosthetic involvement, no severe immunosuppression, and not with a glycopeptide.
mimic: Cefazolin vs ceftriaxone for MSSA
Cefazolin is an anti-staphylococcal first-choice drug; ceftriaxone is weaker against staphylococci.
traps: “Vancomycin” for MSSA mitral IE with septic emboli and HF (DocT Antimicrobials Q5, 61%)
Vancomycin kills MSSA slowly and penetrates vegetations poorly; oxacillin or nafcillin (or cefazolin) wins.
“Add gentamicin to MSSA native-valve IE”
No benefit and more AKI; gentamicin belongs only to the prosthetic-valve regimen.
decode: MSSA mitral IE, multiple septic emboli, worsening HF: most appropriate initial regimen? [DocT Antimicrobials Q5, 61%]
Oxacillin or nafcillin.
Right-sided MSSA IE in an IVDU, prompt response, vegetation 12 mm: duration? [pattern]
2 weeks of (flu)cloxacillin can suffice.
IE-12.punch: MSSA is treated with an anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam, never vancomycin by choice; gentamicin and rifampicin belong only to prosthetic-valve S. aureus.

IE-13.intro: Step 5: enterococci are slow to kill, so the question is always which partner to give with ampicillin, and for how long.
why: **E. faecalis, no HLAR, normal kidneys: ampicillin/amoxicillin + gentamicin, 4 weeks NVE, 6 weeks PVE or symptoms >3 months (gentamicin may be limited to 2 weeks).** Ampicillin alone only inhibits enterococci; gentamicin, let in through the damaged wall, adds the killing.

**HLAR or renal risk: ampicillin + ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly × 6 weeks (ESC 2023 Class I; avoids nephrotoxicity).** Ceftriaxone saturates PBP2/3 while ampicillin binds PBP4/5, so together they kill without an aminoglycoside, and ESC accepts it for non-HLAR strains too.
**Beta-lactam allergy: vancomycin + gentamicin × 6 weeks.** It is the only combination left that kills, at the cost of two nephrotoxins.

**VRE faecium: high-dose daptomycin (10–12 mg/kg) + ampicillin or fosfomycin; linezolid alternative.** E. faecium is usually ampicillin-resistant and intrinsically ceftriaxone-resistant; daptomycin is bactericidal, and a partner prevents daptomycin resistance.
mimic: E. faecalis vs E. faecium
Faecalis: ampicillin-susceptible, ampicillin + ceftriaxone works; faecium: often ampicillin- and vancomycin-resistant, daptomycin-based.
traps: “Amoxicillin + ceftriaxone for 4 weeks” (DocT GrandT1 Q95, 41%)
The combination is right but the course is 6 weeks; with only 4 weeks offered, ampicillin + gentamicin for 6 weeks is the best available answer.
“Ampicillin” or “tigecycline” for VRE faecium bacteraemia in shock (DocT Antimicrobials Q14, 58%)
Faecium is usually ampicillin-resistant and tigecycline is bacteriostatic with low blood levels; daptomycin.
decode: E. faecalis IE, penicillin MIC 4 mg/L, no HLAR: initial regimen? [DocT GrandT1 Q95, 41%]
Ampicillin + gentamicin for 6 weeks.
VRE faecium bacteraemia, ventilated, on vasopressors: agent? [DocT Antimicrobials Q14, 58%]
Daptomycin.
IE-13.punch: Enterococci need two drugs to die: ampicillin with gentamicin, or ampicillin with ceftriaxone for 6 weeks when the kidneys or HLAR forbid gentamicin; faecium needs daptomycin.

IE-14.intro: Step 5: Gram-negatives cause few cases of IE, so the questions test the exceptions: combination for Pseudomonas even when it is susceptible, and the intrinsic resistance of Burkholderia.
why: **Pseudomonas aeruginosa (IVDU): two active classes even if susceptible: high-dose anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (cefepime 2 g 8-hourly, ceftazidime, extended-infusion pip-tazo) + aminoglycoside (tobramycin 8 mg/kg/day), ≥6 weeks; left-sided → early surgery, tricuspid often medical.** A vegetation holds a huge inoculum killed slowly, so one drug lets resistant mutants take over during treatment. Left-sided Pseudomonas IE rarely clears without surgery.

**Burkholderia cepacia on a prosthetic valve: TMP-SMX or meropenem; intrinsically resistant to colistin and aminoglycosides.** Its modified lipopolysaccharide does not bind polymyxins, and efflux pumps with a poorly permeable outer membrane keep aminoglycosides out.
**HACEK: ceftriaxone, 4 weeks NVE, 6 weeks PVE.** Some HACEK organisms make beta-lactamase, so ampicillin is unreliable; they are typical organisms under Duke-ISCVID.

**Other non-HACEK Gram-negatives: early surgery + ≥6 weeks of beta-lactam + aminoglycoside (or quinolone).** Mortality is high with medical treatment alone; ESC 2023 lists non-HACEK Gram-negative PVE as an urgent-surgery indication (IIa).
mimic: Pseudomonas vs Burkholderia
Pseudomonas: beta-lactam + aminoglycoside; Burkholderia: TMP-SMX or meropenem, never colistin or an aminoglycoside.
traps: “Pip-tazo or meropenem monotherapy” because the isolate is susceptible (DocT Antimicrobials Q21, 74%)
Endocarditis needs two active classes; cefepime + an aminoglycoside.
“Colistin” or “aminoglycoside” for Burkholderia (DocT GT6 Q141, 88%)
It is intrinsically resistant to both.
decode: IVDU, tricuspid IE, Pseudomonas susceptible to everything: initial regimen? [DocT Antimicrobials Q21, 74%]
Cefepime + gentamicin.
Prosthetic mitral valve, on haemodialysis, Burkholderia cepacia: which antibiotic? [DocT GT6 Q141, 88%]
Carbapenem or TMP-SMX.
IE-14.punch: Gram-negative endocarditis is treated with two active classes and, if left-sided, early surgery; Burkholderia is the exception that ignores colistin and aminoglycosides.

IE-15.sub: Infective endocarditis → Antibiotics → Fungal and culture-negative IE
IE-15.intro: Step 5 ends with what cultures miss or drugs cannot sterilise: Candida on prosthetic material, and the intracellular organisms behind culture-negative IE.
why: **Candida PVE: liposomal amphotericin B 3–5 mg/kg/day ± flucytosine (or high-dose echinocandin) + urgent valve surgery, then lifelong oral fluconazole suppression if the valve cannot be removed.** Fungi build dense biofilm on prosthetic material that antifungals cannot clear, so medical treatment alone relapses; fungal IE is a Class I surgical indication.

**Supporting test when cultures are negative: (1→3)-β-D-glucan (not cryptococcal antigen; galactomannan is for Aspergillus).** Glucan is in the cell wall of most fungi except Cryptococcus and the Mucorales; false positives come from haemodialysis membranes, albumin, immunoglobulin and surgical gauze.

**Coxiella burnetii (Q fever): doxycycline + hydroxychloroquine ≥18 months; phase I IgG >1:800 is a major criterion.** Coxiella lives in the acidic phagolysosome where doxycycline is inactive; hydroxychloroquine raises the pH so doxycycline can kill it.
**Bartonella: doxycycline 4 weeks + gentamicin 2 weeks.** B. quintana (homeless, body lice) and B. henselae (cats) are found by serology or PCR, rarely by culture.
mimic: β-D-glucan vs galactomannan
Glucan: Candida and most fungi; galactomannan: Aspergillus.
traps: “Antifungal alone” or “echinocandin and wait” for Candida on a mechanical mitral valve (Marrow QB25-Q35)
Antifungal plus early surgery; biofilm is not sterilised by drugs.
“Galactomannan” or “cryptococcal antigen” to confirm invasive candidiasis (DocT Infections (Part 3) Q6, 75%)
These detect Aspergillus and Cryptococcus; β-D-glucan is the Candida test.
decode: Mechanical mitral valve, candidaemia, EF 35%: next step? [Marrow QB25-Q35]
Antifungal plus early surgery.
Septic shock, suspected fungal endocarditis, cultures unhelpful: best non-culture test for Candida? [DocT Infections (Part 3) Q6, 75%]
(1→3)-β-D-glucan.
IE-15.punch: Fungal prosthetic IE needs amphotericin and the surgeon, then lifelong fluconazole if the valve stays; culture-negative IE is diagnosed by serology and treated with long doxycycline-based courses.

spine: The setting names the organism

Who the patient is and how fast the illness moves predict the bug before cultures return: days and destruction mean S. aureus, weeks on a damaged valve mean streptococci, the first year after valve surgery means hospital organisms.
Proving it: cultures, echo, Duke

Three sets of cultures before antibiotics and an echo feed the Duke-ISCVID count, where a typical organism needs two sets, a rare one three, and definite means two major, one major plus three minor, or five minor.
What the vegetation destroys
A vegetation throws emboli to brain, spleen and lung, drives immune complexes, burrows into the annulus to cause abscess and heart block, and can wreck a valve in days.
When the surgeon must come

Surgery treats what antibiotics cannot (a failed valve, walled-off infection, a vegetation that keeps embolising), timed as emergency, urgent or non-urgent, and only a bleed in the brain usually makes it wait.
Killing the organism

Treatment is long, bactericidal and chosen by organism and valve: beta-lactams first, gentamicin only where it adds synergy, rifampicin only on prosthetic material, combinations where one drug selects resistance.
TU-IE.primer: Infective endocarditis is infection of the endocardium, usually a valve, where platelets, fibrin and organisms build a vegetation on endothelium that has been damaged (by a jet, a prosthesis, a catheter or injected particles) or, for S. aureus, sometimes on a normal valve. The vegetation sits in fast-moving blood but has no blood supply of its own, so organisms inside it reach huge densities and are killed slowly; that is why treatment is long, bactericidal and often combined. Native-valve (NVE) and prosthetic-valve IE (PVE: early under 12 months after surgery, late after that), and right- vs left-sided IE, behave differently throughout this deck. Management follows the ESC 2023 guideline; diagnosis follows the 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria.
